I know that by criticising this game, I may receive some criticism myself, but I'll be honest, Dark Souls 3 (in my opinion) is awful.
First of all, the camera - The camera in Dark Souls 3 is one of the worst cameras i have ever seen
in my life. I have died many times simply because the camera isn't
satisfactory. You will find yourself looking in the
opposite direction from an
enemy against your will many times. Even when the camera doesn't
freak out, you will then have to deal with targeting the enemy that you
want among a cluster of
enemies if you are dealing with a group, and my goodness, if you ever
have to deal with that, goodluck.
Second, the controls   - The tutorial is pointless on pc as none of the button prompts are pc keys,
instead, they are console controller buttons. To find out which key does
what, you will have to look into the keybinding options and slowly scan
through each key. This isn't that big of a problem, mostly just
personal expectations, and after a while, I definitely got used to this.
However, I cannot stand the fact that input lag is present, in a game
where split - second timing could make or break a play.
I'm not sure if consoles have this input lag, but it's unbelievably harsh on
pc. To solve this, you must turn off V-sync manually, but even after turning
it off, there is still a slight delay between
pressing a key and having the character engage in the action, and it
seems to have no effect on
the roll delay. (there is a delay of about 0.40 to 0.50 seconds for rolling, I
am not sure how to fix this)
Third, the "difficulty"   - Dark Souls 3 is quite "difficult" at times, I must say. However, I found the
game to be difficult mostly because of the awful input delay which is
always present. Many times I have timed a roll
perfectly only to have a 0.5s delay mess it up and get me squashed by
some giant hammer or axe. Also, I sometimes find enemies to have cheap
ways of being difficult, such as having super high hp. This can easily be
countered by understanding the game, but it tends to get boring and
frustrating if you keep dying to the same boss over and over again simply
because of technical reason like the camera.
Fourth, fov                  - This reason could tie in with reason no. 1. The fov in Dark Souls 3 is way
too low, I can't see jack at this fov, coupled with the awful camera.
There are many other dislikes I have about this game which I will not mention, but with all that said, I want to enjoy this game, I can see why people like this, but I just can't stand some of the problems this game has, including the ones listed here. Anyways, this is just my personal taste of the game, and if you have a different take on it, that's fine by me, we all have unique tastes and preferences.
Thank you very much for reading my review

I'll start with the short version.  I thought I loved the first game...  but after playing this one, I only kinda like the first one (I mean, it got me introduced to the series so I feel I have to).  The sequel, however, is nothing short of AMAZING!
I never played the original series, but after hearing how much Jake Solomon loved the original and was excited to be bringing it back, I decided to give it a try.  I loved it.  Loved it so much I purchased it on 3 different systems, played hundreds of hours and even bought the expansion.  Eventually I had seen every map and got to the point where I had hit my limit for a while.  I remember seeing that they were going to make a proper sequel but I never really got excited for it.  I just figured I get it a few years from now, you know, once I had the craving again.  It wasn't until I saw that they were going to have random maps that I started to have a glimmer of excitement... then they were changing the premise so that you would be doing infiltration missions rather than just explore and wait to be surrounded.  Even then, I thought, that sounds interesting but I think I'll still wait.  Finally I saw the reviews.  I know, I know, people are all over the map when it comes to how much they like/dislike reviews, but it was the final nail in the coffin.  I HAD TO GET THIS GAME.
Yes it has some bugs that need to be patched and some extended time issues (honestly, it's nothing that has hurt MY enjoyment but I get that it would be nice to have these cleaned up).  In the end, this game has won me over, HARD, and I can't stop wanting to play (if you want to know more, watch any review and it provide you with more infor than I can).
What I think sets this above the other:
+ Infiltration mission
+ Randomized areas/maps
+ Destructible environments
+ Characters who recover from stress (This is HUGE by the way)
+ Being able to carry wounded
+ Being able to recover items
+ Randomized abilities
+ Different (IMO better) Enemy's (staying away from spoilers)
+ More options (armor, colors, etc).  Really helps provide an attachment to your soldiers.  Hell, you can write bios and epitaphs if you want.
+ Graphics
This list can go on but I've hit the biggies for me.
Also, I'm not anywhere near done (i.e. beat the game), but I thought I owed it to the developers to write a review and share with them and others how excited I am to be playing XCOM again.

I like what XCOM 2 is trying to do here, and at its core it's a very fun, challenging game, but I would not recommend it AT ALL in its current state.  It's a mess.
Regarding gameplay, there are some familiar elements here from XCOM EU/EW, but some refinements as well.  Even if it ran smoothly, I'll say that the game gets better the more you put into it.  The timers that so many people have mentioned don't "break" the experience, it's something that can be adapted to as you play and improve your team and your own skills.  But I found that the game requires a lot of outside effort--there is a LOT that you'll encounter on your first playthrough that just isn't explained well at all.  An in-game "encyclopedia" like what's found in the Civ games really would have helped with a lot of the newer elements.
And regarding the technical aspect, as mentioned, it's a hot mess.  Even if you don't experience any hard crashes or freezing, there are so many minor glitches that it can make the game nearly unplayable at times.  Here's an example: you have visibility on a group of aliens just on the edge of your vision.  You move your troops into strategic positions, finding good cover, to see where the alien units will move.  That won't work, though, because often the camera will snap to your units and LOCK there during the AI turn, making it impossible to see enemy movements.  You'll hear a bunch of sounds, and when you get control of the camera again after their turn is over, the aliens are nowhere to be seen.  You know they've moved outside of your vision, but you have NO idea where they went.
There's also a major problem with "line of sight" in the game.  I have seen this multiple times, with the aliens doing it as well as my own units.  You have a soldier on the ground floor of a building, something with NO STRUCTURAL DAMAGE.  An alien runs across the roof above your soldier and somehow triggers his overwatch, as you watch your Ranger fire his shotgun directly at the ceiling.  This was not a one-time glitch, I have had this happen on different missions with different enemy types.
The bottom line is, I would not recommend this game at all until these issues get addressed.  I've decided to step away from it until Firaxis can release a patch.  I *could* play the game, but it's not in the least bit fun when I'm constantly running into these issues that take you out of the game, and these things all add up to a very frustrating experience that has nothing to do with the actual difficulty or challenge of the gameplay itself.  When the game is patched, I'll be more than happy to edit my review.

Everyone who knows me well enough knows that I had a ton of hype for this game, and oh boy was it worth it. However, I'm going full ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ critic here, leaving my love for the franchise aside and will do my best to give a fair review. And as usual, I'll start with the stuff the game doesn't do right. Luckily, there's only three things:
First and most important, the difficulty spikes. I'm not sure who tested the game, but he was high as f#cking f#ck. I know XCOM is not known for being easy and forgibing but COME ON, THE EARLY GAME HAS A BIGGER DIFFICULTY SPIKE THAN CORRUPTED PEOPLE ON THE SPANISH GOVERNMENT! Since the second mission (the first one being the tutorial, unless you disabled it), you'll be usually facing with normal and fair enemies like the ADVENT troops AND THEN THE SECTOIDS COME ARROUND. This early on, the Sectoids have MORE HP than your soldiers, have three powerful PSI attacks, and also a Bracelet-Gun they never seem to f#cking use for some reason. And it's not like in XCOM 1 when they could waste their turn to make another Sectoid better or at times cause panic. Here they still have the panic skill, and can also Mind-control AND reanimate dead people into zombies. ON THE SECOND MISSION. If that ain't enough to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off, wait until the game tasks you to "hack" an ADVENT Officer. It's similar to capturing aliens in XCOM 1, but with a LITTLE SURPRISE the game forgot to tell you about: hacking an ADVENT Officer spawns a MID-GAME enemy, which early on will feel like out-right cheating and artificial difficulty. This enemy can TELEPORT AND INSTANTLY FLANK YOU, can cause some sort of Black-Hole which will instantly unload your weapons AND explode for too much damage on the early game on the next turn, has double the HP than any of your soldiers by that moment, AAAAAAAAAAAND will split in half when you injure it. Now you'd think that splitting in half makes it easier to defeat, but no. It doesn't. His clone will usually spawn in the completely direction, and they share no cool-downs. If you're not careful, you'll go from facing one Codex to facing TWO, THREE OR EVEN FOUR CODEX. Sure turning a hard battle into f#cking ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
The second people is one I don't really give a ♥♥♥♥ about, but a ton of people do; Performance. This game is not well optimized. I usually blame games for it, but I must admit it looks good and it's a turn-based game, so playing in low FPS ain't that much of an issue... But I must admit that it got old pretty fast, and the devs yet have to fix most of that, as it took them nearly two weeks to release ONE update. No idea what's going on with that.
The third and last problem are the bugs. I haven't played since last week but Oh God I was finding some weird crap. Most of them are LUCKILY only animation errors, but still there's some weird crap out there that will make you either mad or lose it completely. Things like rooms on the ship not loading and literally being see-through as there's LITERALLY NOTHING IN THERE. Things like characters stuck on the wrong animations, now being forced to teleport arround the map and for some reason take 30 seconds to do each action. Things like your character showing as he's on the completely wrong place where he should be. Those are fun. However, thing as having one of your soldiers stuck in mid-air while enemies fire at him, and forced to use EXPLOSIVES to take him down, literally bleeding out, IS NOT FUN AT ALL. There's also weird crap such as pieces of buildings floating all over the places, sh#tting all over gravity, or both XCOM soldiers and aliens dropping through the floor. Things like that make you even wonder if the game was properly beta-tested.
That being said though, what do we got left? A seriously good sequel for a seriously good game.
Gameplay, ignoring the early game insane spikes, is enjoyable, fun and adds more flavour to a really enjoyable XCOM 1 experience. There's a bigger focus on explosives on this game (as they weren't really that good on the first one), and that goes hand to hand with the mostly completely destructible escenarios.
And talking about maps, they're randomized. One time or two they looked similar, but they're always different and that's something I totally love.
Customization is not only back, it went Super Saiyan: there are AN INSANE TON of options, and it trully feels amazing.
Even better than that though, proper Mod support. And the workshop of Steam already has some fun things on it. Personally I only went so far with customization mods but OH GOD, IS IT FUN TO KILL ALIENS WITH CLASSY TOP HATS AND OVER-SIZED MARIACHI HATS.
I haven't played multiplayer yet, so I'll avoid that, but ♥♥♥♥ing hell it was worth the money. And it already has DLC's coming, which I decided to pre-order as I do trust there guys. However, the price tag will scare people off. WAIT for a sale. 50€ ain't cheap at all.
Just get ready to miss point-blank shotgun shots. It will happen.

I wanted to give this game thumbs up for the early game it had. Would i recommend the whole game for others? No.
Darkest Dungeon is roguelike game that has psychological stress conditions on characters. First couple of hours are fun, you will be spending most of the game grinding same dungeons, same monsters and same loot.
The game relies heavily on the RNG aspect, character that you have trained from start can simply die to few crits if you are unlucky. Leveling up new character to replace the dead main party is not fun.
Pros:
* Unique Graphics style
* Sound & Atmosphere
* First hours are fun to play
* Trying to min max party and use the abilities in combination
Cons:
* Way too much RNG
* Way too much Grinding
* You spend most of the game fighting same enemies on same locations
* If you lose major character, well bad luck.. time to grind and level up another one
* Game is long just because you have to grind so much
* Minimal story
* boring town events
* corpses and other ridiculous game rules (turning them off is good thing)
Total:
Graphics - 7
Sound - 8
Gameplay - 4 (early game 9)
Story - 6
---
;TLDR awesome early game, after that the game becomes very boring, frustrating and repetitive.

I highly recommend this game. I actually prefer this to Terraria, it has more content in their beta stage, then Terraria has in the newest update (1.2). The progression system is challenging, and time consuming, you can rack up endless hours just finding new blocks in the game. The combat system is really fun, as well as the "Creature Capture" feature, allowing you to capture any ground animal, with 50% or lower health. And as many species as the game already has, they're are so many unique creatures to capture and make your own. Seeing a game, this early, do like this is doing, is very encouriging for its future. I am a really big fan of Terraria, I've racked up a lot of hours in that game, but for those who are burnt out with Terraria, and need something to fill that void, Starbound is your game!
Summery: Worth the $15.00, Fun game for all ages, numerous hours of gameplay (no need for multiple characters to get the full experiance), the game is in BETA stage, new updates coming out in the near future.

Darkest Dungeon hits the right spots of player knowledge based progression. Your understanding of your fighter's capabilities and your resource management are key to successful dungeon runs that don't cripple/maim your characters.
However, where it misses the mark is over the "pointless grind" issue. The best roguelikes (despite being party based, it's very much in the genre) aim to minimize XP scumming, while in Darkest Dungeon it takes up the majority of your playtime. You have to spend a lot of time grinding up characters to be strong enough to take the next difficulty level. One mistake and poof, they're dead and you have to start over on their replacement. With enough experience you can grind lower level characters with little to no challenge or mental effort, just going through the motions with the appropriate precautions.
After 10 hours I understood enough of the mechanics to progress, but I just wasn't having enough fun to want to anymore.

Xcom2 is more Xcom. It isn't classic Xcom. Go play openXcom for that!
Keep in mind the time of this writing.
The bad:
Odd pauses, technical issues that interfere directly with gameplay such as:
>Line of sight issues with visibly solid walls (why did the enemy see me through an entire skyscraper... oh no, now I'm unexpectedly being shot through the walls, too), the hacking gameplay menu information being obscured by in-game objects, the rare instance of enemies getting extra actions.
Balance issues
>Hacking is poorly weighted in favor of failure: The rewards for hacking are often too temporary and too impotent to roll the dice on when the penalties are so incredibly severe.
>Swords are overall too risky to use either and stand only as a backup that, more often than not, complicates things by overextending and often ending up causing a new "pod" to join the battle.
>Psionics and Meme Beacons are intensely overpowered. Think "What if ghost grenades were even easier to deploy?"
>The AI is still shackled, and this isn't more evident than when you get used to how Sectoids' fearsome psionics are used.
The good:
The script source is supposedly totally open, and the mod pack is as well. Modding for the game couldn't be any more supported and who can live without Hatsune Miku hair or Stop Wasting My Time.
Timers are good. Forcing the player to take action and take *some* risks made for a more interesting game. I found myself moving soldiers completely out of cover in order to commit to attacks I would not have taken in Xcom1.
The temptation of MELD, in the previous game, wasn't enough because there was no true penalty for ignoring it other than falling slightly behind in the tech race. Now, you stand to lose soldiers, and all the droppable equipment you outfitted them with.
The soldiers are given so much value through equipment and visual customization that losing them almost always hurts.
Escaping from some mission types makes for interesting choices as well. I found myself seriously considering taking on some missions, weighing the likelihood of losing soldiers, or the advantage it would earn should it be a success. Eventually recognizing when a mission is unwinnable and running away to fight another day helps write interesting personal stories that aren't just "and we won again easily!" The struggle gives depth.
The eh:
The game arc is still the same as before: The early and mid game are the most interesting segments of the game. They're the moments where you make tactical sacrifices so that the whole group can survive. They're the moments where you're rooting for a critical to land.
The late game is still a victory lap where your abilities match or exceed all the challenges the game throws at you except in being outnumbered.
It's still Xcom, so what else can I say?
Update: Some elements of this review have fallen out of date due to the recent patch in March.
Mimic Beacons were significantly balanced (Made more expensive and will now only waste 1-2 enemy actions instead of nearly a *full enemy turn*).
Framerate/graphical performance was significantly improved.

Dark Souls has remained my favorite game series ever since I started playing Dark Souls 2 back when it came out in 2014, and the reason has always been the gameplay. Not the challenge or the environment or even the artisitic decisions made to create a fantastical fallen world. I could go on and on about how amazing the world is, and how it instills a sense of dread and despair, but the main thing that always brought me back to the series was the combat. It is simple enough to learn all the buttons but with the way the enemies attack you, the game forces you to learn more about its combat and slowly makes you better at realizing the implications of your style of play, whether it be a more defensive approach or an approach that just swings without hesitation. Dark Souls rewards players who pay attention to their surroundings and to their own actions. There are an extremely large amount of weapons in this game, and every one of them is viable to beat the game, and each weapon has a unique style of play to it that can completly change how the game feels. You can go full srength and wield a huge sword that does massive damage, but is very slow, or use a longsword you find at the beggining of the game and quickly swing it multiple times for good dps. The crown jewel of the games are always the bosses, and Dark Souls 3 may have the fastest and most difficult ones yet. FromSoftware has created bosses that feel like real living things, each boss having its own backstory in the lore and personality in the way it fights. I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who has enough money and enough time and patiance.

This is probably one of the most fun games I've ever played.
Yes, it's frustrating.
Yes, there are times when you'll have this really awesome group all set up and geared and ready to go and then a steady flow of negative things happen and you end up losing the group.  It's part of the game and part of what makes it so freaking amazing.
Sure, you're going to get mad and rage quit from time to time..but that shouldn't impact the overall awesomeness that this game gives you.
At first it's probably a lot to take in, because it's a totally different take on your typical dungeon running game.  No one has really implemented the stress of wandering in these horrific places, but it is certainly something that would occur. You don't watch your friend die and immediately become super-strengthed and run through a place hacking and slashing (okay, so maybe you would, everyone reacts to things differently and some people would go on the adreniline rush suicide mission of slaughtering their way to the exit)...most of the time that's going to cause you stress. The more things like that happen, the worse the stress will become and that's something that this game managed to capture and build around.  Honestly, this is one of the most unique dungeon games I've ever played and I've played a plethora of them.
All these negative reviews are more likely from people who think that they should just be able to run and gun their way through the game, but that defeats the purpose of the mechanics.  You're supposed to lose people.  You're supposed to be wiped. Yeah, sure, there's the chance that you'll roll into the game and whip through parts of it like they're nothing, but all in all you're bound to lose a favorite character, or have to run from the dungeon to prevent it and that is part of the fun. You can't look at it like a game that you're just going to decimate your way through and that's that, because that isn't at all what the game is designed for and honestly, I have yet to have a really clean run that didn't mess at least one of the group members up. You'll make mistakes.
If you enjoy dark humor and don't mind watching as your favorites are slaughtered in otherwise seemingly easy circumstances, this game is definitely one to check out.  Even if you do mind seeing them slaughtered, it's still worth checking out because the humor is fantastic and the dungeons are relentless, making the game probably one of the best games in my entire Steam Library and maybe even my overall video game library (which is not really a small number by any means). The art is really cool and gives you that gothic feel that a game similar to this should and when you coat that with the over all concept of mechanics in the game, I simply do not see a better one out there.
Easy to learn and a vast open world you and your frineds can play and fight dungeons.

Just finished this game in about 40 hours on record, no lost soldiers, and very little save-scrumming. I swear! Here’s the proof that it’s doable with timers and all:
I can recommend this game to anyone who enjoyed the previous game, and likes military, turn based strategy games. Be forewarned though, this game has a pretty steep learning curve. I looked at some of the previous reviews and thought I would put some worries to rest…
Everything is on a timer. Well, not really. I kept track of the last half of my game, and roughly 65% of the missions I played were on a timer. You get used to it. Everybody saying you can’t think tactically or strategically with such pressure, well, they just need to start thinking differently. It’s a challenge, and one we aren’t used to. For those that can’t deal, well there’s save-scrumming. I took my time with the game, and finished it in early December of 2035. I wanted to build and research everything… the AVATAR project timer is managed very easily, once you get a hang of it.
Resource Drops. While my favorite game mechanic, it makes sense in the theme of the world being occupied by a hostile entity. Yes, they get interrupted all the time, yes it’s hectic, and yes you won’t always have all the money for everything… it makes you think and make choices which aren’t always easy.
You’re in trouble when your A-Team dies. Yes, you will be. Same as in Xcom, if you have six colonels and 20 rookies, about two months’ game time into the game you’re gonna end up in the deep end of the pool…
This game does math behind the scenes. Yeah, some of the hit/miss rolls have me yelling and cussing, but hey, it’s a game that constantly does the math. It doesn’t see that there’s a wall there someone’s punching through, or that an enemy is big. It has set parameters to work with, and it calculates. And gets an answer… one a lot of people don’t seem to like.
Perfermonce issues. They exist. They’re working on a fix. I am playing on a maxed out later 2013 15” Retina MacBook Pro, and on the lowest possible seetings I still have a neat looking game with a solid 25-30fps performance. Which, by the way, is fine, this is turn based, not live-action. Just saying.
All in all I loved this game because it required me to think on my feet, and no one tactic worked 100% of the time. It’s a game that you can really use to learn, and a game that’ll keep you on your toes.

I now put around 100 hours into this game and I can definetly recommend it. Long story short:
+ graphics are really good. Most if not all locations look beautiful. The developers paid a lot of attention to details.
+ sound is great and "realistic". Dark Souls 3 features by far the best soundtrack in the series. The theme of the Abyss Watchers is a prime example. The voice acting is also pretty good.
+ combat is fluid and faster as in Dark Souls and Dark Souls 2.
+ a lot of armour, weapons, spells, miracles and pyromancies.
+ great multiplayer - yeah, it is basically the same as in 1 and 2 but this kind of multiplayer is unique compared to any other franchise (I include Demon's Souls and Bloodborne into the Souls franchise).
+ really good quests which enrich the story and are not thrown into your face like in any other RPG.
+ really good length. Doesn't matter if you include the DLC or not.
- invasions or PVP in general can be annoying due to latency issues or lag. Only the arena (accessable while playing the DLC) features a server. The rest is P2P.
- backtracking for additional armour doesn't make much sense - discover location A, 5 hours later, at location X, you kill a certrain unique enemy, armour can now be found at location A. I'm talking about Havel's armour to be specific.
- the first DLC, Ashes of Ariandel, is pretty poor on it's own when it comes to length and variety. But since anybody who buys the game probably buys the complete edition anyway, this does not mean much. I just wanted to point that out. Especially since both DLC's belong together - literally.
- some enemy types can be seen as a recycled version of an earlier enemy later on. It is not that obvious as in other games but still. Seems kinda lazy.
I can definetly recommend the purchase of this game. It does not matter if it is on sale or not. In my opinion, it still is worth 60 bucks. Compare it to "triple A" trash from Activision or EA and you can pay 100€ without batting an eye.

I wanted to give this game thumbs up for the early game it had. Would i recommend the whole game for others? No.
Darkest Dungeon is roguelike game that has psychological stress conditions on characters. First couple of hours are fun, you will be spending most of the game grinding same dungeons, same monsters and same loot.
The game relies heavily on the RNG aspect, character that you have trained from start can simply die to few crits if you are unlucky. Leveling up new character to replace the dead main party is not fun.
Pros:
* Unique Graphics style
* Sound & Atmosphere
* First hours are fun to play
* Trying to min max party and use the abilities in combination
Cons:
* Way too much RNG
* Way too much Grinding
* You spend most of the game fighting same enemies on same locations
* If you lose major character, well bad luck.. time to grind and level up another one
* Game is long just because you have to grind so much
* Minimal story
* boring town events
* corpses and other ridiculous game rules (turning them off is good thing)
Total:
Graphics - 7
Sound - 8
Gameplay - 4 (early game 9)
Story - 6
---
;TLDR awesome early game, after that the game becomes very boring, frustrating and repetitive.

Darkest Dungeon hits the right spots of player knowledge based progression. Your understanding of your fighter's capabilities and your resource management are key to successful dungeon runs that don't cripple/maim your characters.
However, where it misses the mark is over the "pointless grind" issue. The best roguelikes (despite being party based, it's very much in the genre) aim to minimize XP scumming, while in Darkest Dungeon it takes up the majority of your playtime. You have to spend a lot of time grinding up characters to be strong enough to take the next difficulty level. One mistake and poof, they're dead and you have to start over on their replacement. With enough experience you can grind lower level characters with little to no challenge or mental effort, just going through the motions with the appropriate precautions.
After 10 hours I understood enough of the mechanics to progress, but I just wasn't having enough fun to want to anymore.

Now that I've had a decent amount of time with the controls & have played through all 4 available levels I believe I can write my own take on the game. Note: I'm not great at this game, I have failed countless times. This is all based on my experience as someone playing this for fun & taking my time towards the goal.
I am Bread, from the makers of another favorite of mine Surgeon Simulator, leaves you in control of a slice of bread as you try to toast yourself by any means possible. I love the concept itself; it's silly, fun and frustrating beyond belief. It's more of a hit or miss if you'll like it. I'd suggest watching the game play and understanding that the controls are difficult and the game isn't completely serious before you buy it & suddenly find yourself upset because it's not perfect. It's Early Access & the developers are still adding a lot to this so I'm pretty content with what we have so far, though there's still a long way to go. *This means go to the Discussions and make suggestions, not whine over not besting the controls in 20 minutes* With that said...
Pros:
- You are bread
- You can roll in jam & butter to aid you in your goal
- Be creative! There are other ways to heat bread other than a toaster, have fun with it.
- A short narrative that follows our destructive path.
- You can crawl in cereal or other things.
- Make your heat source with destruction.
- Smash things.
- Take your time, have fun!
- Playing/Watching this over live broadcast with a group of friends is very entertaining.
- Procrastination simulator.
Cons:
- The controls are hard. I don't see any way of this being improved, to be honest. It takes time to get used to them but once you are it's more of a challenge of not touching the floor.
- The floor is lava.
- This guy's house is disgusting. There are some walls you can't touch without dying if you don't respond fast enough. The carpet is not always so forgiving depending where you land.
- The grip meter is necessary but it goes from fun to frustrating when you spend all that time climbing but you miss a beat & drop onto the nasty carpet again.
- The timer. I beat a level in 5 minutes without soiling my bread & I made a D at best. Unless you're hardcore going for that heat source I wouldn't expect a great rating.
- The camra angles.
- ^ I stepped on hair & couldn't see it at first.
- He's worried about bread wrecking his house yet he has garbage/germs littered everywhere. Why did you even leave the loaf out.
- I have a hard time removing the top concealing the butter.
- Please make the counters less "edgy" in some aspects. I realize desks & the like have an edge sticking out on top but at times it's nearly impossible for me to get over that tiny lump.
Possible Bugs:
- I can't seem to lift myself up vertically with 3 & 4 anymore the way I do with 1 & 2.
- After flinging myself along the wall I can only grip again with maybe 1 or 2 keys or my bread won't grip at all.
- On the bathroom level I always drop down & end up grasping the toothpaste. This causes it to spasm in all directions and nearly send me flying.
Possible suggestions could go on forever so I'll just leave it at this. Enjoy bread simulator & if you're thinking about whining instead of a "this is why I don't like/recommend this game," turn off your computer & walk away. 10/10

This is probably one of the most fun games I've ever played.
Yes, it's frustrating.
Yes, there are times when you'll have this really awesome group all set up and geared and ready to go and then a steady flow of negative things happen and you end up losing the group.  It's part of the game and part of what makes it so freaking amazing.
Sure, you're going to get mad and rage quit from time to time..but that shouldn't impact the overall awesomeness that this game gives you.
At first it's probably a lot to take in, because it's a totally different take on your typical dungeon running game.  No one has really implemented the stress of wandering in these horrific places, but it is certainly something that would occur. You don't watch your friend die and immediately become super-strengthed and run through a place hacking and slashing (okay, so maybe you would, everyone reacts to things differently and some people would go on the adreniline rush suicide mission of slaughtering their way to the exit)...most of the time that's going to cause you stress. The more things like that happen, the worse the stress will become and that's something that this game managed to capture and build around.  Honestly, this is one of the most unique dungeon games I've ever played and I've played a plethora of them.
All these negative reviews are more likely from people who think that they should just be able to run and gun their way through the game, but that defeats the purpose of the mechanics.  You're supposed to lose people.  You're supposed to be wiped. Yeah, sure, there's the chance that you'll roll into the game and whip through parts of it like they're nothing, but all in all you're bound to lose a favorite character, or have to run from the dungeon to prevent it and that is part of the fun. You can't look at it like a game that you're just going to decimate your way through and that's that, because that isn't at all what the game is designed for and honestly, I have yet to have a really clean run that didn't mess at least one of the group members up. You'll make mistakes.
If you enjoy dark humor and don't mind watching as your favorites are slaughtered in otherwise seemingly easy circumstances, this game is definitely one to check out.  Even if you do mind seeing them slaughtered, it's still worth checking out because the humor is fantastic and the dungeons are relentless, making the game probably one of the best games in my entire Steam Library and maybe even my overall video game library (which is not really a small number by any means). The art is really cool and gives you that gothic feel that a game similar to this should and when you coat that with the over all concept of mechanics in the game, I simply do not see a better one out there.

I would only recommend Darkest Dungeon to someone who can unironically say that "losing is fun."
The game is hard. It genuinely is. It'll take you maybe twenty hours to learn the system to a point where you can tell a good gamble from a bad and start to maximize your odds. Even when you do that, though, it always remains a gamble, and THEN the game starts adding NEW monsters, just as you were getting the hang of the old ones.
Your heroes will die. That grave robber you named after your wife? She's going to get critted by a cultist and bleed before your healer gets a turn. That amazing highwayman? He's going to have the same thing done to him by a spider. Your leper? He's going to have a heart attack and die.
Most games, I get tired of the music after about 300 hours. I have never gotten tired of Darkest Dungeon's music. That said, I can't recommend the music pack dlc, because it only has like, half of the game's OST.
Wayne June's voice remains amazing.
You are not going to complete this game in a week. You are probably not going to complete this game in a month, unless you are playing for more than six hours every day and using guides. Relax and enjoy poking around in dungeons, and the game will be very fun.

I thought long and hard about this, but I came to the same conclusion as everyone else.
XCOM2 is a very good, although unfinished game. It's funny to have to call it unfinished seeing how it is basically the exact same thing as XCOM1, running on the same engine, and fundamentally with the same gameplay, albeit with sensible balance improvements. What's new?
These are very welcome and well thought-out mechanics, but it's also where the praise runs out. XCOM2 has all the glitches XCOM1 had, and then some. The optimization is absolutely pathetic - this game has higher requirements than GTA5 and unplayable with any kind of anti-aliasing enabled. During the last mission there were so many enemies on screen that the game's engine kicked the bucket multiple times and gave epileptic textures requiring a reboot.
The action cam is an incredible drag as well. XCOM1 could handle rapid fire in one animation, but XCOM2 pauses the game twice. Or three, or four, or five times. This is ridiculous considering how many abilities let you shoot 3+ times per turn, and since it used to work on the same engine in 2012. It's basically like aircraft animations in Civ5.
The frequent loading screens approach 40 seconds in length, despite using an SSD drive. Also the stats and leaderboards don't work.
One thing to be particularly weary of is being able to destroy the floor underneath an enemy. It seems like a great idea, but it guarantees that enemy will be glitched out and freeze the game for 15 seconds each time it moves or shoots. It also guarantees a desync in multiplayer.
Speaking of which, most disappointing of all is by far the multiplayer. It comes with questionable limitations (only 2 types of each class as opposed to 5, cannot choose weapons, cannot choose armour, not even half of the utility items are available, no PCS, no deep pockets etc.) These are the gameplay aspects. Gameplay aspects, however, do not matter if you can't play the game.
Once again, in this third installment, the multiplayer an unplayable and completely broken mess.. It is beyond unstable. It is even worse than EW, which, in turn, was worse than EU. I have yet to finish
without it collapsing under desyncs and glitches, and finally disconnecting. How hard can it be to do multiplayer in a turn-based game? Legacy XCOM had multiplayer over email for crying out loud. It's unacceptable to sell this game as "having multiplayer".
But enough of that. I was going to give a negative review for as long as the extremely high price coincided with technical issues, but ultimately I chose acquiescence. It's a good game with tons of fantastic little flavours you won't notice, extensive moddability (!) and significantly improved balance (except for that one item). I'm sure that the modders will find a way to improve many completely of the broken aspects that the developers clearly didn't have time to finish.
I'll admit that I was worried about XCOM2 being geared towards "a wider audience", with a huge amount of guaranteed hit, guaranteed miss, guaranteed protection, never trigger overwatch, mind control lasts for ever and other such items & abilities, but they pulled it off just fine, it wasn't as bad as I thought. Token black guy and woman of colour turned out to actually have a personality instead of being there as a strategic resource. Higher difficulty still has an insanely low margin for error. You will always be gradually losing over time. Sometimes a screwup will cost you a near guaranteed game over 3 hours later, but you won't know until then. Time limits work, but they feel like a lazy and artificial solution to mask the AI's shortcomings.
XCOM2 will sell a lot of copies and make a lot of money. This means we'll see a lot more like it, and by that I mean games being released in an unfinished state. The complete lack of optimization feels like penny-pinching to maximise profits at release, while♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off a lot of people in the long term. The "multiplayer" is blatant false advertising, there is no multiplayer. Personally, I am disappointed and would probably write a negative review if I paid more than I did.
You will have to ask yourself whether the couple of bullet points above are worth the incredibly hefty price tag. As with all Firaxis titles, it is a questionable purchase until an expansion comes out.

A very good game with an interesting setting but it is weighed down by a few flaws. There is too much grind, too much RNG, and an unpredictable turn order which really hold it back. I should clarify that this was originally a negative review but I think the game is still good enough to be worth it's price tag despite it's issues.
At first i was really enjoying the game, the grind seemed more than acceptable and the combat was quite fun, however after getting quite far into the game the 'difficulty' quickly started to ruin the fun. What I noticed was that any kind of strategy is usually crushed by the overbearing RNG which forces you to grind until your characters are strong enough to deal with some of the unreasonable situations that the game puts you in. This really draws the game out and it becomes extremely repetitive in the later stages.
The boss fights seem to be well structured and were always quite enjoyable as the challenge presented in picking the right team for the job and getting them there relatively intact was always quite fun. Unfortunately these enjoyable runs were eventually outweighed by the negative aspects of the game, the constant micromanagement of stress and negative quirks along with repetitive grinding to keep your team up to scratch and the occasional RNG based death sentences were more than i was willing to bear to finish the game which I consider to be a real shame as I was really interested in the cryptic story and exploring the deepest parts of the dungeon.
Overall I'd say the game is well worth it but don't expect to finish it unless you are willing to put some serious hours into grinding through the same content you've already seen a hundred times before.

Dark Souls III, The one game i managed to get over 1500 hours on.
Where to start with this...
Short Version
The Pros
- Engaging gameplay
- Beautiful scenery and soundtrack
- Tons of replayability
- Varied PVP With both strangers and friends.
- Co-op with strangers and friends, to get past those pesky dogs
- Memes that may or may not give conniptions
Cons
- Connectivity may sometimes be an issue when fighting strangers
- Requires patience and determination, not for the easily angered.
- Difficulty may be a turnoff for people who enjoy more casually toned games
- Those people who use a greatshield with great magic weapon in pvp
(Skip to bottom for roundup)
Long Version
As someone who has enjoyed the Dark Souls series thoroughly, I feel that Dark Souls 3 has fixed many control issues apparent in previous installments. The combat feels active, rewarding proper timing and enemy management, whilst punishing rushing into battle without a plan and carelessly swinging your blade around. Enemies are placed strategically across the levels, neatly tieing in with their surroundings and backstories. It feels like all of them have a reason to be where they are. Surroundings are interesting, and tell their own little part of the story.
The bosses are their own kind of combat. Whilst in the levels themself the challenge is in enemy management, and level exploration. The bosses give you a one on one (usually) death battle, where careful dodging and reading your enemy's movement is key to surviving the encounter. They are larger, stronger and faster then any other enemy in the game, and are not to be taken lightly. Defeating these formidable foes is quite the challenge, and also very satisfying.
About the story: you will have to look for it. Although DS3 doesnt hide its story as much as the previous titles, Item descriptions, surroundings and NPC dialogue are essential to finding out what exactly is going on in lothric. Finding all these tidbits of lore makes it exciting to find new weapons and/or items, aside from their obvious use.
The singleplayer aspect is fun enough on its own, but the multiplayer aspect makes it whole. being able to summon both strangers and friends to aid you in your journey makes each journey different. Naturally, recieving more aid makes the enemies tougher, along with other risks, like multiple invaders. the arena is always full with people at almost any level, providing unlimited entertainment as players duke it out 1 on 1, or in teams.
All in all, its a experience that changes from person to person. with bountiful amounts of weapons to choose from, and more armor than one sane person could collect. theres endless combinations of character builds at your disposal. knights, mages,  pyromancers and clerics, and combinations in all forms.
Ive ran through the entire game over 60 times at this point, finding new secrets and tidbits of story still. and with PVP being one of the most entertaining things i have ever come across. The enemies, story, soundtrack and scenery are a joy to return to whenever i launch this game.
(continue here for roundup)
Basically, if youve played the first two games, youll find a familliar yet refreshing style of gameplay before your eyes
If DS3 is your first dark souls, Youll find a easy to learn, difficult to master game that will keep you busy for quite some time.
Overall, I think this is my favorite game in my entire library.

What greater satisfaction you need than hitting your opponent right after weakening them with a terrible finishing blow?
What greater frustration can you suffer than seeing the enemies dog-pile on a single hero, rendering it useless in a single turn?
Make no mistake, this game can be incredibly frustrating at times. The difficulty constantly ramps up, as you try to keep your heroes health and stress in check. Enemies poison you and leave you bleeding with ease, and a bad turn can easily screw an entire expedition, and cost you good men.
But as soon as you get in rhythm. As soon as you understand how to manage your items, what characters have the better synergy together, how to position them in a fight, and how to counter the monstrosities you find in every mission, what once seemed unfair becomes just a challenge. A hard challenge, that you can still loose; but when you do, you learn to just arm another party and send them to prevail where the others failed.
The game makes it's own the despair and hopelessness of the Lovecraft mythos both in aesthetic and theming, while adding a splash of cinical and dark sense of humor.
You are not here to become an immortal, unstoppable force of nature, you are here to try and survive an onslaught of horror way beyond what men can really handle. And the game will make sure you feel that in every corner, just as the men you send to fight, and leave the dungeons more and more psychologically crippled every time they go out. But so what? We are all doomed anyway, right?
If you like turn-based RPGs, Rogue-like games, or just challenging experiences, this one is worth a shot.

XCOM 2 is definitely a huge improvement over its predecessor, seemingly at all levels. Lets see:
1)The sub-par air encounters are gone and not missed.
2)The construction and production of items are redone better. Workshops make sense now(actually you can build only one and it is enough).
3)You can train your rookies in the GTS for the next rank(Hurrah!) and your psionic soldiers advance through training, not combat.
4)All available facilities for construction are useful.
5)Concealment and ambushes: Cool!
6)More mission variety
7)The replacement of the Panic system with the Avatar Project counter is a huge improvement on the strategic aspect. The way that counter works is great, too.
8)You can evacuate at any place on the map on most missions.
9)You can carry the bodies of your dead or unconscious squad members
10)Better soldier classes with better skills.
11)Defend the avenger missions are epic!
12)Infiltrators among the civilians. Brilliant!
13)Most timers in missions are only related to specific objectives. Once the pressing objective is met, you can clear the AO at your leisure. It makes sense. Only VIP rescue and capture missions have a timer for the whole mission but you do not need to clear the AO. RUN FOR IT, squad!
14)Hacking! Yes! Nicely done!(Although a mini-game instead of random would be super-great)
15)Overwatch redone much much much better!
16)Skullmining!
17)Enemy variant and the same enemies keep improving all the time by gaining abilities as time passes!
18)Dark Events!
19)No CTDs(at least not for me, after 81 hours of gameplay) which is very important if you only play Ironman, like I do.
Of course this is not to say the game is perfect. What I would like to see:
1)Ability to carry the bodies of the enemies to the evac zone, so that you can take corpses and goodies in missions that you do not need to clear the AO or in missions that you can still get your primary objective without clearing the AO.
2)Missions that you obtain your primary objective and evacuate without clearing the AO should still count as success. E.g. Hack the terminal, destroy the transmitter, get the item out of the box. It goes without saying that you cannot obtain any AO-depended rewards(except for the ones you managed with (1)) but counting them as a failure does not make sense.
3)More mission variety. For example, you could get a rescue mission for squad members captured in previous missions(THAT would be great!). Also, optional missions(i.e. missions that you can fail without any consequences other than failing to acquire the rewards) would be great.
4)More useful Medical tree for the Specialist. As it is, I do not see why one would take that tree over the combat one.
And, of course, I would like to see, for once, a bug-free game. The bugs are not game-breaking but they are still very annoying.
And, for those that make it through all this, here is a tip:
Contrary to what the tip says about ambushes DO NOT put all your squad on overwatch for an ambush. If even one enemy escapes, they still get their own turn and you can kiss at least one trooper goodbye. Unless the odds for hitting are pretty high(ambush overwatch does not suffer aim penalties) you are better off planning your moves after the enemy scatters.
Also, starting the ambush with a grenade or heavy weapon fire works miracles :).
Certainly recommended if you like this genre.

This has to be one of my favorite games of all time; Red Hook did a phenomenal job creating this masterpiece.
The Gameplay in Darkest Dungeon is quite challenging from a casual perspective (and with mods, can be even more challenging), and features a fairly unique hero system. The heroes in Darkest Dungeon are disposable, unlike basically any run-of-the-mill RPG you'll find out there. The difficulty in Darkest Dungeon, disregarding the RNG which at times (in the nature of RNG) can ruin your day, comes from managing your heroes; their stress, their ailments, and their quirks can all empower, or cripple a hero. Death, in Darkest Dungeon, is always a hair's breadth away, even for the hardiest of adventurers.
Gameplay aside, it is for the art, narration, lore, and music that I keep coming back to this game. The creative expression is fantastic in Darkest Dungeon, so much so that I often find myself watching the beginning intro even when I don't feel like playing the game: how many games can you say that about? The art is striking, and in its disparity with conventional gaming art, is quite beautiful in its dark shadows and sharp, contrasting edges. The music, as with any good score, wonderfully enhances the gravity of the situation in Darkest Dungeon; you are left feeling at all times that this could be your party's last moment--that at any time, in a myriad ways, your favorite heroes can meet their untimely demise. The lore, too, adds to the gravity of Darkest Dungeon, and in a strange way: its sparsity. The game does not feed you the storyline, other than the overarching goal given to you by your ancestor. The lore, though seemingly absent, is deep and rewarding... when you find it. Darkest Dungeon forces you to eke out each scrap of lore through bosses, journals, and narration. And the narration... Wayne June is a fantastic and talented voice actor, and his voice so lends itself to the style of Darkest Dungeon and the Lovecraftian horror that it entails that I find it almost startling. You will grow to love the voice of your ancestor.
This game, if my review wasn't clear, is wonderful, with much replayability, and very engaging gameplay. The world of Darkest Dungeon that Red Hook strove to create is vibrant in the tones of horror that are displayed; the monocromatic nature of fear is displayed in a cacophonous din and shocking visage of terror. This game is a must have at any price. You owe it to yourself to give Darkest Dungeon a shot.

I'll go ahead and say: it's tough to recommend this one if you don't fall in love with the combat system right away, because a lot of it feels downright unfair unless you start out by being careful and learning as much as you can.
That said, I LOVE the aesthetic of this game. The Stress mechanic is really innovative, and causes you to rethink approaches to fights, as to whether you go in guns (or swords) blazing, or try to conserve your fighters for longer by taking a long way around, or by stocking up on lots of healing items.
The core of the experience is solid, and the progression feels meaningful throughout. It is a little grindy, but that comes with the territory for a lot of "Roguelite" games these days.
Edit: One gripe I had about the game is the framerate slowdowns and lack of optimizations. Not only is it fixed, but the game feels SO much better to play than ever since I started playing in beta. So many improvements have been made, and if you dropped the game for a while, you won't regret playing it now.

I now put around 100 hours into this game and I can definetly recommend it. Long story short:
+ graphics are really good. Most if not all locations look beautiful. The developers paid a lot of attention to details.
+ sound is great and "realistic". Dark Souls 3 features by far the best soundtrack in the series. The theme of the Abyss Watchers is a prime example. The voice acting is also pretty good.
+ combat is fluid and faster as in Dark Souls and Dark Souls 2.
+ a lot of armour, weapons, spells, miracles and pyromancies.
+ great multiplayer - yeah, it is basically the same as in 1 and 2 but this kind of multiplayer is unique compared to any other franchise (I include Demon's Souls and Bloodborne into the Souls franchise).
+ really good quests which enrich the story and are not thrown into your face like in any other RPG.
+ really good length. Doesn't matter if you include the DLC or not.
- invasions or PVP in general can be annoying due to latency issues or lag. Only the arena (accessable while playing the DLC) features a server. The rest is P2P.
- backtracking for additional armour doesn't make much sense - discover location A, 5 hours later, at location X, you kill a certrain unique enemy, armour can now be found at location A. I'm talking about Havel's armour to be specific.
- the first DLC, Ashes of Ariandel, is pretty poor on it's own when it comes to length and variety. But since anybody who buys the game probably buys the complete edition anyway, this does not mean much. I just wanted to point that out. Especially since both DLC's belong together - literally.
- some enemy types can be seen as a recycled version of an earlier enemy later on. It is not that obvious as in other games but still. Seems kinda lazy.
I can definetly recommend the purchase of this game. It does not matter if it is on sale or not. In my opinion, it still is worth 60 bucks. Compare it to "triple A" trash from Activision or EA and you can pay 100€ without batting an eye.

My feelings about this game have definitely seesawed in the time that I've spent playing it, so I felt it was necessary to update my review.
My first review for Darkest Dungeon, written while I was still fairly new to the game, was unabashedly positive, though I acknowledged the game was designed with punishment in mind.
Then, as I passed 250 weeks on my first playthrough, I was beginning to get frustrated. Maybe this game was TOO hard. Maybe it was deliberately wasting my time and heaping on artificial difficulty in order to pad gameplay time. I was strongly considering giving it a thumbs down because of this, even though it would've hurt me to do so. There were plenty of things about Darkest Dungeon that I liked, but how could I, in good conscience, recommend a game that had caused me so much grief?
Having played the game a little further and overcome some of the challenges that had me stumped before, I've mellowed out a little. I realized the problem was me. Darkest Dungeon is hard, and the RNG is BRUTAL, but it's not impossible. Far from it. Optimizing your party correctly can make even the most intimidating bosses a cinch. So if you're having trouble with a particular fight, look up some strategies. Every class has its uses. You might discover that the one you thought was useless before is in fact crucial to winning a challenging fight. And for God's sake, don't ignore debuffs and status effects!
That being said, there do appear to be some genuine balance issues with the Crimson Court DLC, judging from what other players are saying. So if you think the vanilla game is too hard, you might want to stall buying the DLC. More I can't say, as I haven't played CC yet.
I now feel confident recommending Darkest Dungeon, but with a strong word of caution: It's not for the faint of heart. Those who dislike grinding and are prone to fits of table-flipping rage when RNG deals them a bad hand might want to look past this one. It can be particularly challenging for people who, like myself, are not so keen on obsessive-compulsively analyzing stats and perfecting their party's synergy; good strategy is essential to winning in DD. But if you like a game that doesn't hold your hand and are in the market for something unique, then I heartily recommend Darkest Dungeon.

They gave me my own ship, along with that I was given one tool that I would cling to dearly as I prepared for my arduous journey to this planet that my ship was conveniently anchored too.  And off I went, beaming down onto this planet of new possibilities, resources, and local inhabitants both peaceful and not. This is Starbound; where the purpose is to explore different galaxies, harvest resources, and create things to help you better survive the planet you are on at any given time.  Starbound is vast and it contains thousands of planets of many varieties. Ranging from the cold harsh Snow planets, to the intimidating and highly dangerous Magma planets. There is even a Tentacle Planet if you’re feeling curious! Right off the back you’re given a hand full of quests to get you familiarized with the games crafting system which has you building bonfires to stay warm, a table to make your various crafts, and a furnace to smelt the metal that you have gathered. The rest was left for you to discover.
No matter how simple and innocent this game may look, don’t let it fool you; it’s quite unforgiving. Beaming down to my very first planet I was greeted with my first contact of alien life.  And let’s just say they didn’t appreciate my presence, which resulted in a swift death for me. The game’s difficulty is challenging but not unbearable and what keeps you coming back is the games complex and deep mechanics. For example upon building my first pick axe and digging through my first few levels of rock my pick axe quickly broke and I was left with my first tool, to harvest at a slower rate than I previously was. Along with this mechanic there are a plethora of others including the crafting system which allows you to build everything you need to make your game more unique, from new armor and weapons to different star maps to travel to more distant and difficult galaxies. Or perhaps you would like to craft a few rainbow bricks to give your new house some much needed color.
There are no real limits in this game and the items, mechanics and worlds are always being discovered. Each time you pick it up you will find yourself doing something entirely different than you did the time prior. Who knows you may find a guitar along the way and find yourself playing a marimba with your friends over multiplayer. Another time you may find yourself coming across a local village on a new planet and raiding it like Genghis Khan! Regardless of play style, fast or slow, hostile or peaceful this game offers many different ways to be played and hosts hours and hours of enjoyment. I would highly recommend Starbound.

Darkest Dungeon is not for everyone; if you're not a fan of games that can't revert saves, take brutal shots to your ego, and have never lost a full skyranger in XCom, then flee for the hills right now.
If you're still here, then this is a game for you.  Lush visual and sound design converge on what can only be described as a perfectly executed bleak endeavor.  The voice over narration is spot on, and reminds you that even in victory, death is right around the corner.
The core gameplay of DD is turn based squad combat.  You customize a group of 4 adventurers and dive in for a delve of varying lengths.   This is no where near the tactical complexity of something in the D20 system; picture short-bursts of brutal action.  The true skill in the gameplay is balancing a never ending battle of attrition with the need to be tatically efficient.  ie, do I buff my guy this turn for a bigger strike next, knowing that the guy i leave alive could very well inflict stress on a character that makes him less valuable in the long run?  There is no right answer.
In between missions, it's more of the same.  Limited resources make you feel behind the curve as you level up, and your motley crew of Dungeon crawlers slowly build up insanities and afflictions.  De-stress one and watch him go on a druken bender and lose that artifact you just found.
The good news is that the game knows it is hard, and clues abound on how to execute better and survive with aplomb.  Many classes have complimentary skills and combos, and there are always newer heroes to replace fallen ones as needed.
I've read many comments about how this game has limited replay and I have no idea wtf people are talking about.  With 12+ classes and only 4 roster spots per mission, there is a massive amount of combos available.  In addition, each class can learn 8 moves but only can slot 4, making for choices and customization even before you get to the mission.  The variety of skills and team keeps me coming back.
Yes, it sucks when you lose people, but it's all in keeping with the game's flavor.  If you're looking to fall in love with Dark Fantasy, this is an amazing game.

Fantastic atmosphere, visuals, and style are completely marred by the RNG-based grindfest gameplay.
I desperately want to love this game, but all of its charm is sapped by the actual gameplay, wherein commitment to your troops is highly discouraged, and progress is measured by how much RNG punishes you. There are a plethora of strategies the player can use, but in order for any of them to adequately work, RNG will need to bless you with decent items and troops. Every other game in existence allows your troops to grow stronger upon leveling. In Darkest Dungeon, there is a very strong chance they will get weaker, because leveling as an equal chance of inflicting negative effects, as it does postive ones. Meaning, even a character youve invested gold and time into can quickly become a liability upon leveling, hampering their effectiveness in combat, or forcing you to spend resources to cure them. None of this even speaks to how even a moderately poor run of RNG can send a party into an unavoidable wipe, resulting in hours and hours wasted.
Darkest Dungeon is entirely completable, but doing so is almost entirely without any sort of satisfaction. Victory is never obtained through smart play or clever tactics, it's done through luck and persistence.

To this day, Spiral Knights remains one of my favourite "go-to" casual play games in terms of adventure-style games. I think it's time I re-reviewed it.
The core aspect of any game. The gameplay type involved is a dungeon crawler, top-down view, adventure-style game. Think Legend of Zelda, in a mix of Four Swords coupled with Phantasy Star (Albeit very loosely)
It has an interesting perspective, being not overly puzzling, but challenging at places and very atmospheric when it wants to be. Every battle tends to feel slightly different from your last one in some aspect.
Unfortunately, there's one flaw with all this; The game's optimization is rather subpar. As a result, lag spikes do tend to occur at a semifrequent basis. It's unfortunate, considering the game is quite stellar otherwise.
Gameplay-wise, the score is a 8/10.
This game has a rather unique art style. It doesn't seem to stick to one general area, rather being more spaced out in several different directions at once.
The players themselves, the Knights, are a good example of this. You begin as a knight who can look serious or cheerful, in a dark or vivid colour, that's either blacklight or neon, accented by vibrant pastel colours or murky, metallic styles. They look like those little figurines you can get, and can come in either plush, clay, or metal materials.
The Clockworks themselves do a nice little background job, themselves. Each level seems sculpted to fit the design of the level and the family that lives within them. One family, known as Fiends, lives in an office-type scenario, with glyphs sometimes strewn about. Lighting wherever appropriate.
9.5/10 with this one, only because on rare occasions, you get odd-looking pieces that don't seem to belong.
Whoever came up with the music scores did an excellent job setting the mood for the area players are in. This is most noticible in boss levels, and tends to come to one of the most engaging boss themes I've ever heard. And this game's been released for quite a few years now.
10/10 because I really don't see - well hear - any flaws with this one.
Unlike the core gameplay experience, this is how it can be, from start to finish, at a reasonable experience.
Unfortunately, this is the only category where I feel it tanks at. It's nice and smooth at the start, as you typically get everything you need easily enough and can progress. When you hit about Knight or Defender level, however, that's when you start to see the reason as to why the game isn't as popular as it was or could have been.
The main issue is the energy costs associated with acquiring the gear you need to progress. When I first began playing (This was one of my first Steam games), the energy system was Mist and Crystal energy. It took 10 energy to go down a floor. This is where my gears started to grind just a tad. That basically meant that, unless you had a bottomless wallet, you couldn't really play...unless you had an elevator pass.
However, while the new system is better, it's not by much. Yes, there's no more elevator costs, at all, but there's now Orbs of Alchemy, which is the main reason why people stopped playing.
I say it's better, however, because of how easy it can be to simply get a bunch of energy, especially now. You need 3 orbs of alchemy of a certain type to progress in the game. The one minor thing with that is the people don't seem to realize it's the same costs as before, it just takes an extra step, sometimes mitigated entirely if your luck is good enough to get all 3 orbs of alchemy while you get the 200 or so Energy you need for your weapons.
Further, you need only ONE of your weapons at the star requirement (In the example above, 3 stars) to proceed, not the other one, two, or three. Overall, to get all 5-star gear, you either need to get very lucky, or cough up 3200 energy for 12 Eternal Orbs of Alchemy. Which, thanks to the drop system, is very unlikely you'll need to cough up all 3200, if even half that. Besides, some of the orbs appear as mission rewards.
That being said, it's still a grind, thanks to the heat system rework and needed Fire Crystals to get the weapons up to the levels needed to progress. That's where I say not by much in terms of how better it is, but it's still not as bad as people think. One word of warning: Go full-out or you may find yourself experiencing Final Fantasy Luck Syndrome.
6.75/10. As a side note, you can get 100 energy for a set number of crowns, which you'll likely get in 1 or 2 runs of the number of floors, anyway. It's honestly easier to get crowns than you might think.
It's a real shame this game gets the hate it doesn't deserve. In fact, I think it's fair to say this is an underrated gem. Of course, every game has it's flaws, and I pointed out perhaps some of the major ones, the two big ones being optimization and the grind to get to Vangaurd rank.
However, this game has some very fun moments, and at no point do you feel underwhelmed when someone brings in their 5-star gear to your party of 2-star equipment. That's the beauty of it; the game is balanced so no one weapon tends to feel super-souped up over the other, rather just gets the job done a tad faster.
The only other complaint I have is that missions tend to be slow for release. But if that just means they have tweaks to them, or want to make sure everything runs smooth (See the Gunner Update), then I don't care how long I have to wait, personally.
Overall score: 8/10. A definite recommendation of mine. This might not be for everyone, of course, but if you like what you see, download it and give it a go. The grind isn't as bad as everyone makes it out to be, though it is intimidating at first, and when it runs, it's mostly smooth sailing from start to finish.

Xcom was like chess but Xcom2 became a roulette or a poker.
Firstly, Xcom2 has  aquired a major game breaking point - the timer. Instead of first two Xcoms meticulous calculation of moves Xcom2 forces you to recklessly risk your soldiers without any back up plan. If you don't your time will be up you have to.
Secondly, the cover mechanic does not work. Lots of NPCs have some inner defences which defie cover system.
Third, unexpected and unjustified spikes of difficulty.
All of the above make you to reload the saves again and again  hoping that the next time the dice rolle in your favour. It is a daunting grind. It is plainly boring.
Example, an NPC standing on overwatch 5 squares from your unit  with probability to hit 65%. Nil option to back up due to the timer. NIl optioni to push forward because the NPC kills any of your soldiers from overwatch with one hit. And with stated probability  65% there is nil option to score a hit either! I reloaded 15 times to understand it.
If you play Xcom2 your gameplay will primarily consist of waiting for another save to reload while you will be staring at the game's tacky screen cover. It is disappointing how devs managed to spoil nearly perfect tactical shooter.

I made the mistake of buying into the pre-release hype that surrounded this game (along with alowing my past experiences with the fallout franchise influence my decision to buy).  Overall it is not a bad game, but it is not a particularly good or innovative game either.  It has turned out to be a very average game.  It feels like a derviative work of Fallout 3 minus the good dlc.  Even the dlc from fallout NV were superior to those of this game, they were expansive, story-driven, and atmosphereic.  Far harbor was alright, but not particulalry memorable.  Who can recall the Pitt, the big MT, or the final battle with Ulysses?  I suppose I expected more from this title, which resulted in this let down.
Edit:
The concept of creation club is here to stay, this is their second attempt to monetize mods.  The real determination with how this will go will be made when the next major title (the next elder scrolls or whatever) is released.  Right now it is nebulous because the creation kit genie is out of the bottle for all of the currently released titles.   I am going to be watching what Bethesda does with the future games, that is where they will show their true intent.
Personally, I am not going to purchase any of their future titles until I see how they plan to proceed with this system.  What will the dividing line be for what season passes will apply to?  Would the gun runners arsenal from NV now be considered a minor mod and not included in a season pass?
My initial knee-jerk reaction to this was negative, but I have walked that back somewhat to being apprehensive.  I do not believe that all the protest in the world will cause Bethesda to abandon this new creation club, and we will have to wait for the next major title release to see what direction they are taking this concept.

The is my token "first game" review on steam.  I never write reviews because I think that they're a drop in a nearly incomprehensible bucket, but here goes.
I just finished commander difficulty on ironman.  It's a great game, in some ways better than XCOM Enemy Unknown/Within.  I was surprised by the levels of hate of reviewers following release day and the few days after release, and that's why I felt compelled to write this review.
This game is not polished.  Some of the animations are unfinished/buggy, and the game could be optimized better.  My GTX 770 could not handle max settings.  However, the moment I reduced the game to medium settings the game played like a well-oiled machine.
I would definitely recommend this game to tactical RPG veterans.  It's punishing in the right way.  And thank the Elders the devs avoided a steep reverse difficulty curve like that of XCOM Enemy Unknown.  The game gets easier the longer you survive but not by much.  It felt like Dragon Age Origins where stacking mages substantially altered the difficulty of the game - psionic operatives are so overpowered.
Anyways, please play this game - it's pretty great.
Absolutely worth every penny. And I backed it with 95 dollars in their Kickstarter. More addictive than cocaine.

I wanted to really experience the game and all the various classes before I wrote a review of this game. The current reviews are so polarizing.
Overall this game is a very enjoyable dungeon crawler. The classes are diverse enough that they feel unique, the items matter significantly and yes it is a challenging game but overall you can win with time and patience. Deaths are painful but the fear of death is what makes success so much more sweet. Also, death of a character is not as bad as some reviewers make it out to be. You can rebuild, the game is not completely ruined.
But the most important thing, is this game fun, yes, now it is not some super deep strategy game, nor is their an incredible amount of diversity to the story or dungeons. But the processes of planning fighting, dieing, rebuilding and eventually overcoming the Darkest Dungeon were very enjoyable. I usually recommend going into games blind, I.E no wikis, no guides and so on. But this game I would recommend reading up on different strategies, there is no dominant one. It makes the game feel less punishing while still maintaining the element of suspense.
7/10 would recommend.
EDIT: One last thing, even though I gave the game a positive review I would recommend waiting to pick it up when it goes on sale.

Starbound is a game very similar to Terraria, and I can't decide which is the better of the two. There are so many things in both games but something in Starbound makes it stand out. Perhaps it's because there are hundreds of thousands of solar systems scattered across 5 different sectors of the universe. You can play as different races, get tech items with cool abilities, fight a monster that spits sand at you and sounds like a horse in an asteroid belt; heck, you can even fight some mechanical spiders in a stinky sewer. But that's just the beginning.
There is so much content in Starbound, and so many places to go. You can even find other races and interact with them while they're living in a planet made of tentacles. There are probably as many ores as Terraria has. The music can be very calm and serene (unless you're fighting a one-eyed howling pig-stegosaurus), and it is only early-access, so there is so much more content to be introduced.

I am very disappointed with how Bethesda is changing Fallout 4 with the creation club. For many years there has been a modding community for Bethesda games, which includes Fallout 4. These mods are done as a hobby for fun. Due to the more causal nature of mods, the lawyers of IPs used to create these mods have turned a blind eye to what is happening. They may no longer turn a blind eye if the creation club starts making money.
If the creation club is not for mods, but professionally developed add-ons then they should not treat these add-ons as paid mods. StarCraft: Insurrection, which was developed by Aztech New Media, is was an official licensed add-on to StarCraft, which was developed by Blizzard. The relationship between Blizzard and Aztech should be the model that Bethesda uses when making professionally developed add-ons.
Given Bethesda’s current choice of actions, I cannot recommend Fallout 4 in its current state.
