Dark Souls III, The one game i managed to get over 1500 hours on.
Where to start with this...
Short Version
The Pros
- Engaging gameplay
- Beautiful scenery and soundtrack
- Tons of replayability
- Varied PVP With both strangers and friends.
- Co-op with strangers and friends, to get past those pesky dogs
- Memes that may or may not give conniptions
Cons
- Connectivity may sometimes be an issue when fighting strangers
- Requires patience and determination, not for the easily angered.
- Difficulty may be a turnoff for people who enjoy more casually toned games
- Those people who use a greatshield with great magic weapon in pvp
(Skip to bottom for roundup)
Long Version
As someone who has enjoyed the Dark Souls series thoroughly, I feel that Dark Souls 3 has fixed many control issues apparent in previous installments. The combat feels active, rewarding proper timing and enemy management, whilst punishing rushing into battle without a plan and carelessly swinging your blade around. Enemies are placed strategically across the levels, neatly tieing in with their surroundings and backstories. It feels like all of them have a reason to be where they are. Surroundings are interesting, and tell their own little part of the story.
The bosses are their own kind of combat. Whilst in the levels themself the challenge is in enemy management, and level exploration. The bosses give you a one on one (usually) death battle, where careful dodging and reading your enemy's movement is key to surviving the encounter. They are larger, stronger and faster then any other enemy in the game, and are not to be taken lightly. Defeating these formidable foes is quite the challenge, and also very satisfying.
About the story: you will have to look for it. Although DS3 doesnt hide its story as much as the previous titles, Item descriptions, surroundings and NPC dialogue are essential to finding out what exactly is going on in lothric. Finding all these tidbits of lore makes it exciting to find new weapons and/or items, aside from their obvious use.
The singleplayer aspect is fun enough on its own, but the multiplayer aspect makes it whole. being able to summon both strangers and friends to aid you in your journey makes each journey different. Naturally, recieving more aid makes the enemies tougher, along with other risks, like multiple invaders. the arena is always full with people at almost any level, providing unlimited entertainment as players duke it out 1 on 1, or in teams.
All in all, its a experience that changes from person to person. with bountiful amounts of weapons to choose from, and more armor than one sane person could collect. theres endless combinations of character builds at your disposal. knights, mages,  pyromancers and clerics, and combinations in all forms.
Ive ran through the entire game over 60 times at this point, finding new secrets and tidbits of story still. and with PVP being one of the most entertaining things i have ever come across. The enemies, story, soundtrack and scenery are a joy to return to whenever i launch this game.

XCOM 2 feels like a much cleaner and refined game than XCOM Enemy Within. There finally is an actual reason for the limited resources that was so puzzling in the first XCOM game. XCOM 2 has you make choices about what you should pursue, without punishing you with rising panic levels in XCOM Enemy Within. This is done through a smartly designed map that allows the Avenger to move around to individual sites and scan for the materials or resources you are attempting to acquire. The map also works very well to give you a visual representation of your progress, as you make contact with the resistance in the different parts of the world. Ultimately, I found this screen and the method of presenting missions to you to be XCOM 2's biggest failing. Why do I have to make contact with the resistance of a region before taking on the story missions? I get that it's to slow the game down, but I was delayed by a huge amount of time between these missions in order to build the necessary buildings. What was also immensly frustrating was the amount of missions that were shoved in my face. The objectives quickly got repetetive, and it was incredibly aggravating to go from a challenging mission into having another "crucial mission" given to me just two or three days after I got back from the last one. Honestly, does the Council want me to destroy the AVATAR project or rescue this one scientist? The time it takes soldiers to recover from wounds is painfully slow; even if they only took one hit the whole mission, they still spend 9-12 days recovering, which is 2-3 missions in XCOM 2's staggering speed of missions. I so rarely had a full squad of my best soldiers for one mission, and had to resort to stealthing several story missions with rookies on occaision, leading to me throwing away 3+ soldiers and killing maybe 2 aliens in a mission with 22. On one hand, it was pretty fun to sneak up to the objective, but it also was frustrating because I was missing out on the reason XCOM 2 is such a magnificent game: it's combat.
Thankfully, XCOM 2's combat is easily the best in the series, almost making up for the aggravating mission placement. The heavy, sniper, assault, and support classes have been replaced with the grenedier (think demo man from tf2, great for destroying cover), sharpshooter (skilled sniper that is also great with pistols and can do a devestating amount of damage to multiple enemies a turn), ranger (assault-esque reconnaisance unit that weilds an awesome sword and a shotgun that can do incredible damage at close range), and specialist (specialist replacement that can heal, revive, hack mechanical enemies, and provide bonus defense to an ally from range) classes. All these classes feel very unique and immensly fun to control and use their unique abilities. I especially enjoyed the ranger's slash ability, though rangers scale the worst out of any class in the game. The new enemy units are also brilliantly designed. In the first 8 hours of the campaign, XCOM 2 really delivered the feeling that XCOM is a shadow of what it once was. The aliens feel technologically superior and pack a serious punch. However, after the first weapons upgrade and armor upgrade the fights become much more even. While the AI does occaisionally make some seriously baffling mistakes, it is largely improved. I enjoyed the combat the most about XCOM 2, and seriously have very little ground to take a negative stance on anything. There were several circumstances (much more frequent than I would have liked), where everything goes wrong to no fault of you. I've had turns where all 6 of my soldiers have missed their 70%+ chance shots or overwatches on the following turn, and several of them have wound up dead and most of the others heavily wounded. This happened a little too often for my liking, not enough to really complain about, but persistant enough to remember.
Overall, XCOM 2 is an amazing game that perfects the satisfying combat of the XCOM franchise. The combat is crisp and the action cam makes your heart leap at every great hit and plummet with every enemy strike. If it wasn't for the crippling soldier recovery times and short spacing between missions, XCOM 2 would be the best single play game I've ever played. I would give XCOM 2 an 8.5/10.

Bottom line up front: this game is terrible. Don't buy it. Buy Xenonauts or XCOM Enemy Unknown.
To be more specific, the game itself builds upon the more or less solid foundation of Enemy Unknown, and manages to add numerous problems while adding very few improvements on the original.
The major problems with the game are mostly in design, but there are some technical issues as well. The game loads slow, stutters, and suffers from numerous bugs and problems. The insane focus on cinematics to give me simple information is absolutely out of control, and probably contributes heavily to the technical stutters.
For example, I don't need a movie of my guys walking off the ship after every mission. I don't need movies every time I fly somewhere or basically do anything in the game, or a minimovie whenever I run in to a group of enemies in the game that, oh by the way, stutters for 3-5 seconds before starting. It drags the game out tenfold, and makes it feel so slow and clunky.
The overworld game is one of the few improvements, with a change to the old formula that is fun enough. There does seem to be a lot going on all the time, and needless obtuseness in the system, but overall it works well.
It's not bad, but the game really falls apart in the tactical battles. First of all, who thought it would be a good idea to put a time limit on everything?  The gameplay is just as punishing as ever, with a misstep leading to glimpsed enemies getting a free move to take shots and head to cover when you get in their sight radius. However, now there are turn limits on the majority of the missions. I have 12 turns to complete a task, and I need to move ahead to do it, but since I can't be as cautious as I'd like, it ends up being very frustrating.
The almight Random Number Generator and computer enemy is just as insane as ever, with 85%+ shots missing on a consistent basis, and enemies shooting me through walls with no line of sight. It is not so much challenging as soul crushing to try and play the game.
"Oh but what about the new ability to ambush? What about the great mod support? What about the customizable characters? What about the new classes and the one with a SWORD?!"
Yea, that stuff is cool, but the game takes forever to load, stutters, rushes you in missions, and is generally not fun or well balanced. Maybe one day someone will make a mod to make the game fun, but that is probably some time off. Don't by it until someone makes a mod to make the game less of a pile of crap.

Where to start with this...
Short Version
The Pros
- Engaging gameplay
- Beautiful scenery and soundtrack
- Tons of replayability
- Varied PVP With both strangers and friends.
- Co-op with strangers and friends, to get past those pesky dogs
- Memes that may or may not give conniptions
Cons
- Connectivity may sometimes be an issue when fighting strangers
- Requires patience and determination, not for the easily angered.
- Difficulty may be a turnoff for people who enjoy more casually toned games
- Those people who use a greatshield with great magic weapon in pvp
(Skip to bottom for roundup)
Long Version
As someone who has enjoyed the Dark Souls series thoroughly, I feel that Dark Souls 3 has fixed many control issues apparent in previous installments. The combat feels active, rewarding proper timing and enemy management, whilst punishing rushing into battle without a plan and carelessly swinging your blade around. Enemies are placed strategically across the levels, neatly tieing in with their surroundings and backstories. It feels like all of them have a reason to be where they are. Surroundings are interesting, and tell their own little part of the story.
The bosses are their own kind of combat. Whilst in the levels themself the challenge is in enemy management, and level exploration. The bosses give you a one on one (usually) death battle, where careful dodging and reading your enemy's movement is key to surviving the encounter. They are larger, stronger and faster then any other enemy in the game, and are not to be taken lightly. Defeating these formidable foes is quite the challenge, and also very satisfying.
About the story: you will have to look for it. Although DS3 doesnt hide its story as much as the previous titles, Item descriptions, surroundings and NPC dialogue are essential to finding out what exactly is going on in lothric. Finding all these tidbits of lore makes it exciting to find new weapons and/or items, aside from their obvious use.
The singleplayer aspect is fun enough on its own, but the multiplayer aspect makes it whole. being able to summon both strangers and friends to aid you in your journey makes each journey different. Naturally, recieving more aid makes the enemies tougher, along with other risks, like multiple invaders. the arena is always full with people at almost any level, providing unlimited entertainment as players duke it out 1 on 1, or in teams.
All in all, its a experience that changes from person to person. with bountiful amounts of weapons to choose from, and more armor than one sane person could collect. theres endless combinations of character builds at your disposal. knights, mages,  pyromancers and clerics, and combinations in all forms.
Ive ran through the entire game over 60 times at this point, finding new secrets and tidbits of story still. and with PVP being one of the most entertaining things i have ever come across. The enemies, story, soundtrack and scenery are a joy to return to whenever i launch this game.

If I could give this game a rating, I would give it a 3.5/5. Edit: post mods and dlc I would say 4/5.
I really enjoyed playing this game through once. If you liked XCOM: Enemy Unknown, then you will like this game, because in my mind it is simply a better version of that game with many cool and new features.
My issues with the game:
1) There is a weird problem a lot of people seem to be having were on the first retaliation mission with Chryssalids reloading the game will cause crashes, the easy fix and what I did is to play this mission through without reloading, after this I never had the problem again, still pretty annoying for save scum like me.
2) I am struggling to find a lot of replay value in this game, playing through once was amazing, but there aren't any second wave options so far as I can see, the only thing you can do is ironman. This means that I basically bought a $60 campaign, a pretty great one but still they could have left this feature in and made replay far more compelling. Edit: I still wish they would add second wave options, but the mods and dlc both gave pretty good replay value later in time.
3) The bleed out mechanic is borderline idiotic to me. In about 15-20 deaths, I have never had one of my soldiers bleed out instead of dying out right, even though I have had a few majors and one colonel die. After looking it up the best explanation I have found is that the bleed out chance is will-100 as a % unless you upgrade it at which point it becomes will-50 as a %. So chance is actually fairly low which seems silly.
4) I got the day 1 edition which came with some sort of personalization pack, I don't remember the name. What I do know is that it was really stupid. If you are looking to buy the game I wouldn't spend more money for the day 1 edition.
All of that said I love this game and don't regret the purchase at all. The above problems were easy for me to overlook. If you like the XCOM series I recommend buying this game. I simply wanted to write the problems I see with the game so that others can make the decision about whether or not they are deal breakers.

We've had platformers, dungeon crawlers, exploration games, spaceship fighting games, farming games and puzzle games for a long time, sandbox games are newer for most of us but they're not exactly rare.
What is incredibly rare is not only to find a game that puts all those things together (in fact, that's what most games seem to be trying at this point), but to find one that actually pulls it off with new twists and yet remains intuituve, accessable, engaging and fresh.
Of course Starbound is only part of its way through the journey of becoming *a game* as opposed to part of a game released in order to attract funding through preorders, but every step of the way the studio is focussing on getting the basic game right. The result is something very stable and enjoyable even before it's *finsihed*, and an open-ness to modding and UGC that will ensure that the game never gets stale.
For $15, Starbound is a real bargain. It may not suit everyone's taste just yet, but like a fine wine or cheese or all too obvious cliche it will only get better with time. If you want a game about digging and building and flyign a spaceship you can have that immediately; you might have to wait a while if you're after the story, town management, RPG and exploration components to be fleshed out but they're already visible with a firm foundation and new content on the horizon.

Most fun I've had in a very long time with a game. The premise is simple and the execution is very well done especially for an Early Access Game (which i normally don't buy because of previous experience). You are a slice of bread and you want to become toast, not any old toast because thats just plain boring. You want to become a delicious edible piece of toast covered in butter and jelly and probley other items i havn't found or they havn't added.
You control the four corners of the slice and can move, break, and climb all over things. The floor is bad, oh and you have a limited amount of grip which is used whenever a corner grabs on to something, which is pretty necessary 99% of the time. When you add butter to one side that side becomes very easy to slide around on, when you add jam to one side that side becomes very hard to slide on. Now you can slow slide down walls if you want, or quickly slide of a ledge. Maybe knocking over a chair to reach a new height.
In the end you have a puzzle game on top of this scrumptious physics struggle, so beyond learning how to walk again like a baby you need to find an object to toast yourself, the first level of course is a Toaster but it changes every level. If this wasnt enough for a -10$ game they have a plot based around a struggling ex buisness owner who now works as a low level city worker for a group he blames for the failing of his buisness.
For me it's a must own.

Immensely fun but immensely glitchy. Any game where I have the combat mission music stuck in my head for 8 hrs at work is a winner in my book, and the only thing keeping me from playing more and more is that I DO have to sleep before work. I tried my best to not save-scum when I first started playing, but I eventually ran into a number of total BS glitches such as
-having a mob pop from one place to another without teleport/burrowing. This happened with a Elite MEC where instead of running to a cliff and jumping up to trigger overwatch, it just popped into its destination.
-having a soldier seemingly run vertically down to the floor THROUGH the ceiling, ragdoll for several seconds (almost an entire minute) then pop back up to the roof.
-mobs vanishing in plain sight. I spotted a turret on the roof and maneuvered to fire, but I could no longer see it even though I had obvious line of sight. I thought it might've gotten destroyed because that part of the roof had collapsed, but then it popped up again next turn.
-mobs not being visible by some squad members but still targetable. I had a sectopod I couldn't target with a heavy hiding behind a fence a few feet away but my snipers in a tower far behind could target it via squadsight.
-mobs taking extra actions. A lancer aggroed on a soldier, ran up to hima nd hit him with the sword, and it missed. Should've been the end of his move. Instead he runs over to ANOTHER soldier and tries attacking again, essentially 5 moves. This was after my turn had ended and enemy activity began.
-missing/inactive models. Sometimes a enemy troopship will drop off mobs and I'll see one mob standing there just stationary in a 'modeling' pose, but it won't immediately show up to target. Then I'll move a troop and boom, mob's there. Also whenever I pick up a target lik ea VIP or a soldier, the carrying soldier will go through the animation but you'll see nothing.
-classical XCOM BS shots. Having a soldier target a mob through a wall, through line of sight behind a pillar, aim at the camera and shoot BACKWARDS behind them.
-doors don't work completely. Instead of opening or being kicked down, mobs will just run through the doors. I've even had mobs aggro through sealed doors/walls even though my soldiers don't have line of sight of them immediately.
The game seems badly optimized too. I'm not sure if its because I'm still running win7 or what, but I had my computer custom-made to handle high-graphics games on max settings, and when I tried to put XCOM on ultra, my framerate was like .01fps. I had to go back to the default medium setting.
None of this, however, is keeping me from enjoying the game. I have to force myself to stop playing so I can eat/sleep/work, and each mission always has me wanting more. I do get very annoyed when you're scanning and you get a priority council mission 1 day from finishing a relay, and I've noticed the world map seems to stick sometimes, like not letting you switch to missions and yanking your cursor back to the Avatar counter. It frustrates me too that dialogue gets cut off. In XCOM EU, npcs would continue talking even if you switched locations until they finished saying their particular segment, but in X2 I missed several lines of interesting dialogue because the npc will start talking just as I swap over to another room then the sentence gets cut off.
It's definately worth buying regardless, just needs additional polishing. Hopefully a optimization or tweak patch somewhere down the line.

After 200 hours and many failed campaign runs, I still find myself returning frequently. It's a mainstay in my library, definitely worth a purchase if you like turn-based strategic alien slaying.
However, performance is still pretty crap (GTX 970, Quadcore 3.1 GHz, Windows 7) and there are some bugs that need to be ironed out. I cut the game slack because I am running with a few mods, and most of the bugs I encounter aren't game breaking. But they are annoying. Like when a character gets blasted with a laser and takes a solid 2 seconds of awkwardly looking around until he flys back from the impact. It's almost like they're on a movie set and they miss-timed their cue to flop over dead.
Also, the DLCs have been pretty unexceptional so far. From what I can tell, the DLCs for the last XCOM were way more substantial. If you're gonna buy the DLCs, wait for a sale and snag the season pass.
But if you can get past these gripes it is a solid game, and the mod scene should give the game a good shelf life and a lot of replayability.

Really amazing aesthetic. Somewhat tedious combat and map exploration aside, the game has a great early game. And a great mid-game. Then you get to the late-game and it's just... so much grinding, and there's no way around it (because you're gonna lose your high-level teams to unknown enemies or bosses) unless you study up on everything you do before you do it.
You end up in this strange situation where you maintain 2-3 whole teams, most of which are expendable and constantly getting replaced as their teams are annihilated while either farming gold for you (ugh) or exploring new areas. And you can't send in your high-level guys to farm gold for yourself because they're all too high level to be bothered to enter the easier areas where the gold is at... which the lowbies you hire to do that for you also become until you kill them off... and mercy on you if you DO lose your main team, because that♥♥♥♥♥♥sets you back HOURS during which you have nothing to do but simply - you guessed it - grind easy content to level up your new team so you can finally do the parts of the game that you actually enjoy.
And then before you know it, you realize you're spending more time grinding than you do enjoying the game.
And then you quit.
But the time it takes you to get to that point is still enough that in my opinion it's worth the price tag.
Really wish they would do something to not make the game so grindy, though...

I made the mistake of buying into the pre-release hype that surrounded this game (along with alowing my past experiences with the fallout franchise influence my decision to buy).  Overall it is not a bad game, but it is not a particularly good or innovative game either.  It has turned out to be a very average game.  It feels like a derviative work of Fallout 3 minus the good dlc.  Even the dlc from fallout NV were superior to those of this game, they were expansive, story-driven, and atmosphereic.  Far harbor was alright, but not particulalry memorable.  Who can recall the Pitt, the big MT, or the final battle with Ulysses?  I suppose I expected more from this title, which resulted in this let down.
Edit:
The concept of creation club is here to stay, this is their second attempt to monetize mods.  The real determination with how this will go will be made when the next major title (the next elder scrolls or whatever) is released.  Right now it is nebulous because the creation kit genie is out of the bottle for all of the currently released titles.   I am going to be watching what Bethesda does with the future games, that is where they will show their true intent.
Personally, I am not going to purchase any of their future titles until I see how they plan to proceed with this system.  What will the dividing line be for what season passes will apply to?  Would the gun runners arsenal from NV now be considered a minor mod and not included in a season pass?
My initial knee-jerk reaction to this was negative, but I have walked that back somewhat to being apprehensive.  I do not believe that all the protest in the world will cause Bethesda to abandon this new creation club, and we will have to wait for the next major title release to see what direction they are taking this concept.

The last time I had this much fun and enjoyment with a game prior to its actual release, was Minecraft years ago, and I think the correlation in concentration of fun and innovative ideas to be meaningful.
I was a big fan of Terraria, and put many hours into it both here and on Xbox Live as well, so the obvious visual similarities and familiar control scheme made Starbound very accessible to me right from the get-go. That said, the game isn't at all difficult to play, so a new player shouldn't have much (if any) trouble picking up the keyboard-and-mouse schema for movement and mining. I see a lot of discussion on here where people are either insisting that Starbound is a completely different game from Terraria (which is untrue of any game with an essentially identical control scheme and visual style, regardless of genre, UI, or crafting mechanic tweak differences), or else insisting just as loudly that it's the exact same game and, as a copy, not worth purchasing if you already own Terraria (which is equally untrue, since if it were Dark Souls would never have sold a single copy to anyone who owned Demon's Souls, when in fact players who owned Demon's Souls were among the most excited and anticipatory to grab a copy of Dark Souls when it came out).
The truth is that neither comparison, be it for or against, is accurate or even meaningful
. By which I mean, there
a lot of basic similarities; they just don't mean as much as one might assume they would. Sometimes more of a good thing is better, and after my extensive experience with Terraria I find that pertinent here. After crafting the best weapons and armors in my Terraria world, building a big base, and defeating all the bosses alongside my sister in multiplayer, Terraria's appeal started to fade, as the game was about as complete as it could get with its current arc of content, and my only option to continue became to start over entirely. Starbound's contrasting ability to warp to your ship and jet off to a new planet or moon from amongst hundreds of thousands of generated choices at any time addresses this content ceiling limitation beautifully. By folding the limit break into the game's very design and tonal feel (the joy and freedom of space exploration!), the total effect is one of
, both of game concept and content. Moreover, the crafting system is indeed different both in design and execution, being less linear-progression-by-material and more sprawling could-you-ever-find-them-all in its variations, down to the idea that each different species you can play as has a unique list of cooking recipes they begin with reflecting their species' unique tastes.
My goals and priorities shifted: I was less likely to feel like building a huge base early on, focusing instead on function over form. I just needed a safe place to sleep on each moon I visited to explore, not a massive tree fortress or vast underground complex. Only later, once I had a solid battery of resources and equipment, did I suddenly realize I both could and wanted to focus on designating a "home" planet and location from which to serve as a larger base of operations for future explorations to originate from. That's added depth right there, from the start: I had to
the right, the means, to even feel like putting down anything beyond the shallowest of roots was a wise or materially justified notion. And on top of that, TWICE I thought I'd found the perfect planet for that base (verdant, green, beautiful!), only to discover that the wildlife on one was more aggressive and troublesome than I wanted to deal with on the regular, and on the other had already begun substantial construction when it began to rain
on me and I had to recognize that I maybe didn't want to live permanently on a planet that had constantly-forming pools of poisonous and damaging liquid everywhere. When I did finally build that base, it felt like I'd earned it. It was more exciting and rewarding building that complex, for me personally, than breaking ground or adding onto my massive underground hotel of NPCs in Terraria had ever been.
So yes. This is not a clone of Terraria, it is merely
to Terraria players, and I find this game to be a true
to that gem of a couple of years ago: More. Better. Broader.
And on top of all of that,
at the time of this writing, which means new massive additions of content and refinements of play concepts as time goes on! I am very excited to see what this sprout grows into as time goes on.
Fair warning to new Early Access purchasers, though! Many of the game's version updates enact "universe-wipes" out of necessity, erasing all established progress, characters, and any and all build progress on all worlds. This is understandably necesary to incorporate new game mechanics and content, but can be jarring to the player who eagerly invested hours without knowing that storm lay on the horizon. One of the necessary evils of Early Access! You've been warned.
Now go explore that galaxy.

The game is a great new take on the XCOM series, and I enjoyed every minute of playing it. The story (in my opinion) was very engaging, and the game drew me back in every time. I wholeheartedly recommend this game. However, with every game there are some cons.
STOP READING NOW IF YOU DONT WANT THE STORY SPOILED!:
Many animations throughout the game are dragged out to a point where its ajust frusterating to have them there. For instance, when you find a patrol of aliens, the game will freeze on the patrol for a good 10-15 seconds before making any other actions. Another example is when you kill an alien, it freezes on the dead body for a few seconds before letting you play again. However, none of these pauses are bad enough to make you want to stop playing, just slightely frustrating. As well, if it really bothers you as much as it did me, you can install the "Stop Wasting My Time Mod" which will get rid of these pauses and speed certain aspects of the game up. These next few opinions are coming from a guy who played the old game extensively. The game seemed to be lacking something the whole experience and I found out what it was. Enemy Unknown had you doing almost boss fights throughout the game, which got you progressing in the story. XCOM 2 just doesnt have that, and it feels empty. Also, the old game had tons of options in the beggining that allowed for so much more replay value, however in this game, there are no options but Ironman, which doesnt allow you to load old saves, and makes all your moves permanent. However you can install the "Long War Mod" to get all the options back. Lastly, the old game made you have soldiers with psionic powers to finish the game, however, in XCOM 2, psionic soldiers are nothing but an advantage in combat. A special psionic soldier is given to you from the beggining of the last level, making your other ones nothing special from the rest of your squad. The ending was much less satisfying than the other game as well, and it seemed way easier. It did set up for XCOM 3 though which was cool.
Conclusion:
A really fun game that if you are new to the XCOM franchise you will definitly enjoy. However, if you have played Enemy Unknown and Enemy Within, you will notice aspects of the game that were in the old games, that you wish would be there. Overall, I would give it a 8/10

Harder than Dark Souls ++++
Honestly, though, this game is hard to master. In fact, it's designed to be hard to master, just like its predecessor 'Surgeon Simulator'. The difference this time, though, is that you yourself are not in a fixed position. Also you are a slice of bread. This lends to some awkward hand-eye mishaps and equally awkward doughy propulsion. Eventually you get the hang of it and start cartwheeling and breadboarding all over the place. Once you figure out basic movement, you can conquor any environment. I have come to write this review shortly after beating all of the available campaign, and I plan on trying to get higher scores than straight Fs and Ds.
The health system of the game, I think, is actually great. It is 'Edibility', how appealing your spongy self looks. Seeming loosely based on the Five Second Rule, you can't spend too long touching the floor/rolling in ants or hair. This subsequently results in many restarts from mishaps in your yeastly yaw, which is also hilarious to watch. Who doesn't like watching a piece of bread fail at a highly unlikely adventure by spinning out of control across the room?
There's more than one way to slice a loaf. You can navigate through the room the way you decide, be it by skateboard, wall climbing, or by the 'easiest' path. With many different ways you can go, I am Bread is like an open world game. Just... open room. Swing from cabinets, smash the plates, hang off ledges: there's a whole bathroom of adventure out there!
With hope of more amazing content (and secrets), this game is worth every dime (and possibly penny). Definitely a must if on sale. It's truly a game, and not just a 'flop til you pop' gimmick.
This game is a crusted challenge. You will not succeed often. Persevere. One day you will be toast.

You know about the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ dialogue system, the utter lack of care put towards the main story, how you get endgame gear in the 3rd mission, etc. etc.
You probably also know how Bethesda's Fallout games don't really adhere to the original series, and arguable never tried to. They're great games in terms of open-world exporation and some light survival elements, but terrible for role-playing.
Let me use one side story to describe my feelings toward Fallout 4.
I came across an elementary school with a basement door blocked by a gate. I got past the gate and found a vault: Vault 83. I go down inside and am greeted by people who look like half vault-dweller, half soldier. They're immediately hostile and I mow them all down as they come. The vault is way more interesting than the one you're frozen in; it's actually been lived in, and early on you'll find some very strange places like a playground and a fake small town inside. The real meat of this side story is in the notes and journals you find, not only the information you recieve but the order in which you find it. You discover the rules of the vault (no one over 17 is allowed), and get some vague ideas of what they do to the kids who grow up. Later on you find out about a group of kids who plotted to break the system in place, and after they overthrow the overseer they hung around and ultimately just went full brute. It's tragic, disturbing, and super though-provoking.
I stopped playing shortly after I completed this vault, becuase I realized that this would probably be the high point of the game for me. See, despite all the awesome environmental storytelling, the full potential of this story was undercut by Fallout 4's core systems. Big suprise, you can't interact with any living thing inside aside from killing it. After knowing the full story, it doesn't make sense that they would all just be basically feral; it would have really opened up the story of this place if you could talk to even one person (maybe the sheriff-looking guy in the fake town), but no. Also, once you go full circle in the vault (i.e. fight through everyone, explore the place, find a shortcut back to the entrance), that's it. You're done. Vault 83 and it's remains are now completely irrelevant to the player and the player-character. I stepped out, was about to start another mission, and then just closed the game.
It's clear that some of the people working on this game really had a passion for what they were doing. Hidden in the burning pile of trash that is the main story, some of the little vignettes and random locations are really strong. And on top of all that, the act of just wandering around is still fun. I can't play it anymore because none of it distracts from the fact that this game is clearly not building up to anything substantial. It's a content-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, nothing more.

This is the best stratagy game i've played in a long time. I never write reviews but the critism this game is recieving game play-wise is unwarrented. Rather than review I'd like to address complaints and convince those who got frustraited to give the game another shot.
The performance issues are warrented, and i don't blame people for being upset.  I had some weird things happen, and the game crashed 3x during my 60hr playtime.  I wonder if operating system plays a role. I have Windows 7,  i have an average card but have lots of gpu and ram memory.  I wonder if MS W10 is causing issues.  i havent seen anyone post if this plays a role. Still For the most part i've not had many problems.
Gameplay: I'm not the best Xcom 1 player, but still i started Xcom 2 on vetern the first game, suffice to say it was very frustraiting.  I restarted it on the easiest difficulty and its much much better. There is no shame in playing on this lvl, and saving and reloading when things got out of hand. Remember its Xcom its suppose to be hard, u need to learn how to play the game, once u figure things out and "get the game" its awesome.  You can always play through it again later on iron man.  As far as the timers they make sense "in the context of the game", be sure to know the mission parameters and plan accordingly.  If you go in every mission guns blazing every mission you will get into trouble.  Use stealth and ambush, save constantly, flank your opponent, get the heck out of there (u need not kill everything on certain missions) use the tools the game gives you, once you learn the game, you won't need to as much.  Also if the ai is cheap reload, if u make a big mistake reload. Keep trying till u beat the mission. I have never had an expired timer yet, the game has a learning curve.  Firaxis made a very old school difficuly type game, back in the early 90's it took weeks to figure out how to play a stratagy game.  If you give up on this game your just cheating yourself.  I'm playing on veteren and am holding my own so far. If i can do it, most of u can, just give it another chance!

Harder than Dark Souls ++++
Honestly, though, this game is hard to master. In fact, it's designed to be hard to master, just like its predecessor 'Surgeon Simulator'. The difference this time, though, is that you yourself are not in a fixed position. Also you are a slice of bread. This lends to some awkward hand-eye mishaps and equally awkward doughy propulsion. Eventually you get the hang of it and start cartwheeling and breadboarding all over the place. Once you figure out basic movement, you can conquor any environment. I have come to write this review shortly after beating all of the available campaign, and I plan on trying to get higher scores than straight Fs and Ds.
The health system of the game, I think, is actually great. It is 'Edibility', how appealing your spongy self looks. Seeming loosely based on the Five Second Rule, you can't spend too long touching the floor/rolling in ants or hair. This subsequently results in many restarts from mishaps in your yeastly yaw, which is also hilarious to watch. Who doesn't like watching a piece of bread fail at a highly unlikely adventure by spinning out of control across the room?
There's more than one way to slice a loaf. You can navigate through the room the way you decide, be it by skateboard, wall climbing, or by the 'easiest' path. With many different ways you can go, I am Bread is like an open world game. Just... open room. Swing from cabinets, smash the plates, hang off ledges: there's a whole bathroom of adventure out there!
With hope of more amazing content (and secrets), this game is worth every dime (and possibly penny). Definitely a must if on sale. It's truly a game, and not just a 'flop til you pop' gimmick.

Immensely fun but immensely glitchy. Any game where I have the combat mission music stuck in my head for 8 hrs at work is a winner in my book, and the only thing keeping me from playing more and more is that I DO have to sleep before work. I tried my best to not save-scum when I first started playing, but I eventually ran into a number of total BS glitches such as
-having a mob pop from one place to another without teleport/burrowing. This happened with a Elite MEC where instead of running to a cliff and jumping up to trigger overwatch, it just popped into its destination.
-having a soldier seemingly run vertically down to the floor THROUGH the ceiling, ragdoll for several seconds (almost an entire minute) then pop back up to the roof.
-mobs vanishing in plain sight. I spotted a turret on the roof and maneuvered to fire, but I could no longer see it even though I had obvious line of sight. I thought it might've gotten destroyed because that part of the roof had collapsed, but then it popped up again next turn.
-mobs not being visible by some squad members but still targetable. I had a sectopod I couldn't target with a heavy hiding behind a fence a few feet away but my snipers in a tower far behind could target it via squadsight.
-mobs taking extra actions. A lancer aggroed on a soldier, ran up to hima nd hit him with the sword, and it missed. Should've been the end of his move. Instead he runs over to ANOTHER soldier and tries attacking again, essentially 5 moves. This was after my turn had ended and enemy activity began.
-missing/inactive models. Sometimes a enemy troopship will drop off mobs and I'll see one mob standing there just stationary in a 'modeling' pose, but it won't immediately show up to target. Then I'll move a troop and boom, mob's there. Also whenever I pick up a target lik ea VIP or a soldier, the carrying soldier will go through the animation but you'll see nothing.
-classical XCOM BS shots. Having a soldier target a mob through a wall, through line of sight behind a pillar, aim at the camera and shoot BACKWARDS behind them.
-doors don't work completely. Instead of opening or being kicked down, mobs will just run through the doors. I've even had mobs aggro through sealed doors/walls even though my soldiers don't have line of sight of them immediately.
The game seems badly optimized too. I'm not sure if its because I'm still running win7 or what, but I had my computer custom-made to handle high-graphics games on max settings, and when I tried to put XCOM on ultra, my framerate was like .01fps. I had to go back to the default medium setting.
None of this, however, is keeping me from enjoying the game. I have to force myself to stop playing so I can eat/sleep/work, and each mission always has me wanting more. I do get very annoyed when you're scanning and you get a priority council mission 1 day from finishing a relay, and I've noticed the world map seems to stick sometimes, like not letting you switch to missions and yanking your cursor back to the Avatar counter. It frustrates me too that dialogue gets cut off. In XCOM EU, npcs would continue talking even if you switched locations until they finished saying their particular segment, but in X2 I missed several lines of interesting dialogue because the npc will start talking just as I swap over to another room then the sentence gets cut off.
It's definately worth buying regardless, just needs additional polishing. Hopefully a optimization or tweak patch somewhere down the line.

I’m awful at writing methodical, comprehensive reviews, so I’ll stick to bullet points.
Flawless. The gritty comic book style creates for an intense and immersive atmosphere befitting of lovecraft's literary style.
Hard to learn, harder to master. The game’s mechanics are complex and not always well explained. This can be frustrating at times, particularly when your band of heroes is steamrolled by a boss you’ve never encountered, simply because you didn’t know what to expect. I recommend playing the game for a few hours, beating a few bosses, then skimming the wiki so you can better understand the in-depth mechanics of the game’s RNG. Nonetheless, its amazingly fun and satisfying.
Perfect. Stuart Chatwood did an amazing job on the soundtrack. The music is also well implemented with the game mechanic of light, making for some intense battles where you feel like a true badass.
There’s only one voice actor, Wayne June, and yet his performance easily lends to 50% of Darkest Dungeon’s enjoyability. His succulent voice invades my ears like some obscure lovecraftian alien lifeform.
While I love June’s lines and delivery, my one complaint with the entire game is that around the end of my first playthrough, I found myself tired of the repetitive lines from the characters and Ancestor. One can only hear the “Remind yourself…” line so many times before it loses its majesty.
I absolutely love The Darkest Dungeon. It was worth every penny and more. It even got me interested in Lovecraft’s stories. Given the new DLC coming in early 2017, I can’t see any better time to pick up Darkest Dungeon. Is rly gud.

Fallen Guardians of the land, beasts of an unspeakable nature, and undead abominations await you in Lothric, where the massive adventure that is Dark Souls III takes place. You are one of the unkinded, awakened from your eternal slumber to link the fire and preserve the light from the coming age of darkness through sacrifice and toil, where all others have failed. The task ahead of you: to find the four Lords of Cinder, those who were mighty enough to link the eternal flame, and return them to their towering thrones, through the only way which they can understand: violence. These four lords reside in lairs woven throughout your adventures, in such breathtaking landscapes as massive regal throne room of the Twin Princes, or the chamber of the Abyss Watchers, filled with corpses of the fallen. In Dark Souls III if you see a location off in the background then chances are you’ll be going there at some point during your quest. Not only do the locations get increasingly captivating as the game progresses, the enemies do as well, becoming more and more interesting and challenging as you near the end of your great journey. Exploring Lothric is a joy like no other, but what sets Dark Souls III out as a true gem among other such Role Playing Games is that not only will the world fill you with joy to explore, but in many cases will also fill you with terror.
In Dark Souls III you can count the amount of beings that don’t want you dead on one hand, ensuring that your quest will not be as easy as you may have thought. Enemies in Dark Souls III can be likened to puzzle pieces, each with their own backstory and every single one of them connected. Dark Souls III not only builds an exemplary game, but an enthralling world behind it just as well, absolutely no easy feat. There is no main storyline you’re following other than the quest to return the four lords of cinder to their thrones, instead Dark Souls opts to give even the most miniscule part of their world a backstory and a place in the universe as a whole. The best way that I can describe this is that Fromsoft seems to have designed every enemy in the game as if they were a boss, not in difficulty, but in the amount of work and story standing behind them. Dark Souls III has also managed a level of environmental design that few others have ever come near, rarely can a game balance the looks of an area, with how that area flows and connects with the rest of the game. Dark Souls III’s areas are filled with nooks and crannies brimming with goodies to be snatched up and put to use, many of which are so secret you won’t notice, or know how to get to them, on your first playthrough. The sheer amount of secret or hidden items and areas that Dark Souls III has is mind-boggling. Sets of armor which you have to do a hidden questline to obtain, zones and bosses that you can easily miss, all of these await throughout the perilous walks of Lothric. There’s this indescribable feeling of both satisfaction and glee you get after noticing a secret alcove or nab that out of reach piece of armor that encourages even further exploration. A critical part of every environment, one often ignored or unnoticed, is how everything in it sounds. Dark Souls III has some exemplary sound effects that enhance both the gameplay and the whole experience both inside and outside of battle. Not only are the sound effects definitely worthy of high praise, the same can be said for the music. In the more sinister areas, the music helps build tension, while in frantic boss battles it helps to keep the adrenaline flowing and ends up as one of the most memorable parts of the fight. There aren’t really a whole lot of games with a soundtrack so good I would pay money to have it, Hotline Miami and Payday 2 being notable examples, however I find myself adding Dark Souls III to that list as well. The soundtrack doesn’t just make the fighting and the ambience better, it adds to the characters, the bosses, in ways that aren’t tangible or really there. This sounds like I’m insane, a charge to which I plead the fifth, but just hearing a bosses soundtrack you’ll feel as if you know them, and in some cases you may even regret putting them down. Music is a part of many games, but in Dark Souls III, in Lothric, it’s not a part of the game, it’s a part of a living, breathing world.
Now after all of that talking about the environments, music, and how Dark Souls III feels you may be wondering, isn’t this a game? Shouldn’t there be gameplay? There most definitely is. Dark Souls III has some of the most fluid combat I’ve ever seen in a souls game, making it enjoyable to play, not just enjoyable to walk through. The combat hasn’t changed much from previous souls games, with some notable exceptions, but that absolutely does not mean it’s any easier to master, this is Dark Souls after all. A major change from the other souls games is that in Dark Souls III you now have a mana bar for casting pyromancies, spells, and miracles, forcing you to split your total estus flasks into health flasks and mana flasks. You choose how many estus flasks you want to be mana flasks and how many you want to be health flasks, so you aren’t being forced to either use spells or hold on to useless estus. The biggest change though is the combat: combat in Dark Souls III takes heavy inspiration from Bloodborne and is significantly faster paced any other souls game. Dodging costs less stamina, the enemies are significantly more aggressive, and as a general rule everything seems to move much faster than previous games. This is a welcome change and makes the combat flow a lot better and just generally more fluid, helping to make the game seem more fair. There’s also the PvP to consider, though I won’t talk much about this because that just isn’t my thing, so I didn’t play much of it. Player versus player combat in Dark Souls III from what I can tell is just about the same as it’s always been, however the cooperative experience has been massively improved. They got rid of the dysfunctional soul rating system from Dark Souls II, now you can be summoned just about anywhere and by just about anyone, though you can regulate this by creating a password that your partner needs to match in order to connect. With such options you now have the ability to actually control your co-op experience, rather than using the needlessly complex systems forced upon you in the previous game. That seems to be a big theme with Dark Souls III: controlling everything. You control your co-op experience, you control the battlefield with the new and improved combat, and you control the power to link the flame. All you have to do, is find it.
Dark Souls III is a not just a game, but an experience that pulls you in like a mimic and won’t ever let go.

The last time I had this much fun and enjoyment with a game prior to its actual release, was Minecraft years ago, and I think the correlation in concentration of fun and innovative ideas to be meaningful.
I was a big fan of Terraria, and put many hours into it both here and on Xbox Live as well, so the obvious visual similarities and familiar control scheme made Starbound very accessible to me right from the get-go. That said, the game isn't at all difficult to play, so a new player shouldn't have much (if any) trouble picking up the keyboard-and-mouse schema for movement and mining. I see a lot of discussion on here where people are either insisting that Starbound is a completely different game from Terraria (which is untrue of any game with an essentially identical control scheme and visual style, regardless of genre, UI, or crafting mechanic tweak differences), or else insisting just as loudly that it's the exact same game and, as a copy, not worth purchasing if you already own Terraria (which is equally untrue, since if it were Dark Souls would never have sold a single copy to anyone who owned Demon's Souls, when in fact players who owned Demon's Souls were among the most excited and anticipatory to grab a copy of Dark Souls when it came out).
The truth is that neither comparison, be it for or against, is accurate or even meaningful
. By which I mean, there
a lot of basic similarities; they just don't mean as much as one might assume they would. Sometimes more of a good thing is better, and after my extensive experience with Terraria I find that pertinent here. After crafting the best weapons and armors in my Terraria world, building a big base, and defeating all the bosses alongside my sister in multiplayer, Terraria's appeal started to fade, as the game was about as complete as it could get with its current arc of content, and my only option to continue became to start over entirely. Starbound's contrasting ability to warp to your ship and jet off to a new planet or moon from amongst hundreds of thousands of generated choices at any time addresses this content ceiling limitation beautifully. By folding the limit break into the game's very design and tonal feel (the joy and freedom of space exploration!), the total effect is one of
, both of game concept and content. Moreover, the crafting system is indeed different both in design and execution, being less linear-progression-by-material and more sprawling could-you-ever-find-them-all in its variations, down to the idea that each different species you can play as has a unique list of cooking recipes they begin with reflecting their species' unique tastes.
My goals and priorities shifted: I was less likely to feel like building a huge base early on, focusing instead on function over form. I just needed a safe place to sleep on each moon I visited to explore, not a massive tree fortress or vast underground complex. Only later, once I had a solid battery of resources and equipment, did I suddenly realize I both could and wanted to focus on designating a "home" planet and location from which to serve as a larger base of operations for future explorations to originate from. That's added depth right there, from the start: I had to
the right, the means, to even feel like putting down anything beyond the shallowest of roots was a wise or materially justified notion. And on top of that, TWICE I thought I'd found the perfect planet for that base (verdant, green, beautiful!), only to discover that the wildlife on one was more aggressive and troublesome than I wanted to deal with on the regular, and on the other had already begun substantial construction when it began to rain
on me and I had to recognize that I maybe didn't want to live permanently on a planet that had constantly-forming pools of poisonous and damaging liquid everywhere. When I did finally build that base, it felt like I'd earned it. It was more exciting and rewarding building that complex, for me personally, than breaking ground or adding onto my massive underground hotel of NPCs in Terraria had ever been.
So yes. This is not a clone of Terraria, it is merely
to Terraria players, and I find this game to be a true
to that gem of a couple of years ago: More. Better. Broader.
And on top of all of that,
at the time of this writing, which means new massive additions of content and refinements of play concepts as time goes on! I am very excited to see what this sprout grows into as time goes on.
Fair warning to new Early Access purchasers, though! Many of the game's version updates enact "universe-wipes" out of necessity, erasing all established progress, characters, and any and all build progress on all worlds. This is understandably necesary to incorporate new game mechanics and content, but can be jarring to the player who eagerly invested hours without knowing that storm lay on the horizon. One of the necessary evils of Early Access! You've been warned.
Now go explore that galaxy.

Spiral Knights is an amazing game that gets you hooked the moment you start playing it. I started playing Spiral Knights when a friend of my introduced me to it. At first I didn't actually know it was on steam until I found out about it.
(May contain spoilers to the game)
The game is very addicting so be warned if you don't want to spend most of your life playing it. The game has good graphics you can see everything cleary. In the game there are ranked missions and certain arcade areas. The ranked missions are basically the main story line of the game, to rank up you have to play these missions/quests.
At first you won't know but this game has items that are ranked 1 star - 5 star, the more starts there is in it the better the gear is and the more expensive it is.
During the ranked missions process you will eventually come to a mission that will ask you to buy certain star items and to make those you require ingredients and a recipe. If you don't have all the certain items in your inventory be warned there will be some grinding.
Grinding basically means your going to have to go and redo or play arcade games that are provided for you in the game to get money.
There are two types of currently in Spiral Knights crowns and energy. Crowns are ones you can easily get by doing missions. Energy requires you to buy with real money or (and this is a really good thing that most games don't do) you can trade crowns ingame and recieve 100 energy, but of course it won't be cheap.
In the game you can also recieve pets. These pets are called Battle Sprites. There are three types that everyone will eventually achieve (if you complete the ranked missions an follow the storyline) you can choose from 3, a Drakon (This is perfect if you like close combat), a Seraphynx (Basically a support pet) and a Maskeraith (If you like sneaking this is the one for you).
Overall there are many other features but this game that is entirely great, I enjoyed it a lot. I would recommend this to anyone who is into Muilt-player online games. The community is also amazing I've met manly nice people on this game.

I’m awful at writing methodical, comprehensive reviews, so I’ll stick to bullet points.
Flawless. The gritty comic book style creates for an intense and immersive atmosphere befitting of lovecraft's literary style.
Hard to learn, harder to master. The game’s mechanics are complex and not always well explained. This can be frustrating at times, particularly when your band of heroes is steamrolled by a boss you’ve never encountered, simply because you didn’t know what to expect. I recommend playing the game for a few hours, beating a few bosses, then skimming the wiki so you can better understand the in-depth mechanics of the game’s RNG. Nonetheless, its amazingly fun and satisfying.
Perfect. Stuart Chatwood did an amazing job on the soundtrack. The music is also well implemented with the game mechanic of light, making for some intense battles where you feel like a true badass.
There’s only one voice actor, Wayne June, and yet his performance easily lends to 50% of Darkest Dungeon’s enjoyability. His succulent voice invades my ears like some obscure lovecraftian alien lifeform.
While I love June’s lines and delivery, my one complaint with the entire game is that around the end of my first playthrough, I found myself tired of the repetitive lines from the characters and Ancestor. One can only hear the “Remind yourself…” line so many times before it loses its majesty.
I absolutely love The Darkest Dungeon. It was worth every penny and more. It even got me interested in Lovecraft’s stories. Given the new DLC coming in early 2017, I can’t see any better time to pick up Darkest Dungeon. Is rly gud.

You know about the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ dialogue system, the utter lack of care put towards the main story, how you get endgame gear in the 3rd mission, etc. etc.
You probably also know how Bethesda's Fallout games don't really adhere to the original series, and arguable never tried to. They're great games in terms of open-world exporation and some light survival elements, but terrible for role-playing.
Let me use one side story to describe my feelings toward Fallout 4.
I came across an elementary school with a basement door blocked by a gate. I got past the gate and found a vault: Vault 83. I go down inside and am greeted by people who look like half vault-dweller, half soldier. They're immediately hostile and I mow them all down as they come. The vault is way more interesting than the one you're frozen in; it's actually been lived in, and early on you'll find some very strange places like a playground and a fake small town inside. The real meat of this side story is in the notes and journals you find, not only the information you recieve but the order in which you find it. You discover the rules of the vault (no one over 17 is allowed), and get some vague ideas of what they do to the kids who grow up. Later on you find out about a group of kids who plotted to break the system in place, and after they overthrow the overseer they hung around and ultimately just went full brute. It's tragic, disturbing, and super though-provoking.
I stopped playing shortly after I completed this vault, becuase I realized that this would probably be the high point of the game for me. See, despite all the awesome environmental storytelling, the full potential of this story was undercut by Fallout 4's core systems. Big suprise, you can't interact with any living thing inside aside from killing it. After knowing the full story, it doesn't make sense that they would all just be basically feral; it would have really opened up the story of this place if you could talk to even one person (maybe the sheriff-looking guy in the fake town), but no. Also, once you go full circle in the vault (i.e. fight through everyone, explore the place, find a shortcut back to the entrance), that's it. You're done. Vault 83 and it's remains are now completely irrelevant to the player and the player-character. I stepped out, was about to start another mission, and then just closed the game.
It's clear that some of the people working on this game really had a passion for what they were doing. Hidden in the burning pile of trash that is the main story, some of the little vignettes and random locations are really strong. And on top of all that, the act of just wandering around is still fun. I can't play it anymore because none of it distracts from the fact that this game is clearly not building up to anything substantial. It's a content-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, nothing more.

This is the first Dark Souls game I played, and I absolutely love it. I play with a Steam controller and it works very well.
Needless to say, the game is very challenging and you're expected to die a lot, so be ready to learn from your mistakes often. There is hardly any guidance in the game, as the tutorial simply tells you the game's controls and then it throws you into the thick of it. Expect a steep learning curve that will test you before you even finish the tutorial.
There is co-op, but it exists atomically with random PvP encounters. So, you can get help from other players (random ones or specific ones that share your password), but not without making yourself vulnerable to invasion by enemy players. While sometimes annoying, it's hard to deny that this fits with the hardcore tone of the game.
The one thing I will complain about is about is the camera. The FoV is pretty narrow and you can't change it, so you don't always get to take in all of your surroundings. This sucks because the game has gorgeous levels.
Use the wiki to your advantage since hardly anything about the game's mechanics is explained in-game. Don't let frustration ruin the game for you, and you'll git gud in no time.
Overall, the game is fun. Im only giving it a negative review for my inability to report hackers.

If you want to play this for a Fallout experience, don't buy it. RPG mechanics were downgraded and have no depth. Skills are removed and replaced with useless perks.
DIalogue system doesn't have the same flowchart design as the other games. For example: In New Vegas you could talk with the leader of the NCR and ask him about how it was formed, why they wanted New Vegas, what they think of other factions, ECT. Here, however, you're limited to only four options for every conversation, which REALLY hurts the immersion you should be getting from an RPG.
Combat is fun, a much needed improvement from the other games, but they didn't pour enough effort into the other aspects of the game to actually make it feel like a world and not a shooting gallery. There's factions that have interesting premises but are left aside as one-off explanations are made for why you need to kill them and not want to join them.
The ending doesn't conclude anything, since the game doesn't actually conclude. The final cutscene is just a wrap-up of the main questline, and not the whole game. It devalues anything you did in the side-quests by doing this. Endings in Fallout 3 and New Vegas could take ten minutes to make sure everything you did will show a cause and effect on the world, while here it's just a simple "You finished, but there's still work to do."
Side quests can be interesting, but the lack of options and effects on the world remind you that these were just put in for flavor and not to make the Fallout universe shine.
What this game ends up doing is removing all of the essence of Fallout, and creating a cookie-cutter product that has nice graphics but no substance.

Fallen Guardians of the land, beasts of an unspeakable nature, and undead abominations await you in Lothric, where the massive adventure that is Dark Souls III takes place. You are one of the unkinded, awakened from your eternal slumber to link the fire and preserve the light from the coming age of darkness through sacrifice and toil, where all others have failed. The task ahead of you: to find the four Lords of Cinder, those who were mighty enough to link the eternal flame, and return them to their towering thrones, through the only way which they can understand: violence. These four lords reside in lairs woven throughout your adventures, in such breathtaking landscapes as massive regal throne room of the Twin Princes, or the chamber of the Abyss Watchers, filled with corpses of the fallen. In Dark Souls III if you see a location off in the background then chances are you’ll be going there at some point during your quest. Not only do the locations get increasingly captivating as the game progresses, the enemies do as well, becoming more and more interesting and challenging as you near the end of your great journey. Exploring Lothric is a joy like no other, but what sets Dark Souls III out as a true gem among other such Role Playing Games is that not only will the world fill you with joy to explore, but in many cases will also fill you with terror.
In Dark Souls III you can count the amount of beings that don’t want you dead on one hand, ensuring that your quest will not be as easy as you may have thought. Enemies in Dark Souls III can be likened to puzzle pieces, each with their own backstory and every single one of them connected. Dark Souls III not only builds an exemplary game, but an enthralling world behind it just as well, absolutely no easy feat. There is no main storyline you’re following other than the quest to return the four lords of cinder to their thrones, instead Dark Souls opts to give even the most miniscule part of their world a backstory and a place in the universe as a whole. The best way that I can describe this is that Fromsoft seems to have designed every enemy in the game as if they were a boss, not in difficulty, but in the amount of work and story standing behind them. Dark Souls III has also managed a level of environmental design that few others have ever come near, rarely can a game balance the looks of an area, with how that area flows and connects with the rest of the game. Dark Souls III’s areas are filled with nooks and crannies brimming with goodies to be snatched up and put to use, many of which are so secret you won’t notice, or know how to get to them, on your first playthrough. The sheer amount of secret or hidden items and areas that Dark Souls III has is mind-boggling. Sets of armor which you have to do a hidden questline to obtain, zones and bosses that you can easily miss, all of these await throughout the perilous walks of Lothric. There’s this indescribable feeling of both satisfaction and glee you get after noticing a secret alcove or nab that out of reach piece of armor that encourages even further exploration. A critical part of every environment, one often ignored or unnoticed, is how everything in it sounds. Dark Souls III has some exemplary sound effects that enhance both the gameplay and the whole experience both inside and outside of battle. Not only are the sound effects definitely worthy of high praise, the same can be said for the music. In the more sinister areas, the music helps build tension, while in frantic boss battles it helps to keep the adrenaline flowing and ends up as one of the most memorable parts of the fight. There aren’t really a whole lot of games with a soundtrack so good I would pay money to have it, Hotline Miami and Payday 2 being notable examples, however I find myself adding Dark Souls III to that list as well. The soundtrack doesn’t just make the fighting and the ambience better, it adds to the characters, the bosses, in ways that aren’t tangible or really there. This sounds like I’m insane, a charge to which I plead the fifth, but just hearing a bosses soundtrack you’ll feel as if you know them, and in some cases you may even regret putting them down. Music is a part of many games, but in Dark Souls III, in Lothric, it’s not a part of the game, it’s a part of a living, breathing world.
Now after all of that talking about the environments, music, and how Dark Souls III feels you may be wondering, isn’t this a game? Shouldn’t there be gameplay? There most definitely is. Dark Souls III has some of the most fluid combat I’ve ever seen in a souls game, making it enjoyable to play, not just enjoyable to walk through. The combat hasn’t changed much from previous souls games, with some notable exceptions, but that absolutely does not mean it’s any easier to master, this is Dark Souls after all. A major change from the other souls games is that in Dark Souls III you now have a mana bar for casting pyromancies, spells, and miracles, forcing you to split your total estus flasks into health flasks and mana flasks. You choose how many estus flasks you want to be mana flasks and how many you want to be health flasks, so you aren’t being forced to either use spells or hold on to useless estus. The biggest change though is the combat: combat in Dark Souls III takes heavy inspiration from Bloodborne and is significantly faster paced any other souls game. Dodging costs less stamina, the enemies are significantly more aggressive, and as a general rule everything seems to move much faster than previous games. This is a welcome change and makes the combat flow a lot better and just generally more fluid, helping to make the game seem more fair. There’s also the PvP to consider, though I won’t talk much about this because that just isn’t my thing, so I didn’t play much of it. Player versus player combat in Dark Souls III from what I can tell is just about the same as it’s always been, however the cooperative experience has been massively improved. They got rid of the dysfunctional soul rating system from Dark Souls II, now you can be summoned just about anywhere and by just about anyone, though you can regulate this by creating a password that your partner needs to match in order to connect. With such options you now have the ability to actually control your co-op experience, rather than using the needlessly complex systems forced upon you in the previous game. That seems to be a big theme with Dark Souls III: controlling everything. You control your co-op experience, you control the battlefield with the new and improved combat, and you control the power to link the flame. All you have to do, is find it.
Dark Souls III is a not just a game, but an experience that pulls you in like a mimic and won’t ever let go.

This is an incredibly hard game. It requires you to learn a lot about heros, enemies and items. But, the game mechanism is so well-designed that it is rewarding to do so.
When you play this game as a beginner, the game is so hard that it may make you think the game totally depends on randomness, but once you learn about the game and then if you carefully and sensibly make your plan, you will reduce the influence from the randomness quite effectively.
Despite its difficulty, it provides players a lot of means to get through tough situations in variuos ways. All of those means have advatages and disadvantages, so you need to think about how you want to combine them, based on your situation. Like when you want to collect a lot of gold in a single quest, you can take an Antiquaria, increase scouting chance to find a secret room or explore a dungeon with a low light level. Each of those comes with its unique risks that you need to add another strategic factor to compensate for. You keep applying strategies until you get satisfied.
I totally recommend this game to those who love a challenge and have a chunk of time to spend.

You may be cautious as first, being bread isn't easy, and it may seem easy to just rub yourself againt the butter or make out with the jam. . . but soon you will feel the call of the warm silvery embrace of your true calling.
Just remember to take your time at first, get used to your new quadrilateral form, flex your crusts, and soon you will begin to feel as if this was the body you were always ment to have.
This game is truely, the best thing since sliced bread.

i've played this game for about three years and it's got it's ups and downs. i don't think i'd recommend this to anyone without telling them first that it's hilariously forgettable and not as fun as it is to someone who's played a while.
it has some decent replay value, for a while. the community is okay, and i've met a lot of nice people.
but if you don't have friends to play this game with, it's definitely not worth it.
up until you hit knight elite it's plenty fun and quite an adventure. after that, it becomes a decent balance of having to grind for supplies and materials to make gear to move on. once you pass vanguard and all the missions after it, that's when it hits the downfall.
once you've cleared all your missions, and maybe operation warhammer, the only reasons to play is:
-for cosmetics. OOO and sega love their costume promotions. :T
-to get more gear, mostly to show off with. can round out your gear for PVP or for PVE if you want, though, which is what i've been doing.
-if you're in an active guild, really
-the events are decently fun until you get everything you want from them, at which point it's forgettable.
the game becomes one long "grind for materials to make more weapons so you can grind for materials to make more weapons/armor so you can...ect", with the occassional "grind for event tokens until you get an incredibly rare RNG drop/box prize or the small token item you want".
all in all, i forget this game exists for about a week or two, get on for a day or two unless someone invites me, and repeat this schedule. it has good music and graphics and an interesting plot, but it's more or less a teidious forgettable grind once you hit a certain point - and that point is honestly not that far into the game.
it's fun with friends to mess around with, though - i have more fun sitting in parties or arcade levels dead chatting with friends then i do actually playing the game. definitely worth it if you have a lot of free time and friends who want to play with you.

This is an incredibly hard game. It requires you to learn a lot about heros, enemies and items. But, the game mechanism is so well-designed that it is rewarding to do so.
When you play this game as a beginner, the game is so hard that it may make you think the game totally depends on randomness, but once you learn about the game and then if you carefully and sensibly make your plan, you will reduce the influence from the randomness quite effectively.
Despite its difficulty, it provides players a lot of means to get through tough situations in variuos ways. All of those means have advatages and disadvantages, so you need to think about how you want to combine them, based on your situation. Like when you want to collect a lot of gold in a single quest, you can take an Antiquaria, increase scouting chance to find a secret room or explore a dungeon with a low light level. Each of those comes with its unique risks that you need to add another strategic factor to compensate for. You keep applying strategies until you get satisfied.
I totally recommend this game to those who love a challenge and have a chunk of time to spend.
