Music:
===========
Great. Nothing special but it rarely ever felt off or repetitive.
===========
Planets:
===========
The visuals of each biome feel distinct but feature-wise the different biomes don't offer much unique from one another right now. Also, we can only "bookmark" one planet so finding other old planets can only be done by writing down the co-ordinates, seems counter-intuitive. Let us write an entry about the planets we've visited so we can remind ourselves what was unique about it and why we would want to visit it again.
Some events happening across multiple planets would be cool and would break up the tedium. Like chasing down some space pirates that flee when you destroy their base, going from planet to planet.
===========
Progression:
===========
In about 2-3 hours you can advance two ranks in equipments. Aside from the unique aesthetics of each rank, there's no other reason to ever go back. This is fairly common in games but what this means in gameplay is that soon after you get the equipment you'll be discarding it for the next thing, and that loop continues. While that avoids some grinding it could probably be handled in a more satisfying way.
The challenges for each sector are basically the same. Find best ore, craft boss-summon with ore, defeat boss, go to next area, repeat. What they have is a good start though.
===========
Combat:
===========
It needs to be more versatile. There's no good reason to use anything but the best hammers and swords thanks to their hit-range and DPS. There also needs to be a bunch more ranged weapons. But really the biggest issue is that later in the game everything boils down to this:
- Have the strongest available weapon? You'll one/two-hit 90% of enemies.
- Don't have the strongest available armor? You'll be one/two-hit by most enemies.
The bosses have one major flaw. 3 out of 4 of them can be trapped rather easily with any blocks and then they present no challenge while you whale on them behind safety. The irony being only the weakest boss can break terrain, which is a good idea to prevent a cheap fight.
Also, I ONCE randomly ran into a boss-like dinosaur-enemy on the surface. That was unexpected, fun, challenging, and it dropped a fancy weapon. Those kind of random encounters need to happen much more often than once in a 20-hour playthrough.
===========
Crafting:
===========
Good art for individual items. But there needs to be more useful items so we can do more beyond different aesthetics.
===========
Misc. Thoughts
===========
Allow us to do a lot more with our ship. Change the design if we have the right materials, or maybe add weapons/defenses and fight other ships.
The UI needs a lot of streamlining. It's functional but not straightforward. Example: We can't click and move the scrollbars in the crafting menus.
Since there is already some high-tech items in the game for player-convenience, add to that by allowing us to eventually make some radar or sensor so we know when we're getting close to important things like a chest or a certain kind of ore. It would make mining much more enjoyable.
Going really deep into a planet with no checkpoint is annoying. Allow us to set one, similar to the beds in Terraria.

I don't really write reviews, but I've made an exception for this game.
Now, I admit, I went into this expecting it to be very similar to the more recent "Simulator" style of game, such as Grass Simulator or Rock Simulator; i.e total crap. Considering that this is made by the people who created Surgeon Simulator, I shouldn't have worried. Like the game the restarted the Simlator genre (and, sadly, inadvertently caused it to spawn things I hesitate to call games), I Am Bread is a "QWOP" style of game, where it is purposefully dificult to control. It does this very well. Perhaps a little
well, but I'll get to nitpicking later.
It, like SS, has little humorous touches throughout. For example, I'm up to the second level, and on the bookshelf, all of the books are parodies of famous books in our world; "Grainspotting" and "A Hat Full of Rye" are two hat stood out to me. The real humour, though, comes from the therapist's reports at the beginning of each level. You can practically feel his emotions through the writing.
Now, the nitpicking. One major complaint, two minor. The small things; firstly, increase the grip timer by a tiny bit, and it'd be perfect. Either that, or make moving slightly smoother. I had great difficulty moving around with keyboard and moue, before switching to a controller, and the grip timer seemed to give way a second before I expected it to. Secondly, make the music non-directional. Of course, that'll be something you'll change as it develops, so I'm not too worried.
Now, my only big gripe. Make it apparent what things do. For example, there's nothing that tells you that jam/jelly makes you sticky, or that butter makes you slippery. Also, show us what things can toast us! Or, if that's supposed to be a secret, give us hints. I passed the first level not by hopping into the toaster, but by
Admittedly, the trailer did show someone being toasted using a hair dryer, but it would be nice if it would be more apparent asto what can toast us, and where such objects might be found.
Oh, and please add a free roam mode!
Overall, I like the game. It's not cerebral or profoundly deep, but it's fun, and I appreciate it. It knows what it is, and that's always a strength. It's certainly not hollow like some of those
Just needs some fleshing out with little story details or easter eggs and it'll be perfect.

This is an incredibly hard game. It requires you to learn a lot about heros, enemies and items. But, the game mechanism is so well-designed that it is rewarding to do so.
When you play this game as a beginner, the game is so hard that it may make you think the game totally depends on randomness, but once you learn about the game and then if you carefully and sensibly make your plan, you will reduce the influence from the randomness quite effectively.
Despite its difficulty, it provides players a lot of means to get through tough situations in variuos ways. All of those means have advatages and disadvantages, so you need to think about how you want to combine them, based on your situation. Like when you want to collect a lot of gold in a single quest, you can take an Antiquaria, increase scouting chance to find a secret room or explore a dungeon with a low light level. Each of those comes with its unique risks that you need to add another strategic factor to compensate for. You keep applying strategies until you get satisfied.
I totally recommend this game to those who love a challenge and have a chunk of time to spend.

I've read quite a few negative reviews comparing this game to a slot machine with perma-death.
Actually, there is significantly less RNG than a lot of people seem to think. There is a fair amount, but it is tightly constrained. If the game says something has an 80% chance to hit, it is PROBABLY going to hit... but you shouldn't bet your last 2 health on it.
Overall, it takes a fair bit of thinking and planning ahead, and (and this is what I see a lot of people not stopping to think about) NOT opening every container in sight. There are some objects that, unless you drop the right item on them first, are going to kick a character's heiny. Also... be careful what objects you place a torch on. Seriously.
To the complaints of the maps being repetative: that is a COMPLETELY valid point. The map layout changes drastically, but the scenery does NOT.
There are more than just the ruins. Most recently added was the free content: The Cove (don't bother bringing bleed skills), and there is some new DLC planned that I'm hoping will bring another new area to stumble around through, screaming in panic.
Darkest Petunia Garden... er... Dungeon... is not for everybody, but it can be a very fun dungeon crawler, and despite my usual preference for games that don't slap you around with insane "difficulty challenge yay go time gogogo yeah hardmode doood", I still love this game to pieces.

Dark Souls is just a great overall game trilogy. I'm personally drawn to games that base themselves heavily off skill and PvP aspects over equipment and stats. Sure stats are important, but if you have skill it makes you all the better.
That said, I always enjoy the dark atmosphere, the constant unknown of what might be waiting. Always fun to conquer the bosses that cause you the most headache. It reminds me of the definition of insanity; "doing the same thing over, expecting a different result."
Perhaps I'm insane, but I usually just slam myself against that brick wall, and eventually. Something different does result from slowly learning the boss's movements, learning where to be, and where not to be...
Anyway, invasions are also fun! Hard to find at lower levels, most people say the "meta" level for invading and PvP is about 120; so if you want to reach that, you'll have a lot of grinding to do.
But I thrive off pummelling others into the ground, so I love Dark Souls. I guess I'd classify under the "Killer" label in Bartle's Taxonomy... ((The splitting of gamers into groups based on what they enjoy most in gaming; such as: "Explorers, Socialists, Achievers, and Killers"... Go check out ExtraCredits on youtube if you're interested in game analysis and insights from a game developer and team of others. If you haven't already, there is quite a lot to see there. Anyway...))
So I thrive off knowing someone else is feeling the pain of lossing, but vise-versa; I hate losing. So... Anyway, whether you like exploring every nook and cranny for items/loot, or just slashing, hacking, and destroying enemies through the kingdom of Londor. I'm sure you'll agree, Dark Souls 3 is pretty great!

Daha önce de yazmıştım, steam tavsİye ediyorum, etmiyorum dışında bir de kararsızım seçeneği koymalı. Olsaydı kararsız olarak işaretlerdim.
Oynadığım en arıza sıra tabanlı RPG’lerden biri. Oyunun atmosferi, öyküleme ve seslendirmenin etkisiyle gayet iyi. Fakat başlamadan önce el emeği göznuru karakterlerinizin öleceğini bilmekte fayda var ki sonradan sinir bozucu hale gelmesin. RPG’de karakter ölmesi bir nevi oyunun bitmesi gibi zaten. Zindan, RPG, sıra tabanlı, karakter geliştirme kelimeleri bir arada cazip geliyorsa ve karanlık atmosfere razıysanız alınabilir. Yok ben onca zaman harcadım, bütünleştim, karakteri geliştirdim zart diye öldü geri de dönemiyorum, klavyeyi kırarım diyorsanz uzak durun. Mis gibi Helion’u az önce daha ne olduğunu anlamadan kaybettim delirmek üzereyim.
Oyunun tadını kaçıran kısmı kısa bir sürede rutine dönmesi ve bu rutinin içinden çıkılmaz bir hale gelmesi ve bunu geriye çevirme ihtimalinin olmaması. Bu rutini ben aşamadım ve bir süre sonra sıktı. Sürekli aynı şeyi yapıyor hissiyatı var. WoW oynayanlar bilir, daily quest ve grind gibi. Karakter gelişsin diye aynı zindanı tekrar babam tekrar yapmak gerekiyor. Bu rutini keşfedene kadar oyun hiç fena değil ama ondan sonra sıkıyor.
Oyunda ve arayüzde bazı eksikler var. Sırayla yazıyorum:
- Şehre geldiğimizde zamanın nasıl geçtiğini görebilsek güzel olurdu. Hava bir kararıyor bir aydınlanıyor. Uzun süre etkisi var mı diye bekledim ama görebildiğim bir şey yok.
- Yine şehre geldiğimizde kahramanları ille de dinlenmeye, stres atmaya yollamak zorunda olunmamalı. Yeni bir göreve gitmeyenlerin stres seviyesi şehirde bekledikleri için otomatik olarak bir miktar azalsa daha iyi olurdu.
- Roster filtrelemesi geliştirilse oynaması daha kolay. Örneğin tedaviye gönderdiğimiz, müsait olmayan hero’lar gözükmesin.
- Şehirde kaynaklarınız bitince vakit harcayamıyorsunuz ki bu hakikaten güzel değil. Kendinizi hazır hissetmediğiniz halde göreve gitmek zorundasınız, oyun sizi buna itiyor çünkü yapacak başka bir şey yok. Bir süre sonra sanırım şehir topladığınız hatıratları (heirloom) hemen harca git gibi zevksiz bir hale gelecek. Elinizde yeterli hatırat yoksa oyun “grind”’e dönme tehlikesiyle karşılaşıyor. Aynı zindanı tekrar tekrar yaparak karakteri geliştirmek zorunda kalıyorsunuz.
- Zindan da ilerlerken karşınızda düşman çıktığınızda hero sıralamanız birden bozuluveriyor. Biraz anlamsız. Aynı zamanda meşalenin ışığı farklı odalarda farklı hızda azalıyor bazen hızlı bazen daha yavaş. Bir sayaç veya meşalenin nasıl azaldığını gösteren ibare olsa daha iyi olur. Fare ile üzerine gelmden anlamak son derece zor.
- Bir önceki zindandan artan meşale, bandaj gibi malzemeler neden geri dönmüyor anlaşılıyor gibi değil. Nereye gidiyor bu malzemeler?
- Inventory tamamen sıkıntı. Nasıl genişletiliyor bulamadım.
OYNARKEN DİKKAT
- Zindanlarda son odadaki dövüşü kazandıktan sonra görev bitti şehre dönmek ister misin sorusu otomatik karşınıza çıkıyor. Hemen kabul etmeyin. Hayır dedikten sonra sandık çıkıyor, içindekileri alıp şehre öyle dönün.
- Trinket’leri karaktere giydirmeyi unutmayın. Kolay bir yolu var. Inventory menusunu açın. Roster’daki her karaktere sırayla sağ tıklayın. Eğer trinket uygunsa zaten belirginleşiyor, ondan sonra takıp takmayacağınıza karar vermek için okursunuz.
- Tavsiye karakterlerim Leper, Helion. En sevdiğim leper. Öne Helion veya crusader arkasına leper. 3. sıraya istediğinizi dizebilirsiniz. Bende ustura kamil Highwayman var çok nadir arbalest veya occulist kullanıyorum. En arkaya Vestal (mümkünse aynı zamanda self-heal özelliği olan). This is the first Dark Souls game I played, and I absolutely love it. I play with a Steam controller and it works very well.
Needless to say, the game is very challenging and you're expected to die a lot, so be ready to learn from your mistakes often. There is hardly any guidance in the game, as the tutorial simply tells you the game's controls and then it throws you into the thick of it. Expect a steep learning curve that will test you before you even finish the tutorial.
There is co-op, but it exists atomically with random PvP encounters. So, you can get help from other players (random ones or specific ones that share your password), but not without making yourself vulnerable to invasion by enemy players. While sometimes annoying, it's hard to deny that this fits with the hardcore tone of the game.
The one thing I will complain about is about is the camera. The FoV is pretty narrow and you can't change it, so you don't always get to take in all of your surroundings. This sucks because the game has gorgeous levels.
Use the wiki to your advantage since hardly anything about the game's mechanics is explained in-game. Don't let frustration ruin the game for you, and you'll git gud in no time.

Firaxis is kinda infamous for buggy releases but this time prelease reviews were claiming it's relatively free of game-stopping bugs, only chock-full of visual animation/camera bugs. While it seems like there aren't a ton of of game-stopping bugs there's still one pretty major one: During any mission the game can crash and corrupt every single save made during the mission, including autosaves. On ironman this means game-over - you have no chance of salvaging the run. Without ironman you can go back to the latest save made on the world map - though considering that the intended/prefered way to play xcom as stated by the devs is ironman a bug like this is unacceptable. Personally I ran into this bug around 3 times even before the final mission but what takes the cake is that this bug seems to be most common during the final mission - several prominent streamers had their ironman-run killed right during the final mission due to this bug and one streamer I occasionally watch is now waiting until there are any fixes for this bug before attempting the final mission.
Other noteworthy bugs include the enemy AI completely borking out which in turn has the effect that the AI's turn takes an abnormal and aggravatingly long time while actually remaining completely stationary and inactive.
Another common bug is the alien viper enemy being able to use their tongue-pull to pull your soldiers without any line of sight and through entire buildings.
Combine these technical issues and game-stopping bugs and the extremely poor optimization that a lof of people already have drawn attention to and I don't see how Xcom 2 deserves to be supported/bought at full prize in its current state. If you put aside the technical issues Xcom 2 is a fairly fun and decent squad-based TBS/RNG-BS game and would be worth the full prize for fans of the genre like myself - in its current state it's a lot less clear cut.
My advice would be to hold off and wait until patches are out and while you're at you might just as well wait for a sale. Personally I won't buy any Firaxis game at launch anymore and instead hold out for patches and sales. At this point I just don't trust Firaxis to not release a game with game-stopping bugs and I don't think they should be rewarded with full-prize sales for a MO like that.

I started the day as a slice of bread. Not the end piece, because no one likes the end piece. No, I was the second slice in. I emerged from my loaf in glorious fashion, spreading my crumbs all over as I flew from what I once called home. This was the start of my journey.
I emerged in to a world of culinary decadence. To my left was Mt. Butter, and to my right was Jelly Valley. There were so many places to see, so many things to do. Life had finally begun.
I began my voyage to Toaster Kingdom by first heading for Mt. Butter. It was always a dream of mine to stand-atop the hills on Mt. Butter, and I did just that. I paraded to the top in mere seconds, only to slide down Mt. Butter and splash right in to Jelly Valley.
It was like a slip-n-slide of deliciousness.
I emerged from Jelly Valley covered from bread to toe, only to come to the edge of the world. I could see it all from here; the vast landscapes of Breadland, the hills of Crumbilina, but most of all, I could see Toaster Kingdom, and I knew my journey was far from over.
In a moment of serenity, I took a giant leap of faith, and I floated through space and time, in an absolute moment of glory. I didn't know what was waiting for me below, but I knew this was what had to be done.
Falling for what seemed an eternity, I thought this to be the end. Just then, something emerges below me, and I land softly on to a giant looking board with wheels. My savior.
I thanked it for saving me, and we bonded very quickly. It turns out, we are both heading to the same destination, and he agrees to let me travel on him. I hold on tight, and off we go. We travel through canyons, wastelands, hell, we even traveled through large ravines.
We're almost there.
We arrive at the Counter-Top Haven. The final stop before Toaster Kingdom. Just when we are in-reach of the Toaster Kingdom, my new friend informs me that he can go no further, for he is not capable of climbing. He entrusts me with a gift for King Toaster, a serum of sorts. He called it Maple Syrup. I am clueless what it would be used for, after-all the King is french. I don't understand what he would possibly do with such a thing. Nevertheless, I say thank you for everything, as a tear of jelly starts rolling down my face, and I start my ascent to reach the top of Counter-Top Haven.
It's a rough climb. It takes me about a minute or two, as I seem to be slipping and sliding all over the cliffs and peaks of this place. Maybe it's the jelly, maybe it's the butter, but all's I know is that I must persevere. I must make it to Toaster Kingdom.
I finally reach the top of Counter-Top Haven, and Toaster Kingdom and the Toaster King are in my line of sight. I flop towards them as fast as my nimble body can take me, battered and buttered and bruised. I reach the entrance to Toaster Kingdom. I can feel it now. I'm almost there. I only have to climb once more and I will have completed my first voyage.
With all the strength I can muster, I grip tightly on to the walls of Toaster Kingdom. I manage to hoist myself a-top this beautiful landscape. I'm here. I made it. The Toaster King is in sight. I just have to decend to the throne room, and I will have fulfilled my purpose in life.
Just as I am readying myself to decend towards the king, a gust of wind blows me off of the top of the kingdom. Down I fly, past Counter-Top Haven. Below I go, to the ends of the earth. No one to save me this time. I fall. I fall.
I land in the dirt.
Ruined.
I wither and die.
10 / 10. Would play again.

Gameplay:
Darkest Dungeon is an immacuatly balanced rougelike RPG where managing your heros' psyches is just as important as their HP. Fighting horrible monsters in the dark is stressful. Stressed heroes are prone to erractic action. Therefore minimizing stress is key to survival. Darkest Dungeon heroes are unique and will develop positive and negative traits (e.g. Quick Reflexes, Claustrophobia, etc). It's up the player to manage these as well. Battles happen in narrow passages so heroes positions (front or back) are tremendously important. This simple mechanic adds an entirely new twist to combat. For example, a ranged character will be useless in front of the party, bu devestating in the back ranks. Manipulating the enemies' positions is equally important. Like most roguelikes, characters are succeptible to permadeath. However, (unless playing NG+) it's not possible to lose Darkest Dungeon. Character deaths will serve as a setback, but there are always more waiting in the ranks. Lastly, while enemies and dungeons are highly varied, late game can feel somewhat repetitive.
Story:
Don't expect a fleshed-out RPG story in Darkest Dungeon. A narrator guides you through the game and gives some inital backstory, but aside from boss fights, the storyline is rarely present until the final encounter in the Darkest Dungeon.
Design:
The tone, art style, and music of the game is DARK. This was originally a turnoff for me, but after a dozen or so missions it began to grow on me. Hand drawn enemies are horrifying and creative without being cartoonish. The soundtrack and narration is enjoyable, but got old eventually. Now I often play my own (more upbeat) music while dungeon crawling.
Overall:
Darkest Gundeon's unique mechanics and time-tested turn-based combat make for an addictive and challenging combination. If you like rougelikes and turn-based strategy games, Darkest Dungeon is absolutely the game for you. Reccomend to fans of XCOM, FTL, Don't Starve, or anyone who wants a serious turn-based challenge. The biggest complaint I've heard from other players is an unfair RNG. The RNG can be brutal, but like other roguelikes, missions in Darkest Dungeon are a balance of risk vs. reward. Darkest Dungeon has a steep learning curve, but mastery is highly achievable and extremely rewarding.

So imagine that Mount Your Friends got an extra dimension and became less suggestive, open world, and also bread. You play a slice of bread and your objective is to become toast. You have an edibility bar that is effectively your health. The floor and other dirty places will lower that and once it hits 0 you fail the level. You have no time limit, but if you take too long, you get a worse rating. I finished the first level three times. I got E, D, and C. The next level didn’t unlock till I got a C.
Controls were frustrating at first and after an hour of play.... were still rather frustrating. That said there are two possible schemes of control: mouse/keyboard and controller. They both will give you a different level of control.
You have 4 buttons corresponding to the corners of the bread slice you control. Pressing a button will cause that corner to stick to the environment. You then can use the mouse or analog stick to move yourself. With a mouse you have far more force behind your movements. With an analog stick, it feels like the bread is struggling to move. You also have a limited amount of time for consecutive grip.
Despite the odd feel of the controls, the game has some fun moments. There is something special about sliding across the wall like a piece of spider-bread. The feeling of mastering the controls is a rewarding experience if nothing else. It’s an interesting and unique game that I expect to become into something more interesting, if Surgeon Simulator is an example.
In conclusion: Wonky controls, not much content, but an early access game that’s been out for about a week or so. If you don’t buy now but are still interested, keep an eye on its development to see what comes of it.

Daha önce de yazmıştım, steam tavsİye ediyorum, etmiyorum dışında bir de kararsızım seçeneği koymalı. Olsaydı kararsız olarak işaretlerdim.
Oynadığım en arıza sıra tabanlı RPG’lerden biri. Oyunun atmosferi, öyküleme ve seslendirmenin etkisiyle gayet iyi. Fakat başlamadan önce el emeği göznuru karakterlerinizin öleceğini bilmekte fayda var ki sonradan sinir bozucu hale gelmesin. RPG’de karakter ölmesi bir nevi oyunun bitmesi gibi zaten. Zindan, RPG, sıra tabanlı, karakter geliştirme kelimeleri bir arada cazip geliyorsa ve karanlık atmosfere razıysanız alınabilir. Yok ben onca zaman harcadım, bütünleştim, karakteri geliştirdim zart diye öldü geri de dönemiyorum, klavyeyi kırarım diyorsanz uzak durun. Mis gibi Helion’u az önce daha ne olduğunu anlamadan kaybettim delirmek üzereyim.
Oyunun tadını kaçıran kısmı kısa bir sürede rutine dönmesi ve bu rutinin içinden çıkılmaz bir hale gelmesi ve bunu geriye çevirme ihtimalinin olmaması. Bu rutini ben aşamadım ve bir süre sonra sıktı. Sürekli aynı şeyi yapıyor hissiyatı var. WoW oynayanlar bilir, daily quest ve grind gibi. Karakter gelişsin diye aynı zindanı tekrar babam tekrar yapmak gerekiyor. Bu rutini keşfedene kadar oyun hiç fena değil ama ondan sonra sıkıyor.
Oyunda ve arayüzde bazı eksikler var. Sırayla yazıyorum:
- Şehre geldiğimizde zamanın nasıl geçtiğini görebilsek güzel olurdu. Hava bir kararıyor bir aydınlanıyor. Uzun süre etkisi var mı diye bekledim ama görebildiğim bir şey yok.
- Yine şehre geldiğimizde kahramanları ille de dinlenmeye, stres atmaya yollamak zorunda olunmamalı. Yeni bir göreve gitmeyenlerin stres seviyesi şehirde bekledikleri için otomatik olarak bir miktar azalsa daha iyi olurdu.
- Roster filtrelemesi geliştirilse oynaması daha kolay. Örneğin tedaviye gönderdiğimiz, müsait olmayan hero’lar gözükmesin.
- Şehirde kaynaklarınız bitince vakit harcayamıyorsunuz ki bu hakikaten güzel değil. Kendinizi hazır hissetmediğiniz halde göreve gitmek zorundasınız, oyun sizi buna itiyor çünkü yapacak başka bir şey yok. Bir süre sonra sanırım şehir topladığınız hatıratları (heirloom) hemen harca git gibi zevksiz bir hale gelecek. Elinizde yeterli hatırat yoksa oyun “grind”’e dönme tehlikesiyle karşılaşıyor. Aynı zindanı tekrar tekrar yaparak karakteri geliştirmek zorunda kalıyorsunuz.
- Zindan da ilerlerken karşınızda düşman çıktığınızda hero sıralamanız birden bozuluveriyor. Biraz anlamsız. Aynı zamanda meşalenin ışığı farklı odalarda farklı hızda azalıyor bazen hızlı bazen daha yavaş. Bir sayaç veya meşalenin nasıl azaldığını gösteren ibare olsa daha iyi olur. Fare ile üzerine gelmden anlamak son derece zor.
- Bir önceki zindandan artan meşale, bandaj gibi malzemeler neden geri dönmüyor anlaşılıyor gibi değil. Nereye gidiyor bu malzemeler?
- Inventory tamamen sıkıntı. Nasıl genişletiliyor bulamadım.
OYNARKEN DİKKAT
- Zindanlarda son odadaki dövüşü kazandıktan sonra görev bitti şehre dönmek ister misin sorusu otomatik karşınıza çıkıyor. Hemen kabul etmeyin. Hayır dedikten sonra sandık çıkıyor, içindekileri alıp şehre öyle dönün.
- Trinket’leri karaktere giydirmeyi unutmayın. Kolay bir yolu var. Inventory menusunu açın. Roster’daki her karaktere sırayla sağ tıklayın. Eğer trinket uygunsa zaten belirginleşiyor, ondan sonra takıp takmayacağınıza karar vermek için okursunuz.
- Tavsiye karakterlerim Leper, Helion. En sevdiğim leper. Öne Helion veya crusader arkasına leper. 3. sıraya istediğinizi dizebilirsiniz. Bende ustura kamil Highwayman var çok nadir arbalest veya occulist kullanıyorum. En arkaya Vestal (mümkünse aynı zamanda self-heal özelliği olan). İkinci grup tercihimde ön iki aynı 3’e occulist 4’e Vestal. Bu setup’la daha yavaş ama daha emin ilerliyorsunuz.
- Birde hayvani damage var. Öne düşmanı işaretleyebilen tank, hemen arkasında işaretli düşmana hasarı %90 daha fazla vuran bir Bounty hunter ile yardır yardır gidilebiliyor.
- Yiyecek, meşale ve bandaj olmadan yola çıkılmaz. Yiyecek 12’li, Meşale 8’li alınabiliyor. Grup seçimine göre ve birkaç zindandan sonra karar verilebilir.

Avoid this and every other Bethesda game. They don't care about consumers, and here's why:
a) Yes, they're introducing a "paid mods" system, but while surely there's a way such thing could benefit creators, this system isn't it. Creators have to work under restrictions and have to give up their rights to a mod as soon as they publish it. Not to mention that they don't receive royalties.
b) The paid mods update forces an extra 2.1 GB download. If you have a data cap, this is a problem. Worse, most of that is not necessary, as most of the data are assets for the mods. That's right, you're forced to download something even if you don't intend to use it.  Expect that 2.1 GB number to get larger as soon as soon as more mods are added.
c) You can't just pay for the mods with regular money. You're forced to purchase packs of their own currency. Similar to the old Bioware Points, this benefits no consumer.
The game's quality (or lack thereof) is entirely unimportant when the publisher treats you like crap. Don't buy Bethesda games, at least until they learn to respect the consumers.

XCOM2 is a proper and well-executed successor of XCOM:Enemy Unknown (XCOM:EU/EW). Every gameplay system from XCOM:EU/EW is improved upon and expanded upon in a good and well-designed way.
It is also a huge value proposition, full playthrough took me 65 hours and lots of replayability is granted through its well-designed randomization.
Everything known from XCOM:EU/EW is turned up a little "in volume" in an exciting way, even "small" things. Example: upon mission start, the skyranger / avenger doesn't land... The squadmates f*cking jump out of the flying thing, rope down and then unsheathe their firearms, ready to receive orders. Small things like this make this game very exciting, "even though" it is turn-based.
Also, as another honorable mention, most missions start with a mission timer BUT the player also vaguely decides from which position he wants to start that timer ticking through the addition of concealment to the game. Basically, your squadmates can move around the map as long as they remain undetected from enemy sight. The turn timer only starts ticking once a squadmate is revealed or fires a shot at an enemy. That way, the game becomes a lot more interesting, as the previously most viable strategy in XCOM:EU/EW, i.e. stutter-stepping forward with the whole squad on overwatch, is overwritten in a well-designed way by careful selection of one's starting position within any given mission.
Wholeheartedly recommended! :)

The special effects and the different colours schemes are amazing, they really put a lot of work into that. I feel that this is more of a dungeoneering game than an rpg but whatever floats your boat. There are so many classes that I haven't had time to explore them all and some classes are definitly more interesting than others but that is personal preference. The dungeon battles are great, so is the battle music, they are very challenging. Only unfortunate thing about them is that they are stacked on a line 4 vs 4 so anybody can't reach anybody, depending on classes, I'd rather have it a 4v4 where everyone can attack everyone so no turns/movements need to be wasted. Death is inevitable in this game so you'd better get used to characters dying. The death system is fair, whenever the hp equals 0 of course, the character stands 'at deads door' with a 50% procent chance of surviving next attack or dying by the next attack. Although I do not like how less healing there is, either they should implement potions (make em decent/expensive priced) which heal 5 instead of only relying on food which heals a max of 2. I also don't like the narrator, nothing personal, but there is too much repetitive stuff occuring to be narrated.
Overall a good and hard game, will try to beat it somehow. I do not know yet how because it was extremely hard from the start.

Imagine playing a slot machine. If you win enough on the slot machine you can then play the next level. But if you lose the slot machine you have to start back at the first one. Finally completing all bosses and recreating new top tier team they get killed in the new patch of levels. Back to grinding the small guys again.
Now they didn't die because I failed to play a certain way, they died because the combat system is entirely random number generated. There is nothing to learn from a loss to help on the next run. Just repetition.

Oh boy, where to begin with this? During April to May, I finished the first Dark Souls, and I simply couldn't get enough of it. It was to the point that I was thinking of Dark Souls 24/7 during my finals, checking the wikia, looking up the lore, thinking of how to beat certain bosses, etc. So when I saw Dark Souls II and Dark Souls III on sale, I absolutely can't let it slip my radar. Naturally, since I finished the first Dark Souls, I'd absolutely play Dark Souls II then Dark Souls III... well, that isn't what happened. Much of Dark Souls II was so slow and clunky (which I feel better elaborating in detail in my possible Dark Souls II review), that I quickly abandonned it in favor of Dark Souls III, since I already know how much better it is after playing at a friend's copy.
Boy did it deliver.
Dark Souls II had many bad first impressions, one of them being just how slow it feels compared to the first game. Dodges feels incredibly delayed and the parrying animation felt slower to me, don't get me started on how they changed the instant gratification of a riposte. Dark Souls III however seemed to have taken more lessons from Bloodborne, and I definitely thought it paid off. Dodging is even more viable than it ever was before in Dark Souls, thanks to the decrease of claustrophobic levels, which does let you run away from enemies to the next bonfire more viable as well, but I don't think that hurts the overall experience. With that said, I don't think the level design is anywhere near as memorable as Dark Souls I. I never found any level that gave me the insane gratification as the archers in Anor Londo, but I feel this is all compensated by just how damn well the bosses are.
Remember when I said Dark Souls III took more cues from Bloodborne? I think most of that design philosophy goes to the bosses more than anything else, you can see how much this is in play when you're as early as the Abyss Watchers. If they were in Dark Souls I, they'd most likely be a mid to endgame boss. In here however, they're most likely your third to fourth boss you'll face. If you're anything like me, that is to say constantly turtling and not having the balls to be aggressive, then they will wreck your♥♥♥♥♥in ways you never knew could be wrecked. If you did somehow managed to beat them that way, his second phase will utterly destroy you. Second phases are also played up much more dramatically in this game than the first game, they will force you to think of new strategies on the fly as you try to familiarize yourself with whatever they will do next. It's why Dark Souls III feels much more faster and aggressive, there's more emphasis on impromptu strategies and quick reflexes more than ever. It's also part of why I think it's definitely more difficult than previous Souls game, and also far more rewarding, giving you those moments where you just fistpump after killing that one boss you struggled all weekend on.
There are probably some things I haven't touched on more like the new FP system or the Weapon Arts, but I feel they don't really change the overall experience by much. I barely use any of the Weapon Arts in the base game, since they don't do much different to a normal attack, and the FP system at best just makes the Attunement stat more important if you intend to play with magic, which I just used for the heals.
I also just want to say that the music is as good as ever, probably won't sell you on the game if you didn't intend to buy the game based on this review, but I just like pointing out good music.
TL;DR: If you wanted a faster Dark Souls I with better emphasis on the bosses, then this is it.

After almost 100 h of playing Darkest Dungeon I'm inclined to write a little review. First of all: i think it is a great game! I love it! It has a fantastic gritty artstyle and cool graphics, amazing soundtrack and challenging game mechanics with exciting turn-based combat. On top of it one gets the somewhat spooky narrator who tells the story of his downfall and sometimes seems to mock the player. But beware: never get to cocky! You will lose heroes whether they just die or get mad so you have to kick them out. You have to play carefully and calculate the risks to get your people back to the meager safety of your Hamlet. You need patience to make it to the Darkest Dungeon.
Pros:
+ interesting combat system
+ large variety of heroes of which none is useless. One just has to figure out how to use them.
+ every hero has a up to seven skills but only four can be active at the time. You have to experiment what works best for oneself.
+ plenty of different group constellations with different tactics. The player has a lot of options on this one and can                      experiment on how to make a group work.
+ great lovecraftian atmosphere
+ intense immersion. You really suffer if one of your beloved level 6  heroes dies of a heart attack.
+ long campaign especially if you take your time and play carefully
+ atmospheric dark fantasy setting
+ mod support
Cons:
- sometimes it gets  grindy
- only five different types of dungeons
- not much variety in the character design
- sometimes you just have bad luck which can be frustrating.
neutral:
sparse tutorial. I  consider it not too bad because it's part of the game to drill yourselt into it!
bottom line:
I would give Darkest Dungeon 9/10, really a must-buy if you enjoy rogue-likes with permadeath and a real challenge.
It can be frustrating at some point or the other but that makes every victory just tastes sweeter.

No pay 2 win as of yet. Graphics are mediocre but friendly for lower spec PC's. What matters is gameplay and it's actually pretty good. It is the snappiest shooter I have played, surprisingly. This is all about aiming for the head and reacting the fastest, just like CSGO/CSS, but with elements of Call of Duty into it. It's not a bad thing at all. Assassination is a really broken game mode with the VIP running TO the attacking team. Demolition(S&D) is fun, just like other modes. TDM is just like other games.
My biggest problem with this game is the community. As with every free game, you will get people of all ages and skill levels, and you will get called a hacker for hitting absurd shots or having faster reactions than them and it's incredibly immature. Apart from that, the tutorials show nothing about educating people different game modes so we have people rushing with horrible aim in demolition, literally giving the opposing team free kills.
TL;DR worth a download. Try it out. Your results may vary with the community.

TLDR: Fallout 4 is a horrible RPG, but a barely-passable game. It is also the manifestation of pure greed reaching its final form with the Creation Club. Do not buy this game. Do not give Bethesda money.
Fallout 4 is the last straw for me with Bethesda produced games. While they may publish some fantastic titles such as last year’s Doom reboot and I’m looking forward to Quake Champions, Fallout 4 has been nothing but a disaster and a cash grab. The issues with Fallout 4 as a game are well documented on YouTube (seriously, go watch just one of the multiple hour-long teardowns of this turd), so I’ll keep this section brief.
Any amount of player freedom in character backstory and personality is gone in order to have a voiced protagonist who is nothing more than a glorified yes man. I don’t think I failed a single quest in the fifty or so hours I played across two characters. There was no way to♥♥♥♥♥♥an NPC off to the point where I could fail a quest. I’ll repeat that:
. Even worse, my only options for player expression were violence and being “sarcastic”, and there is not enough air-quotes in the world to put around that word. Save for a few conversations, your character is essentially pre-determined by the developers to act a certain way in conversation, or, to act as a pop-culture reference spewing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with the “sarcastic” option. Seriously, someone get Bethesda a copy of the dictionary, I truly think they don’t know the definition of sarcasm.
Alright, so, the dialog sucks. Maybe you’re thinking “That’s fine, I wasn’t going to play much of a talker anyway”. Don’t worry, they thought of other ways to ruin this game for you. The character progression is ♥♥♥♥ed beyond all belief. Since, apparently, people are too stupid to understand that “bigger numbers = better stats”, the skill system has been completely removed in favor of the perk system. The consequence of this is that most of the perks are boring as hell and flat bonuses that you are required to take with every character. You can’t pass up the 20% damage boost weapon perks since the game scales the health of every enemy to match your level—if you get too high level without these core perks then every enemy will become a bullet sponge even on normal difficulty. The only good thing about this system is that you have fewer SPECIAL points to spend during character creation, but it doesn’t matter since you can use a perk point to raise a SPECIAL stat anyway. Oh, and just in-case you thought that maybe this system would force you to make difficult decisions about what perk to take, think again. There is no level cap so you WILL get every perk in the game if you suffer through it long enough.
So, the character creation and player interaction are fubar. That’s fine, maybe you just wanted to shoot things. In that case: don’t buy an RPG. Buy literally any other First Person Shooter on the market. The gunplay in Fallout 4 may be leagues better than the gunplay in Fallout 3 and New Vegas, but that puts in on par with 2010. There are multiple better FPS games with more deep and engaging gunplay that deserve your money. I could go into detail on HOW it’s bad, but just watch any YouTube playthrough or critique and you’ll get the idea. It’s passable, nothing more.
Alright, so the shooting is passable, that’s a point. Here, I’ll have to point out the only good thing in this semi-polished turd of a game: the world design… kind of. I really, really feel bad for the art department at Bethesda, since they put together a stunning represent of a post-apocalyptic Boston only to have the idiots in the story and game mechanics departments♥♥♥♥♥♥all over their work. The textures aren’t the highest resolution, and the lighting effects are passable if not a little underwhelming, but the amount of care and effort that went into making a surreal representation of an American city gone to hell is evident. If anything, Fallout 4 is fun to just walk around in to explore. Just make sure you shut your brain off and don’t think about how 200 years have passed too hard. Or question why there’s raider and super mutant encampments literally 50 feet away from the biggest settlement in the game.
I could go into detail about how the story is asinine, with your character making stupid decisions and unable to figure out the most obvious things against the player’s own choice, but people have already pointed that out more effectively than I ever could. No, what made me write this tirade was the release of the Creation Club today. Bethesda has lost every ounce of respect I have given them with this thinly veiled cash-grab. The Creation Club has astronomical prices for pieces of content that are either available for free from NexusMods, or is so amazingly expensive that you’d have to be a complete ♥♥♥♥ing moron to pay for it. There are no high-quality quest mods with voice acting, nor major gameplay changes or overhauls. The only items for sale are simple retextures or a single new weapon or piece of armor at best with a minim price of $1. There’s even “horse armor”, which is a set of power armor crafted from giddyup buttercup parts, which is on sale for a whopping $2, the replica of the Enclave Hellfire Armor from Fallout 3 is about $7.
. That is inexcusable. The Creation Club promised a higher standard of mods more akin to the expansion packs and game overhauls of the late 90s. There isn’t any content remotely worth it on the Creation Club at launch when Bethesda would want to put their best content forward. Instead, they put forward some embarrassingly overpriced content that is literally lower quality than the stuff modders offer FOR FREE. Do not give Bethesda a cent through this service, and if you do, enjoy your life as a sucker.

Beautiful art, effects, story and voice over, but horribly designed. The games sole purpose seems to punish the player with sheer randomness that is heavily weighed against the player. Once a single event goes wrong such as a failed save, 99%  of the time it will turn into a domino effect that completely wipes a party of veterans in a round or two. The underlying strategy seems to be to throw as many bodies at a dungeon as possible, and never get attached to anything in the game no matter how much effort or time was put into it. If you like pure randomness that flies in the face of strategy and planning, then this is the game for you. If you like playing games to experience frustration instead of enjoyment after a hard day of work,  then this is the game for you. If you like having characters you spent weeks building up to be flush down the toilet,  then this is the game for you.It is a shame, everything about this game is top notch and amazing, except the combat design which is just plain amateurish and unbalanced.
Don't get me wrong I love hard games like Dark Souls, Don't Starve and Super Meat Boy where you can learn from failures and overcome them, but with this game there is no learning or overcoming randominess.

I really, really like this game. I don't typically read reviews, but after reading a few negative ones for this game I felt the need to.
This game essentially sets you as a dungeon crawiling party's HR manager. You send parties of recruits into dungeons on basic quests to retrieve equipment and loot to build up your town so that you can outfit your parties with better gear so that you can send them on tougher quests... rinse and repeat. Note that your characters leveling up doesn't actually make them stronger, but allows you to use your resources to make them stronger.
The other big parts of the game are stress, traits, and diseases. Stress damage can be dealt to your heroes, and once it reaches a certain threshold they will start acting irrationally, and hitting the next threshold puts them at risk of having a heart attack. (There's also a chance that they'll hit that threshold and focus, becoming stronger and providing buffs for themselves/your party).
In broad terms, traits are positive/negative permament buffs that your characters can get, really at any time during your adventure. Diseases are treated similarly, but all diseases have bad effects and only sometimes will also have good effects (for example, rabies decreases accuracy but increases damage).
I don't think this game is really about the story that the game designers wrote, but more about the stories that you create on each adventure with your party. Not saying the story is bad or uninteresting (and, since I don't know where else to mention it, the art direction and general feel of this whole game is fantastic and very cohesive) but your own stories are just that much better. You start to care about the traits your characters do/don't get, and whether or not they make it through the entirety of the dungeon. And if you've been upgrading your town properly, you (hopefully) won't get set too far back from a wipe.
Just use the character creation to make all your agents you friends. Now you get to tell them irl how you saved them or how they died.

XCOM 2 is to XCOM what Beyond Earth is to Civ V. The same game, made slightly different and released with a lot less features than you might come to expect after playing the previous game. If you're unfamiliar, Firaxis seems to be making a habit of releasing the bare minimum required to catch people's interest and to then release $50 expansions that slowly bring the game in line with what you were actually expecting.
The game plays out much the same way, including all the graphical bugs we know and love from the previous game. There's no real graphical change, just a slight alteration in overall aesthetic. The Avenger is a simplified xcom base with an ideal layout that is obvious once you work out just what things do. Put the power on the big power things, put the workshop in the middle and then build everything. That said, I always enjoy the dark atmosphere, the constant unknown of what might be waiting. Always fun to conquer the bosses that cause you the most headache. It reminds me of the definition of insanity; "doing the same thing over, expecting a different result."
Perhaps I'm insane, but I usually just slam myself against that brick wall, and eventually. Something different does result from slowly learning the boss's movements, learning where to be, and where not to be...
Anyway, invasions are also fun! Hard to find at lower levels, most people say the "meta" level for invading and PvP is about 120; so if you want to reach that, you'll have a lot of grinding to do.
But I thrive off pummelling others into the ground, so I love Dark Souls. I guess I'd classify under the "Killer" label in Bartle's Taxonomy... ((The splitting of gamers into groups based on what they enjoy most in gaming; such as: "Explorers, Socialists, Achievers, and Killers"... Go check out ExtraCredits on youtube if you're interested in game analysis and insights from a game developer and team of others. If you haven't already, there is quite a lot to see there. Anyway...))
So I thrive off knowing someone else is feeling the pain of lossing, but vise-versa; I hate losing. So... Anyway, whether you like exploring every nook and cranny for items/loot, or just slashing, hacking, and destroying enemies through the kingdom of Londor. I'm sure you'll agree, Dark Souls 3 is pretty great!

The snakes are super nuts... their tongue attacks have just as much range as your ranged attacks (because aliens), and they can drag your squad through anything and keep them coiled up. Good, silly experiences are hard to come by. Most end up just being one trick ponies and gimmick-a-thons. And the few decent ones end up being more like physics toys than actual games (Looking at you Turbo Dismount).
I am Bread turns out to be an actual GAME rather than a toy. It's challenging, strategic and most importantly fun to play.
The game is rather short. Right now there are 4 levels, each of which you could beat in 5 minutes (you won't, but you could). It took me 3 hours to complete. Might take a little longer if you choose to explore more.
Most levels have alternate routes and if that's not enough you could just scoot along the ceiling.
I've seen people complain about the controls, and I admit, the keyboard controls are pretty horrofic, so I suggest you use a controller. Learning and mastering the controls is the main challenge.
You start out clumsily flopping around, smashing everything your way. And by the end you'll be making flips from wall to wall like a preschooler on acid.
Cons mostly consist of some unwarranted failures due to wonky physics knocking over a toaster you desperately need. The learning curve is pretty harsh too. And the lack of real tutorial can be an issue if you get frustrated easily.
Overall. The game if real fun. It didn't feel samey and I can't wait for more to come.
A nod to the developers for showing us that a dumb game doesn't have to be braindead.

A truly fantastic game with a criminally low review rating. This stems from the game having changed a fair bit since early access, but all the changes have been positive. Making the game less exploitable is a good thing, people! The other complaints I hear are usually "The RNG is too severe! No skill!" Which is entirely untrue. All RNG in Darkest Dungeon can be avoided by careful planning and thought. On my second run through the game, I survived 100 weeks without a single death or a single quest failure and with only one resolve check encountered. (Edit: I've now finished the game twice consecutively with no deaths!)
Pros!
- Highly addictive gameplay that keeps you coming back for more
- Tons of replayability as no run through the game is the same
- Very strategic combat; party compositions, trinket speccing, synergies... the list goes on
- Beautiful in every sense. Stunning art-style, effective animation, fantastic soundtrack
- Diverse and varied characters make for a lot of experimentation and fun
- Fair difficulty curve, challenging the whole way with difficult but achieveable boss fights at the end
- Lots of content for the price
- Unique regions to explore with thematic enemies and procedurally generated dungeons
- Perfectly managed stress and health systems with intriguing "Death's Door" and "Resolve Check" mechanics to keep you on your toes in and out of combat
- Wayne June's narration is golden. It sets the Lovecraftian atmosphere perfectly and oozes quality with such sophisticated, verbose vocabulary
- Town Events make things more varied in the Hamlet (For better and occasionally for worse!)
- Somewhat frequent updates with new heroes, new content, bug-fixes, and fine-tuned mechanics
Cons
- A little beginner unfriendly in some places like cluttered tooltips, lack of game-mechanic introduction, etc
- The fact it's not in your game library! Absolutely criminal!
There's plenty more praise I could sing this game but I should stop now. This game captivated me and I fell deeply in love with it. I hope other people do too after reading this review!

I'd like to preface this review by saying that, truly, I was actually looking forward to this game.  It seemed quirky, sandbox-y, and hopefully enjoyable, and the reviews seemed to be overall positive.  It couldn't all have been just people rating it highly, just because you're playing as bread, right?  This had to be actually fun!  However, having now given this game a try, I can say that it doesn't live up to the hype at all.
First, I should state, from the trailers, it would seem like the game takes place in a sandbox-type game style.  Run around, cover yourself in crud, do stupid stuff, etc.  Tons of fun, right?  Well, if you're looking for that kind of gameplay, you've come to the wrong place, currently.  Perhaps when the game is more developed, there will be a free-play mode, but currently, there is only an objective mode, wherein you must make it from one side of the kitchen to the other, and toast yourself.  Still sounds fun, right?  Now, I imagine you may be sitting there going, "At least you can cover yourself in all sorts of stuff!"  Except, you can't, or your edibility bar hits zero and you get a game-over.  "Well, I can still climb all over the place, and swing from shelf to shelf like some gluten-based Tarzan, right?"  Well, bad news, you've only got a limited grip gauge that very quickly depletes, and you need to let it recharge again before you can grab anything, once it runs out.  Anddd when you hit the floor, your edibility quickly drops, as well.  I'm sure that, as it's early access, some of these issues will probably be addressed, but at this point, the trailers look much better than the game is.
Still, you know what?  That could still be a fun, challenging game.  Could be.  That is, if not for what me be perhaps the worst problem with this game: the contols are just awful.  And no, I don't mean like Surgeon Simulator's "haha this is hilarious" awful, I mean "why is the mouse suddenly inverted?  It didn't move like this before.  Why is it not responding to my movements?!" awful.  Seemingly at random, the game decides that you're now pulling back when you're pushing forward, swinging left when pulling right, etc., and then, at the drop of a hat, decides to go back to normal again.  Usually while you're climbing the walls with your quickly depleting grip gauge, or trying to finagle your way into the toaster slot, resulting in you either falling to the floor (at which point, the process repeats until your
edibility bar hits zero) or you flinging the toaster down to the floor, where toasting is not really an option (again, inevitably resulting in the edibility gauge hitting zero, but even more heartbreaking is victory is wrested from your fingers.  Er... Crust?).  If these controls didn't decide at random not to work, perhaps I could have had fun.  Perhaps this could have been a worthwhile game.  However, as it stands, the game is not challenging, it is just downright frustrating, and it is NOT worth your money.  Wait for them to improve the handling (if they ever do).

TL;DR: For all new players out there, be warned! Bethesda has just implemented their horrible "Creation Club" system wherein you pay for mods that used to be free. If you just want to play the base game, go ahead, but if you want the full modding experience then stay away!
Hello all. Welcome to the fifth installment of the Fallout series. The road up until this point has been paved with great storylines, interesting mechanics, and terrific characters. However, it seems that Bethesda has (like many companies) changed their worldview, and is now more interested in making money and screwing their fanbase (in the bad way, not the pleasurable way) than developing a good game. Now, you may say, "But sir, they're a company! They need to make money!" and you would be correct. Making money is ultimately the end goal of any company, and Bethesda is no different. However, be aware that the latest update to this otherwise enjoyable (if repetitive) game has completely changed the way mods work, and, in turn, changed how Bethesda makes money. That's right, we're talking about...
If you were around for the Paid Mods fiasco of early 2015 (wherein Valve in conjunction with Bethesda attempted to monestize mods on the steam workshop) you'll know that any sort of monetization of originally
created NOT by the developers but by COMMUNITY MEMBERS is, frankly, a stupid idea. I, personally, supported the idea of paying mod creators for their hard work, especially for mods that people had put a lot of time and effort into. But the way that Valve and Bethesda went about it was, yet again, stupid. If a person, wolf, or apache attack helicopter downloads a mod, goes through the installation process, plays it, and thoroughly enjoys it, then and ONLY then should they be given the option of paying the creator. Not before, and definitely not in a way where ANY company can profit from works
And now, even though the backlash was extensive, and Valve having since completely reverting their stance on paid mods (bless them), Bethesda has gone ahead and done it again. Congrata-♥♥♥♥ing-lations Todd. Enjoy swimming in the dough you didn't earn.
But what am I going on about? There's no "Pay now!" option on the steam workshop. Of course there isn't, what did I just say about Valve reverting their stance (No seriously, I know everyone's mad about Artifuc-it: The Dota♥♥♥♥♥Cash Cow, but props to them for not endorsing Bethesda)? No, instead, Bethesda has released the, "Creation Club", where you can, "Support your favourite mods!" and "Enjoy officially supported content!" and "Obtain our super originally named premium currency called Credits!" and "Give us more money!" and "Support mod creators (but also us!)!" and "Give us more money!". Sounds fun, right?
Now, look, I know this review is gonna get bashed by Bethesda♥♥♥♥♥♥riders and people who play Fallout for for the "plot", saying that, "Oh, this change is no reason for you to bash the whole game!" or "Stop diluting the reviews with your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ing!" or &quot♥♥♥♥♥u u pace off shet♥♥♥♥♥♥falut foar is aa graeat game u jus t suk atr it lol n00b i fukd ur mum" and, honestly, I don't care. Modding holds a special place in my heart ever since I first tried it with Skyrim back in 2012. Five years of sitting at my desk, looking for that one special mod that would make my playthrough that much better. I know, cringey, and I will admit, from an outside perspective it probably is. I haven't made any mods, I've only donated to one (CBBE ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°)), and I haven't been with TES or Fallout for as long as some people, but I can say with surety that I, and most of the rest of the community, have fought the idea of paid mods with a passion since the beginning. Not because I hate mod creators, not because I don't want to see them thrive, no, it's because in this day and age I'm tired of greedy companies like Bethesda, Ubisoft, Take Two, etc. trying to take something that we, the people who play their games and put up with whatever♥♥♥♥♥♥they do, create for ourselves.

*Sigh* I look at my clock, and, wow, this took me nearly 3 hours to write. And I enjoy writing. I wanted to make sure I made this right, and that what I said would be clear and understandable. If it wasn't... well, sorry. Personally, I believe (unlike the usual general consensus) that Fallout 4 is a pretty good game. It doesn't hold a candle to the other games (at least in terms of story) but it's still enjoyable in it's own way. Let me make this clear,
. Yes, it has it's faults, and I'll be the first to admit them, however it's still a Fallout game. A Bethesda game. A buggy, unfinished mess that is like a guilty pleasure, something you can hate, but you'll still come back to, whether it's after a week, a month, or a year. And part of this longevity is the terrific modding community. Bethesda's "Creation Club" kills the spirit of modding. And, if we, as a community, don't speak out like this, or vote with our wallets, Bethesda'll think this sort of thing is okay. And, if a gaming giant like Bethesda can do this, then what's stopping other companies? Think about that. Think, if you aren't already completely braindead.
Peace.

Spiral Knights is a cute and fun hack and slash almost MMO style game.  It's free to play and you can purchase the premium currency with the in game currency.  This game is definitely freemium, you can achieve anything you need to with enough time whether you feel like spending money or not.  Once you start advancing in the game it becomes impossible to get further without actually spending time playing it so while using the premium currency can speed things up, anyone you see with high tiered gear actually spent time working for it.
The controls are simple and relatively easy to master.  With a wide variety of equipment to choose from it's easy to find a set to match your play style.  Whether you enjoy darting across the level with a stabby sword, kiting the monsters with a spectacular sidearm, using large AOE bombs, or swinging a sword that resembles a telephone pole, there's something for everyone.  Even better, you're not locked into any play style, you can change your equipment out almost every level if you want or need to.
This game has a bright and cheerful art style that's easy on the eyes and music that really works well with it.  Despite its light-hearted exterior, if you delve deeper into the missions you'll find some darker themes here and there that really add depth to the world you've crash landed on.
With the way the arcade runs every expedition is different, the prestige missions rotate every day and special events happen relatively often.
Almost everyone I've met in game has been friendly and willing to work as a team to tackle the tougher challenges of the clockworks.  It's not hard to find people to play with and you have the option to keep your party private if you want to play solo.
I definitely recommend Spiral Knights to anyone who's thinking of trying it, it's free to play so give it a shot and maybe you'll like it.  Bring some friends with you if you can it'll make the experience even more enjoyable.  See you in the citadel and beyond.

I like Fallout 4, as a guilty pleasure. The combat is smooth and enjoyable, and the world looks pretty, BUT...
For everything Fallout 4 does right, it does something of equal magnitude bad in a very similar area. I'll post a few examples.
Settlements: Good - It's an interesting system that allows you to spend hours building things. Bad - It's overused (pretty much 1/2 of open places you come across are settlement sites) and under-utilised by anything other than the goddess-awful Radiant Quests (where settlers often send you to the other side of the wasteland to kill some feral ghouls).
Weapons: Good - The variety is good and they play well, but... Bad - Unlike FO3 and FNV, FO4's weapons do NOT display when not in your hands, despite the fact that dropping them produces a model with all the modifications you made to that weapon (even badly added non-vanilla parts, like a scope on the double barrel shotgun).
World: Good - The world is generally very detailed (often demanding on your system in the city, Hint: Turn Godrays OFF, they crucify performance)m but... Bad - The world seems incredibly small, not helped by the generally flat terrain and huge expanse of water with nothing of note in it besides spectacle island (giant settlement) that takes up around 1/4 - 1/3 of the entire map.
Main Story Quests: Good - You aren't railroaded down the good guys path, and the 3 main factions (Minutemen are just a failsafe) give you some choice of morality. Bad - Before the big airship shows up (It's in the trailer, so not a spoiler), the main story is just dire. I didn't want my character to have a effing baby or be married to a male, I want her an eternal unmarried virgin like me, yet that awful main story focuses heavily on the baby until the airship arrives (then it sort of gets totally forgotten a few quests later and you can finally start RPing as one of the faction members).
Quests: Good - Some of the quests are pretty solid, but... Bad - It seems 90% of proper (AKA Not Radiant, those are a time waster for levelling and getting caps) are tied to the main story factions, so once that's over, you will be hard pressed to find a quest with any substance. If you want interesting things, read all the Terminals and notes you can find.
DLC: Good - Far Harbour and Nuka World are fun for different reasons, FH has a good story much better than anything Vanilla and has a large interesting worldspace. Nuka World skips on decent quests for the most part, but uncovering the history of the park and the park's jingle are good fun. Automatron and the Vault DLC are OK and can be fun but are basically just build-a-bot and build-a-vault with tiny quests attached. Bad - The Contraptions and whatever that other one is called Workshop DLCs are just a waste. Only bother with them if you get the season pass (I did, got it when it was at it's cheaper price before DLCs 4, 5 and 6 were officially announced).
Levelling: NO. Not going to go into this, as I'll be attacked by FNV Fanboys (catch-all term referring to more militant members of a fandom regardless of their gender).
Extra: Creation Club. Just no. It promised high quality mods, sorry "Creations" what we got was mostly things that modders have already done better, a joke (Horse Armour), a Gauss Rifle (about the only thing that is worth having as it's about the only thing modders haven't already done), and some item reskins. All for insane prices. When 100 points = 1 USD, and a pip-boy retexture costs 50 points while most things are 400 points, you start to see the issue.
On a final note. I KNOW FO4 is not great, but it's also not bad, as it's bad is balanced by it's good so it equals out as average. I personally think a LOT of FO4's hate is coming because it's not amazing (or merely good in the case of FO3, it's just too primitive to be great, although modders have fixed it with the TTW mod) like previous Beth, but merely average. More recently, a lot of (justified, but to a different product) hate will pour onto FO4 because of the creation club.
Give it a few years, and I'm sure mods like Fallout Cascadia and Fallout 4 Capital Wasteland (FO3 remake in FO4, you WILL NEED LEGAL COPIES OF BOTH GAMES for this to work) will fix a lot of Fallout 4's flaws and make it great, but until then, FO4 is merely average.

♥♥♥♥ this publisher and ♥♥♥♥ this game.
The last update broke Script Extender so I can't play it with the mods I have installed.
I came to Steam to roll back to the previous patch only to find out that I don't have that option and that they are implementing a paid mod scheme.
Now I'm sure that Script Extender will be updated in a few days, but until it is I can't play.  And even once it is there is a very good chance that many of the mods I've been using for free will no longer work.  And while this game is awesome with mods, it is♥♥♥♥♥♥without them.
Edit:  I want to expand on this just a bit.  I waited to buy this game.  I bought it 2 years after it's release.  I bought it a year after it's final DLC was released.  I expected what I bought to be the final form of the game.  I did not expect there to be any changes unless I made them by installing a mod.  I would not have bought it had I known that was not the case.  I want my money back, and I will not be buying anything released by this publisher in the future.  They broke my trust.
If you want to implement a paid mod scheme, fine.  But don't do it on a game that has been out for 2 years.  Do it on your next release, at release so everyone knows what they are getting.
Now, having said that I will not be buying any game that has a paid mod scheme (that the publisher gets a cut of).  Too many games are unplayable messes at release.  Fallout 4 was no exception, and Bethesda relied heavily on the mod community to fix problems with the game.  Now they have an incentive to create games that are filled with problems, whether it be bugs or incomplete and poorly thought out content.  They have an incentive to be careless, because now they can sell the fixes instead of doing it right from the start.
If someplace like nexus want's to create a system for paid mods to cover their operating costs and pay modders, that's fine.  I have no problem with that.  However, giving the game publisher a cut creates perverse incentives and I do not trust them to do the right thing.

Discovered a high-security prison known to house a VIP who has Intel on the Avatar project.  Sent 6 of my best soldiers in to infiltrate, and secure the target. Our snipers positioned themselves in a small tower nearby, while the Ranger proceeded to close the gap between herself and the Advent Troopers.  Our Specialist was on standby to compensate for any injuries or to hack into their systems where possible, and the two Grenadiers, who backed everyone up, were primed and ready with Acid as well as Incendiary grenades.
This is where all hell broke loose, our Ranger being a little overzealous decided to run in guns blazing ignoring any and all stealth training that was given, and proceeded to shout, "Suck my **** you ****suckers!"  While it's anyone guess as to why she would shout profanities pertaining to the male genitalia, she not only managed to startle the opposition but take out 3 advent troopers in the process with just her fusion blade.
The snipers tried their best to keep up, but she was on a roll.  A turret spotted her, but that didn't shake her determination, and her untouchable training paid off as the turret tried to gun her down, allowing her to dodge with ease.
Then it was the Grenadiers turn, while not the most subtle of the bunch they proceeded to rupture the turrets defenses to nothing, and allowed our Specialist a kill of his own (mind you it was against an inanimate object with minor programming that could've easily been stopped with a simple hack, but I digress).  There's a reason they are called "Special"ists.
Our soldiers moved forward into the prison itself and found themselves surrounded by 2 Andromedans and 2 more Advent troopers.  The Ranger, being a little more cautious this time around, decided to let the Snipers have a go before finishing off the troopers with her own rifle.  Although truth be told, I would have much preferred if the snipers would have used their high powered Plasma Lances instead of just Facing Off against the troopers with their hand guns.  Seriously?  I pay 500 bucks for a gun that can quite literally hit a mosquito off an elephant, and you decide to use your .45 colt because it's more "fun"?
The Andromedans unfortunately flanked one of the Grenadiers and before he was mercilessly killed, he did rain down a hail of bullets, depleting his ammo in the process.  However I'm told it was a "glorious death" by his partner Grenadier who decided to take it upon herself to launch an acid grenade into the fray for good measure.  As the Andromedans high powered suits went into auto-pilot mode and proceeded to run into melee range of our Specialist.

+ Snazzy new graphics. Weapons and armour look amazing.
+ Environments are varied and look a lot better than XCOM:EW.
+ Environmental destruction! Need a quick exit? A grenade on the far wall will do the trick nicely!
+ Psionic soldiers and powers are a lot more fleshed out.
+ Skills and abilities a lot more interesting.
+ Customization options.
+ Weapon upgrades.
+ Ammunition mods.
- Everything needs to be scanned and everyone is always in a rush and demand your immediate attention. There's a lot of flying back and forth across the world map. "Commander, we have supplies waiting for pickup in Asia." You fly over there to pick them up and then immediately something else pops up and requires you to deal with it. Then another thing. And another thing. And so on... It's annoying.
- Missions with timers are a Run-and-Gun gauntlet. This severely prohibits you from playing how you want and it detracts from the overall enjoyment of the game.
- Psionics are overpowered. Field a squad of Psi-Ops and you'll rarely want to run any other soldiers.
- Poorly optimized. Plenty of framedrops even with certain options turned down/off.
- Suffers from typical Firaxis-sequelitis with a touch of Bethesda-modanium - okay that was bad, but still. The fans are expected to "fix" the issues in the game with mods because it was half-arsed during development.
- Hacking and the weird randomness of it. Having a high hacking skill seems to do naff all. I've had a lot more success with non-specialist soldiers hacking things than with the class that is supposedly an expert on it.
- Accuracy is incredibly wonky. Standing in front of an alien, in the tile right next to it, does not give you a 100% to-hit chance.
- Pull mechanics from the Viper-alien is horribly broken. They can pull you straight through walls and obstacles.
- Melee attacks are also broken. Attacks through walls and obstacles are commonplace. Cover does nothing. I've had instances where I was able to strike an alien standing on the floor above me.
- Overwatch and shooting in general isn't making much sense, either. You can shoot through walls and hit the poor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ standing on the other side of the map as long as someone has spotted the enemy.
- The delays after every. single. action. Heal someone? Delay. Hack something? Delay. Shoot something? Delay.
- Unskippable cutscenes and Central bugging you constantly.
XCOM2 isn't bad but it isn't good either. The lack of quality assurance is clear; everything from poor optimization and broken pull-mechanics to all the delays after every single action. It's not much but every little thing adds up. I've spent over 300 hours in XCOM:EW (and god knows how many more in the originals) and I've enjoyed every single one of them, from the missed high-percentage shots to the one-shotting of the Über-Ethereal in the final mission. I have 50 odd hours logged in XCOM2 and I think I'll log another 30-40 to get the last few notable achievements (not Multiplayer, not touching that in an XCOM game) and after that, I don't think I'll play more. Not unless a major optimization patch fixes things.
Good question. I honestly don't know. I don't dislike the game but I don't like it either. It's all very "meh". It has so much potential but it is held back by its own failings.
Final verdict on XCOM2 is a 6/10. It is just... average. I only barely recommend this. It needs to be fixed before it can turn into a truly great game.

This game is
1. Challenging
2. Funny
3. Fun
This game also has alot of replayability. From changing the ways you proceed through the level, discovering funny things or maybe something cool, doing tricks and stunts, etc.
There is one thing you will need in order to play this game though...and that's patience. At first the game is VERY hard. Simply because you have to get used to and learn the controls. With a bit of patience you will be able to master the controls and be on your way as Top Bread. If you've learned to master the controls, you will find your self doing stunts, tricks, and even leaping across areas to get around the map. Not to mention that you can also use things that you find in the world around you to help you as well.
The point of the game is to turn into toast. There are multiple ways of doing so in every level. Either with a heater, toaster, hair straightener, etc. That adds some puzzle elements to the game. You proceed to the next level by toasting both sides of the bread. Make sure you don't over-toast though!
You also have an edibillity meter. You can think of this as your health. If you touch anything that can spoil the bread (a dish of fish, floor, bugs, dirt, etc) you will find the you will lose edibiillity. Once it reaches 0, you lose and must restart. Once you beat a level, you are scored with a letter grade based on your performance. You also have a Grip meter. You can't stay griped onto an object forever. So be quick and make sure that every move is worth it or else you will find yourself losing your grip and possibly falling all the way to the floor. It only takes about 2 seconds to fill up once you stop gripping things though.
Overl this game is very fun and very challenging.
The game only includes 4 levels at the moment, but more levels are planned.
As an Early Access game, there are very very few bugs. 85% chance of you being able to play without a problem.
The developers are also very active on the forums. They tend to joke around with the community, have fun, help players with troubleshooting errors, work on bugs, etc. They are a very awesome dev team to talk to on the forums!
At the moment, I see a possible 10+ hours of gameplay with the games current stage. But with more planned content (levels, easter eggs, more features, etc) I can see the amount of gameplay hours sky rocketing to a huuge amount.
This game is worth your $10
