Oh boy, where to begin with this? During April to May, I finished the first Dark Souls, and I simply couldn't get enough of it. It was to the point that I was thinking of Dark Souls 24/7 during my finals, checking the wikia, looking up the lore, thinking of how to beat certain bosses, etc. So when I saw Dark Souls II and Dark Souls III on sale, I absolutely can't let it slip my radar. Naturally, since I finished the first Dark Souls, I'd absolutely play Dark Souls II then Dark Souls III... well, that isn't what happened. Much of Dark Souls II was so slow and clunky (which I feel better elaborating in detail in my possible Dark Souls II review), that I quickly abandonned it in favor of Dark Souls III, since I already know how much better it is after playing at a friend's copy.
Boy did it deliver.
Dark Souls II had many bad first impressions, one of them being just how slow it feels compared to the first game. Dodges feels incredibly delayed and the parrying animation felt slower to me, don't get me started on how they changed the instant gratification of a riposte. Dark Souls III however seemed to have taken more lessons from Bloodborne, and I definitely thought it paid off. Dodging is even more viable than it ever was before in Dark Souls, thanks to the decrease of claustrophobic levels, which does let you run away from enemies to the next bonfire more viable as well, but I don't think that hurts the overall experience. With that said, I don't think the level design is anywhere near as memorable as Dark Souls I. I never found any level that gave me the insane gratification as the archers in Anor Londo, but I feel this is all compensated by just how damn well the bosses are.
Remember when I said Dark Souls III took more cues from Bloodborne? I think most of that design philosophy goes to the bosses more than anything else, you can see how much this is in play when you're as early as the Abyss Watchers. If they were in Dark Souls I, they'd most likely be a mid to endgame boss. In here however, they're most likely your third to fourth boss you'll face. If you're anything like me, that is to say constantly turtling and not having the balls to be aggressive, then they will wreck your♥♥♥♥♥in ways you never knew could be wrecked. If you did somehow managed to beat them that way, his second phase will utterly destroy you. Second phases are also played up much more dramatically in this game than the first game, they will force you to think of new strategies on the fly as you try to familiarize yourself with whatever they will do next. It's why Dark Souls III feels much more faster and aggressive, there's more emphasis on impromptu strategies and quick reflexes more than ever. It's also part of why I think it's definitely more difficult than previous Souls game, and also far more rewarding, giving you those moments where you just fistpump after killing that one boss you struggled all weekend on.
There are probably some things I haven't touched on more like the new FP system or the Weapon Arts, but I feel they don't really change the overall experience by much. I barely use any of the Weapon Arts in the base game, since they don't do much different to a normal attack, and the FP system at best just makes the Attunement stat more important if you intend to play with magic, which I just used for the heals.
I also just want to say that the music is as good as ever, probably won't sell you on the game if you didn't intend to buy the game based on this review, but I just like pointing out good music.
TL;DR: If you wanted a faster Dark Souls I with better emphasis on the bosses, then this is it.

Tough dungeon crawler with a lot of replayability. There is a lot of % and RNG based mechanics and skills included, though it may be annoying at times (rip Dismas virtue 6), it is what makes this game as difficult as it is. Without the RNG and "level cap", anyone could barrel through this game without any trouble by just grinding. On top of that, the "RNG" can be controlled to some extent by equipping trinkets and changing/removing negative passives, called quirks, that the heroes gain.
Aside from what I've seen as the general complaint/issue with this game, basically, you create a party of 4 heroes from a well-sized cast of options, grab some supplies, and venture through dungeons while managing your health and stress. Stress builds up from certain actions and can end up making your hero act irrational, which basically means you lose control over their turn from time to time. Either succeed in your quest and leave with a pile of loot, or fail and retreat back to the hamlet to grab another set of heroes and then start all over again. All your efforts amount to eventually facing the Darkest Dungeon and hopefully clearing it and achieving victory.
Gameplay is turn based in the form of a JRPG. The environment, music and atmosphere all come together to create a midieval and dark setting perfectly.

XCOM 2 is pretty much XCOM 1 but with more hair pulling action. The story has taken refreshing viewpoint, which makes this interesting for anyone who was already burnt out on XCOM 1. Nearly everything is on a timer and you really do feel the stress and urgancy. The combat of XCOM2 feels more tactical as well place nades and wall breaking situations are frequent. The character customization is very detailed, resulting in much heartache when you get blindsided by that lucky crit.
However as I've bought this game fairly close to launch, I've been met with some unfortunate experiences. The graphics presets are insane and will require tinkering if your pc wasn't built in the past 2 years. The graphics are still fairly solid even if toned down though. However that hardly matters when the game tends to randomly crash or soft lock. I've had many good runs just end because of these reason, including the final mission. If the game gets patched later, I'd definitely say buy it now.

You can really get absorbed into the story and atmosphere of this game. It has a very interesting stress mechanic system; where your characters gain stress over time from fights, exploration, and interactions with other party members. It really comes down to party management in this dungeon crawler and trying to get all your people out alive. And even if they come out alive, they won't be entirely unscathed: they'll end up with vices, diseases and disorders. Prepare to lose your favorite characters. Might even lose an entire party in the dungeons. And imagine a stress meter above your own head, slowly building up as you play :)
PROS:
-Some interesting mechanics, fun to find team synergies
-Large roster of characters to take care of, upgrade and level
NEGS:
-Very grindy after awhile. Especially if you lose characters, you have to level up new ones as replacements
-There aren't as many synergies as I'd like, so you usually play the same optimal team in the same dungeons
EDIT: Looks like there's a group downvoting positive reviews. Those people have reached their maximum stress meter playing this game lol.

Great game with many improvements over the previous XCOM: Enemy Unknown.
I'll start by saying I did not experience any of the bugs or performance issues experienced by other players. I purchased on launch and my experience has been very smooth. I have a mid to high-end computer and the game runs flawlessly. I did experience some crashing but it happens infrequently. Users with low-end PCs may have issues until the game is better optimized.
The biggest change that players seem to be complaining about is the timer. The whole campaign is basically on a timer and you have limited time to research, make contacts and hunt down supplies as there are constant alien interruptions. You would think the aliens would have the courtesy to leave me alone for 11 days while I research the plasma rifle that is going to triple their losses in battle. How dare they try to prevent me from destroying their race. All kidding aside, I enjoyed this mechanic as it forces you to make the most of the time you have available and doesn't allow you to rush through the research and create early super soldiers. There are many ways offered to halt and reverse the progress the aliens make essentially giving you more time for your own activities.
The only real flaw (and it is a major one, in my opinion) of the game is the RNG, or more specifically the in-game indicators of RNG are completely inaccurate and frankly, make no sense. I seem to hit more often with 43% chance than I do with 91% chance. The terrain also effects hit chance in a really weird way and the whole cover system seems to be broken.
Overall I'm 18 hours in and having a blast. I'll freely admit I've re-run some missions that have gone poorly for me in order to minimize the loss of a favored soldier, but half the fun in my opinion is seeing what happens differently during a mission by taking various actions.

You can really get absorbed into the story and atmosphere of this game. It has a very interesting stress mechanic system; where your characters gain stress over time from fights, exploration, and interactions with other party members. It really comes down to party management in this dungeon crawler and trying to get all your people out alive. And even if they come out alive, they won't be entirely unscathed: they'll end up with vices, diseases and disorders. Prepare to lose your favorite characters. Might even lose an entire party in the dungeons. And imagine a stress meter above your own head, slowly building up as you play :)
PROS:
-Some interesting mechanics, fun to find team synergies
-Large roster of characters to take care of, upgrade and level
NEGS:
-Very grindy after awhile. Especially if you lose characters, you have to level up new ones as replacements
-There aren't as many synergies as I'd like, so you usually play the same optimal team in the same dungeons
EDIT: Looks like there's a group downvoting positive reviews. Those people have reached their maximum stress meter playing this game lol.

This is my first review on steam, I just thought I should make a counter point to a lot of reviews that make complaints about the game play I definitely don't share and that are in my opinion mostly a misunderstanding.
Darkest dungeon is a challenging permadeath rpg with very appealing art style and cthulu'esque back story. The game makes it clear to the player that it is meant to be sressfull, to punish him for bad decisions and poor preparations, to surprise him with seemingly unfair enemies and crippling disadvantages. It tells you time and again that your heroes will die, so don't get attached. Each dungeon could be the last for your favorite crusader MountCrushmore or your beloved vestal Bones. But that's not so bad, new heroes arive all the time.
That mechanic can and will be frustrating for many, you will curse RNGesus and your computer for every crit you receive and every miss you get. Some deal with this by writing a bad review how unfair the game is, others try to learn from and prepare better for the next fight.
Having said that, I didn't really have those problems. Sure, in other games your tank doesn't loose have his hitpoint with a single stroke, but you can get used to it. Throughout the game (except the final battle, but I won't spoil that), I only lost two heroes. One was a low level newb I sacrificed deliberately in a story related decision. The other I lost because I didn't want to retreat and was counting on my luck... well... don't do that. I only had to retreat from two dungeons. I did consult the wiki for the bosses from about half the game onward, so that helped. It takes away the surprise, but you can prepare, which I preferred. I also disabled some the harder optional game play settings later on. All in all, you can fine tune your own difficulty setting. If you disabel those options and read the wiki, the game is almost easy, so it's for you to decide. I still cursed and lamented my losses though, but I see that stress as a bonus in this case, it fits the background and art style very well: You don't command immortal and nigh invincible heroes here, but you are suposed to fight a hopeless and losing battle against evil itself.
I personally also liked the changes the devs made to the game. The new quest dungeon "Wolves at the door" nicely forces your hand and is well crafted. The corpses are a nice gameplay element you can even use to your advantage. The antiquarian is an original addition to your roster and fun to play with.
Some reviewers criticise repetitiveness and lack of quests. That is partly true. You play very similar dungeons throughout the game and the enemies you saw in the first 10 hours will mostly not change dramatically, but enough to keep it interesting. What kept me going is restructuring my party: Since your heroes have to recuperate regularly in town and won't take low level quests, you have to change your line up all the time. I discovered new useful combinations of skills and characters right until the end. The "quests" are mostly the dozen or so bosses, most of which you will kill in 3 different difficulties, they are in some way the heart of the game. And each one is original and interesting.
The trinket system (Main equipment of your heroes is generic, but they are not supposed to survive for long anyway ;) is of a rather reduced complexity, but it's very rewarding when you can equip just the right baubles and shinies for exactly this line-up and this quest, so I liked it.
All in all, I got a full 28-hero roster of lvl 6 heroes (including 3 antiquarians, that was some stressfull "dungeoning") but it didn't feel like a grind since I always switched up my party. I also generally detest grind.
I spent 80 very enjoyable hours in this game (1 play-through), but I guess most people will be quite a lot faster. I just wanted the perfect line up and best equip.
I wholeheartedly recommend this game to everybody who enjoys turn-based rpgs.

This game is essentially Terraria in space. If you like Terraria, you'll love this game. I don't like Terraria. I don't like this game. It's as simple as that. The comparisons will be made as the two games are similar. Out of the two, I prefer Terraria but that really isn't saying much.
I also feel like the early access feature of this game isn't working in its favour. The character erases really only served to help fix bugs that should have been obvious to begin with if the creators of the game actually played what they had before releasing it to the public. It also forced players to have to play through the entire game again, with little if any changes that made the character erases worthwhile.
As for the races, the only differences between them other than apperances is what foods they can eat and the flavour text of examining objects. Nothing worth noting, and really no draw to play other races unless flavour text is your thing. Character customisation is minimal and matters little beyond the "personality" stance and the appearance of hair and face pixels as the armour usually covers up what you wear. Costume changes in the game are few and far between, but I can appreciate the call to pop culture that is the hilarious horse head mask.
The best part of the game for me were the weapon names.
Even with the minimalistic graphics of the game, I constantly lagged while playing with my friend which really soured the experience for me. I realise this has a lot to do with my own personal internet connection, but if I can play a modded minecraft server with five other people with no issues, I should be able to play this with no issues.
The game itself held up. Nothing was inherently broken. Game play was logical and getting from point A to point B was no problem, even if I had a frequent experience with jamming in mid air due to waiting for the next five inches of terrain to load.
All in all, not my thing. I would probably be able to look over the issues I had if I actually cared for the game style.

I TRIED to like this game... I REALLY did, but I just can't do it.
- The PVP is terrible (Greatsword meta and Hyper armor =/= Poise)
- The bosses are on crack rushing around the boss room, can't even make sense of them
- The only proper strategy is to rollspam through attacks (no sense in ACTUALLY dodging a boss' attack)
- The "new" mechanics are just ripped from prior games (like FP meter from Demon Souls, or Hyper Armor from Bloodborne)
- The lore on some parts is terrible (The Ringed City and The Nameless King for example)
- The fanservice is so obvious that it hurts (like Soul of Cinder's second phase, or Anor Londo? REALLY?!?)
- The colors give the game a very dull and depressing mood (can't see anything but gray everywhere) which fits Bloodborne, but not a Dark Souls game
- They act like Dark Souls 2 never happened, but still take aspects from the game (some of which make no sense, like the armor sets or Laddersmith Gilligan)
- The chugging meta in PVP is terrible and even NPC phantoms can chug estus (anyone who has fought Hawkwood the Deserter knows what I'm talking about)
- They removed many good aspects that were in Dark Souls 2 (like the Cracked Blue Eye Orb or the Small White Soapstone)
- The players are bullied into NG+ and NG+2 by placing +1 and +2 rings there
- The covenant rewards are annoying to get, especially when you are trying to get all of the achievements (waited over two hours to get summoned for the Blade of the Darkmoon covenant, immediately got kicked out of session -.- )
- Slaveknight Gael is a terrible ending boss battle to the souls- series, his cape has a hitbox? REALLY?!? (Manus was the real final boss battle in the souls- series for me, and even Nashandra was a better final boss than Gael)
In my opinion Dark Souls 3 is game which started with a LOT of potential, but they ruined it by filling the game with fanservice and taking too much influence from Bloodborne. The fast combat of Bloodborne doesn't fit Dark Souls, and the rollspam strategy is a result of it. If you're going to double the speed of the enemies when comparing to prior games, you HAVE TO make the player move twice as fast too! The speed difference stands out really clearly. Even though Dark Souls 2 was a failure in many players' eyes, it still tried to be unique and use original ideas... I wish I could say the same about Dark Souls 3...
If you're like me and you just HAVE TO get this game (just because it's a souls- game), I recommend playing it in offiline mode to get the best experience and not getting the DLCs (they aren't worth it). The first DLC (the Ashes of Trailer Spoilers) is a terrible excuse for a DLC, which plays on the nostalgia of players who went to the Painted World of Ariamis in the first game. The second DLC is just a sh*tstorm with maybe ONE good boss (I'll let you figure out which one of them that is). I know that my opinion is of the minority, but that's because I'm not going to hop on the bandwagon of Dark Souls 1 fanboys and praise Miyazaki for another great game.
As a singular entity this game is great, and I would give it much praise, but when comparing it to prior games of the soulsborne- series, it really brings nothing new into the mix. It really is an unholy abomination stitched together from mechanics of prior souls- games and with a paint layer of Bloodborne. I hate to say this, but I don't think this game is worth buying.

Great game with many improvements over the previous XCOM: Enemy Unknown.
I'll start by saying I did not experience any of the bugs or performance issues experienced by other players. I purchased on launch and my experience has been very smooth. I have a mid to high-end computer and the game runs flawlessly. I did experience some crashing but it happens infrequently. Users with low-end PCs may have issues until the game is better optimized.
The biggest change that players seem to be complaining about is the timer. The whole campaign is basically on a timer and you have limited time to research, make contacts and hunt down supplies as there are constant alien interruptions. You would think the aliens would have the courtesy to leave me alone for 11 days while I research the plasma rifle that is going to triple their losses in battle. How dare they try to prevent me from destroying their race. All kidding aside, I enjoyed this mechanic as it forces you to make the most of the time you have available and doesn't allow you to rush through the research and create early super soldiers. There are many ways offered to halt and reverse the progress the aliens make essentially giving you more time for your own activities.
The only real flaw (and it is a major one, in my opinion) of the game is the RNG, or more specifically the in-game indicators of RNG are completely inaccurate and frankly, make no sense. I seem to hit more often with 43% chance than I do with 91% chance. The terrain also effects hit chance in a really weird way and the whole cover system seems to be broken.
Overall I'm 18 hours in and having a blast. I'll freely admit I've re-run some missions that have gone poorly for me in order to minimize the loss of a favored soldier, but half the fun in my opinion is seeing what happens differently during a mission by taking various actions.

Trove is a casual and social online game comparable to the unfortunately vaporware'd Cube World, with a heavy focus on collection.
Like Minecraft and so many others, Trove's world is composed of dynamic voxels and gameplay heavily revolves around gathering resources from the environment and building stuff. However, Trove uses Cube World's more detailed graphics (characters are composed of many small squares, not a few big ones painted), and relies on a series of procedurally generated instances for its adventure & combat content, while player-made content is confined to Cornerstones and Club Worlds.
The name you register on signup is your account name, and all of your classes are effectively separate "characters" on that account who will be identified only by that name. Trove will individually remember all of their equipment and style options, allowing you to decorate your Knight as a burly man while your Fae Trickster is a cute girl with pigtails; you won't need to readjust every time you switch classes.
Your classes each have a base level that maxes out at 20 and is increased by earning experience, but this is not from where the bulk of your power will originate. Equipment that is upgraded far enough will begin to earn Shadow Levels, and those levels are added to your base level, affecting what level-gated worlds that class may access and better representing your ridiculous strength. The current maximum level when including Shadow Levels is 42, at level 20 with 3 Radiant (Shadow Level 6) gears and a Shadow Level 4 Ring.
In addition, you have an account-wide Mastery Level that is raised through leveling up each class (+15 XP per class level) and by collecting build recipes, styles, and specialty equipment (mounts et al.) Every 100 XP is one Mastery Level, and each level adds a perk such as a Max HP bonus or a special style item to signify your achievement.
Chaos Factor is a valued commodity - for every 1 Chaos Factor, you will receive 1 Chaos Chest every day that you log in. Chaos Chests have a chance of giving exclusive items not obtainable in any other way.
The primary way to gain Chaos Factor is to consume Chaos Coins, items so valuable you can't fit enough money in the trade window for them. Each coin adds 1 Chaos Factor. You will receive non-tradable Chaos Coins at Mastery Level 100 (~1 week of play) and 200, while tradable coins can be found rarely in Chaos Chests and are given out by the Trion Worlds official stream at certain viewer milestones.
Patrons (monthly subscribers) automatically benefit from +2 (or is it +4 I forget) Chaos Factor for as long as they are subscribed. Keep in mind it's possible to buy Patron Passes from other players with ingame currency. In addition, for every $1000 spent on the game, you get +1 Chaos Factor permanently, but that is ONE THOUSAND DOLLARS you could have spent on keeping your PC up to date or padding your bottom with unnecessarily fancy confections.

You can really get absorbed into the story and atmosphere of this game. It has a very interesting stress mechanic system; where your characters gain stress over time from fights, exploration, and interactions with other party members. It really comes down to party management in this dungeon crawler and trying to get all your people out alive. NEGS:

This is my first review on steam, I just thought I should make a counter point to a lot of reviews that make complaints about the game play I definitely don't share and that are in my opinion mostly a misunderstanding.
Darkest dungeon is a challenging permadeath rpg with very appealing art style and cthulu'esque back story. The game makes it clear to the player that it is meant to be sressfull, to punish him for bad decisions and poor preparations, to surprise him with seemingly unfair enemies and crippling disadvantages. It tells you time and again that your heroes will die, so don't get attached. Each dungeon could be the last for your favorite crusader MountCrushmore or your beloved vestal Bones. But that's not so bad, new heroes arive all the time.
That mechanic can and will be frustrating for many, you will curse RNGesus and your computer for every crit you receive and every miss you get. Some deal with this by writing a bad review how unfair the game is, others try to learn from and prepare better for the next fight.
Having said that, I didn't really have those problems. Sure, in other games your tank doesn't loose have his hitpoint with a single stroke, but you can get used to it. Throughout the game (except the final battle, but I won't spoil that), I only lost two heroes. One was a low level newb I sacrificed deliberately in a story related decision. The other I lost because I didn't want to retreat and was counting on my luck... well... don't do that. I only had to retreat from two dungeons. I did consult the wiki for the bosses from about half the game onward, so that helped. It takes away the surprise, but you can prepare, which I preferred. I also disabled some the harder optional game play settings later on. All in all, you can fine tune your own difficulty setting. If you disabel those options and read the wiki, the game is almost easy, so it's for you to decide. I still cursed and lamented my losses though, but I see that stress as a bonus in this case, it fits the background and art style very well: You don't command immortal and nigh invincible heroes here, but you are suposed to fight a hopeless and losing battle against evil itself.
I personally also liked the changes the devs made to the game. The new quest dungeon "Wolves at the door" nicely forces your hand and is well crafted. The corpses are a nice gameplay element you can even use to your advantage. The antiquarian is an original addition to your roster and fun to play with.
Some reviewers criticise repetitiveness and lack of quests. That is partly true. You play very similar dungeons throughout the game and the enemies you saw in the first 10 hours will mostly not change dramatically, but enough to keep it interesting. What kept me going is restructuring my party: Since your heroes have to recuperate regularly in town and won't take low level quests, you have to change your line up all the time. I discovered new useful combinations of skills and characters right until the end. The "quests" are mostly the dozen or so bosses, most of which you will kill in 3 different difficulties, they are in some way the heart of the game. And each one is original and interesting.
The trinket system (Main equipment of your heroes is generic, but they are not supposed to survive for long anyway ;) is of a rather reduced complexity, but it's very rewarding when you can equip just the right baubles and shinies for exactly this line-up and this quest, so I liked it.
All in all, I got a full 28-hero roster of lvl 6 heroes (including 3 antiquarians, that was some stressfull "dungeoning") but it didn't feel like a grind since I always switched up my party. I also generally detest grind.
I spent 80 very enjoyable hours in this game (1 play-through), but I guess most people will be quite a lot faster. I just wanted the perfect line up and best equip.
I wholeheartedly recommend this game to everybody who enjoys turn-based rpgs.

Spiral Knights is an Isometric Real-Time Adventure game, where you play as a knight who has crash landed on an alien clockwork planet. The lower levels of the planet shift continually, making navigation hazardous and unpredictable. You can go solo or party up in groups of four.
PROS: Soundtrack, level design, graphics, story, auction house
CONS: Occasional hit-detection wonkiness
This game is oddly addicting. Its art style combined with its soundtrack make it instantly memorable. Gameplay is really solid and fairly simple. You can spend hours delving through randomly generated levels, or simply spend hours browsing the auction house looking for a great deal on your next sword or gun.
As stated above, occasionally you will die from hit-detection lag. This can be very irritating when navigating high-level monster rooms, but it is not game-breaking.
If you decide to try this game, be warned. It will charm you into giving away hours of your time.

I'm a vet of XCOM:EW (won Classic several times, and even beat Long War) and unfortunately this game gets a thumbs-down, for many of the same reasons others have said.
(And before people downvote saying "but there's a mod to help with that" - games shouldn't require mods to be fun. Mods should make the game more fun. Mods shouldn't make the game less bad.)
1. Timer-based everything. It was a cool mechanic once in a while in EU/EW, but the now most the game - both the missions and the geoscape - are all on a ticker, as Bradford frequently reminds you. Even on normal it's easy to find the Avatar project completed by June if you haven't done many plot missions yet.
EDIT: There are many good mods out there that change the timing, though after a few games it looks like my RNG handed me a lot of timed missions in a row which put a bad taste in my mouth. You can even disable the doomsday clock with mods though I'd advise against it.
2. HEY COMMANDER OVER HERE. The game is constantly interrupting you on the geoscape. New mission, supply drop available, whatever. It's arguably interrupting you all the time even during missions because Bradford won't shut up about how civilians are being massacred after someone gets shot the first time a five-turn dash away.
EDIT: "Shut up, Bradford" is a must-have mod.
3. RNG on steroids. In EW you had RNG but it was your job to help mitigate it, by having a backup when that 95% chance shot missed. Here, the RNG controls everything. The difference on whether a retaliation mission is relative cakewalk or not depends on whether four civilians spawned next to the drop point, or whether there is an unscalable mountain (with no cover on top) between you and the camp. I've seen a base defense where the objective was within sniper range from the Avenger, and ones where it was down a gully or on the other side of a hill. That's not something you can just mitigate with squad loadout, that's the difference between achieving the mission with minimal losses and a meatgrinder, all based on the roll of a die. And that can make the difference in whether a campaign is feasible to win or not. No, that is not XCOM, baby.
EDIT: This is still an issue. Especially with Avenger Defense, a hill in between can mean the difference between being able to send out a scout and snipe from close to the LZ, or having to move your squad out while simultaneously having to defend the Avenger from aliens. Really not great design and a mission that I never look forward to.
4. Performance. Beyond awful. A 970 that can handle Witcher 3 on mostly ultra has gotten one-two FPS in the Avenger. Loading screens longer than a Mass Effect elevator ride. How did this game even ship?
EDIT: Fixed for the most part but still taxes the system heavily for a turn-based game.
5. Buggy LOS. I've had a mission where I had to rescue a scientist and (for whatever reason) they were "sighted" by my squad on the other side of a building. The scientist - inside a van - resulted in enemies outside the van being activated as well, who proceeded to take shots at the scientist because my squad was too far away. That's just one example, there are others where you have a choice between reloading and hoping the LOS doesn't bug out again, or trying to honestman it through and hope the berserker that your squad shouldn't have seen doesn't outright murder you.
EDIT: Haven't had this problem recently, perhaps it was fixed, though I still see LOS glitch out. Save early and often!
I've seen the final fight of the game, and am not really looking forward to it. In fact I think I'd bail on the last mission due to the BS it throws at you.
EDIT: Final mission has unlimited enemies which... I dunno, it's slightly better than the canned XCOM:EU end mission, but also forces you into certain squad composition (heavy on cooldown-based classes like PSI, light on limited use classes like grenadiers.)

Once again, this game is almost made as a joke. Not implying that it's bad, but it's one of those jokes that in the past people would make fun of. "HAH! Who'd want to play a game where you're a slice of bread?" Apparently alot of people.
KEEP IN MIND that the goal in this game is to become toast. By any means necessary. Be it Toaster or Radiator, your goal is to become toast.
---
Now i'll note why I believe the keyboard / mouse controlls are wonky.
To grip onto things, you have 1,2,3, and 4. To grab things, you have Q,W,E, and R. To look around, you use Right Click, and to move around, you use Left Click. I believe this control scheme could have been improved in some fassion. Such as look around being locked onto the cursor.
So ways I think they could improve the mouse & keyboard controlls;
1. Make the camera snap to the cursor, so you look around by moving the mouse.
2. Use a control layout that's a little bit more natural, for instance;
---When I place my left hand on my keyboard, my fingers naturally will rest on (From left to right); Left Shift, A, W, D and the Space Bar.
---A Good Idea would be to change it from 1234 to LShift, A, D, and Space Bar, using W for push away from camera and S for being pull towards the camera (Or the direction that the camera is facing).
---Another way to change the control scheme, is to do what's listed above, but change the camera look from mouse to arrow keys. This would make gameplay better on laptops, and users who prefer playing with a keyboard.
The game is in early access, so again, things will change over time. Hopefully the controlls for keyboard/mouse will become more naturall over time.
Aside from that, I do reccomend this fun quirky little game.

To summarise my opinion on this game, the learning curve is like trying to climb an overhanging cliff, both literally and metaphorically.
There isn't much really to say about it, the controls are almost unusable;, they worked in Surgeon Simulator where you where the camera was always the same, however in this the camera has a variable orientation, and so relying on the direction of the bread which isn't easily distinguishable when you're stuck on something of the horribly balanced first level or fell onto the floor because you don't want to move the camera around to see if the gap between the fridge and the cubbard is too big to gap (protip: the cubbard receeds so far in you cannot scale it whatsoever, avoid at all costs) and while you can get used to the controls, you do so in the manner someone who recently was disabled learns to use the toilet while in a wheelchair. I'd reccomend changing it so that the arrow keys move in relation to where the camera is facing, and WASD are fixatedly assigned to a corner, and overlap each other the further away they are from the camera.
Also, the camera has the sensetivity of my rib cage being perforrated by the fingers of someone with anorexia. Even the slightest movement will cause it to jerk 180, and if you were grabbing onto something good luck getting where you were planning on going before you fall to the floor with the (at least what I interpreted) message "♥♥♥♥ you thats what you get for trying to rotate the camera".
Also, the trailer is very misleading. While it advertises a simple game that tells the tale of a slice of bread on its quest to become toasted, when you get in game you get a happy upbeat song to the tune of a level whose traversability resembles that of a poorly made game with graphics that don't match the lacking quality of the level. The Jenga blocks are evil and you will get stuck on them because you're a loaf of bread with a big area and those jenga blocks don't leave much room on either side for you to pass.
You are virtually immobile when not grabbing onto something, and I think that is just stupid. Grabbing should be a method to assist you to get from A to B, not be the only way to do it. Just have the bread flip and timble according to what edges/surfaces are touching what and in what direction the bread is travelling.
Finally, make getting past the fridge easier. If you try to go up it you'll run out of grip before you realise there is no space at the top to climb over, and if you try to go in front of it you'll realise that the cubbard handles protrude so much that the stale bread you represent cannot bend the majority of its body mass around the corner of a fridge ever so slightly to grip the recessed area of the cubbard, which if you didn't know is basically everything except the handles.
I said it once and I will say it again, stay away from the cubbard because it will ♥♥♥♥ you up.
First level needs some SERIOUS rebalancing, music is too upbeat, camera is on steroine and the controls are aparaplegic.
Those problems need to be fixed fast, because thats not how you add challenge to a game, thats how you make it unplayable, a hugely unappealing game, and a waste of €8.

It is a side-scrolling TBS / dungeon-crawler with a small side of hero / town management.  I love the difficulty but it is too much for some gamers.  If you can't deal with losing or if you ragequit easily, this game is not for you.
+Amazing narration by Wayne June (joyful when winning, condescending when losing). Great graphics and sound. Lots of classes for varied party builds. DD has come a long way since I called it "dungeon-crawl lite" in early access. I really like the stress management system. Game mechanics are easy to learn and understand.
-A lot of the difficulty is stacked on the front-end. In the end-game, non-tank types feel too squishy. I don't care for fighting the same bosses three times each (feels grindy).  Some RNG can make you feel like strategy is out the window.
Played through in about 100-120 hours (some idle time and I'm not the fastest). Had some wonderful fights along the way both win and lose. Terrible things will happen despite your best intentions.  Thankfully, the game warns you every time you start it:

So Spiral Knights... I played back in ye olde days before the steam release. For quite a while actually. months of playtime, possibly half a year. I went through the hell that was the CANT LOG IN phase in the game, stopping me from playing for a couple of weeks, which really killed me. That event seriously injured the game, and if I remember, wasa caused by some hacking over at Sega (but dont quote me on that). This little paragraph was just a backstory to what I've been through with this game, just to let you know that I LOVE this game, or atleast used to more than I do now, so the actual review is down below...
One last thing, I have not played this game in over a year, but I've looked at the update logs and such, so I atleast know what's happened.
Alright, the pros of this game. The gameplay itself is basic, but not mind-numbingly boring. You move around, attack, pick things up, dodge, etc. Better than most MMO's today, with all that clicking on something to blindly attack whatever bull. The art style of the game is quite nice. The soundtrack...boy, I REALLY like the soundtrack, one of my favorite things about this game. The community (in-game, why this is will be said later...) is probably one of the best things about this game. I made many in-game friends playing this game, some in particular were very nice and cool. And as I see in other reviews, Im not alone. The shop that drives the economy is the auction house, where you can put things up for crowns (currency). There are npc vendors, but I'll be honest, no one uses them, unless they have something unique.
Alright, now the bad stuff, the stuff I really hate to see. In the old days of Spiral Knights, there was mist energy. It regenerated quite slowly up to a maximum of 100. Elevators in the game were used to continue on through the levels, but cost 10 energy to use. So that's basically 10 levels a day, maybe around 12 if you use it at specific times. Crystal energy is considered the premium currency in this game, since every f2p game ever has to have one. But on one fateful day, mist energy was removed, but elevators are now free to use. This was a very smart decision, I thought, except when the rest of the update was revealed. Originally, to craft things, pretty much the only way to get high tier gear, you used energy and materials dropped from enemies. You would also pick up heat for your gear, which is used to level it up and make it better. But then, they added Orbs of Alchmey and Fire Shards. Orbs weren't that awful for me, but only because the game requires you to have a certain level weapon in order to craft the next tier of weapon. With the new fire shards, you had to have a specific fire shard, and depending on the amount you used, would show a percentage that the heat level up would be succesful. So you had to have lady luck on your side unless you want to potentially waste all your crystals on one of 10 heat levels (the max). Basically, the game became a grindfest for orbs and shards (and I didnt mention that lower grade shards cant be combined to make bigger shards, but bigger shards can be smashed into smaller ones. BUT you had to have the recipe to do that, which was given to you when you completed the gear check once you had all the same tier gear. Ex: Full tier 4 gear check, you go through, you can now get tier 5 gear. You get a recipe for smashing tier 5 shards, the ones you need, for tier 4 shards, the ones you USED to need. The system is very broken, and I dont think its changed at all.)
Before missions, there was the arcade, a place where gateways led to branches of levels, and players could influence which levels showed up in next weeks gates. This was were you went to actually PLAY the game. That always struck me as interesting. But when the missions came out, you could just skip all those levels and go straight to the boss levels, the main reason people were going down certain gates. Sure, it saved time and wasnt as much as a pain to get there, but missions literally KILLED the arcade. I dont see anyone there anymore, even though it still exists. I just feel it takes some exploration out of the game.
But what about the crystals? Now they're used for feeding your pet, which you get through a line of missions. Everyone freaked out at this since every MMO must ALWAYS have pets. When they came out, you could choose a mini dragon that shoots fire, a phantom ghost that shot out caustic needles and could go invisible, and a cat. You know, just a  cat that flies around. Guess which one no one ever picked...(the cat). Thing is, once I got my pet, I used him some, leveled him up a bit, but I always forgot about him. I never used him as often as he was intended, even though when I did remember him, he did help some. Doesn't this show that we have come to not need pets? We played the game to work as a team of knights traversing through the unknown depths of an alien planet, cut off from the rest of our home. Now its more like pet simulator.
And last but CERTAINLY not least, the new updates. I looked at over 30 update logs within the past year or so. All but about 2 had ACTUAL content. The rest of them were just adding limited time reskins of cosmetics, that cost money to get. This is just sad...  this isnt tf2.
Ok, so I sound like I dont like this game right? Well, I dont like what its become. I liked it before, (except for the elevators becoming free, that was the best thing ever) where it was actually different from other games. Like I said, I love this game, and I hate to see it die like this.
TL;DR (because i'll be honest, this review is frickin long) The game is fun, enjoyable, and all around a cool experience, although its taken some turns for the worst. I wouldnt want to see this game die, since it seems to be bleeding out right now. But overall I give this game a 7/10, or if nostalgia is added to the equation, 8/10. This game is a fantastic f2p, and I recommend it to anyone who is willing to try it out. Do note that the bad things kick in later in the game. You can enjoy the game starting out up til then.
Thank you for reading, and I hope you enjoy Spiral Knights.

The game is interesting enough, atmosphere and art are well done, the stress mechanism is very immersive.
On the other hand, the permanent death mechanism attracted me, but eventually I found it anti-fun. When you lose four guys at level 3 (max level is 6), you are kind of screwed, but well you just hire four other guys and you keep the game rolling.
However, when your four-man party gets wiped in the final dungeon, after a dozen or so of hours just to level and equip these guys, all that's left for you is to grind more hours. And then get wiped again, and... You get the idea.
I play hardcore Diablo 3 (and played hardcore Diablo 2 before that), so grinding and restarting is not something I am opposed to. But Darkest Dungeon is not a grinding game, what is fun in this game is making progress towards an end goal (while in the Diablo series, trashing monsters and finding loot is what's fun). When your entire game is reset, it just feels like you've lost your time.
For the record, this is one of the very few Steam games I own that I quit without finishing (too lazy to check, but in fact it may be the only one). Some would say I am just not good enough, I would say that it is not rewarding enough.

So, it was an interesting FOS that tried to merge some parts of a class based loadout system from games like the Battlefield and CoD lines. The game has simple objective game modes (TDM, Search and Destroy, Protect/Assassinate the VIP) that do not have any kill streak (or rather, point streak) perks. The one ground war-esque game mode has two teams vying to destroy 5 objectives owned by the opposing team. This is the only one with the point-streak perks active. Weapon loadouts are separate from the different perk paths you can choose in the ground war game mode. Weapon handling is okay, really varies based on weapon. Some weapons feel like laser guns without recoil where as others feel like you're lugging a giant stick around.  All in all, I would've said this game was acceptable for a free FPS... until recently. Hackers showed up, infinite rocket launchers ruining the ground war maps. The other game modes are done better in other games, so I played those far less.
Pros:
Decent weapon variety with wildly different handling on each gun.
No noticable rubber-banding while I was playing (decent servers).
Perk variety is fairly wide accross the 4 current classes. (Although they currently do not have any additional perks from the base set)
Fairly easy to earn in game currency between matches, daily log in, and initial welcome pack.
I found the VIP mode to be quite interesting as the killing team also needed to escape; a nice move towards balancing the game mode (disliked the VIP being AI).
Cons:
On the slippery slope of pay 2 win model. (Some things currently are locked behind pay wall)
Guns do not reliably feel like they handle well. They are missing something to make them each feel more... real.
No try mode for guns in the shop. You don't actually know what you're getting besides some numbers on the side.
The hackers have arrived.
In many small ways, the game feels unpolished. It's the same thing that many other F2P FPS games suffer from.
Overall, it was a fun little time sink for a bit, but the amusement is fleeting and the hackers rapidly drained the remainder of the fun. No apparent report system (not that it matters in a F2P). If you want a game to play for a few hours to have fun, this is fine. If you want a game to commit to and play for a while, I'd say avoid this one.

I have no desire to build at the moment, because they will wipe the worlds again when they finalize the universe map.When progression is changed to center around various hazards that will be found on the planets, it will probably be safe to build again. I cant' complain about the lack of content too much since the game simply isn't finished yet, but they really havn't made much progress towards their ideal, randomly generated game structure; as the current quest line ends after the first boss. Progression after the fourth boss is so fast, I'd really have prefered they left out the remaining levels.
The game is VERY FUN and addicting, right up until you hit the "Impervium Wall." A damning blow that launched all my friends out of the game, and confined me to my ship. The game will need much more substance than what is currently available before I could recommend it as it is now. That all being said; dont' buy this game YET, but you'll definetly want to play it later on. Starbound will have far more, longer lasting appeal ONCE ITS READY for showtime. Q: Give me a TL;DR version.
A: Buy the game and git gud.
Q: I heard the game is hard. Is it good for causal player?
A: Yes.
Q: Is it good for Skyrim player?
A: Yes, but you'll need to learn new mechanics such as parrying and roll timing.
Q: Is it a good game for family, friend etc?
A: Yes. The game has a password feature to co-op with friend. I think the game is educational for children, as it teaches people to not give up and overcome hardship.
Q: Is this game full of rainbow and candy?
A: No, it's closer to a horror game, especially in some later areas. Even prettier areas are infested with monsters. The atmosphere of this game is very grim and grey-ish.
Q: Tutorial?
A: Check the signs in the first map. You can check the keyboard-controller maping in setting. The first map has mooks, a mini boss and a boss for you to play with. The tutorial boss, Gundyr, teaches you various evasion technique.
Q: Is there a mini map?
A: No. But since you might die a number of times you'll get familiar with the map. There are many shortcuts.
Q: Is there an easy mode?
A: It's called greatshield, you can get one in the second map but need some levelling up to use it. Starting as knight (default) also counts as an easy mode in early game.
Q: I don't like invaders.
A: Start the game in offline mode, you can change this in setting. You can still play with NPC phantoms but cannot co-op. If you are online, stay unembered prevent invasion but you cannot co-op. If you are invaded you can also run toward the boss fog gate. Edit: you can join Way of Blue in the second map, that will lower the chance of being invaded as well.
Q: Mooks attack 100 times in a row.
A: Try spacing.
Q: Mooks gank me. Unfair!
A: Try looking around, this game is known for enemy trolling you every corner. Lock on feature will spot enemy above.
Q: Bosses are too fast.
A: It's kind of counterintuitive, but you sometimes need to roll toward them. Check Youtube if you have trouble. Don't worry, dying to boss is a learning process.
Q: What's the main strength of this game?
A: Best video game soundtrack.
Q: What's the weakness of this game?
A: Too short compared to DS2, not enough armor/weapon/spells.
Q: Should I buy DS1 and DS2 instead?
A: DS1 is more noob friendly IMO, and a better defined story. DS2 has many different mechanics, better PvP but terrible PvE ganking. It's completely up to you.
Q: Will I feel confused by the story when jumping directly into the third game?
A: The story is always vague, so it doesn't matter. Check Youtube lore channels for better understanding.
Q: I've heard that NPC questlines are hard to complete without guide.
A: Just talk to people and do what they say, check the shrine to see if there are new dialogue. One thing you need to remember is that progressing in Rosaria's Finger (a guild, you cannot equip the guild item or offer the leveling item) will end another questline. Also the magic merchant will leave if you ignore your promise.
Q: I'm a completionist. What if I miss some gear?
A: You need to reach NG++ for 100% achievement, so feel free to look online for checklist in NG+.

Due to popular demand Ive decided to add a more ‘wholemeal’ first look review for people who like that sort of thing.
The game is essential qwop combined with the floor is lava. You navigate your slice of bread around various obstacles on a quest to get yourself nicely toasted (insert your own joke there).  Encountering dirty items reduces your edibility and therefore your overall score, whilst getting smothered in tasty tasty jam boosts it.
The game controls exactly how you would imagine it does. Each corner is assigned a different button which when pressed holds that edge in place apparently regardless of the surface/physics. The mouse or thumb stick flicks the bread around of can be used to nudge it around for precise movements. Practiced or naturally skilled will surely be able to cartwheel their way onto the leaderboards quickly whilst people starting out will ultimately spend more time flailing around like a dying Magicarp. Your main opponent is your own frustration.
If the play style is sounding very familiar that’s because it is. Anyone who has already played Surgeon Simulator or Octodad will immediately recognise the pattern of destruction and failure. This means that behind its freshly baked exterior the game is likely to become stale fairly quickly. Like its sister games there is a big potential for fun workshop content but ultimately you cannot judge a game on what could possibly be made by fans later on.
It is worth pointing out that it is an early access game, meaning that it is essentially unfinished, although this game does feel a lot more complete than most. It is very much playable with the exception of a few minor bugs. Enabling the gif record mode makes the game basically unplayable and the music always seems to be coming out of a random corner of the room.

I think overall most people will have already made a decision about this game, and whatever your thoughts they are probably correct. It’s ultimately a casual iPad-destined meme-maker but it clean fun and will give most people a few laughs for less than the price of an average cinema ticket. If flinging a slice of bread around for a few hours is the sort of thing that will brighten your day, then this is probably for you.

“You remember our venerable house... opulent and imperial. It is a festering abomination!”
Darkest Dungeon is a game that just oozes ambiance out of its many orifices; from the excellent art design to the deeply powerful narration of the Ancestor. The game is difficult, and you can expect to bury many of your heroes before you manage to cleanse the taint of eldritch horrors from your ancestral home (the game tells you as much on the title screen.) On the other hand, outside of the NG+ mode, there’s actually no way to lose the game, either – new recruits, available for free, will show up at your gates every week… and if you don’t have the cash to outfit them with weapons, training, torches, or even food… well, hopefully they’ll be able to make a quick run into one of the low-level missions, kill some cultists, grab some gold and gems, and beat a hasty retreat to refill your coffers… and if not them, perhaps next week’s batch….
I think it’s a superbly well executed game. The low and medium level dungeons are forgiving enough that you can make some mistakes or run with suboptimal parties without getting your head handed to you, giving you the experience needed to face the elite dungeons, and eventually even the darkest dungeon itself.
I think my only complaint would be that you do end up needing to run a lot of missions to collect the materials needed to upgrade your hamlet and level up your heroes. It never reaches what I’d consider a slog; but I also really, really enjoy both the turn-based combat and the amazing narration that goes along with it.

When you look at the amount of hours I've spent on this game you might question why I don't recommend the game. Well, there is a plethora of reasons.
1)PvE is absolute garbage in this game. There is pretty much no challenging content. Sure a mission might get you once or twice but once you know what's going on it's easy peasy from there. This hinders replayability value substantially. It wouldn't be a problem if the game had massive amounts of levels all of which payed out decently to be worth your time but no, it has one mission which must be done for money otherwise you're wasting your time.
2)Serious balance issues. Many weapons/armours are rubbish and completely avoided most of the time. Now you might be thinking that every mmo has tons of weapons which are rubbish and the good weapons are the rares which are difficult to obtain. Well you'd be thinking of a normal mmo. In this game there is no such thing as rarity as far as a weapon goes. Each weapon is obtained in the same way as another and it is not based on random drops, it is based on you crafting them. No luck involved either(unless you're aiming for variants, I'll touch on those later). So, why is the majority of the weapons/armours useless ? Cause the developers can't be arsed to fix them.
3)Developer. The developer of this game is one of the absolute worst. They don't even put out updates or even reach out the community. All they do is put promos into the game(essentially cosmetic items you need to pay for) every 2 weeks which half the time actually end up breaking some of the game.
4)This game has quite a lot of pay to win elements. It isn't really a big issue in PvP because it is largely based on skill there(and thank god) but there is still pay to win elements meaning you can theoretically buy gear which makes you quite a bit better than your enemy(can take more hits to kill you, faster attack speed etc) which should not be in a pvp game!
5)Servers. This game has awful servers and that's coming from a guy who has single digit ping on the EU server and only double digit ping on the USA server. I'm not sure if it's the actual servers or the net code that the game has but either way, the game has some serious connectivity problems. I obviously don't expierence those(most of the time) but many, many others do. In fact this game is usually a battle of the ping rather than a real fight.
6)Horrid optimisation. Based on Java, nuff said.
There's many more reasons that this game just isn't worth your time while there are other games out there however if you do decide to play the game there is only a handful of things that this game is worth playing for.
1)PvP. Even though it has many issues it is still a pretty fun PvP expierence.
2)Community. One of the best communities ever. Made so many friends in the game.
3)Kind of gimmicky mechanics which can be interesting for a short while.
4)Actually good combat system unlike every mmo.

“You remember our venerable house... opulent and imperial. It is a festering abomination!”
Darkest Dungeon is a game that just oozes ambiance out of its many orifices; from the excellent art design to the deeply powerful narration of the Ancestor. The game is difficult, and you can expect to bury many of your heroes before you manage to cleanse the taint of eldritch horrors from your ancestral home (the game tells you as much on the title screen.) On the other hand, outside of the NG+ mode, there’s actually no way to lose the game, either – new recruits, available for free, will show up at your gates every week… and if you don’t have the cash to outfit them with weapons, training, torches, or even food… well, hopefully they’ll be able to make a quick run into one of the low-level missions, kill some cultists, grab some gold and gems, and beat a hasty retreat to refill your coffers… and if not them, perhaps next week’s batch….
I think it’s a superbly well executed game. The low and medium level dungeons are forgiving enough that you can make some mistakes or run with suboptimal parties without getting your head handed to you, giving you the experience needed to face the elite dungeons, and eventually even the darkest dungeon itself.
I think my only complaint would be that you do end up needing to run a lot of missions to collect the materials needed to upgrade your hamlet and level up your heroes. It never reaches what I’d consider a slog; but I also really, really enjoy both the turn-based combat and the amazing narration that goes along with it.

Its free, and for a free game it isn't bad gameplay wise. Really fast paced, instant action. The netcode is a bit dodgy though and has the same annoyance as CS where you can headshot across the entire map without aiming. The thing that annoyed me most though was that if you fire a rocket launcher or a grenade and then die as you fire, it will most likely cancel your shot/throw which is just stupid.
I started being tactical and using my scope, but got more kills just spraying and pre-firing corners.
Equally you can be killed by people pre-firing or lagging around corners too. Overall not that tactical, more luck based.
However, it's fully pay2win/grind2win. The upper weapons and special weapons are MUCH better than the base items. Picked up some high ranked weapons and it was easy, the normal ones may as well not function. There is a 14 day trial on most weapons via the free DLC or by picking them up off the ground.
An OK number of maps for a free game, but most of them you can spawn camp too easily.
I only have a few hours so can't confirm it, but it looks like really high level players unlock stuff quicker (or are cheating). One guy I was playing with got over 30k points (when everyone else had 2-3k) in 2 minutes and had all the point based unlocks (like turrets, rockets) almost immediately on my team with 1 (ONE) kill. I encountred one or two cheaters which isn't uncommon, but more than games like CSGO/TF2 etc
The tutorial was OK though and gave it more of a tactical feel.
Overall, it's OK to kill a few hours on, and think a lot of a positive reviews give it too much leadway because it's free.

This is a tough one. But to sum it up I just can't recommend the game.
There are some bright spots. First and foremost the atmosphere is great. The narration is just so on point. And it really gets you going. Then the game starts and its just draws you right in. The game goes great. The rougelike keeps its interesting with permadeath and the random stat changes can keep the characters interesting. The art is fantastic. The areas seem interesting and deep.
Then the turn, evetually though the game switches. It really stops being fun it becomes a grind with a capital G. Now I actaully enjoy the grind mostly. Played RPGs all my life and there can be something nice about grinding. However, this game swtiches so hard from the fun of exploring and a very real adventuring sense to this MASSIVE grind that it is jarring and incredibly unfun. The game turns into work there is no progression you feel from anything for a long, long, LONG time.
Due to the atrociousness of the grind the other flaws really start to show. The RNG becomes a bit unbearable. RNG can be really fun and leave a sense of the unexpected in the air. However, when its combined with the Mt. Everest of a grind it becomes this ulgy mechanic that can just ruin any gameplay. For instance, you are forced to run the same area for the millionth time just to grind out some charcters when RNG strikes and you lose someone important. This sucks so much, not that permadeath is bad or that RNG + permadeath can't offer really fun games, but because that it wasn't due to ANYTHING you decided. YOU didn't take a risk, YOU didn't overextend, YOU didn't do anything. The game forced you into a boring task and then punished you for it anyways. Then you realize the maps are the same, the monsters are the same, everything is the same. The rougelike randomness and vareity of monsters in each area that started off very cool has become so very boring. Simply becuase you spend a lifetime in each area trying to grind things out. And switching back and forth does little to break this up due to the sheer number of times you have played a map there.
It is sad it is an amazing game off the bat. You will love it right away, then it will slowly make you hate it, dread turing it on. It becomes a job you can't stand. The polar oppostie of Civ's "One more turn" instead being "Ugh, do I have to".

Q: Give me a TL;DR version.
A: Buy the game and git gud.
Q: I heard the game is hard. Is it good for causal player?
A: Yes.
Q: Is it good for Skyrim player?
A: Yes, but you'll need to learn new mechanics such as parrying and roll timing.
Q: Is it a good game for family, friend etc?
A: Yes. The game has a password feature to co-op with friend. I think the game is educational for children, as it teaches people to not give up and overcome hardship.
Q: Is this game full of rainbow and candy?
A: No, it's closer to a horror game, especially in some later areas. Even prettier areas are infested with monsters. The atmosphere of this game is very grim and grey-ish.
Q: Tutorial?
A: Check the signs in the first map. You can check the keyboard-controller maping in setting. The first map has mooks, a mini boss and a boss for you to play with. The tutorial boss, Gundyr, teaches you various evasion technique.
Q: Is there a mini map?
A: No. But since you might die a number of times you'll get familiar with the map. There are many shortcuts.
Q: Is there an easy mode?
A: It's called greatshield, you can get one in the second map but need some levelling up to use it. Starting as knight (default) also counts as an easy mode in early game.
Q: I don't like invaders.
A: Start the game in offline mode, you can change this in setting. You can still play with NPC phantoms but cannot co-op. If you are online, stay unembered prevent invasion but you cannot co-op. If you are invaded you can also run toward the boss fog gate. Edit: you can join Way of Blue in the second map, that will lower the chance of being invaded as well.
Q: Mooks attack 100 times in a row.
A: Try spacing.
Q: Mooks gank me. Unfair!
A: Try looking around, this game is known for enemy trolling you every corner. Lock on feature will spot enemy above.
Q: Bosses are too fast.
A: It's kind of counterintuitive, but you sometimes need to roll toward them. Check Youtube if you have trouble. Don't worry, dying to boss is a learning process.
Q: What's the main strength of this game?
A: Best video game soundtrack.
Q: What's the weakness of this game?
A: Too short compared to DS2, not enough armor/weapon/spells.
Q: Should I buy DS1 and DS2 instead?
A: DS1 is more noob friendly IMO, and a better defined story. DS2 has many different mechanics, better PvP but terrible PvE ganking. It's completely up to you.
Q: Will I feel confused by the story when jumping directly into the third game?
A: The story is always vague, so it doesn't matter. Check Youtube lore channels for better understanding.
Q: I've heard that NPC questlines are hard to complete without guide.
A: Just talk to people and do what they say, check the shrine to see if there are new dialogue. One thing you need to remember is that progressing in Rosaria's Finger (a guild, you cannot equip the guild item or offer the leveling item) will end another questline. Also the magic merchant will leave if you ignore your promise.
Q: I'm a completionist. What if I miss some gear?
A: You need to reach NG++ for 100% achievement, so feel free to look online for checklist in NG+.

However trying to steer this bread or moving it it's extremly tedious... i HATE the controll sceme (I tried both Keyboard and Gamepad (xbox controller)  It's very hard and takes tons of time to get used with the controls.

* How you control the bread...

It may not appeal to everyone, but I love this game. Watch some gameplay videos and read some reviews if you're still on the fence.
Pros:
- The aesthetics, music, narration are all top-notch
- The narrator is so good he deserves a second mention. Seriously
- The gameplay is turn-based, so you can play strategically and thoughtfully
- There's more than one way to "succeed" at the game - there's no single strategy that works better than everything else (but also see below)
- The setting and unfolding storyline are great. Very Lovecrafian and Grimdark
Cons:
- Punishingly difficult. Some may see this as a pro. Be ready to cut-and-run, be ready to dismiss heroes that are damaged beyond repair, be ready to accept failure and death on a regular basis
- Some classes/heroes feel noticably less useful than others, though there's not 100% agreement on which heroes
- Though there's not one game-winning strategy that works all the time, some enemies and bosses DO require specific tactics to defeat, and if your group isn't ready for them, victory may not be possible. Again, that's part of the game, but this may bother some players.
If you know what you're in for, and you're still interested, I'd give this game a shot, for the graphics and music (and narration) alone.

Overall, I do recommend the game, but only for people with the patience of the common rock.

Horrible game! I really hated this game for a variety of reasons:
1) Steep learning curve.
You're thrown into the different items, equipments and the UI does not keep things simple. For example while equiping a particular armor the UI should automatically show the character sheet so that you know where it's giong. But instead it just disappears from the inventory. It takes a while to figure out where it's going.
2) Horrible map.
You see the map and try to figure out where an NPC is but you can only zoom in so much. So you need to keep running around the main world to figure out where is what NPC
3) Broken chat system.
I tried asking for help in the world chat. My message showed up 2-3 times. Later on for some reason none of my messages were showing up in chat while other people could communicate. I don't know if it was some kind of a shadow ban or some other glitch. It made it impossible for me to communicate with other players.
4) Monotonous gameplay.
You keep destroying demons and keep running around with no end in sight. There's no co-op quests so everyone is on their own. The community is horrible. I asked 3 times for help as a beginner but no one responded. I'm sure invalidating experts out there will read this and say "oh you cant ask for help as a beginner". NO! I can! Other MMOs have this kind of thing. This is also a way make friends, form connections. You can't say "you can't ask for help" for ANY phase.
5) Free gameplay is full of grinding
You grind and grind and grind while others around you who're paying for mounts, weapons etc are able to make quick progress. You need to spend more than 200 dollars to truly reap in some fun items. Else you have to spend a huge amoutn of time grinding.
6) Horrible server connection
The connection keeps getting disconnected every 3-5 minutes. Seriously you call this an online game? It's horrible!
Summary
Even though this game is being offered for free I would ask people to NOT skip this useless piece of crap. Thanks for your time.

This is a tough one. But to sum it up I just can't recommend the game.
There are some bright spots. First and foremost the atmosphere is great. The narration is just so on point. And it really gets you going. Then the game starts and its just draws you right in. The game goes great. The rougelike keeps its interesting with permadeath and the random stat changes can keep the characters interesting. The art is fantastic. The areas seem interesting and deep.
Then the turn, evetually though the game switches. It really stops being fun it becomes a grind with a capital G. Now I actaully enjoy the grind mostly. Played RPGs all my life and there can be something nice about grinding. However, this game swtiches so hard from the fun of exploring and a very real adventuring sense to this MASSIVE grind that it is jarring and incredibly unfun. The game turns into work there is no progression you feel from anything for a long, long, LONG time.
Due to the atrociousness of the grind the other flaws really start to show. The RNG becomes a bit unbearable. RNG can be really fun and leave a sense of the unexpected in the air. However, when its combined with the Mt. Everest of a grind it becomes this ulgy mechanic that can just ruin any gameplay. For instance, you are forced to run the same area for the millionth time just to grind out some charcters when RNG strikes and you lose someone important. This sucks so much, not that permadeath is bad or that RNG + permadeath can't offer really fun games, but because that it wasn't due to ANYTHING you decided. YOU didn't take a risk, YOU didn't overextend, YOU didn't do anything. The game forced you into a boring task and then punished you for it anyways. Then you realize the maps are the same, the monsters are the same, everything is the same. The rougelike randomness and vareity of monsters in each area that started off very cool has become so very boring. Simply becuase you spend a lifetime in each area trying to grind things out. And switching back and forth does little to break this up due to the sheer number of times you have played a map there.
It is sad it is an amazing game off the bat. You will love it right away, then it will slowly make you hate it, dread turing it on. It becomes a job you can't stand. The polar oppostie of Civ's "One more turn" instead being "Ugh, do I have to".

(Don't take my hours in account for experience of this game. I've played the majority off-steam.)
So, imagine you want to buy this game because you've been seeing it a bunch on Twitch and such, but before you purchase it, you want to see if the game is any good. So naturally, for a quick peek, you look into the Steam reviews.
And there are waves and waves of downvotes.
This is mostly because of one thing in the game, one element, one mechanic in the game that is too hard for those people to overcome apparently.
And that is RNG.
Admittedly, it is pretty annoying at times. Enemies dodging a bunch or your guys missing, like, everything.
But, there are so many ways to overcome misses and dodges, and to have the RNG on your side.
First of all, debuffs.
Debuffs in this game do all sorts of things, have the enemy take more damage, or less resistances to certain damage types. But it can also reduce their dodge- and accuracy stat. Which means you'll be hitting more and they'll be missing more. Use this.
Secondly, buffs.
Buffs are just the opposite of debuffs. Give your guys a higher resistance to a bunch of damage types, or higher damage. And just like with debuffs, you can make them hit more.
Mainly accuracy increase, which just makes them miss less, and hit more.
Nevertheless, RNGesus will always have a role and will always make you miss something. But that's fine. That's the game. It will never be on your side.
And then there is also the "undodgeable" (I'll get back on this) damage type. Or actually two.
Bleed and Blight.
Very simply, bleed does damage over time in bleeding damage, and blight does the same in poisonous damage. Your enemies cannot cure/dodge this once it has struck. And everytime they take a move, the damage will be applied first. So when an enemy is about to make a move, he can die before he even gets to do anything.
However, they can dodge the intital attack that causes said damage type. Be wary of that.
And then there's stuns, too.
Stuns make it so that the enemy that you've hit with a stun cannot make his next turn. This. Is. Enormously. Good.
Whenever you stun an enemy, he can't take his next turn. Which either means you can take free swings at the guy, or that you won't have to worry about him for a turn.
Now of course, there are resistances in the game, including bleed, blight and stun resist.
How do you work your way around this?
Increasing the base stat of your abilites!
And yes, I know that the skellymen cannot bleed, and the fishpeople are highly resistant to bleed. Same goes for the filthy skrubs in the Weald when it comes to Blight. But the game encourages you to make use of alternatives. And there are rarely any enemies that have resistances on all types. Mainly tanky guys have this. You can still debuff 'em, though.
TL;DR: Its a great game, and dont be fooled by the negative reviews. See for yourself if you like it. Its not a game for everyone, though.
