I'm very happy to be able to finally recommend this game.
When I first bought the game I was very dissapointed by the RNG grind, heart attack chains and just general unfairness. In my previous review I lambasted the fact that there was no difficulty setting, as I genuinely wanted to delve deeper into the story and tackle the darkest dungeon. However I found myself stuck in an endless grind fest, constantly tackling low level dungeons to try get my scrubs up to scratch and conquer the later levels. But I'd find myself time and time again being completely mulched by a boss or have one of my characters turn abusive, hurl insults at all the other characters and then one by one perish to the heart attack mechanic.
It was with a heavy heart that I uninstalled Darkest Dungeon and got on with my life.
However due to a lot of negative feedback about difficulty the developers finally added a new "radiant mode". Obviously you can google the exact ins and outs about this mode but I finally found myself enjoying the game. I think my biggest complaint previously was not being able to take your squad into lower level dungeons, and this seems to have been removed for the radiant mode so you can finally get a sense of actually becoming more powerful and get attached to the characters. In fact now i've started to find it a little bit too easy, even with lower level squads. Maybe I've just got used to the enemies and know how to put squads together a little better, maybe the radiant mode has tweaked more than I realised (when radiant mode was initially released I honestly could not tell the difference.) But this is the beauty of gaming, having options on how you approach things and how you play. Having difficulty options has breathed new life into the game for me, once I complete my radiant run I can play "darkest" mode (normal) or "stygian" (hard).
So now that the game doesn't feel like a giant waste of time, I would definitely recommend it. The art is something to behold, the narrator is fantastic, no game really gives you such a sense of despondence and the mechanics are extremely solid. The characters are actually original too, it's not a generic barbarian, rogue, mage set up, you have occultists, plague doctors, and even a guy with a dog.
I think the only thing that's really missing is a bit more customisation of character just so you could truly get invested in your squad, X-com style.
Other than that a fantastic game.

This is a very good game, worthy of the attention of people with the highest levels of intelligence. Only a person with a high level of intelligence (IQ 120+ or more) can fully appreciate this game, as it requires much executive planning that is denied in the case of lower intellects (below IQ 120).
Having an IQ of 160 on the Wechsler scales myself, I truly appreciate the complexity and realism of the game, alongside its beautiful use of prose in its many narrations. Its vocabulary is dense enough for me, and I enjoyed editing the config files to customise this game completely (I play on 200% HP modifier, among many other changes).

This game is great if you liked XCOM: Enemy Unknown and XCOM: Enemy Within. Your soldiers have interesting abilities and different loadouts give you interesting possibilities. Just like the original game, the enemies can be punishing. I feel there is a greater variety this time around though. The game has mod support, and there are already some nice mods out there.
That said, this game too suffers from shooting through walls, and some abilities simply not hitting like they appear to be. Using AOE abilities can sometimes be somewhat of a hassle. Units can fall into solid objects when they die, and when being reanimated will stand inside said solid object, preventing melee attacks. Civilians will gather in the strangest places. Units will be concealed when entering most missions, but missions are almost always timed with an arbitrary timer. I mean, why the hell would you blow up a chest with valuable things if you are not aware someone is making a move on that chest. It can be hard to move a unit to a specific location, even when you have selected the correct elevation.
The second and third DLC add a lot to the game and are worth the price. It is extremely satisfying to use the "boss" monsters against their underlings. The special voiceover for mech units (without giving spoilers) is great. The unit itself is interesting to play with.
Amazing way to pass the time with friends or family. :)

This is a pretty innovative game with some pros and a decent bit of cons, I have more then 650 hours clocked on my older account just grinding, and that could be a  good or  bad thing I suppose. Here are my pros and cons:
Pros: SK is a flourishing multiplayer experience that has been ever expanding since I started playing it which is wonderful. You have an array of options for weapons and armor that rewards you for specializing well. There are changing events that are always occuring that will keep you coming back to check on them. There are plenty of layers to go through in the arcade with friends and strangers for never ending possibilities of loot inside.

I could complely drop the side scrolling dungeon crawl aspect (the most undeveloped portion of the game IMO) and simply keep the battles and I would have a blast. Dungeon crawling is good fun, but it could be done better.
Coming up with the right combos of abilities and then working hard on getting their gear and skills leveled up, all the while hording trinkets and gold to build your wealth. At any moment, you could lose one of your favorite heroes, or come out victorious with loads of new stuff.
Darkest dungeon, at the very least, is worth a shot to try. Don't expect fast twitch based gameplay. Appreciate it for what it is: a truly artistic development with excellent strategy.
edit: look at the recent reviews: Most complaints are that this game is grindy. Well I'm here to tell you that yes, it is.
But I still enjoy the game, probably because after the initial honeymoon period was over, I just now occasionally come back to the game to enjoy 1 or 2 runs into a dungeon and do my town management duties. I play it casually and that's good enough for me. I'm still progressing, so theres a reason to come back to it and I am not getting burnt out on the lack of depth when it comes to dungeon crawling (not a fan of the constant 1 way sidescrolling).
Yes, this game is grindy and it can be frustrating to lose hours of play because your favorite guy died (TIP! Don't get attached to ANYONE). But if you're like me, who can come back to a game casually, this game is just great to have as a part of your collection. I'm a pretty big strategy fan so this is great for me.

(Don't take my hours in account for experience of this game. I've played the majority off-steam.)
So, imagine you want to buy this game because you've been seeing it a bunch on Twitch and such, but before you purchase it, you want to see if the game is any good. So naturally, for a quick peek, you look into the Steam reviews.
And there are waves and waves of downvotes.
This is mostly because of one thing in the game, one element, one mechanic in the game that is too hard for those people to overcome apparently.
And that is RNG.
Admittedly, it is pretty annoying at times. Enemies dodging a bunch or your guys missing, like, everything.
But, there are so many ways to overcome misses and dodges, and to have the RNG on your side.
First of all, debuffs.
Debuffs in this game do all sorts of things, have the enemy take more damage, or less resistances to certain damage types. But it can also reduce their dodge- and accuracy stat. Which means you'll be hitting more and they'll be missing more. Use this.
Secondly, buffs.
Buffs are just the opposite of debuffs. Give your guys a higher resistance to a bunch of damage types, or higher damage. And just like with debuffs, you can make them hit more.
Mainly accuracy increase, which just makes them miss less, and hit more.
Nevertheless, RNGesus will always have a role and will always make you miss something. But that's fine. That's the game. It will never be on your side.
And then there is also the "undodgeable" (I'll get back on this) damage type. Or actually two.
Bleed and Blight.
Very simply, bleed does damage over time in bleeding damage, and blight does the same in poisonous damage. Your enemies cannot cure/dodge this once it has struck. And everytime they take a move, the damage will be applied first. So when an enemy is about to make a move, he can die before he even gets to do anything.
However, they can dodge the intital attack that causes said damage type. Be wary of that.
And then there's stuns, too.
Stuns make it so that the enemy that you've hit with a stun cannot make his next turn. This. Is. Enormously. Good.
Whenever you stun an enemy, he can't take his next turn. Which either means you can take free swings at the guy, or that you won't have to worry about him for a turn.
Now of course, there are resistances in the game, including bleed, blight and stun resist.
How do you work your way around this?
Increasing the base stat of your abilites!
And yes, I know that the skellymen cannot bleed, and the fishpeople are highly resistant to bleed. Same goes for the filthy skrubs in the Weald when it comes to Blight. But the game encourages you to make use of alternatives. And there are rarely any enemies that have resistances on all types. Mainly tanky guys have this. You can still debuff 'em, though.
TL;DR: Its a great game, and dont be fooled by the negative reviews. See for yourself if you like it. Its not a game for everyone, though.
And remember...great is the weapon that cuts on its own.

I'm very happy to be able to finally recommend this game.
When I first bought the game I was very dissapointed by the RNG grind, heart attack chains and just general unfairness. In my previous review I lambasted the fact that there was no difficulty setting, as I genuinely wanted to delve deeper into the story and tackle the darkest dungeon. However I found myself stuck in an endless grind fest, constantly tackling low level dungeons to try get my scrubs up to scratch and conquer the later levels. But I'd find myself time and time again being completely mulched by a boss or have one of my characters turn abusive, hurl insults at all the other characters and then one by one perish to the heart attack mechanic.
It was with a heavy heart that I uninstalled Darkest Dungeon and got on with my life.
However due to a lot of negative feedback about difficulty the developers finally added a new "radiant mode". Obviously you can google the exact ins and outs about this mode but I finally found myself enjoying the game. I think my biggest complaint previously was not being able to take your squad into lower level dungeons, and this seems to have been removed for the radiant mode so you can finally get a sense of actually becoming more powerful and get attached to the characters. In fact now i've started to find it a little bit too easy, even with lower level squads. Maybe I've just got used to the enemies and know how to put squads together a little better, maybe the radiant mode has tweaked more than I realised (when radiant mode was initially released I honestly could not tell the difference.) But this is the beauty of gaming, having options on how you approach things and how you play. Having difficulty options has breathed new life into the game for me, once I complete my radiant run I can play "darkest" mode (normal) or "stygian" (hard).
So now that the game doesn't feel like a giant waste of time, I would definitely recommend it. The art is something to behold, the narrator is fantastic, no game really gives you such a sense of despondence and the mechanics are extremely solid. The characters are actually original too, it's not a generic barbarian, rogue, mage set up, you have occultists, plague doctors, and even a guy with a dog.
I think the only thing that's really missing is a bit more customisation of character just so you could truly get invested in your squad, X-com style.
Other than that a fantastic game.

I used to be a big fan of Terraria...then I came across Starbound. Starbound, to me, offers a much more fun and exciting experience. There are an infinite number of planets that you can explore, all different, all unique. There is no limit to where you can go! And the crafting! There's so many things you can craft! Furniture can come in wood, steel, gold, crystal, you name it!
Weapons aren't hard to make at all. They also make a big difference from your starting weapon, as the creatures attack frequently on some planets. You can craft bows to gain meat from animals. You can also find weapons in randomly generated chests on the planet surface or underground. The first weapon I ever found was a huge brown hammer called Poop Beater! And it kicked some serious booty! How awesome is that?
Mining is pretty good, but MAN do you have to GRIND for fuel and armor! You'll sometimes find yourself spending hours underground to collect enough silver or gold for that new chestplate and enough coal for a stockpile of torches and fuel for your ship to travel to different sectors. In the end, all the grinding is worth it, because you'll have huge stockpiles of resources that you have extra of. Also beware that your pickaxe won't last forever, as you can repair it with ore and/or ingots.
The randomly generated dungeons and villages are phenomenal. Many planets have villages of different species where you can purchase goods such as food, clothing, and weapons. Other places include secret underground facilities, airships, prisons, military bases, castles, and much, much more! Over the 50+ hours I've played, I don't think I've even found every dungeon and village you can find!
I highly recommend Starbound if you're looking for an exciting adventure, something unique. If you're a Terraria fan, this is a must have. I can't express how awesome Starbound is, even in it's Beta phase!

If you want to go with WASD and you're perfectly fine with it, be my guest because you're not missing out on anything much other than the ability to strafe. Also, shielding is perfect in this game. Bouncing enemies back before they attack gives you a chance to catch them when they're open to damage. Speaking of, most enemies have a tactic for dealing with you, and you should have a tactic for dealing with them. Especially trojans. New players absolutely hate trojans.
All in all, you're gonna love this game if you look into it, the only bad things are the lag spurts on big servers, the attack endlag on most charge attacks which leave you open in both PVE and PVP, and the helplessness you feel when you enter a new tier without any knowledge gained from the previous tier. If you're reading this, congrats because you made it past a few paragraphs of reading. And reading is boring, and by the time you had finished reading this review, you could have downloaded the game and started playing. Imagine that!

Edit:
I did finally play through and complete the game a couple times.  Things smoothed out a lot since my initial review.  Didn't notice any choppy animations, no shooting through walls or doors anymore, however, getting shot or shooting through floors is a thing (from the right angle).  Hacking is not quite as frustrating, cutscenes are still unnecessary and don't add anything.  No more crashes.  I did have a couple times where the animations stopped. Things were still happening, just not being animated, then everything would snap into place.  One time a soldier died, but I could still control him (wonky animations, clearly not working as intended).  Marched his corpse to the evac point.  Docs fixed him right up.
Each of the classes has cool things it can do.  Some more flexible than others.  Cross-training has potential to be awesome.  Sometimes it's meh (Deep Cover on a Sharpshooter... It's not terrible) sometimes it's ridiculous (Killzone on a Specialist, Serial on a Ranger OMG).  The weapon upgrades are a nice layer of customization.  Each class kinda has a mandatory upgrade set.  Laser sights for all your Rangers, extended magazines and autoloaders for Sharpshooters, etc.  You may change things up if they got certain skills from cross-training (I gave my Serial Ranger an extended magazine instead of an autoloader).  The new ammo and grenade types work well with this system.  However, the randomness of which type you get (of anything you build in the proving ground) was not ideal.  AP rounds, Shredder rounds, Acid Bombs, and Shredstorm Cannons were the only things I really wanted from there.  I may have done some save scumming...
The Psy class is ok.  Teach them a few skills, then look at their stats.  If the RNG is not being good to them, cut them from the program and start training a new one.  By the time I got them, I didn't really have room on my teams for them.  A Ranger, a Sharpshooter, two Heavies, and two Specialists can pretty much deal with anything (RNG willing).
Anyway, it's true to its time based strategic/turn based tactical roots, and has enough new stuff to be more than just a clone with updated graphics.  I'm fairly satisfied with how it turned out.
End Edit.
Pros:
It's XCOM.
Cons:
Buggy gameplay.  Choppy animation.  Vipers targetting through walls.  Enemies shooting through closed doors.  Don't hack.  You'll fail.  Annoying cutscenes every time anybody does anything.  Cutscene when you take off for a mission.  Cutscene when you land, cutscene when you spot an enemy, cutscene when enemy reinforcements arrive, cutscene when you return to base.  It's not dramatic after the first 17 times.  I get it.  I landed.  There are aliens.  Start the mission.  Game crashed 3 times in 12 hours of play.
I could handle it if I was losing soldiers because of mistakes, or even tactical risks, but not because snakes can shoot, poison, or pull people through walls.
Do not buy until the beta is over.

Wew, Okay lets go..
This game is probably the best f2p FPS you got out there.. No P2W (Unless you count skipping playing a few hours to unlock a gun permanently p2w). It is important to note that you also start with enough gold to buy 3 weapons of your choice.. However you can only have 3 loadouts so you don't actually need more at the start.
The steam promo allows you to have all the guns for free for 15 days to test out which 3 you want to buy with your initial cash..
The maps are quite average, decent but nothing special (so far). There is a few game modes as well and I'll review each one really quick.
Team Deathmatch: Generic team deathmatch with a short spawn protection and fast paced gameplay.. My personal favorite because it's quick.
8v8 Demolition: 8v8 Csgo clone thing; One team plants the bomb, other team defuses.
5v5 demo: 5v5 csgo clone thing; One team plants the bomb, other team defuses.
VIP: Confusing i still dont get it, You have to protect a vip that is like, a npc I think? Sometimes it starts running off, sometimes it dies and you still win.. It's just weird.
Battle match: Some kind of objective based map with 16v16 and classes and tons of fancy stuff.
Overall guns feel mostly good, the game has a high skill ceiling.. I found a lot of weapons to be very viable.
1: Get a SMG like the Kris Vector or SIZMPX and rush enemies akin to Quake/Teamforteress
2: Get a shotgun and play your corners. You will easily one shot enemies.
3: Get a sniper and hold an unpopular long hall. This gives a lot of room for your team to push.
4: Get AK47/ AK12/ HNK / SR-47, keep crosshair head level and slow turn corners to one tap.
5: Get a steady weapon like the MDR or G36 and follow someone, using them as bait to steal their kills.
Those are all effective ways to end up with 40+ kills per game. (TDM)
Bad players trying to empty their guns into your arm dealing a fraction of the damage while if you aim right you can 2-3 shot kill them very easily.. The game is quite good to make good players snowball which results in a lot of people crying about hackers every single game.
About the hacker situation, this game does fairly well. While you do see some of them once in a while, they're far less common than say CSGO.. (Let alone other f2p games)
While it's not a AAA title. Given their budget and the playing cost. It was far higher than my expectations.. To the point that this is now my main game even if i have 2100 hours on csgo.

I’ve been anxiously waiting for this game since I finished Firaxis’ reboot in 2012, and I really wanted to like Xcom 2. Really. After spending 24 hours across 10 days, however, I finally admitted to myself that I'm not happy with this game. At least, not in its current state shortly after launch.
I’m a big fan of turn-based tactics and strategy games. I love series like Vandal Hearts, Shining Force, Fire Emblem, Civilization, Age of Empires, Shadowrun, even Xcom: EW. And, while I'm generally not a fan of games that are so heavily governed by RNGs, I can easily overlook that as long as good planning and preparation can help you overcome the chaos. Disappointingly, Xcom 2 is not so much a challenging game, such as those previously mentioned, as it is an unbalanced and buggy mess.
When a game like this has so much promise, I can forgive its erratic framerates and un-optimized load times, but then there are the game engine-breaking bugs. Example: my favorite ranger has an ability that grants “free sword attacks on enemies that enter or attack from melee range.” Several times, however, when enemies walked right up to her and swiped her in the face she just took it. No reaction slash. Upon reloading, the Blademaster skill would work correctly. Or it wouldn’t. Other times the game would say one of my snipers has nice line of sight on a faraway enemy, but reload a save from that point, it would just as easily tell me that’s no longer the case.
Why does the game break it's own rules?
Other gripes: hacking is essentially useless (unless it’s story or mission necessary), overwatch shots are missed so often I’m having difficulty remembering one that actually landed, and how is it that a trained soldier can miss a point-blank blade slash? When you’re outside of combat, so many events are outside of your control, yet you’re constantly being bombarded with menial tasks. Couple this with a lack guidance as to which objectives are important for long-term survival and which can be put off, and you’ve got more than just a steep learning curve, you’ve got lazy, unintuitive game design. Considering how much Bradford pesters you about civilian deaths, you’d think he’d give you a more detailed explanation on how the Avatar Project countdown clock works.
The sense of risk and reward in Xcom 2 has been severely diminished from its predecessor. This game doesn't only penalize my mistakes, it is at times abusive towards logic and sound tactics, rather than making the player feel like they've learned or mastered something new about the game's ruleset. No victory is left unpunished.
Most frustrating of all, the game is over-reliant on multiple timers to create a superficial and unnecessary sense of urgency. Sadly, this seems to be a crutch to mask a lack of polish on the game’s too numerous and unwieldy layers.

This game is built for the old-school gamer. The gamer that grew up before this hand-holding AAA garbage-fest we see today. Press F to pay respects. Darkest Dungeon gives you just enough of a tutorial to get you on your feet, but even then the tutorial itself is difficult. One of my heroes died on the first mission, something that would not happen again until several missions later. I've seen many negative reviews in the "most helpful" section complaining of bad RNG and steep difficulty. The only conclusion I can reach is those reviewers are millenials that need their hand held. If this game were any easier, I would not enjoy it. If this game had player-favored RNG, I would not enjoy it. If this game told me what to do and when to do it, I would not enjoy it. These seem to be the qualities some people desire however.
There is a disclaimer before you even start your first save file and every time you load the game thereafter which states that this is an extremely challenging game. Your heroes will die. You will be compelled to abandon some missions (or face a party wipe). You will be forced to make many difficult
I mainly wanted to write this review in an attempt to dispel the false rumors you see in the "most helpful" section. The great atmosphere, art style, voice acting etc. can all be witnessed via the gameplay trailer.
The RNG that people claim to be unfair is actually quite the opposite. The RNG in Darkest Dungeon is actually the most balanced I've seen in a game in a long time. Your players will get crit often, but your crits will land just as well. Your player will get their attacks dodged, but you can dodge just as many enemy attacks. Your players will go from 100%-0% in a single strike, but you can land the same blow. You are not favored in any fight. Neither is the enemy.
The problem people have with this game isn't the RNG, but instead the difficulty curve. The game is always hard, but it goes from hard during the level 1 and 3 dungeons, to brutal in level 5 and insane in level 6 dungeons. The massive spikes in difficulty catch the average player off-guard and once a level 5 dungeon is started for the first time with the usual crew and they get demolished, discouragement is had and RNG is blamed when in fact it was their lack of preparation.
In level 1 dungeons you can pick any composition you want, and still succeed. You could go in with 4 of the same class, all with no trinkets and still complete the quest. During level 3 quests, you need to mix up your roster a bit and start thinking about good class combos but it's still straightforward and can be tank and spanked. Then comes level 5 dungeons. I have a feeling once most players reach level 5 quests is when they start blaming "RNG" and stop playing out of frustration. The difference in difficulty between a level 3 and a level 5 dungeon is immense. In level 5 dungeons, your party composition is extremely important. You need to have a clear idea of what each class brings to the table along with their strengths and weaknesses. It's no longer a zerg rush where all your attacks land and you can just go full offense. Debuffs need to be applied. Stuns are your friend. Movement skills become necessary. You must camp at the right time. Your trinket selection is
All of these mechanics aren't new, but they weren't really a factor until now. Once you figure out how to correctly utilize all of the mechanics the game has to offer, level 5+ dungeons become "easy" again.
So in conclusion Darkest Dungeon is not the unfair game with imbalanced RNG that the "most helpful" reviews would like you to think it is. It is a beautifully difficult game that has steep learning curves. These nightmarish creatures can be felled! They can be beaten! Confidence surges as the enemy crumbles!
TL;DR
Darkest Dungeon has fair RNG. It is the most fun you'll have while simultaneously wanting to rip your hair out. Buy it.

If you enjoy slowly dipping your feet into a game, with a "learn as you go" approach, Darkest Dungeon returns to the days of the cane and beats you merciliessly until you get it right.
The artwork is fantastic and the setting, while not entirely original, nears perfection in execution. The narrator is astounding and truly immerses you into the situation. The interface has been tweaked over time and whilst it initially is somewhat overwhelming, gives you all the information you need to make an informed tactical decision.
Your heroes will die. Your favourite champions will become so twisted that you are either forced to lose your savings to keep them sane or merely discard them to the pit. There will be times where everything has gone right for you in the quest, but suddenly a role of the dice will ruin the run.
The bosses are varied in tactical approach and always feel threatening, moreso the minibosses that roam the dungeon with the intent of taking advantage of low supplies and loads of loot.
I suppose that's what this game does best; it does away with the RPG leveling curve  that will allow you to remove most of the challenge in the game. Even notably difficult ones, such as Etrian Odyssey, suffer from this fate. However, Darkest Dungeon constantly pushes you in to uncomfortable positions and forces you to make the best of, sometimes, dreadful situations.
Darkest Dungeon might possibly be the best RPG I've ever played, most certainly the best one I've played on Steam.

Having a good angle on an opponent means nothing if their plane of cover is between you and your target.  Fog of war prevents you from being able to make rational ambushes more than once per mission. Honestly had way more fun with the Front Mission series.  It's not that I expected this game to be that series, it's that it doesn't offer anything more than it.  A good tactical game should allow you to recover from an initial mistake if you play your cards right, not heavily punish you for scouting fog of war. XCOM 2 is a worthy yet buggy sequel to 2012's XCOM. It's more challenging (sometimes artificially so) with an overall better sense of urgency and desperation than the original had. Firstly, the game in its current state (Feb 2016) requires patching. There are frequent slow-downs, weird pauses between turns, and the occasional lengthy loading time. The game has trouble maintaining a stable FPS. A lot of these issues were actually present in XCOM 2012's release though and they were (mostly) patched out. Give them time to fix it.
In terms of gameplay the core elements of the XCOM francise remain the same - strategic decision-making with turn-based tactical combat against an alien threat. The Geoscape strategic portion has the biggest changes with more choice of "missions" which often serve to take up time rather than being tactical missions. For example you can search for supplies or alien materials. Tactical missions pop up with some defined benefit for their completion and a penalty for ignoring them - and the penalty at least up until the end game is punishing, so you often can't ignore them. The game will infrequently give you a choice of 3 missions - these missions will negate one of the bonuses that the aliens acquire for that month. The aliens play a much better strategic game and you can't simply sit and wait for the next plot point to trigger. In XCOM 2012 you could halt progress by simply not completing some objectives, giving you all the time in the world to advance. In XCOM 2 the aliens are constantly making progress on Avatar, their final solution to humanity. You can delay it but you cannot stop it. This increases that urgency and desperation that XCOM desperately needed; you can't simply wait and research your way to victory.
The tactical game remains largely the same with the added benefit of better map randomisation, a more aggressive AI, and a few new mechanics. Firstly some missions start you troops in concealment, giving you the ability to move around the map without triggering the enemy unless you get too close (or they patrol into your group), allowing you to set up ambushes. Many missions also have a turn limit. I can see why they did this - a very popular tactic in the original was simply to put everyone into Overwatch and advance cautiously, creating a wall of reaction-fire death. Turn limits stop you from relying on this tactic; you have to find the enemy and objectives quickly instead of creeping forward. Overwatch is still useful but you need to be more aggressive. That said, some of the limits feel awfully restrictive, especially at higher difficulty levels (especially when the aliens are just plain stronger across the board). There are still plenty of "XCOM fail" moments where shots miss despite a high probably of hitting (90% isn't 100% guys!) but they hurt a lot more with the new aliens.
Overall I actually do recommend XCOM 2 to fans of the original. Plenty of people complain about turn limits, and they do have a point - but plenty of people whinged that XCOM 2012 was too easy with its Overwatch death-squad tactic, so I guess some people just won't be happy either way. There are some technical issues that will no doubt be mostly resolved, but this is still a fantastic game. Incidentally, the original XCOM's successor, Terror from the Deep, was well known for being XCOM except underwater and with a much higher difficulty level. I guess they just followed the same plan this time.

This game is built for the old-school gamer. The gamer that grew up before this hand-holding AAA garbage-fest we see today. Press F to pay respects. Darkest Dungeon gives you just enough of a tutorial to get you on your feet, but even then the tutorial itself is difficult. One of my heroes died on the first mission, something that would not happen again until several missions later. I've seen many negative reviews in the "most helpful" section complaining of bad RNG and steep difficulty. The only conclusion I can reach is those reviewers are millenials that need their hand held. If this game were any easier, I would not enjoy it. If this game had player-favored RNG, I would not enjoy it. If this game told me what to do and when to do it, I would not enjoy it. These seem to be the qualities some people desire however.
There is a disclaimer before you even start your first save file and every time you load the game thereafter which states that this is an extremely challenging game. Your heroes will die. You will be compelled to abandon some missions (or face a party wipe). You will be forced to make many difficult
I mainly wanted to write this review in an attempt to dispel the false rumors you see in the "most helpful" section. The great atmosphere, art style, voice acting etc. can all be witnessed via the gameplay trailer.
The RNG that people claim to be unfair is actually quite the opposite. The RNG in Darkest Dungeon is actually the most balanced I've seen in a game in a long time. Your players will get crit often, but your crits will land just as well. Your player will get their attacks dodged, but you can dodge just as many enemy attacks. Your players will go from 100%-0% in a single strike, but you can land the same blow. You are not favored in any fight. Neither is the enemy.
The problem people have with this game isn't the RNG, but instead the difficulty curve. The game is always hard, but it goes from hard during the level 1 and 3 dungeons, to brutal in level 5 and insane in level 6 dungeons. The massive spikes in difficulty catch the average player off-guard and once a level 5 dungeon is started for the first time with the usual crew and they get demolished, discouragement is had and RNG is blamed when in fact it was their lack of preparation.
In level 1 dungeons you can pick any composition you want, and still succeed. You could go in with 4 of the same class, all with no trinkets and still complete the quest. During level 3 quests, you need to mix up your roster a bit and start thinking about good class combos but it's still straightforward and can be tank and spanked. Then comes level 5 dungeons. I have a feeling once most players reach level 5 quests is when they start blaming "RNG" and stop playing out of frustration. The difference in difficulty between a level 3 and a level 5 dungeon is immense. In level 5 dungeons, your party composition is extremely important. You need to have a clear idea of what each class brings to the table along with their strengths and weaknesses. It's no longer a zerg rush where all your attacks land and you can just go full offense. Debuffs need to be applied. Stuns are your friend. Movement skills become necessary. You must camp at the right time. Your trinket selection is
All of these mechanics aren't new, but they weren't really a factor until now. Once you figure out how to correctly utilize all of the mechanics the game has to offer, level 5+ dungeons become "easy" again.
So in conclusion Darkest Dungeon is not the unfair game with imbalanced RNG that the "most helpful" reviews would like you to think it is. It is a beautifully difficult game that has steep learning curves. These nightmarish creatures can be felled! They can be beaten! Confidence surges as the enemy crumbles!
TL;DR
Darkest Dungeon has fair RNG. It is the most fun you'll have while simultaneously wanting to rip your hair out. Buy it.

Darkest Dungeon has a great balance between difficulty and engagement.  You will be frustrated, you will find yourself at your wits end, but if you're like me you won't be able to quit.  It gives you just enough progress for you to hope for a better run next time.  I can honestly say it's been a long time since I've played a game with such balance.
The game has great depth.  Multiple character classes with a wide selection of skills and items to customize your party.  Each party make up plays different and feels different.
The game is turn based but the art style, graphics, and sound give it a thrilling feel.  It's easy to get lost in the game and the stress of the dungeon.  I'm not usually a fan of this style but I found myself often on the edge of my seat wondering just how I'd make it through to the next battle.
The only con I would give this game is some of the battles difficulty is so upscaled it's almost left to chance whether you'll succeed or not.  A lucky hit can determine the whole fight and a loss can lead to a lot of grinding and laborous replaying to rebuild your characters.
I highly recommend this game and for the price I guarantee you won't be dissapointed.  I've had 35 hours in it and I'm still going.

If you enjoy slowly dipping your feet into a game, with a "learn as you go" approach, Darkest Dungeon returns to the days of the cane and beats you merciliessly until you get it right.
The artwork is fantastic and the setting, while not entirely original, nears perfection in execution. The narrator is astounding and truly immerses you into the situation. The interface has been tweaked over time and whilst it initially is somewhat overwhelming, gives you all the information you need to make an informed tactical decision.
Your heroes will die. Your favourite champions will become so twisted that you are either forced to lose your savings to keep them sane or merely discard them to the pit. There will be times where everything has gone right for you in the quest, but suddenly a role of the dice will ruin the run.
The bosses are varied in tactical approach and always feel threatening, moreso the minibosses that roam the dungeon with the intent of taking advantage of low supplies and loads of loot.
I suppose that's what this game does best; it does away with the RPG leveling curve  that will allow you to remove most of the challenge in the game. Even notably difficult ones, such as Etrian Odyssey, suffer from this fate. However, Darkest Dungeon constantly pushes you in to uncomfortable positions and forces you to make the best of, sometimes, dreadful situations.
Darkest Dungeon might possibly be the best RPG I've ever played, most certainly the best one I've played on Steam.
I'm not proud of the time I've spent playing this game.

Fun, brutal, and oh so unforgiving. This is truly what a sequel should be, improving on the bad, making the good better, adding some new features, and taking away anything unecessary. This game feels exactly like the original (the one in 2011) and former Xcom players will have no problems jumping in. Likewise, newcomers will find this game to be a bit harsh at first if they don't know what they're doing or if they don't know what the best strategy is, though there are lots of guides to help with that. To me though, the hardest part definitely comes in management. The Avatar Project, or the main thing you're fighting, can only be slown down by certain operations, it's no longer the take your time that we're used to in EW, but it still can feel a lot like it the further in the game you go. On a similar note, combat has been revamped and with all the other people talking about concealment and timed missions, I won't go into it, though I will say I like both. Another good thing is the multitude of ways to finish missions. In EW it was straight up kill all enemies or rescue certain amount of civs then kill all enemies. Now, there are missions such as hostage rescue, comm defense, comm destruction, vip capturing, and even detonating bases. The way they all function is great as well, they have multiple ways of finishing them, you can either go in guns blazing with a full squad, or use a lone soldier to capture an objective and then high tale it out without killing anyone. In general, it's a fun game and a great way to feel mad after seeing your rookies constantly mess up. 9/10

Starbound is an indie game developed by Chucklefish Games. The game is set in space, and the environment is randomly generated featuring: creatures, dungeons, items, and planets. It's massive, and that is a huge understatement. There are moons, which orbit thousands of planets, which are located within hundreds of galaxies, which are situated within dozens of universes. I'm sure you get the idea. The game has only recently entered beta-testing, which has allowed hungry fans to be sated. Starbound was extremely hyped, and the figures definitely show it. Chucklefish decided to launch the game via the kickstarter program, and with it, easily reached all of it's stretch goals; also gaining over $1,000,000. Anyway, I've given you enough of a history lesson, let's begin.
Starbound almost looks like a clone of Re-Logic's Terraria, however, I believe there is a huge divide between the potential enjoyment in these titles. When I first glimpsed Starbound on the Steam marketplace, it looked very appealing, and at this point I had already purchased a copy of Terraria - convinced by my friends to do so, and by the cheapness of the game. Terraria was not a game I enjoyed actually, even though it's of a similar sub-genre. I felt Terraria's graphics were bland and the gameplay was overall unsatisfying. This almost swayed me away from purchasing such a great title, but I took a chance and gave it another shot. Starbound impressed me in every way that Terraria didn't manage too; it was captivating and exciting. Starbound's graphics have a stylistic edge to it; possessing a retro feel, but still managing to stand out. The gameplay structure will now capture a wider audience, and is also more profound in general - it focuses more on exploration and experiencing various parts of the game; rather than laborious mining and gathering, prominent in Terraria. Both these factors have fulfilled the most important point: making the game fun. Let's look a bit more about what the game provides, rather than comparing it endlessly with it's counter-part Terraria.
Starbound's character creation system is somewhat limited, but compared to a lot of other games, there's no complaining. You can choose from multiple races embedded within it's sci-fi universe and customize your character minimally. The races are a cool concept, it allows you to imagine the character yourself, even with limited customization options; as the creators have developed back-story/history for each individual race. Take this example of the Apex:
"Apex are ape-like creatures with naturally humanoid features. Due to a process that Apex researchers discovered, they are able to upgrade their intellectual state while degrading their physical state. There is much dissent among them, as individuals chosen for researching a better process never return."
As you can see it's reasonably brief, but they've actually given the player a bit of breathing room; like I said before, it allows you to imagine the character yourself and create your story. It's an open-world game, and it's massive. You have the choice to do whatever you want, whenever you want, and however you like.
After you design your character, you arrive on your ship; soon after deducing that you should use the portal on your ship, which beams you down to your starting planet - one of many.  The game starts of quite slow, since mining minerals and gathering resources will be slower before you can craft half decent items; however, once you do get past that starting point, the game becomes a blast. It's an exciting single-player experience, there's a fantastic atmosphere; the sound and visuals can really evoke the essence of the game at moments. The multi-player mode entirely augments this experience, everything that you thought was boring before is now exhilarating.
When playing multi-player, you can do everything you can do in single-player, but with your friends - as expected, but that's the beauty of it. Playing single-player can make the game feel extremely lonely, which is it's own experience, but will become stale after awhile, and you will find yourself playing the game only in short bursts. An important feature of multi-player is visiting your friends planet. You are able to beam to your space ship at will (as long as you aren't underground) and do several things whilst in it. In multi-player you can beam to your friends ship and explore his planet from there. Exploring the vast universe with a gang of friends must sound like a captivating adventure, even at first glance.
Starbound has colossal amounts of potential thanks to it's understanding developers and dedicated fan-base. It has a great base model as it is and can only improve. I hope you will purchase Starbound and have a fascinating time playing - watching it grow, plus getting involved with it's great community. Have a tremendous time exploring space.

XCOM 2 is a worthy yet buggy sequel to 2012's XCOM. It's more challenging (sometimes artificially so) with an overall better sense of urgency and desperation than the original had. Firstly, the game in its current state (Feb 2016) requires patching. There are frequent slow-downs, weird pauses between turns, and the occasional lengthy loading time. The game has trouble maintaining a stable FPS. A lot of these issues were actually present in XCOM 2012's release though and they were (mostly) patched out. Give them time to fix it.
In terms of gameplay the core elements of the XCOM francise remain the same - strategic decision-making with turn-based tactical combat against an alien threat. The Geoscape strategic portion has the biggest changes with more choice of "missions" which often serve to take up time rather than being tactical missions. For example you can search for supplies or alien materials. Tactical missions pop up with some defined benefit for their completion and a penalty for ignoring them - and the penalty at least up until the end game is punishing, so you often can't ignore them. The game will infrequently give you a choice of 3 missions - these missions will negate one of the bonuses that the aliens acquire for that month. The aliens play a much better strategic game and you can't simply sit and wait for the next plot point to trigger. In XCOM 2012 you could halt progress by simply not completing some objectives, giving you all the time in the world to advance. In XCOM 2 the aliens are constantly making progress on Avatar, their final solution to humanity. You can delay it but you cannot stop it. This increases that urgency and desperation that XCOM desperately needed; you can't simply wait and research your way to victory.
The tactical game remains largely the same with the added benefit of better map randomisation, a more aggressive AI, and a few new mechanics. Firstly some missions start you troops in concealment, giving you the ability to move around the map without triggering the enemy unless you get too close (or they patrol into your group), allowing you to set up ambushes. Many missions also have a turn limit. I can see why they did this - a very popular tactic in the original was simply to put everyone into Overwatch and advance cautiously, creating a wall of reaction-fire death. Turn limits stop you from relying on this tactic; you have to find the enemy and objectives quickly instead of creeping forward. Overwatch is still useful but you need to be more aggressive. That said, some of the limits feel awfully restrictive, especially at higher difficulty levels (especially when the aliens are just plain stronger across the board). There are still plenty of "XCOM fail" moments where shots miss despite a high probably of hitting (90% isn't 100% guys!) but they hurt a lot more with the new aliens.
Overall I actually do recommend XCOM 2 to fans of the original. Plenty of people complain about turn limits, and they do have a point - but plenty of people whinged that XCOM 2012 was too easy with its Overwatch death-squad tactic, so I guess some people just won't be happy either way. There are some technical issues that will no doubt be mostly resolved, but this is still a fantastic game. Incidentally, the original XCOM's successor, Terror from the Deep, was well known for being XCOM except underwater and with a much higher difficulty level. I guess they just followed the same plan this time.

Positives:
-Mechanics, aesthetic, and theme harmonize tremendously well
-Innovative position-based combat system
-The art and sound design manage to create atosphere and punch out of minimal animation
-The stress and death's door mechanic do entirely what they are meant to do
-Very well balanced
-Wayne June's voice
-Earns every bit of the anxiety and tension it demands
-Weird note, but the "timing" of all the sound cues and animations is absolutely perfect (actions hit suddenly, give you just enough time to process the possible consequences before revealing the result to relief/despair; it's never boring or confusing)
Negatives:
-Some wonky UI elements (taking torches from the first, not the smallest, stack; Not being upfront with duration of buff skills; Very poor information about enemy attacks)
-Wiki-dependent (why not collect curio and enemy information, and Darkest Dungeon maps, in an in-game encyclopedia that exapands as you encounter the subjects?)
-Some character classes have intriguing abilities and build possibilities that lack complements from the other heroes (I'd love a reliable front-line healer, or for the houndmaster to be able to use stress-relief from position 2, or for the arbalest to be able to heal every position; you're probably going to end up taking a vestal/occultist and jester/crusader on near every run for reliable support, which feels like a lot of wasted opportunities)
-The Darkest Dungeon levels could be rebalanced. The 2nd might just be too punishing.
-There is sometimes too much temptation to cheese out an encounter for heals in a way that breaks the atmosphere
-Each hero class has only one sprite with different pallette swaps.  It's a more developer-intensive thing to address (if you add more characterization, you have to animate for all of them), and may even have been an intentional design choice, but still is noticeable at times for it's repetitiveness.
***
Darkest Dungeon might not be for everyone.  It's not for those who want to charge through a game before getting to the next one.  It's not for those who are easily frustrated by setbacks or some bad luck.  You will go on lots of missions, lose heroes you spent lots of time building up, and have pivotal moments go against you at the worst time.  But for those who enjoy the core gameplay loop, it won't feel like a grind, and the stakes and unpredictability reinforce the core appeal of creating meaningful, stressful choices for the player to tell the story of their own playthrough.
Darkest Dungeon is my favorite game of the past year.  It's a quirky but elegant game that uses a near-perfect collaboration of several disparate elements to create exactly the sort of emotional response it's going for. You'll notice that the negatives above are more specific than the positives.  Well, that's because when the overall package is so well put-together, the small blemishes are easier to articulate.
The basics: You have an overworld strategy element (the hamlet), where you recruit heroes, upgrade them, and so on.  You send these heroes into various areas on expeditions to map out areas, kill bosses, etc.  You have to buy supplies for the expedition, so inventory management is one key part of the game: Do I take the shiny treasure if it means dropping survival equipment that might net me a greater return if I keep going long enough to make use of it?
Inside the dungeons, you'll have many combat encounters.  The basic system is a turn-based one that is position-dependent.  Your heroes have skills that can only be activated from certain ranks (it just stacks you and the opposing party in lines) and can only target enemies in certain positions.  There are a few strategic elements that this opens up.  First is that, since you can only take four combat skills per hero at a time, you have to balance maximizing their ability from the position you prefer, and having options if they get shuffled out of it (which can happen in a variety of ways).  Second is that it means that a single character class can have different behaviors and builds based on where they are supposed to be in your line-up, which makes for some interesting variety (and stressful decision-making, when you want to have it both ways).
Then, you have the death's door mechanic.  Death is permanent and there is only one auto-saving slot per game.  However, reducing a character to 0 hp does not kill them right away.  Instead, it puts them on "death's door", a weakened state in which any additional damage has a chance to kill them.  Even a 1 hp heal gets them off death's door, so they're ensured to survive one more shot.  This creates some very tense moments as you pray that your heroes get to go first and get that crucial heal in before the potential death blow comes in.
And finally, you have stress, the mechanic that might most make Darkest Dungeon the game it is.  Characters don't just have health points.  They also accrue stress from things such as traps, enemy abilities, critical hits, etc.  Stress can be alleviated by killing certain opponents, landing crits, allied abilities, etc., but if a character's stress hits 100, they have to make a virtue check.  If they fail (which is the majority of the time), they take on an "affliction", some devastating personality defect such as Abusive, Paranoid, or Hopeless.  These are stat debuffs, but more importantly, also take the character somewhat out of your control.  A character might skip their turn, or hurt themselves.  Afflicted characters can actively refuse others' attempts to heal them, and their negativity causes stress to their comrades.  A failed stress-check can quickly snowball and doom an entire expedition, so managing it is key.  Otherwise, a character can get to 200 stress and have a heart attack, which puts a character at 0 health and on death's door, or kills them outright if they are already there.
This blends with the global strategy element because, while healing physical damage is free, you have to spend gold to fix stress levels and afflictions, or remove negative personality quirks that stressed characters develop.  You're put in a position where you constantly have to evaluate whether to invest a significant amount to get a decent character back in fighting condition, or replace them with a newbie (for free).
Darkest Dungeon succeeded in punishing me for cherishing my characters, and encouraged me to play in a more cold-blooded way than I normally would without literally forcing me to.  But the incentive isn't so overwhelming that I don't still get attached to characters.  And no matter how much I try to protect certain heroes, a few cruel rolls of the dice mean that no one is ever truly safe.
I got to a point where I simply did not want to continue.  Not because it wasn't fun, but because I was just too anxious about the possibility of things going wrong.  I researched ways to save-scum, and made back-up files in case the worst happened.  But I never used them.  It never felt justified.  The game is harsh, even cruel, but refrains from pitching into the absurd or unfair (usually).
There are so many great things going on that it feels weird to acknowledge that none of them could make the game on their own.  The narrator's voice (the incomparable Wayne June) is always enjoyable even after it gets repetitive, but in a lesser game it would just be a detail.  The graphics aren't AAA, and aren't trying to be.  The sound is good.  The mechanics are sound.  But the reason they make for such a good game is that they all drive toward the same purpose and theme.  From the quirk mechanics to stress afflictions, to the degree of rng, they all reinforce the Lovecraftian themes of madness and futility in the face of incomprehensible horrors.  It just works.  It's a delicious experience that really shows how much the design team cared about and understood what was special about their own project.

Fun, brutal, and oh so unforgiving. This is truly what a sequel should be, improving on the bad, making the good better, adding some new features, and taking away anything unecessary. This game feels exactly like the original (the one in 2011) and former Xcom players will have no problems jumping in. Likewise, newcomers will find this game to be a bit harsh at first if they don't know what they're doing or if they don't know what the best strategy is, though there are lots of guides to help with that. To me though, the hardest part definitely comes in management. The Avatar Project, or the main thing you're fighting, can only be slown down by certain operations, it's no longer the take your time that we're used to in EW, but it still can feel a lot like it the further in the game you go. On a similar note, combat has been revamped and with all the other people talking about concealment and timed missions, I won't go into it, though I will say I like both. Another good thing is the multitude of ways to finish missions. In EW it was straight up kill all enemies or rescue certain amount of civs then kill all enemies. Now, there are missions such as hostage rescue, comm defense, comm destruction, vip capturing, and even detonating bases. The way they all function is great as well, they have multiple ways of finishing them, you can either go in guns blazing with a full squad, or use a lone soldier to capture an objective and then high tale it out without killing anyone. In general, it's a fun game and a great way to feel mad after seeing your rookies constantly mess up. 9/10

I heard a lot of things about Darkest Dungeon,
positive, when I first bought it. The game had been out in Early Access for some time, and I had purchased it not long before it went into its non-Early-Access full release. Most of the negative comments around that time focused on very specific changes made during the later stages of Early Access development (primarily PROT, Corpses, and Heart Attacks, for those of you who are wondering).
Not only is this one of the most original concepts for a game in recent memory, rooted in the innovative Stress system - not only does this game exude a strong Lovecraft-inspired atmosphere and style with it's excellent thick-borders bold-colours approach to artwork and gloriously bassy/baritone voiceover narration - not only is this game incredibly adept at creating tension, making you beg RNJesus for the dice to roll your way, and break down when it inevitably doesn't - and not only is this game addictive as all hell, but it's
I admit, sometimes the game feels extremely unfair - very rarely are the odds in your favour, and often you'll find yourself simply trying not to die, as opposed to trying to succeed; in other words, trying to make the best of a bad situation. But the game tells you this right from the beginning. Your favourite hero will probably die, missions will fail (either from your mistakes, or from a particularly unpleasant dice roll). Bad stuff happens. But as long as you are patient, methodical, and prepared to face the consequences of your actions, the game becomes cold and indifferent, as opposed to cruel and vindictive.
TLDR: To summarise - Darkest Dungeon is a fun and well polished (if rather challenging) game which tried and succeeded to deliver not just a great gameplay experience, but a great horror experience too.

Its very clear that Firaxis learned from the Long War moders. Nearly every aspect of XCOM 2 is an improvement over XCOM. The few areas that are not as smooth are the room building game play and the overall rush you are put in due to PLOT.
Room building in XCOM 2 removed the synergy element that was in the previous game, making room placement less important overall, yet there is still some stratigy to it due to the new Workshop, and its bonus to adjacent rooms.
The other area where the game may falter is the main plot element, the Avatar Project. As you progress in the game, you are racing to stop the aliens from completing the project, with their progress being visable from the world map. This rushed gameplay is also transfered into most missions where you have a turn limit before the game auto fails the mission. Again this is visable to you in every mission, so you can plan around it. However, being forced into a faster paced gameplay may not be attractive to vet XCOM players.
Overall, great game, but it does have its less then stellar aspects.

I have a hard time putting into words the feelings that this game provokes. The atmosphere that's been created by the narrator and unique art-style really adds to the emotional roller coaster that is Darkest Dungeon. To see your favorite hero overcome their blaring imperfections, combat madness and despairity, cut down hordes of enemies with a few hitpoints left, and stand fast against the stresses of the unnatural, unholy and unforgiving is uplifting. You'll spend heaps of gold investing in their equipment, abilities, survival tactics, physical fortitude and mental health - only to have them ripped away from you by an unexpected critical blow from a beast you've slain a hundred times previous. The unpredictable nature of this game is one of its most appealing factors; life is unpredictable. Life is fragile, life is gruesome, and life is downright unfair. This is a MUST-play for fans of RPG's, base-builders, and turn-based games. An indie masterpiece.

A worthy addition to the fantastic XCOM series, and a compelling addendum to XCOM: Enemy Unknown.
A fantastic game with a fair learning curve, good replayability, and rich storyline (which is largely unnecessary in a setting of "aliens have invaded, go kill them", but there you go). As such, I'll mainly be judging the game in comparison to the first one.
The new additions are good, and make an effort to appeal to the "rebel resistance" theme of the new game. There's hacking, concealment, randomized loot drops, a new resource "intel", a remix of the classes, and the XCOM "base" now spends its time shooting all over the globe to try and sustain the resistance. Also, many missions now require the squad to complete an objective and extract rather than just giving the player the "kill all enemies" mission in different terrain settings. Concealment adds a fantastic new dimension to the tactical game, allowing you to launch ambushes, bypass enemy squads entirely, and scout for your opponents. The new classes all operate very differently from each other, and their abilities are now categorized based on what you want that particular soldier to do: blow stuff up, or support with heavy fire? Scout, or assault? Heal or shut down robotic enemies? Gone are the days where most of your soldiers of a given class took the same upgrades because most were just plain better than the other choice. There's still some of that (I'm never going to NOT take Long Watch or Threat Assessment, guys), but with most of the skills you're making a clear choice between what sort of role they'll play in future battles. Psychic soldiers are also a class of their own now, rather than being ordinary soldiers with additional powers. The Avenger is a neat little change from the single XCOM facility, both in terms of gameplay and theme. It's also nice that the organization is always doing something, rather than the "scanning" option that the first game used to fast-forward until something interesting happened.
Hacking and looting are less interesting. Neither are particularly tactical, and the loot has that bizarre video-game quality where a chrysalid can apparently come loaded down with weapon attachments. There's also only one enemy in each mission that drops loot, and it can explode if you kill the enemy with explosive weapons or don't get to it in time. These things change the character of each mission, but not in any meaningful or important way.
Some things that are missing from the game that were in the last one are alien capturing, shooting down UFOs, and lasers. Laser weapons have been replaced by "magnetic weapons" as the second-tier weapon technology, but other than a lack of red beams don't represent any kind of meaningful change. Aliens can't be captured, but don't worry; the game finds other ways to make you charge up to extremely unsafe range and try to punch at enemy troops with the Skulljack. That said, I didn't actually get much use out of it; there are only two occasions in which you have to use it on enemies. The removal of UFO-hunting is quite a blow, and unfortunately takes out a big part of the original XCOM game. There are UFOs, but they're rare, and unlike before don't yield critical supplies and components on the (very uncommon) chance that you actually get to assault one. I realize that the dynamic of the second game makes the idea of XCOM shooting down UFOs with interceptors very unlikely, but considering that scavenging alien technology is supposed to be more important than ever it feels like they could have worked it in somehow.
Finally, general criticisms: the research tree is too short, and there aren't enough types of buildings. After having finished the game, I regretted all the investments I'd made into scientists and engineers, because I'd spent the last third of my game time with the scientists standing around doing nothing and two engineers (and room spaces) with nothing to do. I feel like there was definitely room for another technology tier of weapons and armor; how about magnetic, then laser, THEN plasma? And maybe an improved power armor suit for late game? A slew of very late-game projects would have been nice, just to give my scientists something to do. Perhaps give them an option to create PCS upgrades? Or maybe some marginal weapon improvements that have extremely long research times? We need SOMETHING.
Some more variety in weapons would also be nice. Just as before, the Assault (now the Ranger) class is the only one that gets a choice of main weapon, and that choice is rifle or shotgun. It's nice that you put a flamethrower in the game at all, but on top of being a one-shot weapon, you make me choose between that and the rocket launcher. COME ON, PEOPLE.
Finally, bugs. SOOOOOO many bugs. The vast majority are inexplicable graphical bugs that don't hurt the gameplay; the "bound" animation causes constant problems, enemies that have the floor suddenly explode under them freeze and then re-appear instantly on the ground, and every time I killed an Andromedon with overwatch fire I was afraid my computer was going to crash. Sometimes when I got shot the damage counter would just show an empty box, and sometimes my soldiers would get stuck in an unusual animation like being knocked unconscious. There's a lot of work to do, which just seems bizarre in a game with this level of sophistication.
I'll be playing through again once some more DLC gets released and we get some more content. Hopefully those falling animations will make it in there in the meantime.
As a last note, the final battle was pants-ruiningly intense and incredibly satisfying. But I couldn't understand a single thing the aliens were saying. Good job, guys!

I love this game. It's definitely not your run of the mill turn based RPG for better or worse. It's true the RNG is punishing even ridiculously so at times;however, this game is meant to be punishing  and goes way out of it's to make sure you know it. I enjoy a nigh impossible challenge, but simply put if you don't like extremely difficult games then this is definitely not for you. As far as the multitude of other characteristics that make up the game, everything is quite interesting and unique in my opinion. I love dark gothic/cthulhu-esque atmosphere as well as the great voice acting on the story narrative. The combat gameplay is pretty standard as far as how it handles. The dungeon crawling is simple and interesting enough to make every dungeon a bit different along with a little loot to make it a bit better. Again the the difficulty and RNG affect all these greatly, but to me this is what makes the game so rewarding. I can definitely see how 100+ hours would become grindy and burned out, but I'm not there yet and will enjoy until I do. Money well spent.

XCOM 2 should be at the top of the list for any strategy fan and is likely going to be one of my most played games for quite a while. It has terrific gameplay short of a few bugs and long load times, wonderful support for mods that can continue to grow the game, a story that helps make the game feel real and makes much more sense when compared to Enemy Unknown and a terrific sense of accomplishment. The visuals are inviting and the customizations will further suck you in.
XCOM 2 is absolutely one of the best releases of the year so far, and will likely remain so.
Definitely recommend.

positive, when I first bought it. The game had been out in Early Access for some time, and I had purchased it not long before it went into its non-Early-Access full release. Most of the negative comments around that time focused on very specific changes made during the later stages of Early Access development (primarily PROT, Corpses, and Heart Attacks, for those of you who are wondering).
Not only is this one of the most original concepts for a game in recent memory, rooted in the innovative Stress system - not only does this game exude a strong Lovecraft-inspired atmosphere and style with it's excellent thick-borders bold-colours approach to artwork and gloriously bassy/baritone voiceover narration - not only is this game incredibly adept at creating tension, making you beg RNJesus for the dice to roll your way, and break down when it inevitably doesn't - and not only is this game addictive as all hell, but it's
I admit, sometimes the game feels extremely unfair - very rarely are the odds in your favour, and often you'll find yourself simply trying not to die, as opposed to trying to succeed; in other words, trying to make the best of a bad situation. But the game tells you this right from the beginning. Your favourite hero will probably die, missions will fail (either from your mistakes, or from a particularly unpleasant dice roll). Bad stuff happens. But as long as you are patient, methodical, and prepared to face the consequences of your actions, the game becomes cold and indifferent, as opposed to cruel and vindictive.
TLDR: To summarise - Darkest Dungeon is a fun and well polished (if rather challenging) game which tried and succeeded to deliver not just a great gameplay experience, but a great horror experience too.

By far the worst of the Dark Souls games. Most of what is good about it is just directly copied from Dark Souls 1, trading on nostalgia rather than offering anything new.
What is new is a much more buggy game with a horrible interface. The camera does not let you redirect it reliably. Lock on randomly fails, leaving you rolling in the wrong direction. Enemies regularly kill you by just thrusting their weapon directly through a wall/floor/ceiling.
Hit boxes are unreliable - sometimes arrows end up hitting and getting stuck floating in mid-air, other times they fly right through stone to hit you when you thought you were hiding behind something. Similar problems with other attacks that miss despite clearly intersecting the enemy, or attacks that count as hits despite not coming close.
Result is a game decided as much by random error as by skill. It's not that this Dark Souls is harder than the others, it's just much more frustrating because when you die, it's much more often to be because of some glitch rather than something you did wrong. The sense of "I could have killed him if I just did X instead of Y" is gone; instead it's "I could have killed him if random glitch Z hadn't happened, guess I'll try again and hope it doesn't happen this time".

Overall, I enjoyed XCOM 2. I plan to play a lot more of it when the performance issues have been (hopefully) fixed and when some more substantial mods are released.
It should be noted that I played on Veteran difficulty. Commander might fix some of the issues I had.
What I liked:
+ FX
+ Story (Plot, characters, missions, VO)
+ Customisation
+ Combat
+ Stealth
+ Loot became meaningless pretty fast but it was fun customising weapons.
+ Classes
+ AI
Mixed opinions:
~ The randomly generated levels are hit or miss. Usually miss. I found myself fighting in streets and hiding behind chest-high walls and pylons most of the time. Everything that’s interesting in the level tends to not be in the B-line you have to make just to make it to the objective in time during a timed mission.
~ BLOOD FOR THE RNGODS. The RNG can get pretty crazy at times, which is both good and bad. Good when it’s funny and satisfying to hit a 30% shot + crit and bad when you miss two 94% shots then proceed hit a 43% shot.
What I didn't like:
- Overabundance of timed missions. Timed missions are too short to do any meaningful planning, recon, or strategy. You have to make a B-line for the objective. This was my biggest peeve and I’d say it hurt my experience the most.
- OST. The tracks Lazarus and Out of the Ashes and the main battle theme are good. Everything else is pretty generic orchestral music and ultimately forgettable. I was really hoping for more heavy percussion and synth.
- The setting isn’t interesting. I never found the ADVENT intimidating.
- Atmosphere. I never felt one outside of the cutscenes.
- The enemy variety isn’t great. A lot of the enemy types stopped being scary pretty quickly. The only ones to really be worried about are the ones with a lot of armour. Most of the time you just fight the MEC's from Enemy Within and ADVENT soldiers. I was really surprised at how I barely fought any Mutons. I only fought the Muton Berserker three times, one of those times being the final mission.
- Performance issues.
- Mission variety. There are only a handful of mission types. The most interesting and enjoyable ones like UFO capture and base defense only happened once each in my playthrough. Most of the time you're tasked with making a B-line to something you have to hack. I did enjoy the Avatar facility sabotage missions though.

There is something I want to say about this game. I think this title truly has some of the best turn based party/group combat I've ever come across.
When I think on turn based combat that has bored me in some sense it always comes down to same thing. That is, one or two simple "routines" that carry you through most every encounter. "Strategy" dissolves altogether with turn-based combat when it becomes lather rinse repeat.
In the most simplistic of ways, DD completely negates this ^^ even being possible. With the inability to utilize the same team members consistently, keep them in static position/ranges and with gameplay that is completely hinged on it's unique brand of ailments and buffs each and every battle is something that NEEDS to be thought about. And it is something that needs to be thought about carefully to dodge penalty of death.
I'm not saying this is "the best game ever" but I would certainly argue it a contender for some of the finest battle mechanics of it's kind. At the very least the game is built for someone just like me who, after decades of turns and menus, is just completely bored of spamming "attack" and "X-spell" over and over.
