+++Edited Feb 27 for Summary+++
1. Similar mechanics to XCom EU, reskinned mostly for the better
2. Awesome tactical combat
3. Annoying mechanics that interrupt gameplay
4.  Someone shoot Bradford (There are mods that will shut him up)
5.  Expanded use of mission timers adds tension, but to me it feels heavyhanded (again, can be modded out).
++++++
Okay, I am not going to say that this game is flawless.  In fact, by time this is over (if you read all of my review) you might think I hate the game due to its annoyances, but you would be wrong.  It's another awesome XCOM game.
Despite the big change in the premise, the game mechanics are much like the XCOM from a few years back.  The premise is that you lost the original XCOM game, the commander (you) got captured and was imprisoned by the evil aliens who set up a velvet gauntlet world government.  Some of  XCOM remains as a resistance who fights the aliens with little success for 20 years.  The 'some remaining' part is Central Officer Bradford, who in the previous game was your chief of staff who briefed you on missions and showed up in a lot of cutscenes.  They re-voiced actored and reskinned him so that he went from a pencil neck support guy to some generic G.I. Joe type.  For some reason, Bradford decides that they only way the resistance can survive is to rescue the guy who lost the last war for them (you), and that's where the game begins.
The guts of the game will be very familiar to players of the old game.  You have a squad of up to six members.  Instead of an underground base that you can expand to add new capabilites, you have a mobile spaceship that you clear out to add new capabilities.  Instead of a doom clock tracking angry countries who turn their back on XCOM, you have a sinister alien project that fills in little red boxes - when they are all filled the game ends, but if you do specific missions you can un-fill boxes.  Instead of building facilties to launch satellites to add countries and their revenue, in XCOM2 you add comm rooms to spread your defiant message to new areas of the subjugated world.  You also reasearch and build new technologies to upgrade your squad's weapons, like in the old game.
Some of the tinkering changes I like.  The have new classes, which are also mostly improvements.  Some are familiar, but the speicalist is a big change that worked for me.  Like the orignal, most classes generally have two training tracks -- specialists can focus on taking out mechanical creatures (vital in this game) or healing your squad.  But also, they have some decent general combat cacabilities such as some overwatch bonuses.  They are also the best at hacking enemy facilities and possibly getting good personal or squad bonues.  Or, if they screw up, they can give the aliens adantages.
The changes to base building are generally good too. In the old game if you wanted new scientists or engineers, you either bought them through facility upgrades, or got them through missions.  They were all faceless and nameless.  In XCOM2, you can recruit them from places on the map or rescue them from missions.  They all have names and their own appearce.  Moreover, they changed how engineers work.  In the old XCOM they were part of an equation on how fast you build stuff and were packed into the labs like Jack's Links in an economy pack.  Now, you can upgrade the effectivness of most of your facilties by assigning an specific engineer to a specific facility.  This is kind of scary when you assign an engineer to the med bay so your soldiers will heal faster.  Dear Firaxis:  Ability to build bridge does not equal ability to perform surgery on human being.
In general, the base building I think is an improvement on the old XCOM, but the combat, which is the meat and drink of XCOM is still good - in fact it's better.  I have never had as many fun, interesting tactical challenges and fun responses to those challenges as I have experienced in this game.   The different ways of opening up a can on alien butt is astounding.  I personally like explosions, so I carry a squad heavy in grenadiers who strip away armor and weaken the bad guys so my other squad members can mop up.  They also added more useful pistol skills to the sharpshooter to give them more tactical flexibility.  Rangers have some pretty amazing close quarter skills, and psi guys can unload lots of white-haired, purply awesomness.  There is a thread on the forums about favorite XCOM2 moments that will demonstrate just how versatile, fun and rewarding the combat is.
Some parts of the game are no so much fun.  The game seems to be designed to too frequently rip the controls out of your hands and show you things that you already know or don't care about.  For example, most of the strategic game involves flying to a part of the world map to pick up supplies, start missions, etc.  These actions typically take time.  While you are doing this, the game keeps interrupting you to tell you about side missions, new supplies, or alien progress in their doomsday weapon.  It doesn't do this by just having a message on the screen or an announcement -- no, it highjacks your screen through a cutscene or force-scrolls you over to some other part of the map like the middle of the pacific or wherever.  Then you have to manually scroll back to whatever you we doing.  It does this a lot, and its annoying.
Second, I am not sure why the world got overrun after XCOM, but I'm going to blame Bradford.  Not because its his fault or anything, but because he is an annoying, bossy little twit.  Even more than XCOM, his voiceover druing missions is aggravating.  For example, there are missions where the aliens are attacking reistance settlements.  To 'win' the mission, the aliens can't kill more than 6 civilians.  At civilian death #1 he starts screaming that the civilan casusalties are "massive" AND YOU MUST DO SOMETHING NOW.  He does this several times again in this mission as more unfortunates on the other side of the map die.  He also similarly hyperventalates during every other timer mission.    When you are in a nasty firefight while he is at home in his comfy chair, it gets a little hard to take.
On this issue of timers, there has already been a lot written so I won't spend much time on them except to say I have mixed feelings.  I played vanilla throughout my first playthrough and disliked being on the clock.  Also, XCOM is a tactical game about squad combat.   I don't think charging into 60% of all missions at full bore while some desk jocky screams "Hurry, hurry, hurry.  My god, the damage, the casulaties..." into your ear is the culmination of 2000 years of tactical doctrine.  However, I never really had a problem meeting the deadlines, and a part of me also says the combat would not be as fun and as engaging without that artifical sense of drama.  On my next playthrough I've decided not to load one of the mods that extend or remove the timers.  But you can if you want, its really up to you.
In short this game is a must for anyone who likes tactical, turn-based combat, and I hope you enjoy it as much as I do.

tl;dr - Fallout 4 is a decent game with a better engine than the ones that came before, but now Bethesda is trying to add microtransactions.
Fallout 4 is a great improvement in many ways over its predecessors. It looks better and works better (although it struggled at launch with some bugs).
There are problems however, such as the dialog options, oversimplification of levelling, removal of ammunition crafting, and more. Some of these have been fixed by modders, but some just cannot be fixed. Not all of these are truly atrocious either and are merely a matter of taste, which is why I held off on writing a review for this game.
Now, there is the Creation Club. Some people had high hopes for it, some did not trust it. Bethesda said it would be a way to give incentives to modders to make better content, and many people were excited about what that could possibly mean.
Obviously Bethesda would learn from their mistakes, right? Nope. Not at all. The Creation Club is filled with currently only tiny bits of content in singular packages, such as a shotgun for ~$4. That is not what people expected, and you might think that it is just because the Creation Club is new. Well, prepare to be dissapointed. It may only be a rumor and it may change, but for now it is impossible for any major content to show up on their platform due to a record limit. If you dig around you can find people talking about it (CC mods are basically limited to roughly 1/10 the size/scope of the Automatron DLC), and that doesn't sound hopeful.
Finally, lets discuss the FAQ on the CC website.
One of the entries is "Is Creation Club paid mods?" To which the answer begins with "No." Very funny, guys.
Next phrase of interest is "we won't allow any existing mods to be retrofitted into Creation Club, it must all be original content." Funny, as how a large number of items already exist elsewhere AND one of the items looks an awful lot like a straight-up model rip from another Bethesda game.
Finally, "there's a constant demand from our fans to add more official high quality content to our games..." - Yes, but selling Pip-Boy color variants is not what people mean by "high quality content", official or not.
Overall, Bethesda could probably make this system work, but it looks like they just don't care enough to actually make the effort. Hopefully, they will eventually fix it up and make it the system that the people who believed in it thought it would be.

XCOM is back and aside from a few annoying details, it's better than ever.
Virtually every area of the game has seen an improvement in some way. The strategic layer, combat, classes, soldier customization, enemy AI, enemy variety, mission variety, maps, resource management, all improved. But optimization and overall polish has definitely taken a hit, and there are a few questionable decisions that hold it back from being perfect.
On the strategic layer back at the Avenger, managing your base's allocated space has seen a pretty drastic overhaul, and the new contact system replaces the satellites of previous games. In general, you have a lot more control over what missions you take and what you spend your time doing, instead of always passing the time by scanning for activity like in Enemy Unknown. Now as different scanning opportunities pop up with all different kinds of rewards, you can proioritize which place you'd like to take the Avenger to scan based on the rewards that each location gives out.
As far as managing your space goes, the new upgrade system is a welcome improvement over EU. Now you don't need to wait until late-game to get the most out of building generators, for instance. When you unlock the next level generator that increases output, you can just upgrade the generators you have. It's a system that punishes you for early building considerably less than EU did. In addition, each facility can now be staffed with engineers, which are a resource that you'll gather over the course of the game. Staffing facilities gives different bonuses depending on each facility, and you can switch up which facilities are staffed on the fly to focus on what you need at any given time.
Combat is much the same as EU and EW, with some subtle refinements and UI improvements here and there. Grenades and explosives are more powerful and more important now, as you'll often fight armored enemies who need to have that armor shredded by explosives before they become vulnerable. Verticality plays a larger role now as the new maps are built more with setting up for height advantages in mind. The procedural map system works brilliantly and honestly feels like these maps were handcrafted.
Each of the replacement classes for the classes from EU is a step up from the last game, and each one has two distinct paths of skills that almost make each side feel like their own class. The Ranger replaces EU's Assault class, and can be specced for stealth melee or a shotgun vanguard. Sharpshooter replaces the Sniper and be specced for pure sniper or as a gunslinger (a pistoleer that actually has distinct advantages over a sniper -- I once took shots at 8 aliens in one turn using the Faceoff skill that lets you take a free shot at every enemy in range). The Specialist replaces the Support and can be set up as either a field medic or a hacker, and comes with a drone that allows him to heal or hack remotely. The Grenadier replaces the Heavy and can be either a demolitionist focused on explosions or a heavy machine gunner that focuses on the usage of miniguns. And there's a fifth class this time around, the Psi Operative can be acquired earlier in the game than Psi troopers of EU, and is its own distinct class with tons of great abilities. My favorite is being able to permanently mind control one enemy per mission. And the best part of all of these classes is that you can mix and match skills from both sides of each class, so you have a lot of freedom in builds.
Soldier customization is great. You have a lot more control over how your soldiers looks, with customizable faces, names, nationalities, bios, props like shades, headbands, bandannas, headgear like hoods and helmets, full control over weapon and armor color, you can add patterns to weapon and armor (and might I add, weapons and armor can be customized separately), you can pick variants armor torsos, arms, and legs (except for the  middle tier of armor -- you can't change the torso there for some reason) and can even upload your characters to a global character pool so the people you've created will appear in future playthroughs. One big missing feature: If you save a character, you can't load that appearance/description onto a rookie, you just have to hope you bump into that soldier again randomly if you want to use him. To that end, I refrained from using the character pool and will just manually recreate my soldiers next time if I want to re-use those characters. But you can also create characters to be engineers, doctors, or bad guys if that's more up your alley. And finally this one is to Firaxis (thanks for reading, Jake): Give us some more helmets, please. Such a great selection in EU and EW and yet there's only a handful in XCOM 2, and they don't look so good.
Now for some negatives: The game is not optimized well. At all. Back at the Avenger it's  not uncommon for dips down to 10-20FPS, and I have a capable rig playing on reasonable settings. I had better performance on missions after the initial ten-second stuttering as the map first loads, but many people have terrible performance all around. Here's hoping Firaxis addresses this in a future patch and manages to make this game more playable for more folks. It's unacceptable that a game in 2016 that was delayed and made exclusive for the PC runs this poorly, especially when the visuals, while ultimately good, are nothing crazy. There are also frequent hitches like the game hanging in between turns, actions taking longer than they should to start/stop playing, UI and sound bugging out. It's hard to understand why the game shipped like this when Firaxis generally knocks optimization and overall polish out of the park.
Mission timers. Oh boy. Mission timers are a divisive topic within the community. Some people love them, some people say they ruin the game, some people don't care much either way. I played on normal ("veteran", as it's known in-game) and won my first campaign, and on normal the mission timers are very tolerable. On higher difficulties however, the general consensus seems to be that they're only there to force you to rush and make mistakes. I definitely agree that they're artificial difficulty at best and while they didn't bother me so much at my difficulty level, if I had the choice, I probably would have disabled them. They didn't detract much from the game, but at the end of the day they didn't really add anything.
Wounds. My biggest gripe with the game. Injuries for your soldiers are much, much more prevalent this time around than they were in EU. If a soldier takes any hit, no matter how strong their armor is, and no matter if they get healed with a medkit, they're wounded. Wounds come in three flavors, lightly wounded, wounded, and gravely wounded. Grave wounds last up to an in-game month, and while this isn't so bad in the early game, by late-game you're going to be on missions where high-ranking soldiers feel almost mandatory to counter what you're up against. There's a facility where you can staff an engineer to cut recovery times in half, and even then the amount of time your soldiers spend wounded is obscene. The EU system of soldiers only being wounded when they take more damage than their armor adds to their health was much, much better, and I hope this new system is addressed in a patch.
Negatives aside, the game that we got is pretty much just EU but bigger and better in every way. It's not perfect, but what is? It's got some problems, but what doesn't? I would still wholeheartedly recommend this game to anybody, especially people who liked Enemy Unknown.

Alright, DS3 holds a very special place in my heart because it was the first souls game I fully played through and beat. I had previously played most early and mid game in bloodborne (up to rom the spider) and played through a tad bit of early game in the first ds game. So if your looking for a review from someone who played the predocessers FIRST then keep scrolling (Keep in mind I did play through the rest of the series including demons souls afterwards). Okay so enough rambling here it goes, First off DS3 is hard, if you enjoy playing games like call of duty then dark souls probably isn't for you. That "high" feeling you get from killing someone in COD is still there but you actually have to work for it and I think thats what makes dark souls so succesful and why it has simply become my favorite franchise. In DS3 your going to come across bosses and enemies that kill you countless times which causes you to get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off and throw your controller/keyboard around your room, but if your lucky and that controller/keyboard didn't break and you perservere and defeat that difficult enemy/boss you feel like a goddamn legend its like getting a 6 man feed in COD but multiplied by 11! So before you buy this game you need to be prepared to get brutally destroyed by enemies but its the perserverance that really gets you anywhere in this game. Now with this in mind I'm going to compare this game to the prior entries in the franchise. The overall biggest change in this game is that the movement doesn't feel clunky and unfair which in the prior just felt like another barrier to overcome and perhaps one of the hardest. DS3 also has a much faster pace to it then the prior games which made me feel more comfortable taking risks, perhaps it was just the prior experience with bloodborne I had though. Although I have mentioned good things (and will be mentioning more) I wanted to bring up a con to people with previous souls experiences or people who want a game closer to the ds1/ds2 feel rather then the BB feel, DS3 unfortanutly feels much more linear then the prior installments but at the same time its not linear as in Halo campaign or most aaa titles, what I mean by this is that the game uses more bonfires then shortcuts unlike the previous 2 games in the series. I'd assume most people reading this wouldn't care about this though considering they most likely haven't finished any prior games. I want to shortly talk about the dlc before I conclude my review, for the first dlc "ashes of ariendel" I really enjoyed the snowy setting and the challenge the new painted world offered especially the final boss fight and as for "the ringed city" dlc It basicly took the tremendous difficulty of darksouls and bumped it up to 11, the dlc includes 4 new bosses which I consider all of them harder than the base game bosses and adds a lot of cool aspects to the lore/story of the game. I'm going to conclude this review here since it has essentially become an essay at this point but I appreciate it if you read through this huge wall of text and I sincerely hope that this helped you in your decision to purchase this game. +++Edited Feb 27 for Summary+++
1. Similar mechanics to XCom EU, reskinned mostly for the better
2. Awesome tactical combat
3. Annoying mechanics that interrupt gameplay
4.  Someone shoot Bradford (There are mods that will shut him up)
5.  Expanded use of mission timers adds tension, but to me it feels heavyhanded (again, can be modded out).
++++++
Okay, I am not going to say that this game is flawless.  In fact, by time this is over (if you read all of my review) you might think I hate the game due to its annoyances, but you would be wrong.  It's another awesome XCOM game.
Despite the big change in the premise, the game mechanics are much like the XCOM from a few years back.  The premise is that you lost the original XCOM game, the commander (you) got captured and was imprisoned by the evil aliens who set up a velvet gauntlet world government.  Some of  XCOM remains as a resistance who fights the aliens with little success for 20 years.  The 'some remaining' part is Central Officer Bradford, who in the previous game was your chief of staff who briefed you on missions and showed up in a lot of cutscenes.  They re-voiced actored and reskinned him so that he went from a pencil neck support guy to some generic G.I. Joe type.  For some reason, Bradford decides that they only way the resistance can survive is to rescue the guy who lost the last war for them (you), and that's where the game begins.
The guts of the game will be very familiar to players of the old game.  You have a squad of up to six members.  Instead of an underground base that you can expand to add new capabilites, you have a mobile spaceship that you clear out to add new capabilities.  Instead of a doom clock tracking angry countries who turn their back on XCOM, you have a sinister alien project that fills in little red boxes - when they are all filled the game ends, but if you do specific missions you can un-fill boxes.  Instead of building facilties to launch satellites to add countries and their revenue, in XCOM2 you add comm rooms to spread your defiant message to new areas of the subjugated world.  You also reasearch and build new technologies to upgrade your squad's weapons, like in the old game.
Some of the tinkering changes I like.  The have new classes, which are also mostly improvements.  Some are familiar, but the speicalist is a big change that worked for me.  Like the orignal, most classes generally have two training tracks -- specialists can focus on taking out mechanical creatures (vital in this game) or healing your squad.  But also, they have some decent general combat cacabilities such as some overwatch bonuses.  They are also the best at hacking enemy facilities and possibly getting good personal or squad bonues.  Or, if they screw up, they can give the aliens adantages.
The changes to base building are generally good too. In the old game if you wanted new scientists or engineers, you either bought them through facility upgrades, or got them through missions.  They were all faceless and nameless.  In XCOM2, you can recruit them from places on the map or rescue them from missions.  They all have names and their own appearce.  Moreover, they changed how engineers work.  In the old XCOM they were part of an equation on how fast you build stuff and were packed into the labs like Jack's Links in an economy pack.  Now, you can upgrade the effectivness of most of your facilties by assigning an specific engineer to a specific facility.  This is kind of scary when you assign an engineer to the med bay so your soldiers will heal faster.  Dear Firaxis:  Ability to build bridge does not equal ability to perform surgery on human being.
In general, the base building I think is an improvement on the old XCOM, but the combat, which is the meat and drink of XCOM is still good - in fact it's better.  I have never had as many fun, interesting tactical challenges and fun responses to those challenges as I have experienced in this game.   The different ways of opening up a can on alien butt is astounding.  I personally like explosions, so I carry a squad heavy in grenadiers who strip away armor and weaken the bad guys so my other squad members can mop up.  They also added more useful pistol skills to the sharpshooter to give them more tactical flexibility.  Rangers have some pretty amazing close quarter skills, and psi guys can unload lots of white-haired, purply awesomness.  There is a thread on the forums about favorite XCOM2 moments that will demonstrate just how versatile, fun and rewarding the combat is.
Some parts of the game are no so much fun.  The game seems to be designed to too frequently rip the controls out of your hands and show you things that you already know or don't care about.  For example, most of the strategic game involves flying to a part of the world map to pick up supplies, start missions, etc.  These actions typically take time.  While you are doing this, the game keeps interrupting you to tell you about side missions, new supplies, or alien progress in their doomsday weapon.  It doesn't do this by just having a message on the screen or an announcement -- no, it highjacks your screen through a cutscene or force-scrolls you over to some other part of the map like the middle of the pacific or wherever.  Then you have to manually scroll back to whatever you we doing.  It does this a lot, and its annoying.
Second, I am not sure why the world got overrun after XCOM, but I'm going to blame Bradford.  Not because its his fault or anything, but because he is an annoying, bossy little twit.  Even more than XCOM, his voiceover druing missions is aggravating.  For example, there are missions where the aliens are attacking reistance settlements.  To 'win' the mission, the aliens can't kill more than 6 civilians.  At civilian death #1 he starts screaming that the civilan casusalties are "massive" AND YOU MUST DO SOMETHING NOW.  He does this several times again in this mission as more unfortunates on the other side of the map die.  He also similarly hyperventalates during every other timer mission.    When you are in a nasty firefight while he is at home in his comfy chair, it gets a little hard to take.
On this issue of timers, there has already been a lot written so I won't spend much time on them except to say I have mixed feelings.  I played vanilla throughout my first playthrough and disliked being on the clock.  Also, XCOM is a tactical game about squad combat.   I don't think charging into 60% of all missions at full bore while some desk jocky screams "Hurry, hurry, hurry.  My god, the damage, the casulaties..." into your ear is the culmination of 2000 years of tactical doctrine.  However, I never really had a problem meeting the deadlines, and a part of me also says the combat would not be as fun and as engaging without that artifical sense of drama.  On my next playthrough I've decided not to load one of the mods that extend or remove the timers.  But you can if you want, its really up to you.
In short this game is a must for anyone who likes tactical, turn-based combat, and I hope you enjoy it as much as I do.

To clarify recommendation, I'm on the fence.  If you're into Xcom.. Buy it.  If you're not. Don't.
As far as a follow on goes, it's good.  Good idea, quite a basic storyline, but it's fairly involving.
The missions after awhile become quite samey.  But they're fun to complete.
The big let down for me is enforced gameplay and timed missions.   I prefer open non linear games.  Xcom 1 was non linear, sure you have to take out aliens, do missions etc but it wasn't forced on you.
In Xcom2 You spend a few days gathering intel, then a few days picking up supplies(money) then you're given a mission, which you can't ignore doing so looses you the game. In fact you can't really ignore any of the missions or you'll either loose the game outright or you'll loose the county you've spent a week getting.
Then there's the avatar project, which even if you hold every country in the world, can still be completed by the aliens.  Your hand is forced throughout the game and during missions via the timer, forcing you to make moves you'd never make without the timer.  Forcing you to rush and loose essentially.
The game world is excellent, the ai in general is very good, sure there's issues with line of sight and some cosmetic glitches but overall the "idea" of the game is superb.
It is just let down by poor balancing, poor performance issues and mostly by poor design.
I've beaten the game twice on veteran difficulty.  I lost maybe 2-3 soldiers in each game.  I don't mind loosing soldiers if I'm outplayed, but at times the game just seems to decide that you've lost, it's predetermined this and there is nothing to you can to stop it.
Is it value for money? Sure.  I expect with time at least by summer, when the dlc's are introduced it'll be patched and updated.  Will I still be playing it then.. I doubt it.
If xcom 1 had random maps, intelligent ambush and overwatching, the ability to carry wounded soldiers there would really have been no need to even release xcom 2.   It's really just the same game with added insult.
Games aren't about being frustrated and bored they're about having fun and winning. Xcom 2 is about loosing, it's about not getting to do what you want to do when you want to do it.   The physical game is replayable, but do I want to play it again and again.
Nope.  There's just too many annoying mechanics in the game.  Where there's a great idea, it's just poorly implimented or they clearly, just don't care.
7/10 I really tried to like this game, but overall, after everything, I just can't.  Everytime I think of something good about it, I remember 5 bad things.
*Edit*
I hoped the dlc would add more to the game, but it hasn't.  Missions that should appear in mid or late game are appearing almost at the very start, pitting you against insanely powerful boss aliens and you just don't stand a chance.   Without some heavy modding of the dlc to reduce the hitpoints of these bosses, the dlc is worthless.  The added weapons rubbish.   Essentially it's a joke dlc, it's insulting.   Jake Soloman should be fired from firaxis for making this mess.

From the begining.
Gameplay; 8/10
I personally loved the way the game portrayed itself as a survival game, and with the introduction of more guns and other misc. items, it really has gone a long way. The game seems easy during the first few days, but beware of the full moon, as you can get killed easily during it. The only thing stopping this from being a 10/10 rating was how long the day/night cycle lasts, as well as how you can always assure yourself to get the best of the best items at any "military" base.
Story; 8/10
The notes hidden around the various maps hinting to what might have happened was another reason I spent so much time on the game. Getting to explore the maps and searching everywhere for the hidden notes was fun, but got boring after time. Once you find all of them on one map, you have to start a new playthrough entirely just to get to find more on another. Not to mention the many holes in the story, with some notes even seeming to contradict others. The main group of Scorpion 7 was also sort of boring, as you could always find the good loot at any Scorpion 7 base.
Online; 6/10 (Not really related to the game, as it is entirely optional.)
While it can be fun to play online, it is always ruined by the players who just camp the military bases and launch a missile at anyone who comes within a 100 ft. radius of any base. The servers are usually laggy, and you can find cheaters rardless of the BattlEye anti-cheat.
Overall; 9/10
The blend between gameplay and story really makes for a fun time playing the game, especially with the advanced settings and diversity between maps. I can get a solid 50 frames on my computer with the high settings and around 250 on low. All around a wonderful game, I would definitly recommend this to anyone.

tl;dr - Fallout 4 is a decent game with a better engine than the ones that came before, but now Bethesda is trying to add microtransactions.
Fallout 4 is a great improvement in many ways over its predecessors. It looks better and works better (although it struggled at launch with some bugs).
There are problems however, such as the dialog options, oversimplification of levelling, removal of ammunition crafting, and more. Some of these have been fixed by modders, but some just cannot be fixed. Not all of these are truly atrocious either and are merely a matter of taste, which is why I held off on writing a review for this game.
Now, there is the Creation Club. Some people had high hopes for it, some did not trust it. Bethesda said it would be a way to give incentives to modders to make better content, and many people were excited about what that could possibly mean.
Obviously Bethesda would learn from their mistakes, right? Nope. Not at all. The Creation Club is filled with currently only tiny bits of content in singular packages, such as a shotgun for ~$4. That is not what people expected, and you might think that it is just because the Creation Club is new. Well, prepare to be dissapointed. It may only be a rumor and it may change, but for now it is impossible for any major content to show up on their platform due to a record limit. If you dig around you can find people talking about it (CC mods are basically limited to roughly 1/10 the size/scope of the Automatron DLC), and that doesn't sound hopeful.
Finally, lets discuss the FAQ on the CC website.
One of the entries is "Is Creation Club paid mods?" To which the answer begins with "No." Very funny, guys.
Next phrase of interest is "we won't allow any existing mods to be retrofitted into Creation Club, it must all be original content." Funny, as how a large number of items already exist elsewhere AND one of the items looks an awful lot like a straight-up model rip from another Bethesda game.
Finally, "there's a constant demand from our fans to add more official high quality content to our games..." - Yes, but selling Pip-Boy color variants is not what people mean by "high quality content", official or not.
Overall, Bethesda could probably make this system work, but it looks like they just don't care enough to actually make the effort. Hopefully, they will eventually fix it up and make it the system that the people who believed in it thought it would be.

Now, if you're a terraria/minecraft player, you may be a little annoyed that Starbound turned up to join the 'Block Games' party.
But starbound is significantly better that Terraria or Starbound as it has way more features, such as...
1. Much bigger game world
This is kind of obvious, but Starbound's map spans entire sectors of the universe.
Minecraft's map spans 510,000,000,000,000 blocks, Terraria's is determined by the world size at the start, but Starbound's universe is seemingly infininite.
2. Random loot generation
Starbound's loot is randomly generated, Not as in, the game picks pre-made items and places them in a chest. No-no-no
Starbound creates its own loot, like Borderlands, then puts it in the chest. Minecraft has some things that you won't find in chests, like swords, armour, ect. Terraria picks random items from the game and makes them more powerful the deeper you go.
3. Items!
Starbound has LOADS of items. I'm serious. You can find Link's hood, a rainbow cape, tents, guns, even more vanity items...
The list can go on untill the end of time itself!
4. Passive Abilities
Minecraft instantly gets destroyed on this one, as passive abilities are nonexistant, Terraria gives you accessory slots that you can slot passive items into, however Starbound is going to get passive upgrades with the racial armors
(increased inventory, faster movement speed, higher jump height, increased energy regen while in broad daylight ect, ect.)
5. Techs
Starbound has techs that consume energy. These techs can be Samus Aran's Morphball, a double jump, a rocket jump, defying gravity (Is that how you spell defying? Please correct me on this, Reddit.), a dash, and even ED-209!
6. Biomes
Starbound has so many biomes, such as Arid! and Desert! As well as.. wait, tentacles? 7. Progression
Starbound's progression is fairly linear. Build boss summoning item, use boss summoning item, collect loot, craft starmap upgrade, use upgrade, travel to next sector when bothered.

I recall about 13 or 14 years ago when I was first blown away by Bethesda's game Morrowind. Now I find this whole new creation kit... Paid mods with a new name. Fallout 4 was a slight let down to me in the beginning, however I came to love the open ended first person shooter feel and the even the crafting system etc.  I found some interesting mods and it garnered my passion for fallout again.  Now I see this creation club thing as a way to leech money from the work of other people for the benefit of the game company.  I ask myself this is what Bethesda has become? A company that lets the community fix the little bugs it should have set right themselves so they can worry about making the next "great game"? I want to love fallout 4 and all the other games that Bethesda will put out, but after this creation club idea It gets harder for me to find that appreciation that was once there.  Bethesda do yourselves a favor, listen to the gamers and not your wallets thats all I have to say.

I have very mixed feelings on Dark Souls 3. I’m now on my 3rd playthrough, with another on New Game +. I played through primarily as Deprived. After 60 hours I can say finally my thoughts on it and give it a negative review with a score of 5/10.
Dark Souls 3 fails for me as a game for one major reason – and that is inconsistency. In a game about making quick decisions and recognising patterns, inconsistency is an incredibly fatal flaw. The game is meant to be hard, not frustrating because of inconsistency. What do I mean by inconsistency?
For example: Attacks, visuals and sounds not matching up with when things happen. Sometimes you have to dodge on the visual cue, the audio cue or when you can see actual model of the attack. So you’ll go to roll as the person raises their sword to swing and the ‘swoosh’ sound plays, but then they actually do the attack a little over a second later. Attacks hitting things that can’t possibly physically, visually or logically hit (for example a forward attack hitting behind). Attacks that connect visually but don’t deal damage, or make the sound but don’t deal damage.
It’s hard to explain this in a unconvoluted way. For a game about combat, you can’t tell what half the enemies are doing unless you have a reasonable knowledge of the game. You don’t know what/when/how many an attack is, but you know you should probably dodge it.
Online has not great netcoding. And by not great I mean it’s about as shoddy and full of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t as the Australian Greens Party. You’ll hit people when they aren’t there. They’ll hit you when you aren’t there. The fact that you get the hit sound feedback even if you didn’t hit them, and vice versa.
That being said, apart from being frustrating dealing with enemy players, the co-op is pretty okay. I played co-op mostly on my second playthrough and here the networking problems were even more prevalent.  Inconsistency of enemy positions (for example, my friend saw the skeleton boulder was broken when it wasn’t, got hit by it when it was literally nowhere near him at the other end of the tunnel, stuff like this happened very often), connections errors that were primarily linked to wacky server maintenance, passwords not working (seriously, who else is using meme1122 as their password? Why can they summon me?) Co-op was a whole lot of fun when it worked, and you got to do some very silly strategies that completely destroyed the structure and balance of the PvE side of the game. Getting invaded when co-oping was also pretty fun.
“But Algatress, Dark Souls 2/3 sucked! You just have to get good! They aren’t real Dark Souls!”
I mean, the learning of enemies really sucked the first playthrough. By the third you would think I would know what I’m doing, but the game still strikes me as obscenely grindy and inconsistent.
Another thing that’s absolutely sickening is the Dark Souls community in general.
If 2 out of 3 of the games in your series ‘suck’ by the communities own discretion, chances are it isn’t just the devs making mistakes. These games have flaws, from a design point of view.
“Why aren’t you playing DS1?”
I did. It had similar issues, and didn’t strike me especially differently, it had locked 30 fps that ruined it even with DSFix.
“They ruined Dark Souls!”
No, these games area good. Not as nearly as the circlejerk elitists make it out to be. They’re not amazing, but they’re pretty good some of the time. Which comes back to the same thing of consistency: I don’t know if I’m going to enjoy myself if I sit down to play Dark Souls 3, and this is the main aspect that pushes this review into the negative.
Some of the bosses are truly unenjoyable. I don’t mean hard, I mean bland.
Bosses I really enjoyed fighting: Abyss Watchers, Dancer, The Twin Princes, Vordt, Deacons, and (kind of) the Soul of Cinder.
Almost everything else felt like it was needlessly padded with wait times (the 10 second wait time on the Giant Tree AoE slow is ridiculous especially when it’s every other attack) and attacks that were intentionally designed to make you go “Oh” as the screen greys out.
I’m looking at you, Darkeater Dragon. You don’t get massive AoE that does half my hp, a health bar longer than Angela Merkel’s♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and high mobility.
One shots are not fun when you can’t tell what kind of attack they are, or how they’re going to take place. Because chances are you’ll die before you figure out what hit you and how to dodge it.
The one thing I can primarily say I absolutely loved about this game was the music. The soundtrack, as with the other souls games, is admirable. It’s carries the game, especially the boss fights. I can’t compliment it enough. I could write an essay on how excellent this music is (yes, from a musical theory point it isn’t that ‘amazing’, but most people don’t recognise that.)
Oh yes, and let’s not forget XBOX controls. $60, + DLC (I got it with the season pass for $53 AUS to avoid the Steam scam) , so yes, $60 ♥♥♥♥ing USD for a game that doesn’t have native controls. Why is the button for lock on the same button for flipping the camera? Who thought that was a good idea? I’m going to destroy their car breaks without them knowing, I swear to go.
For a $60 game, you should at least have rebindable controls on a port, or maybe, I don’t know, have fully supported controls for the platform you’re playing on?
I’ve coded control schemas cross platform before. This♥♥♥♥♥♥isn’t hard. It really isn’t. The fact that this made it to release and multiple patches is honestly unprofessional.
What else haven’t I covered? Oh yes, the Lord of Cinder’s Sunlight Spear (yes, the thing you get for beating the FINAL BOSS of the game) does minimal damage even with a build surrounding it, and generally damage, spells and scaling doesn’t make sense.
The things which are cool mostly suck or have been nerfed until they suck.
I hope you like Dex builds. And I hope you like needlessly painful areas (for example the artillery areas because you probably haven't done the thing which you couldn't possibly know to do), the Swamps where you take unavoidable damage and are almost perpetually slowed against masses of enemies, the quests which can be failed from the slightest thing and exist only to punish you and force you to play through this garbage game a second time to see if maybe something interesting happening.
This game was hit or miss, like my review score.
5/10.

Spiral Knights was a GREAT game.
Summary in one sentence: Spiral Knights is not new user friendly and adds next to nothing to keep its veteran players interested.
I loved the music, the art style, and the MMO element combined with the Zelda like combat. Imagine Four Swords with online multiplayer and (in the beginning) lots of players.
Sadly the game itself has been stagnant while the developers copy paste stuff to make a quick buck.
Updates just make getting to the end game take longer and longer unless you empty your pockets. But at the same time, once you get there, there's almost nothing to do. New end game content hasn't been added since the "hard more" Shadow Lairs fights added three years ago. Combat is skill based (it's quite obvious who bought their equipment and who got it before they made it painful to try to get to end game without coughing up dough) but acquiring and upgrading equipment is not-so-micro-microtransaction based.
Their cash currency for example will allow you to purchase most end game equipment without any effort on your part. Been playing this game for a very, very long time. I got it near when it just released, and I was very impressed and excited about it. However, since I can't give numeral or decimal ratings, I have to choose what I think of the game now: I just can't recommend it. I'll tell you why my love has been watered down as we go.
You and many other robotic knights crashed on a mysterious planet. This is no ordinary planet; the massive underground is filled with massive machines and gears that are constantly shifting levels. It's sometimes gloomy, sometimes cheery. It is inhabited with many monsters and gremlins who don't want you to explore. This place is called the Clockworks. In its center is your only hope of escape: the energy from the core.
GAMEPLAY
Newbies get to customize their character with various cosmetic armors and ascessories. You can change your knight's color, which affects your eye color and any parts of armors that allow change. You can also change their height.
By default you start with Proto gear, which includes an armor (this covers your body), a helmet, a shield, and two weapons: the Proto Sword and Proto Gun. You are taken through a tutorial that teaches you how to kill meanies and the beginning of your story. Following the tutorial are beginner missions with AI companions to give you a taste of the game and its story before you go on your own. These missions are pretty easy to do and reward you with more weapons to help you on your journey. At the end, you are taken to Haven and you get the Proto Bomb, which is the last type of weapon (swords, guns, and bombs). Haven is located at the surface and is where the knights research and train.
More missions can be done later when you are ready. These too will give you rewards. Complete a set of missions to be ranked up and move on to the next set. Ranks allow you to use better gear. Gear is ranked in stars like a movie would be rated. Most weapons can be upgraded to higher levels. Some ranks require you to have a full set of gear of a certain rank for you to continue to the next and to allow you to go down more tiers. Tiers are chunks of depths with sharp difficulty turns. There are 3 tiers in all. Missions can be replayed again and again as much as you want. You can also independantly delve down the clockworks.
There's two currencies in this game (I know what you're thinking): Crowns and energy. Crowns is earned in the Clockworks or by selling things. You use them to buy equipment from shops or you can trade them for energy. Energy is used mainly for reviving yourself if you die or for buying things in the Supply Depot. The Supply Depot is where you get to look at all the things you cannot get because you got no $$$ in your wallet. Energy can be traded for crowns and bought with real money (mhm, you see the picture now).
You can delve the clockworks solo or with 4 player co-op. To beat each level, you have to reach the elevator at the end of each level, which you can use to either continue going down or go back up. There's many areas to explore each level, and you can find materials to "alchemize" new weapons or upgrade weapons. You only have one emergency revive, so be careful! You can buy sparks of life to revive you again if you need to with energy, which are available in the Supply Depot to buy. Sometimes you will run into a set of levels with a boss at the end. You will seldom run into the same level twice, as the levels change constantly at set times. The elevators give you a hint on the type of level it will be by the picture and color of the picture displayed on the screen on it. For example, a haunted fortress themed level would be a castle tower with either purple or red. Purple would be a little generic, and red will usually mean the Scarlet Fortress levels. Further information on the level ahead is given to you when you go down, such as the name of the "series" (I call more specific themed places like the Scarlet Fortress [a haunted, castle-like level] a series) and an area name (Firestorm Citadel: Smouldering Steps).
Near the end of the game comes the Shadow Lairs. The Shadow Lairs require a Shadow Key to enter. One key grants access for everyone in the party. These are boss levels with massive difficulty changes that make even the beginner's boss a challenge for a full party of 5 star players. On top of that are more powerful monsters and enhanced bosses. There's one for each boss. Each Shadow Lair opens the core little by little.
PvP is also a thing here. In the coliseum, you can pay 200 crowns (which is extremely cheap for most players) to play Lockdown or Blast Network. In Lockdown, you can be one of three classes with their own unique abilities that replace your shield (Guardian has a massive shield that protects allies) on two randomly colored teams. All your gear can be used they aside from your shield, but their level goes down to level 1 until you're done playing. You win by capturing and controlling control points. Blast Network is Bomberman. Nuff said.
The game was really fun and the boss runs were wonderfully done, but there's two evil beasts: GRINDING FOR ALL ETERNITY AND DLC. Beginners will have a blast with the game until later in the game, where upgrades are harder and take longer to do. Your gear can level up and become stronger with "heat" which acts like experience points. However, you can't just breeze through and max out your gear because they can only actually go up a level when they're at full heat and you have enough fire crystals. This is magnificent part is called "forging". There's special fire crystals for each star gear, the better ones being harder to find. 4 and 5 star fire crystals are extremely hard to find, and you need frikkin tens of them depending on the level. Even then, you have the option to use less fire crystals for a lower chance of forging or using a crapton at once to confidently move up a level. Unless you have a massive horde of crystals, you'll probably want to go with the 100% chance option all the time. Even worse, 3 to 5 star gear *require* that you level up your gear to a certain level. 5 star gear requires you to max them out (level 10 is the max), and 5 star gear is *always* slightly less strong than their 4 star counterparts until you can level them up enough for them to actually be better aside from a good charge attack, which almost never changes. It takes me about ONE MONTH or more of collecting materials, leveling up gear, and grinding the same boss levels over and over for money and loot just for ONE 5 star piece of equipment. Guess what the Supply Depot has? 5 star weapons for sale for energy. Remember what I said about occasional gear requirements in missions? R.I.P. your wallet.
Guess what else? Shadow Keys cost a lot of energy. That means you better find an efficient way to earn money or pull out your wallet just to beat the game with a couple of friends. When you have nothing else to do but the Shadow Lairs, you can enjoy grinding for 600 years or lose the roof over your head. Another thing: events. Events and prize boxes. I don't need to say anything else about these. It's a tiny bit like the vicious IAP that ruins almost every mobile game you love.
GRAPHICS, UI, AND PERFORMANCE
Graphically, the game looks great. The gear, environment, and overall art style is really neat. The UI has no problems. As for performance, the game runs perfectly on my 5 year old Dell laptop with no upgrades on low settings. It appears to be well optimized. If I had a newer computer, it would be perfect. No strikes off here.
There you have it. A great game with painful grinding. I give this game a 6.8/10, and I don't recommend it because I don't like being enslaved in grinding for years or PC games + mobile IAP. I'd also like it if I could actually do some cool stuff aside from the Shadow Lairs and getting gear as a Tier 3 player.

Now, if you're a terraria/minecraft player, you may be a little annoyed that Starbound turned up to join the 'Block Games' party.
But starbound is significantly better that Terraria or Starbound as it has way more features, such as...
1. Much bigger game world
This is kind of obvious, but Starbound's map spans entire sectors of the universe.
Minecraft's map spans 510,000,000,000,000 blocks, Terraria's is determined by the world size at the start, but Starbound's universe is seemingly infininite.
2. Random loot generation
Starbound's loot is randomly generated, Not as in, the game picks pre-made items and places them in a chest. No-no-no
Starbound creates its own loot, like Borderlands, then puts it in the chest. Minecraft has some things that you won't find in chests, like swords, armour, ect. Terraria picks random items from the game and makes them more powerful the deeper you go.
3. Items!
Starbound has LOADS of items. I'm serious. You can find Link's hood, a rainbow cape, tents, guns, even more vanity items...
The list can go on untill the end of time itself!
4. Passive Abilities
Minecraft instantly gets destroyed on this one, as passive abilities are nonexistant, Terraria gives you accessory slots that you can slot passive items into, however Starbound is going to get passive upgrades with the racial armors
(increased inventory, faster movement speed, higher jump height, increased energy regen while in broad daylight ect, ect.)
5. Techs
Starbound has techs that consume energy. These techs can be Samus Aran's Morphball, a double jump, a rocket jump, defying gravity (Is that how you spell defying? Please correct me on this, Reddit.), a dash, and even ED-209!

7. Progression
Starbound's progression is fairly linear. Build boss summoning item, use boss summoning item, collect loot, craft starmap upgrade, use upgrade, travel to next sector when bothered.

XCOM 2 is much like its predecessor, except MORE. More enemies, more soldier abilities, more mission types. I played it solidly for 44 hours over 8 days to complete a Commander (Hard) campaign, but that was including dozens of reloads. Next up will be a Commander Ironman run, so I'll have to do a hell of a lot better to get close.
A lot of people have had technical problems with the game, but I was fairly lucky. Playing on medium graphics settings I did experience long level load times (1-2 minutes) and some graphical glitches. The whole engine seemed to glitch out on the last misison, but I didn't have one CTD in 44 hours and a reload fixed the glitches. Initially I was disappointed with the final mission (or at least the first two-thirds of it), but the final area was a fitting (and very difficult) finale to a wonderful game. I can't wait for the DLC and I'm sure I'll easily get 100+ hours of gameplay out of this.
Is it the best squad level turn-based strategy game ever? Not yet. Does it have the potential to be the best ever in time with patches and DLC? Yes, I think it does.

Game summary:
-you don't level up, your gear do from 1 to 5 stars, after investing stuff to transform it :)
-all your gear means a helm, an armor, a weapon (but can carry up to 4), a shield, 2 trinkets and a pet with a collar. In your stash you can have more armors, helms, etc  :)
-you start from surface and via elevators you go underground levels (very small areas, like 3 minutes of walking from edge to edge). "Highest" depth was 29 last time I played. That is the end. Then you go out and go again same route or another to earn extra money or just because you are too bored and there is nothing else to do  :)
-it has missions. You can redo most of them, meaning clearing some depths again.
-very fast your gear will be at maximum level. Then you can gamble your in game money (that can be obtained also with real life cash) to get extra options on your gear, like poison defense low, medium, etc, or maximum - meaning better than smaller versions but still not too much :)   This fun part translates into playing the deepest levels again and again and again untill you have enough money to gamble thirth option on a item. Then you do it again and again and again, becauselast time was a rubbish option and you gamble again to replace it hoping for a maximum :)
-after a while, even gambling for options is over, when you did the deepest missions so many times that you know where to wait every monster before it spawns. All your party members, friends and guild mates are also in same situation. Now it's time for the cosmetic investments :) A moustache or a pair of glasses, or maybe a feather or an antenna. You may do this earlyer, investing your money in a glowing necklace instead of a better armor. This way you look cooler while you lie dead on your back  :)
-OK, now you have everything. Er... well... you do some more runs from top to deepest level. You earn money... Then... you sell some materials..for more money :). Sometimes devs invent new accesories. They drop from boxes that can be buyed with real money. If you buy the box and drops something you don't like you can sell it in auction for in game money. This way other players can have the thrilling experience of wearing a pipe with a brand new yellow, unlike the green, grey and brown that existed before the summer promotion :)
-You start the game. Hm... Nothing new, except the guild leader message to donate more money to the guild to pay rent for guild rooms :)   Your trinket and weapon slots expired, but you buy them again for 1 month each. You do a run with 2 beginners to help them untill they abandon the run and leave you alone at depth 4 :). You try to join a party at biggest boss: Vana, that drops the most expensive tokens. Here you can show off how good is your gear and how impressive you refined your devastating skills. Hi hi :)  Except you can hardly find anyone playing anymore... what happened to the guys?
-You start the game... Same old guild message... No guildies online... 1/86 friends online... What to do now? You look at auction, but you have everything. You are bored of all the missions and all levels that you know like the back of your hand. Maybe you do one for old times sake.  It used to be fun before. Exit game disapointed.
-Start game. Look around. Do nothing for 5 minutes, because there is nothing to do. You are too bored of killing the same wolfs or zombies that you killed tousands of times. Exit game after 10 minutes withot doing anything.
-Start the game... Look around few minutes... Nothing there... Hm... Hm... Exit game.

There is alot to love about this game!  However there is also a lot that is completely unnecessary and infuriating.
I rarely ever review games on here but my hope is some people see this and pause before buying and as importantly the developers see/read and LISTEN...
You can feel the passion in the game from the designers.  It has character, atmosphere and show they really put a lot of thought into the mechanics even though it looks quite simplistic in graphics and gameplay.  I applaud them for that.
I have enjoyed the game immensely but also have quite literally screamed outloud at the some crap they befalls you and your charcters while you are trying to conquer the game.  I was a DungeonMaster for 20 years and understand game design and making a group of players work for their successes...... HOWEVER the designers put way too many negatives in the game that just are overdone.  The whole stress, disease, quirks and maladies that envade your every single playing minute is overwhelming and too much.  Not to mention when you die you are DEAD period!  That alone is like Hardcore mode every scenario.  I understand there is much to be said for making it a challenge and having to deal with issues other finding loot, distributing loot and going out again.  But c'mon!  Seriously tone it down quite a few notches Red Hook.  You do not want to make your players angry, frustrated and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off.  All of which I have felt many times over.  My own son, who got me interested to buy it, himself quit playing it for many weeks before finally going back to it and finishing it.  And before people jump on that and say "see he went back and played it so it worked" get a clue.  A game is suppose to be fun not make you hate it.  And sadly sometimes I hate this game.  Don't get me started on the whole brigand raid on the hamlet crap that you can only bypass by killing off a character unless you want to attempt one of the hardest battles in the game according to the wiki.  Just not cool at all.  Some people aren't ready for that and are still trying build up to neter Darkest Dungeon battles (like me).
Does it have enough greatness to make me continue to play?  Absolutely, but I can honestly say that if they toned down the game on the aforementioned issues they would generate a lot more positive recommendations.

The good: It's challenging, if you're into that. Most of the classes seem well thought through (not sure I see enough benefit in the Antiquarian or the Abomination, but maybe that's just me.) It is very replayable, in that it is basically a RNG-fest with a lot of grinding at the core. If you enjoy it, the cost per hour will be really low. Has sort of a Lovecraftian vibe.
The bad: Doesn't satisfy my explorer urge at all. The dungeons are basically RNG-generated graphs and have no interesting unique content. There is really no story here worth mentioning. I suspect how you feel about this could be predicted by how you feel about rogue-like games. I find them boring; if you are into them, you'll probably enjoy this more.
Mechanically, It's an unforgiving game of tactics and LOTS of grinding to level up fighters. I thought maybe there were plateaus and the mechanics would open up in some interesting way at some point, but not so far. I think I'm done with this game. (I'm still a long way from the end.)
It's ALMOST a game I could like, but at the end of the day, there is way too much tedium and way too little joy for me to want to play this game. It kind of rolls up some of the things I've liked least about D&D dungeon crawls (poor survivability of heros, no real sense of hero's journey, boring resource management) up into one package. If you like games like that -- and I know people who do -- this might be your game. If, like myself, you favor exploration, story, and unique content, well, this probably isn't going to do it for you.

The main complaint people have about this game is the fact that RNG is a big factor in this game but I feel many of them may be missing the point.
This game simply isn't supposed to be about making your characters godlike and being able to beat it with ease. It's specifically about the downsides of adventuring that you Never see in games. The struggle, emotional toll, and most irritatingly the reality that people will die. That feeling of wondering whether the journey was even worth it after all you've been through.
This game is quite enjoyable if you're willing to accept the fact that sometimes you WILL feel cheated.

XCOM 2 is much like its predecessor, except MORE. More enemies, more soldier abilities, more mission types. I played it solidly for 44 hours over 8 days to complete a Commander (Hard) campaign, but that was including dozens of reloads. Next up will be a Commander Ironman run, so I'll have to do a hell of a lot better to get close.
A lot of people have had technical problems with the game, but I was fairly lucky. Playing on medium graphics settings I did experience long level load times (1-2 minutes) and some graphical glitches. The whole engine seemed to glitch out on the last misison, but I didn't have one CTD in 44 hours and a reload fixed the glitches. Initially I was disappointed with the final mission (or at least the first two-thirds of it), but the final area was a fitting (and very difficult) finale to a wonderful game. I can't wait for the DLC and I'm sure I'll easily get 100+ hours of gameplay out of this.
Is it the best squad level turn-based strategy game ever? Not yet. Does it have the potential to be the best ever in time with patches and DLC? Yes, I think it does.

Darkest Dungeon is a dungeon crawler in which you must grind to survive. The game sells itself on the fact that heroes will die and that you won't always finish quests. Fine.
However, what you notice is that this makes the game into a grind fest. Expeditions cost quite a bit of money, especially due to the harshness of some of the combat and any attempt you can make to make up for that. This means that, without the quest reward, you're going to be looking at a net loss if you decide to retreat, even if you grab a fair amount of loot. It also means your heroes will gain no XP from the expedition, which is the means for upgrading them to complete more difficult missions. The difficulty to obtain money and heirlooms required for upgrades, coupled with the lack of rewards (even most items have fairly harsh negatives) and potential loss of a high leveled character (which is more common in higher dungeon levels), makes for a game that can easily stall and leave you grinding in lower level dungeons. This makes for a rather dull, gameplay wise, and repetitive experience.
The upsides are that the combat is fairly interesting when attempting to make synergies between characters, the world seems to have depth in terms of character development, and the game mechanics are fairly unique. However, the synergies between the characters don't seem to be particularly interesting or impactful, character development quickly washes away when you have 16+ different expendable heroes/weirdos, and any trait can be quickly swapped out for another, since characters get a trait on almost every adventure (the swapping mechanic is new, though, at the time of this review). I would maintain that the game mechanics remain unique with little qualifications in these regards.
The gameplay isn't the worst part, though, and it would probably be tolerable if the aesthetic and world weren't so atrocious. If I were to describe the feeling the game was trying to impart upon the player, it would be "hysterical panic." I don't know about anyone else, but that is probably the single worst attitude to attempt to get a person playing a video game to feel. Panic is bad in and of itself, but the hysterics the game attempts to impart upon you make it intolerable. I had to mute the music because it was mind-numbingly obnoxious. All so the creators can impart some cheap, shallow interpretation of H.P. Lovecraft (the mentally-deranged racist that so many gamers have taken a strange liking to).
I would say that the visual art design is well done. The characters look interesting and the world looks unique and well crafted. It really gives you a sense that you're living in a world, and I would say the game's attempt to give you that sense of living in a world is well done. However, a game is much more than that and my interest in the world quickly faded once I actually engaged the game mechanics and started hearing the horrible music.
Darkest Dungeons is a game that had some promise, but the grinding required to play it and lack of reward coupled with the sense of hysterical panic it attempts to impart, and does a good job imparting, make it not worth playing.

tl;dr - Fallout 4 is a decent game with a better engine than the ones that came before, but now Bethesda is trying to add microtransactions.
Fallout 4 is a great improvement in many ways over its predecessors. It looks better and works better (although it struggled at launch with some bugs).
There are problems however, such as the dialog options, oversimplification of levelling, removal of ammunition crafting, and more. Some of these have been fixed by modders, but some just cannot be fixed. Not all of these are truly atrocious either and are merely a matter of taste, which is why I held off on writing a review for this game.
Now, there is the Creation Club. Some people had high hopes for it, some did not trust it. Bethesda said it would be a way to give incentives to modders to make better content, and many people were excited about what that could possibly mean.
Obviously Bethesda would learn from their mistakes, right? Nope. Not at all. The Creation Club is filled with currently only tiny bits of content in singular packages, such as a shotgun for ~$4. That is not what people expected, and you might think that it is just because the Creation Club is new. Well, prepare to be dissapointed. It may only be a rumor and it may change, but for now it is impossible for any major content to show up on their platform due to a record limit. If you dig around you can find people talking about it (CC mods are basically limited to roughly 1/10 the size/scope of the Automatron DLC), and that doesn't sound hopeful.
Finally, lets discuss the FAQ on the CC website.
One of the entries is "Is Creation Club paid mods?" To which the answer begins with "No." Very funny, guys.
Next phrase of interest is "we won't allow any existing mods to be retrofitted into Creation Club, it must all be original content." Funny, as how a large number of items already exist elsewhere AND one of the items looks an awful lot like a straight-up model rip from another Bethesda game.
Finally, "there's a constant demand from our fans to add more official high quality content to our games..." - Yes, but selling Pip-Boy color variants is not what people mean by "high quality content", official or not.
Overall, Bethesda could probably make this system work, but it looks like they just don't care enough to actually make the effort. Hopefully, they will eventually fix it up and make it the system that the people who believed in it thought it would be.

As someone who is generally skeptical of free-to-play titles, particularly with FPS games, I am shocked at what I've stumbled upon here with Black Squad.
I've been playing FPS games on PC and console for sixteen years and let me tell you, the netcode and hit registration in this game is no joke. It makes CSGO, Battlefield, and CoD netcodes seem like they were hacked together by middle school children; considering the budget difference it’s actually quite embarrassing for the bigger publishers. This is coming from someone who is a long-time Battlefield and Counter-Strike player (and occasionally CoD fan, particularly pre-2010 titles).
Netcode is undoubtedly the most important underlying factor for a shooter, but there's a lot more this game does correctly:
- All weapons unlockable without any premium / monetary investment
- Premium weapons are literally stock weapons with skins. Zero statistical advantage.
So now that we know the game has a solid foundation, let’s get into details:
- Starting weapons shred people, so you are golden from the moment you begin your first game
- No automatic health regen
- Multiple classes, each with their own killstreaks (4 per class)
- Killstreaks (which are obtainable with objective points as well) are reasonable, similar to what you saw in CoD 4
- If you have good muscle memory and decision making, you will not lose a firefight unless it is entirely your fault
Black Squad's game modes are a great deal a fun, and they put together a well-rounded list of options. There's classic TDM, VIP, and Demolition (5v5 and 8v8), however I'm currently gravitating toward Battle Match (16 v 16) which features multiple objectives that need to be destroyed by both sides.
Maps are comparable to current AAA titles -- there's long stretches for snipers, close quarters for runners, and generally an assault rifle or carbine will serve as your adaptable option. You have three class kits to customize, so you can easily adapt to the circumstances of your game.
There are three live currencies:
- Gold (Purchases 14-day items. Earned through many general tasks/games/achievements/etc.)
- Medals (Purchases permanent weapons. Earned through more difficult challenges.)
- BS Coin (Purchases cosmetic variants of weapons)
Overall I'm surprised to see myself get slightly addicted to this game. Did I mention the netcode was perfect? ;)
Considering it's free, this game is worth your time and effort to try. Really hope the developers stick to this formula and just add more maps. Everything else is great.

This game has enormous potential, all of which is ruined by the combination of its two biggest weaknesses: RNG and lvl 5 dungeons.
Starting off the game, it will most likely feel difficult for most people, however, after a few introductory dungeons, you're gonna get a feel for the general strategy the game forces upon you. All is going fine and dandy (except for a few bosses), until you get to the max level (lvl 5) dungeons, which provide the pre-endgame of Darkest Dungeon.
This is where the intro screen isntructions of the game come in at full force. You're not trying to beat a dungeon, you're trying to get through it by the skin of your teeth, almost always losing at least one hero. You are at the mercy of RNGsus, praying so that the enemy unit doesn't crit you twice in a row, instantly resulting in death if you fail your death's door check.
I've put over 80 hours into this game. I've read through most of the wiki, I watch youtubers on a daily basis who mostly play this game. I haven't even reached the final dungeon. You might say "well, git gud", but herein lies the other big issue with this game. The easiest comparison you could make is with Dark Souls: both games are extremely challenging, provide little to no information for the player, and at points seem completely unfair. The biggest difference is that in Dark Souls, most deaths that occur, can be attributed to misplays on the player's side. Here, most of my failed dungeons come from being chain-critted in the second fight of a long dungeon. At best, you're trying to minimalize the losses you're going to suffer at level 5. I've always liked challenging games, but this one is simply unfair.
The new town events somehow, after the community's outrage, emphasize these weaknesses even more (RNG playing a huge part in your success). I'm baffled by the fact that not only does the developer not give two ♥♥♥♥♥ about the biggest problems with an otherwise extremely promising game, they even boost those issues further in newer content.
