Some felt New Vegas was ‘over hyped’, and none will forget its performance issues and game-breaking bugs on release. Likewise, we will also not forget was that it maintained the fundamental structures  that kept 3D Fallout New Vegas feeling like a proper RPG, and allowed us to immerse ourselves in spite of the game’s performance.
Then we got Fallout 4, which somehow never gets lambasted with being ‘over hyped’. It also had problems on arrival, and many of us realized that this was not an RPG game like most of the previous Fallout iterations. Our freedom to explore our own stories in the Fallout universe independently had been scrapped in favor of clutching at passé industry trends like base crafting, voiced player dialogue, and tons of fetch questing.   After two years of patches and updates it is apparent that the only notable advancements in Fallout 4 have been in the combat, menus, character creator, and companion characters.
I really like the companion characters in Fallout 4, even if they get grating at times with dialogue repeats and inconsistent character traits. In spite of its obvious improvements, the combat system still suffers from that ‘samey’ gunfeel between most weapons. It would do Bethesda good to take advantage of some of the knowledge their ID software properties in this regard, which seem to be the only Bethesda produced titles to not disappoint as of late. Few of the weapons are satisfying, which is comparable to interactions with both companion characters and NPC’s. The shallow feel of the world of repeat line-blurting NPC’s played over repetitively droning bleak background music is underpinned by the ‘synth’ problem. The issue of which members of the commonwealth you interact with being human or not is inconsequential and is pretty much only a part of the story to give it a false sense of depth.  Much like the base-building (which can be satisfying); Immersion-wise settlements amounts to little more than a distraction from the gameplay itself and create more false depth. It reminded me of when I stopped playing GTA: San Andreas because eventually the game reduced to ‘one of your hoods is under attack’, pulling Carl Johnson out of his journey only to have to tend to a random fight. FO4 uses this same means of entrapment to waste your time, and while it was incidental in San Andreas (it relents when you take over the whole map area) it is intentional in FO4. Once you stumble upon a settlement it becomes your problem.
If you enjoy The Sims and Minecraft and want to make beautiful hovels for the itinerants of the wasteland (if you can call the Commonwealth a wasteland), you are stepping into a trap of being peppered with alerts and discouraged from discovering new settlements. The only benefit to putting up with this hassle is exploiting the game’s economy, where you can become a purified water tycoon if you keep your populations low and strictly focus on water production in your settlements. This will make ammunition and upgrades easy to access and destroys any sense of in-game scarcity. Two years in and these and other market exploits haven’t been touched by Bethesda and likely won’t because they’re the only reward to induce players into sticking their hands into the settlement system and getting caught, artificially prolonging gameplay.
This is what rubbed me the wrong way the first two years of Fallout 4, even with Bethesda Paid Mods v.3.0™ on the horizon. We all knew Bethesda would try it again for a third time because they know they can bank on enough console players to be naïve enough to not understand how anti-consumer a practice charging for mods is. Prior to this, friends lambasted me for being ‘anti-FO4’, calling me a contrarian hipster. My first bad impressions of Fallout 4 came from the E3 announcement and teasers, which showed us what the beginning of the game would be like. I knew then and there that I would be divorced from my traditional Fallout experience.
You want to be able to treat the game universe as a canvas of your fantasies, and prior to FO4 the Fallout (and Elder Scrolls) games were an amazingly liberal way of doing this. That’s why they became so popular to begin with; the amount of leeway granted to explore your own ideas was staggering.
When I play RPG’s, I create a personal avatar in-game. Not very creative, but it helps with my immersion. I’m the kind of person who can’t quite enjoy a movie or a game if I can see through it, so anything that helps me suspend my skepticism helps. So I
how every other woman in Fallout 3 and New Vegas looked androgynous. It suited the realism of a wasteland devoid of available makeup. Moira’s mustache was good, because it was indifferent to the aesthetic expectations of a non-Fallout world. Don’t get me wrong, Cait is a great companion to have. But what kind of sense does it make for someone in North America whose lineage descends a couple hundred years since the bomb dropped to have a first-generation Irish accent? It makes about as much sense at it makes for her to have Helena Bonham Carter’s complexion and composition, and this goes double for Piper. If you’ve ever checked out their illustrated character designs in ‘The Art of Fallout 4’ (better than the game itself), you’ll find that something was lost in translation when these female characters were modelled in 3D. Much like the colourful buildings and objects littering the Commonwealth unbleached by two hundred years of sunlight or the waves of radiation supposedly emanating from the Glowing Sea to the south, the women of the commonwealth don’t seem to belong to their universe. Even the ghouls of FO4 get the Maybelline treatment, given essentially ‘smooth skin’, previously a slur in the ghoul vernacular. The Nexus mod community typically known for turning ‘Bethesda butches’ into calendar babes has several popular mods for FO4 that attempt to make ghouls more lore-friendly; Unblackening their corneas, returning to the New Vegas ghoul skin textures, returning ghoul baldness, and giving ghouls back their facial variety instead of looking like blobs of wax. Nexus has also stepped up its game with multinational ethnic character presets and traits, allowing for Japanese, Chinese, Black, Latino, and other diversifications to deepen the cultural aesthetics of the FO4 world. Up until this point in the Fallout series, attempting to make a non-Caucasian character in the character creator was a cringey exercise. In spite of the improvements character creation in FO4, none of these improvements assisted in nonwhite traits. I learned this while trying to create Bjork and Tricky as the ‘couple’ at the beginning of the game. It was easy to create the Scandinavian Icelandic pop artist. It was a nightmare trying to create African-English Massive Attack front man, Tricky.
The reason I was trying to recreate this 90’s music couple and not my own avatar was that I couldn’t. I had to be a heterosexual adult member of a nuclear family marriage, something the bulk of players won’t identify with. This partly served as the basis for the surge in ‘celebrity’ character creations that became popular the week Fallout 4 launched. Many of us weren’t fitting the forced story quite like a glove, so we projected the lack of choice onto celebrity proxies for us to identify with. We couldn’t explore the Fallout universe as ourselves. Even if you’re not gay, a teenager or a spinster, this forced character construct adds to the divorcing of player and experience and was a contrived choice.
So without touching on the ravaging of the perk system, the neutered skill tree system, the bad textures and facial animations, Paid Mods™ #3, and so on, I cannot recommend Fallout 4 to anyone who wanted to play either a Fallout game or an RPG. This game exists as an illustration of the problems of  Triple-A 2015-2017 game production: Pure franchise branding hype, tacked-on industry trends, and getting you to pay for what you already own.

Dark Souls III is the final addition to the Soulsborne franchise, did it leave a good end to the franchise or was it forgettable and boring?
TLDR: DKS3 has some bad aspects of PvP but otherwise is very strong in the gameplay department.
The story answers some questions left by other souls games.
Gameplay:
Dark Souls III gameplay is fast, not Bloodborne fast but much faster than the other games.
Let's start with the cons: The game has bosses with long combos and aggressive movesets and fast attacks. However, the game makes rolls take less stamina. This makes roll spamming much more viable and harder to punish in PvP however in boss fights roll spamming can easily get you killed.
Also, the tracking on weapons is way too good and some weapons like Greatswords have guaranteed 2 hits in PvP where if you hit the oponnent once they will be stunned and unable to roll away.
The game has some bad things in PvP but other than that the PvP area is very good and if you are a skilled player you will win.
Also invaders are much weaker in this game, so if you like invading you might not have an insanely fun time.
Pros: The game has something called Weapon Arts where two handing and pressing L2 will use a special ability that requires FP. Some are as simple as a spin attack and some is a bunch of fast katana swings and some is shooting a magic beam out of it.
The leveling system now allows people within completely different levels to be summoned as long as you have the same password. This is much more convinent compared to previous Souls games.
There are so many weapons that increase playstyle diversity however in PvP the better weapons are obvious but in PvP it is usualy preference.
Most bosses are hard but not unfair. Which is something games fail to do nowadays as most games have tedium instead of actual challenge.
The game's areas are pretty diverse.
Magic is now more powerful and not completely useless. Instead of having limited usages of each spell you have FP that depletes when you use a spell, and Ashen estus is there which refills FP and you can freely move around how many Estus vs Ashen Estus flasks you have.
Story, music and replayability: lolnoonecaresabouthtis
STORY
It answers a few questions that were left by the previous games.
Music
It adds to the atmosphere of the game and some songs stand out as being realllllllly good such as Pontiff's theme, SoC's theme, the Watchers theme and the Twin Prince's theme.
Replayability: NG+ is not as good as the previous games but it is still worth going there for more challenge and extra souls.
TOTAL: GITGUD/10
The game control itself is very fluid, very nice to play. The stages in this game are sometimes challenging or just a breeze which makes this game more interesting.

This game… ahhhhhhhh, it filled me with such wondrous feelings! The art style, the exceptional diction of the narrator, the atmosphere—all of this was well executed. Sadly, this is where the merits of Darkest Dungeon end.
Kill all the creatures in rooms, explore this amount of territory, find these items, kill this boss—there is some variety in the missions. However, they all feel the same—none of the choices are unique enough to change up how you approach the areas and play the game.
Playstyle… that reminds me of random number generation! An abhorrent string of words, oft applied to the darkest of debacles. Answer this inquiry: how in the hell do I go into a mission fully provisioned, decked out in magnificent trinkets, and using a squad that is recommended by the developers of the game (certain team combinations have names attached to them) and still lose everybody?
You know, such execrable failures wouldn’t be so bad if it didn’t take forever to pull my heroes back to the summit of strenght. Later in the game you are able to recruit new team members that are experienced… but there are six levels in Darkest Dungeon and new guys can only be found from 0 to 3.
Putting more time in wouldn’t be as bad if there was more variety to the game. The amount of hours I put into Darkest Dungeon is enough for you to witness everything several times. If I’ve mastered something then why do I have to go back and do it again and again because the RNG decided to execute me? Utterly risible and devoid of ratiocinating.
Trudging through worn soil wouldn’t be so bad if you didn’t have to beat the last area in the game four times. This is the very definition of artificial lengthening.
Some of this repetition could have been fixed if the developers decided to actually follow through with the very first sentence of the game’s blurb: “Darkest Dungeon is a challenging gothic roguelike turn-based RPG about the psychological stresses of adventuring.”
A complete lie.
Stress does not come from adventuring: the ever present feeling that death could occur at any moment, horrid sights, injuries, brushes with death. Instead, stress comes from witches casting spells. From the blurb I was also led to believe there would be a narrative in the game, but the story and characterization was so weak it basically did not exist.
Some of the troops have a comic strip that gives insight into what lead them to the hamlet. This makes it seem like the heroes are individuals… but they are not. They are clones, soldiers fresh from a vat and ready to fight. Why not take away the infinite supply of people? Then, there would be room to characterize these heroes and show that stress is affecting them through dialogue, which is more interesting than random barks.
Through characterization, the heroes’ motives could have been shown. These could then influence mission objections and create unique quests that aren’t spat out by a random number generator. Maybe these motives could toy with the chemistry of the party and abilities the heroes are capable of utilizing. Perhaps by taking care of these unique missions the heroes could gain resolve levels.
Remove or weaken witches and skeletons with goblets of liquid stress. It makes no goddamn sense when adventuring should be the source of worry. Make it a slow climb—unless something awful like a hero’s death occurs—and make it difficult to get rid of.
This game was teeming with good ideas. Sadly, Red Hook did not take the time to contemplate how they could make combat less reliant on RNG. They also failed to take the time to flesh out their characters, story, and stress system. Darkest Dungeon is too long for the amount of content that it contains and could use more time in development.

I suppose it might be time for me to write this review, considering I've played since shortly after it became available on Steam. Granted, I've taken some pretty lengthy breaks, but I've logged quite a few hours into this game.
TL;DR: A personally nostalgiac MMO that isn't quite what it used to be.
When I started playing this game, I pretty much played solo. There were no missions, nor was the story something you had to experience along the way - back then, all it took was learning the mechanics and diving into it. It was pretty grindy back then, but definitely manageable. As a new player, and with content being released a little more regularly then, grinding consistently paid off. If that were still the case, I'd probably recommend this game.
I got about halfway through levelling up my first set of gear when I realized how quickly things would go if I were in a guild. My first guild experience lasted a day, and I hopped through a few smaller ones until I found my first home. I'm glad to say that a few people from that guild I'm still friends with in real life - and honestly, there are only a handful of MMOs that have actually brought people into my life for an extended period of time outside of game. I suppose that adds to the nostalgia. I got a little more levelled up in that guild, but my interest started to fade and I stopped playing.
When I started again, I hopped around a few more times, settling in for a month or two with some relatively active guilds, but didn't find another in-game group that I clicked with until I joined my current guild. Again, I still keep in contact with several guild mates to this day, not as often lately but it's nice knowing they're there and that they helped me through a time in my life that was a bit troubled. I reached end game with them, and started to feel the interest fade, as well. The mission system took some of the mystery out of the game, but that wasn't too bad. Then energy was replaced with crystals, and the game essentially became pay-to-win. A lot of people stopped playing.
The community in this game has always been one of its strong suits, something that would be a definitive selling point so long as it thrived. However, I don't really see it thriving like it used to. Sure, I have friends that play still, and there are many other great people online pretty regularly. I could go on and on with examples about how changes have impacted the community, though - when I started playing, random clusters of players just chatting away was a regular sight in the more common areas. I don't see that as much now. A lot of community talk has gone from focusing on lore or gameplay elements to constant wondering when something new will happen with the game.
Overall, I concur with what many other reviews say. The Zelda-esque gameplay is really appealing, and the art, both audio and visual, is unforgettable. Yet it has lost its charm. For new players, getting to end-game would take a lot of time or money, or both, and even then, what good does it do? While the journey to the end itself is quite fun, and there is an opportunity to meet some great people along the way, there isn't much to expect after. Even as a completionist, I've pretty much given up on levelling all of my gear - it just doesn't seem worth it, and at this point, things are too repetitive.
Do I recommend this game? A few years ago, sure, but now, I sadly cannot. If that changes, I'll be sure to update my review, but I'm not counting on it.
EDIT: In response to comments questioning how I can dislike a game that I put 1100+ hours into, the answer is this. I actually was quite fond of the game for several years, and during that time, yes, I played it a lot. The game has had many updates (and I do agree that some of them were for the better, especially allowing people to play more without waiting. The energy revamps were much needed), yet the missions system and energy change was, in my opinion, the last "great" update to the game. Considering the grindiness that the game currently has, I don't consider it welcoming to new players in the sense that the game is fun for quite a while, and then becomes rather repetitive and frustrating.
To be fair, the game was *always* repetitive and frustrating - the difference, at least for me, is that at one point it was fun enough that I didn't mind, and now, with a lack of additional content (we've been at the core for a while now and only recently got a glimmer of hope that we'd move deeper into the world), it's less fun and more "I'm playing this game because I used to play this game."
Is this review biased? Of course it is, I logged over a thousand hours into the game. Needless to say it had an impact on my life. I'm definitely grateful for those hours, but I won't simply recommend it to everyone based on the fun I had a couple years ago - especially since the game has become less fun for me. The game will always have a special place in my memory - I just can't say with certainty that it would be anywhere near the same for someone just starting out now. Take from that what you will.
---

I've been a long standing fan of the original Xcom series, and I played UFO Enemy Unknown on the PS1 back in the day for days on end. I have to say I am utterly disappointed with where the new series went, and here is why:
They've taken basically every aspect that made the game great out of it and replaced it with something much more simple and fancy gfx:
- No weapon diversity. In the original title you had loads of standard military weapons to chose from even in the first mission ( Assault rifles, Pistols, RPG's, Sniper rifles, Shotguns, Machine guns, with different kinds of ammo ranging from AP to incendiary ) In this title your soldiers can have one type of assault rifle.
- No character diversity. In the original title your soldiers hat a multitude of stats, action points, hit points, psycholgical abilities, strenght etc .. now all soldiers can move two times or shoot. The direction they face does not matter either, you can not even turn them to cover a specific area. They're like clones with no difference whatsoever.
- Unrealistic feeling and a stupid story. You are trying to tell me that a technologically highly advanced species which took control over a whole plabet with billions of humans can be stoped by a handful of guys with rifles flying around in some sort of airlift transport which - despite the fact that the aliens obviously possess highly advanced spaceships and weapon technology - can move around freely with no interference whatsoever. Of course the aliens have no way of tracking it back to the base and nuke the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the base. Give me a break.
If you want to see what the game should look like, google UFO:AI, which is an open source project based upon the original series. Xcom2 only has a minor fraction of the strategic depth, but I guess people nowadays prefer fancy gfx over complexity and depth.

I really liked the direction Firaxis took with XCOM compared to one of my all-time favorites, the X-Com from '94. But what really made it click for me was the Long War mod. Despite its name, mod's main appeal was not in the game's increased length (stock game was slogging as it is by the end), but its improved variability. Every aspect of the game was thoroughly reimagined, rethought and made more compelling. This brought back some of the "ye olde" X-Com feel without introducing any of the outdated mechanics.
Now, when I fired up XCOM 2, it became clear that Firaxis also realized what a godsend that mod was. And even without directly ripping it off, they critically looked at each facet of the first title, and found ways to make it better. It is not all flawless, mind you, as a fair share of mechanics look half-baked and bolted to the game at the last moment (visible enemies indicators, I'm looking at you), regardless, the changes do make the game more interesting.
I fully recommend XCOM 2 as it is, but what tingles me with excitement is imagining what the community will make of it in the coming years!

A good start isn't a always a good thing, sometimes it might distract you long enough that the refund is not an option anymore.... Here we have a boring, repetitive clicker game, ruled by RNG and artificially extended by one of the most tedious grindfest you'll experience in your gaming "career".
Game isn't hard for real, as long as grinding the same enemies for dozens of hours is ok for you, considering that the combat is a tedious clicker game that might force you to repeat hours of grind over and over again if the RNG decides to screw with one of your heroes.
Arbitrary desing choices like the heroes not going to lesser dungeons once they level over a certain cap or never going back to the Darkest Dungeon artificially extend the lenght of the adventure, forcing you into a spiral of grind that will make you hate every second you wasted on this very mediocre game.
It had some potential, but it's lack of deph and it's horrible design choices kills it as soon as you picture the full scope of it.
It took me some time to realize that this game was garbage, because it certainly doesn't look bad at first sight.
Learn from my mistake.
EDIT post Radiant update: the new update cuts in half the grinding time and allows higher level heroes to grind lower level dungeons, removing some of the atrocius artificial difficulty of the original release. The core simplistic and boring combat grind stays the same, but if you are willing to waste a few dozens of hours (as opposed to many dozens of hours) the unforgivable RNG is now less punishing from a wasted grinding hours point of view.
I still don't recommend wasting your time with it, there are plenty of hard games that are also fair, this one still isn't.
Still, devs deserve praise for putting some effort trying to improve the game.

After a decent amount of time, I think I can give you guys an overview of Trove. If you like my review or not, feel free to like/ dislike and comment on it.
Pros:
- balanced classes, even if you only have 4-5 skills to use

Once upon a time there was a game that played like teamwork based Legend of Zelda, where up to four Links could plow through dungeons that required them to solve puzzles, defeat enemies, and survive so that they may find phat stacks and materials to upgrade their gear with.
It played sort of like a facebook game, a common free to play structure of the time, wherein non-paying players got only limited time per day to play, but it was honestly enough. Because revival costed a player valuable play-time, traveling as a group was a huge benefit, as a teammate who preserved their health could revive a fallen teammate by sharing health with them. It wasn't a perfect game, but it was a fun game, and it held the promise of future content updates in the form of paid DLC, which would allow players to support the company and get actual, different gameplay, weapons, and armor in return.
That game was Spiral Knights. Its charming artwork and engaging gameplay were enough to get me sucked into it, even though for a long while I thought it wouldn't be my thing. At first it felt like it would take forever to outfit myself in the armor I wanted, or to have the weapons I wanted, but the more I played, and the more I learneda bout how to use the time I was given each day efficiently, the more I realized it was all realistically obtainable, and in only a month or so, I had a lot of what I wanted without ever dropping any money on the game. There was still so much more for me to do, entire levels and bosses still unbeaten, and at the rate I was going, it would take much longer to truly reach endgame, since the relatively simplistic looking mechanics actually began to spread out and demand a player to be ready to serve multiple roles. It was all well and good, and I can honest to God say I enjoyed the game.
Then everything changed. The game went to a new model of keeping itself afloat. Players were free to play as much as they wanted per day. It sounded like a dream come true, but it was actually the beginning of a long nightmare that eventually brought this once entertaining game to the shambles that it is now. Content updates went out the window in exchange for the equivalent of TF2's hats, nothing but cosmetics that have no impact on the game itself. Not a crime, but it became more and more obvious that this game wasn't bringing in enough money to do much else but justify the cost of running the servers. I'd be surprised if there's even a content development team anymore - I'm certain a more realistic picture of the studio that designed this game is now nothing but someone to post lies to their official forums, and someone else to reskin already existing models - making new models, even as low poly as this game's assets are, is above his paygrade.
The aspect of teamwork was removed entirely. A fallen comrade cannot be revived by sacrificing your health, it was removed in favor of sparks of life, just another scheme at cashgrabbing that this game's developers had to resort to. Shortsighted developers overlooked that this made certain armors cmopletely worthless, as players now no longer had a healer role to fill. From day 1, the game had balance issues, and these issues were made worse by negligence. For a game that tried to offer a nearly completely customizable experience, it boiled down to a handful of viable weapons and armors - anything else is just robbing you of time and money.
I haven't played this game in more than half a year. It isn't worth the time it takes for it to boot up. Thanks to the removal of the daily limit of stages to play, I was able to accomplish everything I ever wanted to in almost no time at all. I reached the end of the game, and without any meaningful content updates, there is nothing else. There was one update that looked like it would extend the story and add more levels, but it felt like only a sampler platter for a complete meal that will never arrive.
A tragic story for sure. If you're wanting to find a new MMO to play, stay away from this one - it is the shambling corpse of a game once filled with promise. You'll have more fun elsewhere.

I've been a long standing fan of the original Xcom series, and I played UFO Enemy Unknown on the PS1 back in the day for days on end. I have to say I am utterly disappointed with where the new series went, and here is why:
They've taken basically every aspect that made the game great out of it and replaced it with something much more simple and fancy gfx:
- No weapon diversity. In the original title you had loads of standard military weapons to chose from even in the first mission ( Assault rifles, Pistols, RPG's, Sniper rifles, Shotguns, Machine guns, with different kinds of ammo ranging from AP to incendiary ) In this title your soldiers can have one type of assault rifle.
- No character diversity. In the original title your soldiers hat a multitude of stats, action points, hit points, psycholgical abilities, strenght etc .. now all soldiers can move two times or shoot. The direction they face does not matter either, you can not even turn them to cover a specific area. They're like clones with no difference whatsoever.
- Unrealistic feeling and a stupid story. You are trying to tell me that a technologically highly advanced species which took control over a whole plabet with billions of humans can be stoped by a handful of guys with rifles flying around in some sort of airlift transport which - despite the fact that the aliens obviously possess highly advanced spaceships and weapon technology - can move around freely with no interference whatsoever. Of course the aliens have no way of tracking it back to the base and nuke the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the base. Give me a break.
If you want to see what the game should look like, google UFO:AI, which is an open source project based upon the original series. Xcom2 only has a minor fraction of the strategic depth, but I guess people nowadays prefer fancy gfx over complexity and depth.

Ok, let me just say I've been playing this game since early access, and its only been getting better with every update. Its very fun, very addicting, the art and atmosphere are spot on, and its insanely (haha) stressful. One thing you have to accept is that your heroes will die. A lot. Even if you plan ahead with a perfect roster with no negative quirks, that doesn't ensure victory. This game is HARD, and if you don't want a hard game that can be potentially frustrating this game isn't for you. I see a lot of negative reviews saying that the RNG is stupid and the game is to grind heavy, but you always have the option to flee a dungeon if things aren't going well, and with some upgrades to the stage coach you can get higher level heroes right away, so the grinding problem isn't nearly as bad anymore. The game feels stacked against you, but that makes it all the more rewarding when you actually win, sort of like a mix between Dark Souls and X-com in a way. The game isn't about flawlessly winning every dungeon, its about improvising and making sacrifices for the greater good. I'd give it a 8/10 overall. Great atmosphere, art, gameplay, and music, but definetly not for people who don't like hard or stressful games.

I really liked the direction Firaxis took with XCOM compared to one of my all-time favorites, the X-Com from '94. But what really made it click for me was the Long War mod. Despite its name, mod's main appeal was not in the game's increased length (stock game was slogging as it is by the end), but its improved variability. Every aspect of the game was thoroughly reimagined, rethought and made more compelling. This brought back some of the "ye olde" X-Com feel without introducing any of the outdated mechanics.
Now, when I fired up XCOM 2, it became clear that Firaxis also realized what a godsend that mod was. And even without directly ripping it off, they critically looked at each facet of the first title, and found ways to make it better. It is not all flawless, mind you, as a fair share of mechanics look half-baked and bolted to the game at the last moment (visible enemies indicators, I'm looking at you), regardless, the changes do make the game more interesting.
I fully recommend XCOM 2 as it is, but what tingles me with excitement is imagining what the community will make of it in the coming years!

If we purely look at the content, the game is absolutely great. Possibly the best thing that developers have introduced are procedurally generated maps. Maps are not random, instead they are a combination of huge number of ‘modules’ (sets of these modules are exclusive to locations) that are picked and shuffled in a new way every time you start a game. If that was not enough, there is a number of weather conditions that take place – rain, night, flying burning ashes, etc.
Classes have been revised, now you have five of them (sword person; hacker; sniper; heavy; and psi-soldier) and sixth will be added as part of the pre-purchase DLCs later this year. I really like the new psi mechanic, you now train your psi soldiers within the base, but you can take them to mission when needed and they will jump in back to complete their current education upon return to the base. If you train the psi-soldier long enough, they become a bit too powerful.

Ok, let me just say I've been playing this game since early access, and its only been getting better with every update. Its very fun, very addicting, the art and atmosphere are spot on, and its insanely (haha) stressful. One thing you have to accept is that your heroes will die. A lot. Even if you plan ahead with a perfect roster with no negative quirks, that doesn't ensure victory. This game is HARD, and if you don't want a hard game that can be potentially frustrating this game isn't for you. I see a lot of negative reviews saying that the RNG is stupid and the game is to grind heavy, but you always have the option to flee a dungeon if things aren't going well, and with some upgrades to the stage coach you can get higher level heroes right away, so the grinding problem isn't nearly as bad anymore. The game feels stacked against you, but that makes it all the more rewarding when you actually win, sort of like a mix between Dark Souls and X-com in a way. The game isn't about flawlessly winning every dungeon, its about improvising and making sacrifices for the greater good. I'd give it a 8/10 overall. Great atmosphere, art, gameplay, and music, but definetly not for people who don't like hard or stressful games.

If you have liked Terraria, Minecraft, Starbound, or Unturned (other great games, you should play them as well :D) you're going to like Trove. It is a 3D block based game, similar to Minecraft, but weapons and armor have more detail. Graphics such as fire are smoother and aren't pixelated, however, which brightens up the landscape up a bit. There are many biomes including Dragonfire Peaks, The Neon City, and Candoria. Each one has it's own dungeons, mobs, color scheme, etc. Mobs and bosses will drop related weapons and hats, so if I defeated a boss in Candoria, I might get a Lollipop wand or something candy related. There is also a block called the Loot Collector. It lets you put old weapons you don't need anymore, or an extra Lollipop wand in and gives you Flux, a common crafting material, and the item's style. You can put these style on the weapon you are using and you will get the graphics of the style and the damage of the weapon you are using. So now you can use a Lollipop wand forever and ever, (seriously, who doesn't like defeating their foes with a piece of candy?!) However, once you have made a weapon into a style, you won't be able to use it as a weapon anymore. Another col feature in Trove is your Cornerstone. It's like a portable base. All aroung the world, there are places where you may place your cornerstone. It has a place to fill up your potions, change the look of your character, as well as other things you get later on. You can customize it with blocks you find around the world and trophies. There is a lot more to the game, but I won't spoil it all for you, so go get the game and find out for yourself!

This game is an instant must-have for anyone who even dabbles in the FPS genre. Whether you play all the time or just a match or two a week, everyone wants a shooter that runs well, finds matches fast, and isn't P2W.  It's a free game that I would have gladly paid $20 for as it stands now (fresh after launch). I'm excited to see how the devs and community are going to shape this game.
Pros:
-Quick match finds matches very quick.
-Fantastic servers. I've never once disconnected or had a teammate lag out on me.
-I really like the in-match leveling system. Basically, every match you start as a private and move up in the ranks based on score. This rank is displayed above your head for the team to see. This allows you to see who's worth sticking with on your team and who might need extra help without constantly checking the scoreboard. It's also just a cool way to measure your contribution to the team.
-No disadvantage for new players. You can buy the gun you consider the very best before you play your first match.
-Fantastic hit detection.
-Fast-paced. No killcams or lengthy respawn timers.
-Maps (while they will also appear in the "cons" list below) are easy to memorize, have clear hotspots, and at least 2-3 main pathways from your spawn.
-Invulnerability on spawn lasts long enough to prevent spawn killing, but not long enough for you to run into the fight with magic armor.
-Combat rewards patientce and skill. There's no aim assist or generous hitboxes. Spray n' pray has no place in Black Squad.
-Free DLCs let you try every primary weapon in the game for 15 days. So, if you're like me and jumped the gun (no pun intended) with your purchases in the beginning, you can use every AR, DMR, PDW, SMG, and shotgun in the game for 2 weeks, which is more than enough time save up for your newfound favorite.
-Personally, I haven't seen any hackers yet. *knock on wood*
-Community seems fine. I've seen more "gg" than "kys," which is always a good sign. Still too early to tell.
-Low system reqs-- because war doesn't have to look pretty. Still, it doesn't look bad at all IMO.
-Ragdolls are satisfying, though some might think they're over-the-top. Idk. I think it adds character to the game when bodies go flying across the room.
-No OP melee, meaning that pulling out your knife is either for movement speed or a true last resort, as it should be.
Cons:
-Maps are ridiculously small, which is great sometimes, but they're too easy for a good team to dominate. I realize that introducing larger maps is risky for a game with no sprint mechanic (especially if you advertise being fast-paced) but it's not a true military shooter if everything is close quarters.
-Guns aren't fully balanced, but who was expecting that this soon after launch? Sniper rifles zoom in just as fast as an AR or SMG, and there was nearly no sway on the one I used, if any. I suspect this is to make them even somewhat relevant on these small maps and that this will be changed later. KSG could use a slight range nerf, etc.
-No weapon customization at the moment aside from a few skins, but I hope we'll be able to use different sights and attachments on compatible guns.
-Everyone looks the same by default. You can pay real money for new models if that's your thing, though. Still, I hope we'll be able to unlock cosmetic options in-game as well.

Dark Souls III is the final addition to the Soulsborne franchise, did it leave a good end to the franchise or was it forgettable and boring?
TLDR: DKS3 has some bad aspects of PvP but otherwise is very strong in the gameplay department.
The story answers some questions left by other souls games.
Gameplay:
Dark Souls III gameplay is fast, not Bloodborne fast but much faster than the other games.
Let's start with the cons: The game has bosses with long combos and aggressive movesets and fast attacks. However, the game makes rolls take less stamina. This makes roll spamming much more viable and harder to punish in PvP however in boss fights roll spamming can easily get you killed.
Also, the tracking on weapons is way too good and some weapons like Greatswords have guaranteed 2 hits in PvP where if you hit the oponnent once they will be stunned and unable to roll away.
The game has some bad things in PvP but other than that the PvP area is very good and if you are a skilled player you will win.
Also invaders are much weaker in this game, so if you like invading you might not have an insanely fun time.
Pros: The game has something called Weapon Arts where two handing and pressing L2 will use a special ability that requires FP. Some are as simple as a spin attack and some is a bunch of fast katana swings and some is shooting a magic beam out of it.
The leveling system now allows people within completely different levels to be summoned as long as you have the same password. This is much more convinent compared to previous Souls games.
There are so many weapons that increase playstyle diversity however in PvP the better weapons are obvious but in PvP it is usualy preference.
Most bosses are hard but not unfair. Which is something games fail to do nowadays as most games have tedium instead of actual challenge.
The game's areas are pretty diverse.
Magic is now more powerful and not completely useless. Instead of having limited usages of each spell you have FP that depletes when you use a spell, and Ashen estus is there which refills FP and you can freely move around how many Estus vs Ashen Estus flasks you have.
Story, music and replayability: lolnoonecaresabouthtis
STORY
It answers a few questions that were left by the previous games.
Music
It adds to the atmosphere of the game and some songs stand out as being realllllllly good such as Pontiff's theme, SoC's theme, the Watchers theme and the Twin Prince's theme.
Replayability: NG+ is not as good as the previous games but it is still worth going there for more challenge and extra souls.
TOTAL: GITGUD/10

I'm sure at least five times as many were though. We like our dollars a lot.
Now of course I'm not talking about everyone, nor are the devs entierly blameless, but I do feel like, when my fellow vets look at how much of the cash shop content was also throwm right into their hands as an appology for an update, or an event, or as a log-in reward, or for so many other reasons, what would compel you to spend? I'm just your average gamer. I'm not hardcore, I'm not particularluy serious, and trove, while an amazing game, was behind a lot of other games I enjoy in my list of priorities. While any good roguelike serves to punish you for make mistakes, Darkest Dungeon takes this a step further. The game is designed to punish you regardless as to your choices--not just by making the game more difficult, but my making the game pointlessly long. The game forces you to continually grind lower level quests while your highest level heros have to relieve stress (possibly for multiple weeks). Late game forces you to only use your heros once for the final quests, meaning if you have a great team comp and you complete one of the final quests, you have to start from square one if you want that team comp again. Certain quests sack your village causing you to have to restore it--yes you can stop this, but after beating it the first time it offers you no reward for doing so, making the game even longer.
I would say that 3/4ths of my play time was spent mindlessly grinding just so that I could get on with the story, only to fail because of a bad miss and have to start again. The core concept and gameplay is interesting, albeit repetitive, but it is unneedingly punishing in ways that don't make the game interesting. Punishment should come due to making bad decisions, but in The Darkest Dungeon, punishment comes because they want to keep you playing longer. And that just isn't fun.
Is it any good? Well, if you never played a decent FPS, it is.
Worth it!

Great combat system, art, and style;mediocre everything else. The narrator has WAY too little variety basically making it a necessity to mute him, while the lore and story are better left ignored. That doesn’t matter too much in a game like this, since the gameplay is what’s important.

Unfortunately, the exploration mechanics are so obtuse and set against the player with cheap RNG to the extent that you can't even capitalize off of what’s supposed to be a positive result. For example being surprised basically dooms your party in certain circumstances, and almost always results in a hero dying or being brought down to 0 hp based on the order they’re put in, while surprising the enemy just results in the enemies going twice in a row, which means you're still taking more unmanageable and frankly unreasonable damage considering that you have to survive consecutive fights and losing heroes has lasting effects on what you have to do next. Each time you lose a hero or they become inflicted with something you need to heal, it is not money you primarily lose, it is time. Not a resource in the game, but your actual free time. Whenever you lose a hero, you more or less have to play a couple more hours just to grind out new heroes to replace dead ones, which can easily result in you losing more heroes due to bad rolls, making it so you need to grind even more. The game is just a perpetual meat grinder where you’re going to spend 10 hours just trying to reach where you were before a bad roll killed your party. This reliance on RNG for the main difficulty ruins the fun of the combat, since whenever you do beat a difficult run it feels less like something you earned, and more like you just got lucky.

In the end for a game that expects you to put 50 hours into it to beat, it doesn't nearly make itself feel worthwhile enough to bother finishing. While I enjoy a lot of the time I put into it and I will probably put more time into it in the future, considering how frustrating it can be to play, how much of a time investment it is, and the repetitive nature of the game, I cannot recommend Darkest Dungeon, as I cannot recommend a game that doesn’t feel worthwhile to beat.

This game has several good points, unfortunately the bad points outweight them.
1. RNG. Many of those giving the game a "recommend" instead of a "non-recommend" claim that the problem is that people are upset that their characters die. Well, no. Not really. I don't care that my characters die. What I care about is that they are not dying because of a lack of skill (which can get better through practice and thus make the grindfest rewarding) but that they die through sheer chance. Gamers like to know that we have succeeded, that we are able to triumph, and while Cthulu is supposed to make things hopeless, this is a game not a book. You have to consider enjoyment of the players. And when whether you live or die has nothing to do with how you play, and everything to do with the dice rolls? You have a problem. There should be a balance between what the dice do and what the players do causing success or failure. Always.
2. Goals. The characters are hired help. Yet apparently once they are higher level they will refuse to go into lower leveled dungeons. This is an arbitrary mechanic just to make the game harder for no reason. It also breaks immersion since it has no lore reasoning. What hired guard refuses to go somewhere because "it's too easy?" No such thing. Mercenaries love easy jobs that guarantee cash for little risk.
3. Characters that enter the final dungeon refuse to return. This is the final killer. You finally grind up enough people to be suitable, and then a dungeon that you MUST enter more than once to complete the game, is no longer accessible by those you specially molded to be used in it.
Between these three features, the only way the game is any fun is to cheat so as to make the grind-fest as limiting as possible, and just enjoy the story. Waste of something that held great potential.
Positive for superb single, tho multiplayer is just broken, so many steps back from improvements in DS2.

This game was really, really fun and enjoyable when it first was released back in 2011 – however, over the years the game has become stale. Don’t get me wrong, I still really enjoy playing it despite its faults.  However, this game has MASSIVE problems, and I therefore cannot truly recommend it for new players.
Since the beginning, Spiral Knights always had an element of grinding and farming to it; want better gear? You’re going to have to earn it. Farm a bit for some ‘crowns’ and some ‘heat’ to level up equipment, and eventually your equipment will reach level 10 and you can then craft it into a bigger and better version with the right recipe.  Equipment with higher star ratings (higher stars = more powerful equipment) obviously took a bit longer to fully upgrade – something of which makes perfect sense. If needed, you could always sell off minerals you found while exploring to make some easy crowns (Minerals were also originally used to alter the construction of areas you could explore – different minerals type combinations lead to different forms of monsters and level themes you could encounter). In my experience, most of my crowns went towards buying more Energy, as it was used in both crafting and level exploration (originally, to use the elevators to explore, you had to pay in Energy – eventually this was scrapped entirely).
Today, the game in itself has simply become a farming and grinding mess.  Trying to upgrade equipment is tedious and far more time consuming than it needs to be.
Equipment can no longer be leveled up with heat unless it is forged first – once equipment levels up it can no longer consume heat to continue leveling up until it is forged. This just adds another step of unnecessary farming to the mix – as forging requires ‘fire crystals’ (these can either be rewards from missions or bought with Energy). In essential, you have to farm for crowns in order to buy energy, to buy fire crystals to forge equipment, to level up equipment,  to farm for heat and more crowns, to buy more energy, to buy more fire crystals…and so on and so forth. If you farm and grind enough, you may be able to finally upgrade your equipment to one star level higher than it was. Minerals themselves are now used to feed Sprites – which are essentially just another part of upgradable equipment that takes far too long to upgrade.
I'm not even sure where the plot related portion of this game disappeared to - I haven't seen a plot related update in years. The only updates I see nowadays are for weapons and gear packs - and those are for only those that are willing to shell out money for them.
The design and art for the game is still very appealing, and the basic gameplay is still fairly solid – all however, are greatly overshadowed by the game’s horrendous upgrading mechanics. If you have the patience for time-consuming farming and grinding, this just may be the game for you. If not, look elsewhere.

I haven't played this game that much....only about 9 hours as I'm writing this.
From what I've played so far, I would recommend this game. And this is only hoping that the developers will soon add more content! What is available so far is not too much, but the game is so unique and I can see so much awesome potential with it. It is definitely playable with what is implemented so far though.
If you like to play sandbox games (like Terraria), you will love this game. It's actually very similar to Terraria, but has it's own unique spin on it....where you live in a Spaceship and beam down to different planet types. You can pick your own species type between 6 different races, and you can customize your sprite from there (hairstyle...color....etc). And the sprites are actually quite attractive (unlike Terraria...where they are so ugly). There are only a few monster types and they tend to get stale after a while.
I LOVE all of the different decoration items you can find throughout the planets. Different beam types....posters.....tvs.....lights.......planters......you name it. It's rewarding to find the buildings and collect materials and such for building your own creations. The worlds are very pretty, I think, especially compared to other "pixelized" games.
Mining can get stale quickly, I felt like I reach the bottom of the planet too quickly (the lava). And there could be more (different) undergound moster types and ores and chests to find. I love how you can soemtimes find a little tent to rest up in and heal yourself. I also love the "mini bosses" you can encounter and beat.
The game is rather difficult to get the hang of at first. (I had to go online to find out how to do everything). I wish you could change your hotkeys. (But I'm sure this is a feature that will come with future updates).
Overall, I think the game needs a lot of updates before it can be played for a much longer time. I realize this game is in beta,,,,,and this is why I still recommend this game. I am going to wait wishfully for any updates and I have very high hopes for this game!

This game is what RNGesus prays to.
I am not recommending this game because I don't believe that it is for everyone. At least the very least, I recommend waiting for a decent Steam sale.
I currently sit at 9.2 hours clocked into this game which is not a lot, I know, but every one of those hours were played separately after having to step away for breaks from the grinding. Not solely because of the grind, mind you. I have an affinity for reptative and tedious tasks in general. BUT I draw the line when said tasks result in absolutely no personal skill improvement or in-game reward.
As far as personal skill is concerned: all of the meticulous memorizing and party/skill combo experiments are thwarted against the game's RNG.
For in-game progress: I've yet to complete a dungeon. Most of my time has been spent so far purely farming for curing characters enough to continue farming. The game has a very minimalistic approach to leveling and upgrading. There's no stat or trait selections, no large armour, weapon, jewlery, trinket, and silk panty customization. It seems that a little is meant to go a long way when upgrading which should make it exciting when you finally get the cash and/or materials to upgrade...
But that just has not been the case. Not only is it very hard to gain the cash/materials needed for upgrading when you can only complete 3 or 4 rooms per run, but I've also realized quite early on that spending money on upgrading characters is pointless. They WILL die. I believe I have only 1 original character left and that is mostly by chance. Not to mention that the skill upgrades seem very low. Buffing helps a lot but when enemies are throwing out an average 10 damage per hit (not including dot damage like bleeds), sometimes raw healing is needed. But the healing skill I have is upgraded from 5 to 6 points for one character per turn. No matter how I spam, it is impossible to keep up with the damage output of many enemies across all of my characters.
Not being able to upgrade characters has lead to a real stagnation in any progress. I have spent about 9 of the 9.2 hours just grinding the same enemies in the same dungeons which is just getting dull. Yes, I have been able to upgrade my little Hamlet place a bit, but saving a couple hundred gold on curing afflictions has not made a significant dent in my ability to keep up with curing. Most of my cash goes to this, recruitment, and food that doesn't do anything anyway except negate occasional 20% damage hits in the middle of crawling.
I get what the developers were trying to do here. The game has cool visuals, the audio is great and the idea of dungeon crawling taking a toll on the average adventurer both physically and psycologically is an interesting concept. I just don't believe that the execution was very good. The story, or what little there is of a story, has really been stamped out by the mechanics and I would prefer a more in-depth, story-driven look at the affects of taking on your nightmares than this. As it stands, I don't care if my characters go mad. The only reason it bothers me is it messes up my combat strategies. At that point, I'd rather just let the person die because it's cheaper to just recruit a carbon copy than care about the psycholical stresses and recovery from them for that character.
I will likely continue playing this game for many hours into the future just to see if I can progress anywhere and learn any sound strategies as I simply enjoy the environment and ambiance offered by the visual and audal work that has been implemented.
With that, I did have a pretty funny experience at the time of losing most of my starting characters. And this might contain some spoilers if you can consider a cautionary tail about one of the game's surprise prostate exams a spoiler.
I approached this strange, glowing stone that was wrapped by a twisted tendril protruding from the floor. There was a bit of information that popped up on my screen--perhaps as one of my character's dialogue boxes--that mentioned I should use an item on this cute piece of contemporary art. Upon doing so, my entire party was sucked into some vortex and trapped in an abyss with quite the impressive-looking boss which I could best describe as a wonderful rendition of an actual purple people-eater. After a couple of love taps to the monster's belly, I realized my quest to loot this guy was going to be futile. Even the game itself was quite aware of what a s**t storm I had gotten myself into. My first tool tip informing me of the "retreat" mechanic popped up on screen. "Thank God!" I thought as I began spamming that bad boy before the monster could lay another finger/tentacle/whatever on my party; the same party that was now looking more like that box of raisins that have been floating about at the bottom of a juniour high kid's backpack for an entire semester. That is to say, there wasn't much left of my party at this point. My relief was quickly dashed, however, when the message that the attempt to run away had failed! With a well-recorded "slap" from the boss (love the audio), one of my party members fell dead...permenantly. My next couple of turns were spent just trying to run away with the message that the attempt had failed popping up on my screen before it could even completely dissolve after the last click. Just before my party was about to be completely wiped, the game had the audacity to pop another tool-tip up for me to REMIND me that the retreat function exists and that if my party wipes, it will be entirely my fault for not timing the get-away properly. I would have been livid if I weren't laughing through my face-palm. The next couple of minutes were spent by me sipping mineral water and enjoying the high quality recordings of people dying and the monster blurgeling while the narrator chastised me in his low, sensual voice. Needless to say, I've since avoided all future art school projects that I've come across in the hallways of the Darkest Dungeon.

I really wanted to write a more positive review, but two things made this a negative..

XCOM 2 is a a rare game for me. Often times I will only play games for an hour or two at a time. XCOM 2 is a game that I find myself playing for hours. Simply put, it is a fun game. There has been a great deal of backlash towards XCOM 2 regarding timed missions and poor optimization. For me, the timers were a nonissue. They never felt unfair, even at higher difficulties. From my perspective the timers added another layer of tactical consideration, where unlike Enemy Unknown, or the expansion Enemy Within, one could play as cautiously as they wanted. For XCOM 2, sometimes you have to take risks; and that's okay, since it adds more than it takes away.
I've poured nearly 40 hours into the game so far and I am not tired of it. The game has a great deal of replayability and the fact that Firaxis had the foresight to give XCOM 2 full mod support is just another welcome bonus. I plan on adding several mods my second go around with the game to change up how everything plays out. Furthermore, I've actually invested in my troops due to the new character creation system. With the plethora of options I can at least make rough outlines of my friends and family (who will be lucky not to die), where unlike the last game everyone looked rather generic.
However, XCOM 2 is not without its problems. I am somewhat displeased by the optimization of the game. To some this alone has been a major turn off. However, with a few adjustments I have managed to get the game to run relatively well. While I have heard complaints about crashes and game breaking bugs, I have yet to experience any myselt, except for a single crash after a session which lasted 4-5 hours. I am hoping that the game is properly optimized soon so that it can be experienced equally by any who can and are willing to invest time into this game.
Overall I would give XCOM 2 a 7.8/10.

Great combat system, art, and style;mediocre everything else. The narrator has WAY too little variety basically making it a necessity to mute him, while the lore and story are better left ignored. That doesn’t matter too much in a game like this, since the gameplay is what’s important.

Unfortunately, the exploration mechanics are so obtuse and set against the player with cheap RNG to the extent that you can't even capitalize off of what’s supposed to be a positive result. For example being surprised basically dooms your party in certain circumstances, and almost always results in a hero dying or being brought down to 0 hp based on the order they’re put in, while surprising the enemy just results in the enemies going twice in a row, which means you're still taking more unmanageable and frankly unreasonable damage considering that you have to survive consecutive fights and losing heroes has lasting effects on what you have to do next. Each time you lose a hero or they become inflicted with something you need to heal, it is not money you primarily lose, it is time. Not a resource in the game, but your actual free time. Whenever you lose a hero, you more or less have to play a couple more hours just to grind out new heroes to replace dead ones, which can easily result in you losing more heroes due to bad rolls, making it so you need to grind even more. The game is just a perpetual meat grinder where you’re going to spend 10 hours just trying to reach where you were before a bad roll killed your party. This reliance on RNG for the main difficulty ruins the fun of the combat, since whenever you do beat a difficult run it feels less like something you earned, and more like you just got lucky.

In the end for a game that expects you to put 50 hours into it to beat, it doesn't nearly make itself feel worthwhile enough to bother finishing. While I enjoy a lot of the time I put into it and I will probably put more time into it in the future, considering how frustrating it can be to play, how much of a time investment it is, and the repetitive nature of the game, I cannot recommend Darkest Dungeon, as I cannot recommend a game that doesn’t feel worthwhile to beat.

Trove is a fun game to play with friends. You can do dungeons, collect loot, go fishing, craft some rings, build your home on your own plot, have a club with friends. So here's a list of some pro's and cons. And a view tips if you really intend on reaching max level.
Pro's
- A decent amount of classes that are actually very well balanced. Even though you only have 4 abilities.
- A lot of different worlds for different levels. ( You have to be a certain level to get to a world higher.)
- Various dungeons. ( Dragonfire peaks, fairy stuff, candy themed, etc.)
- Multiple biomes.
- An ingame shop and currency to buy items with. ( in game transactions are also possible if you'd like to do it that way.)
- Club worlds.
- Professions.
- Portals to travel.
- quests can be fun.
- The ability to add friends in the game.
- Teleporting towards friends.
- Most people are pretty helpfull.
- Crafting bombs, they can be very usefull.
- Build mode and combat mode.
Con's
- Quests get grindy. Yes they really do.
- No end game content, you just reach max level cap. and then there's pretty much nothing.
- Profession levels are grinded by doing the same thing all over again.
- Your first shadow arena quest.
- It's fun for a view hours. Because it gets boring fast.
- After a while you will know most dungeons by heart.
- Needing to go to the sky realm without wings.
- Blindly teleporting on friends in a skyrealm without wings.. ( Yeah, pretty stupid xD)
- Mining with your laser. But seriously, don't do that.
Those are the things I found out while playing Trove without the expansions or what so ever.
It's a fun game to play for a short period of time. I'm a WoW player, so I'm used to rushing all the quests and content, and doing as much dungeons as possible. But you will find out that you can get in trouble with Trove if you rush quests. So here is a little list of tips too.
Tips and Hints, Do's and Dont's.
1. It is easy to join a club, just stick around for a while and decide if this is a nice club or not. And if people are helpfull and active, if they are, you have a reason to stick around.
2. Pick a class that suits you. I made a dracolyte, not knowing this was a pretty tanky class. But it is. And it turned out to be the right class for me.
3. Remember to check the stats on items. Get the correct stats for your type of character and class.
4. Items that you can't use, are best to be thrown into a loot collector.
5. Try not to rush your questing and do some dungeons in between. There will be a level where you actually get wings ( I thought it was 20.) You can use those wings to collect skyshards? Don't really remember the name. But it's gathered in the skyrealm.
I had a real problem because I grinded quests. I didn't have enough money to buy wings and I was level 14 when I got to that quest. I just didn't feel like grinding dungeons. So I just decided to quit for a while.
6. Shadow key's are used for shadow dungeons. You first have to grind dungeons in uber worlds. There you usually get up to 4 Shadow Key Fragments. You need a lot of those to craft a shadow key. I thought it was around 100? Or it might have been 200 fragments. So it takes a lot of grinding to get a key. Best thing to do is to work with a group of friends and get the fragments together.
After you managed to get all the materials for a shadow key.. Here it comes.. You will have to find a shadow portal within a normal dungeon in an uber world. I found these extremely hard to find. Once you found it you need to use your key. There is a limited amount of people that can enter the portal. I'd advice you to get a group together for completing the dungeon.
Shadow Dungeons can't be solo'ed. You can get good loot out of them, but these dungeons are way harder than regular dungeons. Don't hesitate to ask "Who wants to join me in a Shadow Arena?" Because a lot of people will be willing to do so.
---
Have fun playing Trove, hope this was helpfull.

This game has several good points, unfortunately the bad points outweight them.
1. RNG. Many of those giving the game a "recommend" instead of a "non-recommend" claim that the problem is that people are upset that their characters die. Well, no. Not really. I don't care that my characters die. What I care about is that they are not dying because of a lack of skill (which can get better through practice and thus make the grindfest rewarding) but that they die through sheer chance. Gamers like to know that we have succeeded, that we are able to triumph, and while Cthulu is supposed to make things hopeless, this is a game not a book. You have to consider enjoyment of the players. And when whether you live or die has nothing to do with how you play, and everything to do with the dice rolls? You have a problem. There should be a balance between what the dice do and what the players do causing success or failure. Always.
2. Goals. The characters are hired help. Yet apparently once they are higher level they will refuse to go into lower leveled dungeons. This is an arbitrary mechanic just to make the game harder for no reason. It also breaks immersion since it has no lore reasoning. What hired guard refuses to go somewhere because "it's too easy?" No such thing. Mercenaries love easy jobs that guarantee cash for little risk.
3. Characters that enter the final dungeon refuse to return. This is the final killer. You finally grind up enough people to be suitable, and then a dungeon that you MUST enter more than once to complete the game, is no longer accessible by those you specially molded to be used in it.
Between these three features, the only way the game is any fun is to cheat so as to make the grind-fest as limiting as possible, and just enjoy the story. Waste of something that held great potential.

I currently sit at 9.2 hours clocked into this game which is not a lot, I know, but every one of those hours were played separately after having to step away for breaks from the grinding. Not solely because of the grind, mind you. I have an affinity for reptative and tedious tasks in general. BUT I draw the line when said tasks result in absolutely no personal skill improvement or in-game reward.
As far as personal skill is concerned: all of the meticulous memorizing and party/skill combo experiments are thwarted against the game's RNG.
For in-game progress: I've yet to complete a dungeon. Most of my time has been spent so far purely farming for curing characters enough to continue farming. The game has a very minimalistic approach to leveling and upgrading. There's no stat or trait selections, no large armour, weapon, jewlery, trinket, and silk panty customization. It seems that a little is meant to go a long way when upgrading which should make it exciting when you finally get the cash and/or materials to upgrade...
But that just has not been the case. Not only is it very hard to gain the cash/materials needed for upgrading when you can only complete 3 or 4 rooms per run, but I've also realized quite early on that spending money on upgrading characters is pointless. They WILL die. I believe I have only 1 original character left and that is mostly by chance. Not to mention that the skill upgrades seem very low. Buffing helps a lot but when enemies are throwing out an average 10 damage per hit (not including dot damage like bleeds), sometimes raw healing is needed. But the healing skill I have is upgraded from 5 to 6 points for one character per turn. No matter how I spam, it is impossible to keep up with the damage output of many enemies across all of my characters.
Not being able to upgrade characters has lead to a real stagnation in any progress. I have spent about 9 of the 9.2 hours just grinding the same enemies in the same dungeons which is just getting dull. Yes, I have been able to upgrade my little Hamlet place a bit, but saving a couple hundred gold on curing afflictions has not made a significant dent in my ability to keep up with curing. Most of my cash goes to this, recruitment, and food that doesn't do anything anyway except negate occasional 20% damage hits in the middle of crawling.
I get what the developers were trying to do here. The game has cool visuals, the audio is great and the idea of dungeon crawling taking a toll on the average adventurer both physically and psycologically is an interesting concept. I just don't believe that the execution was very good. The story, or what little there is of a story, has really been stamped out by the mechanics and I would prefer a more in-depth, story-driven look at the affects of taking on your nightmares than this. As it stands, I don't care if my characters go mad. The only reason it bothers me is it messes up my combat strategies. At that point, I'd rather just let the person die because it's cheaper to just recruit a carbon copy than care about the psycholical stresses and recovery from them for that character.
I will likely continue playing this game for many hours into the future just to see if I can progress anywhere and learn any sound strategies as I simply enjoy the environment and ambiance offered by the visual and audal work that has been implemented.
With that, I did have a pretty funny experience at the time of losing most of my starting characters. And this might contain some spoilers if you can consider a cautionary tail about one of the game's surprise prostate exams a spoiler.
I approached this strange, glowing stone that was wrapped by a twisted tendril protruding from the floor. There was a bit of information that popped up on my screen--perhaps as one of my character's dialogue boxes--that mentioned I should use an item on this cute piece of contemporary art. Upon doing so, my entire party was sucked into some vortex and trapped in an abyss with quite the impressive-looking boss which I could best describe as a wonderful rendition of an actual purple people-eater. After a couple of love taps to the monster's belly, I realized my quest to loot this guy was going to be futile. Even the game itself was quite aware of what a s**t storm I had gotten myself into. My first tool tip informing me of the "retreat" mechanic popped up on screen. "Thank God!" I thought as I began spamming that bad boy before the monster could lay another finger/tentacle/whatever on my party; the same party that was now looking more like that box of raisins that have been floating about at the bottom of a juniour high kid's backpack for an entire semester. That is to say, there wasn't much left of my party at this point. My relief was quickly dashed, however, when the message that the attempt to run away had failed! With a well-recorded "slap" from the boss (love the audio), one of my party members fell dead...permenantly. Summary:  The experience is similar to playing Dungeons & Dragons with a somewhat goth and very depressed version of Debbie Downer.
The main problem is *not* the difficulty, it's being around depressed characters.  When you go into a dungeon your characters  go from "Let's do this!" to "Why the crap am I here?" to "Life sucks and is utterly pointless, and I might as well kill myself now."  Further, when you do conquer a dungeon, the game is very lame about it ("Well, i guess you didn't die *this* time...") and your characters are so PTSD'ed out with neuroses (becoming suicidal, stealing treasure, etc.) that they need to de-stress.  So how do they do this, you might ask?  Gardening?  Hunting?  Playing frisbee?  Nope.  You have to send them to go drinking, gambling, a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, or to flog themselves, etc. which is actually not nearly as fun as you might think since you just move the character icon to another slot and have to pay $$$ to try to bring them back.  (More on economics below)
I am used to old-school games that are hard, where you die a lot, and I wanted to like this one based on the art style and old-school interface.  On the difficult/balance: if you have a few missions go sideways (which is extremely easy, since your characters can randomly die of heart attacks during battle), then you find that the $$$ situation has gone so wrong that you are actually *worse* off than you were when you first started the game, and you are better off just deleting your save file (game auto-saves) and starting all over again.
Conclusion:  *IF* you like wearing black berets and saying things like "Life sucks and then you die" in a French accent (even though you are not actually French) while chainsmoking for no apparent reason, then you might enjoy this game.  Otherwise,  save your $$ and go do something fun with your friends.

XCOM2 takes everything that XCOM1 did and does it better.
Three great things:
1) The world map is vastly improved, with interesting strategic decisions laid out, rather than all that stuff with panic and satellites. The crummy airforce minigame is gone, as is the passive 'scanning for something to do' gameplay that you had to put up with in the first game. What's left in its place is a globe that you have to steadily allocate resources to as you build long-term plans. I quite like that.
2) Combat has been vastly improved with the addition of Fire Emblem-ish customizable equipment. If you kill an alien and they drop a scope, you can duct tape the thing to your gun for a nice accuracy bonus. If whoever is holding it dies and isn't rescued the equipment is gone forever, unless you successfully retrieve the soldier's corpse. This adds a nice layer of depth to the game's combat. They've also added a nice hacking mini-game for good measure. Great stuff.
3) The new stealth mechanics make the game a lot more proactive. No more tiptoeing around hoping you don't run into 6 Mutons as you move your last guy.
Two lingering frustrations:
1) The game is still merciless with its RNG. There is no worse feeling in the world than having your squad go through a series of six 80%+ chance to hit shots and having them all miss. It wouldn't hurt to have some sort of mechanic in place to let you break those kinds of streaks.
2) Some of the shots the aliens take are still highly questionable. Go into this game prepared to have a robot guy shoot through two walls and a ceiling to bullseye your sniper. Bleh.
Still, it's an amazing and immersive game that is worth your time. Now get out there and fight for humanity.
