I currently sit at 9.2 hours clocked into this game which is not a lot, I know, but every one of those hours were played separately after having to step away for breaks from the grinding. Not solely because of the grind, mind you. I have an affinity for reptative and tedious tasks in general. BUT I draw the line when said tasks result in absolutely no personal skill improvement or in-game reward.
As far as personal skill is concerned: all of the meticulous memorizing and party/skill combo experiments are thwarted against the game's RNG.
For in-game progress: I've yet to complete a dungeon. Most of my time has been spent so far purely farming for curing characters enough to continue farming. The game has a very minimalistic approach to leveling and upgrading. There's no stat or trait selections, no large armour, weapon, jewlery, trinket, and silk panty customization. It seems that a little is meant to go a long way when upgrading which should make it exciting when you finally get the cash and/or materials to upgrade...
But that just has not been the case. Not only is it very hard to gain the cash/materials needed for upgrading when you can only complete 3 or 4 rooms per run, but I've also realized quite early on that spending money on upgrading characters is pointless. They WILL die. I believe I have only 1 original character left and that is mostly by chance. Not to mention that the skill upgrades seem very low. Buffing helps a lot but when enemies are throwing out an average 10 damage per hit (not including dot damage like bleeds), sometimes raw healing is needed. But the healing skill I have is upgraded from 5 to 6 points for one character per turn. No matter how I spam, it is impossible to keep up with the damage output of many enemies across all of my characters.
Not being able to upgrade characters has lead to a real stagnation in any progress. I have spent about 9 of the 9.2 hours just grinding the same enemies in the same dungeons which is just getting dull. Yes, I have been able to upgrade my little Hamlet place a bit, but saving a couple hundred gold on curing afflictions has not made a significant dent in my ability to keep up with curing. Most of my cash goes to this, recruitment, and food that doesn't do anything anyway except negate occasional 20% damage hits in the middle of crawling.
I get what the developers were trying to do here. The game has cool visuals, the audio is great and the idea of dungeon crawling taking a toll on the average adventurer both physically and psycologically is an interesting concept. I just don't believe that the execution was very good. The story, or what little there is of a story, has really been stamped out by the mechanics and I would prefer a more in-depth, story-driven look at the affects of taking on your nightmares than this. As it stands, I don't care if my characters go mad. The only reason it bothers me is it messes up my combat strategies. At that point, I'd rather just let the person die because it's cheaper to just recruit a carbon copy than care about the psycholical stresses and recovery from them for that character.
I will likely continue playing this game for many hours into the future just to see if I can progress anywhere and learn any sound strategies as I simply enjoy the environment and ambiance offered by the visual and audal work that has been implemented.
With that, I did have a pretty funny experience at the time of losing most of my starting characters. And this might contain some spoilers if you can consider a cautionary tail about one of the game's surprise prostate exams a spoiler.
I approached this strange, glowing stone that was wrapped by a twisted tendril protruding from the floor. There was a bit of information that popped up on my screen--perhaps as one of my character's dialogue boxes--that mentioned I should use an item on this cute piece of contemporary art. Upon doing so, my entire party was sucked into some vortex and trapped in an abyss with quite the impressive-looking boss which I could best describe as a wonderful rendition of an actual purple people-eater. After a couple of love taps to the monster's belly, I realized my quest to loot this guy was going to be futile. Even the game itself was quite aware of what a s**t storm I had gotten myself into. My first tool tip informing me of the "retreat" mechanic popped up on screen. "Thank God!" I thought as I began spamming that bad boy before the monster could lay another finger/tentacle/whatever on my party; the same party that was now looking more like that box of raisins that have been floating about at the bottom of a juniour high kid's backpack for an entire semester. That is to say, there wasn't much left of my party at this point. My relief was quickly dashed, however, when the message that the attempt to run away had failed! With a well-recorded "slap" from the boss (love the audio), one of my party members fell dead...permenantly. My next couple of turns were spent just trying to run away with the message that the attempt had failed popping up on my screen before it could even completely dissolve after the last click. Just before my party was about to be completely wiped, the game had the audacity to pop another tool-tip up for me to REMIND me that the retreat function exists and that if my party wipes, it will be entirely my fault for not timing the get-away properly. I would have been livid if I weren't laughing through my face-palm. The next couple of minutes were spent by me sipping mineral water and enjoying the high quality recordings of people dying and the monster blurgeling while the narrator chastised me in his low, sensual voice. Needless to say, I've since avoided all future art school projects that I've come across in the hallways of the Darkest Dungeon.

The game is good.  I recommend it.  But, if you have not yet played XCom:  Enemy Within, I recommend you start there.  The improved graphics in XCom 2 don't justify the extra money, in my opinion, and the game isn't actually better.  In fact, it might not be quite as good.
I'm really glad that Firaxis didn't just give Enemy Within a new coat of paint and republish it.  They took several risks.  Some of them worked out and some of them did not.
I'm going to start with what didn't work.
Failure 1.  Concealment:
The biggest feature that I think failed is Concealment.  In theory, it's a great idea.  You get to sneak up on the enemy and set up an ambush.  And, it did provide some pretty cool moments across my playthrough.  Unfortunately, it provided far more frustrating moments, while I learned the rules.  (The game does very little to teach you how to use the feature.) The issue compounds with the fact that the game is generally more punishing than Enemy Within.  Unlike Enemy Within, you can't really "hang tough" if you engage an enemy squad sub-optimally, as XCom 2 is quite a bit more punishing.  The result is that I found myself reloading my game far more often, which I don't think is very satisfying.
Failure 2.  Snipers/Sharpshooters:
Snipers were too good in Enemy Within, so I'm not surprised that they did some things to limit their power in this game.  They seem to do less damage, and their hit percentages are lower, at least initially.  While all of the new pistol talents are cool, they also seem to slow the rate at which a pure sniper build can get rolling.  All of that might as have been alright.  As I stated, snipers were probably too good in previous iterations of the game.  But, (possibly as a result of the new, more randomized stage generation) there seem to be far fewer strong sniper perches in the game, forcing you to move your sniper more often. Since they can't shoot in the same turn that the moved, that's a hefty reduction in power.  That, by itself, seems like it might have been enough of a 'nerf.'
Anyway, I never actually pulled the trigger on it, but I spent most of my time playing this game wondering if I would be better off benching my sniper in favor of a third grenadier.
What worked:
Success 1.  Armor:
The new armor system adds another interesting layer to the tactical choices that you make during a mission.  In short, a unit's armor value is subtracted from the damage you do them.  But, certain attacks can "shred" armor, opening the unit up to taking full damage from other units.  It makes you have to actually think about the order in which you utilize your own unit, which can sometimes lead to interesting trade-offs within your decision making.
Success 2.  All of the other classes:
Aside from the sharpshooter, All of the other classes feel really great.
The ranger's sword attack really helps to make them feel strong in the early game.  I didn't find that it scaled well into the late game, but by then they have so many other options that you won't miss it.
The grenadier is just pure fun.  Environmental destruction is one of the best things about XCom games, and grenadiers are the best at doing this.  All of the various grenade types add to the fun.  This class might even be too good.
The specialist can now deploy medkits remotely via his drone, which is an AMAZING change, because it means you can use him as an actual soldier, who moves around the battle field and shoots at his own targets, rather than following other units around so that he can heal them.
The psi operative has far more interesting abilities than she had in the previous games.  Her abilities are far more offensive, and have some really cool applications.
Success 3.  The increased time pressure:
I'll make this one short.  Many of the missions force you to be very efficient with your turns, or you lose.  The added time pressure is a great tension booster.  I enjoyed trying to finish missions with as much time to spare as possible.
So my review probably sounds like a mixed bag, but this game is excellent.  It's just not the wonderous improvement that you might have been hoping for.  If you are an XCom fan, you are going to love this game because its definitely more XCom.  If you are thinking about making this your first XCom game, don't bother.  XCom:  Enemy Within is just as good as this game (again, graphics aside) and is half the price.

I have not completed the game but from what I have played, this game is amazing. I love the different changes from XCOM and they really make a difference. One major change is the concealment mode which is very useful in wiping out as many enemies before they spot you. Another noticeable change that is really nice is reloading only takes up one turn which means you can reload then attack or reload and heal etc.
Below, I talk about some pros and cons that I found with this game.
Pros:
- Graphics
- Randomized maps (From my time playing, all the maps feel different in ways and you never feel like playing the same map)
- Challenging (This is a pro if you like the extra challenge, combat seems harder than XCOM (more casualities), the control map is different, you move around it collecting intel, resources or recruits and that takes a few days. It is also very hard to get engineers and scientists.)
- Customizability (Lots of different options you can choose, even how your soldiers behave or the things they say)
- New and awesome classes (I have had so much fun hacking the robots or these control panels you can find in the map to get bonuses for your soldier, entire squad or even things like 50% faster research time for your current project! The ranger is also fun, just beware to not find new enemies when using the melee or your ranger is in deep trouble.)
- Aliens have objectives (Now you need to also prevent the aliens reaching their objective. At first it is hard to keep up but after you gain more countries in your resistance it becomes easier to stop the aliens. Dark events also give a unique play through.)
Cons
- Buggy (So far I have not run into too many game breaking bugs but I will list some that I found here. Sometimes you cannot see inside buildings when looking or mousing above it and it is very annoying, sometimes enemies disapear for a bit but reapear after their turn, when it is the enemies turn the screen goes black for 10 or so seconds. That last bug only happened twice when no enemies are visible. The game would freeze for 10 or so seconds. I know there are quite a lot of bugs and glitches in this game but it does not take away the fact that this game is amazing.)
- Lots happening all the time (There is always something you need to do and planning can get more complicated, planning what to do. The control map of the world is also in real time meaning the more time you spend there the more time will pass.)
- Load times (They are terrible, much more worst than XCOM. I guess because there is so much more but it should not take 30+ seconds to load a map and a minute or so just to go back to base.)
- A huge game (The game is 25 GB. For me at least, it is insane. I do have room for it but that is more than 1/4 of my internet cap. I guess it wont bother people who have unlimited but I thought I will mention it here.)
The main con is being buggy. If they fix this then the game will be that much better and I am sure so many more people will enjoy this game because the actual gameplay is phenomenal. Enjoy it so much more than XCOM.

Summary:  The experience is similar to playing Dungeons & Dragons with a somewhat goth and very depressed version of Debbie Downer.
The main problem is *not* the difficulty, it's being around depressed characters.  When you go into a dungeon your characters  go from "Let's do this!" to "Why the crap am I here?" to "Life sucks and is utterly pointless, and I might as well kill myself now."  Further, when you do conquer a dungeon, the game is very lame about it ("Well, i guess you didn't die *this* time...") and your characters are so PTSD'ed out with neuroses (becoming suicidal, stealing treasure, etc.) that they need to de-stress.  So how do they do this, you might ask?  Gardening?  Hunting?  Playing frisbee?  Nope.  You have to send them to go drinking, gambling, a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, or to flog themselves, etc. which is actually not nearly as fun as you might think since you just move the character icon to another slot and have to pay $$$ to try to bring them back.  (More on economics below)
I am used to old-school games that are hard, where you die a lot, and I wanted to like this one based on the art style and old-school interface.  On the difficult/balance: if you have a few missions go sideways (which is extremely easy, since your characters can randomly die of heart attacks during battle), then you find that the $$$ situation has gone so wrong that you are actually *worse* off than you were when you first started the game, and you are better off just deleting your save file (game auto-saves) and starting all over again.
Conclusion:  *IF* you like wearing black berets and saying things like "Life sucks and then you die" in a French accent (even though you are not actually French) while chainsmoking for no apparent reason, then you might enjoy this game.  Otherwise,  save your $$ and go do something fun with your friends.

I can not recommend buying this game. I really want to love this game, but I can't suggest to anyone to buy it with a clear heart. First lets give points where it's due, then I will talk about the shortcomings.
-very atmospheric (great narrating voice and music)
-the art style is fantastic
-the story is interesting
-town events really add to the game
-real sense of loss and/or accomplishment after missions
-horribly unbalanced gameplay
Seemingly the positives are overwhelming the negatives, but anyone who ever played a dungeon crawler or rogue-like knows how important balance is. Here I am not talking as someone who dislikes hardcore games, it is not simple whining about the game difficulty.
My concern is the lack of options the player is given to combat the challenges the game sets for us. The character skills and identities are just lacking.
: you have a single character (the jester) who can manadge stress level of the party, making them camp and preparing a feast using all your time on stress relief is far from enough, even with the torch lit bright you have no real way of combating the problem. Even striking 3 critical strikes will only give the benefit of a single one, so you can not even depend on luck)
Stress level is just one, the party lockout (a leper refusing to serve with a moster, because reasons) and level capping are ridiculous concepts, not to mention you MUST bring 4 people at any time, forcing you to keep at least 4 people of every level in your roster, and if you overlevel 2 of them your party just broke up and you can not use half of it until you somehow level the remainng guys up with a makeshift party.
Forcing players to lose with setting impossible goals and forcing them to try and complete them is not a hardcore game, it is just lazy design. Real challenges can be solved, even if you ahve to spend a lot of time on them. If no sollution os presented it is not a challenge, it is a timewaster.
Until the horrondous balance gets fixed in a way, turning the game into a real hardcore game from the current state, I can not wholeheartedly suggest this game to anyone. That is why it gets a downvote from me.

Honestly this game is amazing, it has almost every feature I would want in a tactical strategy game. I should go into more detail on the positives, but instead I am going to get into the dirt, the info that doesn't make sense to me.
So I am on this mission, taking advantage of the fact that your auto save feature saves every turn, before you take your turn. I have come to notice that all of a sudden I have the option to hack this turret, as a specialist obviously, about half the time. That's right, I mean I am reloading the game and moving one character, to the exact same spot then using my specialist as the second move and sometimes I have the option to hack the turret and sometimes I don't. I wish the buggy issue stopped there, but it doesn't. I have a 42% chance, apparently, to hack this turret. That being said I have attempted to load so many games that I have managed to attempt to hack it 8 times, at a 42% chance, and have failed every. single. time. Doing the math gives me a 0.164% chance that I have missed every time, so clearly the game is not giving the actual math. BS.
At the end of the day I still love the game and would beg every other tactical turn based gaming fan to give the game a shot, because it really is amazing. That being said, be prepared to use the load feature built in, because the odds are NOT at all in your favor...either that or I am either a liar or just insanely unlucky as hell...seriously, do the math and that is how unlucky I am.....crazy.

Seemingly the positives are overwhelming the negatives, but anyone who ever played a dungeon crawler or rogue-like knows how important balance is. Here I am not talking as someone who dislikes hardcore games, it is not simple whining about the game difficulty.
My concern is the lack of options the player is given to combat the challenges the game sets for us. The character skills and identities are just lacking.
: you have a single character (the jester) who can manadge stress level of the party, making them camp and preparing a feast using all your time on stress relief is far from enough, even with the torch lit bright you have no real way of combating the problem. Even striking 3 critical strikes will only give the benefit of a single one, so you can not even depend on luck)
Stress level is just one, the party lockout (a leper refusing to serve with a moster, because reasons) and level capping are ridiculous concepts, not to mention you MUST bring 4 people at any time, forcing you to keep at least 4 people of every level in your roster, and if you overlevel 2 of them your party just broke up and you can not use half of it until you somehow level the remainng guys up with a makeshift party.
Forcing players to lose with setting impossible goals and forcing them to try and complete them is not a hardcore game, it is just lazy design. Real challenges can be solved, even if you ahve to spend a lot of time on them. If no sollution os presented it is not a challenge, it is a timewaster.
Until the horrondous balance gets fixed in a way, turning the game into a real hardcore game from the current state, I can not wholeheartedly suggest this game to anyone. That is why it gets a downvote from me.

First off I should this game is fantastic, regardless of whether one enjoys it or not. While its inspirations are obvious, it doesn't rest on the work of others. It adds both its own take on Lovecraftian lore and takes dungeon crawling in a fresh direction with a combat and stress system. I could ramble on about how great the elements of this game are, but I'm writing this review not so much to review the game as to address the complaints about the game's RNG.
First off it should be said that, yes, a lot of the mechanics rest upon an RNG. However the strategic element of the game is not rigidly controlling the flow of battle but rather doing everything you can to mitigate that risk - y'know, like how real strategy is. Planning your supply, your party and its formation, your route through the dungeon, your finances - if you plan sufficiently the RNG is little threat, something that was fairly obvious 5 hours in and something I'd grown proficient in 50 horus in. I worry players griping about the RNG are coddled by other dungeon crawler and strategy games.
I'm usually the first person to gripe about RNG in games, but the unpreventable possibility that something could go wrong is not a flaw in this game - it's entirely necessary for the game to strike fear in the heart of the player. This is working from Lovecraftian horror after all. Why feel scared if you can comepletely control the outcomes? At the same time Red Hook has done a stellar job constructing the strategic elements of this game to allow skilled players to not eliminate that risk, but survive it.

This is by far the best XCOM game.
If you played and liked the previous XCOM game, then you will like this one aswell, because it more of that with better graphics and then some. Within the genre, this is a great game. I would give it either 8 or 9 out of 10.
Pros:
+ Story is an alright XCOM story.
+ Gamemechanics works fine (works like the previous XCOM, but with some new features build on top of that)
+ Support modding
+ Graphics looks beautiful (especially playing it on 4k, which I do)
+ Campaign map and campaign gameplay (a bit like Total War)
+ several distinct different classes for your soldiers with different special abilities and style
+ Good crafting system
+ Good economic system and balancing economics with time pressure on the campaign gameplay
+ AI works fine
+ voiceacting
+ cool cut scenes
+ soundtracks are great
+ many different aliens to fight with distinct strengths, weaknesses and abilities
+ animations looks good
+ sounds in the game sounds cool
+ good customize options (soldiers looks and weapons can be customized)
+ even the loading screens are cool
+ combat is very intense on high difficulty and tactical
+ good leveling system for your soldiers
+ good autosave system, so you can always go back, when you screw up.
+ lots of hours of content (you can't finish this game in a few hours)
Cons:
- There are a few minor bugs (for example, an animation bug) and I have experienced 2 crashes. No big deal though.
- The stealth mode could be better or more advanced than it is.
- Faces do not look very good and looks very "generic".
- If they had time and resources, they could have implemented even more cool gameplay mechanics in, for example, in the campaign map gameplay.
- They is a lack of variety of maps (some maps are reused and some looks almost the same).
- The last mission is like 10 times harder than any other mission. It is insane.

I think I'll use my example of their lack of an armor mechanic, everything is health, no joke, other than a few abilities for some class if an enemy does 10k damage, you're gonna take 10k damage. Welcome back, Masochist, ahem Commander.
Xcom2 is a worthy successor to Xcom Enemy Unknown. You will weep as your soldiers fall to the oppressor and marvel as others step up the ranks. The game pulls no punches even on Normal. Expect to see bodybags at some point during your play.
The concealed overwatch mechanic is a thing of beauty. In most missions you start concealed and can move around freely as long as you don't wander into someone's sight range. This allows for some wonderful ambush opportunities. Position is everything. Do it right and enemy patrols will be erased by a sweet turkey shoot just like Mom used to make.
The Ranger, a new melee unit, glides across the field of battle. They have a blade attack which can be tweaked which allows you to go toe to toe with some of the alien bruisers. They also have an ability which allows them to keep killing after their first melee target dies.
Fair warning there are several missions that have you racing the clock to complete the objectives. I find them mildly irritating on normal sometimes but not too bad. I imagine on harder difficulties that could get down right annoying.
The aliens have some new mechanics too. The thin man has evolved into something else... and its bind attack will have you on the edge of your seat. Can you rescue the captured soldier or would that risk too much of your squad. I won't say any more less I ruin the surprises ahead of you.
The Avenger is a nice twist for a base and very fitting given the guerilla nature of this conflict. I am gritting my teeth as I figure out where and how to place things and hoping I don't blunder too badly.
There is one issue that in all fairness I need to bring up. There are points where there is significant slowdown. But Firaxis is said to be working on it.
All in all I am glad to see this new addition to the Xcom family. Just remember to keep your ammo dry and to check those corners.

Of course other times nothing can stop your party of heros as you smash the hoards of enemies with ease. Not to say that rng is ultimately the deciding factor in winning or losing but it holds a part. poor play and decision making is punished regardless of rng. strong play and persistence seem, to me, to be what will defeat every dungeon even when there are crushing losses from time to time. I would caution away anyone who doesnt like rng element that have the potental to lose missions or character progression with little to no fault of your own or anyone who doesnt like games with very high difficulty. I plan to put many more hours into Darkest dungeon and cant wait to see what else Red Hook has planned for the future.

First and most importantly I find this game fun. The game has a shallow learning curve and the FBTHF (From Boot To Have Fun) ratio is about as low as any game since Doom & Doom2.
Now, one thing you will immediately notice is that your heroes have flaws. Yes, thats right, not the super hero movie kind of flaws that are "cool to have flaws" ("I'm not a hero, I kill people" or "I'm too perfect for my own good"); no your heroes have real flaws like being a cheat, petty thief, or having a "holier than thou" attitude. These quirks manifest themselves in game by preventing you from easily managing stress levels and lowering combat attributes among other things. This is part of the game. Its what makes the game fun. If you are looking for perfect heroes who just need a healing potion and then off to the next adventure you probably don't want this game.
In my opinion the game is well crafted with bonuses like cool narration and a well done Gothic art style to boot.
Also, the game makes me believe that Red Hook, the organization behind this game, realizes that people are going to be imperfect and yet they can still offer great value. Perhaps this game should be used by management students and/or in onboarding processes to prepare management for the complexities of real world personalities -- or maybe they can just play it as a stress relief activity :-D . In any case I would bet that most would find the game fun. I sure do!

First, My system ran the game satisfactory with a few minor graphic's hitches.  My System has an Intel i7-3770K CPU @3.5hz, Geforce GTX 970 (driver  361.43 at the time of game), Windows 10 Home 64-bit. I played the game at the veteran level.
I finished the game after 60+ hours, I could have finished sooner but I wanted to "cover" the world and build evetything.
Many reviewers  complain about the timer in many missions  but I found that a steady pace worked ok, not to say, that sometimes especially difficult pre-battles didn't force a clearing the path for a run to the goal.  I had several missions on the last count.
The enemy are strong and many have area attacks but are usually grouped only by three.  If you don't  pull more than one group, you will have a fair chance.  I found even with the timer, you can set up a defense and pull a group into a kill zone and then move on to the next group.  As the game proceeds, you will have many new options for strategy with advancements in ammo,skills,etc.
Despite the difficulty, I found that I didn't have to go to a saved game to correct a bad out-come too many times.  Usually when my scout advanced too far and pulled too many groups.  It was rare for my teams not to suffer injuries and healing is slow which means many missions did not have an ideal team.
There are substantial strategic decisions to make in the game , as an example for an advance team, the enemy can have shield and armor however there are weapons/ammo that by-pass armor, so if you hit a group with an area attack that does substanial damage despite heavy armor and follow it with a sniper with a rifle with extended magazine and the serial ability (kill shot doesn't use action point) and AP ammo , that sniper can take out the entire group. This is just one of many possibilities based on skills, equipment, etc,
Overall, I very much enjoyed the game.  It is difficult but very satisfying in surviving.

I have to admit, when first looking at the images I was a sitting on the fence wondering if this would be as good as xcom: enemy unknown and UFO aftershock. But I thought screw it and bought it anyway, hoping for the best and it certainly didn't disappoint!
I was suprised how much of an improvement this game had over xcom enemy unknown, with xcom enemy unknown already being a great game.
Positives:
- Very good graphics, huge improvent from previous game
- Lots of gameplay, with an amazing story line, continues from xcom enemy unknown very well, the storyline is intrigueing, I found myself logging on early and logging off late to uncover more of the storyline
- Lots of different AI enemy, you discover new ones often as the game goes through, forever making you to rethink your strategies, to the point where your have to re-do tactics in most games, which furthers the thrill of gameplay.
- It's hard, your squad will haves losses, wounds, promotions, get shaken, furthering the fun and excitement of which of your soldiers can make it through all of your missions with you superior tactics ;)
- Lots and lots of research, ammo, armor, weapons, utility items, storyline research.
- Fully customizable characters and weapons, litterally build your dream team!
- Character pool, create some pretty cool characters before you start playing, or subscrive to some through workshop, you'll then have the option to recruit them ingame!
Negatives:
- Turn based can be good, but can be frustrating a lot at times, when the AI seem to 'technically' have more turns than you, and some units can obliterate your plans by vialating what you would of thought was the 'turn based rule'. Once you get used to it, you'll realise you can still counter and do a good job in every mission if you truly strategized your squad, but of course, some losses are near un-avoidable, and only improves the amazeballs this game gives!
- Timer based. 90% of missions are timed to 8 turns, failing to reach, or complete the objective within 8 turns will fail the mission. This can prove to ruin any strategy plan and make the game a guns-blazing typed plan in every mission, however, their are mods to change/configure or completely disable them.
- Actual storyline progress can push you pretty quick and catch you offguard (won't go into detail because of spoilers) just remember to keep up your pace in fighting the alien threat and you should more than keep up with the game progress. Once again, theirs a mod to slow this (game pushing) progress down.
All in all, I highly recommend this to anyone who likes tactical games, strategy games, squad managing games, and of course, any previous xcom owners that enjoyed playing! Amazing game! I will be playing this game all over again some time soon just for the hell of it!

PROS:
-------
- One (if not the best) of the best tactical turn-based action games out there.
- Once you learn the game, tough battles are extremely fun.
- Recruit, train, customize, and take your soldiers from rookies to bad♥♥♥♥♥veterans. (getting attached can be risky...)
- Main campaign is long and intense especially when everything is seemingly going the Advent's way.
- Good soundtrack.
CONS:
-------
- The punishing RNG in battle (especially on harder difficulties) can really demoralize newcomers to the XCOM universe.
- Having timers in almost every battle is a hinderance to the tactical part of the game. (More on this below)
- Panic attacks from rookies are over the top and frustrating to play through in the early game.
- Advent Project ticker on the campaign map is also a hinderance to the overall flow of the game (More on this below)
- Tons of performance issues even on top notch PCs. This has been fixed for the most part in the War of the Chosen DLC.
ABOUT BATTLE TIMERS
------------------------
In XCOM, there were a small handful of battles where the objective required you to complete the task before the timer ran out. These missions included the likes of bomb diffusions or securing a supply pod before it is destroyed. These were a refreshing change since most battles were not timed. In XCOM2, about 80% of all battles are timed for some reason. This is suppose to be a tactical turn based game where you spend time meticulously planning your attack, ambush, or flanks. When you are faced with a 12 turn time limit to retrieve data from a console surrounded by Advent forces, your strategy becomes drastically limited. You always feel rushed and this forces you to put your soldiers in positions of risk that you would normally not do. I absolutely hate this concept. I got around this by cheesing the game. In battles where I have to fight, I bring 5 Assault + 1 Healer. In battles where I have to retrieve something or plant bombs, I just deploy one super Assault guy with the Wraith Suit that allows him to walk through walls. One man can infiltrate and escape faster and more efficient than deploying a full team against a timer.
This brings me to the Advent Project tracker on the main campaign map. This is basically an overall timer for the campaign. If the Advent are allowed to fill all the bars, then you are forced into a do or die mission to try and save your campaing. If you fail, then you lose indefinitely. On paper this doesn't sound so bad but then you have to take into account the sheer amount of time it takes you to just do the most basic things like building a room, waiting for a soldier to recover from wounds, or scanning a region for supplies. It takes considerable in-game days to get anything done meanwhile the Advent ticker keeps adding on. Again, this doesn't sound so bad on paper or even when plaing on the easier difficulty. But on harder difficulties, this forces you to submit to a strict build order for your base and all your research or you will lose. It's bad design because what seems like challenging micromanagment reveals itself to be more a tedious cookie cutter format in order to survive.

This is a fantastically developed and thought out RPG title.   It reminds me a lot of the Xcom titles in that you're developing both a base (Hamlet) and a roster of characters from which you make parties for various missions.
Darkest Dungeon is however devilishly and unrelentingly punishing and difficult.   While many games have an "Ironman" mode and tougher difficuty levels than normal, Darkest Dungeon has only those options.    There are no save games, the game saves what happens in just about real time.   So you always pay for your mitakes - and dead characters stay dead.
If you're up for challenge and like Xcom type challenges - upgrading your Hamlet to best support your troops, and deploying them with the best tactics in the dungeon areas - don't miss this game.    Great narration only intensifies the stressful, punishing atmosphere as you learn your way to better chances of survival.

First, My system ran the game satisfactory with a few minor graphic's hitches.  My System has an Intel i7-3770K CPU @3.5hz, Geforce GTX 970 (driver  361.43 at the time of game), Windows 10 Home 64-bit. I played the game at the veteran level.
I finished the game after 60+ hours, I could have finished sooner but I wanted to "cover" the world and build evetything.
Many reviewers  complain about the timer in many missions  but I found that a steady pace worked ok, not to say, that sometimes especially difficult pre-battles didn't force a clearing the path for a run to the goal.  I had several missions on the last count.
The enemy are strong and many have area attacks but are usually grouped only by three.  If you don't  pull more than one group, you will have a fair chance.  I found even with the timer, you can set up a defense and pull a group into a kill zone and then move on to the next group.  As the game proceeds, you will have many new options for strategy with advancements in ammo,skills,etc.
Despite the difficulty, I found that I didn't have to go to a saved game to correct a bad out-come too many times.  Usually when my scout advanced too far and pulled too many groups.  It was rare for my teams not to suffer injuries and healing is slow which means many missions did not have an ideal team.
There are substantial strategic decisions to make in the game , as an example for an advance team, the enemy can have shield and armor however there are weapons/ammo that by-pass armor, so if you hit a group with an area attack that does substanial damage despite heavy armor and follow it with a sniper with a rifle with extended magazine and the serial ability (kill shot doesn't use action point) and AP ammo , that sniper can take out the entire group. This is just one of many possibilities based on skills, equipment, etc,
Overall, I very much enjoyed the game.  It is difficult but very satisfying in surviving.

This is the kind of RPG that harkens back to the bad old days where the DM is out the get the players in the most unfair manner possible. Old adventure modules that have traps everywhere and often penalize the party for not being prescient are not too far off from the game style of Darkest Dungeon. If this sounds like your cup of tea, then you will enjoy the game very, very much. It makes no bones that the RNG can screw you over and make even the best laid plans fall apart. For example a boss was just 2 HP from death when my dudes decide to just stab themselves to death due to stress. Frustration is a key feature of the game as it can easily leave you with an unwinnable situation very rapidly. Manage your expectations accordingly. It is not recommended for busy adults though as the set backs often necessitate a long rebuilding period. A couple of bad runs can mean having to start over since you lack the gold and men to tackle the current dungeons. Back in college, that would have meant a couple of nights of gaming to get back on even keel. As a working adult, it means a couple of weeks. Best played over holiday periods where the nail biting intensity can be truly felt as opposed to half a dungeon at a time which often leads to a loss in tension.

I have to admit, when first looking at the images I was a sitting on the fence wondering if this would be as good as xcom: enemy unknown and UFO aftershock. But I thought screw it and bought it anyway, hoping for the best and it certainly didn't disappoint!
I was suprised how much of an improvement this game had over xcom enemy unknown, with xcom enemy unknown already being a great game.
Positives:
- Very good graphics, huge improvent from previous game
- Lots of gameplay, with an amazing story line, continues from xcom enemy unknown very well, the storyline is intrigueing, I found myself logging on early and logging off late to uncover more of the storyline
- Lots of different AI enemy, you discover new ones often as the game goes through, forever making you to rethink your strategies, to the point where your have to re-do tactics in most games, which furthers the thrill of gameplay.
- It's hard, your squad will haves losses, wounds, promotions, get shaken, furthering the fun and excitement of which of your soldiers can make it through all of your missions with you superior tactics ;)
- Lots and lots of research, ammo, armor, weapons, utility items, storyline research.
- Fully customizable characters and weapons, litterally build your dream team!
- Character pool, create some pretty cool characters before you start playing, or subscrive to some through workshop, you'll then have the option to recruit them ingame!
Negatives:
- Turn based can be good, but can be frustrating a lot at times, when the AI seem to 'technically' have more turns than you, and some units can obliterate your plans by vialating what you would of thought was the 'turn based rule'. Once you get used to it, you'll realise you can still counter and do a good job in every mission if you truly strategized your squad, but of course, some losses are near un-avoidable, and only improves the amazeballs this game gives!
- Timer based. 90% of missions are timed to 8 turns, failing to reach, or complete the objective within 8 turns will fail the mission. This can prove to ruin any strategy plan and make the game a guns-blazing typed plan in every mission, however, their are mods to change/configure or completely disable them.
- Actual storyline progress can push you pretty quick and catch you offguard (won't go into detail because of spoilers) just remember to keep up your pace in fighting the alien threat and you should more than keep up with the game progress. Once again, theirs a mod to slow this (game pushing) progress down.
All in all, I highly recommend this to anyone who likes tactical games, strategy games, squad managing games, and of course, any previous xcom owners that enjoyed playing! Amazing game! I will be playing this game all over again some time soon just for the hell of it!

PROS:
-------
- One (if not the best) of the best tactical turn-based action games out there.
- Once you learn the game, tough battles are extremely fun.
- Recruit, train, customize, and take your soldiers from rookies to bad♥♥♥♥♥veterans. (getting attached can be risky...)
- Main campaign is long and intense especially when everything is seemingly going the Advent's way.
- Good soundtrack.
CONS:
-------
- The punishing RNG in battle (especially on harder difficulties) can really demoralize newcomers to the XCOM universe.
- Having timers in almost every battle is a hinderance to the tactical part of the game. (More on this below)
- Panic attacks from rookies are over the top and frustrating to play through in the early game.
- Advent Project ticker on the campaign map is also a hinderance to the overall flow of the game (More on this below)
- Tons of performance issues even on top notch PCs. This has been fixed for the most part in the War of the Chosen DLC.
ABOUT BATTLE TIMERS
------------------------
In XCOM, there were a small handful of battles where the objective required you to complete the task before the timer ran out. These missions included the likes of bomb diffusions or securing a supply pod before it is destroyed. These were a refreshing change since most battles were not timed. In XCOM2, about 80% of all battles are timed for some reason. This is suppose to be a tactical turn based game where you spend time meticulously planning your attack, ambush, or flanks. When you are faced with a 12 turn time limit to retrieve data from a console surrounded by Advent forces, your strategy becomes drastically limited. You always feel rushed and this forces you to put your soldiers in positions of risk that you would normally not do. I absolutely hate this concept. I got around this by cheesing the game. In battles where I have to fight, I bring 5 Assault + 1 Healer. In battles where I have to retrieve something or plant bombs, I just deploy one super Assault guy with the Wraith Suit that allows him to walk through walls. One man can infiltrate and escape faster and more efficient than deploying a full team against a timer.
This brings me to the Advent Project tracker on the main campaign map. This is basically an overall timer for the campaign. If the Advent are allowed to fill all the bars, then you are forced into a do or die mission to try and save your campaing. If you fail, then you lose indefinitely. On paper this doesn't sound so bad but then you have to take into account the sheer amount of time it takes you to just do the most basic things like building a room, waiting for a soldier to recover from wounds, or scanning a region for supplies. It takes considerable in-game days to get anything done meanwhile the Advent ticker keeps adding on. Again, this doesn't sound so bad on paper or even when plaing on the easier difficulty. But on harder difficulties, this forces you to submit to a strict build order for your base and all your research or you will lose. It's bad design because what seems like challenging micromanagment reveals itself to be more a tedious cookie cutter format in order to survive.

I saw this a few days ago and I thought it would be bad. Then I realized that it just came out so obviously it wouldn't be that popular, so I decided to give it a try. After messing with a few settings and playing nothing but 5v5 demolition, I can say that the one thing that really stands out are how good the maps are split into lanes and obvious paths to go. The 5v5 demo game mode is obviously inspired by CS:GO with the paths top the A and B objectives being painted in red. This is a really weird mix of CS and COD mechanics that surprisingly mixes well. For example, there is no sprint (Which I love in games because it influences good map design) There is only walk with shift, and walk faster with your knife out. Gunplay definately feels like COD but more like the older ones like COD4 and MW2. Snipers are OP but they are not always practical, Its actually exactly like how snipers work in MW2 and MW3. Lots of borrowed traits from other games, and thats what makes this game seem so familiar but new at the same time. As long as it doesn't become Pay to win and sticks with skins, then this will be a good free to play game.

I am a huge fan of XCOM Enemy Unknown and I have to say XCOM 2 is a big improvement. It polishes core game-mechanics (although still very buggy) from the previous title and adds in couple new elements that make the game feel more complete.
Pros
- Deeper customization for soldiers
- Better system for building facilities
- Improved graphics
- Tough and interesting enemies
- New soldier classes
- Decent story
- Grittier than previous title (as it should be)
- Very well balanced (felt somewhat equal to my enemies when facing them)
- New HQ system (gives player more flexibility and control)
- Difficulty (difficult as always)
Cons
- Poorly optimized like the previous title (didn't stop me from putting in 50+ hours)
- Buggy (you will run into dozen of minor bugs)
- Camera angles during sequence are terrible as always
- Inaccurate shot success rate (too many times have my soldiers missed 98% hit rate from flanking positions)
Overall, this game is pretty amazing and I highly recommend to anyone that enjoy hard tactical turn-based shooter.

Here are couple of early game tips for beginners:
Upgrade
Make sure to research "Predator Armor" and upgrade "Increase Squad Size 1 & 2" in the beginning of the game. This is critical when facing harder enemies in early stages.
Soldier Classes
XCOM 2 included new and tougher enemies however, you also have access to new and better gear for your soldiers.
Grenadier: Tank and splash damage expert that should always be included in each mission.
Ranger: Rangers can be very powerful late in the game, but in beginning stages, they aren't that prevalent.
Specialist: I found Specialists to be critical in certain missions that involve mechanical enemies as you are given opportunities to hack those enemies using one of Specialists skill. You could even get control of the unit for 2 turns which can turn the battle in your favor significantly. They also have a perk that allows 4 heals via gremlin that can be spammed twice in a single turn.
Sharpshooter: Just like rangers, they aren't that great early game, but very very useful late game.
Psi Operative: Psi soldiers can be OP so I recommend them, but it takes quite bit of time training them.
Items
Best item in the game hands down - Mimic Beacon. I don't even know how many times decoys saved my squad, but I carry 3 of them for each mission.

This is the kind of RPG that harkens back to the bad old days where the DM is out the get the players in the most unfair manner possible. Old adventure modules that have traps everywhere and often penalize the party for not being prescient are not too far off from the game style of Darkest Dungeon. If this sounds like your cup of tea, then you will enjoy the game very, very much. It makes no bones that the RNG can screw you over and make even the best laid plans fall apart. For example a boss was just 2 HP from death when my dudes decide to just stab themselves to death due to stress. Frustration is a key feature of the game as it can easily leave you with an unwinnable situation very rapidly. Manage your expectations accordingly. It is not recommended for busy adults though as the set backs often necessitate a long rebuilding period. A couple of bad runs can mean having to start over since you lack the gold and men to tackle the current dungeons. Back in college, that would have meant a couple of nights of gaming to get back on even keel. As a working adult, it means a couple of weeks. Best played over holiday periods where the nail biting intensity can be truly felt as opposed to half a dungeon at a time which often leads to a loss in tension.

I had some concerns about this game before it came out and they all proved to be true; combining that with exceptionally poor performance issues, I can't recommend this game right now.
Pros: New aliens, new maps, more customization.  Concealment mini-game is okay but is just a much-hyped minigame that only takes up a couple turns at the start of some missions.  After that it's normal XCom.  These things are new and passably good but they also could have been put into expansions / DLC instead of a sequel.  Making this a sequel was basically an excuse to upgrade the graphics, which as you've probably been reading, was actually a mistake...
Con: System performance is amazingly bad.  The game 3d renders everything in the base but you can't actually view those things in 3d, so you will get your biggest performance hit WHILE IN THE BASE.  If that sounds manageable to you, it's not; I write that as an example of how badly optimized this game is.  Returning to the base after a mission takes up to several minutes for an average system, apparently for no reason since people discovered that if you push capslock during a return, it has a 50% chance to instantly let you back into the base.  I can confirm the capslock trick is true.  I could run XCom: EU on high with no problems but have to run this on minimal, at which point it looks worse than EU did on minimal, and it still has a lower framerate.  I'm sitting there wondering if capslock will work on this run or if I have to get up and do something else for 5 minutes while returning to base after a laggy and annoying mission.  What the heck?
Con: Lots of melee units dashing into combat just doesn't work for a game like this.  In the early game it's really overpowered for the enemies and makes the majority of timed missions aggravating.  Also, timers in missions are not optional (like meld was in EW) which is annoying when you also have melee aliens suicidally charging at you.  Yet in the mid-game you can get a sword character who counter-attacks anyone that gets close.  At this point melee enemies will just run up to the closest character and die immediately on their own to the counter-attack mechanic.  This means you can completely ignore them with a proper setup once you have a character like that.  So melee is either too hard or too easy and makes everything annoying because the melee aliens have suicidal AI.  Close range? In XCom? Why?
Conclusion: System performance issues and the few good things about the game could have both been solved by making this an expansion and not a sequel.  The close range stuff and extremely poorly optimized graphics didn't warrant a 2-year wait and full-game price tag.

Short story: Black Squad has good graphics, high Frames per Seconds, excellent weapon balance, solid rising community. It is truly Free to Play. Black Squad is simply the best F2P PvP shooter on PC !
Long story: Black Squad is a kind of brilliant mix between CS GO and Ghost in the Shell (another Korean game). Let’s look first at its strong points:
* Runs smoothly on old computers. My January 2012 PC runs great with all details on. What a change from games such as Ark Survival ! Also no network lag.
* Weapon balance is impressive. ARs are versatile, SMGs / shotguns are close to mid range, snipers mid to long range. At first I believed snipers were at a disadvantage because characters move so fast. But if you pick the right spot you can do many kills and also deny access to enemy. Killing is great but blocking enemy is important too.
* Maps are well designed. There aren’t many per game mode but they are subtle.
* Black Squad is really Free to Play. You can download free access to weapons for 14 days. Twice. Great for testing before unlocking. In a month you can gather enough gold and medals to buy really many weapons. Only skins require real money.
* Developers seriously listen to the community. Recently many players complained that shotguns were OP. Nerfed in the next patch !
* Character leveling up and daily / weekly missions are well designed. They give a purpose. In CS GO you play for ranking. In BS for medals and gold.
Now let’s look at the weak points:
* Servers are often down. Let’s hope this is just a youth issue.
* Characters move too fast. Bunny hops are lame. It’s okay to move fast with the knife. It makes the game fast paced. But it should slow down when carrying primary weapon. Slow down more than it does. Arcadish sprint and jumping around is good in a hero shooter such as Overwatch. But in a ‘serious’ military shooter it does not fit.
* No matchmaking based on ranking. Ranking is very important in a PvP shooter because it allows fair games. When noobs are crushed by vets they get frustrated and leave the game. Hopefully as the game grows, Elo based ranking will be implemented.
* Game modes. This is the main flaw of the game. Firstly there are too many game modes which spray the community. Secondly several game modes are sub optimal. Team Death match is great. Battle 16vs16 with skills like Overwatch / Paladins, why not. At first it seems chaotic. But a deep strategy is possible. Next game mode, Assassination 8vs8 is boring: when you die you might wait for a long time because a team of 8 is huge. Same for demolition 8vs8. Demolition 5v5 seems good. But it requires coordination. Unfortunately, contrary to CS GO, nobody uses a mic. And many players don’t even understand the basic strategy of demolition. They play like death match. And they get crushed.
What lacks badly is a capture the flag mode.
To sum-up, despite game modes flaws, Black Squad is the best and most popular F2P PvP shooter available. Give it a try !

This sequel iterates from the previous game, it is definitely a good game, it improves in some points like map generation and usabilty but sadly it takes a step backwards in many others, i admit i am biassed by the 600+ hours i spend with the Long War mod but i just had higher expectations for this game
The random map generation engine is pretty great but i feel does not get exploited to its complete potential by the gameplay, the maps will tend to "feel the same" because it will keep giving you missions around the same area and that means that while the game can have widely different looking maps, it will keep sending you to similar looking ones, i must also mention that, as a consequence of the random generation, the maps just dont have the detail and love the handcrafted maps from XCOM had
I am sad to say that the Legendary mode is a big dissapointment, instead of being "commander but much harder" its more like "commander with 5-10% more enemies per map and pointlessly much much longer", i played legendary for my first playthough since the game looked easy in the previews, and i while it started hard the difficulty curve went into free fall once i got veterans, psi operatives and better items, instead of being challenged i was just burnt out by the sheer amount of missions i had to do with soldiers not leveling up, research not finishing and day counters barely advancing. I recently started a commander ironman playthrough and the pacing is soooooo much better, i recomend avoiding the legendary difficulty, there is only grind to find there, nowhere near as challenging as XCOM's impossible mode
I am also dissapointed at the changes in the strategy layer, after the huge step back taken with the XCOM reboot i was hoping for a little more complexibillity to get put back into the game but they decided to go further on into dumbing it down, everything has being reduced, research is simpler, item making is simpler, character development, etc, you would think as the "agressor" in this game you would get to pick your fights right ?, well no, you just wait to be given missions, to be honest it feels a lot like a mobile game, you just click and wait for content to be delivered, it doesnt sound as different from the previous game but it feels far less interesting
A few other nitpicks:
*There is a greater reliance on RNG for this game, it is easier to miss even against uncovered/flanked targets, melee attacks miss, even 100% attacks can get dodged, better ammo, better grenades, hidden abilities you characters get, you throw a dice instead of choosing, i never liked RNG in XCOM so i cant see how this helps anything
*While they added a line of sight indicator and a "you are going to get poisoned" indicator, the sight indicator is very hard to use because you need to keep the aliens on view to use it and several expected indicators that are missing like the "you will get flank" indicators and "you will trigger overwatch from a seen enemy" indicator
*The weapon upgrade system is nice but very underused, there should have been more options and ammo types should have been part of the upgrades
*The soldier upgrade trees again have pretty obvious "better paths", in most levels one of the two are just better, more than two options would have made more builds viable
*There is little reason to have more than a single proper squad, you can actually buy replacement colonels with intel and get them in missions, making squaddies a lot less important
*I hate the way the "hidden" ability works, by being completely random it just ends up making you abandon characters you liked for those that got abilities, i would rather choose, why wont you let me choose ?

Darkest Dungeon is a chance-heavy, atmospheric, dark, turn-based dungeon crawler where you really have to make the most out of an incredibly ♥♥♥♥♥♥ situation that gets worse as you play.
I have a few complaints about the game, but I'm giving it a positive score based on a few things it does really well:
- Really cool atmosphere, this game drips with it. Like Lovecraftian horrors and hopeless situations? This is for you. Each character has things to say in the dungeon and in the base (i forget if it's the hamlet or the abby or whatever)
- Interesting and visceral turn-based combat. Each thing that happens feels great. Tons of things to manage: buffs, debuffs, bleeds, stun, and unit position. Corpses are even a concern in battle
- Base management. You'll be using the treasures you find in the dungeons to improve each part of the HQ, but most of your money will go to stress management and other things to help you survive
- Character classes. Each week sees new adventurers with unique abilities and playstyles. I really like the variety of abilities and their effects. The occultist is an interesting character that can heal you really well, but has abilities that debuff the enemy and lower your torch value. The grave robber is constantly shuffling position.
Complaints
I understand that this game is all about making the most out of a bad situation, but it really goes out of its way to ♥♥♥♥ you.
The stress mechanic is neat, but stress comes too easily. Your party is stressed when in combat, when they hit a trap, when they read a book, when they stub their toe on a rock, when someone says something mean, and just by walking.
When they are stressed above 100, they get a mental affliction and will often not respond to commands and sometimes will act on their own. They will also not allow a character to give them a buff sometimes. What the hell. This gets way too out of hand. I was just in a dungeon when a surprise encounter completely destroyed an otherwise good run. Everyone was full health, but my occultist couldn't heal for some reason because his stress was above 100. My cleric died because she decided not to accept a heal from the crusader and attacked an enemy without my input and bled to death. The Occultist got the mental affliction hopeless and wouldn't shut up about everything and gave everyone stress damage every turn. By the end of the battle only the arbelist or whomever was left and I had to leave because she has no abilities that allow her to target an enemy in the front position.
There are also some things about combat that aren't too clear or I don't like:
- No indication of turn order or speed. Unless i'm just being really unobservant, there's no way to tell when your dudes or the enemy are going to act.
- Why can some melee abilities target guys in the back row and some can't? This seems unevenly weighed toward the enemy, but I could be wrong.
- Some abilities can hit multiple enemies, but there's no UI tool which displays this effect, you just kind of have to guess who is getting hit.
Maladies come a little too easily. I rarely end a complete run without every adventurer getting 1 or 2 mental or physical disabilities. This is on top of what I suffer in the dungeon. The game just piles it on and expects you to manage this with the high cost of stress management in the town. Everything that can repair these things cost 1k or more. Some characters even receive new negative traits while "relaxing".
You have to upgrade the blacksmith before you can even do anything there...
Someone else mentioned this in another review, but you don't keep  any of the provisions you have when you end a dungeon run. It'd be nice if there was storage for the stuff you don't use or the game let you use them on your next run. Considering how much♥♥♥♥♥♥you go through and how much it costs, that'd be a minor relief in an otherwise relentless game.
Overall
This is a good game with some things that prevent it from being great. Don't let those things turn you off, if you have been thinking about playing this, then give it a shot. The combat is fun, the atmosphere is superb, and the rewards are good if you can survive the tsunami of crap that comes your way.

Just finished the game after nearly 200 hours. And I feel it's 200 hours well spent.
The game has some flaws, but hopefully they will keep working on it and adding new stuff. Otherwise it's damn easy to mod, so it's just a matter of time before the community creates something even more awesome from this gem of a game.
Some tips for beginners:
- Don't favor a particuilar hero. Because he WILL die.
- Don't be afraid to abandon quests. There's nothing worse than a total party wipe-out.
- Pay attention to stress.
- Don't think that every class is a one-trick pony, they excell in many things when needed.
If your team is fully healed, get your Occultist to the front and start stabbing and stunning!
- Don't make your characters dependant on one exact spot in your setup. Otherwise your run will mess upp completely if your party get's shuffled around and none of your characters can use any attacks. Some characters have abilities that makes them jump forward or backward towards their favored position, try to have at least one in your party with such ability.
Some things I did find annoying is;
- The long grinding mid-game.
You run SO MANY runs thats just boring, just to get enough gold or to level up that partivular character. There's just not enough mid game to keep the game interesting at that point. Just the same quests over and over again.
- Unfair deaths.
I don't know how many times I go into a dungeon run, and my team get's surpired by the first monster encounter, and then they deal 2 or 3 crits in a row on one of my guys and he just drops dead, before I have the chanse to do anything. The game is hard, but sometimes it isn't fair.
- Useless items(trinkets).
There's a lot of items in the game to find, but most of them are just better versions of items of lower tiers. When you find the better version of an item, you can sell your old one and won't bother with it if you ever find it again. This makes about 90% of the total item count garbage in the long mid-game and late game, and suddenly you feel like there's not enough items in the game. You just keep using the same over and over again.
- Trinket stats.
Speaking of using the same items over and over again... All items are just stat changes. So they really don't feel that interesting. You will always get a +ACC on your Leper cause of his low base hit chanse, and always give a +Healing to your Vestal for example. The different classes in the game can make great synergies together, to bad the same can't be said about the trinkets. I would love to see something like "critical hits gives a +speed buff" or "hits has a chanse to instantly use up all Bleed-stacks on your target, dealing the damage they would deal over time instantly"
Oh, I forgot to mention... All items gives a penalty to some stats as well. So you usually pick one trinket that is good for your character, and then an other one to cancel out the negative stats from the first one.

People play games; they play it with such passion.  Why do we play games?  I probably have only a cut of the sense, but I play them to have fun; I play them to compensate for my terrible lack of success in reality: at least I could seem competent in the fantastical world created by these games.
To a program-level basis, this game is terribly optimized, spending as much as a whole gigabyte of memory for who-knows-what.  The servers seem particularly laggy, even for an MMORPG; be prepared to blame some loss of success to that...
However, what bothers me the most is what follows:
Everything in this game is driven by micro-transactions and connections.  If you go in blind without a guide or some cash, you'll be trudging along the bottom-of-barrel content of the game for quite some time.  Assuming you do have some guidance or you, just maybe, legitimately reached the top you begin to realize something about the game...  There are these extremely jam-packed messy missions that just throw everything they have at you, making you waste an incredible amount of revives as the days pass by.  Yet, we remain frugal, knowing that each of these revives we lose, we have just lost a few cents of our time or money.  All that frustration knowing that, or the tenacity you have to practice to keep your calm under the sort of lag and buffer speeds you have to experience...
One day, I just stopped to think... Why do we play games again?  I certainly didn't play games to get frustrated over proving myself to be a competent player in a certain environment, or throw in time or money to accomplish more of the former...  All to impress who?  What am I going through all this frustration for?  Then I realized: this is hardly a game to be played at all.
From why I play games, this game is an atrocity.  I felt so angry after such a realization that I uninstalled the game, wished I didn't even have that account or those crowns in it, wished I didn't even start that wretched game, wondered how I was even blind enough to get as far as I did without realizing this, hid it from my library, and after much thought: decided to give the game this senseless tirade of a review.
Don't want to bother reading this review?  Fine: don't play the game; it goes against why I play games in the first place.

This is a fantastically developed and thought out RPG title.   It reminds me a lot of the Xcom titles in that you're developing both a base (Hamlet) and a roster of characters from which you make parties for various missions.
Darkest Dungeon is however devilishly and unrelentingly punishing and difficult.   While many games have an "Ironman" mode and tougher difficuty levels than normal, Darkest Dungeon has only those options.    There are no save games, the game saves what happens in just about real time.   So you always pay for your mitakes - and dead characters stay dead.
If you're up for challenge and like Xcom type challenges - upgrading your Hamlet to best support your troops, and deploying them with the best tactics in the dungeon areas - don't miss this game.    Great narration only intensifies the stressful, punishing atmosphere as you learn your way to better chances of survival.

Trove is a great, free-to-play, open world MMO. There is no real story or purpose to the game, other than doing dungeons. It is a great game to play with friends and family, or to just plain have fun.
In the game, you get a place that only YOU can build on, called a cornerstone. To use one, you have to claim it, and then build on it whatever you want. The best part about the cornerstones is that you can claim others, and your house will appear there. This helps a LOT when doing dungeons, castles, and just exploring and gathering materials for crafting. There are also little missions in the game, and a shop, where you can buy coins, mounts, wings, and other classes.
I will say, however, that I do dislike the newer update to the game. I personally dislike it, and feel that, yes, the update did improve somethings, but changed some things that I find rather stupid and uncalled for. Yes, the Battleverse, (which is a PVP mode), was an okay thing to add. But, my only thing against this update are, A, the "power ranking" system, and B, how you can no longer buy classes with Cubits, (thein-game curency). I find that the original level system was better, and a little less confusing, than the power ranking system. However, I do see why they changed it from level to power ranking.
Over all, this is a fantastic game. From the design of everything, to the fact that Glyph lets its players create sword, enemy, and dungeon designs through Reddit, which I think is a great way for people to feel included, Glyph made a fantastic game.

Darkest Dungeon is a brutally brilliant game with a fantastic artstyle and voiceover that is second to none.
RNG in Darkest Dungeon is mitigated by your play and skill which is why the overwhelming majority of people calling it an RNGfest have so little hours put into it. It's because they don't understand the importance of concepts such as party setups, camping, ability combinations, trinket choices and resouce efficiency at that point.
Progression and leveling in Darkest Dungeon is the game itself. There is end game but if you know what you are doing it takes a fraction of the time compared to building up your teams. The worse you are at the game, the slower progression is and the more grindy it feels but there is no failstate, you can always recover!
If you want a game where you have one party, they never permadeath and you focus entirely on them then this is not the game for you. This is very obvious right from the beginning of the game. Even the introduction text points to this.
If you want an easy rpg dungeon crawler that requires zero thought or effort then there are plenty out there. Darkest Dungeon is not that game but if you stick with it and get a good grasp on it, you will never think any part of it is unfair. Instead you will learn something and realise there was a decision you made somewhere that could have prevented it.

Following XCOM: Enemy Unknown (EU) and Enemy Within (EW) which successfully proved a point to publishers: turn based strategy games can have a space in the mainstream AAA market.
XCOM: EU and EW has for better or worse modernized X-COM. While different aspects of the game has been streamlined or "dumbed down", the combat is the key sauce of the game and it is executed very well. No other titles has made the cover system as well as XCOM at the time of release. The franchise is relevant once again.
XCOM: EU/EW- Long War mod has added and deepened a wide range of mechanics from EU and EW, providing a whole lot more of reasonably well balanced tactical options, a better geoscape strategy along with brutual difficulty that increases the replayability of XCOM EU/EW ten folds, with the pacing being somewhat of an issue.
XCOM2 is in essence eliminating the bad and odd parts from XCOM EU, adding procedural generated maps and rebalancing the game from Long War's "inspiration" while still maintaining accessbility to the mainstream.
TL;DR: If XCOM: EU/EW is a 7/10, Long war is a 9.2/10, then XCOM2 is a 8.5/10.
Read more for details below...

Differs from EU/EW, the geoscape straegy in XCOM2 is influenced by Long War, Enemies have their own research progress and you can choose which 1 out of 3 to stop. The guerrilla theme setting of the game has rebalanced the satillite game and got rid of air space battles completely in a believable way, as well as making the geoscape gameplay abit more balanced. Also following Long War, rushing satillites (radio relays) is no longer the absolute no brainer optimal strategy.
The first half of a campaign in XCOM2 is actually very fun, unlike XOM EU/EW where Thin mints appear early and they have a high chance to kill your early soldiers out right and there’s little you can do about it, XCOM2 instead provides group of enemies with a variety of attack patterns that gives you a much fairer chance and a much more tactical game right out of the gate. It is in fact so much better that new enemies from the later parts of the campaign actually feel dull and uninspired in comparison.
Enemy AI remains as fun and challenging as before, with tweaks to them that encourages, or often forces a more aggressive gameplay style.
Procedural generated maps are also a godsend, every battle is now slightly different in ways enough to keep them unpredictable.
More mission types are available in XCOM2, and quite a lot of them includes a mission timer. I am personally not against the idea of limited time missions but losing soldier(s) until you get a chance to rescue them just because you are 1 tile away from the evac zone in a cleared map is sort of jarring and doesn’t make much sense.
XCOM2 soldiers' builds balance are quite a step up from EU/EW, where a squadsight flying sniper is all you need to roll over everywhere. Most of the classes are quite balanced and useful in their own way without a single class being way more desirable. (Psi operatives are kind of an oddball class that does not follow the growth rules like others so I don't count them). However, the tactical options of each soldier still pales comparing to Long war. At best case, XCOM2 is apparent that the general builds are inspired right from Long War.
There are new elements that have become part of the loot system in XCOM2- PCS and weapon mods. PCS are basically a character gem mod that passively increases a stat for a soldier, and weapon mods adds additional minor passive perks. Both helps giving each soldier more uniqueness, along with the character customization system that is now actually a proper thing.
Being one the most improved feature in XCOM2, soldier appearance customizations is actually decent, if not one of the best foundations made for a turn based strategy game in recent years. I personally love customizing all my soldiers, and XCOM2 made it very easy that I can save my character to appear in future play throughs again. The only thing I hope for is a lot more of them: especially faces, hair style and such, in which mods will likely help on that front.
