XCOM: EU/EW- Long War mod has added and deepened a wide range of mechanics from EU and EW, providing a whole lot more of reasonably well balanced tactical options, a better geoscape strategy along with brutual difficulty that increases the replayability of XCOM EU/EW ten folds, with the pacing being somewhat of an issue.
XCOM2 is in essence eliminating the bad and odd parts from XCOM EU, adding procedural generated maps and rebalancing the game from Long War's "inspiration" while still maintaining accessbility to the mainstream.
TL;DR: If XCOM: EU/EW is a 7/10, Long war is a 9.2/10, then XCOM2 is a 8.5/10.
Read more for details below...

Differs from EU/EW, the geoscape straegy in XCOM2 is influenced by Long War, Enemies have their own research progress and you can choose which 1 out of 3 to stop. The guerrilla theme setting of the game has rebalanced the satillite game and got rid of air space battles completely in a believable way, as well as making the geoscape gameplay abit more balanced. Also following Long War, rushing satillites (radio relays) is no longer the absolute no brainer optimal strategy.
The first half of a campaign in XCOM2 is actually very fun, unlike XOM EU/EW where Thin mints appear early and they have a high chance to kill your early soldiers out right and there’s little you can do about it, XCOM2 instead provides group of enemies with a variety of attack patterns that gives you a much fairer chance and a much more tactical game right out of the gate. It is in fact so much better that new enemies from the later parts of the campaign actually feel dull and uninspired in comparison.
Enemy AI remains as fun and challenging as before, with tweaks to them that encourages, or often forces a more aggressive gameplay style.
Procedural generated maps are also a godsend, every battle is now slightly different in ways enough to keep them unpredictable.
More mission types are available in XCOM2, and quite a lot of them includes a mission timer. I am personally not against the idea of limited time missions but losing soldier(s) until you get a chance to rescue them just because you are 1 tile away from the evac zone in a cleared map is sort of jarring and doesn’t make much sense.
XCOM2 soldiers' builds balance are quite a step up from EU/EW, where a squadsight flying sniper is all you need to roll over everywhere. Most of the classes are quite balanced and useful in their own way without a single class being way more desirable. (Psi operatives are kind of an oddball class that does not follow the growth rules like others so I don't count them). However, the tactical options of each soldier still pales comparing to Long war. At best case, XCOM2 is apparent that the general builds are inspired right from Long War.
There are new elements that have become part of the loot system in XCOM2- PCS and weapon mods. PCS are basically a character gem mod that passively increases a stat for a soldier, and weapon mods adds additional minor passive perks. Both helps giving each soldier more uniqueness, along with the character customization system that is now actually a proper thing.
Being one the most improved feature in XCOM2, soldier appearance customizations is actually decent, if not one of the best foundations made for a turn based strategy game in recent years. I personally love customizing all my soldiers, and XCOM2 made it very easy that I can save my character to appear in future play throughs again. The only thing I hope for is a lot more of them: especially faces, hair style and such, in which mods will likely help on that front.

Darkest Dungeon is a brutally brilliant game with a fantastic artstyle and voiceover that is second to none.
RNG in Darkest Dungeon is mitigated by your play and skill which is why the overwhelming majority of people calling it an RNGfest have so little hours put into it. It's because they don't understand the importance of concepts such as party setups, camping, ability combinations, trinket choices and resouce efficiency at that point.
Progression and leveling in Darkest Dungeon is the game itself. There is end game but if you know what you are doing it takes a fraction of the time compared to building up your teams. The worse you are at the game, the slower progression is and the more grindy it feels but there is no failstate, you can always recover!
If you want a game where you have one party, they never permadeath and you focus entirely on them then this is not the game for you. This is very obvious right from the beginning of the game. Even the introduction text points to this.
If you want an easy rpg dungeon crawler that requires zero thought or effort then there are plenty out there. Darkest Dungeon is not that game but if you stick with it and get a good grasp on it, you will never think any part of it is unfair. Instead you will learn something and realise there was a decision you made somewhere that could have prevented it.

I was late to xcom enemy unknown, passing it off as a silly sci fi wannabe strategy game. But I got it for free from some deal on amazon with all the xcom games. So I tried it out and got hooked.
Fast forward to xcom 2, which I had only heard about a month or so ago. So with Xcom Enemy unknown still fresh on my mind, I can say that this is exactly what I had hoped for.
It still feels just like enemy unkown which is important since it works, and works well. The base layer of strategy is essentially the same (Cover system, research/engineering/recruiting etc) which like I said is good, but many small features have been reworked or are new altogether.
The game is definitely tougher and more unforgiving. I've had to restart several times whereas on enemy unkown, bad situations didn't always have such hard long term consequences. Of course the game gets easier the longer you are into it, that's by design of the game, but the early portion is sure rough and for a new player they do throw a lot at you at once (and a lot of small useful stuff they don't tell you).
One thing to note about combat missions is that they have you thinking a little more on your toes than before (In the sense of turn based), due to the fact that in many missions are designed to eliminate a tactic called overwatch crawling. This is where you only move your soldiers up far enough to use 1 action, and then use the second action on overwatch so as to always have a jump on the aliens when they are spotted. I think a tactic is a tactic regardless of intentions, but I also see why the makers didn't want people to abuse a game that is supposed to be punishing. So what they've done to eliminate this in some missions is to add a turn based timer to complete the objective, or suffer a mission failure. Not all missions are like this, and honestly it's not that bad unless you're completely new to strategy games in general. For me, it adds a sense of immersion in the sense of decision making during critical operations.
Visually it's the same type of artwork as enemy unknown, but with much improved graphics and effects.
Character creation is very expansive, and very role play friendly.
New concealment system adds an extra layer to combat if used properly, otherwise it's relatively useless. You could theoretically win some missions without combat at all. Or you could use a concealed soldier as a spotter for long range snipers. Surely a welcomed system.
No more satellites, instead replaced by another (better) system.
Xcom 2 is basically a much improved version of enemy unknown. If you liked that game, you will like this game too. If you did not like enemy unknown, you probably won't like this either. If you're simply looking for a drastic change in any of the game's mechanics, you won't find it. In my opinion Xcom 2 is a faithful sequel of enemy unkown, and is a better version of an already great game.

I previously reviewed this game and my verdict was a negative, after having played this game some more recently, I have had a change of heart.
Spiral Knights is a cute Action RPG game with a simple yet engaging combat system, a prestige system with useful rewards and an indication as to how much progression you've made.
Positives:
Artsyle - This game looks pretty, it's basic and not overly fancy, but colourful and pleasent to look at.
Combat - Nothing too special however, the weapons are great and blocking is nice to have.
Music - Harry Mack did a great job with the soundtrack, certainly a great listen for atmosphere.
Missions - Before you would just travel the Clockwork, using materials gained to upgrade equipment, reach the bottom and you fight the final boss, now you have progress tracking and rewards.
This may not seem much, but the game does have a fair bit to offer, overall, it makes quite a nice package of content, providing missions, lots of weapons and armors, a replayable clockwork system and daily missions for extra prestige.
However, like all games, there are some negatives, pretty big ones at that.
F2P model - To begin, when the game first came out, to travel the clockwork, transmute and do some other stuff (I forget), you would require energy, this was similar to what some mobile games use, perhaps fatigue points is another term people might recognise. Essentially you are required to use energy to traverse the clockwork, costing 10 energy per descent, you would also have to use energy to revive, doubling per consecutive revive in a day starting at 2 energy, or you would use some to transmute (craft) items. This was the stance on the free to play model, you could pay money to refill your energy to continue playing for the day, it wasn't great, but it wasn't awful.
Instead, energy is now used as a "Premium currency", you can buy things from the supply depot, giving you rare items, cosmetics or straight up weapons, sheilds armors ect, you can also open gates during the clockwork for a cheap amount of energy for small bonus', not much but it's optional. Due to the change in energy and the lack of a need for it, they instead increased the time spent on getting materials, by adding more required items. Here's the biggest problem for me:
Alchemy orbs and heat crystals were introduced to solve the change in the free to play model. Alchemy orbs are required to transmute items, you are required to collect 3 of a certain rarity orb to craft the item corrasponding to the rarity of the orb e.g You need 3 Advance orbs to craft a 3 star item. These could be rewarded through quests or by VERY rarely finding them throughout the clockwork, these aren't so bad in the early game as a lot of equipment is either: Cheap enough to buy already made, gifted via missions, orbs awarded via missions in bulk of 3 so you don't need to farm or buy them, this meant that orbs up until rarity 2 aren't a problem to get.
Once you get to Rarity 3 for Alch orbs, things get pretty bad, you won't spend time farming for the orbs, once you've done all your missions, you won't have enough for a full set of 3 star gear, which you NEED because there are missions that validate if you're strong enough for the content up next, you can't complete this missions if you don't have the prerequisite items, being a full set of 2 star, 3 star ect gear. You will instead spend most of your time farming for crowns to buy orbs off of the aunction house, which sucks. Orbs are high priced, it takes about 45 minutes + to get 1 orb, and that's if you win the auction as well, if you don't, it's not the end of the world, you get your crowns back (really nice) and you can just try again, but you have to wait for a while to complete the auction.
Essentially, orbs really suck and slow the progression down by a lot, if you're impatiant, you will most likely end up spending money and just buying orbs for energy or just getting the gear right off the bat.
Heat Crystals aren't so bad so I won't go into so much detail, they're required to level up your equipment, you get heat from killing enemies and treasure boxs, then when you max heat, you need to use crystals to actually get to the next level. This is kinda meh because it's a chance unless you use 3 crystals, but you can get bonus' and crystals are much more common than orbs as drops and mission rewards.
For the most part, these 2 factors really take away from the game for me, Orbs of Alch suck a lot, they make you play the Auction house game, pay money or spend ages farming for them.
The only other real issue I have with this game is the netcode/servers. Lag is a real big killer in this game, you can get hit despite blocking, your attacks will phase through enemies, you skate around the floor and teleport around, enemies will hit you from a mile away and so on and so forth. A little bit of lag can really be detrimental and ruin a lot of things.
I might have missed some things out, but I wanted to "try" and keep it short, not that I did. Overall, this game is a nice time waster, it's nothing to take too seriously but has a nice end game to it for the most part, there are plenty of problems with it and since Grey Heaven purchased it, nothing has really happened, it's just sitting on a shelf gathering dust but it still remains charming and a nice little time sink.
I would have love to seen it flourish a bit more and get some new toys after Grey Heaven took it but that's not the case, as most of us expected.

The weapon customisation is impressive as well, the settlement system still feels like an after thought, with a lack of tutorial and the snapping feature being relatively finicky at times with some things requiring an act of congress to snap to other built structures.
The story also lacks in many respects, in my opinion Bethesda is skilled with world building and not in actual game development.  With an aged engine that still suffers with the above mentioned bugs as well as the low resolution of shadows.  The game looks like something that could have been released on previous gen consoles and platforms rather than current platforms.  There is also the issue of Bethesda disabling achievements if you utilize mods, even worse with the idea that you now have a freemium way of downloading mods.

I bounced between liking and disliking the game.  At first I liked it, then I hit a wall, and it became an annoying grind.  The Town Events patch made the game more dynamic, and I began to enjoy it again, and completed it.  Here's what you need to know:

2.  The game is hardcore.  Some parts are easy, but mistakes and RNG can easily kill off your characters.
3.  It is a grind.  The grind is enjoyable, but if you don't like grinding at all, this is not your game.
4.  You WILL need to research strategies and such.  If you try learning by trial and error (as I did at the start), be prepared for lots of frustration.
5.  Although I was very frustrated at points, the game style kept me poking at it until I got the hang of it.
I recommend it, but you will have to hang in there to get the most of this game.

I've only spent about, I think less than an hour at this game. Now, you may think that "Pffft- don't go judge the game yet without even spending a couple of hours playing it," BUT, let me tell you this: If the player doesn't kill you, the lag kills you.
Here's the thing. I like the game! Just from the tutorial itself and I had already gotten myself enjoyed it! The graphics? It's like you're playing with Crossfire (fellow asian players will understand) with COD4 graphics. Other players will of course, won't quite like it. But for me, I do like it. I'll let the other reviews point out the rest of the game since the message that I'm trying to get across here is this: If you live in any part in Asia, your ping will go above the roof!
The game right now, has only three available servers: North America, South America and Europe. Unforunate players, like me, will have no choice but to play in one of those three servers. I tried out playing my first game in NA and my ping is over 300! Sure, it may not sound like much to some, but whatever I do while I play, there will always be a SIGNIFICANT delay! The "teleportation lag" is real here. At one point, I was trying to walk towards the stairs and the next thing I knew, I was UNDERNEATH of it! And this 'teleportation lag" happens every 5 or 7 seconds! Reloading is a hassle! When you press 'R', it will take at least 5 seconds before the actual reload starts! Heck, I can't even swith loadouts in-game! I keep pressing 'F3' so I can equip my sniper, and as soon as I respawn, I still have my SMG! Believe it or not, I actually am stuck to using the same gun every game, with no hope of switching in-game! WTF!
And you know the worst part here? I'm not alone. I checked out the leaderboard, and the ping of other players are so high, ranging from 280 to as high as 900! ALL OF THEM! I'm not kidding. Apparently, my fellow Asians wanted to play in the NA, so if you're American slash Canadian and want to try out this game, prepare to get overwhelmed with laggy players.
"Well then, switch to other servers! What about in South America and Europe?"
Sure! If I wanted to suffer the same lag with no difference, then sure! :D
/sarcasm
Point is, the game is good. I like it, and it's really easy for anyone to get hooked into playing it, but the only thing that sets them back from truly enjoying the game is the latency lag. I will keep the game installed in hopes that the developers will add dedicated Asian servers (maybe even more), but for now, this game is a good "NO".

Ok first of all, if you are still thinking about wither to buy this game or not, just buy it. The game is simply amazing and worth every cent spent on it.
To be clear, this is my first souls game and I enjoyed it thoroughly. The concept is amazing. Having to study an enemy and dieing to him several times just to learn his patterns, combos and tendencies is something we gamers don't do in a game very often. The feeling of finally defeating an enemy after god knows how many times you died to is simply a very satisfying one(I'm looking at you abyss watchers, nameless king and sould of cinder). The lack of music in areas puts you in edge and when the music rolls on during a boss fight is just art. Heads up though, you will be jump scared in a few areas to your surprise.
My only complain would be the new journey system. The game simply gets harder with no actual rewards. The bosses simply hit harder and have higher HP and they don't exactly get a new move or anything. Which is a dissappointment. Don't get me wrong though, it becomes very unforgiving and punishes even harder for your mistakes. It would have been nice to see levelling up not become pointless after a certain level of each aspect (usually 40-50) and even nicer if there was loot specific to the new journies afetr you beat the game except for rings.
I will always recommend this game and it's worth your money. However if you don't have the patience to learn from you mistakes and remeber patterns etc. walk away form this game.

XCOM® 2 is now my favorite strategy game of all time!
First lets talk short about the story:
It's been 20 years since the aliens took control over earth, and you are the only hope to stop them.
You are the commander on a mothership that fights against the aliens in secret. I like to think of it as the "Resistance".
The aliens is working on a AVATAR Project and your mission is to stop them before they finish their project.
You have to use strategy outside combat and also in combat. This is something I love, cause It kinda reminds me of the Total War series.
What I like:
-The Graphics are kinda the same as the first one if you ask me, but they have re-made the weapons, armors, aliens and your soldiers so this is a massive plus to the game. Anyways the Graphics is great.
-The strategy in combat is amazing! You can feel the adrenaline when you're concealed and you make a huge overwatch attack on the aliens when they have no idea you're there. And you can feel the stress when you have to escort the VIP to the extract zone when there's only 3 turns left. Plus, the feeling of finishing a mission with only one soldier left is really a relief. You get so excited in combat and that is something I love!
-The strategy outside combat is something I also enjoy. You'll have to choose what to research, what your next Shadow Project is, what are you gonna build in the mothership to help you on your mission, and where to go around the world and what your next move is. You are the commander. You control everything.
-I also love the animations in this game. When your jumping out of the small aircraft at the beginning of every mission and you see your squad of soldiers jumping and grabbing a rope and lands safely on the ground, pulls out their weapons and getting in position is so cool! when you fire your weapons, when you do melee attacks, how the aliens move and their taunts. The animations are really doing a huge impact in the game, you can "feel" their powers and strength and that gets you even more excited.
-Perma-Death. When a soldier dies, he's dead forever. This is something I find great cause it brings some realism to the game.
What I don't like:
-This game have some glitches. Sometimes it takes some time after a turn to see what happends, it can "freeze" for a few seconds. Also sometimes the camera gets locked so you can't see what the aliens are doing after your turn. But theese glitches are small, so I don't mind them at all.
-There's a new mission you HAVE to do once you get it. You don't have much time in the mothership because there is something happening all over the world, all the time. so your researches takes a long time. Some missions can you skip but approximate 90% of the time you can't skip at all.
Final Words from me:
XCOM® 2 is really an AMAZING GAME!
It takes strategy, dedication and skills to complete this game! I have not finished it yet but this is allready my favorite strategy game of all time! it is a few glitches and bugs, but it's still worth playing through! This game is really worth what it costs!
My personal score: 9.5/10

Despite its pretensions, this is by-the-numbers dungeon crawling wrapped in a typical upgrades grind. In theory, I like the way stress acts as a persistent form of damage across runs, but it doesn't amount to anything. Somebody's numbers get too high, and then something bad happens, and then you pay gold to make it go away. It's just another HP bar to manage. Also in theory, the fact that it forces you to swap out party members should make things more dynamic, but it doesn't. While the classes do have different abilities, the only thing that actually matters is damage output. There's no point in buffing and defending when you can just kill things before they can hurt you. Crucially, the game doesn't get interesting when it gets hard; it just gets annoying. Non-damage-dealing abilites aren't effective enough to allow you to manage stronger opponents, so there's ultimately no real gameplay outside of the grind. Which, ironically, completely kills the horror effect, because you're never really at risk of losing anything. It's all one big grind, it'll just take more or less time to finish depending on how lucky you are. This is why grafting an upgrades system onto a roguelike fundamentally doesn't work. Meanwhile, the story is generic pop-Lovecraft (pro tip: Lovecraft sucks, get over it), and whoever wrote the narration needs to have their thesaurus privileges revoked.
The graphics are good, though.

I'm a bit dissapointed with XCOM2 so far, have to say.
I come to XCOM having played Laser Sqad in the 80's, then the Original UFO, then XCOM. XCOM and Enemy Within sacrifice a *lot* of the micromanagement for a more accessible and fantastically entertaining turn-based game. Still a long way from perfect, but I have maybe a couple of hundred hours in XCOM / EW - one of my top 3 games ever.
XCOM2 has a lot going for it. It is MUCH harder (thankfully). New (and the welcome return of old) aliens, great maps, the rebel mechanic seems interesting and the ambush idea is probably superb. I say probably because almost every mission has a turn limit - which seems a wierd juxtaposition to 'take your time and be sneaky sneaky' new tools. How can I set up a great ambush, reach the objective on the other side of the map and get back to the exit in 8 turns? It makes no sense at all and is very frustrating. I can't develop a play style and learn the nuances of a squad whene everything is done on a sprint. I've had one map so far (a Blacksite) which wasn't time-based and it was superb - but only one. And now I have the avatar project counting up on the geoscape, so I don't feel I can explore the world either.
I realise that modern gaming is all about instant gratification and I'm an ancient 40 year old who likes 'the good old days' - but honestly XCOM was superb in being almost alone in bringing a more thoughtful pace of play and probably thanks to that we have rising popularity of the more faithful UFO clones out there, which I'll be getting into more. We wrinklies have disposable income as well - it's not all wasted on providing games for our grunting, twitching, sleep and daylight deprived offspring :o) I just wish there was a game with the visual appeal, AI, enemies and interface of XCOM2 with at least the depth and freedom of XCOM/EW.
Would be great if there was a third thumb on the rating system - not recommending sounds harsh (if you like being under endless overly-contrived countdowns and want maps as quick as a round of CS:GO, this is the game for you), but I can't really recommend it either - can we get a 'meh' thumb? :o)

Not only did Bethesda create the worst canonical Fallout to date with this entry, they also showed us they will try to squeeze every bit of money out of us for nearly nothing. This review has two short parts. The nickel and diming of Bethesda and the horrible development of Bethesda Softworks.
If you buy this game because you love Fallout, go for it, but I say buy it on sale and I mean like 10-15 dollars sale. If you want the DLC buy the Season Pass on sale for like 5 or 10. The Season Pass was originally 30 USD but was raised to 50 USD for all the content that would be included. That content was mostly random items you can place in your settlement, horrible sidequests that last under 4 hours if you can even bear it that long. Now, they're trying to get people to pay for mods that are free on the Nexus.  Boy, I can't wait for all the mods to be paid content when they were previously free with the optional donation to the creator.
Fallout 4 misses the mark on many levels. While every entry to a series that has so much information will eventually mess up its own lore, Fallout 4 doesn't even care and neither did Pete Hines when asked about it. The jarring tweet about the ghoul in the fridge putting "fun" over lore consistency was a middle finger from Bethesda to you. The jet being spawn in Vaults as a loot table oversight is one thing, outright saying it was Pre-War is another. It wasn't even necessary. Todd Howard also likes to talk about character freedom but we get locked out of so many things. In Fallout 4 you can't kill anyone you'd like. Essential NPCs litter the game. You can't even make your own dialogue choices with the voiced protagonist. You get 4 options at all points and they usually loop back into the original options again.
When it comes to talking to people you get options like: 1. Be nice 2. Just talk 3. No 4. Be horrible at trying to be sarcastic.
When you are asked to do a quest you get the options of: 1. Yes 2. I want more money for it 3. No (but I really mean SURE WHY NOT) 4. I'll be back later
The game isn't Fallout. There is no decision making outside of a few quests and the main quest. There are no skills just perks that act as skills and perks. There's too much backstory on the character. There's no character development to get involved into the characters they want you to be emotionally invested with. It's fun for a while, but it's really superficial. If you want Roleplaying Game where you sink hours, look elsewhere.

I bought it as kind of an experiment, because I've seen a friend of mine playing it a lot and I was somewhat interested how can it be that my friendlist constantly shows Darkest Dungeon under his name - I did't see a screenshot of the game before buying it.
Glad to report, I regret nothing. Darkest Dungeon is a point and click dungoneer rougelike, where you are controlling a wide variety of heroes (4 at a time) with the rest of them living in the ruined town above the dungeons. Each exploration attempt in the 4 differently themed dungeon (seamonster caves, bandit road leading to town, ruins, and the darkest dungeon) you'll recieve loot that you can use to rebuild the town, restore it's buildings that provide your heroes equipment, relaxation, new heroes, cure and training, with each upgrade opening up a better option or making them cheaper. The combat and exploration is turn based with the latter being "real time", and the distance you make equals to turns per specific sections.
The cartoony looks is really working, the audio effects are nothing special but do their job well calling the deathly atmosphere to life. The strongest and most essential part here is the Narrator, the only human voice you'll hear in the game aside from the accusations of that damn depressing risen who hides his mouth. The Narrator has an interesting speach pattern, not shakespeare english but similarly "higher" poetic, really being the icing on the gothic cake. So the atmosphere is a perfect hit, but how's the gameplay?
At first, you are going down to all the various exploration trips out of curiosity and wanting to see everything, but once the 4 (really 3, because the darkest dungeon is far, far endgame content) different enviroments become familiar and you spent all the at first seemingly plenty resources, sooner than later you'll face that for your next desired upgrade you have to clear 3-4 dungeon runs. I understand that some kind of scaling is necessary to keep the game the longtime fun it is intended to be, but the scaling is way too harsh. I consider myself lucky I upgraded my town in a way I did because after a point the dungeons won't offer low level exploration trips anymore, and make no mistake, you WILL die in this game, you WILL see your favourite heroes die a horrible death in combat, fall to madness, have a heart attack, and the endless resupply of newcoming adventurers to the town can leave you with amateurs who have to face that they don't have low level challange to beat anymore, happy that did not happen to me... yet. Also the game works towards almost entirely unavoidable failure of your heroes though the stress mechanics that cause a wide variety of mental illness / personal flaws such as addictions, selfishness, mazohism and these lead to uncontrollable actions that futher stress the entire party, so you have to put away your "sick" hero and throw in a lot money on his/her cure, which means somebody has to take the place in the meantime, so you'll have 2-3 full set of heroes varied all the time. More countermechanisms to pressure would have been nice, and could have been done without making it "comfortable" for the user, but having 17-25 stress points added to all 4 heroes per turn vs some enemies when you can "heal" those in the dungeon IF you are lucky on top of IF you are landing a critical hit / multikill with one move to heal 3-7 points on one or two heroes is ridicolously unfair.
One thing that I think is just a minor thing on the end user side but a major flaw from the development side, is having so little visual custimization options for your heroes. You can choose from 4 premade color patterns and rename them, but that's all. Having the option to choose from 3-4 different armors, maybe hairstyles, or just the actually visible clothes / armor upgrades at the blacksmith change the looks on the hero too not only on the armor in the inventory, would have a HUGE boost on being connected to your favourite heroes and caring for them, making their fall all the more painful (which the game intends to do so, just could do better. After a point I see them as easily replacable throwaway tools, a bunch of statistics that help me along, that's it).
I really focused on the negatives here, but that is only because the game otherwise is so good, I love it so much that I cannot help but want to make it even better. Among all my recent purchases this year, this was definitly the most worth it.

UPDATE/EDITED VERSION AT THE BOTTOM !!
At first I was very hesitant to buy this game due to the following 4 reasons:
1 - I was not sure if my Geforce GT 740m could run this.
2 - I read about the terrifying mission timers.
3 - I read about the performance issues and glitches.
4 - I read about the terrifying Avatar Project.
Well, I took the leap of faith and bought it, thinking I could refund it if any of my nightmares become true. This however - was not the case. Let me explain what happend to m above-mentioned points:
1 - My laptop can run this game 100%, even given the fact that my graphics card is a bit below the recommended specs. Albeit I play on all the minimum settings, honostly the graphics are really still amazing and more that satisfying to look at. It may be a bit personal opinion as I play a game more for the gameplay (which is soooo so so good), rather than the graphics, but even so...I am really impressed with how great this game still looks even on lowest settings.
2 - The mission timers, in one word, they are awesome !! I read a lot of people complain, saying it takes tactics aways, makes you stress, ensures you can't play the game like you normally would etc etc, and although I was also not keen on mission timers as I also like to not feel rushed, take my time with overwatching enemies and so forth, mission timers are a great addition. It creates a sense of urgency, while making you stress yes, but in a good..and fun way. It most certainly does not take away tactics, and if you feel it does, it replaces it with other tactics. When your country/earth gets invaded, you have to play by their rules, and these timers mould into this theme brilliantly. I mean for example...if they want to execute someone, they are going to execute them..and it's up to you to save the person if you have what it takes. If not, they won that mini battle, but you can retaliate in other ways. So again - do not be afraid of the negative reviews saying mission timers spoil the game, they don't, and if you truely feel they do, there's mods to extend the timers or completely remove them.
3 - Performance issues...well honestly, there is a few, but NOTHING game breaking at all. Yes sometimes you wait 10sec for enemies to make their move, or sometimes you struggle for a bit to see the middle floor of a building, but this, for me at least, does not take anything away from the other 99% of bugfree amazing gameplay. Performance issues and fps drops, I have not encountered them, even on my sub par setup. In my 11hours I've had 1 time where my fps dropped noticebly for 2sec, that is ALL. In al honesty, I can live with that if I get a great game like this in return.
4 - Ahhhh the Avatar Project aka the doomsday tracker. Again..same as my second point, there is ways to stall this "timer". Honostly if you make sure you expand early on and play very slowly and carefully, I can't see why this will ever be an issue....and if you REALLY don't want this tracker..again, there is a mod for that.
Summary:
All in all an excellent game, the base building is awesome, the combat is awesome, everything is great and I could not see a reason not to buy this game other that if you are not into these type of games. On that note though, I was also not into these games, not at all. I used to cringe at the sight of turn-based games, then decided to give the demo a try when XCOM Enemy Unknown released on PS3 back in 2012...well, look where I am now - praising it's sequal. I think that says enough, whether it is to buy this game or simply try out a new genre...I can promise you it is worth it !!
8/10
UPDATE (12 August 2016):

Despite its pretensions, this is by-the-numbers dungeon crawling wrapped in a typical upgrades grind. In theory, I like the way stress acts as a persistent form of damage across runs, but it doesn't amount to anything. Somebody's numbers get too high, and then something bad happens, and then you pay gold to make it go away. It's just another HP bar to manage. Also in theory, the fact that it forces you to swap out party members should make things more dynamic, but it doesn't. While the classes do have different abilities, the only thing that actually matters is damage output. There's no point in buffing and defending when you can just kill things before they can hurt you. Crucially, the game doesn't get interesting when it gets hard; it just gets annoying. Non-damage-dealing abilites aren't effective enough to allow you to manage stronger opponents, so there's ultimately no real gameplay outside of the grind. Which, ironically, completely kills the horror effect, because you're never really at risk of losing anything. It's all one big grind, it'll just take more or less time to finish depending on how lucky you are. This is why grafting an upgrades system onto a roguelike fundamentally doesn't work. Meanwhile, the story is generic pop-Lovecraft (pro tip: Lovecraft sucks, get over it), and whoever wrote the narration needs to have their thesaurus privileges revoked.

Even though I am an older player when the game first ever came out, years ago, I'm going to bias this review upon it's current state, rather than babbling on what was better etc.
Pros:
~Entire game from start to finish is not blocked by a pay wall and is free, for those who actually can work for their gear, it's actually quite easy.
~For a java based game, the graphics are heavy and nice when maxed out, and there are even 16X AA options along with cull transients and effect rendering for faster CPUs.
~The combat system is very balanced and easy to pick up while also familiar to that of older retro games with the convenience of online play, with all of your friends.
~Battle sprite pets make great companions to the game, and there are 3 different types to choose from, with the option to have as many as you want, building their skills as you go up in the game.
~Vanity in this game is as refined as TF2's costume system, heavily impacting the market, and with the great art designers, I would say the costumes and accessories and possibilities of vanity in the game are awfully full of variety, and more so for end-gamers with more crowns to spare, and the designs on their own look very well worked and taken into consideration by the game's lead art designer.
~The game can offer optional challenging difficulties and has a variety of monsters to fight, as well as Danger rooms found randomly in arcade runs, and Danger missions which tend to strain player skills with high density monster battles and emphasis on either status resist and defense, or dragging a player's dodging skills and giving large consequences should they make any mistakes, in say a low defense set like the chaos set. Many ways to play yet simplistic.
~Game community is very good and still better compared to other MMO's I have personally seen, and guilds and their halls are greatly refined to freshen up the experience for many players, and coax guilds to work together to build their halls to great lengths and maintaining upkeep, and working towards boss statues later on as they grow.
Cons:
~Player controlled economy maintains the idea that more or less than half the player base will pay real money for the in game commodity, Crystal Energy, and will push it into the market for free to play players to buy with their earned crowns, now the problem in this is, that, the company, Three Rings entertainment, doesn't directly control the market and instead uses risky marketing methods, such as flash sales, promotions, prize boxes, and auction house featured flagship items and accessories and more, in hopes that players will buy more Crystal energy to obtain such things, which I think is not a bad marketing technique, but that would technically mean the game isn't entire Free for the whole player base, whether they spend or not, so in order to have energy, someone, somewhere in this game has to spent money and put it up on the market, so that the free player may obtain the same resource for free without real life money and instead in game goods. I call it a con because the economy is unstable and needs to be deflated at times, but as long as Three Rings can keep the market from inflating too much, I suppose this isn't such a big matter, but as I say with thus being said, this game isn't free for everyone.
~Players who prefer to be solo in the game may not get such a refined experience and may not play this game much considering the game itself doesn't offer too much for single player features, and reasons to stay in the game, some MMO's can be done entirely single, but the level design is too simplistic just for one player to analyze and enjoy long term, as there are certain limitations in place.
~Updates are quite slow due to the small development team, and there isn't really a whole lot of content for end gamers to enjoy, thus making the community solely keep some players from quitting because of the theoretical experience of playing with others making it more enjoyable.
Final Verdict:
~Play this game, see how you like it, it has a great lore that keeps theories coming almost like FnaF (though not as much lol) there are guilds, and still quite a bit of good mannered players and potential friends to make here, and the combat system while only having 3 types of technical weapon classes and sprite types, yet the large arsenal available allows anyone to create their own style of playing, silly or serious, or just something to do the job.

I bought it as kind of an experiment, because I've seen a friend of mine playing it a lot and I was somewhat interested how can it be that my friendlist constantly shows Darkest Dungeon under his name - I did't see a screenshot of the game before buying it.
Glad to report, I regret nothing. Darkest Dungeon is a point and click dungoneer rougelike, where you are controlling a wide variety of heroes (4 at a time) with the rest of them living in the ruined town above the dungeons. Each exploration attempt in the 4 differently themed dungeon (seamonster caves, bandit road leading to town, ruins, and the darkest dungeon) you'll recieve loot that you can use to rebuild the town, restore it's buildings that provide your heroes equipment, relaxation, new heroes, cure and training, with each upgrade opening up a better option or making them cheaper. The combat and exploration is turn based with the latter being "real time", and the distance you make equals to turns per specific sections.
The cartoony looks is really working, the audio effects are nothing special but do their job well calling the deathly atmosphere to life. The strongest and most essential part here is the Narrator, the only human voice you'll hear in the game aside from the accusations of that damn depressing risen who hides his mouth. The Narrator has an interesting speach pattern, not shakespeare english but similarly "higher" poetic, really being the icing on the gothic cake. So the atmosphere is a perfect hit, but how's the gameplay?
At first, you are going down to all the various exploration trips out of curiosity and wanting to see everything, but once the 4 (really 3, because the darkest dungeon is far, far endgame content) different enviroments become familiar and you spent all the at first seemingly plenty resources, sooner than later you'll face that for your next desired upgrade you have to clear 3-4 dungeon runs. I understand that some kind of scaling is necessary to keep the game the longtime fun it is intended to be, but the scaling is way too harsh. I consider myself lucky I upgraded my town in a way I did because after a point the dungeons won't offer low level exploration trips anymore, and make no mistake, you WILL die in this game, you WILL see your favourite heroes die a horrible death in combat, fall to madness, have a heart attack, and the endless resupply of newcoming adventurers to the town can leave you with amateurs who have to face that they don't have low level challange to beat anymore, happy that did not happen to me... yet. Also the game works towards almost entirely unavoidable failure of your heroes though the stress mechanics that cause a wide variety of mental illness / personal flaws such as addictions, selfishness, mazohism and these lead to uncontrollable actions that futher stress the entire party, so you have to put away your "sick" hero and throw in a lot money on his/her cure, which means somebody has to take the place in the meantime, so you'll have 2-3 full set of heroes varied all the time. More countermechanisms to pressure would have been nice, and could have been done without making it "comfortable" for the user, but having 17-25 stress points added to all 4 heroes per turn vs some enemies when you can "heal" those in the dungeon IF you are lucky on top of IF you are landing a critical hit / multikill with one move to heal 3-7 points on one or two heroes is ridicolously unfair.
One thing that I think is just a minor thing on the end user side but a major flaw from the development side, is having so little visual custimization options for your heroes. You can choose from 4 premade color patterns and rename them, but that's all. Having the option to choose from 3-4 different armors, maybe hairstyles, or just the actually visible clothes / armor upgrades at the blacksmith change the looks on the hero too not only on the armor in the inventory, would have a HUGE boost on being connected to your favourite heroes and caring for them, making their fall all the more painful (which the game intends to do so, just could do better. After a point I see them as easily replacable throwaway tools, a bunch of statistics that help me along, that's it).
I really focused on the negatives here, but that is only because the game otherwise is so good, I love it so much that I cannot help but want to make it even better. Among all my recent purchases this year, this was definitly the most worth it.

Though, my time on this game is pretty short on Steam, I played this as a standalone client for a long time, so I have a ton of time not logged on Steam. Having said that, here's a semi-involved review on the game.
Pros:
- Customization: You can customize your character to look however you want, able to wear any armor, weapon, shield, costume, etc. You can also choose your main color and it's able to be changed (for a price). Your role isn't defined by choosing a role, but rather by the weapons and armor you choose. You can be a sword/bomber hybrid, a pure gunner, or whatever combination (or not) that you want. The interface makes it easy to change between all of these things so you can prep for any mission with relative ease. You can also choose your own kind of pet with its own unique abilities. Choose Charmander, always!
- Involved Storyline: One great thing about this game is that it sticks to its storyline and there is a lot of background behind the clockworks. Unfortunately, this is mostly displayed through the course of the storyline missions. Outside of the main missions, there isn't much lore going on.
- Guilds + Guild Customization: Unlike other games, you can actually purchase a building for your guild and it's able to be customized pretty highly. You may use materials to make statues, decorate it for your favorite holiday, have your own office, dorm rooms, or whatever you'd like. The more you build, the more it costs, but it's a nice touch.
- Changing dungeons: The clockworks changes based on real-time. Every time you go in, you'll be in a different generated room/floor/type than before. It's great for not feeling like you can only run through the same floor all the time.
- Seasonal Events: Every so often, there will be a seasonal event going on for holidays and you can score some pretty cool costumes, gear, or items. There are holiday missions and clockwork dives that you can do to earn them and celebrate with others in the game or in your guild hall! (also see cons below)
- PvP / Side-Games / Side Missions: The pvp in this game is pretty great, actually. You'll be in a team and each map will have different objectives for how to gain points. Mostly capturing a spot and then for how many kills / deaths are on your team. Between Sword fighting, gun shooting, and bomb placing you'll always be kept on your feet and the matches are long enough to be fun and engaging, while also being short enough to allow for many matches and much playability. The "bomberman" game that is in here also provides a fun distraction from the daily grind. It's not as popular as the fighting pvp, so it takes longer to get in game, but it's pretty fun and has rewards for accruing points. Crimson Hammer is an expansion for another great mission, as well as Shadow Dungeons. Try them all!
Cons:
- Endgame: There is not much to do at endgame, other than just keep grinding for the gear that you want to have. There are daily missions that change with every day, but after a week's change, they are the same every week. Once you finish off the storyline missions, all that's left is to either run the clockworks themselves or replay the missions. While they do offer tokens to trade in for gear, it becomes really grindy.  Even with shadow dungeons, which provide an extra challenge, there are only 4 shadow dungeons and shadow keys are NOT cheap, but that's about what you have to look forward to.
- Seasonal Events (Pt. 2): These should change it up a bit, right? Wrong. The seasonal events are the same every year and rewards haven't changed much. The devs keep saying that content will be added, but there isn't much going on. While it may be great and fun the first time you experience all of them, you'll be disappointed to find that the next year won't change much at all and new rewards will either not be worth your time or not added at all.
- Looting: This may not seem like a big issue, but what used to be awesome about this game was that while running with a party, you wouldn't have to pick up every bit of loot. If a monster died, anyone could pick up the loot and it would be shared amongst everyone, so if you wanted to divide the map amongst players to clear the room more quickly, they could pick up their loot in their section and you could pick up yours and it would still count for everyone. As changes came along, OOO made it so everyone has to pick up their own loot now. A friend and I used to duo run the last mission boss and divide up the floors, so now it's a big time waster if you want all of the loot. You have to run to all of the areas where enemies were killed and pick it up yourself. I'm not sure why this feature was prompted, but it was a terrible change.
- Reviving mechanics are terrible: Again, this is a change that was implemented at some point, but what used to happen was that when a party member died, you could run to them and give them half your life to revive them, so it really encouraged teamwork and coordination to keep each other alive. If you were running solo, you could spent your energy(which was removed from the game) to revive yourself. What it changed to now is that you have to find items called "Spark of Life." These items revive either you or a party member, but TRUST ME when I say that these don't drop very often at all. That means, if you used up all your sparks, you have to forfeit running the dungeon. You'll be forced to grind the clockworks to find more sparks of life just so you can have them handy in case. It may not sound too bad, but when you are having trouble finding more than just a few sparks, it'll become irritating.
All in all, it's a pretty great game while you are still ranking up, but like I said, once you hit endgame, it's kind of a bore. I hope you can like the game for the most part though. It did provide a lot of good friends for me and a lot of really good times.

I'm a bit dissapointed with XCOM2 so far, have to say.
I come to XCOM having played Laser Sqad in the 80's, then the Original UFO, then XCOM. XCOM and Enemy Within sacrifice a *lot* of the micromanagement for a more accessible and fantastically entertaining turn-based game. Still a long way from perfect, but I have maybe a couple of hundred hours in XCOM / EW - one of my top 3 games ever.
XCOM2 has a lot going for it. It is MUCH harder (thankfully). New (and the welcome return of old) aliens, great maps, the rebel mechanic seems interesting and the ambush idea is probably superb. I say probably because almost every mission has a turn limit - which seems a wierd juxtaposition to 'take your time and be sneaky sneaky' new tools. How can I set up a great ambush, reach the objective on the other side of the map and get back to the exit in 8 turns? It makes no sense at all and is very frustrating. I can't develop a play style and learn the nuances of a squad whene everything is done on a sprint. I've had one map so far (a Blacksite) which wasn't time-based and it was superb - but only one. And now I have the avatar project counting up on the geoscape, so I don't feel I can explore the world either.
I realise that modern gaming is all about instant gratification and I'm an ancient 40 year old who likes 'the good old days' - but honestly XCOM was superb in being almost alone in bringing a more thoughtful pace of play and probably thanks to that we have rising popularity of the more faithful UFO clones out there, which I'll be getting into more. We wrinklies have disposable income as well - it's not all wasted on providing games for our grunting, twitching, sleep and daylight deprived offspring :o) I just wish there was a game with the visual appeal, AI, enemies and interface of XCOM2 with at least the depth and freedom of XCOM/EW.
Would be great if there was a third thumb on the rating system - not recommending sounds harsh (if you like being under endless overly-contrived countdowns and want maps as quick as a round of CS:GO, this is the game for you), but I can't really recommend it either - can we get a 'meh' thumb? :o)

After rescuing him from the alien, the Lovecraftian deity falls madly in love with Mahiro and forces herself into his household, much to his chagrin. And oh my goodness, so many things to collect if you're into that.
I will note, though, that while I have been playing quite a lot, it's not as much as Steam thinks; Trove has a launcher, Glyph, that I just leave open. Still--I leave that open because I might want to jump in at any point through the day. Once you get a few mastery levels under your belt, hourly challenges open up, and they're delicious.
This is everything I ever wanted in a multiplayer voxel game. And it's just a fine game on its own right.

Despite its pretensions, this is by-the-numbers dungeon crawling wrapped in a typical upgrades grind. In theory, I like the way stress acts as a persistent form of damage across runs, but it doesn't amount to anything. Somebody's numbers get too high, and then something bad happens, and then you pay gold to make it go away. It's just another HP bar to manage. Also in theory, the fact that it forces you to swap out party members should make things more dynamic, but it doesn't. While the classes do have different abilities, the only thing that actually matters is damage output. There's no point in buffing and defending when you can just kill things before they can hurt you. Crucially, the game doesn't get interesting when it gets hard; it just gets annoying. Non-damage-dealing abilites aren't effective enough to allow you to manage stronger opponents, so there's ultimately no real gameplay outside of the grind. Which, ironically, completely kills the horror effect, because you're never really at risk of losing anything. It's all one big grind, it'll just take more or less time to finish depending on how lucky you are. This is why grafting an upgrades system onto a roguelike fundamentally doesn't work. Meanwhile, the story is generic pop-Lovecraft (pro tip: Lovecraft sucks, get over it), and whoever wrote the narration needs to have their thesaurus privileges revoked.
The graphics are good, though.

XCOM 2 is a continuation of successful 2012 XCOM enemy unknown and should be treated with caution. Buyer beware, any player who doesn't have the stomach to deal with RNG should stay clear of this game or risk losing your monitor or keyboard through sheer frustration.
Pro
- Better graphic compared to EU.
- More mods with easier modding, you can find modders adding or deleting parts they don't like already.
- More soldier customization.
- Weapon customization. Adding rare parts to your weapon and rocking it is extremely satisfying.
- Better stroryline compared EU. The characters are more fleshed out than their 2012 counterparts.
- Concealment system allowed your first engagement to be planned ambushed.
- Procedurally generated maps.
- Radically different theme from EU. You are now a rebel, not a govenment force.
Con
- Severe performance problems for many players (I had occasional stutter throughout the game and failure to load texture during the last mission).
- Some gameplay from EU went missing ; interceptor play, advanced armor like archangle armor, gene mod and MEC unit from EW, Advanced Muton.
- Rather strict base building order which inherited from EU.
- Armor customization for high-tier armor is extremely limited (they just change the pattern on the armor) and mass effect-ish compared to low-tier armor which offer quite a variety.
Controversy about 'timer' gameplay design.
IMO, most missions can be finished within 8-12 turns and concealment system has a positive effect on speeding up the first engagement. If the players don't dawdle and try to use overwatch turtle tactic from EU with every move then most missions should be doable within time limit. However, procedurally generated map can sometimes create an almost impossible mission which can be painful.
Do I recommend the game? Yes, after Firaxis patch it.

XCOM 2 takes the basic concepts and ideas of XCOM Enemy Unknown and builds upon them to create a newer, fresher take on the events of the first game. There are a lot of mechanical fixes and gameplay changes, but the core of the game remains the same: build up a team of badass soldiers, lead them into glorious battle, then gasp in horror as your mans get killed horribly by alien monsters.
On the other hand, the game is horribly optimized, suffers from a bunch of stuttering problems, and at one point somehow messed up my save files so that I couldn't load any of my save games that took place during the final mission, The new vision and line-of-sight indicators help mitigate some of the problems of the isometric perspective, but it isn't quite enough, and I had one early mission nearly go awry because I couldn't tell where my Specialist could stand to get line of sight on a laptop computer I needed to hack.
There have been a lot of complaints over the timed missions: I personally don't mind too much. The turn limits add tension, but don't particularly feel unfair: of course, I haven't yet tried my Commander Ironman run, so that might change in the future.
Finally, the game's story really does expect that you've played the Tutorial level: otherwise, the explanation for how your main character ended up where they are is kind of glossed over. The replacement first mission if you choose not to redo the Tutorial feels a bit disjointed from the story in consequence: I would have much preferred to replay that Tutorial level, except with a full squad of random soldiers, some more enemies, and without the hand-holding prompts.
TIPS: Forego Guerilla Tactics in favor of Advanced Warfare: the improved healing rate is a godsend, and the chance that your soldiers will get bonus perks as they level up is too good to pass up. For Sharpshooters, tend towards Gunslinger over Sniper: those aforementioned Timed Missions mean that you really need your squad to be as mobile as possible. For Specialists, Combat Hackers over Medics: Given a choice between shutting down or even taking over an enemy mecha (which can keep an entire squad alive) or healing up hit points from one or two soldiers in your squad, I'd rather take the former. I have no strong opinions on Rangers or Grenadiers.

Get this game if you:
- like to imagine storys and background to characters.
The game is full of atmosphere but very little story. When you camp and your vestal uses the skill "sanctuary" and says something like "may this circle of light protect us in the night" and everybody's stress level goes down, I can just imagine a whole ceremony with candles, incense, praying and listening to the priest's incantation. Suddenly a glimmer of light surrounds the camp and everybody feels the weight of worry lifted off of their shoulders...
That's the kind of thing that should happen in your mind. If you're not the person for that, you partly miss out on the experience.
- like to fiddle around with stats and skills
Just picking characters you like and stroll into a dungeon isn't going to take you far. You should have fun optimizing your party, finding the most synergistic composition, modifying stats with items to improve your strategy and take into account every little advantage and disadvantage. You don't need to crunch numbers though.
- like turn-based combat (pretty obvious this one)
- can accept risk and failure as a part of the experience
That's a thing many people don't like about this game. They are perfectionist and love to find out how to beat the game flawlessly. This is not possible here. Even if you do everything the right way, sometimes RNG can screw your run anyway. You can lower that impact by turning off enemy crits in the options though.
Checked all the points? You will probably have a great experience. I certainly had and still have.

Throughtout all the time I've spent on this game, I can honestly say that it was one of the funnest experiences I ever got from a video game, and an MMO at that. It reminded me of another game that I know called Cube World, which I was legitimately interested in for a LONG time. Having all this in mind, I played the game to it's full potential alongside my sister and a friend: leveled up, slayed hundreds of shadows, built a house, raided dungeons, and even created a Club (basically what a guild is called in Trove) straight from scratch, and made friends along the way as well. On occasion, the game would close down due to the scheduled updates and patches being implemented into the game. Most of them would fix up the game, while others changed the game a bit here and there and gave things more flavor.
However, after spending so much time playing the game consistently and noticing it's only aspect was raiding dungeons, the game grew boring with each passing day from that point onward. Don't get me wrong, the game is great and they are constantly adding new things into the game so it's still growing in my opinion, but this is one of those games where if you spend WAY too much time on, things become bland and the spark just isn't there anymore. As a final verdict, I'll have to say that you should play the game and see how things go for you. Just, you know, play it at a pace that won't cause you to become extremely bored and tired of it; that way, it'll be much more fun when you get on the next time.

There’s nothing I can say that hasn’t already been said about this game. Across Morrowind, Oblivion, Skyrim, FO3/NV and Fallout 4, I’ve put in almost 3000 hours, and for the most part I’ve enjoyed every minute, when the game wasn’t crashing, freezing, or bugging out. To me, had Fallout 4 been released as new IP, with no previous titles, I would have thought it was nothing more than a rip-off of Far Cry 3 and 4, but worse in almost every aspect. Also, I’m not going to be talking about any of the DLCs in this review/rant, or even the lack of RP elements, the quests, or how the game isn’t a Fallout game.
To address the big issue with this game:
. Once again Bethesda is trying to push paid mods for both FO4 and Skyrim, under the “Creation Club”. Until paid mods (or ‘micro transactions’) go away, avoid this game like the plague. Otherwise, TES 6 and FO5 will be even worse than this game.
To be totally fair towards this game, I knew it was going to be terrible before it was even announced. I knew this because I looked at how dumbed down Skyrim was compared to Oblivion, and how much better New Vegas was compared to FO3. It wasn’t hard to work out, and that upsets me honestly.
One of the things that really bugs me with this game is something that very few people address; the gun play.
One of the things that I was excited for during the E3 showcase back in 2015, was the weapon customisation. It looked amazing, being able to turn a pistol into a rifle, make a shotgun into a sniper rifle, I’m sure you get the idea; complete freedom to change up how the gun functions. But when the game came out the weapon customisation was nothing more than a “this part does more damage” system. The weapon customisation was a liner system; you can’t slap on a 4x scope onto a slug firing shotgun, only make the gun to more damage or fire faster. This was a massive let down for me. I was hoping the weapon customisation would be something more in line with Escape from Tarkov. Since Bethesda focused so much on making a 10mm pistol fire faster, they skimped out on adding guns into the game. I mean, why add a 10mm SMG like in FO3, when you can turn your oversized 10mm pistol into a full auto pistol? The game lacks so many weapons from FO3/NV, the Tri-Beam Laser Rifle is one that I deeply miss. Oh, but the normal Laser Rifle has a shotgun barrel! But since shotguns are useless and unrealistic in this game… that can’t hit anything due to their spread…
The combat in FO4 is rather terrible. Many people praise FO4 for having better combat than FO3, which is true, but when compared to games like Far Cry 4, Red Orchestra 2, Call of Duty 1 and 2, or even New Vegas with the Project Nevada mod, you begin to see that the combat is nothing but underpowered guns, with no sense of weight, hitting bullet sponge enemies that barely react to being hit. If you want your gun to fire in full auto, you have to modify the gun, using random metal and tape. You can’t just tap a button and have it firing in full auto, like how you can in real life, or a game with good gun play (i.e. Red Orchestra 2). The Hunting Rifle, (which is a left handed model because reasons) feels like I’m firing a BB gun. No sense of weight or recoil. Most of the recoil the guns have is just an animation, not actual recoil (There’s a mod that removes recoil on the laser rifle, but the recoil animation still plays). There is so many little issues this game has when it comes to the gun play, (many of which people never talk about) that just make the game feel horrible to play.
I’m only going to briefly mention that lack of ammo types. The Hunting Rifle fires .308, .38, and .50. How you’re able to fit a 12.7mm round into a gun that fires .308 is anyone’s guess. But not only is the Hunting Rifle the only (worthwhile) gun that can fire the .50 caliber round, there are no alternative ammo types of it. In New Vegas you had armour piercing, hand loaded, incendiary, and explosive. But in FO4, if you want armour piercing, incendiary, or explosive, you need to find the weapon that has the legendary perk attached with it. Which means you need to luck out and find one of each, and carry each one, if you want to be able to use each type of round. In New Vegas, all you had to do was carry the ammo you wanted, and swap out the ammo you wanted to use.
I haven’t even mentioned the oversized “Assault Rifle”, the lack of a LMG, the left handed AK in Nuka World, how the little PPK fires 10mm and not 9mm or .38, how there is no dedicated sniper rifle, how the Minigun is underpowered and doesn’t let you spin it up before firing like in TF2, how the Submachine gun… is a weird mix between 2 different tommy guns… or how the site on the Submachine gun doesn’t line up…, how the four barrelled Missile Launcher just doesn’t make any sense when you add the stabilizer, how the Combat Rifle fires .45 as standard and not .308, how 10mm and .45 exist in different guns but are more or less the same round, but can’t be interchanged, or how the 10mm can’t be used in the SMG or Combat Rifle, or how .45 can’t be used in the 10mm pistol, how the Fatman is super underpowered against humans… or how the shotguns have more spread than a metaphor about spreading things. At least the energy weapons are alright, for the most part..
EDIT: Completely forgot about how terrible the scopes are. That is nothing more than a black screen with a hole in the middle. If you want to see how sniper scopes should function in games, check out Red Orchestra 2.
EDIT 2: I also forgot how when a gun is convertred to full-auto, it does less damage compared to semi-auto.

I see a lot of displeased users. I didn't play that game for as much as others (yet). Is this game perfect? No, it is not. Is it worth buying and playing? It depends. For me it is.
What is my approach? I use a lot of imagination. And that's what I recommend.
The game is meant to present unequal struggle with terrors from beyond. And almost every element of the game fits this and make this production very immersive. Let's forget for a second it is a game and join expedition into the unknown.
Alongside 3 other adventurers you pass into darkness. You got there for a reason - to purge, to steal or learn. But as the torch slowly dies so does your enthusiasm. You find what you came for. Book, papers and unknown monuments. Sources of knowledge. But it's not meant for eyes of mortal. You no longer want to read them. You want to get rich but anything you try to steal is dangerous for your health. It is not prepared for humans. Then you find evil you swore to purge. But it's not your environment. The fight is not equal. You are stressed, it's dark. And these creatures are superior to you due to some cursed powers.
That way I enjoyed RNG. Instead of frustration I felt fear. Curios? I used to try to open them but now I don't test my luck unless I have already checked something and know it's good. Sometimes however my team check it without my will.
There are however things that I'd love to be different.
- Using abilies outside of battle. - Why not? Not for free ofc, at an expense of light, maybe little stress for a guy using it and risk of encounter.
- Enemies hit hard, make strange effects that last outside of battle and inflict stress. It is unequal fight already. That's why I would consider making them a bit more position dependant. Right now I haven't met enemy who wouldn't be able to get back to the front line dealing damage along the way. Or casters who act distinctively different in the front row. If my arbalest or houndmaster ends up in the first row he is worthless. So does abomination or lepper in the last row. Why not make enemies more position dependant?
- After finishing first level of dungeons the next ones are just the same with higher difficulty. It is quite, hmmm, boring from lack of better word. The worst part is that bosses are the same every time.
- Some minibosses in most of the dungeons would be a nice add-on. DLC maybe? Nothing too fancy, something bigger with distinctive abilities and fair fight.
- Now that I think of it some dynamic goals/problems arising in dungeons would be nice. For instance you find out you are being hunted by creature and if you don't end fights in less then 6 turns it will catch onto you. Or finding a map with some chapel or gold mine that improves your village somehow (faster stress regenaration? extra income?) if you accomplish a challange (defend mine for 3 consequetive battles, prevent desecration by cultist by disrupting them for 3 turns - stun/move/kill one that performs ritual before he finish it). DLC please :)

My opinion on this game is that it is good- to a point. That point being the Veteran level dungeons. The early game is fun, interesting, challenging and good, but by even the mid-game the problems start to show.
First off, your heros become locked away once they are high enough level to go to the next dungeon tier - in others words, you finally got that hero up to max level without one of the many crippling debilitations screwing them over (or paying money to fix them when you can) NOPE! Cant use them now, go to the next elvel of dungeon where they are back to being weak in comparision to the monsters.
Second off, as with everyone else, I have to complain about the RNG. Forget cuthulu, you need to be building your shrines to RNGesus for you to really get anywhere, as basically everything in this game passes by him at LEAST once, if not more. Not that this is a problem in the earlier levels - the game doesn't expect you to be using any of the advanced tactics (which rely on RNG more heavily than just hitting the enemies), so if RNG betrays you a few times while using them, it's not a big deal, you aren't punished (you only aren't rewarded). Any of the later missions though - the game NEEDS you to be using the RNG reliant advanced tactics. This means that, even if you play the more intricate sytle perfectly, should RNG ever betray you, you're suddenly utterly obliterated becuase you apparently didn't know how to use the advanced tactics correctly - never mind if you're in a bad position and have to not spend turns doing things like shuffling openents in order to heal (becuase RNG screwed you over last time).
The game is interesting and fun, and RNG is an important part of it, too, just like many other games. The problem lies in combat that does just involve RNG - it RELIES on RNG, and one failure means that the dungeon run is scrapped, do not continue, hope you didn't get too much stress/diseases/negative-quirks, better luck (litterally) next time, chap. The game can be either one of two things - forgiving of RNG screwing you over, or not letting RNG screw you over completely. Unfortunately, the game si currently a third thing - BAD, unfun, and punishing in the bad way (especially becuase it will punish you for RNG rather than your actions).
Overall, I think that beucase of the games good comcept, ideas, and character, it makes for a good 7-10 hours or so in the quite great early game before you hit the veteran RNG-wall. I think it's a great 10 hours, though, so I recond buying the game but only if you're willing to spend it on only 8-10 hours of pretty good content. If you're looking for a longer life out of you game, look elsewhere. The game is basically a fun evening, but one you leave with a bad taste in your mouth.

Overall I recommend this game, despite some hefty gripes.
Pros:
A fun, strategic game with loads of content.  A huge (even if overcomplicated) meta game with research, upgrades, decisions and resource management.  Customizing your squad members is the best part and really makes you care about losing your soldiers.
Cons:
Some poor, frustrating design choices.  Instead of presenting you with a challenge and forcing you to strategize or adapt, you are often forced to save/reload or start missions over after enemies appear from offscreen or ambush you with no chance to react.  Situations often require you to have prior knowledge of upcoming enemies instead of reacting to them which is lame.
Some smaller cons include enemies with abilities with insane cast range, either offscreen or half the map away.  We also have the same wonky dice rolls where your soldier is point blank with no visible way to miss, but will aim straight up and fire into the sky instead.  Enemies will also shoot through 3 walls and cover to hit you, you'll often find yourself saying "what..." to illogical hits and misses.
Overall its a great game, but not without some strange and frustrating moments.

So I have a decent computer and I have to turn the settings down a bit to run this game. The game sometimes locks for a couple seconds in between turns. However, this is a good game I would still highly recommend it. A lot of the negative reviews are people that were somehow unaware that this is an RNG based game and are frustrated, complain about the timers, or are upset about optimization issues.
Maybe I'm insane, but if a game is a bit buggy at launch, but still works I don't just take to the internet to write a scathing day-one review about how I had to turn AA off. Some people's reviews are understandable to where the game did not launch or something or were met with frequent crashes. I get that. I just hate it when people drop a negetive review because of optimisation problems then never bother to change it and artifically drop the rating. If your game didn't work. that's cool. If you couldn't run it on triple-ultra settings with smell-o-vision turned on, then didn't bother to play the game, then give it a negative review, please just don't leave one until you've played the game. Maybe I'm just a butt-hurt fanboy, but I've noticed how a lot more people seem to place flawless optimization over gameplay, which drives me insane.
People keep complaining about the timers on some missions, but the reviews seem to misrepresent the entire game as having timers on every mission. Optional missions often have timers associated with them, but people often leave out how you can use a drone to remote hack into several objectives and stop the timer. Major missions and many difficult missions do not have a timer assoicated with them. You can also back out of a mission if it gets to hot or you can savescum through most of them pretty easily. The game is meant to be difficult and people talk about the timers as if having a time limit somehow doesn't make it a strategy game.
Also, yes, this is an RNG based game. The computer doesn't always fight fair, your soldiers will die, and bad things will happen. Your choices in research priorities, side missions, and dark events will change the outcome of the game later on for better or for worse. You are fighting an alien threat far more advanced than yourself, thus the difficulty curve is supposed to be high. You don't have hardened space maries, a secret weapon, or super powers. What you have is a stolen space ship, a scientist, an engineer, and some guys with guns. This game is hard, but you can always learn the game by playing on easy and saving frequently. If you don't like things there are already a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of mods that tweak the game to different playstyles.
Anyway, tl;dr:
-This game is hard, so try savescumming and playing on easy to get the hang of it
-There's RNG
-There are timers, but not on all missions and sometimes there are ways to stop them, and retreating is always an option
-There are optimisation problems, but it's playable and at the most inconvient for most people
-There are mods that can tweak the game to your play style
-The game is hard. It's supposed to be hard.
-It's a good game and worth playing.
