Dark Souls 3 is the first game I played in the Souls series, and as a rather casual gamer I was quite hesitant to give it a go at first. So yes, if you've never played any Dark Souls game in the past, the third one is definitely a good start.
- An important thing to note is that the keyboard and mouse support is atrocious. You will have a much better experience playing with a controller.
Visually the game is very impressive, especially from an artistic perspective. I've never played a game quite like this - It has a very dark, brutal and grotesque theme which I felt was very unique, even awe inspiring at times. It was smart of the developers to have such a long view distance as it really makes you appreciate the scenery.
Level and enemy design are top notch. It's evident that a huge amount of effort was put into designing various areas that reward exploring and do not feel repetitive. Enemies are also extremely well made: Their design and models are very detailed and the amount of unique enemies I encountered throughout the game is unlike any other game I've ever played, especially when taking into account that almost each enemy has a unique moveset.
The lore in Dark Souls 3 is mostly hidden in the descriptions of items. What little information you get from NPCs is usually vague and there aren't many lines of actual dialogue, but the ones that you do get to hear were clearly spoken by very talented voice actors. I personally enjoyed the fact that lore wasn't being shoved in my throat as this only added to the mysterious tone of the game.
If you're actually invested in the lore, you will have a better time watching lore videos on YouTube since those will bridge gaps that the game will not.
The version of Dark Souls 3 I played appears to not be very stable on certain Nvidia driver versions. I tried a few versions, including the latest one at the time of writing this review, and the most stable version for me was 384.94.
The game is quite difficult at first, but once you realize that dying is part of the learning process you will start understanding the mechanics and movesets of enemies and it eventually becomes a matter of pressing the dodge button at the right second, which also became my first issue with the game: You cannot play as a tank character. It doesn't matter how many defensive stats you invest in to be able to properly wear heavy armor and still be able to dodge, you WILL get absolutely trashed unless you time your dodges and attacks properly. Alternatively, you can play with greatshields, but those require a huge investment in stats, and will not be viable until the later sections of the game, but they do make certain areas much easier.
My second issue is the camera, or more specifically the FOV. Some locations force you to fight grossly oversized bosses and the only thing that makes those fights needlessly frustrating is the game's narrow field of view. There are mods that will aleviate this issue, but those can potentially trigger an online ban.
Which leads me to the online aspect of the game. Most of the online mechanics are great at their core, especially the messages system that allows people to create messages on the floor that other players are able to read and rate (i.e Bad or Good). Those messages can be extremely useful or completely useless. You cannot write whatever you want - you must compile sentences from an existing pool of words and incomplete sentences, but it was clearly well thought-out since the pool of words to choose from contains everything you need to explain yourself. For example, you can leave messages like "Hidden path ahead", or "Be wary of mob enemy, above".
The other nice aspect is the invasion system that allows users to invade the games of players who are enkindled, which is a status aquired by using an item. Users who are in enkindled mode appear as hosts of embers and gain +30% to their health pool. They are also able to summon other players to help them clear a level and even fight a boss off. The downside is that some players will invade the host's world and try to kill them and their co-op partners.
The PVP aspect starts falling short when you realize how laggy it is. The rubberbanding is constant and some players have extremely high pings that will even make the monsters lag. Fights feel very unresponsive and some hits take more than a second to register.
A good example of this is the
boss fight that summons
to fight you.

Nothing changed in DS3, since the debute of Dark Souls franchise. It's still a grindfest with broken hitboxes, outdated graphics, horrible PC port quality (Developers didn't even give a f. about the control revamp - just let you guess what the X button stands for).
Gameplay mechanics are cursory, more of a dance-roll simulator than a Swordfighting experience. And the enemies themselves? Unresponsible Meatbags that can take dozens of hits without even making a sound, specially the bosses.
I'm not sure why is this called "Hardcore", because all you do is typically grind the boss to reveal all it's attack patterns and moves, then come up with countering measure to beat him. And that's not hardcore, but merely patience-trying.
I've beaten up the first boss and this was an utterly boring battle of kiting and repeating the same moves over and over again until he fell dead. Then I uninstalled and refunded.
And to say it once more, because the practice makes perfect, Graphics and animations are incredibly outdated by multiple orders compared to every other game on the market, instantly crossing out the visual aspect of this handicraft.
I gave Dark Souls whole 3 chances with each game, but it looks like it was just not the right approach. Dark Souls is a niche game for masochists who enjoy dying a lot, because you practically can't defeat a boss without dying (to learn his movelist, of course), which is time consuming and tedious.
Not recommended for purchase.

Dark Souls 3.
--
I am honestly elated that FROM managed another high quality sequel to Dark Souls.
To understand the strengths and weaknesses of this game, it's important to also understand that it's most certainly not
for everyone. Dark Souls is not a franchise you play mindlessly, it's not a power fantasy.
I feel that, to some extent, the "Prepare To Die" motto that the first game adopted has tainted the public image of
the Souls games. Not to say it's an inaccurate statement to make about the franchise, but rather, that it puts
emphasis on DIFFICULTY above all else. Dark Souls, against all public image, is not about difficulty.
--
This is especially the case in Dark Souls 3.
I personally believe that any player that has the motivation to beat Dark Souls 3 is fully capable of doing so.
The emphasis in Dark Souls is in challenge versus reward. Completing an area, finding a new weapon hidden behind some
tough enemies, beating a boss you've had trouble with - they leave you with a sense of pride in your abilities, and the
courage to take on the next challenge Dark Souls 3 provides. Sure, you'll die. Quite a lot, actually.
The mistake made by new players is that they believe dying is equivalent to failure, which is far from the case - hell, it can
be abused to the advantage of the player.
--
The most fair comparison I like to make is to The Elder Scrolls: Skyrim.
Both games provide you with a rich world to explore, loot to find and bosses to kill.
However, Skyrim is a power fantasy. In Skyrim, canonicaly, your character never dies. So, in order to accomodate that,
a quick save system is in place. When you reach certain checkpoints, it will save, when you travel, it will save, when you tell
it to, it will save. Whenever you die, you are sent to said previous save. If you can't kill said boss, you reset. Progress gone.
Try again. What this means is, if you want X piece of loot, you better find a way to sneak out with it, or kill all the enemies
in the area. In Skyrim, death is failure. Victory is often dependant primarily on numbers, who has the stronger swing, or the
most health.
In contrast, death is canon in Dark Souls 3.
You will die, over and over - and that's built into the lore. More importantly, it's accomodated mechanically.
You see, death isn't save reset in Dark Souls 3. Death drops your souls on the ground, you lose your "ember", and
you are returned to the last bonfire you rested at. Grabbed an item before dying? You still have it. Killed one of the
enemies that don't respawn? Still dead. Progress has still been made, things aren't just reset. You can even run back to where
you died, and collect your souls once again.
This means, realistically, mechanically, that each death is a way to learn. Each death should leave you thinking
"Well, I can't do that again". Perfect? No - it can be frustrating when you just want a boss dead, and you are on your 50th try.
However, it gives more flexibility to how you play the game, often I'll sprint to an area, grab an item, and die on purpose to
save travel time, especially if I don't have very many souls on me.
--
--Multiplayer/Cooperative features--
--
On top of that, Dark Souls 3 provides you with many features for you to request assistance against areas or bosses
that are giving you difficulties. Through the summoning system, after using an item called an "ember" (which you also gain
the effects of after killing a boss), you are able to see the summon signs of other players or NPC's that will help you. They can
help you fight a boss, and gain a tangible reward of souls, an ember, or other rewards depending on their covenant, for assisting you. In a way, it helps you to choose your own difficulty - if you want to tackle it solo, awesome. If you want
some jolly cooperation, also awesome.
This, however, is where we need to discuss the side of multiplayer that can make your life more difficult.
Invasions. Primarily, red invasions, which are hostile in nature - sometimes nuetrally, sometimes through a covenant with
definite rules, and purplse invasions, "mad spirits", which can choose whether they want to help or hinder you, depending on
how they enter your world. They will try to kill you for your souls, and can gain rewards for their covenants for victory.
This can be frustrating for new players - but that's why there's the Way Of Blue covenant. In a nutshell, it summons players
from another covenant to assist you as blue, righteous phantoms to defend you against invaders - and they gain a reward for
success.
There's also a simple messaging system, where players can leave messages on the ground built from preset phrases, which other players can then see in their world.
These can be helpful hints, or even hostile jokes.
Through these systems, and more, there's no "multiplayer" lobbies as you know from more traditional games.
Multiplayer features are integrated into the game world itself, so unless you are playing in offline mode, you are never truly alone.
--
--Combat Variety--
--
Dark Souls 3 improves on it's predecessors in many ways, notably the much larger variety of useful armor and weapons.
Dark Souls 1 was great, but had a pretty limited set of playstyles and weapons that were viable, and a lot of useless ones.
This has been rectified in 3, where most every weapon and armor set is viable to some extent, from heavy armor with
great swords to naked warriors with daggers.
This is complimented by the fact that Miracles, Sorcery, and Pyromancy are all very viable, both in PVE and PVP.
The main issue with combat variety is that, unlike Dark Souls, Dark Souls 3 leans towards the agile side of the spectrum being
somewhat more powerful for PVP. The pace of combat is simply far faster than that of the original.
--
--World/Storytelling--
--
Dark Souls 3 is a game that doesn't tell a narrative. It tells you a story, or rather, many stories - but there's very little in the
way of your standard AAA game narrative. I've beaten the game many times, and still don't really know what's going on
half the time. Honestly though, I find this to be part of the beauty of Dark Souls 3. I can read vague item descriptions, listen
to short snippets of dialogue - and piece together what I think is going on, on my own. It leaves holes in the story, in history, that provides the player some creative direction of their own.
Storytelling is done through environment, such as the "ghosts" walking throughout Irrithyl, or the bodies stacked in
a building to the side of Firelink Shrine. This is not a joyful game, but it's one that makes you think.
Of course, if you only care about gameplay, the fact that narrative is not shoved down your throat is a real plus, as you can
just not worry about it and still enjoy the game.
--
--Conclusion--
--
Should you buy Dark Souls 3? I'm inclined to say yes - but only if you have the understanding that you won't breeze through it.
That you will feel like you can't win. That you will find yourself frustrated by bosses or areas - but that by pushing forward,
the game rewards patience. This is not a game for people who want instant gratification, or those who want to feel like a
badass - this is a game about overcoming challenges, creatures, worlds FAR more powerful than you.

While the gameplay can be repetitive, it can also be addictive if you can look past the repetitiveness of the dungeon crawl. A wide variety of simplistic classes provides an inwards change of scenery that makes every playthrough feel a little different up until you have to play some of the more lackluster classes. Don't try too hard to play this game as if it were some sort of mlg experience and you just might be able to widen your perspective of the game. Don't be afraid to try some of the more efficient classes as they tend to be the ones that are most fun and allow you to venture into some of the lesser-known areas.
Some features to look forward to:
- Class options are wide in variety and still expanding.
- Character customization is decent enough although you won't be creating renditions of yourself.
- Scenery is beautiful even in its voxel form.
- Content is being added constantly.
- The game is quite populated and might continue to expand a bit further (Should current overnerfing issues eventually simmer).
- Combat can be fun, but may get repetitive after a while so you can switch to classes you are comfortable with.
- You absolutely do not have to spend a single dime in this game to attain anything you've got your sights on, although if you'd like its available to you.
Things that might turn players away:
- The community is slowly, but surely becoming more toxic over time and now with whispers of a pvp scene it may just get worse.
- IE: Select groups of players are spending real-world currency to boost themselves through the game via the market        exchange, utilizing their gain to then achieve  the highest mastery or whatever equipment they desire and while this may not be seen as a negative point initially, these same players utilize their affluence/influence to lessen the morale of those who savor the game and aren't interested in gloating over the rest of the population. Steer clear from these types of toxic players and pay them little mind when they flaunt their 'achievements'.
- The balance team seems to be intent on forcefully shepherding players into different areas of the game by nerfing content such as challenges and soon enough other aspects of the game such as fishing may soon see the same treatment.
- Server instability during challenges or before/after updates may be apparent and with the game's history of long downtimes there's no telling when a hiccup might occur.
- With nerfing of challenges and their rewards we've seen ridiculous fluctuations in the economy that are only being exacerbated by the balance team as well as a handful of very vocal players who already manipulate the economy with their vast stores of in-game currency.
Overall I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a creative voxel experience, but beware the toxicity growing in this community and the misguided balance team. This game has vast potential and in its current state it truly worth playing. I'd hold off on any real-world investments until we have a clearer idea of where the balance team is headed and whether or not the toxicity of player behavior returns to a tolerable level. Gather a friend or two and give this a try.

Current review: Sunday, February 21st, 2016.
Recent updates have challenged the integrity of the development team in my eyes. A hefty number of players now speculate that current changes to the in-game store and the function of dragon coins, monetization changes to classes and the function of mastery ranks were all influences by Trion superiors. Whether or not this is accurate is up for debate. That won't be discussed here. Feel free to review this on this thread:
On to the review with a few major changes.
Dragon Challenges/Dragon Coins/Dragon Souls/Dragon misc.:
Dragon coins were previously tradable and were a quite a contribution to the market and player-made exchanges. They were utilized as a primary source of in-game income and as such were somewhat prized. They were especially useful for the simple fact that players would play challenges even whilst having finished their dragon acquisitions because they could be used for income or saved for months where players simply wouldn't be available for additional future dragons. In a way this was a wonderful thing, but of course all wonderful things eventually fall short with Trion. So why was this important exactly? This drove players to continue to interact and assist in challenges where newer players would take part and as a result, guided users in the general layout of challenge functions and how to operate them. At least seeing a vast number of players taking part in challenges brought a visible and undeniable proof that the game would still carry life through various worlds regardless of time zone variables. Case and point? Restricting them to non-tradable was a terrible idea.
How did they put the nail in that coffin? Previously some dragons only utilized one to two coins in order to unlock a particular dragon PER SOUL. Now a majority of the list utilize 4 coins per soul and as high as 400 for the full unlock. As a remedy, the dev team reduced the additional unique materials required to produce these souls. Unfortunately that did not actually alleviate problems or concerns.
In the past dragon challenges distributed boxes that were dedicated to a particular dragon per tier of the challenges in sets of two with the final tier only rewarding a non-tradable soul for that month's dragon. Challenges now reward a 'lesser' dragon cache in contrast to this and a new 'grand' dragon cache has been introduced to the in-game store(For credits not cubits) that is purchaseable and carries a chance to provide a user with the full set of dragon souls required to unlock one dragon. This chance, however, is low. Of course we all know this is a gamble, but these caches drop a larger quantity of dragon coins to use at the dragon crucible.
It doesn't take a rocket scientist to see the general direction this has taken the game. With the significance of dragon titles and what they contribute to a player's passive functions, this speaks ill of Trion and its dev team's intent for the direction of the game.
Class/Store Changes:
Keeping mastery rank's implication to a character's function, the introduction to power rating has added several dynamics to the playing field that don't favor newer players and further complicates the power divide between veterans and new challengers. This new system takes equipment values into account with a total rating you can calculate based off of your gear as well as your current mastery rank and the dragons you've collected. Why is this a problem? Without focusing too hard on the obvious let us put the situation into perspective. Base health that traditionally accompanied every class' passive bonuses has now been cut, however, with power rating health and damage is now heavily reliant on your mastery/power rating. You could say this was a buff/nerf, but the function has heavily boosted the potential of veteran players while leaving newer ones somewhat handicapped.
There are other problems that haven't been elaborated upon here, but recent class nerfs and vial/emblem changes further disappoint. All in all I can not recommend this game to anyone in its current state. If you aren't a fan of P2W games then simply dodge this bullet. You'll save yourself the disappointment and grief.

Your task in Darkest Dungeon is to hire and train up willing merc's to take on the Darkest Dungeon. This task will put your men/women to the limits as you have to harden them in battle to collect loot and exp to better upgrade not only your team but your town so that you can proceed to more difficuilt areas. This is all well and good and makes for a fun and diffuicult experience, but all this gets thrown out the window when everything you do boils down to RNG and the luck of the gods. You can replay the same level 3 times with the same group of heroes the same way and get 3 different outcomes based on luck. This makes the game less fun and more frustrating when all your hard work goes down the toilet due a random mob getting incredible luck and wiping most if not all your team.
Though in the games fairness the first text box you see basically says "This game is random, so dont be upset if you die a  bunch". This is a game that demands you put it down and take a break rather than sitting and pounding away at it for hours, less you end up stressing out like one of your poor characters.

I am just starting in this game and find it fun and dark.  I am having an issue though with Hunger.  I find it very confusing that in a game where you can keep track of how stressed/sane your character is you don't get to know the more basic question of how Hungry they are.  This would be something that any character should be aware of (or at least more aware of then how stressed out they are).  Currently the mechanic seems to be random.  You walk into a dungeon and have a x% chance to get hungry.  Eat then it goes back to the x% chance.  It doesn't build up, just keeps at the same chance.  Why didn't they pull a mechanic for hunger like they have Stress.  Heck look at legend of Grimlock, they do hunger very well.
I will recommend this game, but if you can get a mod that makes hunger more realistic (or more in line with the games theme of management) then you would be better off.  Ideally they will fix this in some patch.  At the very least a set timer of moves would be better than it is now.

It's a great game, overall. I had a blast with my friends for about a month, then we just suddenly stopped playing. We played hours on end during the summer, it was great. The dungeons are really creative, too, and they always match the biome they're in. It's not pay to win AT ALL. The building is pretty fun and great, and you can make some pretty cool things. The fighting system is really active, too. I played as a neon ninja, and honestly, its a fragile class that requires strategy. It's pretty hard to use(and I sucked at it).
Like all games, it has it's flaws. For example, it got pretty repetitive after like a month or so of playing it. It lacks PvP support, but that could be coming soon. There's very few biomes, so it lacks a bit of variety.
All in all, it's a really nice game to get into. You can venture around and explore, restocking at your portable home(called a cornerstone). Club worlds are private worlds that you can make for your group(you can make them public if you want) and allow you to unleash your creativity. There's a lot of neat stuff to do in the game, but the dungeoneering will get repetetive and will eventually feel like it lacks in variety. It's a nice game, but you will most likely end up uninstalling it after a while because it'll get a bit boring.
Tl;dr
A pretty good game. I do recommend a download, but it will get repetitive after a while of playing.

This is in Early Access,so I will cut it some slack ^^ .
I put into this game 2 hours and I am already falling asleep.One BS thing,is the fact that your health doesn't regenerate.Wait what?I have seen myself COUNTLESS times into the less than 10 health mark,and all you can do is die in the next engagement.What about classes?Well,only 2 game modes allow them.But people mostly play TDM as always.I do not care about this game enough to go deeper into the gameplay.Last thing,the sprinting system is just bad IMO.But,you walk really fast anyway,so,I don’t use it cause you switch to your knife in order to run,so you can die if you meet an enemy by the time you get your weapon.
I know this is the kind of shooter like CS:GO,its the regular shooter with minimal recoil and kick so you can shoot from the hip while moving fast,but you can aim down your sights at least.Though,all you do is peek-a-boo or go in spraying and praying and double kill 2 enemies and have like 6 health remaining because netcode is bad and enemies are missing you 75% of the time.At other times,you die 2 seconds later and do small amounts of damage to an enemy.
To be honest,these are not my biggest complains.The worse thing about this game..is the shooting itself...I know this is not Arma or anything,BUT,any kind of weapon you use,LMG,DMR,assault rifles and Sub-machine guns feels the SAME.I used the scar H DMR and it had a  20 round magazine and it was firing like an assault rifle,full automatic(where is the semi-automatic?What the heck?),it was laugable.If that is a DMR,then I don't know what the heck a DMR is,but whatever,its not meant to be realistic anyway.
But the sound when you hit an enemy?Wow,just wow,its like breaking someones bones infront of a mic,its unbeliavable,replace that sound effect immediately I had to turn it down cause it was too loud and annoying,plus,the sound for the "man in the back",saying the usual,"objective is nearly done",is just mediocre,so,sound effects are mediocre at best,guns do not sound incredible either,and that "tactical reload" from you and your teammates?,hehe,you better be prepared to hear it 1000 times.
But last but not least,one of the most frustrating things about this game is...the maps.The maps are sometimes either a Great selection of...drum roll please...corridors.And small ones at that.Not only of course are the maps bland as always,I barely even remember their names(its a casual F2P FPS,what can you expect),but its just boring.
I remember at the map which is in a cruise or a ship,that you spawn and you either had:Corridor no.1,a narrow corridor where snipers would camp and kill anyone that went there,so,none of my teamates went there after they died 10 times.Then we have corridor no.2,and it begins after a starcase,and what basically happens is that,both teams stand the end of the corridor,shoot each other a bit,maybe move on when nobody is watching,which leads to an actual open area that is...just a point to access most of the corridors.WOW,amazing map design,then to move to the enemy base,there were ways to access corridor no.1,which would mean pure death,and then you had a small corridor at the north of the open area,which basically led to the enemy's base.At one point we were spawnkilling them,which is a bit alarming cause the map is just to damn small.
To be completely honest,most of the maps where just that,a set of corridors and an open area to give more "freedom" to the players.Yeah,I wish,after doing the same thing,in the same maps,in the same corridors?Yeah,tedious is the word to describe the gameplay.There is no "different" way to approach the enemy,just some high Points Of Interest thrown here and there,to give the advantage to people who are willing to go in the same spot,over and over,just because they can ambush people(I am reffering to that tower in the desert town,and a small bridge at an other map,which was like a plant or something).
I can asure you that the Batte match is far more interesting and its where the classes are available,you just have to wait more in comparison to TDM.Also,the maps are bigger(but corridor-ish again),but still better.Also the regular TDM is 8VS8 while this is 16VS16,so go out there and kill each other.
Anyway,to address the “other” portions of a game,I can say that,the Free “DLC” was a good move,cause it gave you a good amount of pretty much all types of weapons,for unfortunately 15 Days,but whatever,positive about that(We will see if that was only for early access).The prices of the  weapons,while a bit high,are actually obtainable,something like 120K+(or even lower),is an OK amount,cause you start anyway with 200K+,and,you get something like 1K and lower “gold” per game,and,you get 15K per day if you login.There are the usual crates,which need premium currency to open(bullets they call them),apart from a 30K gold one that gives you melee weapons and grenades,so,a no for me.
So F2P players?This looks OK,we will see how this will change in the near future.Apart from that,that’s all for now,graphics are OK for the regular potato PC,not amazing,runs smooth.Tutorial was just bad...tried way too hard to get you into the “hell yeah war is badass” mood or whatever.UI needs some tweaking here and there.Servers were unstable,once online and once offline,but this is launch so its OK,now it seems more stable.
So overall,is this CS:GO:poor man's edition?Yes,I would say,if you are into this kind of games,try it,go ahead,but just be prepared to feel the small amount of content.Personally?I would go play dirty bomb,neither is that game great but I find it more interesting and appealing than this.
But one thing I can say,is,that this was one of the “better” experiences with F2P shooters,I played far worse shooters and this was much better,so I am happy about that,if they fix the issues and add more content this will sure be a shooter to play.Wait and see,wait and see.
Maybe this was really good for some,but for me,its was mediocre at best,but hey,the best things are the simple ones.I simply cannot recommend this to someone apart from the fast paced competitive shooter fans,so it's a 5/10 for me.

Overall, game is super fun and I am sure ready to call it my favorite 2016 game.

*DISCLAIMER* I'll admit that I haven't exactly spent too much time with Darkest Dungeon, so I've read up on some other user experiences while also presenting my own. I plan, at some point or another, to go back and give the game another try and see if I just dismissed it too quickly.
While my time with this game isn't much, I do believe that I've seen and heard enough of it to give a solid opinion. Darkest Dungeon stresses realism at its finest and at its absolute worst, bringing a mariad of interesting mechanics and solid designs, but overall presenting us with a very, very frustrating experience.
I had been looking for a dungeon crawler-esque game for a while now that could satiate my thirst to test my greed whilst diving for treasures and loot, and Darkest Dungeon seemed like a nice fit at the time. Unfortunately, only four hours later, I felt completely defeated and a tad bored of what this game wanted me to accomplish. The developers want you to go into various locations that seem to be procedurally generated and complete whatever mission you choose. Most of the time it was a "Complete 100% of the battle rooms" or "Explore 90% of the rooms" or something of that nature. There's the occasional random battles or what have you along the way, and I enjoyed that part.
Initially, I enjoyed every second of combat. It was diverse and very strategic, keeping you on your toes and thinking steps upon steps ahead. Every battle was a fight not to just keep your team healthy enough to venture on, but to
It was thrilling and it was made even harder through the stress mechanic (which I will get to later). After a while of going head-to-head with hordes of bandits, undead, and demons, I started to realize something very grave about Darkest Dungeon in that, for a game that stresses realism, RNG has some very heavy influences. Random crits made your life either a lofty cloud to rest upon or a hellish nightmare to barge through. Every crit landed against you felt like being pushed even further down a hill of an uphill battle.
Then, to continue with this discussion of RNG, there's the largest offender: the stress mechanic. Stress in this game is manageable through various skills of different classes and two locations in the base town. The concept in itself is interesting, but already too overbearing as there's already so much you have to worry about. Every hero or whatever you would like to call your characters has a stress bar that reaches to two-hundred points. In just one mission your heroes, if you don't play your cards right, could very well easily get over one-hundred points of stress. Stress isn't just triggered through combat either; there are a lot of tiny other things that will add up over that period of time that you spend in the area. Once a hero reaches one-hundred points of a stress, a very heavy fifty-fifty will take place that could possibly make or break a character, deciding if they get some virtuous perk that reinforces heroism or some negative effect that just hinders the rest of your group entirely. The stress system is just a dice roll that I dread every single time I'm notified of it.
The game of chance that you play whenever you find a new treasure (called "Curio" in Darkest Dungeon) kind of adds just an unnecessary step of risk and reward. Not to mention running away from a fight is also determined by RNG...but I think that my point has been made clear enough.
Ultimately, this is one of those decisions on whether you're willing to put forth the time and effort that this game requires of you to press on. And you have to be accepting of the fact that your best team could very well be wiped out in a single mission if you're not very careful. I enjoy that cautious and looming feeling that you really should have whenever playing a game like Darkest Dungeon, but with its heavy reliance on RNG when it really matters, it takes away from that experience and oppresses the realism that Red Hook Studious is trying to convey.
I give Darkest Dungeon a solid 4/10 so far. I plan to play the game further and it might give me a better viewpoint if I just give myself more time to bask in the dark fantasy world that the developers have conjured, but I'll always have a sinking feeling that knows that there's always a very large chance of my characters being lost to random crits or afflictions. And unless there's some type of fix in the future, I don't see my opinion chaning all that much.

Dark Souls 3 is the first game I played in the Souls series, and as a rather casual gamer I was quite hesitant to give it a go at first. So yes, if you've never played any Dark Souls game in the past, the third one is definitely a good start.
- An important thing to note is that the keyboard and mouse support is atrocious. You will have a much better experience playing with a controller.
Visually the game is very impressive, especially from an artistic perspective. I've never played a game quite like this - It has a very dark, brutal and grotesque theme which I felt was very unique, even awe inspiring at times. It was smart of the developers to have such a long view distance as it really makes you appreciate the scenery.
Level and enemy design are top notch. It's evident that a huge amount of effort was put into designing various areas that reward exploring and do not feel repetitive. Enemies are also extremely well made: Their design and models are very detailed and the amount of unique enemies I encountered throughout the game is unlike any other game I've ever played, especially when taking into account that almost each enemy has a unique moveset.
The lore in Dark Souls 3 is mostly hidden in the descriptions of items. What little information you get from NPCs is usually vague and there aren't many lines of actual dialogue, but the ones that you do get to hear were clearly spoken by very talented voice actors. I personally enjoyed the fact that lore wasn't being shoved in my throat as this only added to the mysterious tone of the game.
If you're actually invested in the lore, you will have a better time watching lore videos on YouTube since those will bridge gaps that the game will not.
The version of Dark Souls 3 I played appears to not be very stable on certain Nvidia driver versions. I tried a few versions, including the latest one at the time of writing this review, and the most stable version for me was 384.94.
The game is quite difficult at first, but once you realize that dying is part of the learning process you will start understanding the mechanics and movesets of enemies and it eventually becomes a matter of pressing the dodge button at the right second, which also became my first issue with the game: You cannot play as a tank character. It doesn't matter how many defensive stats you invest in to be able to properly wear heavy armor and still be able to dodge, you WILL get absolutely trashed unless you time your dodges and attacks properly. Alternatively, you can play with greatshields, but those require a huge investment in stats, and will not be viable until the later sections of the game, but they do make certain areas much easier.
My second issue is the camera, or more specifically the FOV. Some locations force you to fight grossly oversized bosses and the only thing that makes those fights needlessly frustrating is the game's narrow field of view. There are mods that will aleviate this issue, but those can potentially trigger an online ban.
Which leads me to the online aspect of the game. Most of the online mechanics are great at their core, especially the messages system that allows people to create messages on the floor that other players are able to read and rate (i.e Bad or Good). Those messages can be extremely useful or completely useless. You cannot write whatever you want - you must compile sentences from an existing pool of words and incomplete sentences, but it was clearly well thought-out since the pool of words to choose from contains everything you need to explain yourself. For example, you can leave messages like "Hidden path ahead", or "Be wary of mob enemy, above".
The other nice aspect is the invasion system that allows users to invade the games of players who are enkindled, which is a status aquired by using an item. Users who are in enkindled mode appear as hosts of embers and gain +30% to their health pool. They are also able to summon other players to help them clear a level and even fight a boss off. The downside is that some players will invade the host's world and try to kill them and their co-op partners.
The PVP aspect starts falling short when you realize how laggy it is. The rubberbanding is constant and some players have extremely high pings that will even make the monsters lag. Fights feel very unresponsive and some hits take more than a second to register.
A good example of this is the
boss fight that summons
to fight you.

The game in not perfect, but playing it is a unique experience unlike any other I've had. I strongly recommend trying it out even if you've never played any souls-like game before. It's definitely going in my favourites list.

I've beaten up the first boss and this was an utterly boring battle of kiting and repeating the same moves over and over again until he fell dead. Then I uninstalled and refunded.

Dark Souls 3 is the first game I played in the Souls series, and as a rather casual gamer I was quite hesitant to give it a go at first. So yes, if you've never played any Dark Souls game in the past, the third one is definitely a good start.
- An important thing to note is that the keyboard and mouse support is atrocious. You will have a much better experience playing with a controller.
Visually the game is very impressive, especially from an artistic perspective. I've never played a game quite like this - It has a very dark, brutal and grotesque theme which I felt was very unique, even awe inspiring at times. It was smart of the developers to have such a long view distance as it really makes you appreciate the scenery.
Level and enemy design are top notch. It's evident that a huge amount of effort was put into designing various areas that reward exploring and do not feel repetitive. Enemies are also extremely well made: Their design and models are very detailed and the amount of unique enemies I encountered throughout the game is unlike any other game I've ever played, especially when taking into account that almost each enemy has a unique moveset.
The lore in Dark Souls 3 is mostly hidden in the descriptions of items. What little information you get from NPCs is usually vague and there aren't many lines of actual dialogue, but the ones that you do get to hear were clearly spoken by very talented voice actors. I personally enjoyed the fact that lore wasn't being shoved in my throat as this only added to the mysterious tone of the game.
If you're actually invested in the lore, you will have a better time watching lore videos on YouTube since those will bridge gaps that the game will not.
The version of Dark Souls 3 I played appears to not be very stable on certain Nvidia driver versions. I tried a few versions, including the latest one at the time of writing this review, and the most stable version for me was 384.94.
The game is quite difficult at first, but once you realize that dying is part of the learning process you will start understanding the mechanics and movesets of enemies and it eventually becomes a matter of pressing the dodge button at the right second, which also became my first issue with the game: You cannot play as a tank character. It doesn't matter how many defensive stats you invest in to be able to properly wear heavy armor and still be able to dodge, you WILL get absolutely trashed unless you time your dodges and attacks properly. Alternatively, you can play with greatshields, but those require a huge investment in stats, and will not be viable until the later sections of the game, but they do make certain areas much easier.
My second issue is the camera, or more specifically the FOV. Some locations force you to fight grossly oversized bosses and the only thing that makes those fights needlessly frustrating is the game's narrow field of view. There are mods that will aleviate this issue, but those can potentially trigger an online ban.
Which leads me to the online aspect of the game. Most of the online mechanics are great at their core, especially the messages system that allows people to create messages on the floor that other players are able to read and rate (i.e Bad or Good). Those messages can be extremely useful or completely useless. You cannot write whatever you want - you must compile sentences from an existing pool of words and incomplete sentences, but it was clearly well thought-out since the pool of words to choose from contains everything you need to explain yourself. For example, you can leave messages like "Hidden path ahead", or "Be wary of mob enemy, above".
The other nice aspect is the invasion system that allows users to invade the games of players who are enkindled, which is a status aquired by using an item. Users who are in enkindled mode appear as hosts of embers and gain +30% to their health pool. They are also able to summon other players to help them clear a level and even fight a boss off. The downside is that some players will invade the host's world and try to kill them and their co-op partners.
The PVP aspect starts falling short when you realize how laggy it is. The rubberbanding is constant and some players have extremely high pings that will even make the monsters lag. Fights feel very unresponsive and some hits take more than a second to register.

Nothing changed in DS3, since the debute of Dark Souls franchise. It's still a grindfest with broken hitboxes, outdated graphics, horrible PC port quality (Developers didn't even give a f. about the control revamp - just let you guess what the X button stands for).
Gameplay mechanics are cursory, more of a dance-roll simulator than a Swordfighting experience. And the enemies themselves? Unresponsible Meatbags that can take dozens of hits without even making a sound, specially the bosses.
I'm not sure why is this called "Hardcore", because all you do is typically grind the boss to reveal all it's attack patterns and moves, then come up with countering measure to beat him. And that's not hardcore, but merely patience-trying.
I've beaten up the first boss and this was an utterly boring battle of kiting and repeating the same moves over and over again until he fell dead. Then I uninstalled and refunded.
And to say it once more, because the practice makes perfect, Graphics and animations are incredibly outdated by multiple orders compared to every other game on the market, instantly crossing out the visual aspect of this handicraft.
I gave Dark Souls whole 3 chances with each game, but it looks like it was just not the right approach. Dark Souls is a niche game for masochists who enjoy dying a lot, because you practically can't defeat a boss without dying (to learn his movelist, of course), which is time consuming and tedious.
Not recommended for purchase.

I've been playing since November of 2014, as soon as this game came out of closed beta. I really enjoy this game, aside from the hourly challenges. The hourly challenge is like a mad zerg rush to finish as many dungeons as you can in a 20 minute timespan, to fill your "Challenge Bar". Upon completion of each level of the bar, you get a "Dragon Cache" that has (as of this moment) 4 different prizes: Eyeballs, Flux, Dragon Coins or Penta-Forged Souls. All of those items are used for upgrading your gear. You need lots and lots of Flux and Eyes. The classes are good, except the Boomeranger. His boomerang does not always work like it's supposed too. I'm pretty sure it's a glitch/bug that has not been fixed yet. The Shadow Hunter does not do too much damage either, and the Current new class, the Tomb Raiser, is a little OP in my opinion. If you have the Death Defying Vial potion, then you can tank like nobody's business.
Aside from those little issues, there is a building aspect to this game, kind of like minecraft. You get your own personal plot of land called a Cornerstone that you can build on. These plots of land look like a big black square with a little yellow sign on the edge of the square. No matter where you build your home, you can summon it at one of the black platforms, in any land you go to (aside from the club worlds). You can also make your own clubs, or join a club that someone else made. You can have up to 5 clubs in your roster, and you can be the leader of more than one club. I currently have 3 clubs that I own, I joined my Husband's club, and I am in a random club that a single person is in. There are a bunch of different blocks you can build with, and some organic blocks that can add liquids (water, lava, chocolate) to your home/club. There are also musical blocks to play with. I suggest you check out the Trovian Maestroes club, or Voxel Busters. They have some awesome songs setup there. There is gardening you can do. Some plants are decorative, others grow materials that you use for crafting.
With the Club worlds, you can expand beyond the initial land you have by crafting Terraformers. They are not cheap to make, but they do add extra biomes you can bulid on. I think the maximum number of members a club can have is 750? I'm pretty sure. There is no adventuring in the club worlds, sadly enough. Just open spaces to see people pixel-art.
So, do I recommend this game? Yes. You can send me a friend request too. I play almost every afternoon.
I do not mind the grinding for items, but some people might. I'm looking forward to the new class coming out, the Lunar Lancer, since I tried it out on the Player Test Realm. I'm also looking forward to the new Shadow Tower update.

XCOM 2 will Hurt Your Feelings
XCOM 2 builds upon XCOM's winning formula for inducing rage quits and broken keyboards from tears and fists of angry defeat.  It's a fantastic upgrade and story continuation to a classic series with a new life. For the impatient readers: Buy this game, like right now.
I'm guilty of playing the crap out of this game (and Rise of the Tomb Raider) and not editing/uploading vids as planned. So now that ya know this game has my sincere approval here's why.
No zombies. That's right, this game is (mostly) free of the "well overcooked zombie phenomenon". XCOM-2 is about Aliens who have won the war, taken over humanity and are driving the propaganda machine full throttle. It shares elements from Half-life 2 and some book I read 15 years ago.
Take 2 Interactive and Firaxis have really taken the winning XCOM formula and didn't muck it up like Ubisoft did with Assassin's Creed. They instead took the lesser elements and made them that much better, while somehow managing to improve the winning XCOM formula of excellence. Not to say there's issues, but most of them are fixable technical problems discussed below.
Furthering the improvements, passing time no longer consists of staring at a blue globe. You now do your work on the world map, flying continent to continent scanning regions, picking up supplies and other tasks. It grants you a more tactical ( I love that word) overview of the entire game world and the state of your situation.
Lastly for all those dilly dalliers out there, there is the Doom Counter.  The Avatar project is XCOM 2's method of giving a sense of urgency. The game world will not wait indefinitely for you to suck up all the supplies and research as XCOM once did. Now if you take too long, your game is over. This is similar to how the pacing in the board game "Eldritch Horror" is set up.
XCOM's Bad Side
The Bad in XCOM 2 is that it's horribly optimized. On a fairly decent gaming rig, frame rates wildly swing between 24 to 40 fps in 1440 resolution (half 4k). The game also spends a lot of time "thinking" (pausing for no reason despite only 30% CPU use). XCOM 2 also spends too much time focusing on an objective. We're talking creepy stalker length of time staring. It has tons of other weird little bugs. None of these though are a real show stopper, but they're all quite annoying.
Summary
XCOM 2 is very addictive and will mess with your YouTube upload schedule. I highly suggest you buy this game after Valentine's day is over.

I cut my teeth on turn-based strategy games with the original X-com and X-com: terror from the deep. So when I tell you I have played them all, you can believe me.
Xcom: Enemy unknown was the apex of this genre for me, and Enemy Within was an improvement I never even knew was possible to a game I already considered to be perfect.
With this said, let me be frank about Xcom2. I... Love... This... Game! Yes, it has its problems, what new release doesn't. But they are nothing when you line them up with the endless list of positives. Firaxis really did a nice job with Xcom2, and I did not mind in the slightest that I paid $60 back in November for this game.
I feel there a a couple things that should be made known up front before I give you the reasons this game is more than worth the money. First, there is a considerable lag between turns for the charachters, like 3-4 seconds. This may not seem like much, But trust me, it's an eternity when you get wrapped up in the mission and have to wait for you next squad members turn to act.
Second, there are some minor glitches to the graphics. Grenades thrown will do their damage long before it has ever left your squad members hands. Seeing the grenade land in an already demolished and burning pile of rubble does tend to take away from the moment. Also, enemys as well as your own squad seem to have the uncanny ability to be able to see and shoot through walls. Yet another mood wrecker. And the load times between missions is extrememly long, taking nearly 35-40 seconds just to get your troops off the ship and either onto or out of the combat zone. Again, a mood stealer.
And lest you think I'm trying to run this game on a sub-par machine, my specs are:
Windows 10 64-bit
Intel Core i-7-4770k 3.5ghz
16GB ram
64-bit operating system, 64x processing
ASUS Radeon R9 390 graphics card
Believe me, this is the first game to EVER lag on my machine.
Now to the positive. Even with the lag time, this game is worth playing. Xcom2 has already beaten me 3 times, and I still look foward to starting again. The story is rich, the graphis stunning, and the battlefield mechanichs are awesome. Remember in the original Xcom when you could get on top of a ship or building and jump in through a hole, suprising the aliens? Its back. So is destructable terrain. And not just for pretty visuals like in Enemy Unknown, but for tactical advantage.
Does the enemy have an advantage over you by using the roof tops to shoot down on you? No problem, just a throw a grenade up there and blow the roof out from under their feet. Not only will they fall to the ground, taking damage olong the way, but there is a chance you may even set them on fire to boot! :)
Also, in the original game, you could target gas pumps and other explosives on the battlefield to devistating effect. That's back too. And while you still can't target ANYTHING you want, its still nice to see a particuraly stupid alien try to take cover behind a pile of propane tanks or a gas pump.
Then there's the stealth mode. Sometimes, you are dropped behind enemy lines under cover. The enemy won't know you are there until you either open fire, or stumble into the line of sight of a wandering patrol. I like this because it throws a whole new dynamic into the mix.
'Should I stay concealed and go around this sentry post, or open fire on it?'
If you fire, every alien within ear shot will come running. On the other hand, if you by-pass it and continue with your mission, there is a GOOD chance that when the shooting finally does start, any aliens you left behind you will follow the sound of the shooting and open fire from behind your positions. Not a good day, believe me. (resulted in my second re-start}
I could go on, but their are simply too many good things to say about this game, and frankly I want to get back to playing it.
Love turn based strategy? Buy the game.
Want a graphically pretty, solid, squad based tactical game with endless strategic possibilities, Buy the game.
It's worth the $60, so just buy the game.
And if you have the extra resources, pre-purchase the expansion pact. I strongly suspect they will be improvements to the game I did not know were even possible. Just like with Enemy Within.

6. Everything you come across in the dungeons has a corresponding item. Such as locked chests yield more loot when you use a key so buy a couple keys and shovels before each dungeon. Edit: My original review of Trove was negative, but after recently playing the game again, I have to rewrite it.
Trove is, overall, a very good MMORPG, and is perfect for beginners and experienced players alike who are looking for something less intensive than the traditional MMOs. The game is well designed, the voxel graphics are cute and detailed and gameplay is generally interesting,
There is a lot of content to explore, with many different 'biomes' and dungeons, along with a mastery and level system, and a huge array of items, mounts, rewards and gear to aquire. The combat is not the most action-packed, as each class only has 3 abilites and a passive, though it serves its purpose fine. The classes are usually pretty unique to one another, with dynamic abilities, and are nice to play around with.
The game also has a pretty good social aspect, with player run 'clubs' that can hold up to 200 players, and an active population and chat.
The devs have recently reworked many aspects of the game to make the rarer resources, items and mounts (like the dragons) easier to obtain, which is a major improvment from when I originally wrote this review. The game undoubtedly is grindy, as it is an MMORPG, but not ridiculously time consuming.
However, this game has its issues. The main one is that the game is now edging towards being P2W. Trion is not a company with the best reputation, as many of you know. The most recent change is that classes can now only be purchased with a 'premium' currency, which is horrific for new players. The servers are also repeatedly laggy, though it is improving, The classes are completely unbalanced, with the oldest ones hugely weak compared to the newest releases. PVP is directly affected by this, with only 1/4 of the classes being actually viable to use.

XCOM 2 will Hurt Your Feelings
XCOM 2 builds upon XCOM's winning formula for inducing rage quits and broken keyboards from tears and fists of angry defeat.  It's a fantastic upgrade and story continuation to a classic series with a new life. For the impatient readers: Buy this game, like right now.
I'm guilty of playing the crap out of this game (and Rise of the Tomb Raider) and not editing/uploading vids as planned. So now that ya know this game has my sincere approval here's why.
No zombies. That's right, this game is (mostly) free of the "well overcooked zombie phenomenon". XCOM-2 is about Aliens who have won the war, taken over humanity and are driving the propaganda machine full throttle. It shares elements from Half-life 2 and some book I read 15 years ago.
Take 2 Interactive and Firaxis have really taken the winning XCOM formula and didn't muck it up like Ubisoft did with Assassin's Creed. They instead took the lesser elements and made them that much better, while somehow managing to improve the winning XCOM formula of excellence. Not to say there's issues, but most of them are fixable technical problems discussed below.
Furthering the improvements, passing time no longer consists of staring at a blue globe. You now do your work on the world map, flying continent to continent scanning regions, picking up supplies and other tasks. It grants you a more tactical ( I love that word) overview of the entire game world and the state of your situation.
Lastly for all those dilly dalliers out there, there is the Doom Counter.  The Avatar project is XCOM 2's method of giving a sense of urgency. The game world will not wait indefinitely for you to suck up all the supplies and research as XCOM once did. Now if you take too long, your game is over. This is similar to how the pacing in the board game "Eldritch Horror" is set up.
XCOM's Bad Side
The Bad in XCOM 2 is that it's horribly optimized. On a fairly decent gaming rig, frame rates wildly swing between 24 to 40 fps in 1440 resolution (half 4k). The game also spends a lot of time "thinking" (pausing for no reason despite only 30% CPU use). XCOM 2 also spends too much time focusing on an objective. We're talking creepy stalker length of time staring. It has tons of other weird little bugs. None of these though are a real show stopper, but they're all quite annoying.
Summary
XCOM 2 is very addictive and will mess with your YouTube upload schedule. I highly suggest you buy this game after Valentine's day is over.

I cut my teeth on turn-based strategy games with the original X-com and X-com: terror from the deep. So when I tell you I have played them all, you can believe me.
Xcom: Enemy unknown was the apex of this genre for me, and Enemy Within was an improvement I never even knew was possible to a game I already considered to be perfect.
With this said, let me be frank about Xcom2. I... Love... This... Game! Yes, it has its problems, what new release doesn't. But they are nothing when you line them up with the endless list of positives. Firaxis really did a nice job with Xcom2, and I did not mind in the slightest that I paid $60 back in November for this game.
I feel there a a couple things that should be made known up front before I give you the reasons this game is more than worth the money. First, there is a considerable lag between turns for the charachters, like 3-4 seconds. This may not seem like much, But trust me, it's an eternity when you get wrapped up in the mission and have to wait for you next squad members turn to act.
Second, there are some minor glitches to the graphics. Grenades thrown will do their damage long before it has ever left your squad members hands. Seeing the grenade land in an already demolished and burning pile of rubble does tend to take away from the moment. Also, enemys as well as your own squad seem to have the uncanny ability to be able to see and shoot through walls. Yet another mood wrecker. And the load times between missions is extrememly long, taking nearly 35-40 seconds just to get your troops off the ship and either onto or out of the combat zone. Again, a mood stealer.
And lest you think I'm trying to run this game on a sub-par machine, my specs are:
Windows 10 64-bit
Intel Core i-7-4770k 3.5ghz
16GB ram
64-bit operating system, 64x processing
ASUS Radeon R9 390 graphics card
Believe me, this is the first game to EVER lag on my machine.
Now to the positive. Even with the lag time, this game is worth playing. Xcom2 has already beaten me 3 times, and I still look foward to starting again. The story is rich, the graphis stunning, and the battlefield mechanichs are awesome. Remember in the original Xcom when you could get on top of a ship or building and jump in through a hole, suprising the aliens? Its back. So is destructable terrain. And not just for pretty visuals like in Enemy Unknown, but for tactical advantage.
Does the enemy have an advantage over you by using the roof tops to shoot down on you? No problem, just a throw a grenade up there and blow the roof out from under their feet. Not only will they fall to the ground, taking damage olong the way, but there is a chance you may even set them on fire to boot! :)
Also, in the original game, you could target gas pumps and other explosives on the battlefield to devistating effect. That's back too. And while you still can't target ANYTHING you want, its still nice to see a particuraly stupid alien try to take cover behind a pile of propane tanks or a gas pump.
Then there's the stealth mode. Sometimes, you are dropped behind enemy lines under cover. The enemy won't know you are there until you either open fire, or stumble into the line of sight of a wandering patrol. I like this because it throws a whole new dynamic into the mix.
'Should I stay concealed and go around this sentry post, or open fire on it?'
If you fire, every alien within ear shot will come running. On the other hand, if you by-pass it and continue with your mission, there is a GOOD chance that when the shooting finally does start, any aliens you left behind you will follow the sound of the shooting and open fire from behind your positions. Not a good day, believe me. (resulted in my second re-start}
I could go on, but their are simply too many good things to say about this game, and frankly I want to get back to playing it.
Love turn based strategy? Buy the game.
Want a graphically pretty, solid, squad based tactical game with endless strategic possibilities, Buy the game.
It's worth the $60, so just buy the game.
And if you have the extra resources, pre-purchase the expansion pact. I strongly suspect they will be improvements to the game I did not know were even possible. Just like with Enemy Within.

This is definitely by far one of the most unique and fun games I have ever played. After 130 hours and kicking this games♥♥♥♥♥♥in its entirety I think it's safe to say I know what I'm talking about.
Graphics - dark, hand drawn and beautiful. I absolutely love the heroes and bosses. They were exceptionally done..
Music - will play on in my head for a very long time. Very ambient and well composed.
Gameplay - not as hard as everyone claims. Definitely difficult but once you find a hero composition that works for you.. stick to it and steamroll the game.
A few helpful tips.
1. Look up boss strategies to save you from alot of heart ache.
2. Hire and fire heros often.. if a hero continues to play badly or gets stacked up with more negative traits then he is worth or that you can afford to heal... fire him and replace him with a fresh face.. try different hero parties
3. For extra gold play without using torches. Meaning rum the dungeons in the dark.. enemies are slightly tougher but yield greater rewards.
4. Dodge trinkets...
5. Lock down key positive traits at the sanitarium such as traits that give you + speed or eldritch hater
6. Everything you come across in the dungeons has a corresponding item. Such as locked chests yield more loot when you use a key so buy a couple keys and shovels before each dungeon. Not all corresponding items are so obvious I recommend looking up a "curio" guide. It's super easy to understand and will yield you a significant amount more LOOT
7. Heros in order of usefulness.. this is strictly my preference. If it's not yours.. tough.
Vesteal
man at arms
plague doctor
Crusader and hellion tie
Graverobber
hound master
Highwayman

abomination

Trove - это "массивная, мульти-вселенская" приключенческая игра. Ваш персонаж будет исследовать случайно созданные миры, разрушать их, бороться за жизнь с монстрами и добывать сокровища из глубин. Каждый герой будет иметь конечную цель: построить здание для жизни, обезопасить участок защитой от нападения темных сил, обеспечить себя пропитанием. То, что персонаж сможет создать в одном мире, может найти применение другим игроком, уже в другом мире. В Trove каждый игровой мир влияет на тысячи других созданных и хотя бы раз населенных игроками.
И даже если вы решите разрушить свой мир, то сможете забрать его осколки в другую вселенную. Как эта миграция может помочь игрокам? Многие геймеры просто смогут пользоваться плодами, созданными другими, например, универсальной буровой установкой, когда-то и кем-то изготовленной. Это касается не только оборудования, но и монстров, которые также умеют мигрировать и создавать новые виды самого себя. Поэтому исследуя глубокие подземелья вы не будете знать с чем столкнетесь.
А если вы устали от стяжательства и борьбы, то можете просто отдохнуть и порыбачить на живописных берегах. Ну или найдите крылья птиц и сконструируйте из них летательный аппарат, изготовьте волшебные снадобья и приручите, в конце-концов, дракона. Развлечений в игре одостаточно много, лишь бы была фантазия. Скучно и это? Тогда создайте из себя существо другого вида, в игре есть система классов, их можно редактировать, обучать или полностью менять, придав нужные характеристики.

It upsets me to see so many negative reviews bashing this game for being an XCOM game. Let me start by saying I haven't finished the campaign, and things could go south (I doubt they will) but I've enjoyed every minute of this game so far.
As a huge fan of enemy unknown/enemy within my expectations were high, and this game crushed them in every way. It takes a little while to adapt to the new style, and even veteran players will struggle at first. Here goes:
Pros
-Game looks great, not exactly the best looking game ever but everything looks sharp, ESPECIALLY enemy designs.
-Art is amazing, the setting isn't revolutionary but done well. Every alien looks badass, and they're all unique
-customization. Lots of it. Almost too much.
-various QOL improvements, most notably the LOS indicator. No more "I CAN TOTALLY SEE THAT GUY" moments.
-Pretty solid story actually. Helped by the really well done cutscenes
-much more mission variety. VIP extractions, bomb defusal, base attacks, base defense, etc.
-I could go on but you get it.
CONS
-yeah the game is buggy. It has the same issues as the first, meaning enemies still shoot through walls and sometimes you take forever to line up shots.
-With so many systems at play, some things fall by the wayside ending up in a horrible time for your first campaign. Pay lots of attention to every tutorial
Lastly, the issue of timers and difficulty. XCOM 2 is hard. Harder than the first. But do not let that dissuade you. I fully believe that if you beat EU On normal, Rookie is the way to go here.
Timers on the other hand are more complicated. Timers lead to some very frustrating fights but it's always manageable.
And for the love of God, the AVATAR counter is so easy to slow down. You have more than enough time to do everything you need and then some.
In conclusion, this game is fantastic. If you aren't afraid of a challenge, buy it NOW. RNGesus be with you

The game is great, buy it, especially now at 26EUR.
Most important recent change for me: finally "real" (360) Controller support has been implemented, and it is on par with XCOM EU/EW implementation.
SteamController worked fine too (arguably better in places because more options/features - come fight me!), but had some unfixed bugs that are quite annoyng. DoubleClick issue, I am looking at you.
I'd reccomend it to anyone having played XCOM EU/EW, I had little performance issues, and the Mods add so much to this game on top of the inherent changes.
BUT
- My system is technically above the officially recommended specs, so I'm not suprised (it honestly runs as I more or less expect any other unpatched current game to run on this system) - if you have a machine more towards middling/minimum specs your experience may differ, I don't know.
- Others seem to have a lot of performance issues - problem is though that very few people post their system specs and relevant graphics settings when complaining about performance, and I suspect that quite a lot of those people simply did not apply the known "good" graphics settings and just started shouting.. but still, Firaxis said that they "are working on various performance issues", so you might simply be rolling the die on how well this runs on your machine right now
Bugs:
I feel XCOM EW was far worse unpatched. Only "relevant" thing I have noticed a few times (as did others) is that sometimes specific enemies seem to be able to 100% ignore the existence of cover for your guys. That's a major bug, yes - doesn't happen often though.
Beyond that there are a few bugs you might remember from EW/EU in regards to clipping and camera, but I actually feel that they are not as many as EW still has right now, fully patched.
The game itself is great - if you liked XCOM EU/EW, this is more of that in general, but with very important specifics changed (read any actual Review/WatchTotalBiscuit/whatever of the game for details),
I like it a whole lot and I have little doubt that I will rack up similar if not more hours than with EW, but I too do think it's harder/even more unforgiving than before.
Last but not least: Holy mods, Batman!
At time of writing there are more than 200 mods available directly through Steam Workshop, with about 25% not being character pools or just "cheats", and it's day 6 post release. A lot of really cool stuff already, and I am actually quite exited to see what modders will come up with in a months time or so.

Spiral Knights is a free to play four-person co-op dungeon crawler developed by Three Rings and published by Sega. In it you play the role of one of the titular Spiral Knights whose ship crashes onto the surface of unknown planet. The survivors band up together and explore the massive randomly-generated Clockworks to find an answer as to what is going on here.
As far as story goes, it isn't anything really special, but it's nicely presented and keeps you interested enough to keep playing.
Graphics are quite nice, they have that unique feeling of a mash-up of fantasy and sci-fi, with the eponymous Knights and quite a lot of monsters looking somewhat cutesy, I personally like it, but I do understand not everyone might enjoy this.
Gameplay consists of exploring dungeons, either story ones, dailies or the Arcade which allows you to delve into completely randomly-generated Clockworks with your only goal being to progress as deep inside as you can. Each tileset has a different look to it as well as different gimmicks, and while they do reappear very often, each level is random so you will rarely see the same map layout as before. During combat, besides smacking the enemies with your sword or shooting them with your gun, you can also block, dodge, shield bash, use your Battle Sprite's abilities, or items. The boss fights are interesting and beating stuff up feels right, so it's definitely a strong point of this game.
Unfortunately, I can't say the same thing about progression. Your power is based entirely on your gear, so without good equipment you are unable to become stronger in any way. It doesn't help that Orbs of Alchemy, used to craft better gear (you need
per piece) are relatively rare despite being needed in such huge quantities and pretty expensive on the market. Same thing goes for Crystals used for reaching the next Heat Level for your gear (and recipes for more powerful gear require a certain predetermined Heat Level of the weaker gear that's required for crafting). At some point, the game just comes to a grinding halt and forces you to either spend real money or grind out a ton of Crowns to even be able to continue the story missions.
Music is definitely the strongest point of this game. It's a unique mash-up of orchestrated instruments and chiptunes, creating that unique retro-mechanical feel. It's very pleasant to listen to even outside the actual gameplay.
Overall, this is a solid game. Dungeon crawlers and co-op players will be satisfied provided they don't mind spending quite a bit of time grinding money for the neccessary upgrades, which, frankly, I personally don't have enough patience for.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown managed to successfully resurrect the XCOM series, XCOM 2 continues it brilliantly.
Procedural level generation, that was an important aspect of the original XCOM, is finally back for better replayability. Also the new concealment mechanic eliminates some of the randomness of triggering the alien groups and instead allows us to plan deadly ambushes (so satisfying when they work well).
One controversial point is that most missions now have an objective that must be reached within a fixed number of turns. While I was a bit surprised at first, I think this is actually very good. XCOM is all about risk management and without an incentive to go faster, the best strategy is to play extremely defensively, advancing your soldiers as little as possible each turn. With the timers, you have to balance safety vs efficiency and that makes the game a lot more dynamic and interesting.
In terms of story and background, they managed to keep things fresh: XCOM is now the resistance against a well established alien presence (it seems inspired by the "V" TV series).
One negative point is that the game feels quite glitchy (weird line of sights, bad camera angles, silly animations, bugs). That was already the case of the previous one and they never really fixed all the problems. I would have hoped that when starting fresh on a new game, they would have restarted from a more solid foundation but it looks like they just reused the old code (bugs included) for many things.
Overall, I absolutely recommended this game to all XCOM fans or even people new to the series!

XCOM 2 in my opinion is a worthy sequel to the critically acclaimed XCOM: Enemy Unknown. The game features aspects and features integral to the rebbot, expands on others while adding new features, that for the most part work well.
The graphics have been improved and are far more beautiful and impressiev to look at. So an improvement there.
Central gameplay elements such as the turn-based strategy, base management - although this has been downsized, which while disappointing, fits the fact that the Avenger only has so much space with which to work with- and soldier progression which is less symmetrical and has more streamlined and clearer more logical paths of advancement.
Interceptors have been done away with, and honestly this is welcome, as it was basically RNG-based combat with minimal input on tactics or actions by the player. The Geoscape has been improved. YOU CAN INTERACT WITH IT. Directing the Avenger around the globe as you build up the resistance; you select what supply drops, resistance rumors and events you investigate. Beware, a UFO can and most probably will shoot you down.
The enemies are a mix of old and new, familiar faces such as the Muton and everyone's favourite , the Chryssalid. In addition to new faces, such as the ADVENT soldier variants and aliens like the Faceless and Gatekeeper. It is a healthy and expanded roster that will certainly challenge, even the most skilled XCOM player.
Mod support is significant as it adds to the longevity of the game and produces interesting creations. So far only minor mods have been released, but hopefully conversion mods and major alterations will create new, interesting and fresh scenarios.
The maps are always different, this makes for a more appealing and wealthy mission environment and setting, weather effects, terrain based on global position and a day/night cycle that works heralds a noteworthy improvement.
WARNING, the game has several issues that I encountered when playing it. Optimisation is not that good. Expect framerate drops even on high-end gaming PCs and occasional freezes as well. Some graphical bugs such as floors disappearing and enemies not falling down to the floor also do persist. Youy can alter the game's graphics settings to get a higher FPS, although this is somewhat forgivable as turn-based startegy does not require a high FPS for you to play it effectively.
Overall i rate XCOM 2 in its present state an 8.8/10. When all bugs are patched and the game runs properly, it can easily score a 9-9.5/10

XCOM: Enemy Unknown managed to successfully resurrect the XCOM series, XCOM 2 continues it brilliantly.
Procedural level generation, that was an important aspect of the original XCOM, is finally back for better replayability. Also the new concealment mechanic eliminates some of the randomness of triggering the alien groups and instead allows us to plan deadly ambushes (so satisfying when they work well).
One controversial point is that most missions now have an objective that must be reached within a fixed number of turns. While I was a bit surprised at first, I think this is actually very good. XCOM is all about risk management and without an incentive to go faster, the best strategy is to play extremely defensively, advancing your soldiers as little as possible each turn. With the timers, you have to balance safety vs efficiency and that makes the game a lot more dynamic and interesting.
In terms of story and background, they managed to keep things fresh: XCOM is now the resistance against a well established alien presence (it seems inspired by the "V" TV series).
One negative point is that the game feels quite glitchy (weird line of sights, bad camera angles, silly animations, bugs). That was already the case of the previous one and they never really fixed all the problems. I would have hoped that when starting fresh on a new game, they would have restarted from a more solid foundation but it looks like they just reused the old code (bugs included) for many things.
Overall, I absolutely recommended this game to all XCOM fans or even people new to the series!
