The graphics have been improved and are far more beautiful and impressiev to look at. So an improvement there.
Central gameplay elements such as the turn-based strategy, base management - although this has been downsized, which while disappointing, fits the fact that the Avenger only has so much space with which to work with- and soldier progression which is less symmetrical and has more streamlined and clearer more logical paths of advancement.
Interceptors have been done away with, and honestly this is welcome, as it was basically RNG-based combat with minimal input on tactics or actions by the player. The Geoscape has been improved. YOU CAN INTERACT WITH IT. Directing the Avenger around the globe as you build up the resistance; you select what supply drops, resistance rumors and events you investigate. Beware, a UFO can and most probably will shoot you down.
The enemies are a mix of old and new, familiar faces such as the Muton and everyone's favourite , the Chryssalid. In addition to new faces, such as the ADVENT soldier variants and aliens like the Faceless and Gatekeeper. It is a healthy and expanded roster that will certainly challenge, even the most skilled XCOM player.
Mod support is significant as it adds to the longevity of the game and produces interesting creations. So far only minor mods have been released, but hopefully conversion mods and major alterations will create new, interesting and fresh scenarios.
The maps are always different, this makes for a more appealing and wealthy mission environment and setting, weather effects, terrain based on global position and a day/night cycle that works heralds a noteworthy improvement.
WARNING, the game has several issues that I encountered when playing it. Optimisation is not that good. Expect framerate drops even on high-end gaming PCs and occasional freezes as well. Some graphical bugs such as floors disappearing and enemies not falling down to the floor also do persist. Youy can alter the game's graphics settings to get a higher FPS, although this is somewhat forgivable as turn-based startegy does not require a high FPS for you to play it effectively.
Overall i rate XCOM 2 in its present state an 8.8/10. When all bugs are patched and the game runs properly, it can easily score a 9-9.5/10

If you are looking for a simple shooter to kill some time with you won't go wrong here.  Though it does need a little more work in terms of balance and mode design.
On the upside, it runs well, plays well, and if you aren't killed by a blazer
, I never felt at any time I died due to some kind of unfair element. The base game is just good, clean, simple Arcade-FPS fun.
The biggest downside to me so far is balance. There are some OP guns (

, and to a much lesser extent, blazer) and some rather underpowered abilities (Seriously who uses The Medkits or ammo restore abilities? And I havent seen juggernaut armor used once because of how stupid expensive it is)
The game modes are....mixed. Demolition is basically Counter Strike or COD Search and Destroy, though not as graceful as either. TDM is Probably the most fun IMHO, just good clean simple shootin fun.
The two unique modes however require a bit more to talk about
VIP: Good in theory, needs work in practice. Like in Demolition, there are zero respawns, one team is trying to prevent another team from getting into a room where once they enter it an Executive looking guy in a purple suit appears, after downing several rifle rounds in this guy, he goes down and the attacker survivors need to run back to spawn to get to a helicopter.
The big problem here is that it's hillariously lopsided in favor of the defenders. Three things typically happen.
1) The Attackers never make it because everyone dies
2)The Attackers make it, but the defender's superior defensive positions allow them to get the jump on them as they are attacking the VIP
3) The Attackers kill the VIP cause someone slid right through, but they gotta go ALL the  way back to spawn....and the other team knows, since the VIP is on one side of the map and the spawn on the other, since the defenders are nearer to the the helipad, they go and camp it, and because they..again have superior defensive positions around the helicopter, they kill the oncoming attackers one by one
I have never won as attackers or lost as defenders, though it is possible for the attackers to win, most likely by killing everyone else
Finally there's the Battle mode, which is their unique mode. it's a mode where you have to destroy five armored crates (or do as much damage as you can before time runs out) before the other team destroys yours. Whoever does the most damage or destroys the other team's crates win. In this mode you get access to classes which give you a passive bonus and Black-ops 2 Style Killstreaks
It's not bad, it's actually a lot of fun once you get your head around how to avoid the sniper killzones, but some abilities could use a buff or redesign...and maybe give smokes as an ability for attacking snipers in horrid spots (more on this later)
Off the top of my head:

, Nobody uses health/Ammo packs (ESPECIALLY AMMO PACKS), and Juggernaut is too expensive
Netcode is fine if your connection is fine, if it starts to die on you then the game starts to die on you
The F2P Model isn't bad, but it's not perfect. It is by no means Pay2Win, as advertised, The guns you start out with are servicable enough and you can fight back with them (Unless of course you come across a well entrenched Blazer sniper or a KSG runner...but you can easily get those for free early in the game).
You spend money on "Bullets" which give you access to Counter strike style loot crates...and that's pretty much it! Everything else you get more or less through grinding (and you get enough money to buy 2-3 guns at the start...depending on what you pick of course)
My only complaint with the model so far is the timed grenades...not only are they relativley expensive in relation to the amount of gold you get per game, but they also only last for a DAY. This is only a problem with Smoke Grenades. Smokes are sometimes your ONLY option against a well entrenched sniper, and you can very much run into a situation in Battle where you have none, BECAUSE of those restrictions! Flash or frags are nice force multipliers, but you can live without them so I don't have a problem with those being timed. Maybe there can be a weak smoke or a visual screen to replace a less-used ability to ablate this?
Like I said, if you are looking for a simple Arcade-y FPS, you wont go wrong here. I enjoyed my time so far, despite issues.
Other than that, my only other request is that I think it could be cool to have class-variants of the existing modes...

XCOM: Enemy Unknown managed to successfully resurrect the XCOM series, XCOM 2 continues it brilliantly.
Procedural level generation, that was an important aspect of the original XCOM, is finally back for better replayability. Also the new concealment mechanic eliminates some of the randomness of triggering the alien groups and instead allows us to plan deadly ambushes (so satisfying when they work well).
One controversial point is that most missions now have an objective that must be reached within a fixed number of turns. While I was a bit surprised at first, I think this is actually very good. XCOM is all about risk management and without an incentive to go faster, the best strategy is to play extremely defensively, advancing your soldiers as little as possible each turn. With the timers, you have to balance safety vs efficiency and that makes the game a lot more dynamic and interesting.
In terms of story and background, they managed to keep things fresh: XCOM is now the resistance against a well established alien presence (it seems inspired by the "V" TV series).
One negative point is that the game feels quite glitchy (weird line of sights, bad camera angles, silly animations, bugs). That was already the case of the previous one and they never really fixed all the problems. I would have hoped that when starting fresh on a new game, they would have restarted from a more solid foundation but it looks like they just reused the old code (bugs included) for many things.
Overall, I absolutely recommended this game to all XCOM fans or even people new to the series!

XCOM 2 in my opinion is a worthy sequel to the critically acclaimed XCOM: Enemy Unknown. The game features aspects and features integral to the rebbot, expands on others while adding new features, that for the most part work well.
The graphics have been improved and are far more beautiful and impressiev to look at. So an improvement there.
Central gameplay elements such as the turn-based strategy, base management - although this has been downsized, which while disappointing, fits the fact that the Avenger only has so much space with which to work with- and soldier progression which is less symmetrical and has more streamlined and clearer more logical paths of advancement.
Interceptors have been done away with, and honestly this is welcome, as it was basically RNG-based combat with minimal input on tactics or actions by the player. The Geoscape has been improved. YOU CAN INTERACT WITH IT. Directing the Avenger around the globe as you build up the resistance; you select what supply drops, resistance rumors and events you investigate. Beware, a UFO can and most probably will shoot you down.
The enemies are a mix of old and new, familiar faces such as the Muton and everyone's favourite , the Chryssalid. In addition to new faces, such as the ADVENT soldier variants and aliens like the Faceless and Gatekeeper. It is a healthy and expanded roster that will certainly challenge, even the most skilled XCOM player.
Mod support is significant as it adds to the longevity of the game and produces interesting creations. So far only minor mods have been released, but hopefully conversion mods and major alterations will create new, interesting and fresh scenarios.
The maps are always different, this makes for a more appealing and wealthy mission environment and setting, weather effects, terrain based on global position and a day/night cycle that works heralds a noteworthy improvement.
WARNING, the game has several issues that I encountered when playing it. Optimisation is not that good. Expect framerate drops even on high-end gaming PCs and occasional freezes as well. Some graphical bugs such as floors disappearing and enemies not falling down to the floor also do persist. Youy can alter the game's graphics settings to get a higher FPS, although this is somewhat forgivable as turn-based startegy does not require a high FPS for you to play it effectively.
Overall i rate XCOM 2 in its present state an 8.8/10. When all bugs are patched and the game runs properly, it can easily score a 9-9.5/10

Fallout 4 feels like a Fallout game for the Mountain Dew generation, where every game needs to have crafting elements (check) and zombies (check - Feral Ghouls now more closely resemble zombies). It is an overproduced and underwhelming parody of its predecessors.
The most disappointing design choice, in my opinion, is the crafting and settlement building. While crafting elements have been part of Fallout canon at least as far back as Fallout 3, here the player is expected to build settlements Sims-style and maintain them, providing for the settlers' needs for food, water, power and defense. So far, I've played 140+ hours of Fallout 4 and very little of that time has been spent on building settlements, apart from what's required for the Minutemen quest line. The game doesn't punish you for this. What's the point? I simply don't give a sh*t about building settlements and I wonder why Bethesda thought I would. Sim City doesn't belong in Fallout. I would much rather be out there exploring the Wasteland.
There are also some very obvious signs that Fallout 4 is trying to ride the coattails of Mass Effect. The biggest is the "romance" system, which is - let's be real - a joke. While some of the characters are likable, the payoff for achieving "love interest" status is not at all worth it. You have to travel with them for a very long time and please their demands of you, whether it be by avoiding theft, drug use and violent crime (for pacifist companions) or indulging in it (for violent ones). This can be HIGHLY frustrating, particularly with Paladin Danse, who seemed to disapprove of literally everything I did. Of course, you could choose to travel without a companion and do whatever you like...
Also, the romances have none of the mature content we expect from Bioware titles. There isn't even a kiss scene, and all you get for putting in all that effort to build your relationship with your companion is a minor perk. After that, you may as well dump them in Sanctuary to rot with the rest of your romantic conquests. They don't seem to mind. At least the original Mass Effect confronted you if you tried to Casanova it with all of the potential love interests. Maybe I expect too much, but it certainly feels like a letdown when Bioware let me see Cassandra's naked t*ts. Hey, Bethesda, if you're gonna try and be Bioware, maybe do a little more research on why Bioware titles sell so well...
The game also has the ME-style dialog wheel, which is a frustrating step backwards from the complex and interesting dialog system from earlier Fallout titles, where you could earn new dialog options and even open alternate quest routes if you leveled your SPECIAL skills appropriately. All of that is gone, including the hilarious r*tarded dialog you got from having a low Intelligence score. All you get now is an overall "Charisma" score (increased via perk points) that can make passing certain speech checks easier or more difficult. Bo-ring. Oh yeah, karma's gone too. You can play all the factions up to a certain point when the game forces you to choose which side to ultimately take.
Finally, the voice actress for the female Sole Survivor isn't Jennifer Hale, but she sure sounds like Femshep to me. Her delivery of her lines also feels very familiar.
The story? Eh. New Vegas had the best story, IMO, with the most interesting factions that I can still discuss with friends today. Was the Legion REALLY that bad? Sure, they were a**holes, but Caesar got sh*t done, while the NCR just sat around bullying small farm owners. Don't expect to have such deep conversations with friends over this game. Fallout 4 took the theme of "synth rights" directly from Blade Runner and didn't do it nearly as well. Play the Railroad quest line and then rewatch Roy Batty's death scene and ask yourself which one had more emotional impact.
Fallout 4 is not a wholly bad game, but I'm thumbing it down because... well, I just don't like it. Fallout 3 and New Vegas were better. And after having played Fallout 4 for so long, I feel qualified to make that judgment. Too many corners were cut and not enough love was put into the parts of the game that I enjoyed. Instead, they gave us SETTLEMENTS. I feel that what we have here is an attempt to make the world of Fallout more pleasing to the lowest common denominator (ie. the Minecraft crowd), and in the process it has lost a lot of its charm. I don't think this bodes well for future Bethesda games. I had a blast with the last two Fallout games, so I wondered why I wasn't having fun with Fallout 4. Now I think I understand.
On the plus side, the DLCs do add some interesting new content, although Automatron feels like a bit of a waste of time. The story is over too quickly and the robots you can build will fill the companion slot you could otherwise occupy with a more interesting flesh-and-blood character. I would recommend skipping Automatron and buying Nuka-World and Far Harbor.
Verdict: 6/10. Buy it on sale, if you can. If you're a fan of the Fallout games, then I suggest you at least give it a chance. You might enjoy it... and you might not.

Its times like these that I wish Steam had a sideways thumb as this is not a bad game by any means, however it does suffer with a couple of issues.
Let me start by saying that I believe Xcom 2 has the potential to be a great game, it has all that I would like in a Turn Based RPG and I’ve only just scratched the surface, however there are a few balance issues that need to be remedied that make certain things in the game impossible.
I have played just under 10 hours on veteran mode on the opening weekend, and have had some really good moments, however there are certain issues which I know will eventually nullify my enthusiasm.
1) Cover
Cover seems to be a bit pointless. More often than not I lose full health squad members who are either in full cover or in half cover (I understand half cover isn’t always guaranteed). On one occasion I was flanking around the side of a garage with two troops at full health. Soldier 1 was behind a road block and soldier 2 behind the garage wall, this gave me both Half-Cover and Full cover respectively. However this didn’t seem to matter because soldier 1 was hit at distance and died instantly loosing 5 health. Soldier 2 was shot through 2 solid non damaged walls and again was killed (How the enemy would have seen her I don’t know). That doesn’t leave a lot of room for setting up your team and formulating a tactical plan if the enemy can just shoot through cover as if it wasn’t there, this for me is a major issue. I feel that either the enemies are too overpowered or the cover isn’t working as it should do. Surely a concrete roadblock would assure a smidgen of protection.
In another instance, I had a full health rookie behind a barrier; the enemy melee unit ran all the way up so he was positioned on the other side of the barrier (half-cover) and killed me with one thwack to the head.
2) Timed Goals
I have no problem with the idea of a timed goal; however there are 2 issues I feel need to be addressed:
a) Harsh countdown times - The timed goals given are on the whole too short, running and gunning doesn’t work as combined with the above issue of cover being like jelly, it makes getting to the goal impossible and in most cases I lose the majority of my team getting there, just to have to spend all of my supplies on new recruits and thus getting stuck in a vicious cycle. (and this was in the Early game).
b) Random reinforcements are too penalising, as you just have barely enough time to get to the goal. But add in the fact that 75% of the time, reinforcements form behind your team, and just mop up with 1 shot kills.
From what I’ve played of the game, there’s a lot that I’ve enjoyed, there's a lot of potential and I’m genuinely excited about it, but I personally feel there needs to be a re-think when it comes to the cover situation and the harsh countdown timers.
There are also a few performance issues that I believe are being looked into, however, I’m not as badly affected as some.
Really enjoy this game, it's cathartic in a way. Be patient it will only get better.

Never before has a game that disregards its player's agency been recieved so well - confusingly well, at that. This is a tactical game in which tactics are irrelevant, and all the good decisions and intelligence in the world will net its players nothing. You can play perfectly, make no mistakes, always make every best decision possible, and still overwhelmingly lose. The only logical way to play XCOM 2 is the cheat by reloading saves that give you infinite do-overs until a favorable outcome emerges.
XCOM 2 is therefore not a game about strategy or tactics, it's a roulette wheel; it's a slotmachine. You aren't playing the game at all, you're simply hitting a button or two and waiting for the game to decide whether you've won or lost.

I decided to give another rogue-lite a try, see if I could get past the old issues I had with them and I have not. So I can't in good heart recommend this title. It is one of those kind of games where everything is based on luck. RNG all over the place. Quite frankly I don't find that to be "difficult" at all, just unfairly unforgiving. Difficulty is giving the player a goal, the means of completing the goal and then allowing the player to show their skill and accomplish what is set in front of them. If the player has to rely completely on RNG to favour them then it is not difficulty. And there are far more RNG's that favour punishing the player than there are RNG's that favour giving the player a helping hand. The scales are tipped too heavily on one side and I just found it frustrating.
The art design is great, I didn't pay much attention to the story as it felt too background'ish to care about, the combat is interesting and has potential, the setting is drearily neat, the sound design is ok I suppose.
What I'm getting at is that the rest of the game is pretty much fine. It is really good in some ways. But the RNG mechanics of the game just kills any enjoyment I could squeeze out of it.

The most anticipated game i've had all year, and i gotta give it a negative review. Great.
So, XCOM 2. The core game is great, awesome in fact. But the problem is once again the bane of all PC gaming for the last few years, performance. Now, devs really need to start understanding something. And that's the fact that you CANNOT release a game in an unfinished, buggy, badly performing POS state like this. You just can't, it's not under ANY circumstance acceptable that a game like this doesn't run on my $1500 rig with even medium settings and 60fps stable.
Now, it's a turn based game. Yeah, i can kinda understand when some people use that as an argument to counter the fact it runs like total bottocks. But that's not all, you heard right the performance isn't even 50% of the real issue. The real creep that ruins this game is the massive, swarming amount of bugs underneath it. In every match i've played in the game so far i've experienced some of the following;
1.) Visual bugs.
2.) AI Bugs.
3.) Animations stall the game to a crawl type of bugs.
4.) Aliens completely bugging out and flat out ignoring the rules of the game type of bugs.
5.) Bugs like the AI getting an extra turn all the sudden because of reasons type of bugs.
6.) Game breaking, game ending, save corrupting and really infuriating bugs.
So yeah, basically DO NOT buy this game until they've fixed it. These are not issues that only me or a few select people are having, these are happening to the majority of the players. And those refusing to accept this fact are either living in denial because their favorite game isn't what they hoped it would be or are just flat out trolling.
Peace out.

This game is...meh.
If I had to describe it, I would call it a side-mission-palooza! Honestly, the vast majority of the game is just you doing missions that feel meaningless and are often quite repetitive. Help this settlement, take out those raiders, synths, supermutants, etc. Here's the thing, the main story isn't very interesting - sole surviving mother/father looking for their lost son. What's worse is that the story unfolds rather quickly. After that, you are just wandering around doing missions for others that have nothing to do with the main plot and all you can think is why should I care? How did I go from parent searching for my lost kid to everyone's problem fixer? Even the settlement building gets boring after a while. It's basically the same thing in a different location.
If you get the game for cheap, like less than $15, then it's a good time killer, and if you like constantly shooting at things, this has got you covered. If you want a deep story, or something that will keep you wanting more - look elsewhere.

TLDR; fantastic game to jump into XCOM with; great game but a tad lazy in some areas for those coming back for round two.

However; the game is a bit buggy, and suffers from framerate dips. I have a 4.2 ghz 5820k 16GB ddr4 2667mhz, 980GTX and i was getting sometimes 15-30 fps at times. That is inexcusable. Combine that with the occasional graphical glitch or black screen with the UI overlay "alien activity" with sound the only indicator the game did not crash.
Would I recommend it? Yes and no. Yes in the fact that its a good successor to the other xcom games, fun, interesting and engaging, deep complex combat, skills, and characters, challenging depending on the setting you put it at(set it at verteran or above be prepared to reload the game lol). And then No, for the bugginess of the game.
I would say if you are willing to put up with the bugs, errors, and performance issues; Go for it, you won't be sorry. It is a great purchase. But for me I got a refund and I will come back to it when a patch or 2 resolves the issues plaguing it right now.

Truly an amazing sequel for a brilliant reboot of XCOM. The gameplay is about what you'd expect from a turn-based game but of course with significant additions compared to Enemy Unknown and Enemy Within. Although I do miss my squad of superhumans and MECs, the new revamped classes are worthy replacements. The combination of rangers, specialists, grenadiers, sharpshooters and Psi operatives make one hell of a squad. Guerrilla Ops is a nice change of pace in which you enter a mission concealed thus allowing you to set up an Overwatch ambush. Fantastic addition to say the least. Gone are the days in which you can send out your Firestorms to shoot at alien crafts, and that is something I do miss at times. I won't spoil anything about the story here, but one thing I can say is that it gave me chills from start to finish and all of it in a good way. After such a long wait, it is good to be back as the Commander.
ps. Optimisation issues are still troublesome as the framerate dips almost constantly from time-to-time, not to mention the loading times can take a considerable amount of time. I give Darkest Dungeon a 9/10. The game forces you to stop and strategise elements such as trinkets, party combination, supplies, and the cost of town and hero upgrades early game means hard choices are forced on the player - and frequently.
This is all aside from the staggering and cumulative difficulty as one progresses through the different levels of dungeons, juggling stress, health, damage, and utility makes the turn-based combat essential. It seems like a lot to handle but the game gives you ample opportunities to prepare; as long as you take them.
Despite the difficulty I personally have had a great experience playing Darkest Dungeon and while I haven't come close to beating it, there's something really thoughtful about the design of this game that has me coming back for more; masochism be damned.

This game basically ruins other games for me. Dark Souls 3 is my first Soulsborne game and I have a lot of fun with it. Everything about this game is superior to other games. The lore, the music, the graphics, the details and overall combat system are astonishingly good. This is the work of art here.
Now you might have heard rumors surrounding Soulsborne games for being extremely hard. I agree, these games are meant to be hard, or should I say "challenging". But it never feels unfair. Soulsborne games are one of the few games that allow players to get punished for their mistakes. Every enemies are deadly enough to kill you if you're not careful. You die mainly because of your own faults, not the game mechanics.
Saying a game is bad because of its difficulty level is like saying football is a bad sport because it's hard to play. It's idiotic, really. The only way to be able to surpass the challenges this game offers is to be patient, don't panic, and get good with it. Once you've overcome all the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ts they provide, you will feel like you have leveled up alongside with your character (because your in-game level means nothing if you're not good at it).
The lore of this game is my favorite part. Soulsborne franchise takes environmental story-telling to the next level. Every aspects of its lore are loose-ended and opened for speculations. Thus providing rooms for arguments based on one's opinion. I will not spoil it for you here but rather let you discover it by yourself.
The final topic I want to talk about is its combat mechanics. Soulsborne games combat mechanics involves around one's ability to quickly react to certain situation, and memorizing the enemies attack pattern. It's PVP, however, is a lot more complicated. It basically boils down to your ability to read your opponents next move, and how to punish them effectively. It feels like you're fighting someone in real life. Although I've heard people say Dark Souls 3 combat mechanics is the worst one out of all three due to its lack of poise and underwhelming spells, I'd say it's a good one, for the person who literally has no experience in Soulsborne games at all. I really love its combat mechanics here. Poiseless means you have to be more careful, more precise, and able to maximize your damage outputs potential with your newly introduced weapon arts mechanics. Overall, I think Dark Souls 3 has the most balanced combat mechanics out of all three.
To sum up, I really love this game. And I'm sure you will too once you've played it. I give it a 10/10 with a badass seal of approval (Angry Joe references here).

The Bad: The game is extremely buggy, whilst not unplayable there is still clearly work to do to here.

To me this is unnacceptable, X-Com is a great foundation, but a bit more imagination and bravery in the game design would go a long way. I think the game is crying out for larger/multiple squad missions. Or how about having a rescue team to secure the pickup location as well as another squad trying to get there, this could offer many new possibilities and new options for the player to consider. Sadly the tactical game (the actual really important part of the gameplay) is exactly the same as the first one.
Overall: Good but if you've played X-Com you've pretty much seen it all before; derivative

Pretty much better in every way than the predecessor. Not taking into account the issues some ppl are having. Some ppl have moaned about graphic performance and until there is a patch optimizing the graphics i would suggest switching the decal setting to "some static" and not to use MSAA anti aliasing. Made a big improvement to the FPS.
Its never suprising to hear folks moan about some game mechanics but those are ppl who arent familiar with xcom.  Sure i might be inclined to tweak an unit here and there but the overall experience is true XCOM where a wrong move can mean party wipe. This game is hard (all previous incarnations were also), its meant to be challenging and you are supposed to be nervous going into most early missions especially on commander or higher difficulty. Dont play ironman mode unless u are a freakin pro, literally a single wrong move or just a spot of bad luck on one or 2 shots can cost the lives of your troops and the mission. Youre going to have to accept that you will fail a few missions on commander or higher and the "call EVAC" function will actually be used, literally all it takes early game is 2 crits in a mish on the aliens side and your screwed.  Frustration will happen, you will miss 80% or even 90% to hit or even higher chance shots, and you will be livid BUT the same can happen to the aliens aswell so bear that in mind.
But the tactics and strategy are of the highest order and the healthy dose of team, base and resource management are some of the strongest aspects of the game. You will love your soldiers but they will die and you will mourn them :3 Randomly generated maps and an event driven non linear campaign makes for great replay value aswell.

2.) AI Bugs.
3.) Animations stall the game to a crawl type of bugs.

5.) Bugs like the AI getting an extra turn all the sudden because of reasons type of bugs.

So yeah, basically DO NOT buy this game until they've fixed it. These are not issues that only me or a few select people are having, these are happening to the majority of the players. Fallout 4 is a good game, not a great game and certainly not living up the the fallout legacy.
Fallout 1 & 2 were deep and engaging games. The world was designed impecably and the writing was a masterpiece of intertwing gameplay and narrative. The world grew between the two games.
Fallout 3 was shallow by comparison. The world felt like it had no history or purpose. You did things and there were certainly outcomes, but it lacked depth. A shift to 3D seemed to have harmed the series. Then New Vegas showed how good 3D could be. The writing didn't pop in the same way as the original and the first sequel, but the game stood up and is a wonderful follow up. The world felt lived in. I believed that there was a history, infact I bought Fallout 3 because I thought New Vegas was built upon it. NV was that well written.
Fallout 4 follows 3 instead though. People ask you to turn up somewhere and kill badies. You do and the people like you. Any quest is a murder-thon. Go and kill. This gets old fast. Your interaction with the world is to lower the population signicantly. Want to negotiate, want to seek a different resolution, you cannot. Do you shot the badies with a big gun, a little gun or smack them with a melee weapon. These are your choices.
As I started this review, Fallout 4 is good. The base building is fun, the world can be geographically interesting, but without a history. This may be the last Fallout game I play. The writing is no longer neuanced. Bethesda cannot make the fallout game that the series deserves.

I often see people criticize Fallout 4 and yet they give no reason or metric in how or why it is a bad game. As a preface I'd like to say that I like the game and although it has it's flaws, I still enjoy playing it. With many imperfections to choose from, I'll boil down to a few of the more apparent defects of Fallout 4.
One of the main reasons is that the quests lack depth. There are no moral decisions to be made and most of the quests follow the same set of actions: receive the quest, kill some♥♥♥♥♥♥ and then loot. There isn't much complexity or diversity in a lot of those quests and I could see why people might find the game dry or boring. It's a solid argument. Afterall, they could have done so much more. The lack of true moral choices that impact the game rob the player from feeling immersed in the game.
This can be said about mosts of the quests in the game, barring the ones in the main quests involved in whichever faction you choose. While the issues I listed above are present in these quests, they're not as egregious as any of the other quests. Some people may disagree with me here or they may dislike the endings offered to them; and while I'm inclined to agree, I think that there was some real effort put into constructing those storylines.
What's sad is that it had potential. Each and every one of those smaller stories could have been explored and refined in order to make a more fulfilling, fun, and complete game.
Also, it's pretty damn buggy game, but I'm sure everyone knows that.
With all that being said about how the writing sucks and lacks depth, the world of Fallout 4, I believe, is a different story.
There is so much to explore and so much to enjoy. The map is massive. It's filled with ruined cities with enemies around the corner waiting for you; cities that despite the war, are thriving; abandoned towns with a history; and so many little jewels of pre-war relics.
You can see how much creativity and imagining went into making this world:
I love The Glowing Sea, the swamps of South Boston and the cities of Cambridge and Boston. There's a whole world to explore.
More than that, you get to explore it with 13 different companions. Each companion has their own distinct personality (if you can call it that) and amusing in their own unique way.
Fallout 4 is by no means a terrible game and when I first bought it, I was a bit let down as well. But with all of the issues I've listed and all of the flaws it has, I still play it from time to time. Why? Because it's fun. Because despite how it may fall short of other fallout games, I still enjoy it.

Starbound is my first 2D-style indie game I have ever played before, so I write this from my perspective, as a person who is new to Terraria-style games; and who is much more experienced with 3D indie games like Starmade, Blockland and Minecraft. I've been playing indie games for many years now and I have begun to get rather bored with nearly everything I play. So, I decided I would play this game hoping to be surprised with a new and unexpected style of gaming.
-------------------------------------------------------
A moderately fun game to play overall, but it tends to get boring after playing it for 3 days, with nothing really new or interesting to do. I mean, sure, it's all different environments everywhere you go, but fundamentally none of it is much different; you'll find pretty much the same stuff no matter where you go.
The gameplay is quite repetitive, with your main goal mostly being to just keep your ship fueled so you can travel to new places, where you will spend yet again most of your time mining for more fuel. And once you level up to the top tier of technology, weapons and armor, there isn't much else that's new to do. There is a quest system but even though I played the game for over a week solidly, I could not seem to find any quests of any sorts to give it any use, other than the tutorial quests I started out with.
It has a considerably steep learning curve. When I first picked it up and played it, I found its controls unintuitive and difficult to use, and the tutorial didn't help much either with figuring this out. If you are a person who is completely new to Starbound and know nothing about it when you start a new game, expect to die many many many times, until you figure out the way to play. Because of this, I highly recommend looking at player-made guides to the game, though those may contain gameplay spoilers.
After you figure out the basics, you will mostly spend your time trying to advance through the different "tiers" of armor, techology and weapons. In search of resources to make better stuff for yourself, you will also stumble across underground ruins, creepy tombs, tribal villages, and even robot/monkey space facilities of sorts. It's also very fun to launch a big attack on a village and burn their buildings to the ground, if you're the sadistic type.
Unfortunately, the resource requirements for items is absurd. To get better weapons and armor and technology, you have to spend many tireless and rather boring hours of clicking and popping your way through layers of blocks to find large amounts of resources for a small piece of body armor or that next gun or sword. And if you get injured while off exploring, you better hope you get lucky enough to find some sort of vine or cactus vegetation in a cave and collect several of them to make a tiny bandage that heals only a small percentage of your health.
As for gameplay difficulty, it's very very difficult to survive when you first play, and the difficulty options don't offer much choices that would go easy on newbies. You have difficulty option choices like that in SCP Containment Breach: Temporary death or Permanent death. There is no "peaceful" or "normal" or "hard" option like in Minecraft. Oh, and you can expect to be constantly falling into pools of deadly poison when stumbling around in dark caves, or getting attacked, with no real way of your body regenerating health on its own. So, have fun with that.
As for aesthetics, it is a rather appealing game and carries its atmosphere of 2D alien planets fairly well, with cute cartoonish textures that reminded me of some nostalgic Cartoon Network flash games I used to play when I was a little kid. The graphics look fairly nice I guess for this genre, but I haven't played any other Terraria-style games so I don't have anything I can fairly compare it to.
One feature I especially like is the way the liquids work. Unlike Minecraft and other games where liquid sources are either just solid blocks or flowing things that don't really spread out evenly but act like an illogical geyser, the liquid physics in Starbound act like you'd expect liquids would in a 2D game. If a pond springs a leak into a cave, you can expect that cave to be filled with all the pond's water quite soon and no water left in the pond. If a pocket of lava is mined into, there's a big danger it could fall right over you and kill you!
There is very little actual space-oriented gameplay. You can't change your ships appearance except for adding furniture on the inside, you cant pilot your ship yourself (everything is done with an onboard autopilot; you just choose a destination), and you cant have space battles. This is a significant blow to the "Star" in StarBound.
Feature wise, there are many different things you can do, though in the current state of the game there are some things which one could obviously wish they could change upon.
Features:
- Build a base/house/evil lair of doom on planets, asteroids and whatnot.
- Fight cool and seemingly procedurally-generated monsters
- Explore endless open planets with different environments and even multiple different biomes on each of them
- Pillage and conquer villages, homes and secret bases built by monkeys, anthropomorphic birds, talking flower creatures, aliens, and even robots.
- Craft and arm yourself with a plethora of different defenses and offenses
- Collect resources for your base by mining for more resources, all the while digging towards the planet's core.
- Research technology to let yourself have special moves and powers to help with combat, climbing and digging.
- Play online with friends and have even more fun building things together, or just messing around and pillaging other players for fun
As for pros and cons...
Pros:
- Game is very stable, quite impressive for an early-access game. Very few crashes.
- Lots of different features, as mentioned in above list.
- Decent graphics
- Online gameplay
Cons:
- Very little actual space-oriented gameplay.
- Unfitting soundtrack of symphony-piano style music.
- Extremely sharp and difficult learning curve.
- Gameplay gets boring after several days
- Not much to do once you get to the top tier aside build more and shoot stuff.
- No story/campaign mode
Overall, the game is like that one gift you get from an estranged distant relative, which you find appealing to look at and hold for several days, and then never touch it again. It's fun and sparkly to play for a little while, but it gets boring fast if you're a serious and dedicated gamer. I can honestly say the experience I had with it was interesting but I wouldn't want to play this game again until it gets a massive future update that fundamentally changes the way it's played. I guess 2D games just aren't for me.

It says I've only played for a little over an hour on steam but I owned it on PS4 since it came out over a year ago. Since then I have gotten all the way to the two Princes, so I have some knowlege.
That out of the way, Holy Cow this game is amazing. Take all the best things of Dark Souls and Dark Souls II and put them together to get this game. The gameplay is solid and masochistically challenging, with the usual cryptic storytelling (or lack thereof) that we've grown accustomed to in our SoulsBorne journey. It is a hard game, it is unforgiving for simple mistakes; you must become an expert at your particular fighting style or which there are many.
PvP is a death sentence for new players and a mental punishment for the adept, where more souls are on the line for you to lose and them to take. You never quite know when your next human enemy will pop up, and it could come at any time.
Gameplay aside, this game is gorgeous inside and out. The story is captivating and tragic, the characters are stalwart in this harsh wastelad of a once-great kingdom, but broken inside as you'll soon find out; and there are a pluthera of characters for you to run into, fight beside, or fight against.
The art in this game is stunning. The attention to detail is beyond amazing with everything from distant objects and backgrounds to little hanging bits and bobbles hanging off your character's armour. The armour is gorgeous and with great variety, everything from leather tunics to giant suits hewn from solid stone. Along with that, the weapons share in their diversity and beauty, from small and fast rapiers to the infamous Ultra-Greatswords, each with their own details and story.
I am a huge fan of this game and series as a whole, playing from Demon souls to Bloodborne to Dark Souls III, and I cannot recommend this game enough. If you crave a challenge, are willing to be smacked down time and time again on oyur quest to the end of the game, and maybe have a bit of a masochist in you, this game is definitely for you.
Drop what you're doing, buy this game, and Prepare to Die.

I guess it's time to add in my two cents into the mix.
Darkest Dungeon is not a game for everyone.
It appeals to old school D&D players like me, many things in this game are based on RNG checks, and most of those will not go your way. Your heroes may get two shot by something ridiculous, and they will be gone forever (unless your lucky with town events). You might lose your whole party and get no loot.
Many people have a problem with this. I don't.
Maybe I'm a masochist.
Or maybe I see the depth of the combat system and how to minimize losses. Learning how classes work, optimizing for team synergy, knowing what supplies to bring, how much of said supplies, taking risky dark runs to get so much loot, and in general getting your perfect team together to go take the fight to the lovecraftian horrors, that's where the real fun of this game is.
The game is rewarding when you stick with it and learn the mechanics. It is going to anger inducing though, make no mistake.
-EDIT-
Oh dang, people hate this review. I do too.
I still love this game, but after another 50 hours (on GOG), the cracks have shown themselves. While at first I loved the almost Dark Souls like cruelty, after spending 10 hours building up a character up to lvl 6, and then having them two shoted in the most frustrating manner, I had enough.
The game has gotten significant updates since I first wrote this. The town event update seemed like the perfect solution to my problem (with your killed character able to come back from the dead ever now and then) , but then my hamlet got invaded by some boss whom is seemingly impossible to kill.
As soon as something comes along that can add an cool dynamic to the game (like Town Events), it comes with yet another brick wall to break down (like Town Raids), so much so that some of the crap I've gotten for defending this game seems justified.
I still recommend this game, it is good.
It's just ridiculous sometimes.

For being a Free-To-Play Open-World Sandbox Zombie-Apocalyptic game, it's not bad.
Here are my ratings:
Default Controls: 3.5/5 could be set up better, but good overall.
Graphics: 2.5/5 considering they aren't *supposed* to be amazing, it still has good shaders, the textures and models look like they're from the N64, but they're still decent and are definitely satisfying enough for the eye, so that you don't get dizzy.
Gameplay/Programming: 3/5 I'm not very good at programming, (As I haven't done it in a long time) but there definitely could be more stuff, of course the game will update over time so i'm sure it'll get better.
Singleplayer/Multiplayer: 2/5 | 4.5/5  Singleplayer can really get boring/annoying quite fast on Normal Mode if you don't know the controls (unless you're willing enough to just dive in), don't take the tutorial, don't know basic PvZ (familiar with the AI),
so I highly recommend you at least eye-ball the list of controls and skim through the tutorial <-This goes for Online too.
--- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- ---
Multiplayer: Multiplayer can be really fun if you play with guns a lot, (Played CoD, Halo, CS:S/CS:GO/CS before and are familiar with aiming and such) and if you have at least 1-2 friends to play with (for co-op or just killing) if you just VC (out of unturned; using TS, Discord, Skype, etc) it can be super fun[ny].
Community: 1.5/5 (rant) There's too many kids on here, screaming into their mics "DONT KILL ME OR I'LL GET THE ADMIN" on a Deathmatch/FFA server or something like that, you kill them anyway but to see all the annoying toxic children on a game like this is just pitiful, but the rest of community is decent. Steam Workshop: 3.5/5 The Steam Workshop is definitely one of the best features of Unturned, with so many cool maps, gamemodes, guns, etc even just offline (singleplayer) can be super fun if you have a small handful of workshop items downloaded onto your client.
Overall Game: RATING The community/rude kids on this game is what prevents me from giving this game a 7 or a 8 out of 10, and a few other flaws about it, but this is a "recommended" review so good luck with me listing them.

XCOM 2 is the sequel to XCOM: Enemy Unknown.  I played over 1000 hours of the first game, including on my Android device, and it was my favourite game of all time... until now.  If you're looking for negatives, scroll to the bottom.  Otherwise, I'm going to discuss all the things about this game that make it better than its predecessor.  (Other than the procedurally generated maps; the feature I was most excited about before the game launched.  The maps feel handcrafted and still provide near endless variation.)
XCOM 2 is a genuine sequel, not a polished re-skin with a few new buttons.  This game is a sequel in terms of story, your opponents, and even the difficulty level.  For that reason, if you haven't played XCOM: EU, I recommend you begin there.  Despite my experience with the previous game, XCOM 2 destroyed me on my first attempt, at the difficulty level I played most on EU.  I'm thrilled about that because fans like myself can experience the challenge, the rush, the highs and lows of the war, and those moments when everything's so intense that your heart pounds but you keep on playing!
The story and the characters in the campaign have been improved immensely.  The tutorial introduces you to them, and the setting, through a series of story missions that'll make you feel connected to them in a way you never did in XCOM: EU.  As the story goes on, the connection you feel to each character continues to develop, and the story might stay with you for a long time.  In addition, the ending is much more thrilling and rewarding than the end of XCOM: EU--however, this game makes that
ending into a spectacular one, and then goes on to give you an even better ending in XCOM 2!
The strategy layer of the game has been significantly enhanced in XCOM 2 as well.  In the past you could do research and construction however you wanted, but that isn't the case in XCOM 2.  No more watching the hologlobe spin while you pass time at the base either--now the Geoscape is like a board game.  Your decisions on the strategic layer have a major impact on the way the game plays out, and the aliens are also playing their own game against you.  You'll need to adjust your strategy on the fly to counter the aliens' projects and prevent their victory.
Additionally, the tactical gameplay is better than ever--and that's where XCOM has always been strongest.  Many games try to copy the tactical combat of XCOM, and you might hear games described as "like XCOM."  I assure you that having two actions per soldier per turn, and a cover mechanic, DOES NOT qualify a game to be declared "like XCOM."  The number of enemies and their combat abilities, combined with psychological effects your soldiers can suffer, really sets this game apart from imitators.  In XCOM 2, you're fighting to liberate the world from an occupying collective of aliens that has superior technology, and many missions will feel impossible--even with fully trained troops, using the best gear.
Last but not least, the audio in this game is phenomenal!  The cinematic scenes and sound effects are as good as a blockbuster action movie.  The voice acting is impressive, and the dialogue feels natural.  The music enhances every moment of the game; from ramping up the tension in the most threatening combat situations, to relaxing you after a hard-fought battle.
Negatives:
1.  XCOM 2 has some bugs and performance issues at launch, but keeping regular saves and back-up saves will prevent some frustrating issues.  I had one crash during my first 65 hours of play, and the save file got corrupted.  I do not recommend playing in Ironman mode until the game is patched.
2.  Some people don't like the pressure of turn timers on some missions.  I love the timers because the tension is part of what makes XCOM 2 special, but not everyone wants to play a game that requires skill.  Don't worry, however, as there's already a mod to take away the timer if you just can't play the game as it was intended to be played.
3.  It will probably be several years before XCOM 3 comes out.

XCOM 2 is largely a refinement of and an advancement on XCOM: Enemy Unknown. It honestly doesn't feel like a full sequel. Feels like XCOM: Enemy Unknown 1.5. But that's not really a bad thing. As mentioned, many things have been refined and streamlined, and there have been a host of new additions that do mix things up to a certain degree. Though yes, at the same time, I must say I am a tad disappointed that things aren't more different.
So, long story short, if you like XCOM: EU you will most probably like XCOM 2 as well. The campaign length for a first run is around 40-50 hours.
Now, the game has some glaring issues. One is optimization. I honestly do not find the graphics to be anything stellar (they don't seem that different from in XCOM EU), but even on the lowest settings I am getting absolutely terrible performance.
Another is from time to time, the game can bug out. I hacked a Sectapod successfully, yet somehow it remains out of my control and kills my troops on the next turn. Then there was once a muton who was actually on the roof, but the graphics made it look like it was at the bottom of the roof. And once my scanning went to -3 days (it just bugged out).
Gameplay wise, too many enemies are just bullet sponges in the mid-to-late game.
Now that I am right at the end of the final mission, I can say that this game suffers the same two issues from XCOM EU.
1) The mid-to-late game is relatively much, much easier than the fiendishly difficult early game.
2) There is no "middle ground" difficulty setting between Veteran (a tad too easy) and Commander (a tad too difficult)
This game is a net recommendation actually but I leave a thumbs down until Firaxis can fix the optimization issues at least.

This is the first game review I have written, and I have been playing online games (MUDs) since 1997.  I have never loved a game as much as I love Fallout 4, and I cannot recommend it highly enough.  Fallout 4 is the only Fallout game version I have played.
No game has ever haunted me like this game.  If I hear music from the 1950s or 1960s, I am reminded of this game and nostalgically think about it all over again.   The real power of this game is in the settings and the ambiance.  In most areas you have enough evidence to easily see the whole story of what has happened there through time.  How the people in the area lived before the war, how they struggled to survive or how they died, and the evidence of one or more post war inhabitant groups (raiders, supermutants, minutemen, etc).
I played the game on the "Very Hard" setting so I could use Fast Travel.  The combat and sneak systems are not perfect.  You feel underpowered and fragile at low levels (1-19) and overpowered at high levels (50+).  Basically, you have 5 weapon types to choose from, and you can either sneak (later with ballistic weave) or wear heavy armor.  You only have to choose in the early game.  By late game, you will have enough perks to branch into something new because there is no level cap.
You can run through the game content with a sledge hammer and powered armor, but you will miss 60% of the game.  You will still be forced into the game's heartbreaking questline of betrayal, but you will miss so much.  Therefore, I recommend you select one of the "Sneak" character builds so you can slow down and see all of the content.  The weapon choice does not matter, because there are silenced versions of all weapons except energy weapons and heavy weapons.  The game settings are so carefully crafted for content, that you will feel nostalgic about the game world each time you are reminded of it.
Here are some recommended builds to really enjoy the game content:
Sniper Build:  Ninja, Rifleman, Sneak, Sniper, Penetrator, Gun Nut, Demolition Expert, Hacker, Locksmith, Armorer, Science (Rifleman Perk works for shotgun as well, so switch to your shotgun in close fighting conditions)
Gunslinger Build:  Ninja, Gunslinger, Sneak, Gun Nut, Better Criticals, Critical Banker, Grim Reaper Spirit, Hacker, Locksmith, Armorer, Science
You need Science to build water purifiers.  This is instant success to make money is the game.  The purified water is valuable.  This is the first Perk I build.  The better store bought gear makes up for having a lower starting combat perk set.
You need Armorer to make Ballistic Weave clothing that is lightweight for sneaking.  You will need to follow the Railroad questline until making Ballistic Weave is available to you.  You can make a huge mistake by being at war with the Railroad before you have learned this skill.  Do not make this mistake.
My normal modus operandi is to Fast Travel in power armor (because half of the Fast Travel destinations are under immediate attack as you arrive).  Kill whatever is attacking you (if any).  I leave my powered armor and sneak to clear the area (this saves the fusion core battery).  I hobble back to my powered armor overloaded with loot.  Once I am back in the powered armor, I am usually unencumbered and I can Fast Travel back to base.
If you want to build settlements with the Minutemen, you will also need Local Leader (2), Medic (1), Cap Collector (2)
When things are darkest, remember the immortal words of the Raider Lieutenant, Bedlam; "I'm Safe In The Light."
**********************CAUTION MILD SPOILERS BELOW:**************************
There were things I did not like about Fallout 4.  I hope Bethesda would consider fixing them for future players.
*There was no way to bury my wife Nora, or bury my neighbors (from before the war).  Adding a graveyard to the game would have been so easy, and leaving their corpses to rot in Vault 111 was a thoughtless oversight.
*When Shaun was terminally ill, why couldn't I just put him back into Cyro-stasis in Vault 111 until the Institute develops a cure.  I went through a heck of a lot more effort to save the little boy Austin Engill (Vault 81) and to save Robert MacCready's son (companion quest) under similar circumstances than I bother with my own boy.  The choices the game gives me concerning my son's illness is inconsistent with other quest line options in the game and inconsistent with what my character already knows is possible.  Given my resources available (I have Science 4 perk, access to the institute scientists, and my Vault-Tec, lab technician, girlfriend Curie), getting the Cyrolab in Vault 111 operational for my boy to use should have been easy.
*Throwing grenades in this game is ridiculous.  I was in the Army and I threw live grenades in training with over 1000 other dumb soldiers and none of us died.  If we were in the Fallout 4 world, you could expect 150 of us would have been dead from our own grenades bouncing back.  Even if you have the Explosives 2 Perk, and you can see the grenade's trajectory before you throw, it can still bounce back (somehow) and kill you.
*Companions are always in the way.  Once I hit level 40, I never used companions because they are so annoying.
But overall, Fallout 4 is an awesome, haunting game, that you will think about for years.

Got this game as a gift from a friend of mine who knows I'm a fan of the series. I am enjoying my time playing around with a heavily modded settlement building system and roaming the wastes, but this is probably the least compelled I've been to actually pursue the story in any of the Fallout games.
For those of you who are fans of the heavy RPG elements and storytelling of New Vegas, the classic Fallout titles, and to a lesser extent, Fallout 3 - you will be disappointed by the dialogue options this game has to offer, as well as a skill tree that suffers from the exact same problem Skyrim had - it is way too easy to become a jack of all trades (and master of everything!) over time due to both the lack of a level cap and the simplifying of the SPECIAL stats/skills/perks progression system. The pacing of the story feels rushed and the lack of dialogue options that actually influence the way events play out, alongside there being hardly any sort of skill point checks, make for ingame conversations that feel like a worse, less interactive, version of those in Mass Effect.
That's actually the most important comment I'd have for those of you on the fence. This game feels more like an open world, first person Mass Effect with survival and base building tacked on, than it does a "proper" Fallout game in terms of mechanics. That being said, I think the worldbuilding is spot on for a Fallout game and for those of you who just want to roam the wastes and soak in the atmosphere, you will find a great sandbox to do it in with this game.
Updates to gunplay and the user interface make it really hard for me to recommend the older Fallout titles over this one to any newcomer of the series on any ground beyond storytelling and depth to RPG mechanics. If you are a huge RPG fan, start with New Vegas. If you are a fan of games like Dying Light, pick this one up first.

Oh, what i wouldn't give to go back to when Fallout 4 was announced and we all still believed the greatest Fallout ever made was coming. Such simple times. I remember how excited I was the day the reveal trailer came out. I remember every second I spent watching the BE3 with my friends and how my excitement grew with every new feature there would be.
- New engine?! (Nah, just an updated creation engine)
- Settlement CREATION?!?!? (Yes, but extremely clunky w/o extreme modding)
- custOMIZABLE WEAPONS OMG!!! ( Honestly, I'm not sure about this but it feels like there are barely any weapons in this compared to New Vegas, and the "unigue" weapons are just normal weapons with different stats)
The gunplay of this game is a significant improvement over NV and FO3 but still isn't nearly as fun as in most FPS games. Yes, I know this is an RPG game, but it falls pretty flat on that aspect as well. Because of the choice to have a fully voiced player (Regardless of this, I still thought Brian, and Courtney were pretty great) many roleplaying aspects were sacrificed. The number of dialogue options is significantly reduced and extremely simplied. (Nearly) Every conversation has the choices of
Down: Yes     Left: Sarcastic/ Alternative Yes    Top: Tell me more, but yes    Right: No (yes)
This ties into another problem with the RPG elements: the
. You pretty much have to be the good guy (until you play Nuka World, where you have to be a bad guy) Unlike New Vegas, where almost every problem seemed to have multiple solutions, most problems in FO4 have to be solved with violence. It's fun the first time, boring every other time. Because of the voiced player cutting out most dialogue options and the removal of skills mean the only special dialogue lines are based on charisma. They are also a random chance of success, meaning you can quicksave/quickload until you get what you want (except for in survival mode) Bethesdaddy also removed the karma system for better or worse. To me, it's not that important, but at least it let you know when you were being a♥♥♥♥♥♥ I remember how I originally thought the replacement of skills and traits with perks was awesome and how "skills are pointless anyway". However, the current system lets you get a god-like character in every playthrough since you can't be locked into a specific playstyle except by choice. Most people like it, but i kind of miss planning out my character and thinking about what perks and skills I was gonna get next.
Now, after complaining about all the cons of the game (I skipped over a few I'm sure, such as lackluster main story), here is why you should play it:

The world building in this game is really quite good. Sometimes i do miss the desolate wasteland of NV, but post-nuclear Boston is filled with tons of interesting characters and fun places to explore. The game definitely has better graphics than it's predecessors (albeit not the best w/o some graphic mods) The power armor in this game is ACTUALLY POWER ARMOR and it makes you feel powerful. I really appreciated the little animations like when taking a stimpak or getting mauled by a deathclaw. The ghouls in this game are actually creepy too, and can be quite a challenge when they gang up on you in the beginning. The companions in this game are really cool in my opinion, especially Piper, Valentine, and Hancock. Dogmeat is an annoying piece of crap who disappears with your stuff and gets in the way, but I still like to use him as a companion. However, the invincibilty of him removes the worry of losing your 4-legged pal, which added some emotional value to FO3. (Also, there isn't much point in stimpaking your companions, since they just get back up later. Hardcore mode is what survival difficulty should have originally been, being an improvement over the NV version. However, it really is hardcore, with no auto healing, fast travel, or saving, so be prepared. Modding in this game is great as it is with all Bethesda RPGs (except for the fact that they made achievements disabled when you mod the game) But seriously, there are some kickass mods either downloadable or being worked on. Personally, I can't wait for
and the Fallout 3 and Fallout NV recreation mods.

All in all, this game is really fun. It falls short in many places but excels in others. The worst part about it is probably knowing that we won't be getting another Fallout for years.

XCOM 2 is the sequel to XCOM: Enemy Unknown.  I played over 1000 hours of the first game, including on my Android device, and it was my favourite game of all time... until now.  If you're looking for negatives, scroll to the bottom.  Otherwise, I'm going to discuss all the things about this game that make it better than its predecessor.  (Other than the procedurally generated maps; the feature I was most excited about before the game launched.  The maps feel handcrafted and still provide near endless variation.)
XCOM 2 is a genuine sequel, not a polished re-skin with a few new buttons.  This game is a sequel in terms of story, your opponents, and even the difficulty level.  For that reason, if you haven't played XCOM: EU, I recommend you begin there.  Despite my experience with the previous game, XCOM 2 destroyed me on my first attempt, at the difficulty level I played most on EU.  I'm thrilled about that because fans like myself can experience the challenge, the rush, the highs and lows of the war, and those moments when everything's so intense that your heart pounds but you keep on playing!
The story and the characters in the campaign have been improved immensely.  The tutorial introduces you to them, and the setting, through a series of story missions that'll make you feel connected to them in a way you never did in XCOM: EU.  As the story goes on, the connection you feel to each character continues to develop, and the story might stay with you for a long time.  In addition, the ending is much more thrilling and rewarding than the end of XCOM: EU--however, this game makes that
ending into a spectacular one, and then goes on to give you an even better ending in XCOM 2!
The strategy layer of the game has been significantly enhanced in XCOM 2 as well.  In the past you could do research and construction however you wanted, but that isn't the case in XCOM 2.  No more watching the hologlobe spin while you pass time at the base either--now the Geoscape is like a board game.  Your decisions on the strategic layer have a major impact on the way the game plays out, and the aliens are also playing their own game against you.  You'll need to adjust your strategy on the fly to counter the aliens' projects and prevent their victory.
Additionally, the tactical gameplay is better than ever--and that's where XCOM has always been strongest.  Many games try to copy the tactical combat of XCOM, and you might hear games described as "like XCOM."  I assure you that having two actions per soldier per turn, and a cover mechanic, DOES NOT qualify a game to be declared "like XCOM."  The number of enemies and their combat abilities, combined with psychological effects your soldiers can suffer, really sets this game apart from imitators.  In XCOM 2, you're fighting to liberate the world from an occupying collective of aliens that has superior technology, and many missions will feel impossible--even with fully trained troops, using the best gear.
Last but not least, the audio in this game is phenomenal!  The cinematic scenes and sound effects are as good as a blockbuster action movie.  The voice acting is impressive, and the dialogue feels natural.  The music enhances every moment of the game; from ramping up the tension in the most threatening combat situations, to relaxing you after a hard-fought battle.
Negatives:
1.  XCOM 2 has some bugs and performance issues at launch, but keeping regular saves and back-up saves will prevent some frustrating issues.  I had one crash during my first 65 hours of play, and the save file got corrupted.  I do not recommend playing in Ironman mode until the game is patched.
2.  Some people don't like the pressure of turn timers on some missions.  I love the timers because the tension is part of what makes XCOM 2 special, but not everyone wants to play a game that requires skill.  Don't worry, however, as there's already a mod to take away the timer if you just can't play the game as it was intended to be played.
3.  It will probably be several years before XCOM 3 comes out.

TLDR: It's better than it was in early access. However, if you havent played Terraria, go play that.
Having finally been released, I'm nonplussed. The game is much more complete as an experience, and has notably changed in terms of depth and direction. There is now a fairly solid story, as well quests that provide meaning to the random environments you're continually thrown into. However, the gameplay is little changed from early access beta. Combat is still awkward and choppy, monsters seem to have little coherence or diversity, let alone any kind of clear typology or sense of structure or logic, and exploring is still essentially a scramble for settlements and loot. Despite all the improvements, I would still heartily recommend Terraria over this to someone interested in 2d minecraft-alikes (minecraftvanias?).
Some Confusion
How does one review an early access game? Is this an impression, a statement of opinion about the direction in which the game is heading? I am supposed to treat this as a product? It's clearly not, hence the early access tag.
In any case, if you haven't played Terraria go play it instead of this. It's cheaper, tighter, more fun and has better netcode, once you work out how to connect to a server. This is just a Terraria world generator with some baseline gear and crafting. The monsters have to be placeholders, as they all look like pokemon and have no biome consistency at all, the worlds are just bottomless terraria maps with random stuff on top, and the gear is very straightforward, consisting of the same suit of armor made of different, better stuff. Its also just as much fun to explore those worlds and stripmine them as it is in Terraria.
Having said that, check back in six months. It could be a completely different game, and chucklefish seems to have a clear direction in mind. Odds are version Rabid Wombat or whatever it's called will be a positive change.

XCOM 2 is largely a refinement of and an advancement on XCOM: Enemy Unknown. It honestly doesn't feel like a full sequel. Feels like XCOM: Enemy Unknown 1.5. But that's not really a bad thing. As mentioned, many things have been refined and streamlined, and there have been a host of new additions that do mix things up to a certain degree. Though yes, at the same time, I must say I am a tad disappointed that things aren't more different.
So, long story short, if you like XCOM: EU you will most probably like XCOM 2 as well. The campaign length for a first run is around 40-50 hours.
Now, the game has some glaring issues. One is optimization. I honestly do not find the graphics to be anything stellar (they don't seem that different from in XCOM EU), but even on the lowest settings I am getting absolutely terrible performance.
Another is from time to time, the game can bug out. I hacked a Sectapod successfully, yet somehow it remains out of my control and kills my troops on the next turn. Then there was once a muton who was actually on the roof, but the graphics made it look like it was at the bottom of the roof. And once my scanning went to -3 days (it just bugged out).
Gameplay wise, too many enemies are just bullet sponges in the mid-to-late game.
Now that I am right at the end of the final mission, I can say that this game suffers the same two issues from XCOM EU.
1) The mid-to-late game is relatively much, much easier than the fiendishly difficult early game.
2) There is no "middle ground" difficulty setting between Veteran (a tad too easy) and Commander (a tad too difficult)
This game is a net recommendation actually but I leave a thumbs down until Firaxis can fix the optimization issues at least.

I guess it's time to add in my two cents into the mix.
Darkest Dungeon is not a game for everyone.
It appeals to old school D&D players like me, many things in this game are based on RNG checks, and most of those will not go your way. Your heroes may get two shot by something ridiculous, and they will be gone forever (unless your lucky with town events). You might lose your whole party and get no loot.
Many people have a problem with this. I don't.
Maybe I'm a masochist.
Or maybe I see the depth of the combat system and how to minimize losses. Learning how classes work, optimizing for team synergy, knowing what supplies to bring, how much of said supplies, taking risky dark runs to get so much loot, and in general getting your perfect team together to go take the fight to the lovecraftian horrors, that's where the real fun of this game is.
The game is rewarding when you stick with it and learn the mechanics. It is going to anger inducing though, make no mistake.
-EDIT-
