Like many of the other reviewers, I'm conflicted about whether I reccomend this game or not. At the start it's very fun and it's a great concept, but in the end there are a few glaring issues with the game:

Buy it when its on sale. The game is a massive overhaul of the former 3D Fallout titles. All actual thinking is removed from the game and now perks mean nothing. Get your overpowered suit of armor 10 minutes in, kill your first deathclaw 12 minutes in. I can't help but ask what is going on in Todd Howard's head. The game revolves around a 3 phase core;
All the "RPG" elements of Fallout are stripped away from the game in favor of a more
representation of combat.
The art style is okay I guess. Some of the locations look bland and boring and quite frankly I prefer the locations from 3 or New Vegas over these. The color choice is honestly quite sketchy at best and at worse just plain boring. It's akin to going outside and looking at dirt, then turning around and looking at a pile of rocks, then turning and looking at a pile of bricks, then turning and looking at a pile of dog♥♥♥♥♥♥ I understand its supposed to be gritty, but couldn't they have made some scenic areas? Something like adding some still functioning neon signs or maybe an area where the vegetation started to regrow? Regardless at its core the game is overall pretty bland on the color choice. Some of the textures look quite hideous for the amount of time and the hardware of todays standards. They don't necessarily detract from the gameplay experience, but when you notice them they do detract from the overall immersion.
Okay, lets talk about the story.
Not a bad premise for the story, but not an original one either
. It's better than being a prisoner who becomes a savior by far, but nothing new on this front. The only problems I have with the story is that it isn't very memorable nor does it have any reprecussions for you ignoring it. You can spend 2000 hours not giving a single ♥♥♥♥ about your
and nothing happens. No synth takeover, nothing. It would have been interesting to have a time limit of sorts to
and if you dont get to
in time then a massive synth incorporation into the society happens. Why this was never thought of or put into the game I'll never know.
Overall the sound design is pretty good. I like the atmosperic sounds of the world and it made me feel more engaged in it. Even the creatures of the world had very wonderful and creepy sounds, I loved it. The guns on the otherhand sounded like... well kinda weak. When I fire a gun in my neck of the woods it makes a loud
, but when I shoot in Fallout 4 it just feels like I'm playing with an
a spring gun. It's unsatisying to hear all these amazing overworld sounds and creature sounds and then when you go to shoot it just feels... meh. In this aspect it makes me feel more obligated to playing a melee character which is really fun. Speaking of which
The combat in the game feels pretty solid, especially the melee parts. Every hit makes nice impact
and its overall an enjoyable experience. The gunplay is very solid too, every shot I can tell exactly where it's going to hit and shooting things is quite a nice experience. The VATS system used in this game is pretty cool, I like how instead of stopping time like some sort of DIO-esque character you instead slow time to slightly faster than a crawl but slower than a second. The killcams also look quite good and allow for some pretty gruesome screenshots. If you want to get this game the best factor of it is the combat hands down. It's not perfect but it's the best its ever been in a Fallout game. The exploration isn't as rewarding as they make it out to be and the randomly generated loot just makes the grind even more of a grind. Adhesive is going to kill your mid to late game if you don't stockpile it as soon as you get started.
I like the idea of crafting upgrades for your weapons and adding say extra damage or extra firing rate give the already lackluster weapons some actual viability on harder difficulties. Of course punching things is the only good meta in the game though and using a suit of power armor just makes the game a cakewalk. I could easily sneak through any area with a power armor and my fists and kill literally anything that moved, breathed, or had a pulse. Giving something that fundamentally broken so early on is a fool hardy move and also given that the combat even on the hardest difficulties is nothing short of♥♥♥♥♥♥easy it makes the fanbase move on to getting mods that increase the difficulty or change the start of the game or the "perk" system.
Alright so let's move on to the meat and potatoes. These aren't perks at all, they're minor passive buffs to stats with specific weapons or with your ability to not eat dogass at picking a lock. The only perk in the entire tree worth getting is Blitz. In fact, its so useful it helped me break through walls and almost broke a quest for me
.
The game at its core is flawed and a mess, however that isn't to say the game is awful. It's an average game full of below average qualities with an above average combat system and a superb sound design. If they would have tried to make the game more like an ACTUAL fallout game (y'know like with choices and stuff) then I think it would have been a far better title. Gutting the perk system and replacing it with this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ized shell ruins the RPG element and basically put it on par with a Call of Duty clone or an MMO but singleplayer only
. The foundation is there but they forgot to put up the walls. And fill in the floors. And put in plumbing. And put in a powergrid. The game falls short on so many levels to its predecesor that honestly I wouldn't even recommend it at all unless you really want to play it for the combat. But then why are you even playing a fallout game if you care about the combat.

It took me a long time to come to terms with the fact that I don't like Fallout 4. I really wanted to, but I just can't.
The world is good and interesting. I like the setting. I also found many of the characters likeable. But that is where the good things end.
The story is insufferable. You are looking for your kidnapped child or to be more precise the poorly built animatronic monstrosity you have somehow convinced yourself is a human child. (Seriously, the baby animation is Twilight levels of creepy wrong.) Everything is connected to this central element. Here is the thing: I have the same emotions towards this baby as any random piece of pre-war junk in the wasteland. No time is spent setting this up. This is not so uncommon, Fallout rarely wastes much time on setting up the macguffin. But a baby is a terrible macguffin. Will not finding it affect the wasteland? Not at all. It is just bad and kills the whole game. Every time you talk to someone the character uses a desperate voice to ask 'have you seen Shaun?', while I could not care less. So no main story line. Some of the sidequests are fun, many are just open world shovelware.
The settlement building is a neat idea, but its hampered by its limitations. There is a ton of DLC to buy if you want a modest amount of customization. Without it you can build a ramshackle shack or another ramshackle shack. And other than tending to a few meters, the survivors you take in have no personality so its hard to be attached to them. The settlement building should be its own game, with characters you can actually care about.
Other than this, the game is a bog standard shooter. I dread to think how it looked if the id team needed to be brought in to polish this up. You aim, shoot, the bad guys fall over. Nothing much to note. Fallout was hardly loved because of its innovative combat, but it seems that it was the focus of 4.
Overall, its a good setting wasted on a thoroughly mediocre game which lacks a heart and sometimes a brain. The protagonist is the least interesting man/woman in the world, almost every single side character has more personality, especially as the limited conversation tree locks you into (a) asking about Shaun helpfully (b) asking about Shaun sarcastically or (c) asking about Shaun angrily. The kid is lucky that the apocalypse happened because the protagonist seem to lack any identity beyond the kid and would have probably gone on to be an insufferable stage parent sans nuclear Armageddon.
However, if you have a weird fascination with dragging typewriters around an irradiated wasteland, this game is sure for you. Otherwise get New Vegas, while it looks uglier (Fallout 4 is no beauty to look at either, especially the main character), it has a heart beyond 'ugh we have to make another Fallout game because we haven't figured out yet how to milk Skyrim until 2277'.
And seriously, Shaun can get nuked. Damned creepy robo-baby.

It says I've only played for a little over an hour on steam but I owned it on PS4 since it came out over a year ago. Since then I have gotten all the way to the two Princes, so I have some knowlege.
That out of the way, Holy Cow this game is amazing. Take all the best things of Dark Souls and Dark Souls II and put them together to get this game. The gameplay is solid and masochistically challenging, with the usual cryptic storytelling (or lack thereof) that we've grown accustomed to in our SoulsBorne journey. It is a hard game, it is unforgiving for simple mistakes; you must become an expert at your particular fighting style or which there are many.
PvP is a death sentence for new players and a mental punishment for the adept, where more souls are on the line for you to lose and them to take. You never quite know when your next human enemy will pop up, and it could come at any time.
Gameplay aside, this game is gorgeous inside and out. The story is captivating and tragic, the characters are stalwart in this harsh wastelad of a once-great kingdom, but broken inside as you'll soon find out; and there are a pluthera of characters for you to run into, fight beside, or fight against.
The art in this game is stunning. The attention to detail is beyond amazing with everything from distant objects and backgrounds to little hanging bits and bobbles hanging off your character's armour. The armour is gorgeous and with great variety, everything from leather tunics to giant suits hewn from solid stone. Along with that, the weapons share in their diversity and beauty, from small and fast rapiers to the infamous Ultra-Greatswords, each with their own details and story.
I am a huge fan of this game and series as a whole, playing from Demon souls to Bloodborne to Dark Souls III, and I cannot recommend this game enough. If you crave a challenge, are willing to be smacked down time and time again on oyur quest to the end of the game, and maybe have a bit of a masochist in you, this game is definitely for you.

I am so pleased to give them thumbs up to this game. I was so stoked to get my hands on this new reiteration of the XCOM franchise, and after finishing the campaign, I am very happy to repport that 2K & Firaxis took it to a whole new level. They improved almost every aspect of the game, cutting off the unnecessary ones and gave us even more control over everything. That is how a sequel should be done! I remember my initial dissatisfaction at the delay in the launch date, but my, now I am so happy that they did, cause all the extra game polish worked wonders!
XCOM2 is all about survival of the human race. The canon story behind XCOM Enemy Unknown/Within is that we lost horribly and the aliens decided to take the role of "benevolent" rulers who are constantly improving and "helping" humanity. Pockets of resistance across the world still remain and one of them is led by none other than "Central" - our trusty right hand, office Bradford from XCOM1. He goes on a hunt to discover YOU - yes, you, Commander are in the game! And so it begins...
In true fashion for my reviews, I will take a look at the good and the bad.
The Good:
1. Extremely immersive gameplay. To me, this point outweighs every single other. You will get immersed in the story, you will care heaps about the world you are living in, you will care about your soldiers as if they are your children, you will feel happy when all of them make it back and sad if someone gets injured or doesn't live through a mission. You will remember and tell their stories, and I can assure you, there will be tons of stories to tell.
2. Amazing story, with great buildup, that only gets better till the final showdown. You will have full CLOSURE in XCOM2, and you will have a lot of fun finding out what happens to you, Bradford, the Council Leader, the old team, new team, everyone! Hell they even tell you why a Sectopod is called like that!!!
3. A soundtrack elevated to the next level. Every single song will get you very pumped up and ready to go kick some alien♥♥♥♥♥♥ Turn up the volume, cause you are in for a treat!
4. Customization brought to a whole new level - every single thing is customizable now. You can totally expect to spend an inordinate amount of time just making soldier(s) look the way you want. You can fully customize:
4.1. Your soldiers - name, sex, race, nationality, voice, posture, armor types, accessories, colors, etc. You can literally do everything.
4.2. Their weapons - as in XCOM1, you have 3 tiers of shotguns, heavy guns, sniper rifles, pistols, and assault rifles that can be named, colored, improved with loot you find on the field, which leads to a ton of new combinations that fit your taste or vision of how the soldier should play out.
4.3. Their armor - once again, you have 3 tiers of armor, which is extremely slick and aesthetically pleasing. In XCOM2 you get to kick♥♥♥♥♥♥and look good doing it. What's more to ask? To make things even better, armor types of the same tier don't get obsolete - and you can even make experimental armors to boot!
5. The new Avenger, the better take on the world map, and the improved research and engineering – you are no longer forced into using the same best strategy over and over again. The Avenger is your base, and even though it is very much like the old one with levels and stuff to clear before building, it is mobile, which lets you get creative. The world map is your playground where you and the aliens both have your goals – they must complete the avatar project, you must prevent them from doing so by making contacts with other resistance cells, hitting them where it hurts, choosing in what way to hinder them, and so on. The research and engineering have seen marked improvement, and you are even allowed to do meta projects that are not mandatory, but can give you better gear, ammunition, powerful psi abilities, bestow skills from other classes to a certain soldier, and so on and so forth. This gives you a plethora of ways to approach the game!
6. The graphics – XCOM2 is undoubtedly gorgeous. Streets, signs, the skyline, everything looks amazing.
7. The Combat – the combat remains very much the same as it was in XCOM1, but there have been a lot of small tweaks to make it more fluid. A lot of actions that used to end your soldier’s turn in XCOM1 are now just half the cost – most notably the reload, which now means you can reload and then shoot! Add to that the whole new concealment mechanic where it is actually YOU stalking the aliens!
8. The enemy variety – there are even more enemies in the game, ready to surprise you and make your life a living hell. Every enemy in this game comes with own set of skills and own danger level, and you will have a lot of “fun” discovering who can do what. And when you think you know everything, the enemy will suddenly use some secondary skill you never know he had… like that time a Muton charged my soldier and melee attacked her. And I was expecting shots or grenades…
9. The soldier class variations – you may be disappointed to learn that you only have 4 main soldier classes (plus a secret one that I am not going to spoil for you), unlike the crazy amount that the Long War mod introduced, but don’t hate on the game just yet. Each class can be customized with skills (some that even belong to other classes!), psi abilities, weapons and weapon mods to such extent, that you can barely recognize your starting guy.
10. The mission timers – so many people hate them, and it is understandable, but as an XCOM veteran, I welcome them. They give a sense of urgency and prevent cheap half move/overwatch tactics. And if you still think this is a bad thing, read No. 11!
11. Modding – as Jake Solomon himself said, once you buy the game, it is yours to do whatever you please with it. Less than a week after release, there are already a good number of mods for you to choose whether to use or not, including ones that extend or flat out remove the mission timers people hate so much.
12. The line of sight indicator – now you always know whether you are going to be able to shoot an enemy if you move to a certain position. While the camera could be a bit finicky to position in order to see whether the cross appears or not, whaddya know – there is a camera mod that helps with this!
The Bad:
1. Bugs, bugs, bugs – XCOM1 was no stranger to bugs on release as well, but so far I haven’t had gamebreaking ones, and 95% of them can be solved with a simple save and reload. Unless you are playing Ironman, you have at least 3 mission autosave points to return to.
2. Only 3 tiers of weapons and armor – while I don’t terribly mind, the Long War team was employed to help 2K/Firaxis, and they did create number of additional weapon and armor tiers for XCOM Long War… I guess it just wasn’t a priority here. I am quite sure there will be mods to remedy this, though.
3. The learning curve – XCOM2 is a whole new XCOM, with many new things for you to discover and learn. It can be quite daunting of a task for a new player and even for veterans with hundreds of hours of XCOM1 under their belts. The game will also force you to break a good number of old habits, which can be quite disconcerting for some.
4. Framerate is all over the place – many other people have found this to be an inconvenience and it is fair to point it out.
5. Hefty hardware requirements – for a turn based strategy game, the recommended specs for the game are actually quite hefty.
Conclusion: XCOM2 is a marked improvement over XCOM1 in every feasible aspect. They learned from XCOM1, cut all the fat and put even more meat where it was sorely needed. 2K & Firaxis took a game that is already awesome and brought it to a new level of brilliance. This game is worth every cent of its purchase price, and then some. Once all the bugs and oversights are dealt with, you will be in for the best combination of turn-based/management/tactical experience to date.

Boring, generic shooter. These are the words that perfectly describe this free-to-play shooter.
This game has no depth to it other than walking and shooting, it doesn't try to do anything new or interesting. It plays it safe by having semi-acceptable netcode, little to no recoil and accuracy loss, basic maps (one of which comes straight from alliance of valiant arms), and a cash-shop system that I am fond of seeing not currently filled with extremely expensive guns that take either your wallet to get or 300 hours.
It's an alright-ish multiplayer shooter, but it gets old faster than the time it takes to download it.
The graphics are kind of passable, but with the unreal engine 3 it's not that hard. It looks like something out of 2010. I will commend that the game runs perfectly with zero stuttering or frame drops on it's maximum settings. Besides that it's not a great looking game.
Overall, if you've played any classic free-to-play multiplayer shooter around 2010 or beyond and you see this game, skip it. It's nothing that will blow you away or be interesting long enough to justify wasting your time downloading and playing it. You'll likely get a kick out of it for a few hours and simply leave it installed collecting dust on your drive, or quickly uninstall it and forget it existed.
The developers can still make this game into something more than a stiff, poor mans cs:go clone, but will they? We'll find out in a year or so. Right now it's a rinse and repeat shooter that's duller than the knives in my grandmothers kitchen.

So right from the beginning when I heard about this game I was excited, a lot of good improvements were shown in the many, many videos cranked out by the development team. But unfortunately maybe a little more time should have been put into developing the game than making videos about it. The game (at launch, it's possible many of these bugs will be fixed on a later date after posting this) is absolutely riddled with game-breaking bugs, the biggest being some severe frame-rate loss on scene changes (eg switching from world view to ship view) as well as at the start and end of levels. Frequently the UI will bug out and perform an action you didn't give. The story is definitely an interesting one, unfortunately I can't go into too much detail without ruining it, suffice to say it's worth the money in that department.
Going into detail like I said my biggest complaint was with the bugs. Frequently enemies will be able to fire through, or even in some cases move through floors, walls, etc that have yet to be destroyed. This can be thoroughly irritating on some missions where you
your in cover only to discover an ADVENT MEC under you firing through the floor. While choosing a target you frequently end up having the game skip the targeting phase as well as the confirmation only to fire at a target you don't want to, or use an item somewhere you wouldn't approve of. (For example using a med kit on a solider who's only lost one hit point with 11 more to go.) The frame rate loss gets irritating between loading screens and transitioning between the world map and the
display but in my experience it's not something that effects game play, just makes load times a little longer.
If you liked the difficulty in the previous games, get ready for more. I ended up having to turn the difficulty down on my first play through because of the new units and abilities. The vast majority of ADVENT forces posses AoE attacks that take two turns to 'cast' but once you know how they work are fairly easy to avoid. Your own forces, until they level up are fairly useless but again, once you level up and get to know the way things work can be used to astonishing effect.
Graphics and Customization have both received a very impressive overhaul. The cut scenes seem to be slightly off on the audio sync but it's negligible. It's about what you'd expect graphically for the time. Customization options have been expanded significantly over the first game, allowing you to pick the colors of your character's armor, the style of the equipment, personality of the troops (which effects their lines in combat and stance) as well as voice, sex, race, pretty much whatever you please. Some options are rank-locked but it doesn't take too long to unlock those options. You can also use the "Character Pool" option to import and export your own characters, as well as create your own.
All in all it's an enjoyable game, the randomization of the levels keeps it from getting stale too quickly but if you drag-out your game you will find yourself getting bored. Can't wait for the expansion packs to come out.

I think this is my first Steam review. I'm posting it because of how much I love this game. I bounced, hard, off Demon's Souls way back in 2009, and after breaking one of my PS3 controllers in frustration over one particular part swore to never touch a game like it again. I skipped Dark Souls, Dark Souls II, Bloodborne and Dark Souls III, dismissing them as an exercise in stress and gratuitous difficulty, not fit for my goals as a relaxing and enjoyable way to spend my time.
However, I also like watching Let's Plays, particularly the Game Grumps. To make this short, watching the Grumps play Dark Souls III made me want to try playing it. I had to stop watching the series because I realized I didn't want them to "spoil" anything else for me. I found DSIII on sale for $20, and thought, "what the hell." I figured I'd get a handful of hours of it at least.
It's now been about a week and I've spent every moment of free time playing it, and the rest thinking about it. I discovered that, far from being "gratuitously difficult and unforgiving," the designers of this game are actually quite forgiving, they just refuse to insult your ability and intelligence. They demand more of you. They want to encourage you to improve, practice, and then feel that immense satisfaction that comes from conquering a tough challenge. They aren't your enemies, they're your friends on your little journey of video game self-discovery.
I now regret missing out on this series until now. DSIII has swiftly become one of my favorite games of all time on a list that has seen barely any movement in many years.
The amount of depth in this game is incredible. The amount of detail and things to find and explore is ridiculous. The combat system is polished, gratifying and exacting. I love everything about it. If you're on the fence about the Souls games, don't be. Get this game and play it. Just remember and accept that you will die, that you will be POed, and that you will have to repeat things, but each time you will learn something new. Your character isn't the only one improving: you are too. Treat it like a sport as much as a game and PRACTICE. Practice against the tough enemies until they're kittens. Practice against the bosses until they fall. Find a playstyle you enjoy and stick with it.
This is perhaps the most rewarding game you'll ever play, but there is no reward without hardship. Enjoy it.
P.S. if this gives you any indication of how obsessed I am with this game: I've been looking forward to Divinity: Original Sin II since it was announced. It released yesterday and I tried to play it but couldn't. I quit and played DSIII instead, because nothing is more fun or interesting to me than this game.

Spiral knights is one of those super casual games that really aren't meant to be taken seriously. Its your typical dungeon crawler you pick up and play with say, your significant other who isn't that hardcore into gaming. The story line is rather dull and uninteresting, so don't really worry if you missed something, all the game is about is reaching the core in long run anyway. Missions spoon feed you half decent equipment, but you can easily craft your own gear if you wanna get ahead of the curve, which, yet again, really isn't anything intensive. Combat is just right click your way to victory as enemies are pretty easy to read.
If you're looking for something casual you don't need to invest a whole lotta time into, or just something to play with that non-gamer significant other, Spiral Knights is a fair choice.
If you want something more hardcore, or even dedicated, I'd give this one a pass.

You guys...don't listen to all these naysayers.
This is an excellent game.
I will admit, the beginning of the game is probably the hardest part. Although, I say this without having actually gone to the final dungeons yet. The trick is to spend your money wisely and to try and build up your town as quickly as possible. Once you start racking up some heirlooms to spend on buildings in town and gather some extra money, you can start upgrading your characters regularly. I would highly recommend upgrading the stagecoach first so that you can recruit more characters more often. After that, I focused on the guild and the blacksmith discounts heavily. Once those are upgraded to a higher level, you can beef up your characters without spending very much money at all!
It seems like a lot of people aren’t approaching this game from a tactical standpoint which is entirely necessary in order to be successful. I would say in the last 20 Dungeons that I've attempted, I didn't have any characters come close to going over their stress limit. There are plenty of characters that heal stress in the middle of the dungeon and that's key. The Jester has become one of my favorite characters simply because he can heal stress. This also means you should be targeting the most dangerous enemies at the beginning of the battle, which tend to be those who inflict a lot of stress damage. When you're coming out of dungeons without having to send your characters to heal their stress you can save a ton of money.
If you want to make this game more enjoyable, then look up a guide of what curios require which items based on location. You can save yourself a hell of a lot of headaches by doing this.
People are right. This game does take a lot of grinding. But there's something satisfying about being able to absolutely ruin enemies that were previously ruining you.
PROS:
+ The story is fun. The monologues have great voice acting and add to the atmosphere. I find myself quoting them whenever I play the game.
+ It’s challenging. I get tired of people giving games a bad review because it's hard (Dark Souls etc.). Is this game unfair at times? Absolutely. But never so much that it made me want to stop playing.
+ There are lots of characters with lots of abilities. You will quickly learn which trinkets work best with which character and which characters form the best group for that particular area.
+ There is very little more satisfying than a critical hit in this game. ASTONISHING!
+ I would consider this game casual. I play it while I'm watching sports or movies all the time. It doesn't take all of your attention all the time. You can take breaks during the action.
+ The artwork is absolutely beautiful for those who enjoy comic book art.
CONS:
+ Can come off a little bit repetitive at times because of the grinding. If you're grinding intelligently then you can rack up a lot of money fairly quickly.
+ Without a guide on inspecting curios, you're going to have a hell of a time. They can inflict a lot of stress or negative attributes to your character. Sometimes it's just better to leave them alone.
+ The boss fights can seem overwhelming at times, but if you really think, you can find a good strategy. One thing to remember about this game is that getting to zero HP does not kill you. In fact hovering just above zero HP is sometimes all you can do with certain bosses and that's OK. I think some of us are trained to panic when our characters get close to zero HP, but that's not a huge issue in this game.
If you're not sure about this game, then wait for a discount. But don't let all these people tell you it's a broken game just because it's hard. Be ready to play for many hours, but don't get the discouraged. Find good tactics and put them to use. You got this.

You guys...don't listen to all these naysayers.
This is an excellent game.
I will admit, the beginning of the game is probably the hardest part. Although, I say this without having actually gone to the final dungeons yet. The trick is to spend your money wisely and to try and build up your town as quickly as possible. Once you start racking up some heirlooms to spend on buildings in town and gather some extra money, you can start upgrading your characters regularly. I would highly recommend upgrading the stagecoach first so that you can recruit more characters more often. After that, I focused on the guild and the blacksmith discounts heavily. Once those are upgraded to a higher level, you can beef up your characters without spending very much money at all!
It seems like a lot of people aren’t approaching this game from a tactical standpoint which is entirely necessary in order to be successful. I would say in the last 20 Dungeons that I've attempted, I didn't have any characters come close to going over their stress limit. There are plenty of characters that heal stress in the middle of the dungeon and that's key. The Jester has become one of my favorite characters simply because he can heal stress. This also means you should be targeting the most dangerous enemies at the beginning of the battle, which tend to be those who inflict a lot of stress damage. When you're coming out of dungeons without having to send your characters to heal their stress you can save a ton of money.
If you want to make this game more enjoyable, then look up a guide of what curios require which items based on location. You can save yourself a hell of a lot of headaches by doing this.
People are right. This game does take a lot of grinding. But there's something satisfying about being able to absolutely ruin enemies that were previously ruining you.
PROS:
+ The story is fun. The monologues have great voice acting and add to the atmosphere. I find myself quoting them whenever I play the game.
+ It’s challenging. I get tired of people giving games a bad review because it's hard (Dark Souls etc.). Is this game unfair at times? Absolutely. But never so much that it made me want to stop playing.
+ There are lots of characters with lots of abilities. You will quickly learn which trinkets work best with which character and which characters form the best group for that particular area.
+ There is very little more satisfying than a critical hit in this game. ASTONISHING!
+ I would consider this game casual. I play it while I'm watching sports or movies all the time. It doesn't take all of your attention all the time. You can take breaks during the action.
+ The artwork is absolutely beautiful for those who enjoy comic book art.
CONS:
+ Can come off a little bit repetitive at times because of the grinding. If you're grinding intelligently then you can rack up a lot of money fairly quickly.
+ Without a guide on inspecting curios, you're going to have a hell of a time. They can inflict a lot of stress or negative attributes to your character. Sometimes it's just better to leave them alone.
+ The boss fights can seem overwhelming at times, but if you really think, you can find a good strategy. One thing to remember about this game is that getting to zero HP does not kill you. In fact hovering just above zero HP is sometimes all you can do with certain bosses and that's OK. I think some of us are trained to panic when our characters get close to zero HP, but that's not a huge issue in this game.
If you're not sure about this game, then wait for a discount. But don't let all these people tell you it's a broken game just because it's hard. Be ready to play for many hours, but don't get the discouraged. Find good tactics and put them to use. You got this.

Spiral Knights is a good idea of a game, however the execution of the game and the later installments made to said game make it not as recommended as most of the community might make you think. I will not be absoulutely negative in this review, frankly because I've played more than enough time on this game (200+ Hours) and I enjoyed a majority of said time spent. It was fun. But now, I honestly can never go back to this game, now that I've taken a long hard look at it after some experience playing it and taking a few years of a break away from it. I realized that this game is great sounding on paper, and the execution was probably spot on at the beginning, but as Sega bought the license and copyright to Spiral Knights, you could say it sort of went a little downhill. It became pay to win rather than a good experience for gamers, and to be honest, I fell into the trap and put a lot of money into the game, not an insane amount but still a lot.
When I was playing the game, if you didn't have money to speed up the process, you we're endlessly grinding for materials you needed to upgrade. Depending on your luck, it would last from 30 minutes to several hours just to get that ONE item you need for crafting. It's tedious and repetitive and overall, negative. Another negative is no real FUN minigames to play. The only side things you could do we're play PvP or play a rehashed version of Bomberman, which doesn't really handle all that well. Two important negatives are the gameplay and the soundtrack. I barely remember any tracks from this game, and some just sound like generic music, give or take. Also, the gameplay feels sluggish, and at it's worst, laggy. Also, there are some really annoying difficulty spikes in this game, such as the second boss where you are forced to use shadow weapons or else you lose ultimately.
There isn't that much you can do in terms of defense and dodging. For example, there isn't a stand-alone dodge that you can use on a basis. This makes bullet-hell bosses and levels incredibly frustrating to push through, especially in a group. You have a shield, sure, but that won't last long, especially since for me, it was always easy to bust through for enemies, even upgraded. Sometimes you even got shield-locked by enemies who constantly attack you. Enviornments are a little dull to an extent, and even sometimes there's too much stuff happening on screen, causing way too much lag which might get you booted from the game, like I did several times. Not like there really was much to do in this game anyway. In fact, as the months went on, I found myself at the end bored because there wasn't really that much content to keep me entertained for as long as I thought, roughly around a few maps and the occasional boss here and then. They have tried to supply us with updates with new content and the such, but even then, it just isn't enough to keep me around longer. Especially that ludicrous dlc or "packs" that they're giving out now, costing far too much than it's actual value. Basically, Capcom level dlc. Would you pay $40 for one armor set and a few items in the game? If you said yes, you really don't value your money as much as you should be.
Last but not least, the servers. How do the servers of Spiral Knights hold up? To be honest, they're kinda bad, especially when they are over-populated. If I wanted a lagless experience, I had to go on some of the barren servers. If you decide to join a populated server, prepare for everyone to lag walk, especially in the central district. This game cannot handle so many players at once if the servers are bad. If they manage to fix the servers and give us plenty of more content, I might look back for some revelations. But for now, that's all the negatives. Let's move on to the positives!
I had a lot of fun with this game with my friends. It was indeed fun to team up on missions together and leveling up your armor and weapons feels good. You can feel a difference in power between weapons and armor and their levels respectibly, regarding the shield. Once you have the materials and money for a new weapon, it feels rewarding to make it and use it. Busting up a monster is fun, especially a boss. The enemies have some variety to them and some are pretty challenging to beat, which is cool. The combat, although sluggish, is pretty solid, if it doesn't lag, ugh. Those are pretty much all the positive I can really think of. I'm not even going to mention the story, because let's be honest: Do any players of Spiral Knights really care for the story at all? Nope, because it's too boring for me to care about and so generic that if this story was in a bad triple AAA game these days, it would fit right in.
----Final Verdict----
5/10 [Average]

After playing Commander/Ironman for 15 hours and constantly getting my butt kicked because I just wasn't good enough I dropped down to Veteran/Ironman. 7 hours in and I'm doing great. No deaths, mag and gauss weapons, predator armor. I'm feeling pretty confident. And then I go on a dark VIP extraction mission and it all goes to hell. A bug treats the mission as failed after I destroyed the VIP's car even though I have him over my shoulder 30 squares away. Then the game calls in reinforcements right on the evac zone in back to back turns. Even though I could have killed them the game treats the zone as overrun and moves it to a place that I can't physically get to in the time left. So that's it. My squad is captured and there is nothing I can do. So my best run is now over and I'm questioning why do I even want to try again when next time something worse could happen 20 hours in.
I'm sure Firaxis is trying to fix these bugs but it is just really disappointing to see a game that was in development for so long and even delayed multiple times is still released in this state. Then again, I guess that is just the norm for video games nowadays.
** UPDATE on February 27th, 2016 **
So I have beaten XCOM 2 on Veteran/Ironman difficulty and it took about 28 hours. I went through the game being much more cautious then in my previous attempts. Sometimes I did not attempt a gorilla ops mission that would have given me the best reward because it had something to do with evac and I just didn't want to risk the game bugging out and me losing a squad again.
While there were a few bugs here and there (enemies suspended in mid air after I destroyed the floor beneath them, somehow triggering pods when I couldn't see the aliens but they could magically see me, kill zone not triggering on enemies that clearly moved, mutons seeing me through a door and throwing a grenade at me) the game was rather uneventful.
The problem I now have with the game is that its difficulty snowballed and didn't push me to experiment with my tactics. Once my soldiers levelled up it was hard not taking them on missions and levelling up replacements because the aliens simply did too much damage. Also my tactic of bring at least two grenadiers (and some soldiers in amor suits with rocket launchers) got boring pretty quick. The problem was whenever I tried to deviate from it by not using my grenadiers or holding them back to the end of the turn I found that I just didn't have the fire power. The game seems really balanced around AoE/shredding damage and killing the aliens before they get any shots on you especially because of the aggressive timers which force you into combat.
The missions also felt more repetitive than XCOM 1. The procedurally generated maps were great. I never really felt that I knew exactly was coming next but the missions were always the same. The guerrilla ops barely changed. The retaliation missions were always the same and you knew exactly when they were coming. The alien facilities were almost identical. The exact same tactics worked on every single one. I was bored my alien facilities by the third one and only did them to lower the avatar project to stall for more time to get supplies. In XCOM 1, looking back with my rose coloured glasses, the randomness of the alien attacks I feel like I enjoyed more. The different types of alien crafts, the landings versus shoot downs, the terror missions which you sometimes didn't see coming.
Also story missions felt better spaced out in XCOM 1. In XCOM 2 I probably went 12 hours between story missions because after the black site there was nothing pushing me on. I literally had taken out every single alien facility on the planet before I attempted a story mission. There was no tech or advancements behind those missions on then the next story mission to eventually get you the final mission.
All of this sounds really negative but I did enjoy a lot of the game.
- The geoscape was great. Tough choices all around. I felt it dragged the game on a little bit because it was hard to get the supplies needed to upgrade everything to tier 3 so I definitely killed time for a month just waiting for attacks because I didn't want to attempt any story missions.
- There definitely were some missions where even with what I feel are my OP tactics of never-ending explosives and mimic bacons I did feel like I was just walking over the aliens.
- The character customization really drew me in. There were so many storylines of all my soldiers and their amazing exploits that are all just inside my head. The ability to customize every character ahead of time and just have them randomly showed up really pulled me in.
On the whole as a die-hard XCOM fan I did enjoy it and I'll probably come back in 2-3 months when some DLC and patches have come out and make my Commander/Ironman attempt. But I am very afraid that I'm just going to have to resort to my same boring tactics again. I'll probably make a couple of attempts at different tactics, maybe rush psionics instead of mag weapons or something but I'm just a bit worried that the game at higher difficulties just isn't balanced for that.

I wanted to give Darkest Dungeon a recommendation, but the make or break for the game is this: it is often woefully unfair.
There's a lot to love about it. It's unique, it allows for a lot of strategy and decisions of every kind really have weight in DD. The art style fits the tone, the tone suits the gameplay, and the gameplay is taxing and demands your attention--you won't last an hour approaching it flippantly.
Randomly generated dungeon layouts and encounters keep you on your toes and make you ask yourself whether you're willing to chance the next room and possible death or retreat to live another day. It's a stressful game, in the way that playing Dark Souls without a guide or wiki is stressful. In the same way, the difficulty makes success, however fleeting, rewarding and exhilarating.
Darkest Dungeon is a really promising title, but the real killer is that you're assaulted at every turn by aggravating percentages and enemy abilities and attacks that always make you feel like you're a step behind. Not only this, but you can never get a step ahead or even keep pace, because skill improvements and equipment upgrades cost substantial amounts of coin--coin that you'll need to be able to provision your party every time you enter a dungeon.
The first character you get is a burden because no matter how many times you start a new game, he'll always have sticky fingers and pilfer loot for himself for the first three-ish dungeons you enter when you're already desperate for startup cash.
Beyond this initial hindrance, you'll find the percentage-chance nature of your abilities to be incredibly frustrating when you find your party missing attack after attack despite good odds and good strategy. A single round of whiffed actions can leave your party in shambles as your foes relentlessly assault you with impunity.
For me personally, progress has been so little and so late that the game goes beyond its intention. The game does a great job of punishing foolishness and lack of foresight, but even when you've checked all your boxes and covered your bases, you'll get backhanded anyways.

The atmosphere in this game is amazing. If you like Lovecraft you'll love this game. Friends I have who don't generally like turn based RPGs still like this game. Combat is fast and action packed. When you press attack you get immediate satisfaction. Skills and heroes are varied and so are bosses (8 bosses + 2 mini bosses + final mission mini bosses and bosses).
RNG is utilized to its fullest to make every dungeon potentially dangerous and to keep tension up. You can never feel completely safe and the awesome narrator will remind you of this. A couple of crits in a row can totally tun the battle around, be it to your favour or detriment. In tense fights when your hero gets stresed out but become vigorous rather than afflicted (strong buff rather than severe nerf) you can feel the stress relief yourself.
I see a lot of negative reviews focusing on the length of the game calling it a "grind". Let me compare it to a soccer game: In those games you can usually change the length of a match and usualy also the number of matches per season to fit different players. You can't do that in this game but you wouldn't call playing matches in a soccer game a "grind", after all that's what you bought the game to do.
Beating a dungeon takes around 30 min. Beating the final boss (ie completing the game) takes around 60 dungeons. 100% completion (except the 104 weeks achievement) takes around 90 weeks and you have to beat the game once first (to unlock "new game plus"). Is this too long? It is of course up to personal preference. I think there's plenty of content to justify 30 hours. Heck, I'm still playing it after 150 hours and that's excluding all the time I played during the alpha.
Just like in many sports games the management aspect is not very big. It is all about dungeon runs. If you don't like doing dungeon runs you should not buy this game. Some peole continue to go into dungeons even after they have beaten and upgraded everything just for the fun of doing them. About 4% of players have made it to week 104 (104 dungeon runs in a single game).
Some people list money management as a negative. I actually think it is a positive. Having a lack of resources adds to the tension and it forces you to take risks. Do you go for that last treasure chest? Do you dare bringing a high stress hero into the dungeon in hopes of removing it for free with hero skills? It of course punishes those who refuse to (or can't) learn money and risk management, but since there is only one difficulty setting you can't satisfy everyone. Some people will find this aspect too easy and some will find it too hard. There's no vac ban for cheating though and you can mod the game to be easier too if you want.

For anyone who has played a Fallout game you'll notice a LOT of changes from Fallout NV & Fallout 3. There is an entirely new crafting system for modifying both weapons & armour. There is also a game changing mechanic of creating settlements (Towns). The base system for settlements is pretty dissapointing. If you become familiar with mods then you'll find that you can fix so much that Bethesda did not include.
Overall, I do recommend this game as I have sunken so many hours into this game and enjoyed a majority of them.
This game has a lot of potential (probably all of its playability after 1 playthrough) with the modding system.
If you do not want any hassle with modding and messing around with files then you'll most likely do a maximum of 2 playthroughs. With mods you'll probably get well over 4 vastly increasing area sizes, guns, NPC's and pretty much everything.
Buy Fallout 4 for the experience even if you don't care for modding. Try to get it on sale for around £20 though.
The DLC is only worth getting on sale too.

After the first day or two it starts getting boring. Every player seems to be running solo. It's definitely a multi-player game, but the "multiple" players are all running by themselves. It's extremely hard to chat with others; most people don't reply, and most people don't want to play with you. The game is structured to heavily influence solo-play. The failure of this game is lack of community. There's no group feature in the game. You cannot party up with other players; all you can do is follow them around and add to friends list. There are "clubs" in the game, but all you do in a club is build things together. There's very little benefits to being in a club, since anyone can join a club's world to run around in it. The only real benefit to being in a club is being able to have the club chat. This game seems like alpha or beta. It should not have been released. After you reach level 8 it seems there's no drive in the game anymore. When I was level 15 or so, I thought "why am I even trying to level up? What's the point?" I don't see anything end-game that's worth the time and effort to level up, or continue spending time playing this game. The developers did a great job at creating a game that takes a long time to level up and reach max "mastery points" but the reward for all of your hard work is not that great. After spending nearly 40 hours playing this in the past 7-10 days, I feel like I havent achieved anything. I feel emptiness-- like I wasted all of my time and didn't accomplish anything. I really came into this game wanting to play with other people, but this is not the game for that. Overall I'm very disappointed and cannot recommend this to others. I really want to like the game, but as time went on I realized that I don't. It's cool to run around and check out what other players built (for 20 minutes or so) but the time required to build awesome stuff w/ no reward is not worth the effort (for me anyway).  If you're looking for a MMO where you actually interact with other players and play with other people, this is not the game for you.

Buy it when its on sale. The game is a massive overhaul of the former 3D Fallout titles. All actual thinking is removed from the game and now perks mean nothing. Get your overpowered suit of armor 10 minutes in, kill your first deathclaw 12 minutes in. I can't help but ask what is going on in Todd Howard's head. The game revolves around a 3 phase core;
All the "RPG" elements of Fallout are stripped away from the game in favor of a more
representation of combat.
The art style is okay I guess. Some of the locations look bland and boring and quite frankly I prefer the locations from 3 or New Vegas over these. The color choice is honestly quite sketchy at best and at worse just plain boring. It's akin to going outside and looking at dirt, then turning around and looking at a pile of rocks, then turning and looking at a pile of bricks, then turning and looking at a pile of dog♥♥♥♥♥♥ I understand its supposed to be gritty, but couldn't they have made some scenic areas? Something like adding some still functioning neon signs or maybe an area where the vegetation started to regrow? Regardless at its core the game is overall pretty bland on the color choice. Some of the textures look quite hideous for the amount of time and the hardware of todays standards. They don't necessarily detract from the gameplay experience, but when you notice them they do detract from the overall immersion.
Okay, lets talk about the story.
Not a bad premise for the story, but not an original one either
. It's better than being a prisoner who becomes a savior by far, but nothing new on this front. The only problems I have with the story is that it isn't very memorable nor does it have any reprecussions for you ignoring it. You can spend 2000 hours not giving a single ♥♥♥♥ about your
and nothing happens. No synth takeover, nothing. It would have been interesting to have a time limit of sorts to
and if you dont get to
in time then a massive synth incorporation into the society happens. Why this was never thought of or put into the game I'll never know.
Overall the sound design is pretty good. I like the atmosperic sounds of the world and it made me feel more engaged in it. Even the creatures of the world had very wonderful and creepy sounds, I loved it. The guns on the otherhand sounded like... well kinda weak. When I fire a gun in my neck of the woods it makes a loud
, but when I shoot in Fallout 4 it just feels like I'm playing with an
a spring gun. It's unsatisying to hear all these amazing overworld sounds and creature sounds and then when you go to shoot it just feels... meh. In this aspect it makes me feel more obligated to playing a melee character which is really fun. Speaking of which
The combat in the game feels pretty solid, especially the melee parts. Every hit makes nice impact
and its overall an enjoyable experience. The gunplay is very solid too, every shot I can tell exactly where it's going to hit and shooting things is quite a nice experience. The VATS system used in this game is pretty cool, I like how instead of stopping time like some sort of DIO-esque character you instead slow time to slightly faster than a crawl but slower than a second. The killcams also look quite good and allow for some pretty gruesome screenshots. If you want to get this game the best factor of it is the combat hands down. It's not perfect but it's the best its ever been in a Fallout game. The exploration isn't as rewarding as they make it out to be and the randomly generated loot just makes the grind even more of a grind. Adhesive is going to kill your mid to late game if you don't stockpile it as soon as you get started.
I like the idea of crafting upgrades for your weapons and adding say extra damage or extra firing rate give the already lackluster weapons some actual viability on harder difficulties. Of course punching things is the only good meta in the game though and using a suit of power armor just makes the game a cakewalk. I could easily sneak through any area with a power armor and my fists and kill literally anything that moved, breathed, or had a pulse. Giving something that fundamentally broken so early on is a fool hardy move and also given that the combat even on the hardest difficulties is nothing short of♥♥♥♥♥♥easy it makes the fanbase move on to getting mods that increase the difficulty or change the start of the game or the "perk" system.
Alright so let's move on to the meat and potatoes. These aren't perks at all, they're minor passive buffs to stats with specific weapons or with your ability to not eat dogass at picking a lock. The only perk in the entire tree worth getting is Blitz. In fact, its so useful it helped me break through walls and almost broke a quest for me
.
The game at its core is flawed and a mess, however that isn't to say the game is awful. It's an average game full of below average qualities with an above average combat system and a superb sound design. If they would have tried to make the game more like an ACTUAL fallout game (y'know like with choices and stuff) then I think it would have been a far better title. Gutting the perk system and replacing it with this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ized shell ruins the RPG element and basically put it on par with a Call of Duty clone or an MMO but singleplayer only
. The foundation is there but they forgot to put up the walls. And fill in the floors. And put in plumbing. And put in a powergrid. The game falls short on so many levels to its predecesor that honestly I wouldn't even recommend it at all unless you really want to play it for the combat. But then why are you even playing a fallout game if you care about the combat.

I really do enjoy XCOM 2 but the bugs and technical glitches are just too much to overlook. I have a 980 Ti and I constantly see frame drops. Kill cams are constantly broken. Aliens are suspended in mid air or teleporting around. But the worst of it all is the game breaking bugs.
After playing Commander/Ironman for 15 hours and constantly getting my butt kicked because I just wasn't good enough I dropped down to Veteran/Ironman. 7 hours in and I'm doing great. No deaths, mag and gauss weapons, predator armor. I'm feeling pretty confident. And then I go on a dark VIP extraction mission and it all goes to hell. A bug treats the mission as failed after I destroyed the VIP's car even though I have him over my shoulder 30 squares away. Then the game calls in reinforcements right on the evac zone in back to back turns. Even though I could have killed them the game treats the zone as overrun and moves it to a place that I can't physically get to in the time left. So that's it. My squad is captured and there is nothing I can do. So my best run is now over and I'm questioning why do I even want to try again when next time something worse could happen 20 hours in.
I'm sure Firaxis is trying to fix these bugs but it is just really disappointing to see a game that was in development for so long and even delayed multiple times is still released in this state. Then again, I guess that is just the norm for video games nowadays.
** UPDATE on February 27th, 2016 **
So I have beaten XCOM 2 on Veteran/Ironman difficulty and it took about 28 hours. I went through the game being much more cautious then in my previous attempts. Sometimes I did not attempt a gorilla ops mission that would have given me the best reward because it had something to do with evac and I just didn't want to risk the game bugging out and me losing a squad again.
While there were a few bugs here and there (enemies suspended in mid air after I destroyed the floor beneath them, somehow triggering pods when I couldn't see the aliens but they could magically see me, kill zone not triggering on enemies that clearly moved, mutons seeing me through a door and throwing a grenade at me) the game was rather uneventful.
The problem I now have with the game is that its difficulty snowballed and didn't push me to experiment with my tactics. Once my soldiers levelled up it was hard not taking them on missions and levelling up replacements because the aliens simply did too much damage. Also my tactic of bring at least two grenadiers (and some soldiers in amor suits with rocket launchers) got boring pretty quick. The problem was whenever I tried to deviate from it by not using my grenadiers or holding them back to the end of the turn I found that I just didn't have the fire power. The game seems really balanced around AoE/shredding damage and killing the aliens before they get any shots on you especially because of the aggressive timers which force you into combat.
The missions also felt more repetitive than XCOM 1. The procedurally generated maps were great. I never really felt that I knew exactly was coming next but the missions were always the same. The guerrilla ops barely changed. The retaliation missions were always the same and you knew exactly when they were coming. The alien facilities were almost identical. The exact same tactics worked on every single one. I was bored my alien facilities by the third one and only did them to lower the avatar project to stall for more time to get supplies. In XCOM 1, looking back with my rose coloured glasses, the randomness of the alien attacks I feel like I enjoyed more. The different types of alien crafts, the landings versus shoot downs, the terror missions which you sometimes didn't see coming.
Also story missions felt better spaced out in XCOM 1. In XCOM 2 I probably went 12 hours between story missions because after the black site there was nothing pushing me on. I literally had taken out every single alien facility on the planet before I attempted a story mission. There was no tech or advancements behind those missions on then the next story mission to eventually get you the final mission.
All of this sounds really negative but I did enjoy a lot of the game.
- The geoscape was great. Tough choices all around. I felt it dragged the game on a little bit because it was hard to get the supplies needed to upgrade everything to tier 3 so I definitely killed time for a month just waiting for attacks because I didn't want to attempt any story missions.
- There definitely were some missions where even with what I feel are my OP tactics of never-ending explosives and mimic bacons I did feel like I was just walking over the aliens.
- The character customization really drew me in. There were so many storylines of all my soldiers and their amazing exploits that are all just inside my head. The ability to customize every character ahead of time and just have them randomly showed up really pulled me in.
On the whole as a die-hard XCOM fan I did enjoy it and I'll probably come back in 2-3 months when some DLC and patches have come out and make my Commander/Ironman attempt. But I am very afraid that I'm just going to have to resort to my same boring tactics again. I'll probably make a couple of attempts at different tactics, maybe rush psionics instead of mag weapons or something but I'm just a bit worried that the game at higher difficulties just isn't balanced for that.

It took me a long time to come to terms with the fact that I don't like Fallout 4. I really wanted to, but I just can't.
The world is good and interesting. I like the setting. I also found many of the characters likeable. But that is where the good things end.
The story is insufferable. You are looking for your kidnapped child or to be more precise the poorly built animatronic monstrosity you have somehow convinced yourself is a human child. (Seriously, the baby animation is Twilight levels of creepy wrong.) Everything is connected to this central element. Here is the thing: I have the same emotions towards this baby as any random piece of pre-war junk in the wasteland. No time is spent setting this up. This is not so uncommon, Fallout rarely wastes much time on setting up the macguffin. But a baby is a terrible macguffin. Will not finding it affect the wasteland? Not at all. It is just bad and kills the whole game. Every time you talk to someone the character uses a desperate voice to ask 'have you seen Shaun?', while I could not care less. So no main story line. Some of the sidequests are fun, many are just open world shovelware.
The settlement building is a neat idea, but its hampered by its limitations. There is a ton of DLC to buy if you want a modest amount of customization. Without it you can build a ramshackle shack or another ramshackle shack. And other than tending to a few meters, the survivors you take in have no personality so its hard to be attached to them. The settlement building should be its own game, with characters you can actually care about.
Other than this, the game is a bog standard shooter. I dread to think how it looked if the id team needed to be brought in to polish this up. You aim, shoot, the bad guys fall over. Nothing much to note. Fallout was hardly loved because of its innovative combat, but it seems that it was the focus of 4.
Overall, its a good setting wasted on a thoroughly mediocre game which lacks a heart and sometimes a brain. The protagonist is the least interesting man/woman in the world, almost every single side character has more personality, especially as the limited conversation tree locks you into (a) asking about Shaun helpfully (b) asking about Shaun sarcastically or (c) asking about Shaun angrily. The kid is lucky that the apocalypse happened because the protagonist seem to lack any identity beyond the kid and would have probably gone on to be an insufferable stage parent sans nuclear Armageddon.
However, if you have a weird fascination with dragging typewriters around an irradiated wasteland, this game is sure for you. Otherwise get New Vegas, while it looks uglier (Fallout 4 is no beauty to look at either, especially the main character), it has a heart beyond 'ugh we have to make another Fallout game because we haven't figured out yet how to milk Skyrim until 2277'.
And seriously, Shaun can get nuked. Damned creepy robo-baby.

TLDR: It's better than it was in early access. However, if you havent played Terraria, go play that.
Having finally been released, I'm nonplussed. The game is much more complete as an experience, and has notably changed in terms of depth and direction. There is now a fairly solid story, as well quests that provide meaning to the random environments you're continually thrown into. However, the gameplay is little changed from early access beta. Combat is still awkward and choppy, monsters seem to have little coherence or diversity, let alone any kind of clear typology or sense of structure or logic, and exploring is still essentially a scramble for settlements and loot. Despite all the improvements, I would still heartily recommend Terraria over this to someone interested in 2d minecraft-alikes (minecraftvanias?).
Some Confusion
How does one review an early access game? Is this an impression, a statement of opinion about the direction in which the game is heading? I am supposed to treat this as a product? It's clearly not, hence the early access tag.
In any case, if you haven't played Terraria go play it instead of this. It's cheaper, tighter, more fun and has better netcode, once you work out how to connect to a server. This is just a Terraria world generator with some baseline gear and crafting. The monsters have to be placeholders, as they all look like pokemon and have no biome consistency at all, the worlds are just bottomless terraria maps with random stuff on top, and the gear is very straightforward, consisting of the same suit of armor made of different, better stuff. Its also just as much fun to explore those worlds and stripmine them as it is in Terraria.
Having said that, check back in six months. It could be a completely different game, and chucklefish seems to have a clear direction in mind. Odds are version Rabid Wombat or whatever it's called will be a positive change.

I wanted to give Darkest Dungeon a recommendation, but the make or break for the game is this: it is often woefully unfair.
There's a lot to love about it. It's unique, it allows for a lot of strategy and decisions of every kind really have weight in DD. The art style fits the tone, the tone suits the gameplay, and the gameplay is taxing and demands your attention--you won't last an hour approaching it flippantly.
Randomly generated dungeon layouts and encounters keep you on your toes and make you ask yourself whether you're willing to chance the next room and possible death or retreat to live another day. It's a stressful game, in the way that playing Dark Souls without a guide or wiki is stressful. In the same way, the difficulty makes success, however fleeting, rewarding and exhilarating.
Darkest Dungeon is a really promising title, but the real killer is that you're assaulted at every turn by aggravating percentages and enemy abilities and attacks that always make you feel like you're a step behind. Not only this, but you can never get a step ahead or even keep pace, because skill improvements and equipment upgrades cost substantial amounts of coin--coin that you'll need to be able to provision your party every time you enter a dungeon.
The first character you get is a burden because no matter how many times you start a new game, he'll always have sticky fingers and pilfer loot for himself for the first three-ish dungeons you enter when you're already desperate for startup cash.
Beyond this initial hindrance, you'll find the percentage-chance nature of your abilities to be incredibly frustrating when you find your party missing attack after attack despite good odds and good strategy. A single round of whiffed actions can leave your party in shambles as your foes relentlessly assault you with impunity.
For me personally, progress has been so little and so late that the game goes beyond its intention. The game does a great job of punishing foolishness and lack of foresight, but even when you've checked all your boxes and covered your bases, you'll get backhanded anyways.

and enjoy this chicken stir fry recpie
- Serves 4
- 10 mins to prepare and 10 mins to cook
- 325 calories / serving
- Healthy
INGREDIENTS:
- 1 orange, zested and juiced
- 2tbsp soy sauce
- 2tbsp sesame oil
- 250g (8oz) tender stem broccoli
- 5cm (2in) piece root ginger
- 1tbsp sunflower oil
- 1 garlic clove, finely sliced
- 1 red pepper, deseeded and thinly sliced
- 150g Straight To Wok Noodles
- 400g (13oz) chicken fillet, cut into thin slices
METHOD
Step 1 - Mix together the orange zest and juice, soy sauce and sesame oil and set aside.
Step 2 - Blanch the broccoli in boiling water for 2 minutes, then drain well and set aside.
Step 3 - Finely shred the ginger. Then heat a large frying pan or wok, add the sunflower oil, heat it until sizzling, and fry the ginger till it's crisp.
Step 4 - When it's done, remove with a slotted spoon. Add the chicken and garlic, and stir-fry until just browned. Remove the meat using a slotted spoon and set aside.
Step 5 - Add the red pepper and broccoli and stir-fry for around 2-3 minutes until it's just tender. Add the soy sauce mixture, bring it to the boil then return the chicken to the pan

The atmosphere in this game is amazing. If you like Lovecraft you'll love this game. Friends I have who don't generally like turn based RPGs still like this game. Combat is fast and action packed. When you press attack you get immediate satisfaction. Skills and heroes are varied and so are bosses (8 bosses + 2 mini bosses + final mission mini bosses and bosses).
RNG is utilized to its fullest to make every dungeon potentially dangerous and to keep tension up. You can never feel completely safe and the awesome narrator will remind you of this. A couple of crits in a row can totally tun the battle around, be it to your favour or detriment. In tense fights when your hero gets stresed out but become vigorous rather than afflicted (strong buff rather than severe nerf) you can feel the stress relief yourself.
I see a lot of negative reviews focusing on the length of the game calling it a "grind". Let me compare it to a soccer game: In those games you can usually change the length of a match and usualy also the number of matches per season to fit different players. You can't do that in this game but you wouldn't call playing matches in a soccer game a "grind", after all that's what you bought the game to do.
Beating a dungeon takes around 30 min. Beating the final boss (ie completing the game) takes around 60 dungeons. 100% completion (except the 104 weeks achievement) takes around 90 weeks and you have to beat the game once first (to unlock "new game plus"). Is this too long? It is of course up to personal preference. I think there's plenty of content to justify 30 hours. Heck, I'm still playing it after 150 hours and that's excluding all the time I played during the alpha.
Just like in many sports games the management aspect is not very big. It is all about dungeon runs. If you don't like doing dungeon runs you should not buy this game. Some peole continue to go into dungeons even after they have beaten and upgraded everything just for the fun of doing them. About 4% of players have made it to week 104 (104 dungeon runs in a single game).
Some people list money management as a negative. I actually think it is a positive. Having a lack of resources adds to the tension and it forces you to take risks. Do you go for that last treasure chest? Do you dare bringing a high stress hero into the dungeon in hopes of removing it for free with hero skills? It of course punishes those who refuse to (or can't) learn money and risk management, but since there is only one difficulty setting you can't satisfy everyone. Some people will find this aspect too easy and some will find it too hard. There's no vac ban for cheating though and you can mod the game to be easier too if you want.

Review with 2nd Impression:
1st Impression: First review I've ever written - fitting that it should be for XCOM 2. I rarely buy games on release, I usually wait until a sale to buy games, but I shelled out $75 for the game and DLC. So far it has been worth it.
As someone who has played nearly 300+ hours of XCOM: Enemy Within/Enemy Unknown, I have to recommend this game. (-Yes, the RNG will drive you crazy and if you don't like it, you won't like it now. I feel that it's always been part of XCOM and while a missed shot will♥♥♥♥♥♥you off, it shouldn't make or break the battle. Mind that I still feel like breaking my mouse when I miss a 90%...)
Positives:
-Customization (Plenty of more options, making your guys more unique and way cooler than the last XCOM. It's also worse when you lose someone. It still irks me when I take the time to make a soldier, only to have them get killed instantly)
-Missions (The variety, the randomly generated maps, the objectives: I love all of it. Refreshing change from XCOM: EW. Some people may be annoyed with the timed missions, but I personally feel that they force action and decisiveness as a whole)
-Story (Been great so far - just finished the Blacksite Mission and am really into the game. Yes, I've played 22.3 hours over the past week when I have lots of school >_>)
-Modding (Long War - enough said)
-Class variety (They all feel unique and have a part to play in a battle)
-Time Limit (I like the real aspect of the game - ex: trying to evacuate a VIP should have a time limit as the enemy is undoubtedly hunting you. It forces less conservative play, and harder missions. However, it's not to the point where it is unbeatable.
Negatives:
-Yes, there are optimization problems. My computer actually runs about 10-15 FPS. Yet the game is so good in itself that I'm willing to play through it. Once an optimization patch comes out, this shouldn't be a problem.
-Glitchy (Phasing through walls, melee through walls, shooting in the opposite direction and hitting the target)
-Camera Angles (Will sometimes show you a view that's blocked immediately off by a wall/ceiling)
Some really quick impression of the game after about 22.3 hours. Excellent game so far, and will be even better with the optimization. Improvements all around - if you liked EU or EW, buy it! 9/10 for me.

Great game, but the chance-hit-system ruins it.  It's hard to recommend this game when it's core mechanic is essentially dice rolling. It allows for even the best tactics and mechanical mastery to be trumped by randomness. (Not saying I'm a god at X-Com, but the argument is still valid.)
Randomness isn't bad in all games, I just don't like the way it's implemented in X-com 2. In a card game like Hearthstone, losing to chance (and in general) isn't so bad. Randomness evens out over multiple matches, and losing isn't so damning. In X-Com 2, losing a mission or operatives is a huge kick in the teeth.
If you have lots of free time, this may not be an issue for you, as you can retry missions plenty of times. But if you have a very limited amount of time to play video games, you may get especially frustrated.
TL;DR X-COM 2 is a good game, but it may not appeal to you due to it's the randomness of its main mechanics.

Genuinely surprised at how salty people are over RNG, and how negatively received many positive user reviews are.
The only real flaw with the RNG is that you can go hungry several times in the span of minutes, which does not reflect any reason or logic conceivable. Missing several times in a row is possible, getting critical'd over and over is possible, starving after every other battle is not.
Despite that, Darkest Dungeon is a better example of coping with stress, death and the inevitable randomness of despair life offers than most games in recent history.
People say this game is more fun as an "experience" rather than a game with fair rules or challenges, and they're completely right. Darkest Dungeon is unfair in a way to remind you that life is unfair, a trait that most games lack for the sake of defining "balanced combat engine" as "let me beat the game".
Darkest Dungeon is not about winning. Darkest Dungeon is openly and intentionally a stress simulator.
The skills this game really tests you at aren't traditional video game skills like timed dodges and attacks, but psychological skills like patience, diligence and mental composure. It's not about a win-state as much as it is about learning how you react to struggle and adversity, and learning to make the best of it. It teaches you the difference between victory and diligence, each one its own virtue and reward.
If you can't handle that, go play an easy game like Minecraft or Dark Souls.
