This is a very well done mmo that manages to stay very simple while still be addicting to play. I haven't spent a single penny on it yet, and I never felt pressured to spend money, unlike most free to play games at the moment. Trove is very easy to learn, and since it's a voxel game, allows you to transform the landscape at your will. I highly reccommend it for anyone who loves mmo's, but feels almost overwhelmed at all the details of mainstream mmo's or just their insane subscription rates.
Also, another HUGE plus this game has: ALL LOOT IS SHARED. Some player can't run by get the last hit off a dungeon boss and steal the loot, since each individual player gets loot simply by being around when the boss is defeated. There is NO downside to having other players around. Even when mining, everyone around gets the materials, no matter who mined the block. This stress on friendly co-op is spectacular and I've never seen anything like it in any other mmo game out there.

Even with the bugs in mind, I would still recommend this game to any fans of the original series or Firaxis' reboot.

I love this game. I've nearly beaten it, it has been very fun. But I can't recommend it in it's current state. It has obviously had a lot of work put into it, but it still needs a lot of work. My main complaint is that for a game that was created with the idea in mind of introducing the player to a world of realism(with fantacy Lovecraftian Eldritch horror themes), of the human mind and body being put to the test and the results of doing so, for some reason they decided the way to do this was with RNG deciding the mechanics they so heavily wanted to emphasize: permadeath and afflictions.
PROS:
+Very well done visually.
+Sound effects, narration, and music are great.
+Strategy based gameplay with many party and skill combinations to use.
+Difficult in a satisfying way (usually).
CONS:
-Too heavily dependant on RNG. Mechanics that are the main focus of the game, such as permanent death (Deathblow at Death's Door) and how heroes react to stress(Affliction/Virtue), are entirely up to chance. I'm fine with RNG when it's used to create the quests, but the combat and progress in general is too heavily dependant on it. To add on to this, the game actually becomes more RNG dependant as you progress. Critical Hits become more common and effects decided by RNG (bleed, blight, disease, debuffs, move) become more common.
-A total grindfest. Seriously. It takes SO LONG to raise heroes to be able to have any chance at surviving the LVL 6 Darkest Dungeon missions. Heroes come with, and gain throughout their quest through RNG, various negative quirks that render them useless against the extremely unforgiving stress and health damage of the late game enemies. So you have to grind low level dark runs, to gain enough gold to afford the treatments to cure their quirks, to make your higher level heroes even usable.

My single biggest gripe about this game is the Avatar Project countdown to doom.  XCOM does NOT belong on a time limit!  Thankfully within the first week or so of the game being out, someone basically modded it out of the game.  So I've been enjoying the game at MY pace!
The graphics are a step up from EU/EW.  The customization options are better, and there are a lot more options to change.
I like the direction they went with changing the aliens, and the introduction of a classic, the Snakemen, called Vipers in this game.  Though serving a different role, it's still awesome to see them!
This game, overall, doesn't play the same as EU/EW.  Again, it's on a timer, and a LOT of the missions you go on have timers as well. Oh, what i wouldn't give to go back to when Fallout 4 was announced and we all still believed the greatest Fallout ever made was coming. Such simple times. I remember how excited I was the day the reveal trailer came out. I remember every second I spent watching the BE3 with my friends and how my excitement grew with every new feature there would be.
- New engine?! (Nah, just an updated creation engine)
- Settlement CREATION?!?!? (Yes, but extremely clunky w/o extreme modding)
- custOMIZABLE WEAPONS OMG!!! ( Honestly, I'm not sure about this but it feels like there are barely any weapons in this compared to New Vegas, and the "unigue" weapons are just normal weapons with different stats)
The gunplay of this game is a significant improvement over NV and FO3 but still isn't nearly as fun as in most FPS games. Yes, I know this is an RPG game, but it falls pretty flat on that aspect as well. Because of the choice to have a fully voiced player (Regardless of this, I still thought Brian, and Courtney were pretty great) many roleplaying aspects were sacrificed. The number of dialogue options is significantly reduced and extremely simplied. (Nearly) Every conversation has the choices of
Down: Yes     Left: Sarcastic/ Alternative Yes    Top: Tell me more, but yes    Right: No (yes)
This ties into another problem with the RPG elements: the
. You pretty much have to be the good guy (until you play Nuka World, where you have to be a bad guy) Unlike New Vegas, where almost every problem seemed to have multiple solutions, most problems in FO4 have to be solved with violence. It's fun the first time, boring every other time. Because of the voiced player cutting out most dialogue options and the removal of skills mean the only special dialogue lines are based on charisma. They are also a random chance of success, meaning you can quicksave/quickload until you get what you want (except for in survival mode) Bethesdaddy also removed the karma system for better or worse. To me, it's not that important, but at least it let you know when you were being a♥♥♥♥♥♥ I remember how I originally thought the replacement of skills and traits with perks was awesome and how "skills are pointless anyway". However, the current system lets you get a god-like character in every playthrough since you can't be locked into a specific playstyle except by choice. Most people like it, but i kind of miss planning out my character and thinking about what perks and skills I was gonna get next.
Now, after complaining about all the cons of the game (I skipped over a few I'm sure, such as lackluster main story), here is why you should play it:

The world building in this game is really quite good. Sometimes i do miss the desolate wasteland of NV, but post-nuclear Boston is filled with tons of interesting characters and fun places to explore. The game definitely has better graphics than it's predecessors (albeit not the best w/o some graphic mods) The power armor in this game is ACTUALLY POWER ARMOR and it makes you feel powerful. I really appreciated the little animations like when taking a stimpak or getting mauled by a deathclaw. The ghouls in this game are actually creepy too, and can be quite a challenge when they gang up on you in the beginning. The companions in this game are really cool in my opinion, especially Piper, Valentine, and Hancock. Dogmeat is an annoying piece of crap who disappears with your stuff and gets in the way, but I still like to use him as a companion. However, the invincibilty of him removes the worry of losing your 4-legged pal, which added some emotional value to FO3. (Also, there isn't much point in stimpaking your companions, since they just get back up later. Hardcore mode is what survival difficulty should have originally been, being an improvement over the NV version. However, it really is hardcore, with no auto healing, fast travel, or saving, so be prepared. Modding in this game is great as it is with all Bethesda RPGs (except for the fact that they made achievements disabled when you mod the game) But seriously, there are some kickass mods either downloadable or being worked on. Personally, I can't wait for
and the Fallout 3 and Fallout NV recreation mods.

All in all, this game is really fun. It falls short in many places but excels in others. The worst part about it is probably knowing that we won't be getting another Fallout for years.

A solid strategy game that improves upon its predecessor in nearly every way. The game presents you with even more strategic and tactical choices than the first, and many of these choices present particularly difficult quandries. Firaxis has also increased the degree to which you can customize your soldiers, making it even harder to see one die because of your mistakes. And they will die; make no mistake about it. Your soldiers will die if you play sloppily, even on the lower difficulties.
There are some performance issues, but even with my not so great system, they're hardly noticable (or perhaps I'm just more tolerant of them than most). There is really only one aggravating bug present at release (that your save game is corrupted if you save while a chryssalid is buried in the ground on a mission).
Even with the bugs in mind, I would still recommend this game to any fans of the original series or Firaxis' reboot.

I'm really happy to say that I've completed this game.  It's pretty hard, and it's different than basically all other games because psychologically you have to be able to work failure into your mind as a normal thing.  It was really strange how good I thought I was doing, just starting out at the game, thinking "Wow!  This isn't so hard.  Characters are supposed to die?  I still haven't lost any!"  Oh, how naiive I was.
This is a minor gameplay spoiler, I mean, if you want to go into it with a clear head and empty expectations (which was part of the fun of it for me, honestly).... but characters WILL die, missions WILL fail, you WILL have to retreat.  It's all about just accepting your losses and trying to make the most out of bad situations.
It can get a bit slow at times, because once you get to a certain part of the game, you will realize that at parts in the game there are certain things you will need, and you don't have them yet.... for example, you know what your next overall goal is, but you look at your bank and realize you don't have enough money to fund an expedition to that dungeon, safely anyway (there's certain things you want to bring with you on every adventure - partly for safety, and partly as a means of opportunity [having the right item to interact with curio, in order to find better treasure or positive effects[).  Once you realize it's not going to go fast though, and you have to go about it meticulously while remembering a lot of things you learned earlier in the game from your mistakes and information gathering, it can be a lot of fun to take on the challenge of the Darkest Dungeon.

I haven't had this much fun naming soldiers after my friends/family and stressing out as I watched them all die gruesome deaths since Xcom: Enemy Unknown.
Darkest Dungeon is at its core a turn based "Encounter-Battle" style RPG (much like pokemon/final fantasy) with elements of base management and dungeon delving.  Oh yeah, and that character you just spent the last 10 hours upgrading?  If they take a fatal hit, they're gone for good.  Death matters in this game, which makes every little battle a stressful experience.  Did I mention stress?  Did you know that all of your mighty men and women not only have a health bar, but also a stress meter?  If your health bar depletes you die.  If your stress meter fills up twice, you risk having a heart attack (you die).  Managing mental states is a blast, and can make for some quite humorous situations.
The art style adds to the games depressing atmosphere, everything is drawn with deep shadows and a dark color pallate, which is something that I feel brings the entire experience together when you add in the equally depressing soundtrack.
Overall I would highly recommend this game.  I have never encountered a bug and have consistantly been kept on edge while playing.  If you enjoy tactical games with high risk and reward then this game is for you.

In Xcom 2 Firaxis have done what many thought impossible and improved on almost every aspect of Xcom EU. And if you are a fan of turn based stratagy games then this is a must-have purchase. That being said however, It does have it's drawbacks.
Pros:
1. Far, far deeper customisation for your soldiers, now being able to choose things such as face paint, camouflage and individual options for the torso, legs and arms of their armour.
2. Randomly generated levels meaning that you won't play the exact same level multiple times like in EU.
3. Consealment. Now when you start most missions you are in consealment meaning the enemies don't know that you're there, Allowing you to move without being attacked and set up abushes.
4. Strong class system requireing you to think tactically about who you bring on each mission and what equptment to give them.
5. Much improved Visuals.
6. Mod support.
7. More varied enemys with unique abilities to each other.
8. More methods of going about the task than just shooting. You can now use a specialist to hack robotic units, or use a ranger to deal massive amount of damage with their sword.
9. More mission types. The missions are no longer just kill everything or escort someone across a map. There are new objectives such as destorying a communications relay. Breaking VIPs out of prison or having to carry an unconcious VIP across the map to the extraction zone.
10. Almost fully destructable environments. Is there an enemy flanking one of your soldiers while on a rooftop, and there is no way that you can shoot it to death in that turn? Get a grenade and blow up the floor beneith it! making it take the grenade damage, fall damage, and if you're lucky, fire damage from the building begining to burn down.
Cons:
1. Clipping issues. Soldiers will often fire through solid walls, break windows that have already been broken, or standing on absolutly nothing in order to shoot an enemy while positioned on a ledge.
2. Performance issues. For some unexplained reason this game is far more demanding than it deserves to be, or that the reccommended settings say it is. Unless you turn off MSAA then it WILL lag. Even without MSAA it will still lag, jusst not as much.
3. long load times. Even on an SSD, expect load times to be 30 seconds+. While it is understandable on the way to the missions due to generating teh map, on the way back the load times are even longer. An issue that can inexplicably be fixed by pressing the 'Caps Lock' button which makes it load almost instantly.
4. Mod support. While I said that it is a good thing that it has it, it has been implimented in a way that means that any mod you turn on creates a dependancy for that mod in that save. This means if you install a mod, play a mission with it an descover you don't like it then you either need to keep playing with it, revert back to a save before you had it, or with Ironman player, restart the game.
5. Steep dificulty curve. While in Xcom EU the first 3 missions would be fighting sectiods, then they intoduce thin men who can spit poison, on Xcom 2 the first 2 missions are fighting nice, weak enemies, then suddenly the introduce sectiods in the 3rd which can panic and mind control your soldiers. In the 5th mission the introduce vipers that can grab your soldiers from 7 tiles away and pull them out of cover. The game gets very hard, very quickly.
6. Mission timers. Most missions now have a timer for you to finish them in before you fail and are either force evacuated or captured by the aliens. The problem is that they give you usually less than 10 turns to kill about 12 aliens, finish the objective then get to a set evac zone on the other side of the map. Another problem is that most of the reasons for the counters are 'drop ships are coming to attack you' or 'the aliens have rigged this thing to explode' but when you enter the missions you're consealed so there is no reason for the countdown timer to start in that case.
Although I listed almost as many cons as pros, the good things that the pros bring by far outweigh the badness of the cons, and none of the cons are things that can't be fixed in updates or by mods. And yes, this is a difficult game and I have rage quit it many times, but i'm not going to be pathetic and post a negative review, just because I wasn't thinking tactially enough to get myself out of those situations.

While I am still fairly new to this game, I felt the need to express my absolute joy and more often than not frustration while playing this game.
Let's first start with the areas of the game. The Graphics and aesthetic of this game are very stunning, more often than not I found myself just standing there and enjoying the scenery. Many locations in the game are memorable whether they are just beautiful or difficult only one or two of the areas in the game felt lacking in depth and content or just had artificial difficulty, those areas being the Irithyll dungeon and The Profaned Capital. The profaned capital in particular had very little to explore when compared to the other levels in the game while the Irithyll dungeon was just annoyingly frustrating with enemies that drain your health by looking at you. But enough about that let's get onto the next topic
Items in the game are not few and far between which I personally enjoy, You can get at least two weapons, armor sets, rings, and spells per area. They all also have a variety which makes not only each class of weapon unique but each weapon in general. In the time that I've run through this game I've mostly used straight and great swords (I know how boring) and even the few that I used were all unique and varied in not only their weapon arts but their ways to acquire them, their looks and even the lore behind them, this brings me onto my third point.
Lore in not only this game but in all of Fromsofts games is just incredibly, and while I have to admit that if you truly and fully want to understand and appreciate this game you might have to do some digging and video watching I believe it is all worth it. The world that FromSoftware builds in the background of this game astounds me, the world isn't just created with visuals but with words, every line spoken by a character seems very important and thorough, making investigation into people's stories worth while. This brings me to my final point.
If you can't tell by now I love pve in games and while I do like pvp I just find pve more fun. This game's bosses have amazed me in a way I thought not possible. I'm going to go over each and every boss in order to add to this already long review so brace yourself.
First boss first: Iudex Gundyr, this is how you start a game, when I first saw him I felt nothing but terror knowing that I would have to kill my first boss here. Even in this first stage he teaches you how to handle things bigger and stronger than yourself and his second stage teaches you to keep your cool when facing giant grotesque monsters.
Next is Vordt he is more simply teaches you to deal with status effects and where big enemies blind spots are, nothing complicated.
Third is the Curse-Rotted Greatwood, I won't be the first to admit that this fight isn't the best (beat him first try blind) he just serves to help make you boss weapons honestly.
Fourth is the Crystal Sage, the first magic boss and while he isn't that tough he'll give new players a bit of a challenge the first time around.
Fifth are the Abyss Watchers, these guys are the first real challenge of the game with their unorthodox moves and fast speed, they are a worthy challenge as your first lord of cinder.
Sixth are the Deacons of the Deep, a mob type enemy that isn't super hard and you can only really die by your own greed and their cursing you, nothing special here.
Seventh is High Lord Wolnir, more of a gimmick boss that doesn't let you hit him because he won't give you openings, I'll be honest this fight kinda sucks.
Eighth is the Old Demon King, if you face this Demon when you're supposed to he is a real and dangerous threat, I fought him before I fought Wolnir and he gave me a run for my money the first few times I tried him.
Ninth is Pontiff Sulyvahn, this is your first real challenge of this game, he's fast tough, and strong all in one package, I died quite a few times my first time through and I a little ashamed to admit that I had to rely on the help of phantoms my first playthrough.
Magic number ten is Yhorm the giant, while mostly a gimmick fight it provides amazing spectacle that gets me every time with its use of the Storm Ruler.
Eleven is Aldrich, Devourer of Gods, he isn't so much of a challenge as all he does is massive damage with magic and his terrifying arrow storm, still good nonetheless.
Twelve is Dancer of the Boreal Valley, in my opinion the hardest main game boss, She tricks you with her size and graceful movements to fool you with a false sense of security and devastates you with massive combos. A worthy boss indeed.
Thirteen is Oceiros, the Consumed King. This fight can be very easy of very hard depending on what he does. His first stage is very easy with little resistance, but his second stage turns him into a dazed bat flying around your house and can offer a very stressful fight.
Fourteen is Champion Gundyr. In my opinion the best main game boss, it combines my two favorite things rolling a lot and fast strikes, this fight is intense until the very end when you let out a gasp of relief when you finally best this former champion.
Fifteen is Dragonslayer Armour. This in my opinion is the very middle ground when it comes to bosses, not to hard not to easy and while his second stage can get annoying it brings a smile to your face when you finally best this ancient piece of equipment.
Sixteen is Lothric, Younger Prince and Lorian, Elder Prince. yes this fight is a double boss but not in the way that you would think Lothric just helps out occasionally and helas his brother while attacking you, this fight is memorable because of all the dirty tricks these two pull with their teleporting, healing, and ranged attacks. One of the more difficult fights in this game.
Seventeen isn't really a boss just a cool set piece, Ancient Wyvern. This boss just lets you plunge attack its head for fun. Nothing memorable here.
Eighteen is what most people to consider the toughest boss in the game, Nameless King. This fight has two stages with his Drake being the first and him being the second, the first stage is very poor in terms of camera and is very frustrating a times, his second stage is my mortal weakness, delayed combos. He is very difficult to predict sometimes and gives even veteran players a run for their money.
Finally at number Nineteen is The Soul Of Cinder. This boss is not only nostalgic but fun as hell too. He changes play styles throughout the first stage making him difficult to predict and his second stage sees him becoming Gwyn himself in an epic final battle with his music and moves.
Now that that's over with I believe I've taken up enough of your time already so I'll leave you with this closing statement. This game is fun, frustrating, sad, happy, and stressful all at the same time, and for that I give in a 10/10 would get ganked in pvp again.

Alright, so around 230 hrs into this game (not that much in my opinion), I feel that this game has been a great game for all of those hours.
This game is hard, I am sure you have heard that many times, and if you are someone who hasn't played or have seen gameplay of any of the past Dark Souls games than here are some tips. This game will throw you against the wall multiple times and wants you to learn and get better from mistakes. This isn't the kind of game with a drawn out tutorial, it's more or less a showcase of a few buttons, some messages telling you vaguely where to go, and the rest is left up to experience. This game is about overcoming obstacles, NOT an ease of access I just play for the story game.
Speaking of the story, if you like secret lore, oh boy are you going to have a blast with this series. This game's lore is best hit on by multiple Youtubers and a great community on constantly figuring out "what other secrets await in this game." It's not a story that "casually" playing through the game. But if you are really good on context clues and the knowledge of past games, Dark Souls III is almost a nerdgasm for lore.
And now PVP. I'll be honest, for the first 30 hours, my only PVP was with invaders (not including NPCs). I had a decent time with them and got my♥♥♥♥♥♥handed to me on more than several occasions. I strayed away from invading people's worlds as well due to the face I had a thought it might effect the story in some way (it can). But later on my first NG+ (New Game Plus / harder difficulty) I decided to go through with the invasions and boy oh boy did I have a blast. It wasn't schooling on kids as much as it was a genuine fight between two people. I learned tricks from fighting people along with making friends. Along with the addition of a new PVP arena, the game has been held at a higher setting for me.
(Side note: the NG+ is a joke, I'm hoping for improvement in the future but might just want to wait till their next game.)
To wrap things up, this game overall is a great game and I would recommend it to those who enjoy an interesting take on combat/ fighting games and or a difficult game in total. 9/10

XCOM 2 is one of those games that gets under your skin. You'll be playing it mentally long after you've finished your session for the evening, you'll be thinking about various strategies long after your first campaign completion too. The fact that this time Firaxis has built modding right into the game client is a real testament to the fact that this XCOM will almost certainly be the one to beat for some time to come, and with it they've made some major steps forward, and a few steps sideways, along with one step backwards. I'll come to that one at the end of the review.
Firstly, let's go over the synopsis. The game assumes that most people failed their first campaign in XCOM:EU (or EW), which is probably correct, and thusly, the governments of the world, having lost faith in XCOM decided to go the route of negotiating for peace with the aliens. On the face of it, this approach worked. The "elders" as they're now called, have on the surface - uplifted humanity - by providing improved technology, health and civic benefits that have improved the race as a whole, but it's very much a vision of humanity that's ruled with a velvet glove belying an iron fist. Any dissent results in the said voice taking a quick trip to "re-education" and never being seen again. A good way to imagine it is China circa 2015 but with an even more hawkish stance concerning human rights and you'd not be far off.
Humanity that wishes to remain free, lives in isolated clusters at the fringes of society, deprived of any real contact with the world. and resists, albeit ineffectually. XCOM, having gone into hibernation, is suddenly awoken as intelligence brings the commander (you) back into play.
So XCOM is now a resistance movement. This rather neatly solves a lot of the story contrivances of the first game, you have limited resources, your base is a very small, but mobile command HQ that can only deal with a subset of what is going on in the larger world. Your options are now reactive, rather than proactive. The enemy is no longer a passive one either, having an active project that it persues. There's no longer a simple "You lose" condition, now the enemy has a "They win" condition that they're going after. This puts active pressure on the player to keep advancing and expanding all the while.
Meanwhile, the tactical layer has had an awful lot of quality of life improvements, with classes now feeling a lot more distinct, and offering a lot more "play" in the 2-AP system that has become a hallmark of the XCOM series reboot. There's now ways to bend, and in some cases, thoroughly break the rules in your favour. The same goes for the aliens, who pretty much right away get the ability to mind control your soldiers, which makes for fun times.
The game isn't -entirely- without faults, there's still numerous bugs and camera glitches (though they're a lot less than the previous game), and unless you have a real monster of a rig, be prepared to scale the graphics back a bit, because whilst the game looks a fair bit prettier, it seems that Firaxis didn't do that great a job of optimising the code, so the game munches resources at a fairly terrifying clip. If you CAN max out the settings mind, it does look awfully pretty, and you can end up with a great looking game when you're fighting the aliens, so it does reward with the eye candy.
Other glitches I've seen include melee attacks through solid walls and closed doors (really -.-) and some pretty amazing instances where the camera decides the one place to be is inside an object, thus clipping everything and rendering the screen opaque for a fair while.
However, the big issue is as ever, the RNG. XCOM 2 uses a "pre-generated" set of rolls over the course of a fight, so imagine a long list of dice rolls prepared at the beginning, as each shot is taken, it checks against the list, ticks off a number, and moves to the next. I've tested extensively against multiple scenarios to isolate this, and have managed to confirm that the current system does not roll independently nor does the seed regenerate with a save reload. This is likely done to prevent save scumming, but unfortunately it also means that the game is robbed of a lot of the actual strategic improvisation that is actually supposed to exist, because it reduces the game to something of a puzzle game, once you understand HOW the pre-RNG system works, you can essentially reload saves to maneuver around it.
It's a design choice, and it's a bad one. Again, likely to prevent save-scumming, which is a legitimate tactic in and of itself, but it essentially makes a game based on making estimates and percentage shots less about good judgment and more about working out what number is on the list. An option to have the game actively re-randomise rolls on -each- shot would be extremely welcome, and currently the only mod available simply forces the game to move to the next tickbox on the list.
XCOM 2 is a great game. It could be legitimately excellent, were it not for the terrible issues with the pseudo RNG that is as far from actual randomness as one could get. When someone actually figures out a mod that corrects this, it'll be the first thing I recommend everyone downloads so we get the XCOM experience we deserve, that said, the rest of the package is so complete and tightly tuned that this game still warrants my highest rating even in spite of this issue.
Firaxis, if you're listening - Regenerate the seed on each roll check, make this an option as a priority yo. Strategy gamers deserve this.

I've played it for seven hours, starting two new games on ironman mode.  I don't really like it.  All of the missions are timed, which is pretty irritating.  I'd like to have an honest fight against these aliens, but the game has decided when I discover the aliens they get to move into cover.  Combined with the time limit, you're forced to run into bad positions and if you stand your ground you run out of time.  This is supposed to add tension, but it isn't any fun to play.  I could deal with maybe one timed mission in every four played, but you're forced to make uninformed risks which defeats the purpose of a tactical game.
Technically the game isn't that great either.  I haven't had any crashes in the short time I've played, but the framerate is pretty bad most of the time.  The graphics look pretty nice but there are some really bad camera angles and sometimes it's hard to tell if the shot you fired missed (it probably did).  Sound is probably the strongest part of the game.  Most of the voice acting is strong but the main characters are kind of wooden.  Bullets, lasers and explosions sound great though.
The story is alright so far, but it feels as though you're almost at too much of a disadvantage.  As soon as the "concealment phase" is over, you're going to be in a heads up fight to wipe out all of the enemies from the map.  This is kind of counter to the guerilla tactics you're supposed to using, which says to hit a target quickly and run.  A time limit to sprint to the end of the map and then kill all the enemies is not a guerilla strategy.  It all just seems a little bit too reactive, when as an underground rebel force with a hidden mobile base I would expect to be directing a little bit more of the action.  The choices you make on the strategic map don't seem to matter either.
I might keep playing it and modify this review, but honestly it's probably not going to get much more of my time.  I don't usually buy AAA games and now I remember why.  I was excited to play this game, since the first XCOM was radical, but this puppy ain't worth the money.

I have played the entire fallout franchise, and I have to say, it is exciting to see how far it has come.  Some differences you are going to notice if you haven't played this yet but did fallout 3 and new vegas is that the power armor is basically like a vehicle you will enter and it needs fusion cores to keep them going. The good news is, stats can be increased when you level and there is a bobblehead for each stat still, as well as a "special" book near the start. As for story, I love how this one worked out, really raises the typical sci fi questions.  It was truly enjoyable.

After 770 hours in this game, streaming, uploading videos, and spending hours aquiring data, this is my honest review of this game:
Pros:
-No pay-to-win.
-Free-To-Play, but doesn't suck. Seriously, this game plays like a mid-tier first person shooter almost on par with CSGO and COD.
-New guns/equipment can be acquired quickly through normal gameplay. No grinding for a week for a new gun, you'll have one in an hour or two.
-Fast Paced: Compared to other AAA competitive shooters, the action is fast and hard.
-Large Variety of Weapons: This game has a gun for everyone! Guns for Sprayers, 1-Tap Gods, No-scopers, whatever playstyle you have, there is a gun/knife for you, and it doesn't take long at all to get!
-Positive Community: Most players you come across are positive, you can easily find people to add and play with.
-Hit Registration: Unlike CSGO, I've never had one instance of a shot I know landed not register.
-Global Support: There are servers being released often, and support for you to play normally with servers around the globe! Definitely give this game a try if you don't live in an area that is usually supported by game developers servers!
-Multiple game modes: There is a game mode for every FPS player! Team DeathMatch for the COD players, Demolition for the CS:GO players, Battle Match for the Battlefield players, BOT TDM for casual players, and Assassination for the awesome players. There is even a PVE mode they have released for Halloween that is a true challenge, and might even stay in the game!
-Holiday Events: They gave skins out just for playing the game during Halloween, introduced a new game mode, and implemented a lot of new items during the holiday update. I hope this trend continues!
-Community: Unlike a lot of other games, this game isn't toxic as hell. Even with random strangers, most of the time you'll have have a good time. The discord is almost always popping with players discussing the game, looking for a clan, or challenging one another. Beware, people still get salty!
Neutral:
-No voice support: You need Discord or another program to communicate via voice.
-Netcode: This works both ways, the greater your lag, the longer it takes for the server to register your shots. If you go up against a lagger, he will have a slight peek advantage on you. If your ping is in the 300+, you will suffer, but there shouldn't be an issue with servers all around the globe.
-Early Access: Now, I'm not going to complain because this game is free, but it's not perfect. I've not run into anything game breaking during my gameplay, but just keep that in mind.
-Hackers: I have 250 Hours in this game, and I've only ran into ONE hacker/cheater during a battle match. In all of my competitive gameplay, I've never observed, or went against any cheaters. People do cheat, but it is rare in this game. Anyone that says they run into hackers all the time most likely aren't used to the game, or don't play on a higher skill level.
-Boxes/Crates: These can be opened by spending Real Money to buy bullets. Bullets is a currency in Black Squad to open boxes, and to also buy exclusive boosters, epic player models, and more. There are a ton of different boxes in Black Squad, so you know exactly what you will get when you open a box. Want a legendary AK-47? You can click the box and know exactly what you might get. Usually they contain an "epic item", such as a rare skin, and all the other prizes include gold, medals, BS coins, and sometimes, even lower tier skins. All the boxes, except for one, require you to pay, and everything inside is purely cosmetic. The only box that you can open for free have exclusive knife skins that you can only get by spending gold to open. Some people get lucky, others do not. This is for you to decide.
Cons:
-Uninspired maps: Most of the maps aren't that great in my opinion, they release new ones nearly monthly, but some of them are just...awful.
-User Interface: The main menu sucks. The friendslist/chat gets in the way of anything on the right side of the screen, you cannot chat in the main menu screen at all, and some items you can double-click to quickly navigate, and other buttons you can't! Why? I blame this on early access, but this goes down as a con for me. I enjoy my efficiency!
-Lack of a competitive scene: Yes, this game is early access, but the only way to find "competitive" players is to either get lucky on a clan match selection, or find a team on the official discord. There are clan ranks, but no one takes them seriously right now.
-Matchmaking: There have been times where I've went against a team of 5 when I was by myself for 3 rounds before other players connected. This has happened when I've went solo, qued with a team, or just randomly jumped around. The game will TRY to match you up based on rank, but after 30 seconds, it will just throw you with whoever is on. Doesn't really happen in the competitive gamemodes, but if you play assassination, it will happen a lot.
-No report system: Early access, I know, but if someone is being really toxic, or is cheating, the only way you can report right now is by posting a video on the discord. It's better than nothing, and the mods actually do their job!
-Currency: There are 4 different types of currency in this game: Gold, which is gained just by playing the game and given as a daily log-in reward. Gold can be used to buy most guns in the shop, and is easy to obtain a huge amount of it. Medals, which is gained every 7 days as a login reward, and is gained every time you level up. It is used to buy guns/knives/characters from the medal shop. (There are two shops in this game, more on that later) BS Coins, which is only gained by opening boxes. They can be used to buy different skins, compared to just winning them from a box. Finally, Bullets, which is the currency that can only be bought using Real Money. You use these to open boxes, or to buy a special model, or EXP/GOLD booster. I spoke about boxes in my Neutral section of this review above.
If you're broke and want to try something new, give this a try! You get free currency just for doing a quick tutorial, and if you look in the DLC section, you can try almost every gun in the game for free for 15 days! That is more than enough time to amass enough gold and guns to supply your own Black Squad. Give it a shot, and feel free to hit me up at IGN SL4DE. Happy Fragging!
(P.S. I spent a while writing this review, a thumbs up would be appreciated! <3)

I have to start by stating that Dark Souls 3 was my first title by FromSoftware that I gave a legitimate shot. I played Dark Souls 2 for a little bit a few years ago but I never felt it would keep me interested. I died a lot and decided to spend my time playing South Park: The Stick of Truth and Middle Earth: Shadow of Mordor. Soon after I completely forgot about Dark Souls.
Fast forwad a few years and I was looking for something to immerse me the same way that The Witcher 3 did. I was busy with Darksiders 2, as the first game kept me well entertained when I saw that Lords of the Fallen was on sale. Following numerous reviews stating that it's worth a buy during sale, I got it. I finished it, and I really enjoyed it, clunky combat included.
Dark Souls 3 started appearing everywhere I looked. I was on the fence with it because of the difficulty flashbacks from the second game. Eventually I got the Deluxe version, and so began my trip into this brilliant work of art. From the start, until you've killed the last boss, it's a journey that will never be forgotten.
I can't say what was wrong with this game because I know nothing about the previous games. However, this game as a standalone title changed the way I look at games. The artwork, the combat, the lore, ALL OF IT. This game was perfect. And I can see myself replaying it for some time to come. This is my first Steam review, as I feel you should always give credit where it's due.
No game has ever had my heart racing like this game did. It's not easy at the start. But you learn, retry, and conquer.
I found myself thinking about this game on a regular basis in my first playthrough, more so while not playing.
I would recommend this title through and through. Even for people that haven't played a game in this genre.

This game is fantastic. It is a very challenging turn based tactical game presented from an isometric point of view on the battlefield combine with a global resource management and territory gaining element against a global doom ticker. You have to try and take the world back from an occupying force one territory at a time, and amass resources to improve your base, research better technologies for your soldiers. One a tactical mission scale, you command a squad of 4 - 6 soldiers (you can mod this to be more) who consist of different classes, earn exp and rank up. There are multiple skills for each class to choose from, and a lot of items to equip them with.
If you're familiar Enemy Unknown/Enemy Within, then this game keeps all the good stuff about that game, and adds stuff to make it even better.
A lot of people are complaining about performance issues. The game is indeed not fully optimized, but will probably be patched soon enough. In general, I meet the system requirements, and even play on mac OS X. I have no issues so far.
A lot of the negative reviews seem to be due to people whinging about the turn timers. Please allow me to give you some context; The developers intentionally put this in to discourage a cowardly and tedious meta that was adopted by many players in the first game. In XCOM, you get to perform 2 actions per turn; you can move a certain distance twice, move and shoot, or move and use a skill. However, if you use your action to shoot, your turn ends (there are ways to change this by ranking soldiers of a certain class). There is a universal skill that all classes have called overwatch; it ends your turn and prepares your squad to shoot at any enemy that paths in sight during their turn.
Due to XCOM being somewhat challenging, many people decided to move half a turn, and overwatch every single turn across every map (maps in XCOM are rather large) because they didn't want their soldiers to die. The devs decided to upend this, and added turn timers to the second game.
HOWEVER, the turn timers are very lenient, you get plenty of turns to reach your objective safely (through your squad being concealed) and to complete it, kill enemies and evac the map with 2 or 3 turns to spare. There are also mods that allow you to tweak these (as XCOM 2 has complete mod support). The people whining about the turn timers are probably the people that I described above. Instead of actually altering the turn timers to be longer, or using the steam workshop mods that disable them completely, they just give a great game a negative review.
What do you feel is more tactical? Option A: Moving with stealth, setting up ambushes for enemy patrols, taking them out efficiently from a roof, blowing up the side of a building to reach your objective quick then evacing after a successful mission, or Option B: tediously moving half a turn and overwatching every turn against an enemy that isn't even actively looking for you in the first place? Yeah, I thought so. Anyone saying the timers remove the tactical layer of this game was never very good to begin with. Also, it doesnt make snipers useless. Fully upgraded snipers can take out multiple squads in a single turn if used correctly. Furthermore, on many missions, the turn timers deactivate after you complete the objective, leaving you with plenty of time to mop up remaining aliens for loot and exp. Many missions dont even have timers (campaign critical story mission, and alien retaliation missions.)
If your pc meets the minimum requirements for this game, and you are interested in this type of game then please try it out. If you dont like the timers, you can easily mod them. This game is incredibly challenging, and has many mechanics to learn, but once you master them, the game becomes very enjoyable and manageable. It also has infinite replay value (and is moddable to be even more infintely replayable)
Just don't listen to the whiners who are moaning because the devs decided that they didnt want people who wanted to cheese the game to be able to do so. Also, the people leaving bad reviews because they found the game too hard are a vocal minority who don't like learning too many things, or having open ended choice based game play that doesnt involve move to the arrow, now shoot that one guy, now move to the next arrow. Head over the XCOM subreddit to see how many people are having so much fun playing this. Other people don't seem to understand how probability works and that 90% is not the same as 100%. There is still a 10% chance to miss, but the majority of the time you will roll the 90%.
Yes the game is challenging and hard, but gives you every tool and opportunity to win.
Make up your own mind and don't listen to impatient self-entitled man children with the attention span of a gold fish.

XCOM 2 succeeds because it fixes the one large flaw with its predecessor: pacing.
Oh, things are still tactical and patience is still important. But in Enemy Unknown, experienced players quickly learned that the safest way to play was at a slow, glacial pace, spamming the overwatch ability (reactionary fire on the enemy's turn) every turn as your squad crept inch by inch across the map, combing it with a net of deadly crossfire. While satisfying, there were few rewards for risk and no sense of urgency at all. The tactical flow was prone to stagnation. The expanion, Enemy Within, took steps towards improvement by introducing Meld, a timed resource that would expire within a handful of turns. Yet even with this incentive, the problem remained.
By now, you've probably heard that XCOM 2 will, more often than not, impose turn limits on the player. This has been a source of much frustration and negative feedback -- just look around on this page for some examples -- yet this change is not only a positive one, it's the core of this game's DNA and vital to its success. You can still end every turn with your troops safely tucked in cover and all prepared to fire (and there are times where this is still a logical strategy), but the clock is ticking and it's going to take some measured risk to reap each mission's rewards. Hidden alien foes await in the fog of war standing between your starting point and your goal -- whether that's a VIP to rescue, an alien relay to destroy, or a UFO to raid -- which is tantalizingly close yet guarded enough to punish recklessness with severe consequences.
To complement the renewed sense of urgency, the soldier skillsets and capabilities have seen a significant overhaul. It's mostly familiar mechanically -- you're still taking cover and seeing percentages and screaming as you miss 85% shots -- but an increased focus on melee combat and destructive environments gives you more strategic capabilities that let you move forward towards your objective while maintaining a tactical approach. There's no longer any time to get bogged down in an entrenched skirmish, so the game provides a multitude of alternatives: you can use a grenade launcher to destroy your opponent's cover or rush his position with a deadly swordsman or hack his mechanized units and bring them under your control or...well, you get the idea. The destruction you'll inflict on the battlefield is both visually impressive -- buildings crumble, floors collapse, and yes, cars still explode -- and tactically crucial.
On the macro level, base-building is functionally similar but given a modern board game-esque overhaul that turns engineers from a simple resource into the pieces in a crucial worker placement mechanic. Do you assign your free engineer to speed up construction or to increase your power supply? Or send him off to clear out more room for a new building? Unfortunately, scientists don't receive the same attention and, consequently, feel somewhat pointless. The first scientist recruited increases your research speed by 50%, but diminishing rewards and a lack of usefulness means you'll find yourself continually opting for missions that reward engineers or supplies instead. The Geoscape has been given a similar gloss of board game paint -- no longer just a fancy hologram showing you where your next mission, the globe now gives you options to pursue additional resources or targets of opportunity. The layout is far from intuitive and the frequency of interruptions can approach frustration (a 5-day scan to make contact with a new resistance cell feels like an eternity) but it's nice to have options.
I could go on about everything else XCOM 2 does well -- the strong skill progression, the balanced classes that make a pistol-specced sharpshooter 100% viable, the smooth escalation of equipment that has just enough randomness to keep things intriguing -- but I want to end by touching again on the turn limitations. Rarely has a sequel taken such a large mechanical risk, one that completely upends the strategies its predecessor and turns the typical XCOM conventional wisdom on its head. And yes, it is absolutely punishing and demands strict execution and the occasional abandonment of your troops on the battlefield...but it's the most important change the game has made and gives XCOM 2 an injection of urgent life. Firaxis could have been safe and given us more of the same -- but as XCOM 2 will teach you, true rewards rarely come without risk.

While I am still fairly new to this game, I felt the need to express my absolute joy and more often than not frustration while playing this game.
Let's first start with the areas of the game. The Graphics and aesthetic of this game are very stunning, more often than not I found myself just standing there and enjoying the scenery. Many locations in the game are memorable whether they are just beautiful or difficult only one or two of the areas in the game felt lacking in depth and content or just had artificial difficulty, those areas being the Irithyll dungeon and The Profaned Capital. The profaned capital in particular had very little to explore when compared to the other levels in the game while the Irithyll dungeon was just annoyingly frustrating with enemies that drain your health by looking at you. But enough about that let's get onto the next topic
Items in the game are not few and far between which I personally enjoy, You can get at least two weapons, armor sets, rings, and spells per area. They all also have a variety which makes not only each class of weapon unique but each weapon in general. In the time that I've run through this game I've mostly used straight and great swords (I know how boring) and even the few that I used were all unique and varied in not only their weapon arts but their ways to acquire them, their looks and even the lore behind them, this brings me onto my third point.
Lore in not only this game but in all of Fromsofts games is just incredibly, and while I have to admit that if you truly and fully want to understand and appreciate this game you might have to do some digging and video watching I believe it is all worth it. The world that FromSoftware builds in the background of this game astounds me, the world isn't just created with visuals but with words, every line spoken by a character seems very important and thorough, making investigation into people's stories worth while. This brings me to my final point.
If you can't tell by now I love pve in games and while I do like pvp I just find pve more fun. This game's bosses have amazed me in a way I thought not possible. I'm going to go over each and every boss in order to add to this already long review so brace yourself.
First boss first: Iudex Gundyr, this is how you start a game, when I first saw him I felt nothing but terror knowing that I would have to kill my first boss here. Even in this first stage he teaches you how to handle things bigger and stronger than yourself and his second stage teaches you to keep your cool when facing giant grotesque monsters.
Next is Vordt he is more simply teaches you to deal with status effects and where big enemies blind spots are, nothing complicated.
Third is the Curse-Rotted Greatwood, I won't be the first to admit that this fight isn't the best (beat him first try blind) he just serves to help make you boss weapons honestly.
Fourth is the Crystal Sage, the first magic boss and while he isn't that tough he'll give new players a bit of a challenge the first time around.
Fifth are the Abyss Watchers, these guys are the first real challenge of the game with their unorthodox moves and fast speed, they are a worthy challenge as your first lord of cinder.
Sixth are the Deacons of the Deep, a mob type enemy that isn't super hard and you can only really die by your own greed and their cursing you, nothing special here.
Seventh is High Lord Wolnir, more of a gimmick boss that doesn't let you hit him because he won't give you openings, I'll be honest this fight kinda sucks.
Eighth is the Old Demon King, if you face this Demon when you're supposed to he is a real and dangerous threat, I fought him before I fought Wolnir and he gave me a run for my money the first few times I tried him.
Ninth is Pontiff Sulyvahn, this is your first real challenge of this game, he's fast tough, and strong all in one package, I died quite a few times my first time through and I a little ashamed to admit that I had to rely on the help of phantoms my first playthrough.
Magic number ten is Yhorm the giant, while mostly a gimmick fight it provides amazing spectacle that gets me every time with its use of the Storm Ruler.
Eleven is Aldrich, Devourer of Gods, he isn't so much of a challenge as all he does is massive damage with magic and his terrifying arrow storm, still good nonetheless.
Twelve is Dancer of the Boreal Valley, in my opinion the hardest main game boss, She tricks you with her size and graceful movements to fool you with a false sense of security and devastates you with massive combos. A worthy boss indeed.
Thirteen is Oceiros, the Consumed King. This fight can be very easy of very hard depending on what he does. His first stage is very easy with little resistance, but his second stage turns him into a dazed bat flying around your house and can offer a very stressful fight.
Fourteen is Champion Gundyr. In my opinion the best main game boss, it combines my two favorite things rolling a lot and fast strikes, this fight is intense until the very end when you let out a gasp of relief when you finally best this former champion.
Fifteen is Dragonslayer Armour. This in my opinion is the very middle ground when it comes to bosses, not to hard not to easy and while his second stage can get annoying it brings a smile to your face when you finally best this ancient piece of equipment.
Sixteen is Lothric, Younger Prince and Lorian, Elder Prince. yes this fight is a double boss but not in the way that you would think Lothric just helps out occasionally and helas his brother while attacking you, this fight is memorable because of all the dirty tricks these two pull with their teleporting, healing, and ranged attacks. One of the more difficult fights in this game.
Seventeen isn't really a boss just a cool set piece, Ancient Wyvern. This boss just lets you plunge attack its head for fun. Nothing memorable here.
Eighteen is what most people to consider the toughest boss in the game, Nameless King. This fight has two stages with his Drake being the first and him being the second, the first stage is very poor in terms of camera and is very frustrating a times, his second stage is my mortal weakness, delayed combos. He is very difficult to predict sometimes and gives even veteran players a run for their money.
Finally at number Nineteen is The Soul Of Cinder. This boss is not only nostalgic but fun as hell too. He changes play styles throughout the first stage making him difficult to predict and his second stage sees him becoming Gwyn himself in an epic final battle with his music and moves.
Now that that's over with I believe I've taken up enough of your time already so I'll leave you with this closing statement. This game is fun, frustrating, sad, happy, and stressful all at the same time, and for that I give in a 10/10 would get ganked in pvp again.

Long time fan of the fallout series.  Wasn't disappointed in another great game from Bethesda.

Good:
- The new classes are generally well done.  In XCOM EU/EW I had a fixed template for each class.  In XCOM 2 I want two of most classes (except perhaps Ranger).
- The weapons, upgrades, and utility items are well designed.  I find myself rearranging loadouts according to mission type and expected enemies (once the shadow chamber is built).  I especially like the way heavy weapons are handled.  (Sniper used one move? Fire the blaster launcher instead!)
- The strategic layer has a bit more strategery.  It feels active, rather than just a satellite spreadsheet.
- The new mission structure and map randomization adds a lot more variety.  Concealment takes some figuring out, but is pretty handy.  Notably, it provides a way to scout the enemy that isn't as game-unbalancing as the invisibility features in XCOM EW.
- Some subtle touches, like civilians are now named.  When a civilian gets killed, you don't lose some guy, you lose Jane Smith.  No difference to gameplay, but it makes everything feel more real.  Seeing your squad members on holographic "wanted posters" in city areas was also nice.
- Stability is generally good, but ironman enthusiasts might want to wait for a couple of patches.
- Feels like an XCOM game.
Bad:
- Long load times, especially when returning from missions.  I think it takes longer to return from a mission than it does to launch the game into the geoscape.  (You can hit caps lock to speed things up, at the risk of causing a crash.)
- Some voice-overs pause the action and can't be skipped ("we're losing lots of civilians"... yes, I know, thanks).  There's a mod for this ("Stop Wasting My Time").
- The pre-mission loadout UI needs a bit of work.  They got the "release armor" / "release utility" buttons done right - they let you take things from other characters, but don't strip the items if you don't take them - but there's no equivalent for weapons.  The UI flow doesn't feel right either... after selecting a weapon I have to back out a couple of layers to customize the weapon.
- The loadout screen music was much better in XCOM EU/EW.
I strongly recommend this to anyone who enjoys strategy games.

While I REALLY wanted this game to be about invading the alien homeworld I don't see that in the near future. However as fan of the series the ending leaves me with high hopes for the DLC.

Even though I feel like Bethesda changed the rpg formula too much with Fallout 4, I still have to recommend it. Even though there is less freedom of choice and the story kinda falls flat, it is the fact that I am creating my own story in this wasteland that makes this journey worth while.
Expect the odd 'Bethesda game wacky' bugs and the sometimes weird looking character models.
The gun gameplay is also a lot better in F4 vs F3, however it subtracts from the rpg system where your shots are calculated on your skill or talent of your character and instead relies on you physical skill to shoot and kill enemies. (That is if you are not using VATS)
I am also let down by the engine. This engine has been used for many of the recent Elderscrolls and Fallout games, even though heavily updated the engine is not keeping up with more modern engines other games are using today. The cracks are clearly visible and a crap ton of god rays is not going to make it all peachy.
However, I have had more fun in this game than I have had in any other game recently. There is something very special about Bethesda RPG games.
Pick it up if you have not already.

While I am still fairly new to this game, I felt the need to express my absolute joy and more often than not frustration while playing this game.
Let's first start with the areas of the game. The Graphics and aesthetic of this game are very stunning, more often than not I found myself just standing there and enjoying the scenery. Many locations in the game are memorable whether they are just beautiful or difficult only one or two of the areas in the game felt lacking in depth and content or just had artificial difficulty, those areas being the Irithyll dungeon and The Profaned Capital. The profaned capital in particular had very little to explore when compared to the other levels in the game while the Irithyll dungeon was just annoyingly frustrating with enemies that drain your health by looking at you. But enough about that let's get onto the next topic
Items in the game are not few and far between which I personally enjoy, You can get at least two weapons, armor sets, rings, and spells per area. They all also have a variety which makes not only each class of weapon unique but each weapon in general. In the time that I've run through this game I've mostly used straight and great swords (I know how boring) and even the few that I used were all unique and varied in not only their weapon arts but their ways to acquire them, their looks and even the lore behind them, this brings me onto my third point.
Lore in not only this game but in all of Fromsofts games is just incredibly, and while I have to admit that if you truly and fully want to understand and appreciate this game you might have to do some digging and video watching I believe it is all worth it. The world that FromSoftware builds in the background of this game astounds me, the world isn't just created with visuals but with words, every line spoken by a character seems very important and thorough, making investigation into people's stories worth while. This brings me to my final point.
If you can't tell by now I love pve in games and while I do like pvp I just find pve more fun. This game's bosses have amazed me in a way I thought not possible. I'm going to go over each and every boss in order to add to this already long review so brace yourself.
First boss first: Iudex Gundyr, this is how you start a game, when I first saw him I felt nothing but terror knowing that I would have to kill my first boss here. Even in this first stage he teaches you how to handle things bigger and stronger than yourself and his second stage teaches you to keep your cool when facing giant grotesque monsters.
Next is Vordt he is more simply teaches you to deal with status effects and where big enemies blind spots are, nothing complicated.
Third is the Curse-Rotted Greatwood, I won't be the first to admit that this fight isn't the best (beat him first try blind) he just serves to help make you boss weapons honestly.
Fourth is the Crystal Sage, the first magic boss and while he isn't that tough he'll give new players a bit of a challenge the first time around.
Fifth are the Abyss Watchers, these guys are the first real challenge of the game with their unorthodox moves and fast speed, they are a worthy challenge as your first lord of cinder.
Sixth are the Deacons of the Deep, a mob type enemy that isn't super hard and you can only really die by your own greed and their cursing you, nothing special here.
Seventh is High Lord Wolnir, more of a gimmick boss that doesn't let you hit him because he won't give you openings, I'll be honest this fight kinda sucks.
Eighth is the Old Demon King, if you face this Demon when you're supposed to he is a real and dangerous threat, I fought him before I fought Wolnir and he gave me a run for my money the first few times I tried him.
Ninth is Pontiff Sulyvahn, this is your first real challenge of this game, he's fast tough, and strong all in one package, I died quite a few times my first time through and I a little ashamed to admit that I had to rely on the help of phantoms my first playthrough.
Magic number ten is Yhorm the giant, while mostly a gimmick fight it provides amazing spectacle that gets me every time with its use of the Storm Ruler.
Eleven is Aldrich, Devourer of Gods, he isn't so much of a challenge as all he does is massive damage with magic and his terrifying arrow storm, still good nonetheless.
Twelve is Dancer of the Boreal Valley, in my opinion the hardest main game boss, She tricks you with her size and graceful movements to fool you with a false sense of security and devastates you with massive combos. A worthy boss indeed.
Thirteen is Oceiros, the Consumed King. This fight can be very easy of very hard depending on what he does. His first stage is very easy with little resistance, but his second stage turns him into a dazed bat flying around your house and can offer a very stressful fight.
Fourteen is Champion Gundyr. In my opinion the best main game boss, it combines my two favorite things rolling a lot and fast strikes, this fight is intense until the very end when you let out a gasp of relief when you finally best this former champion.
Fifteen is Dragonslayer Armour. This in my opinion is the very middle ground when it comes to bosses, not to hard not to easy and while his second stage can get annoying it brings a smile to your face when you finally best this ancient piece of equipment.
Sixteen is Lothric, Younger Prince and Lorian, Elder Prince. yes this fight is a double boss but not in the way that you would think Lothric just helps out occasionally and helas his brother while attacking you, this fight is memorable because of all the dirty tricks these two pull with their teleporting, healing, and ranged attacks. One of the more difficult fights in this game.
Seventeen isn't really a boss just a cool set piece, Ancient Wyvern. This boss just lets you plunge attack its head for fun. Nothing memorable here.
Eighteen is what most people to consider the toughest boss in the game, Nameless King. This fight has two stages with his Drake being the first and him being the second, the first stage is very poor in terms of camera and is very frustrating a times, his second stage is my mortal weakness, delayed combos. He is very difficult to predict sometimes and gives even veteran players a run for their money.
Finally at number Nineteen is The Soul Of Cinder. This boss is not only nostalgic but fun as hell too. He changes play styles throughout the first stage making him difficult to predict and his second stage sees him becoming Gwyn himself in an epic final battle with his music and moves.
Now that that's over with I believe I've taken up enough of your time already so I'll leave you with this closing statement. This game is fun, frustrating, sad, happy, and stressful all at the same time, and for that I give in a 10/10 would get ganked in pvp again.

Unfortunately, I have to echo the sentiments of a lot of other reviewers here. XCom2 delivers a great core game, playing off of the strengths of its predecessors, but a few design flaws (and a LOT of bugs and graphical issues) have sunk the game experience for me.
People have already outlined those issues in detail, but a short list:
EVERYTHING IS ON A TIMER (EVEN THE WORLD MAP). The aliens are working on  the "Avatar Project" (which might as well be named the Deus Ex Machina project), which ticks forward, often out of your control. God help you if you want to try to get anything done, because you'll be spending all your time on...
RESOURCE DROPS. Yes, to get any supplies, you'll now have to sit over them, like a hen laying on an egg, to get any resources. However, you won't be able to do this, because...
EVERYTHING IS ALWAYS ALARMING ALL THE TIME. Missions pop up all the time and while you're sometimes given a choice as to which one to do, you damned sure better do ONE of them, and best of luck because...
YOU'RE S.O.L. IF YOUR A-TEAM DIES. I don't mind difficult games. In fact, I like the permadeath nature of XCom; it gives your missions and decisions weight and I'll admit having to fight the urge to save-scum when one of my favorite soldiers died. However, the random nature of your missions means that it's entirely possible to get three of those "not mandatory but actually pretty mandatory" missions outlined above, and if you take any damage at all, you'll have to bring in fresh recruits. Even by mid-campaign, Squaddies and Corporals are effectively useless because...
THE COVER MECHANICS AND TO HIT NUMBERS MAKE NO SENSE. I take a reasonably seasoned corporal with a Tier 2 railgun, put him directly next to a muton with no cover at all under the effects of suppression, and my to hit is... 18%. What? Are XCom soldiers half-stormtrooper? A big giant unit with big giant HP and armor is apparently faster than a speeding bullet. You'll be surprised when a stun lancer hits you literally through a wall because...
THE COVER MECHANICS MAKE LITERALLY NO SENSE. Hitting through walls? a 20% to hit percentage difference on two of the same creatures literally right next to each other? Sure, why not. I don't care anymore.
I almost never buy anything on launch day, and like I said, I loved XCom EU/EW, and I was excited for this game. But there's a difference between difficulty and gimmick, and the challenge here is not winning the game by playing it; it's winning the game in spite of the game itself.
For now, I'm waiting on a patch to resolve the glitches and bugs (of which there are many), and to fine-tune the numbers, before I download some of the (excellent) mods and go back for another playthrough. There IS an excellent game here, I just hope Firaxis is able to squash enough of the bugs to create the game that should have been there at launch.

Alright, so around 230 hrs into this game (not that much in my opinion), I feel that this game has been a great game for all of those hours.
This game is hard, I am sure you have heard that many times, and if you are someone who hasn't played or have seen gameplay of any of the past Dark Souls games than here are some tips. This game will throw you against the wall multiple times and wants you to learn and get better from mistakes. This isn't the kind of game with a drawn out tutorial, it's more or less a showcase of a few buttons, some messages telling you vaguely where to go, and the rest is left up to experience. This game is about overcoming obstacles, NOT an ease of access I just play for the story game.
Speaking of the story, if you like secret lore, oh boy are you going to have a blast with this series. This game's lore is best hit on by multiple Youtubers and a great community on constantly figuring out "what other secrets await in this game." It's not a story that "casually" playing through the game. But if you are really good on context clues and the knowledge of past games, Dark Souls III is almost a nerdgasm for lore.
And now PVP. I'll be honest, for the first 30 hours, my only PVP was with invaders (not including NPCs). I had a decent time with them and got my♥♥♥♥♥♥handed to me on more than several occasions. I strayed away from invading people's worlds as well due to the face I had a thought it might effect the story in some way (it can). But later on my first NG+ (New Game Plus / harder difficulty) I decided to go through with the invasions and boy oh boy did I have a blast. It wasn't schooling on kids as much as it was a genuine fight between two people. I learned tricks from fighting people along with making friends. Along with the addition of a new PVP arena, the game has been held at a higher setting for me.
(Side note: the NG+ is a joke, I'm hoping for improvement in the future but might just want to wait till their next game.)
To wrap things up, this game overall is a great game and I would recommend it to those who enjoy an interesting take on combat/ fighting games and or a difficult game in total. 9/10

This game is why Fireaxis needs to start implementing emplyee drug testing.  It isn't just broken, it's bad.
It's not the difficulty, it's not the graphics, it's not the lag: It's the horrible, poorly thought out game mechanics that traded in working, balanced gameplay in favor of cheap gimmicks yanked from tacky Korean MMOs (read: lottery loot) and a total clusterfark of a strategic map. And the entire plot was unabashedly ripped striaght from
.
The Doom Clock is nothing more than an arbitrary time limit that does nothing more than artificially force you down a certain research path & gameplay style under the threat of losing if you deviate from it in any way. The fanbois says this game is proactive instead of reactive - that's complete horsepucky.  This series has never been more on rails than in this iteration.
All of the Second Wave options you knew & loved are gone. Random stat bonus on level up? Gone. Random rookie stats? Gone. Flanking aim bonuses have been reduced to a flat rate that doesn't involve any real math. Ditto for criticals. The experience points system have been traded in for raw kill totals.  Comparing the tactical game mechanics of XCOM1 to XCOM2 is like comparing chess to checkers.
Your base experience, likewise, has also been dumbed down. Alien containment? Gone. Interrogations? Gone. Interceptors? Gone.  The once mighty research tree has been trimmed down to a pathetic shrub, mostly so that they could implement their latest gameplay gimmicks over in engineering.
The engineering room is the epitome of XCOM2's failures. Shen tells me that she's got the technology to make a powered armor exoskeleton combat suit with flame throwers in the arms that can phase through reality and walk through walls like a ghost... but then tells me that the only way we can put a scope on rifle is to loot one off a dead enemy, because manufacturing such an advanced piece of obviously alien technology is clearly beyond her capabilities.
And it gets worse. If you want to make a +1 hitpoint vest then you go to engineering, spend the materials, and produce one vest that can be equipped by one soldier. But when you make a single +4 hitpoint armor suit literally all your soldiers can now wear it all at once. But if you want to make a powersuit then you have to manufacture each one by hand, one by one. But if you want to make plasma rifles you can build one and now literally everyone has them. But if you want to make a fancy hand grenade you have to make them one at a time and, oh yeah, they're completely random
But that one hand grenade can be used an infinite number times. But only by one soldier at a time.  Shen, your drug test came back and it says you're a carrot.
Mind you, these are all the game mechanics that are actually working as intended. I haven't even mentioned the bugs and I'm not going to, because that would take another six pages. Sufficie it to say, the graphics aren't the only place where Firaxis slept through their workday.
Yet now I must get to my conclusion and the core of my complaint about XCOM2, and it is thus:
They looked at XCOM1 and how popular LongWar was, and they realized that, oh yeah, they didn't actually have to do any of the work that went into LongWar. The modding community did (specifically, one small and amazingly talented group of modders). They took an already good game and made it great. Firaxis took that lesson and ran with it... and ran with it... past the touchdown line, into the parking lot, and into the next state over.
They released two things at the exact same time: A buggy, barely finished game that featured only a minimal amount of core material... and a modding kit. Golly, I wonder what they expected to happen next? It's rather obvious - they, like Bethesada, are 100% counting on a bunch of talented people from the modding communities to figure out how to use their SDK and finish making their game for them.
Only 4 classes? Eh, let the modders fix it. Only 3 weapon tiers? Eh, let the modders fix it. Poor interface choices? Eh, let the modders fix it. Limited enemy variety? Eh, let the modders fix it. Weak core, lack of variety, poor optimization, bugs and generally bad design decisions all around? Eh, let the modders fix it. It works for Bethesda, right? Why pay our own people to this game's cornucopia of problems when you can make the customers do it for free?
I can sum up all but one of the DLC in two words: "Horse Armor."
In summary, Firaxis has given us lazy, poorly thought out game design that focuses on gimmicks rather than real upgrades & deeper content. The gimmicks are trying to prop up gameplay mechanics that were either devolved or removed outright and they just aren't up to the task.
XCOM2 did succeed in bringing us a
game experience than XCOM1 did, but it failed at bringing us a better one - or even a comparable one.  This is isn't the brutal blend of strategy & tactics that we've come to love.  This is 2/3rds "Barbie's Army Dress-up Playset" and 1/3rd of blatant "
" rip-off.
