This game is good. Like, this game is REALLY f*cking good. If your debating whether or not to get it, or thinking "this just looks like some refurbished mobile game, or a pokemon rip off", throw that thought in the garbage.
The good stuff - Darkest Dungeon punishes you. A lot. This is not a cakewalk. Every choice you make, big or small, has an impact on whether or not you will leave the Dungeon rich will all of your heroes, or carrying 4 bodies back to the Hamlet fortuneless. Each of the main 4 areas has strengths and weaknesses, and you need to assemble your party and supplies accordingly.  The enviroment is very fleshed out, and certain curios of loot can harm you unless you have the proper traits and supplies to deal with them. The camping system is also very nice, allowing you to recover damage and stress, and buff your heroes for the upcoming battles all while your still in the dungeon. The Hamlet is full of depth, and actually feels very interesting to invest in. It is even accompanied by over 40 random events that can occur when you return, good or bad, ranging from running out of meade kegs to being able to ressurect a fallen hero. Hell, the heroes themselves are fun and diverse, and I find myself getting attatched to many of them (Which in this game can be a mistake). The game is also not as repetetive as it may come off as. Sure, its not your Killing Floor 2 action game, but it definatly does something right to keep you on the end of your chair during tough battles.  Finally, the feature to disable features such as heart attacks and unfleeable fights is a nice touch, allowing you to ban mechanics you deem unfair
The flaws - Throughout all of the pros, there are a few problems with the game.  For example, the trinket system could use a little rework. I often find myself not using many of them because they can harm your hero just as much as help them. Even the rarer trinkets come with debuffs, which makes progressing feel slightly unrewarding. I think it is also a drawback that as the game progresses, you will find that enemies have higher resistances to stacking or special abilities such as bleed, blight, stun, or move. It feels like a little bit of a waste of the games mechanics, since a lot of heroes good abilities apply these. The game also does take a dose of luck, but definatly not enough to cause a real problem
In summery, if you are not a patient person, with resistance to rage, then this game is undoubtedly for you. Just remember above all, it is HARD.

Starbound is, at it's core, a flawed game. It always has been since its conception, and no real effort has been made to change the game for the better; they've mostly just added things onto the flawed structure of the game. The game revolves around a lot of farming, due to essentially everything being randomly generated. Not that it's particularly "hard" to get anything, but nothing is really rewarding. If you happen to find a weapon with really good stats, you don't feel like you earned it, you just happened to run into it. Same goes for pretty much every item in the game. Most enemies aren't an issue, more of an annoyance; combat is as basic as it gets. Enemy either chargest at you or shoots you, and you shoot back until the enemy is dead. Enemy variety is very scarce, too; they all move very similarly, attacks are mostly the same throughout the game aside from the rare biome-specific enemy, and so on.
The "story" of the game is a very generic story; you're the "chosen one" and you have to collect six artifacts to open a door and fight the final boss. The bosses are pretty basic, nothing to really write home about; they can be overwhelming, but that's mostly due to poor design than actual difficulty (The boss staying off-screen, cramped combat areas, etc.), and the final boss is monstrously underwhelming. More than anything else, though, is the fact that doing the story doesn't really give you any sort of reward. You get some extra NPCs which provide some extra stuff (which isn't exclusive to them), and you get money and generic "prize bags" which give you some random weapon, but that's it. Bosses (besides the final boss, for no real reason) have a 10% chance to drop a unique weapon, but said weapons generally aren't really worth having to sit through the long, tedious missions (because yes, you have to do the entire mission each time you want to fight the boss) to farm the drop.
That more or less covers the game up to this point, but Chucklefish has recently provided new updates after the game was "released" (which begs the question, why bother exiting early access? What was the point of early access at all? But I digress.). These updates added three major additions to the game, which, initially, I was excited for; at face value, the additions sound great, but as usual, Chucklefish found a way to ♥♥♥♥ it up.
The first addition is a post-final-boss addition, supposedly meant to provide a sort of "ongoing challenge". Once you beat the final boss, you can trade with a vendor to buy temple keys, allowing you to enter an ancient portal to an ancient temple, made by generic "ancient people". It's not exactly prize-winning story-writing, but that's obviously not what you should expect from Chucklefish. Given that this is the end of the game, you'd expect some sort of grand challenge; cool platforming challenges, new, harder enemies, and so on, but of course, you would be disappointed. These temples are just an empty maze of tunnles to the end, populated only by basic enemies you've already seen throughout the game. There isn't really any new loot, either. Once you get to the end, though, you'll find a new boss; at least they could be bothered to make SOMETHING new in these temples, but they're generally pretty basic boss fights. They only really have two or three attack patterns, maybe with one bonus attack as their health lowers. Once you've beaten the boss, it explodes into a new kind of currency, the same currency every other enemy has been dropping, which you use in the final room of the temple. It may also drop a new kind of item, which changes the area around you into a particular mini-biome; a fun little gimmick, but not particularly useful unless you really need to change the biome of a particular area into something else. The final room contains two crafting tables; one allows you to craft machines which change a planet's type at the cost of said currency, and the other upgrades weapons to endgame-tier; again, neat, but nothing really new. It's fun for the endgame, but crafting new weapons isn't particularly useful or fun when combat isn't useful or fun.
Next, Mechs were added. They seem really cool, initially! Finally being able to travel through space, and all. But you can't use the mech wherever or whenever you want; you can only spawn it once going down to a planet/space-area, and it only lasts a limited amount of time before despawning. On top of this, the mech is weirdly balanced; it completely obliterates any planetary enemies, even with the starter gear, but works fine against space enemies. It just seems like space enemy/mech health/damage was scaled up for no particular reason, and leaves everything feeling pretty unbalanced. But, hey, building a mech sounds cool, right? Well, not really, because parts are rare, and cost an absurd amount of materials to craft. Plus, the only thing you really get from exploring through space are some generic pre-generated space ships and buildings, with the occasional space station (which your mech doesn't fit in). And, by space ships, I don't mean you actually get to fight other space ships, or even other mechs, the ships are just stationary buildings meant to look like ships. The only loot you get from going out into space is stuff to upgrade your mech, and the only real use for your mech is to travel through space, so, ultimately, it just feels like a moot cause meant to fluff the game with mindless grinding for parts that only help you grind for more parts. Actual space combat is basic; shoot at stuff that's flying and shooting at you. You don't get to actually fight other mechs, or ships, or anything interesting; the most interesting thing you can fight are floating computers that shoot bullets in your direction. And, naturally, because nothing in this game has any unique drops, there's no reason to focus on fighting them; you're better off just ignoring enemies and flying to the pre-generated space thing.
And lastly, the worst of all, space stations. This one stings particularly badly because of how excited I was for it; being able to build your own space craft, finally! It looked so cool, it looked like you could trade resources and manage your ship and crew members and all this neat stuff and build cabins for your crewmates... you know, stuff that NPC space stations have. But, as it turns out, NPC space stations are actually nothing like the space stations you get. You don't get a crew. You don't manage resources. I say this with no hyperbole; the space station is just a gigantic waste of time and resources that does absolutely nothing. You can't even ♥♥♥♥ing build it. "But wait", you're thinking, "surely you're exaggerating, you must be able to build it! It's a sandbox game, how would you not be able to build it?" You're prevented from even touching the walls of your space station. Forget being able to change the shape of the rooms, the materials, you can't even change the ♥♥♥♥ing color of it. All you're given are pre-generated hallways and rooms. You can build inside of them, but nowhere near to the extent which NPC stations are customized. It just feels like a clumsy, rushed feature which doesn't add anything to the game; you already have a ship, you can already upgrade it, the space stations just feel like an uglier version of your ship that you can't drive or teleport directly to. But that's not even the worse part, if you can believe that. You already have to pick from ♥♥♥♥♥♥, cramped, pre-built rooms, how could it get worse? Well, if each of those pre-built rooms cost literally
of resources. You could build dozens of massive buildings at the cost of just one tiny hallway.
Long story short, don't get this game. The devs are lying jackasses, and honestly, even if you already have Terraria, you're gonna have a much better time playing through Terraria again than trying Starbound. If you don't have Terraria, stop reading this right now and get it immediately.

This game is why Fireaxis needs to start implementing emplyee drug testing.  It isn't just broken, it's bad.
It's not the difficulty, it's not the graphics, it's not the lag: It's the horrible, poorly thought out game mechanics that traded in working, balanced gameplay in favor of cheap gimmicks yanked from tacky Korean MMOs (read: lottery loot) and a total clusterfark of a strategic map. And the entire plot was unabashedly ripped striaght from
.
The Doom Clock is nothing more than an arbitrary time limit that does nothing more than artificially force you down a certain research path & gameplay style under the threat of losing if you deviate from it in any way. The fanbois says this game is proactive instead of reactive - that's complete horsepucky.  This series has never been more on rails than in this iteration.
All of the Second Wave options you knew & loved are gone. Random stat bonus on level up? Gone. Random rookie stats? Gone. Flanking aim bonuses have been reduced to a flat rate that doesn't involve any real math. Ditto for criticals. The experience points system have been traded in for raw kill totals.  Comparing the tactical game mechanics of XCOM1 to XCOM2 is like comparing chess to checkers.
Your base experience, likewise, has also been dumbed down. Alien containment? Gone. Interrogations? Gone. Interceptors? Gone.  The once mighty research tree has been trimmed down to a pathetic shrub, mostly so that they could implement their latest gameplay gimmicks over in engineering.
The engineering room is the epitome of XCOM2's failures. Shen tells me that she's got the technology to make a powered armor exoskeleton combat suit with flame throwers in the arms that can phase through reality and walk through walls like a ghost... but then tells me that the only way we can put a scope on rifle is to loot one off a dead enemy, because manufacturing such an advanced piece of obviously alien technology is clearly beyond her capabilities.
And it gets worse. If you want to make a +1 hitpoint vest then you go to engineering, spend the materials, and produce one vest that can be equipped by one soldier. But when you make a single +4 hitpoint armor suit literally all your soldiers can now wear it all at once. But if you want to make a powersuit then you have to manufacture each one by hand, one by one. But if you want to make plasma rifles you can build one and now literally everyone has them. But if you want to make a fancy hand grenade you have to make them one at a time and, oh yeah, they're completely random
But that one hand grenade can be used an infinite number times. But only by one soldier at a time.  Shen, your drug test came back and it says you're a carrot.
Mind you, these are all the game mechanics that are actually working as intended. I haven't even mentioned the bugs and I'm not going to, because that would take another six pages. Sufficie it to say, the graphics aren't the only place where Firaxis slept through their workday.
Yet now I must get to my conclusion and the core of my complaint about XCOM2, and it is thus:
They looked at XCOM1 and how popular LongWar was, and they realized that, oh yeah, they didn't actually have to do any of the work that went into LongWar. The modding community did (specifically, one small and amazingly talented group of modders). They took an already good game and made it great. Firaxis took that lesson and ran with it... and ran with it... past the touchdown line, into the parking lot, and into the next state over.
They released two things at the exact same time: A buggy, barely finished game that featured only a minimal amount of core material... and a modding kit. Golly, I wonder what they expected to happen next? It's rather obvious - they, like Bethesada, are 100% counting on a bunch of talented people from the modding communities to figure out how to use their SDK and finish making their game for them.
Only 4 classes? Eh, let the modders fix it. Only 3 weapon tiers? Eh, let the modders fix it. Poor interface choices? Eh, let the modders fix it. Limited enemy variety? Eh, let the modders fix it. Weak core, lack of variety, poor optimization, bugs and generally bad design decisions all around? Eh, let the modders fix it. It works for Bethesda, right? Why pay our own people to this game's cornucopia of problems when you can make the customers do it for free?
I can sum up all but one of the DLC in two words: "Horse Armor."
In summary, Firaxis has given us lazy, poorly thought out game design that focuses on gimmicks rather than real upgrades & deeper content. The gimmicks are trying to prop up gameplay mechanics that were either devolved or removed outright and they just aren't up to the task.
XCOM2 did succeed in bringing us a
game experience than XCOM1 did, but it failed at bringing us a better one - or even a comparable one.  This is isn't the brutal blend of strategy & tactics that we've come to love.  This is 2/3rds "Barbie's Army Dress-up Playset" and 1/3rd of blatant "
" rip-off.

Make no mistake: this game is not for everyone. It is the type of game that requires patience, more patience and, every so often, the ability to chant mantras like "I will not rage, I will not smash my keyboard..."
Pros:
Art, SFX, replayability
Cons:
RNG - the gods of RNG are easily angered
Picture this: you get a high level party and proceed to faceroll anything that comes your way, all the while listening to the awesome "ancestor" voice saying "OBLITERATED!", "DESTROYED!", "MASTERFULLY EXECUTED!" as you kill, bleed and poison your opponents. After the dungeon is complete, you collect lots of loot and you feel confident.
Big mistake.
As your ancestor reminds you, "Overconfidence is a slow and insidious killer". But you think that this does not apply to you and so you start another dungeon, with the same party. After all they were successful in the previous run...And this is where DD reminds of who is in charge: enemies start handing out critical hits to your heroes as if it was Christmas all over again. And so, your vestal panics which in turn prevents her from doing her job: TO HEAL. The other members of the party get stressed because she is constantly babbling to herself about the horrors she has seen. This leads to more stress piling up and, quicker than you realise, they are all screaming and cursing and hitting themselves till they are nothing more than nervous wrecks left at death's door...
And then the blissful silence of death...your heroes that so confidently defeated the evil hordes in the previous dungeon are now resting eternally in the graveyard. You look around and find only young and inexperienced recruits, barely capable of lifting their weapons.
How many heroes does it take to appease the RNG gods? Only they know. But if you have the strength to rise from the ashes, you will find the time spent in the Darkest Dungeon rewarding.

I think this is the best fallout game, an unpopular opinion maybe but I'll try to justify why.
Firstly, the gunplay in Fallout 3 and New Vegas was atrocious, some of the worst, most broken, inaccurate shooting I've ever experienced. Unless the enemy is within about 5ft of you you'll miss 99% of the time, this makes the game nigh unplayable without heavy use of VATS. This was fixed by Fallout 4, now the gunplay is actually decent, and you can hit things at reasonable distances without VATS. Of course this doesn't invalidate VATS, it simply makes it not ESSENTIAL to hit anything at range.
Secondly, the crafting system makes it so that junk is actually something that you have a reason to collect. In previous Fallout games, junk was just that: junk. It was little more than a set piece and the fact you could pick it up was really a novelty, as it served little to no purpose. With Fallout 4's settlement building and weapon/armor modification systems this turned what used to be next to useless props into valuable materials, and I spent the majority of my caps on Wonderglue and alarm clocks rather than weapons or armor, which makes the game feel a lot more apocalyptic - the fact the player scavenges for junk which they can repurpose to help them survive is quintessential to post apocalyptic settings and, in fact, makes the player feel like they are surviving.
Thirdly, the power armor has been completely revamped, into what is essentially a mobile tank. Many critics of the power armor mechanics say that it is overpowered and was poorly executed, and there is some basis for these claims. The player is given a suit of power armor at the start of the game, which I believe was a poor decision. However, in the early game/mid game power armor is used scarcely, since fusion cores are quite a valuable resource which are quite rare at lower levels. This makes the power armor feel powerful, and the player can sometimes be hindered by it, as while sprinting with power armor is possible, it heavily taxes the fusion core, so discouraging players from doing so.
Finally, the new perk system, I feel, is more meaningful than the skills system of previous Fallout games. When you level up you now get a "perk point" to spend on perks, similar to Skyrim's leveling. The perks you can access are based on your level and your SPECIAL attributes, making you SPECIAL allocation especially important for what type of character you want to build. This system makes leveling feel monumental, and also provides a motivation to make a less "well rounded" character with the special stats, as you close off some of the best perks in return for being more versatile.
Obviously the game is not perfect, if you are a heavily story driven player the game may leave something to be desired, however, as someone who loves gameplay and fun, I must say that Fallout 4 is by far the best Fallout game to date in my opinion, and highly recommend this game to anyone who is interested in it.

Dark Souls 3 is an awesome game, truly good. And you should buy it.
But then, why am I not recommanding it?
We'll talk about that later.
First the game is worthy of being called Dark Souls, if like me you spend hundreads of hours on the first and second one, you have no reason not to buy it. You'll easily spend a few hundread on this one. A lot of weapons to choose from, and the addition of the weapon art mechanic only encourage you to find and try them all. There is also the new "dual weapon" mechanic, some weapons cannot be two handed, but instead will act like the dual wielding system from dark souls 2 (which was unfortunatly removed), but with a more unique movesets and weapon arts (for example the gothard swords or farron greatsword). You can also now charge your power attacks to do A LOT of damage.
Bosses, are so much better than in Dark Souls 2, where I litterally first tryed (solo of course) nearly all of them, I won't lie, some bosses in Dark Souls 3 are nothing but gimmicks, and those are disappointing, but they aren't bad, just useless. And some bosses can be pretty damn brutal, I'll tell you that much.
There is also this password mechanic which allow you to connect to anyone WITHOUT ANY RESTRICTION (NG cycle, soul level, weapon upgrade), great for coop, or to get some items early for specific builds/cosplays.
So the gamre is great, but what's bad then? Well first the roll sytem. I don't like it, basically Fromsoft wanted to make a bloodborne like game, and I don't know why they wanted Dark Souls 3 to be like that. Dark Souls 2 was slower, and it was good, you had to actually time your rolls, in Dark Souls 1 your rolls could be quick but costed enough stamina to be careful about it. Dark Souls 3 is a roll party, with a base stamina bar, you can, and I'm not joking, roll 12 TIMES IN A ROW.
And it makes PVP, and especially invasions so bad, since it's so hard to roll catch people barely use power attacks, it's just regular attack spam, because yes, in this game, with 20 points in stamina, you can swing an untra greatsword 5 TIMES. If you see someone do so in Dark Souls 1 or 2 you would call the guy a cheater. Well not here. It's so dumb, DEX and other light weapons aren't worth anything in PVP unless you're very good with it, with the hyper armor meta: Basically the game gives you unlimited poise when your swing a heavy weapon, so if your spacing isn't perfect, you can't hit someone using an ultra greatsword with a light weapon, well you can, but you'll loose the trade.
Invasions, are so bad, invaders are so disadvantaged, you can't have fun unless you have a full meta build. Everyone can estus now, so it last forever, in Dark Souls 1 and 2, invaders couldn't heal unless they used a miracle, and when invading the phantoms could not heal either, only the host could use Estus. It was fine like that, why did they changed it?
BTW the blue covenant is still a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to level up, and game isn't dead yet.
But even that, is not enough to call Dark Souls 3 a bad game, however a game forcing PVP via invasions (which are a lot more present in this title than in any other), and with an anti-cheat like that, I cannot recommand. The game has so much cheaters, it took 10 HOURS ONLY to be one shotted/petrified by someone, this is simply unacceptable in a game forcing PVP that much. Don't assume I don't like to invade/be invaded, I absolutly love the mechanic, despite the massive disadvantage invaders get. And the twinks, it's unbelievable, the first area of the game, play it offline, it's just people with DLC weapons and crap there, it's not fun, played it with a friend once, it's not fun. And the password mechanic doesn't help unfortunatly...
To conclude, you should buy this, but play offline if you can't handle the online♥♥♥♥♥♥

Having just finished the main game I thought it was time for a review. FYI it took me 41 hours, didnt do DLC yet,  with a bit of sidetracking but I know I missed a fair few things just from item descriptions on loading screen etc.
If you thought Dark Souls 1> Dark souls 2, this is the game for you. Lovingly crafted and gorgeous return to the origins of the series. It is an amazing game but I think it would be more useful for prospective buyers (who presumably are familiar with the first 2 entries in the series) to compare the games. Here are a few things I noted:
Dark Souls 3 keeps the 'feel' of Dark Souls 1. Environments are WAY more expansive, you'll spend ages looking around. Enemies are more 'monstrous' rather than all knights like in DS2. I found the game really hard and had to stop and grind a couple of times (notably on road of sacrifices).
Dark Souls 3 keeps the bonfire warping of DS2, but environments are far more interconnected. You'll often loop back on yourself in an area. I wont spoil anything, but soon after you start the game you're looking (far off, in the distance) at the area where you'll play out the final chapters. Everywhere you can see, you will go to at some point. Which is cool. However I couldn't find any optional areas like in DS2 or DS1 (- yet?). The game is not TRULY interconnected like dark souls 1. You'll never have the profound mind-blowing moment of going from Firelink->valley of drakes-> blighttown -> ash lake and realising exactly where you are in the game world. But in general environments are far more involving. One downside is that the interconnection seems a bit forced in some areas. Almost every new area you get to will have a locked door or elevator that 'this door will not open from this side'.  Minor issue.
There have been many quality of life improvements. Homeward bones now warp much quicker and they were a bona-fide get out of jail free card on more than one occasion. Weapon arts - I didn't use them very often but they add a lot of variety, as do the different shield powers etc. Rings of sacrifice have gone back to truly one-use items. Very frustrating when you die as a phantom and break them. It's way easier to change covenants now, just equip an item. No more finding the shrine each time.  You can offer multiple medals etc to a shrine at once, too. (you can't see how many you've offered though or what level you're at, which is a distinct regression). You need to be careful who you invite back to the shrine or the c-bombs will kill other c-bombs.
One thing really drove me wild - you can't cancel accidental miracle casts by rolling out of it anymore. It's much harder to level up, more like dark souls 1 than dark souls 2. I finished the campaign at level 70 with about 1m souls saved - didn't have anything to spend them on :( .AFAIK soul memory is gone, player level now drives the multiplayer. You can't improve armour in this version (!)  ( i think?) and it's not really clear how 'absorbption' and 'defence' works. So you only really spend souls on levels, weapons, or consumable items. I really found myself missing several of the armours or shields from the previous games. I would have loved to see a little more info about certain aspects of the first game like those in black iron, or with a dagger for a tail.... Possibly they're there and I missed them. I still haven't managed to completely put the story together yet, so I'm still uncovering it which is enjoyable.
On the topic of story, it nicely wraps up the previous 2 entries. You'll see nods to the war between the giants, and plenty of other bosses and characters. it also gives you a very, very cool taste of what actually *happens* when the fire fades. Previous games were always sunny and then at the end you choose light or darkness with not much context - this shows you what happens when all fades and the darkness comes in. And I was actually kind of scared to choose one of the outcomes at the end.
This is a pretty amazing game with lots of fan service. I only wish it would go on for ever and ever.  If you haven't played it, or any of the games in the series, you're cheating yourself.  Get started.
**Edit**  Btw, I did come across two very frustrating glitches. One, sometimes you will fall through an elevator (seems to be if you are rolling/striking etc as you hit the button). Only happened once but i was on my way back to collect my bloodstain and lost everything. I have seen other people's bloodstains showing they died the same way - standing on the elevator and then just fall through the floor.
Second, you'll often go for a backstab, get pinned in place and strike at thin air while the enemy is free to keep moving - usually to turn around and belt you one while your character is stuck lining up his strike.
**Subsequent Edit**  Yeah....just found a massive optional area I missed.  Great stuff. (also addresses some of my earlier criticisms about lack of interconnectivity....)

This game is why Fireaxis needs to start implementing emplyee drug testing.  It isn't just broken, it's bad.
It's not the difficulty, it's not the graphics, it's not the lag: It's the horrible, poorly thought out game mechanics that traded in working, balanced gameplay in favor of cheap gimmicks yanked from tacky Korean MMOs (read: lottery loot) and a total clusterfark of a strategic map. And the entire plot was unabashedly ripped striaght from
.
The Doom Clock is nothing more than an arbitrary time limit that does nothing more than artificially force you down a certain research path & gameplay style under the threat of losing if you deviate from it in any way. The fanbois says this game is proactive instead of reactive - that's complete horsepucky.  This series has never been more on rails than in this iteration.
All of the Second Wave options you knew & loved are gone. Random stat bonus on level up? Gone. Random rookie stats? Gone. Flanking aim bonuses have been reduced to a flat rate that doesn't involve any real math. Ditto for criticals. The experience points system have been traded in for raw kill totals.  Comparing the tactical game mechanics of XCOM1 to XCOM2 is like comparing chess to checkers.
Your base experience, likewise, has also been dumbed down. Alien containment? Gone. Interrogations? Gone. Interceptors? Gone.  The once mighty research tree has been trimmed down to a pathetic shrub, mostly so that they could implement their latest gameplay gimmicks over in engineering.
The engineering room is the epitome of XCOM2's failures. Shen tells me that she's got the technology to make a powered armor exoskeleton combat suit with flame throwers in the arms that can phase through reality and walk through walls like a ghost... but then tells me that the only way we can put a scope on rifle is to loot one off a dead enemy, because manufacturing such an advanced piece of obviously alien technology is clearly beyond her capabilities.
And it gets worse. If you want to make a +1 hitpoint vest then you go to engineering, spend the materials, and produce one vest that can be equipped by one soldier. But when you make a single +4 hitpoint armor suit literally all your soldiers can now wear it all at once. But if you want to make a powersuit then you have to manufacture each one by hand, one by one. But if you want to make plasma rifles you can build one and now literally everyone has them. But if you want to make a fancy hand grenade you have to make them one at a time and, oh yeah, they're completely random
But that one hand grenade can be used an infinite number times. But only by one soldier at a time.  Shen, your drug test came back and it says you're a carrot.
Mind you, these are all the game mechanics that are actually working as intended. I haven't even mentioned the bugs and I'm not going to, because that would take another six pages. Sufficie it to say, the graphics aren't the only place where Firaxis slept through their workday.
Yet now I must get to my conclusion and the core of my complaint about XCOM2, and it is thus:
They looked at XCOM1 and how popular LongWar was, and they realized that, oh yeah, they didn't actually have to do any of the work that went into LongWar. The modding community did (specifically, one small and amazingly talented group of modders). They took an already good game and made it great. Firaxis took that lesson and ran with it... and ran with it... past the touchdown line, into the parking lot, and into the next state over.
They released two things at the exact same time: A buggy, barely finished game that featured only a minimal amount of core material... and a modding kit. Golly, I wonder what they expected to happen next? It's rather obvious - they, like Bethesada, are 100% counting on a bunch of talented people from the modding communities to figure out how to use their SDK and finish making their game for them.
Only 4 classes? Eh, let the modders fix it. Only 3 weapon tiers? Eh, let the modders fix it. Poor interface choices? Eh, let the modders fix it. Limited enemy variety? Eh, let the modders fix it. Weak core, lack of variety, poor optimization, bugs and generally bad design decisions all around? Eh, let the modders fix it. It works for Bethesda, right? Why pay our own people to this game's cornucopia of problems when you can make the customers do it for free?
I can sum up all but one of the DLC in two words: "Horse Armor."
In summary, Firaxis has given us lazy, poorly thought out game design that focuses on gimmicks rather than real upgrades & deeper content. The gimmicks are trying to prop up gameplay mechanics that were either devolved or removed outright and they just aren't up to the task.
XCOM2 did succeed in bringing us a
game experience than XCOM1 did, but it failed at bringing us a better one - or even a comparable one.  This is isn't the brutal blend of strategy & tactics that we've come to love.  This is 2/3rds "Barbie's Army Dress-up Playset" and 1/3rd of blatant "
" rip-off.

Make no mistake: this game is not for everyone. It is the type of game that requires patience, more patience and, every so often, the ability to chant mantras like "I will not rage, I will not smash my keyboard..."
Pros:
Art, SFX, replayability
Cons:
RNG - the gods of RNG are easily angered
Picture this: you get a high level party and proceed to faceroll anything that comes your way, all the while listening to the awesome "ancestor" voice saying "OBLITERATED!", "DESTROYED!", "MASTERFULLY EXECUTED!" as you kill, bleed and poison your opponents. After the dungeon is complete, you collect lots of loot and you feel confident.
Big mistake.
As your ancestor reminds you, "Overconfidence is a slow and insidious killer". But you think that this does not apply to you and so you start another dungeon, with the same party. After all they were successful in the previous run...And this is where DD reminds of who is in charge: enemies start handing out critical hits to your heroes as if it was Christmas all over again. And so, your vestal panics which in turn prevents her from doing her job: TO HEAL. The other members of the party get stressed because she is constantly babbling to herself about the horrors she has seen. This leads to more stress piling up and, quicker than you realise, they are all screaming and cursing and hitting themselves till they are nothing more than nervous wrecks left at death's door...
And then the blissful silence of death...your heroes that so confidently defeated the evil hordes in the previous dungeon are now resting eternally in the graveyard. You look around and find only young and inexperienced recruits, barely capable of lifting their weapons.
How many heroes does it take to appease the RNG gods? Only they know. But if you have the strength to rise from the ashes, you will find the time spent in the Darkest Dungeon rewarding.

Hello people considering downloading trove. I'm glad you're reading my review still. Trove back in the first 5 months of release was an epic game that I put a lot of time into. It was hard and fun. Every minute had me on edge because of how hard the enemies were. It took forever to get anywhere in the game making it fun and easy to put a lot of time into as there was endless amounts of small updates just adding more loot and some other small tweeks. However the new updates ruined the experience for me:
I don't usually say that I like the older versions better on games but trove is one of those rare cases where the original game was superior to the current version.
Trove has branched off way to far from its roots. It originaly was supposed to be a small indie game that wouldn't grow. However when it did the developers started changing their demographic to a very you audience. It went from a hard rpg that you had to put a lot of time into to a very borring long game. The game no longer has those epic moments that it used to.I feels bland and uninspired.
The game was originaly about fighting monsters and crawling through dungeons with creative ways. Now it has turned into a game about building like minecraft and less focused on the fighting wich is where trove shines.
The people who played trove back in it's glory days had so many amazing experiences with it. The things us "oldies" had like horses or double jumps or cool things took so much time to do. Easily 10 hours in just to get a horse. You were plopped down with no direction or any idea what to do and you had to figure it out yourself. Now there is a pointer at every direction what us "oldies" spent hours working for is now given to you for free and it is very boring.
So to sum it up it no longer feels like and RPG with a block building sandbox game. It now feels like a block building sandbox game with RPG machanics awkwardly shoved in there.
So I give it =3/10
Pros:
A fun combat system +2
Solid Gameplay +3
Very few bugs +3
Cons:
Strayed super far from it's original idea (THAT WAS GOOD!) -2
Everything given to you at the start of the game -1
Super Easy -1
Far too much grinding -1
There are many better F2P games than this. Trove you should have stayed with your original concept.

XCOM 2 is a straight sequel to the 2012 remake XCOM: Enemy Unknown.
In his infinite wisdom, Jake "Sid Meier is the dad I never had" Solomon threw out the expected Terror From The Deep follow-up from the meeting board and offers us instead a "what if ?" scenario where the aliens won and left XCOM in shambles.
Also you get snake girls with♥♥♥♥♥♥cause he swore to never put snakemen in the game. Meta as ♥♥♥♥ !
The game is pretty much a refined version of the first one. If you only swear by the original trilogy and Xenonauts, you might be dissapointed. Still, there are some new nice features.
With no United Nations to back you up and Alien backed EXALT forces trying to hunt you down, the game flow is a little confusing at first. With your mobile base, you need to scan Earth's various regions to find supplies, troops and more importantly make contact with local resistance cells. This new version of the satelite coverage will become crucial as you try to thwart ADVENTs plans. Indeed, the aliens have an endgame, a doomsday counter called "The Avatar Project", which can't be stopped. It's scarier than it looks as completing story objectives and blowing up facilities will slow its progress drastically.
Apart from the cosmetic lifting and the guerilla vibe, two features I really loved are the global revamp of the soldier classes and the concealment system. Every class is back but with a new edge, assaults get a melee machete, supports a cool robot, snipers become gunslingers, etc. It's such a great way to spice up the existing classes and make them much more polyvalent. Since XCOM is now a guerilla warfare operation, every mission makes you start hidden. It's up to you to spot enemies and ambush them WHEN you want it. It's a great way to set up a mission, especially since most of them are now timer-based.
I don't have many problems with the game. The sad motto "Don't spot enemies on your last turn movement is still up or you are ♥♥♥♥ed" is still true and some enemies are pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t (like the lancers). But most of these complains will probably be answered by a "git gud, f4gg4t".
The unsung hero of the game is probably Tim Wynn, the new composer. I was♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at first that McCann didn't make the new score but now I realize it's for the best. XCOM was about mystery and unseen threats which matched the music perfectly. XCOM 2 is all about solemnity and the unshattered pugnacity of humanity. Music is so good it made me swallow a thesaurus.
tl, dr: It's a new version of XCOM 2k12 with cool enemies, tons of customization and MOD supports.

An incredible game worthy of full price, something I have not been able to say about the overwhelming majority of AAA (and otherwise) titles these days.  If you are a fan of turn based strategy combat, and a minor basebuilding overworld that involves an early-mid game frantic pace where you juggle resources and make key decisions, Xcom 2 should be right up your alley.
It improves on almost every facet of the original, though the base building is a little bare bones in comparison, since the nature of this game is quite different and your mothership is your home base so naturally, there are a lot fewer choices to make.  If you played the first one, you will be right at home, nothing is so vastly different that you won't be able to infer what its role or function is.
The story is pretty well done, albeit a little sparse, and towards the end it does feel a little anti-climatic but really Xcom is about having a badass group of marines and the amazing combat.  A gripe many people will have (myself included) will be in regards to the some what questionable RNG that determines the success or failure of your tactics within the game.  When I think of 80-95% chance of success, I think of it as an almost sure thing.  When you miss 4 of those in a row, you begin to really question how accurate the numbers depicted upon the screen are.... but as everyone says Xcom is Xcom, and this is just part of the experience.  You can miss a 95% and you can hit a 20%.  The game isn't without its moments where you'd like to put an axe through your monitor.
Unfortunately, there are definitely some performance issues and bugs/glitches with the current game.  The game, as impressive as it looks, is certainly not what you'd expect to push your gaming rig to its limits, yet your frames will drop inexplicably, mini cutscenes will stutter, and overall you will notice some choppiness.  Where as it's not aggregious for me (GTX980 TI, 16 gb RAM, SSD, I74790k), it still is bothersome that this game isn't running flawlessly.
There is quite a bit of graphical clipping issues, it seems the engine has trouble dealing with structures, walls, doors, windows, and multi-level buildings.  Often your character will stick his gun through a seemingly solid object, or try to smash out a window that is already smashed, walk through a door, be pulled through a building, shot through solid cover, etc.   Where as it is annoying and takes away from immersion, the game is still so robust, deep, and rewarding that I found myself looking past it.  It's just too damn enjoyable to let those things drag down the experience.
One would hope Firaxis is aware and addressing these issues, because once they are fixed, this game is a VERY strong contender for GOTY.   Certainly, this is the best tactical strategy game I've played, and the extensive modding capabilities the game has only means great things when you get guys like the creators of the Long War  working on all manners of new content - for free.
All in all, despite the somewhat unforgivable performance issues of a PC-Exclusive, this game is definitely what I would consider a must-buy for anyone who is a fan of the genre.

While the game has way too many "launch issues" to merit them, reviewers seem to have given Firaxis the benefit of the doubt.  It seems many are taking the long-view of the game down the road, rather tha at launch. Clearly the games large number of fine reviews are largely deserved from a overall design  perspectiveand once all the launch issues are resolved the game may well merit "classic" status.  Personally, I think will end up  a fine addition to the Xcom franchise once many of the launch problems are ironed out. Xcom2 has tons fresh ideas and also pulls off the trick of picking fresh ideas that fit well with into the Xcom Universe. They streamlined gameplay and wanted very tense gameplay. (EW's Meld mechanism to get players to feel tension also seemed a bit contrived. Play balance is definitely geared to the experienced player, and while brutally hard games seem to be more acceptable these days, the casual player may easily be put off.   The customization and mod support up front were great ideas that will really add replayability, and the ease of adding "Mods" is a real plus.  ( One nit-pic there: One would think that game would remember the Mods you picked last time, but that obvious feature was not implemented at launch!)
The game ramps up difficulty exponentially from Easy to Legendary.  Essentially from easy, to brutual and for all practial purposes impossible at the highest difficulty.   Legendary, is,as the designer of Long War commented on his own most difficult setting, "winnable in theory, but not particularly fair."   I've played a whole lot of Xcom but Legendary is so hard as to be simply exhausting.  I suppose someone will beat it on Ironman mode somewhere, but having gotten well into a Legendary campaign, I began to get a little tired of having nerfed hit percentages  mixed with eternal first-gen weapons (it takes forever to ramp up tech) against enemies with enough armor to absorb first gen base weapons damage completely).  Commander difficulty isn't quite as insane, but certainly harder than the Xcom EW Classic difficulty.
There are some rather odd enemy selection choices.  I saw some enemies very frequently (the Archon) while other hardly at all.  while we saw Mutons all the time in EW and it was "Heavy Floaters 24/7" in the later stages of Long War, I almost came to miss my old friend the Muton a bit because I barely encountered them at all.  Additionally, a bias on my part, but I found the choice of the Archon art a big disappointment for the heavy floater replacement.  It's Sci-Fi genre - If I want to play D&D I'll pull out my 20 sided dice.  I,for one, can't waint for a heavy floater mod to ensure me that I'm still in the right genre.
To their credit, when it works well,  the cinematics can be great.  A slow-mo playout of a well designed ambush can be one of the games best moments. On the downside there were really way too many launch issues to merit 9+ reviews - at least for now. While the graphics are far better than Xcom EW optimization is horrible.  The game has barely playable at 1080p when XcomEW, for example, rarely strayed from the the refresh top end of 60fps at the 4k res of 2160p on my 970 GPU powered rig.   Graphics glitches abound, which is bad enough, but I also experienced and  a handful of hard crashes while playing.
The precedurally generated maps are wonderful, but the short-time horizons of the missions mean that you will likely get a "Long War Moment" (A mission that cannot be completed successfully - a Kobiashi Maru Scenario) from time to time because of map layout and enemy postitioning.  I experienced a rescue mission where if I had double moved the whole way with no enemies I might have been able to get the VIP and then double back to the Evac zone.   Now if it is there purpose to basically have an unwinnable mission from time to time thats fine,  but that seems doubtful design decision for "veteran" difficulty - the second lowest difficulty.
The game came with no controller support which I found difficult to understand.  (It does work with the Steam Controller, but the implementation was clunky; frankly I missed the smooth as silk and quick gameplay that came from using the Xbox 360 controller in Xcom EW - one of the reasons I put so many hours into it. ) With alot of PC games being streamed to the couch these days this is a bad oversight.  It's not that much extra code. Sure a PC game but that is a weak excuse for not having controller support.

In my playthrough so far, I had a tank character get gravely injured causing the medic/mage to go into "Distress" and panic screaming "This is hopeless!". This action also effected my secondary tank character with "Selfishness" causing them to scream "Let me finish them off!". These two afflictions carried throughout the rest of the dungeon, causing me to become more and more stressed, as my characters literally lose their minds. This mechanic also had me jumping out of my seat in joy. As one of my main tank characters opened up a cursed book that caused stress, but instead of adding to the multiplier negatively, he became "Heroic" which buffed my entire team and almost completely removed his stress level. To mitigate this punishing system, the game lets you prepare before embarking, lets your heroes rest to remove their stress and gives you ample opportunity to heal dying characters before they get the permanent dirt nap. Just make sure to bring lots of food or else starvation will kill off your heroes before they even find a blightful skeleton to fight. Oh and do watch your step..........

Darkest Dungeon drips style but sinks into rote repetition despite all of its clever ideas. It ultimately feels like a highly polished smartphone game: all treadmill and no destination.
Fundamentally, the game wants you to toy with villainy, tasking you with renovating your haunted estate on the backs of an endless supply of expendable heroes. At first glance, this works pretty well. You send a colorful cast of characters through four zones of procedurally-generated room progressions, encountering spooky doodads, slaughtering monsters, and collecting loot as you protect your heroes' bodies and minds. But after a short while, it drifts into purposelessness. Clear an expedition and you're rewarded with another one that's no different. Defeat a boss only to learn that he has a palette swap (two, actually) standing a dozen missions behind him. Level up a hero and (after jumping though entirely too many hoops) raise all of his numbers a tiny amount while leaving him functionally the same. Lose a hero and replace him with another barely different one. Even the system of perks fails to individualize units, since you'll usually end up selecting for "better at the only thing this class does" traits that don't exactly scream personality.
The expeditions themselves fare no better. Most of your time will be spent in the innovative combat system, which restricts units' abilities and targeting capabilities by marching order. But as before, this makes a great first impression before sinking into drudgery. Heroes generally have little mobility and even less desire for it, encouraging a static formation that spams its most effective abilities. Enemy formations consist almost entirely of meaty tanks up front and stress-inducing mage types in back. It doesn't take long to realize that every fight has you stunning a few folks, killing the back, mopping up the front line, rinse and repeat. When not fighting, you have scattered opportunities to set camp for the night and recuperate or to investigate madness-inducing curios littering the estate, but as with everything else the volume of ideas fails to hide the lack of depth. When each decrepit hall looks and demands the same approach as the last, the tension gives way to tedium.
It bears repeating Darkest Dungeon presents a wealth of excellent ideas worth exploring. It's just a pity that it didn't bother to.

For anyone that does not know, Trove is a 3rd person RPG, that has multiple playstyles and classes, Community made loot, beautiful dungeons (most of the time) addicting gameplay, and a decent community to boot.
Now lets actually get into the review.
Getting into this game at the start is easy. This is because of the tutorial, and all it does is tell you the basics of the game. It has you make a house, go to a dungeon, make rings, etc.
Regarding the artstyle...
It is amazing. The pixelated squares, that give this game it's simple cartoony feel, and the lighting and shadowing is the icing on the cake. However the game can look pretty meh sometimes, especially when looking at a large area.
Now for the combat.
This game has one of my favorite combat systems ever. It is easy to learn, and very simple, with only 1 passive ability per class and 2 extra attacks/abilities. This makes every class simple, but very different. There are three kinds of classes as of  now. My only complaint is there are not ENOUGH moves, me being a dark souls player, i wish there was more depth in the melee characters,
Rangers
sword users
spear users.
There might be more in the future. The rangers are all very balanced and are very damaging, say for the gunslinger. And they are not specifically glass cannons, so you can run through crowds and use your special without getting destroyed.
Now we have the sword based classes. These classes can be kind of weak, like the boomeranger (you can use the boomeranger as a melee OR a ranger, and switch between the two.) But there are some tanks, like the Candy Barbarian, who dual wields.
The spear characters have not come out yet, so i can not say.
Now for the leveling system.
In this game there are two kinds of levels you can increase. Your mastery, that is a collaboration of all of the things that you collect, like weapon skins or recipies, while your character level is a collection of all the XP you gain on ONE character. For an example, i have a level 19 boomeranger and a level 7 candy barbarian, but my mastery will ALWAYS be 12 across all characters, unless i level it up. You also get cool rewards by leveling up your mastery, from wings to ships.
Now for the styles.
Styles are when you collect new loot (like a new gun) and you take it to the deconstructor, and it, of course, deconstructs your weapon, gives you its skin, and some flux (the games main currency and forging material) and sometimes an eye. You can then equip the skin, and that is all there is too it.
Now for the community.
This game has a decent community, spanning from the large amount of humbled squeakers, those damned spammers ( there is a way to block players, so they are really no problem) The anti-bullying activists, and the small minority of enragement children. Most people will help if you ask questions, as long as you don't beg.
Is this game pay to win?
No, it is not. Most paid for things are kind of unnessary.
My final rating is 8.5 shadow keys out of ten.

It does everything XCOM: Enemy Unknown did, and ramps it up way better. For those new to the series, a brief summary:
You get squad members from all over the world with names, genders and personalities all generated either randomly or based on their nationality (all of which are also fully customizable for each soldier). You then take them on missions within a macro-strategy scenario and conduct turn-based tactical combat with them. Youtube videos can probably tell you more about the meat and potatoes than I can.
What I love about XCOM is emergent storytelling. The ability for scenarios to form in your mind around your soldiers. The way you get attached to your squaddies. Then pain when you lose them, and the feeling of triumph when they pull out a difficult battle. The way each battle can turn into its own action movie sort of sequence. And XCOM 2 amplifies all of that over the levels provided by Enemy Unknown.
For the lazy folk who'd rather not dig very much and haven't heard about this game, here are some features you might enjoy:
- Extensive soldier customization.
- Excellent modding community. 220 mods in less than a week, many of which add a great deal to the game.
- Procedurally generated battle maps. No two battles will be fought on the exact same terrain.
- The ability to save soldiers to a pool of characters that future playthroughs will draw from when picking your recruits, scientists, engineers, etc.
- A handful of different mission types to keep you on your toes.
- A whole slew of aliens with a variety of abilities. I've played for nearly 70 hours and still haven't seen all the confirmed enemies that are in the game. (Granted, I've already lost a few times and had to start over! Pesky Avatar Project.)
- Permadeath that matters; you can write epitaphs for your fallen squad members and look back at then to reminisce, if you're so inclined. And with limited resources, every able body counts more than ever.
- Base building! Research! Experimental gear! The engineering team is at the peak of their usefulness in XCOM 2.
- The ragdoll physics and fully destructible environments never get old.
As someone who's logged well over 100 hours in XCOM: Enemy Unknown, I give this game a 9/10. There are a few minor things that could've made it even better, but it's a SUPERB game and more fun than I can fully describe with words. And being fair, most of what could've made the game better is already being improved upon with mods!

Angelo ‘Buzzsaw’ Romano was a pony-tailed, shotgun and sword-wielding Italian. The UI wouldn’t let me make him chew a matchstick, which was unfortunate. Ian ‘Hype’ Kelly was an Aussie sniper who said things like ‘You can’t handle me’, and was also the only member of my squad cool enough to wear the XCOM hairdo, with aviators. Both of these guys had been with me since my second mission, but Ian was recently crushed by a giant snake, and Romano was punched to death by a side of beef.
This is one of the many areas where XCOM 2 improves on its predecessor; somehow, you find yourself caring much more about your squad. The original XCOM did this well, but this time round, when your main characters buy it, it’s gut-wrenching. The flip side of this, though, is that early to mid-game, you’re so short on soldiers that if you have a bad mission and your squad end up crocked for a week, much against the great adversarial spirit of XCOM, it’s difficult to resist reloading and trying again.
This is both the strength and the weakness of the game: it’s evident that much effort has been made by the developers to ramp up the tension, and to make the player feel pressured. For the most part, this works incredibly well, although the game’s perceived difficulty level and learning curve have been met with a mixed reception. Conversely, the prospect can be so bleak when things are going badly, several times I ended up thinking ‘Ah, what’s the point?’, and backtracked by several saves.
The only way to have enforced the ‘pressure’ angle properly would have been to disallow saving as freely as it has been, but that would almost certainly have been unpopular with the more mainstream crowd the reboot franchise has attempted to attract. The result is that you kind of guilt yourself into persisting as much as possible, but in the end, escape key>load game always wins.
All that said, the game manages to be challenging yet enjoyable. Thankfully, there seem to be a lot less ‘grind’ missions now, each one providing a clear goal, and a clear reward, which contributes in a specific way to your progress.
Essentially, it’s a tug of war. The aliens work on their ‘Avatar’ project, as you attempt to sabotage it. A kind of doomsday meter goes up and down, depending on your success. On one occasion in my game it maxed out, and I had about 20 hours to do something, anything, to get it back down again. I was rewarded for my perseverance, and went on to complete the campaign, but it’s moments like that when you find yourself punching the air in sweet victory, and telling the aliens to go and procreate with themselves that highlight what a great job of making a turn-based strategy game not only interesting, but exciting, Firaxis have done – and to a greater extent than before.
There are performance issues, though, as has been widely stated. Even players with great setups (eg i7, GeForce 980, 8 or 16GB RAM) have reported problems with stuttering, hanging, and frame rate dips. It seems that the game is a bit optimistic about its optimal settings, and decreasing these can help. Nevertheless, we await a patch to properly optimise the game. I can confirm all the above issues: I have an i5-4690K @3.5Ghz, Asus Sabretooth Z97, 16GB DDR3-1600, GeForce 960, with the game running on an SSD. There were issues, but not enough to spoil the game for me, but this is something to consider if the game remains unpatched, and you’re a bit dubious about your setup – be prepared to turn some of the graphics settings down, or off.
Performance problems aside, from a graphical and even a design point of view, there are detractors, but the game looks great by all accounts. I was reminded of the original ‘V’ series from the 80s on several occasions: the seemingly benevolent occupation, the black and red uniforms, masks hiding the aliens’ true appearance, the guerrilla shoot-outs at alien PR events, the human spokesperson. The script writer won’t win any awards, but it’s all good fun.
Voice acting is strong, and the dynamic between the three principal characters seems to riff better than it did in the first game.
On balance, I recommend XCOM2 highly to lovers of its predecessor, and of the original series. Maybe hold out for the patch, but if you have an ok system, and you really can’t wait, you won’t be disappointed.

Addendum after initial posting: I really thought I would hate the timed missions. As it turned out, I don't. One thing I loved about X-Com was the rumination: should I do this or do that?. XCOM2 still allows you this, but in the tactical missions, it forces you to be executive and bold. Don't believe the moaners - I finished it on default difficulty, I didn't cheat, and I only lost one squad member on the final mission, which believe me, is thrilling, as many of the missions are - although it came down to a golden shot, which had I missed, the rest of the team would have been wiped out.
Often, you might find that the main problem is that you've beaten most of the enemy, but there aren't enough turns left to get your team to the evac zone. But, with thought, you can do take 2, and it's always possible.
Many scenarios are emergent, but on first try seem impossible. Having reverted to your best save, you are confronted with a kind of Kobayashi Naru, and it's these situations that present the most beautiful, chess-like problems of the game.
Trust me - persist in the face of adversity, and you will be rewarded. Don't give up because things don't go well, or continue to go well after having done so.
It's a bit of a damning indictment on something (or someone) that life advice needs to be given to players of a game that in a way, mimics the themes of life quite well, despite its fantastical setting. But then again, X-Com (or XCOM), is at heart, a strategy game, latterly trying to include action. The original fans will appreciate the upscale, but the new blood might not appreciate this retrospectively.
Oh well!

XCOM 2 is a straight sequel to the 2012 remake XCOM: Enemy Unknown.
In his infinite wisdom, Jake "Sid Meier is the dad I never had" Solomon threw out the expected Terror From The Deep follow-up from the meeting board and offers us instead a "what if ?" scenario where the aliens won and left XCOM in shambles.
Also you get snake girls with♥♥♥♥♥♥cause he swore to never put snakemen in the game. Meta as ♥♥♥♥ !
The game is pretty much a refined version of the first one. If you only swear by the original trilogy and Xenonauts, you might be dissapointed. Still, there are some new nice features.
With no United Nations to back you up and Alien backed EXALT forces trying to hunt you down, the game flow is a little confusing at first. With your mobile base, you need to scan Earth's various regions to find supplies, troops and more importantly make contact with local resistance cells. This new version of the satelite coverage will become crucial as you try to thwart ADVENTs plans. Indeed, the aliens have an endgame, a doomsday counter called "The Avatar Project", which can't be stopped. It's scarier than it looks as completing story objectives and blowing up facilities will slow its progress drastically.
Apart from the cosmetic lifting and the guerilla vibe, two features I really loved are the global revamp of the soldier classes and the concealment system. Every class is back but with a new edge, assaults get a melee machete, supports a cool robot, snipers become gunslingers, etc. It's such a great way to spice up the existing classes and make them much more polyvalent. Since XCOM is now a guerilla warfare operation, every mission makes you start hidden. It's up to you to spot enemies and ambush them WHEN you want it. It's a great way to set up a mission, especially since most of them are now timer-based.
I don't have many problems with the game. The sad motto "Don't spot enemies on your last turn movement is still up or you are ♥♥♥♥ed" is still true and some enemies are pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t (like the lancers). But most of these complains will probably be answered by a "git gud, f4gg4t".
The unsung hero of the game is probably Tim Wynn, the new composer. I was♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at first that McCann didn't make the new score but now I realize it's for the best. XCOM was about mystery and unseen threats which matched the music perfectly. XCOM 2 is all about solemnity and the unshattered pugnacity of humanity. Music is so good it made me swallow a thesaurus.
tl, dr: It's a new version of XCOM 2k12 with cool enemies, tons of customization and MOD supports.

An incredible game worthy of full price, something I have not been able to say about the overwhelming majority of AAA (and otherwise) titles these days.  If you are a fan of turn based strategy combat, and a minor basebuilding overworld that involves an early-mid game frantic pace where you juggle resources and make key decisions, Xcom 2 should be right up your alley.
It improves on almost every facet of the original, though the base building is a little bare bones in comparison, since the nature of this game is quite different and your mothership is your home base so naturally, there are a lot fewer choices to make.  If you played the first one, you will be right at home, nothing is so vastly different that you won't be able to infer what its role or function is.
The story is pretty well done, albeit a little sparse, and towards the end it does feel a little anti-climatic but really Xcom is about having a badass group of marines and the amazing combat.  A gripe many people will have (myself included) will be in regards to the some what questionable RNG that determines the success or failure of your tactics within the game.  When I think of 80-95% chance of success, I think of it as an almost sure thing.  When you miss 4 of those in a row, you begin to really question how accurate the numbers depicted upon the screen are.... but as everyone says Xcom is Xcom, and this is just part of the experience.  You can miss a 95% and you can hit a 20%.  The game isn't without its moments where you'd like to put an axe through your monitor.
Unfortunately, there are definitely some performance issues and bugs/glitches with the current game.  The game, as impressive as it looks, is certainly not what you'd expect to push your gaming rig to its limits, yet your frames will drop inexplicably, mini cutscenes will stutter, and overall you will notice some choppiness.  Where as it's not aggregious for me (GTX980 TI, 16 gb RAM, SSD, I74790k), it still is bothersome that this game isn't running flawlessly.
There is quite a bit of graphical clipping issues, it seems the engine has trouble dealing with structures, walls, doors, windows, and multi-level buildings.  Often your character will stick his gun through a seemingly solid object, or try to smash out a window that is already smashed, walk through a door, be pulled through a building, shot through solid cover, etc.   Where as it is annoying and takes away from immersion, the game is still so robust, deep, and rewarding that I found myself looking past it.  It's just too damn enjoyable to let those things drag down the experience.
One would hope Firaxis is aware and addressing these issues, because once they are fixed, this game is a VERY strong contender for GOTY.   Certainly, this is the best tactical strategy game I've played, and the extensive modding capabilities the game has only means great things when you get guys like the creators of the Long War  working on all manners of new content - for free.
All in all, despite the somewhat unforgivable performance issues of a PC-Exclusive, this game is definitely what I would consider a must-buy for anyone who is a fan of the genre.

Xcom 2 is a brilliant sequel to "modern" Xcom series.  Being someone who completed Xcom: Enemy unknown on Impossible/Ironman, I'm both loving & hating my run on Xcom2's "Commander" difficulty.
This time you are the small insurgence in a strongly narrative driven campaign that turns the tables on your role from the first Xcom.  Stealth is key and losing Rookies is inevitable inorder to level out the odds.
I am drawn to this game, & am so glad it's the game I was hoping it would be. Each time you manage an "excellent/good" on a tight mission you'll feel good & clap, especially when, at higher difficulties.
This game has bugs, poor design choices and incredible AI that'll terrify you.
Bugs noticed: Mission buttons dissappear randomly that make you stuck on World Map.
Possible, significant bugs/coding choices regarding Aim hit chances.  The values are illogical at times &           all over the place which will leave you not "oh Xcom, you devil" but "this is competely broken."
Poor design : Serpent enemies can tongue you through solid walls.
Constant illogical misses that are more than just chance (both enemy & mostly player soldiers)
Terrible "Sniper" class that is literally useless due to beyond broken aim stats.
"Ranger" class is so effective that you'll find yourself having to rely on these at higher difficulty (very little option as other classes fail incomparison)
Enemies again can shoot you through solid object even though you cant shoot them through said objects.
Constant "Timer" missions which are a not fun or rewarding.
All in all, this is well worth a play.  "Commander" difficulty is beyond punishing so save often on multiple saves if you want to try it.  Sadly no "Ironman" mode from the start. :(  Would have loved that.
Recommended for those who have played first game.  Not recommended for those new to series or easily frustrated.

While the game has way too many "launch issues" to merit them, reviewers seem to have given Firaxis the benefit of the doubt.  It seems many are taking the long-view of the game down the road, rather tha at launch. Clearly the games large number of fine reviews are largely deserved from a overall design  perspectiveand once all the launch issues are resolved the game may well merit "classic" status.  Personally, I think will end up  a fine addition to the Xcom franchise once many of the launch problems are ironed out. Xcom2 has tons fresh ideas and also pulls off the trick of picking fresh ideas that fit well with into the Xcom Universe. They streamlined gameplay and wanted very tense gameplay. (EW's Meld mechanism to get players to feel tension also seemed a bit contrived. Play balance is definitely geared to the experienced player, and while brutally hard games seem to be more acceptable these days, the casual player may easily be put off.   The customization and mod support up front were great ideas that will really add replayability, and the ease of adding "Mods" is a real plus.  ( One nit-pic there: One would think that game would remember the Mods you picked last time, but that obvious feature was not implemented at launch!)
The game ramps up difficulty exponentially from Easy to Legendary.  Essentially from easy, to brutual and for all practial purposes impossible at the highest difficulty.   Legendary, is,as the designer of Long War commented on his own most difficult setting, "winnable in theory, but not particularly fair."   I've played a whole lot of Xcom but Legendary is so hard as to be simply exhausting.  I suppose someone will beat it on Ironman mode somewhere, but having gotten well into a Legendary campaign, I began to get a little tired of having nerfed hit percentages  mixed with eternal first-gen weapons (it takes forever to ramp up tech) against enemies with enough armor to absorb first gen base weapons damage completely).  Commander difficulty isn't quite as insane, but certainly harder than the Xcom EW Classic difficulty.
There are some rather odd enemy selection choices.  I saw some enemies very frequently (the Archon) while other hardly at all.  while we saw Mutons all the time in EW and it was "Heavy Floaters 24/7" in the later stages of Long War, I almost came to miss my old friend the Muton a bit because I barely encountered them at all.  Additionally, a bias on my part, but I found the choice of the Archon art a big disappointment for the heavy floater replacement. It does everything XCOM: Enemy Unknown did, and ramps it up way better. For those new to the series, a brief summary:
You get squad members from all over the world with names, genders and personalities all generated either randomly or based on their nationality (all of which are also fully customizable for each soldier). You then take them on missions within a macro-strategy scenario and conduct turn-based tactical combat with them. Youtube videos can probably tell you more about the meat and potatoes than I can.
What I love about XCOM is emergent storytelling. The ability for scenarios to form in your mind around your soldiers. The way you get attached to your squaddies. Then pain when you lose them, and the feeling of triumph when they pull out a difficult battle. The way each battle can turn into its own action movie sort of sequence. And XCOM 2 amplifies all of that over the levels provided by Enemy Unknown.
For the lazy folk who'd rather not dig very much and haven't heard about this game, here are some features you might enjoy:
- Extensive soldier customization.
- Excellent modding community. 220 mods in less than a week, many of which add a great deal to the game.
- Procedurally generated battle maps. No two battles will be fought on the exact same terrain.
- The ability to save soldiers to a pool of characters that future playthroughs will draw from when picking your recruits, scientists, engineers, etc.
- A handful of different mission types to keep you on your toes.
- A whole slew of aliens with a variety of abilities. I've played for nearly 70 hours and still haven't seen all the confirmed enemies that are in the game. (Granted, I've already lost a few times and had to start over! Pesky Avatar Project.)
- Permadeath that matters; you can write epitaphs for your fallen squad members and look back at then to reminisce, if you're so inclined. And with limited resources, every able body counts more than ever.
- Base building! Research! Experimental gear! The engineering team is at the peak of their usefulness in XCOM 2.
- The ragdoll physics and fully destructible environments never get old.
As someone who's logged well over 100 hours in XCOM: Enemy Unknown, I give this game a 9/10. There are a few minor things that could've made it even better, but it's a SUPERB game and more fun than I can fully describe with words. And being fair, most of what could've made the game better is already being improved upon with mods!
