Angelo ‘Buzzsaw’ Romano was a pony-tailed, shotgun and sword-wielding Italian. The UI wouldn’t let me make him chew a matchstick, which was unfortunate. Ian ‘Hype’ Kelly was an Aussie sniper who said things like ‘You can’t handle me’, and was also the only member of my squad cool enough to wear the XCOM hairdo, with aviators. Both of these guys had been with me since my second mission, but Ian was recently crushed by a giant snake, and Romano was punched to death by a side of beef.
This is one of the many areas where XCOM 2 improves on its predecessor; somehow, you find yourself caring much more about your squad. The original XCOM did this well, but this time round, when your main characters buy it, it’s gut-wrenching. The flip side of this, though, is that early to mid-game, you’re so short on soldiers that if you have a bad mission and your squad end up crocked for a week, much against the great adversarial spirit of XCOM, it’s difficult to resist reloading and trying again.
This is both the strength and the weakness of the game: it’s evident that much effort has been made by the developers to ramp up the tension, and to make the player feel pressured. For the most part, this works incredibly well, although the game’s perceived difficulty level and learning curve have been met with a mixed reception. Conversely, the prospect can be so bleak when things are going badly, several times I ended up thinking ‘Ah, what’s the point?’, and backtracked by several saves.
The only way to have enforced the ‘pressure’ angle properly would have been to disallow saving as freely as it has been, but that would almost certainly have been unpopular with the more mainstream crowd the reboot franchise has attempted to attract. The result is that you kind of guilt yourself into persisting as much as possible, but in the end, escape key>load game always wins.
All that said, the game manages to be challenging yet enjoyable. Thankfully, there seem to be a lot less ‘grind’ missions now, each one providing a clear goal, and a clear reward, which contributes in a specific way to your progress.
Essentially, it’s a tug of war. The aliens work on their ‘Avatar’ project, as you attempt to sabotage it. A kind of doomsday meter goes up and down, depending on your success. On one occasion in my game it maxed out, and I had about 20 hours to do something, anything, to get it back down again. I was rewarded for my perseverance, and went on to complete the campaign, but it’s moments like that when you find yourself punching the air in sweet victory, and telling the aliens to go and procreate with themselves that highlight what a great job of making a turn-based strategy game not only interesting, but exciting, Firaxis have done – and to a greater extent than before.
There are performance issues, though, as has been widely stated. Even players with great setups (eg i7, GeForce 980, 8 or 16GB RAM) have reported problems with stuttering, hanging, and frame rate dips. It seems that the game is a bit optimistic about its optimal settings, and decreasing these can help. Nevertheless, we await a patch to properly optimise the game. I can confirm all the above issues: I have an i5-4690K @3.5Ghz, Asus Sabretooth Z97, 16GB DDR3-1600, GeForce 960, with the game running on an SSD. There were issues, but not enough to spoil the game for me, but this is something to consider if the game remains unpatched, and you’re a bit dubious about your setup – be prepared to turn some of the graphics settings down, or off.
Performance problems aside, from a graphical and even a design point of view, there are detractors, but the game looks great by all accounts. I was reminded of the original ‘V’ series from the 80s on several occasions: the seemingly benevolent occupation, the black and red uniforms, masks hiding the aliens’ true appearance, the guerrilla shoot-outs at alien PR events, the human spokesperson. The script writer won’t win any awards, but it’s all good fun.
Voice acting is strong, and the dynamic between the three principal characters seems to riff better than it did in the first game.
On balance, I recommend XCOM2 highly to lovers of its predecessor, and of the original series. Maybe hold out for the patch, but if you have an ok system, and you really can’t wait, you won’t be disappointed.

Addendum after initial posting: I really thought I would hate the timed missions. As it turned out, I don't. One thing I loved about X-Com was the rumination: should I do this or do that?. XCOM2 still allows you this, but in the tactical missions, it forces you to be executive and bold. Don't believe the moaners - I finished it on default difficulty, I didn't cheat, and I only lost one squad member on the final mission, which believe me, is thrilling, as many of the missions are - although it came down to a golden shot, which had I missed, the rest of the team would have been wiped out.
Often, you might find that the main problem is that you've beaten most of the enemy, but there aren't enough turns left to get your team to the evac zone. But, with thought, you can do take 2, and it's always possible.
Many scenarios are emergent, but on first try seem impossible. Having reverted to your best save, you are confronted with a kind of Kobayashi Naru, and it's these situations that present the most beautiful, chess-like problems of the game.
Trust me - persist in the face of adversity, and you will be rewarded. Don't give up because things don't go well, or continue to go well after having done so.
It's a bit of a damning indictment on something (or someone) that life advice needs to be given to players of a game that in a way, mimics the themes of life quite well, despite its fantastical setting. But then again, X-Com (or XCOM), is at heart, a strategy game, latterly trying to include action. The original fans will appreciate the upscale, but the new blood might not appreciate this retrospectively.
Oh well!

This action also effected my secondary tank character with "Selfishness" causing them to scream "Let me finish them off!". These two afflictions carried throughout the rest of the dungeon, causing me to become more and more stressed, as my characters literally lose their minds. This mechanic also had me jumping out of my seat in joy. As one of my main tank characters opened up a cursed book that caused stress, but instead of adding to the multiplier negatively, he became "Heroic" which buffed my entire team and almost completely removed his stress level. Darkest Dungeon drips style but sinks into rote repetition despite all of its clever ideas. It ultimately feels like a highly polished smartphone game: all treadmill and no destination.
Fundamentally, the game wants you to toy with villainy, tasking you with renovating your haunted estate on the backs of an endless supply of expendable heroes. At first glance, this works pretty well. You send a colorful cast of characters through four zones of procedurally-generated room progressions, encountering spooky doodads, slaughtering monsters, and collecting loot as you protect your heroes' bodies and minds. But after a short while, it drifts into purposelessness. Clear an expedition and you're rewarded with another one that's no different. Defeat a boss only to learn that he has a palette swap (two, actually) standing a dozen missions behind him. Level up a hero and (after jumping though entirely too many hoops) raise all of his numbers a tiny amount while leaving him functionally the same. Lose a hero and replace him with another barely different one. Even the system of perks fails to individualize units, since you'll usually end up selecting for "better at the only thing this class does" traits that don't exactly scream personality.
The expeditions themselves fare no better. Most of your time will be spent in the innovative combat system, which restricts units' abilities and targeting capabilities by marching order. But as before, this makes a great first impression before sinking into drudgery. Heroes generally have little mobility and even less desire for it, encouraging a static formation that spams its most effective abilities. Enemy formations consist almost entirely of meaty tanks up front and stress-inducing mage types in back. It doesn't take long to realize that every fight has you stunning a few folks, killing the back, mopping up the front line, rinse and repeat. When not fighting, you have scattered opportunities to set camp for the night and recuperate or to investigate madness-inducing curios littering the estate, but as with everything else the volume of ideas fails to hide the lack of depth. When each decrepit hall looks and demands the same approach as the last, the tension gives way to tedium.
It bears repeating Darkest Dungeon presents a wealth of excellent ideas worth exploring. It's just a pity that it didn't bother to.

Okay to get some things out of the way. I got this game as a gift from a friend and I have played some of this on my friends steam account so I actually do have more hours than what it says on here. And with that out of the way let me tell you why you should play Darkest Dungeon.
One of the things I love about this game is the environment. It just seems to fit for what they are trying to go for and I like it.
Now the gameplay this is where its usually hit or miss for people. Its a turn based game where you have to mange your stress and your health while trying to also mange your inventory since you have limited space. Yes its rng based but to me it doesn't fully relay on rng to play. There is some skill that is involved into playing this game. Yes you will get your♥♥♥♥♥handed so hard you just wanna quit but that's just a learning curve. Take what you learn from that fail and make sure it doesn't happen again. Like some classes work better with certain bosses while others don't do so well. Look at the situation and think what classes would be best for the boss. And some classes work better in certain areas. Take the ruins the crusader works best for that since there's a lot of unholy enemies in it and he has a move that does more damage to them.
Now lets talk about trinkets. Most of these IMO are hit or miss. There are some that I haven't touched just due to how iffy they are. But do not worry there are some guides out there that will make it easier to decide which ones will work best for you and don't forget to look up the kickstarter trinkets also. Some of those are actually good. And there are some kickstarter hero's to acquire which there are also guides for those I would recommend to take a look at them but be warn you can only use them once per playthrough.
Now is this game for everyone no it Isn't far from it but if you can enjoy the game for what it is I'm sure you will love it and conquer the darkest dungeon. I love this game for what it is and I hope you can do thanks to this review.

Dark Souls 3 is an awesome game, truly good. And you should buy it.
But then, why am I not recommanding it?
We'll talk about that later.
First the game is worthy of being called Dark Souls, if like me you spend hundreads of hours on the first and second one, you have no reason not to buy it. You'll easily spend a few hundread on this one. A lot of weapons to choose from, and the addition of the weapon art mechanic only encourage you to find and try them all. There is also the new "dual weapon" mechanic, some weapons cannot be two handed, but instead will act like the dual wielding system from dark souls 2 (which was unfortunatly removed), but with a more unique movesets and weapon arts (for example the gothard swords or farron greatsword). You can also now charge your power attacks to do A LOT of damage.
Bosses, are so much better than in Dark Souls 2, where I litterally first tryed (solo of course) nearly all of them, I won't lie, some bosses in Dark Souls 3 are nothing but gimmicks, and those are disappointing, but they aren't bad, just useless. And some bosses can be pretty damn brutal, I'll tell you that much.
There is also this password mechanic which allow you to connect to anyone WITHOUT ANY RESTRICTION (NG cycle, soul level, weapon upgrade), great for coop, or to get some items early for specific builds/cosplays.
So the gamre is great, but what's bad then? Well first the roll sytem. I don't like it, basically Fromsoft wanted to make a bloodborne like game, and I don't know why they wanted Dark Souls 3 to be like that. Dark Souls 2 was slower, and it was good, you had to actually time your rolls, in Dark Souls 1 your rolls could be quick but costed enough stamina to be careful about it. Dark Souls 3 is a roll party, with a base stamina bar, you can, and I'm not joking, roll 12 TIMES IN A ROW.
And it makes PVP, and especially invasions so bad, since it's so hard to roll catch people barely use power attacks, it's just regular attack spam, because yes, in this game, with 20 points in stamina, you can swing an untra greatsword 5 TIMES. If you see someone do so in Dark Souls 1 or 2 you would call the guy a cheater. Well not here. It's so dumb, DEX and other light weapons aren't worth anything in PVP unless you're very good with it, with the hyper armor meta: Basically the game gives you unlimited poise when your swing a heavy weapon, so if your spacing isn't perfect, you can't hit someone using an ultra greatsword with a light weapon, well you can, but you'll loose the trade.
Invasions, are so bad, invaders are so disadvantaged, you can't have fun unless you have a full meta build. Everyone can estus now, so it last forever, in Dark Souls 1 and 2, invaders couldn't heal unless they used a miracle, and when invading the phantoms could not heal either, only the host could use Estus. It was fine like that, why did they changed it?
BTW the blue covenant is still a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to level up, and game isn't dead yet.
But even that, is not enough to call Dark Souls 3 a bad game, however a game forcing PVP via invasions (which are a lot more present in this title than in any other), and with an anti-cheat like that, I cannot recommand. The game has so much cheaters, it took 10 HOURS ONLY to be one shotted/petrified by someone, this is simply unacceptable in a game forcing PVP that much. Don't assume I don't like to invade/be invaded, I absolutly love the mechanic, despite the massive disadvantage invaders get. And the twinks, it's unbelievable, the first area of the game, play it offline, it's just people with DLC weapons and crap there, it's not fun, played it with a friend once, it's not fun. And the password mechanic doesn't help unfortunatly...
To conclude, you should buy this, but play offline if you can't handle the online♥♥♥♥♥♥

The Darkest Dungeon is a turn-based strategy game with a dark twist on dungeon crawling.  It is masterfully constructed from the ground up.  The dark atmosphere, the tremendous music, the meticulous artwork, and the accomplished characters all construe an extremely well-rounded game that I recommend to just about anyone with a taste towards grotesque and repulsive looking enemies.
However, this game certainly comes with a price (I'm not talking about 25 dollars).  The game clearly contains some crazily and ridculously difficult/punishing moments that could be tremendously hard to recover from.  On some quests, you will need to retreat, your favorite hero will die, and you will lose all of your gold.  But it's all in good fun... Right?  Therefore, if you are the person who enjoys getting beat within an inch of failure and barely managing to pull off a victory and then feeling totally awesome about yourself!  Then, by all means, buy this game (It's worth it)!

A lot of people tend to describe this game as the spiritual successor to Terraria, and they wouldn't be wrong.  But they're not entirely correct, either.  In a strange mix of Star Trek, Terraria, and the .hack// franchise, Starbound manages to really astonish players with what it has available, considering it's still in early Beta, as of this writing.
In it's current state, the game is extremely playable.  It has enough content early-game to hook you quick, and keep you pulled under for hours on end.  Between four bosses, ten tiers of content, and a virtually endless supply of planets to explore both inside and out, you'll rarely find yourself without something to do.
At first glance, anybody can see the obvious relations to Terraria.  It's a 2D, side-scrolling sandbox survival game with very high-quality pixil art.  But, it is so much more than just "Terraria in Space".  It takes a lot of elements (intentional or not) from the .hack// franchise as well.  The game procedurally generates planets using the star map coordinates as a seed, similar to how .hack// uses a three-word system to generate fields.  And like .hack//, those planets are fairly unique in a variety of ways, from the surface elements, monsters, to the very core of the planet containing molten lava or frigid ice.  The planets often contain procedurally generated dungeons with varying degrees of valuable treasure, suitable for that tier of planet, with higher tiers containing more powerful loot.
For the current asking price, the game is more than worth it.  However, the best part is that the development team has announced plans to completely revamp the current progression system; add additional bosses and quest lines; and give farming and NPC interaction much larger roles.
And, if everything I've said so far isn't enough, the game not only has a full multiplayer scene, but also has modding support and a thriving modding community on the developer's own site.
This game is nothing if not a labor of love.  Few games earn this high of praise, but Starbound is definitely deserving of it.

When a Player was defeated in battle they could be revived by another player who would give them 1/2 their remaining health. If your whole team went down you could revive using energy that doubled after every death so the more your team died the more it would cost to try again. Teamwork was key to survival and worked very well. NOW Now its just every man for himself, you cant revieve another player, instead of energy theres just sparks of life that are rare to find of you can buy for around 1500cr but the most Important element was the stratagy you went through with making the best of your health and keeping everyone up and fighting as a team.

A lot of people tend to describe this game as the spiritual successor to Terraria, and they wouldn't be wrong.  But they're not entirely correct, either.  In a strange mix of Star Trek, Terraria, and the .hack// franchise, Starbound manages to really astonish players with what it has available, considering it's still in early Beta, as of this writing.
In it's current state, the game is extremely playable.  It has enough content early-game to hook you quick, and keep you pulled under for hours on end.  Between four bosses, ten tiers of content, and a virtually endless supply of planets to explore both inside and out, you'll rarely find yourself without something to do.
At first glance, anybody can see the obvious relations to Terraria.  It's a 2D, side-scrolling sandbox survival game with very high-quality pixil art.  But, it is so much more than just "Terraria in Space".  It takes a lot of elements (intentional or not) from the .hack// franchise as well.  The game procedurally generates planets using the star map coordinates as a seed, similar to how .hack// uses a three-word system to generate fields.  And like .hack//, those planets are fairly unique in a variety of ways, from the surface elements, monsters, to the very core of the planet containing molten lava or frigid ice.  The planets often contain procedurally generated dungeons with varying degrees of valuable treasure, suitable for that tier of planet, with higher tiers containing more powerful loot.
For the current asking price, the game is more than worth it.  However, the best part is that the development team has announced plans to completely revamp the current progression system; add additional bosses and quest lines; and give farming and NPC interaction much larger roles.
And, if everything I've said so far isn't enough, the game not only has a full multiplayer scene, but also has modding support and a thriving modding community on the developer's own site.
This game is nothing if not a labor of love.  Few games earn this high of praise, but Starbound is definitely deserving of it.

Overall, I love this game.  I have been playing since March 2012, with more than 2k hours, but I did not start off on Steam, so you can't see that.
Graphics:
The graphics are amazing, that's all I really have to say.  They are very smooth and refined, unless you have low graphics or graphics glitches, which I don't.  Both on the knights and on the monsters, there is detail, but not so much to make them realistic, which I think would ruin the game.
Advancing:
It's an MMO, be prepared to grind.  I have completed the game (mostly) so I don't have to worry about grinding, but there is a massive grindwall.  For the most part, I got over this grindwall F2P, which is possible, but it is hard.  If you want to get over this grindwall, I suggest grinding with friends.  If you don't have any friends, go make some!  This game has an awesome community!  As long as you're not a beggar...
Weaponry:
I will be rather blunt here.  Some of the weaponry is extremely unrealistic, and some of it is waaay too OP.  The Dark Retribution (the DLC bomb) is rediculously powerful.  It can cause massive damage in a matter of seconds, redering everything else obsolete, depending on what you are fighting.
The rapiers in the game (flourishes and Snarby swords) are the only swords of their damage type, leaving you no other options, unfortunately.  Personally, I love them, but if you don't, you're out of luck.
The guns in the game are fairly well balanced, but, as with everything, some are better than others.  Recently, the Magnus/Tundrus line has become OP, but before they were useless.  Pulsar lines are not as powerful as before, but they are still a good choice of weaponry.  The Antigua lines are situational: you don't want to use them against just anything.
Lastly, some of the weaponry is just terrible for everything, even though they look powerful.
PvP:
P2W. P2W. P2W.  PvP is based on unique variants that you have to spend a lot of money to get.  You also have to have the right armor, some of which is hard to acquire.  The weapons are NOT balanced.  Rocket Hammers, rapiers, Pulsars, Sealed Sword lines, and Brandishes are all OP, but some other things that are great on monsters, such as the Blitz Needle, are terrible.
Community:
The community is very small, which is an advantage.  A lot of the players are older, mature people.  If anyone acts like a♥♥♥♥♥♥ EVERYONE soon knows it, and they can be shunned.  The P2W Lockdown players (PvP) can be those♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ but, knowing some of them myself, not all of them are that bad.  One problem with the general community is the noobs that don't know how to grind.  They sit there begging for money in Haven (the safe zone).  Personally, I hate it.
Guilds are an amazing part of the game, which boost the community.  Guilds are groups of players, and your guild is sort of like an entension of your friends list.  You can do guild versus guild Lockdown, which can be very enjoyable, unless you are a small guild person like me.  Unfortunately, the guilds with the richer players have more members.  Wealth attracts people.
Conclusion:
Although I have found many faults in this game, it is my favorite game.  This game has ruined my life.  If you are a player of MMOs, you would enjoy this game greatly.  I think I'll give this game a 9.5/10.

So, unless you love trying to launch your game like 2 billion times hoping it will work, stay out of this game until the developers read the community complains (which they don't so far unfortunately), and start fixing their bugs. This is such a shame for 25 bucks. Now you are warned.

Trove, by trion worlds
PS, there is alot of conflicting information in this review, but i think its all important and shows a sort of timeline of how far trove has come and how far it still has to go, with the most relevant information being at the back end of the review as it will be the newest
just a side note before we get into the review, the game as of 30/12/2015 is very oriented towards new players, it doesnt reward returning players who are max level and high masterys, with some tasks like getting to mastery 100 and doing things that can give you boosts that can take  over 150 hours on their own not helping even a smidge in PVP and making very little differance to farming and dragon challenges in the high ubers
now here is my review of Trove, by trion worlds
trove is a "block" based casual mmo, what does that mean? it means the game is more relaxed than games such as WoW and has a blocky almost minecraft like look.
personally my favourite mmo as it is a pretty calm enjoyable experience
Pros-
game is free, in game purchases are an option, and wont hinder your gameplay if you decide to opt out
always new content, as you progress through the game, theres always a new challenge, always a new task or item to get or complete. thus making the game never feel empty, with weekly updates helping too
graphics, the game looks pretty good, with hundreds of clothes and weapon styles that have been player made adding to the large array of unique content not to be seen in any other game (apart from the odd pop culture reference here and there)
Cons-
some grinding can be a drag, its never too bad, it never gets to the point where you're aobut ot have a mental break down, goals are always reachable and fair, but sometimes can take alot of work to achieve.
servers, as the game is still fairly new, you can expect the odd server crash once in a while, and if the servers arent crashing, then they have a tendancy to run slowly, making navigating difficult as the ground beneath your feet disapears.
community- while not all players are bad, there are a lot of minges, spammers, trolls, scammers about theses days, however with the recent addition of a report spam button the population of minges is decreasing
Trade- pretty much its too easy for new players to get a hold of rare items, the economy is bust at the moment, good for new players, bad for returning or current players
summary-
the game is fun,free,laid back, at first i was hesitant but now its become a hobby, not an addiction though. if you where thinking of picking up the game you might as well start as of now (2/10/2015) as rare loot, pickups and others things are way too easy to get right now, the game is definatly trying to welcome new people.
so what are you waiting for? go play it!

Well, it pains me to write a review of this matter but it has to be done.
When this game first released I started seeing the negative reviews that were just some poorly written sentences thrown together complaining about the performance and bugs, and I got defensive because I always hated when games get a bad wrap because of issues not actually related to the game.
After nearly completing the game though with about 40 hours of time, I have to say I have changed my mind.
The performance issues in this game are so apparent and evident that it reminded me of several instances in the past where I was severely unhappy with a game purchase. Those include Might and Magic X, which I still to this date have not finished or trudged through because of the horrible performance in an "average" looking game that should have ran flawless (Legend of Grimrock looks 5x better and runs flawless for instance). The other one is X-Rebirth which ran completely and utterly horrible and unplayable and I ended up getting a steam refund.
It's disturbing that a game could be released that looks "decent" but nothing exceptional and yet perform this bad. The game performs decent on some maps, but other maps it is completely and utterly unplayable (or at least not enjoyable) and there are seemingly no reasons for it in some cases. Some maps have weather effects and other things that can cause issues, which makes sense, however even putting all settings on MINIMUM make no impact on the performance. Other maps run poorly for no reason at all if there are any enemies at all on the screen. Then there are the out of actual combat issues, such as on the world map, or in the Avenger (the mobile base). There is absoltuely no reason to have FPS/Stutter issues on the World Map and in the Avenger! Utterly ridiculous!
But now let's just talk about the game itself. I love this game. At first I was annoyed by the constant rushing of things. You are forced to act quick in almost everything, building, doing missions, everything feels forced and timed. However after 40 hours of play I realize that this makes for a unique and dynamic game experience that I really enjoyed, despite the stress it can cause. As you increase your soldiers levels and abilities, armor and weapons, these timed missions become easier and easier until it is a fun and rewarding "beast mode" type experience.
The game makes several improvements over it's predecessors and omits some of the annoying things as well. So I can't say too many bad things about the game itself outside of performance. It feels like an X-Com game with enough changes to make it a new experience but not too many to make it feel like something else. So yes, I love the game.
In conslusion, I love XCom2. The game itself is very good, at least from my standpoint as an X-Com fan. However, because of the lack of response from Firaxis/2k about performance issues, and because of the plethora of performance issues and bugs themselves, I cannot recommend this game at this time.
It saddens me because I like to latch on to developers who make games I enjoy. Companies I tend to respect and follow and when one screws up it really bothers me. The key is how they respond (poorly so far) in earning that trust and respect back. Time will tell in the coming days.
Just for Reference:
i7 4790k
ASUS Maximus Hero VII
MSI GTX 980 4gb
16gb G.Skill 1866mhz
Windows 7 Ultimate on Samsung Evo 8xx SSD
Steam and Steam games on another Samsung Evo 8xx SSD
Playing at 1080p, no DSR or anything unusual.

*The F2P model is good, with the devolpers kind enough to hand out 15 day trails of ALL current available weapons in the game, letting you try them and figuruing out if you want to purchuse.
*Medals are a form a currency earned by leveling that let you be buy gear and such.
*Bullets are premium currency to spend on lotos that can get a permament weapon. All weapons reskins have the same stats but just look cooler.
*The currency to buy weapons is earned a reasonable pace compared to the prices, weapons are bought for permament.
-GAMEPLAY-
*It a standard FPS, with multiple games modes and maps to play on.
*Team Deathmatch is as it sounds letting people score points by kills, these maps are a bit chokey as in  they are small, but it does breath a much more classic approach to team deathmatch seen in older FPS games.]
*demolition and assassin are standard elemention and VIP modes
*Battle Match is where this game shines, as a very unique mechanic comes into play as you get kills you level up, with objectives helping as well, in match, and can go down the route of classes with abilities which can only be used after being a certain level, encouraging objective gameplay, in order to use cool abilities. This is a insane thing that often can get misinterpited if someone doesnt know what it is, which I will explain in a bit.
*Training allows you to spawn bots and set up situations to test a weapons damage and such. A really neat option if you ask me.
*The games guns function in a modular manner with the ability to take on/off suppresors mid game, and turn on lasers to assist aim (Depending on your team the laser is red/green)
-THE FLAWS-
*Every game has its issues and this one is no diffferent*
*Hackers are not as a big issue as the people make out things entirely wrong. Sure hackers are there but its easier to see if I contrast TDM and Battle, the accalims i've seen in TDM have been about aimbot's (which ive seen a few) but Black Sqaud's gameplay is where each limb does a different amount of damage, where legs arm, and torso shots can kill somone slower, where a headshot can kill with 2 hit, if using a Auto Rifle. So its more of the multiple limb system that can confuse people, but in BATTLE mode is where its gets bad, with Aimbot and Wallhack being thrown around in the wrongest ways, Wallhack can be used by RECON to see behind walls and prefire to deal maximum damage and find out where they are. Its part of the game so I dont understand why people insist its hacking when the accused is using a recon class at the time. The other is Aimbot regarding the sniper rifle recon has acess to, its high explosive and easily kill most things quickly and effecnitl in a AOE pattern, so even if it misses it has potentinonal to kill. Hackers are a issue but low level people dont know the mechanics and call it hacking.
*The games flaws are kinda done here, hacking is a flaw, and I personally cant find a flaw other than two things
1. Blazer sniper rifle is a 1 hit kill almost anywhere, completely brutal, but i understand why it does that
2. This was from a couple of friends I tried to get in the game and thats the lack of iron sights, no not ADS, because you can do that, but all guns are fitted with optics already, they complain about no IRON sights, I find this a dumb flaw but some people consider it one.
-MY THOUGHTS-
This game has huge potentinal, the opening tutorial felt much like a actual single player campaign so i hope its expanded with co op or maybe a zombie mode, more maps and guns would be nice, but i very much like this game and hope it continues to grow.

The sad thing about this, is that you can stop playing at night, turn your PC off, and when your switch it on in the morning there is no way you can have the game start. Like that. For no reason. Even not a Windows update...

I played two seperate versions of this game for about 15-30 game weeks each.  Recently I decided to buy it because this is probably one of my favorite games I've played in a long time.
The first build I played which was probably dated from around 06/15, was a gruelling experience.  Many parties were wiped.  I was constantly barely hanging on, and everything was quite rough.  But it was intriguiging.  I later on found a more recent build dated from around 2/2015, and started a second playthrough, taking the grueling lessons I learned on my first playthrough by heart.   I started out much stronger this time, but still I made mistakes, and eventually I had a double party wipe combined with bankruptcy.  I set the game down for a bit a few weeks.
Finally, I decided to buy the game.  So far Im about 40 weeks into this playthrough with at least one of every class above level 3.  I have no deaths, and have not started a single run without optimized equipment.  At this point I am unsure if the game has been made easier in recent patches (Healing seems much more available).  Though this is not necesarily bad.  There is always that faint line of balance where if I focus the wrong target, everything will go to hell (It's happened).
I also noticed a large number of complaints about the rng.  From what I've experienced, The Rng is much less random than people paint it out to be.  The worst case scenario is usually the norm, and anything other than that is a blessing.  When you play with this consideration in mind, the game becomes much more maneagable and feels much better.
I think the Rng Mirrors the style of the game.  On the outside it's hopeless, but deep underneath it creates  am environment primed in equal measures for hope and hopelessness.
Also in terms of art review, It's fantastic.  The diction is beautful, and the writing lends to it so well.  Overall this is very very well done from an artistic standpoint, and can easily be worth about 10 hours of play to experience it on the surface

This game encouraged me to write my first review here on steam. I know X-com since the first game in, I think it was 93 and I really love it. Its a round based stragey game with many facets. So if you´re looking for an exciting and deep game which you can play when youre not in the mood for say a hectic round of battlefield with 64 people on a server but still want to be entertained very well, then I would say this is the game you are looking for.
The situation:
All started with the alien invasion in the 90s and you were the defence force which hunted them over the whole planet, shot down their ufo´s, examined the crash grounds, discovered their technology and researched how you could use this for your own purposes to fight them back.
The last part of the X-com seríes was a remake of this.
The current game X-com2 is drawing the the scenario of a world turned upside down. The aliens ran over the planet and pushed youre organisation back into the underground which now needs to regroup and get organized to disintegrate the current alien leadership and to establish a new world order.
Pretty exciting ha`?
As the game is very deep you probably expect to go through a big tutorial or so but the little cutscenes and helps are really taking this burden off you which is making it possible to find access to the game without being a fanboy of the series. Its pretty much self explaining. You need to think wisely and make the right moves off and on the battlefield to choose the right missions to surpress the alien progress, prevent enemy events, to research the right things, to not lose youre squad which per round has two moves for moving on the map to place it right for the next action, seek cover, firing your weapons, hacking stuff, using the bushwhacka, throwing nades, or more. You can shred the enemies cover, break through walls and more. With each rank the soldiers (Specialists, Rangers, Sniper, granadier) gain new abilities and as usual you can research better weapons, armor, ammo, and so on.
The playing style is a bit more agressive than known from the predecessor but its matching the story and your situation of being under pressure to prevent the so called avatar project from progressing. This includes that you in some missions have a round timer which is ticking down. But don´t worry, because after you hacked a device or achieved a specific goal it gets shut down and you can take your time to kill the other enemies. In your own round you have no time limit at all, so it is really not as bad as some people describe it. I think it actually adds an extra bit of excitement.
The game can be played on many difficulty levels but after all it sometimes is not easy. And please dont understand this wrong but there are games and games... Those where you just go with the flow and somehow make it through the content anyway. And there are those games where you sometimes need to restart a mission (Advice: Save at the start of every round) because you f´ed it up and need to overthink your tactics. But the reward is priceless, because if you make it through a difficult mission, the game really gives you the feeling of that you really achieved something.
The graphics are awesome and very pleasing for the eye. My system is consisting an Asus x79 mainboard, a Intel i7-3820 3.6Ghz, 16GB Corsair Detonator RAM, a NVIDIA GeForce GTX 670 OC2 2GB and a Samsung 840Pro SSD and I can play the game with the Graphics cranked up to max. At the moment the game has got a few performance issues still which is causing the frame rates to go down sometimes but I guess its only a matter of time. Despite of this I didnt experienced any incidents so far.
My only criticism is that you sometimes can shoot through seilings and floors where it shouldnt be possible. But facing all the upsides of this game its really not that bad even though it would be nice if fireaxis would fix this issue.
Theres a lot more to say about this game and seeing how it developed from X-com to X-com2 already makes me curious about what they plan for the next X-com. From me this game gets 9 of 10 Points and a crystal clear recommendation to buy it, no matter if you´re a fan of the series or completely new to this game.

The list can go on...
As you can see there are many great mods to choose from to enhance the Fallout 4 experience. You can be lore-friendly or you can do whatever you want, the modding community has a variety of choices.
As for the main game. Fallout 4 improved:
-Exploration
The world is handmade, there are an endless amount of stories told in a subtle way to make the world more believable.
-Combat
Combat animations are smoother and the AI are smarter. Most NPCs and enemies have a diverse set of animations to make an intriguing combat experience.
-Scavenging
Junk has purpose, you can collect whatever you find and scrap them for materials, only a small amount of items are not scrappable. The materials gathered can be used to expand and build your settlements.
Fallout 4 failed to deliver a satisfactory experience on:
-Roleplay
You play as Nate or Nora, you can customize their appearance but you are forced to experience their story. You can not construct your own background. You can not build your reputation the way you want 'cause dialogue options are short and bland.
-Dialogue
Most dialogue options end the same-way. Your choices do not have meaningful effect on the overall storyline. The dialogue options only portray two personalties; Good or an inconvenient-not-as-nice-but-still-good character.
-Lore
The game's storyline expects you to care about these characters and if you don't it falls flat and fails. Characters are black and white and slightly not white. There is no complexity added to any character. So you have bland characters expanding Fallout lore which is very upsetting to most.
I can go on and on about the pros and cons of Fallout 4, I think this is enough though. In The end Fallout 4 does not deserve its negative reputation. It does deserve its constructive criticism. Mods are the game's saving grace. So give modded Fallout 4 a try and you'll be surprised it is not as bad as you thought it was.

I'll start this by saying, Darkest Dungeon is not for everyone. In my opinion however, it is an amazing game with fantastic artstyle, music, and characters. The combat is actually in-depth if you go beyond "this move deal damage", "this move heals", and "this move stuns" as well as intresting maps and fights. Now, the main downside pretty much everyone is complaining about is "bullcrap RNG, enemy crits way too often, spend hours grinding, no fun, holy crap this is totally unfair, games with challenge should allow me to bypass these challenges in a fun and manageable manner". However, THIS IS THE POINT OF DARKEST DUNGEON. The game isn't about how well you can defeat these challenges, it's about how well you get slapped and hit in the face, and press onwards. The game is about persistance, and attrition. Who will lose first? You or the Dungeon? When you get anihillated by crap RNG, that is a test of if you're the kind of person that says "THIS IS BUL**** OMG AWFUL GAME UNFAIR" or if you are the person that goes, "K, two can play at that game" and rebuilds. In fact, thats what you do throughout the whole game, rebuild your legacy, the hamlet, and most of all, the justice of the world. The game isn't about being fair and fun, it's a game that tests your spirit and determination. While some may say a game based off awful luck and RNG and difficulty is a poorly designed game, it isn't. It's a game that tests you and you WILL PREVAIL. As the Ancestor once said
"A Spark without kindling, is a goal without hope".

Really enjoyed this game despite minor flaws.  Played it to its end over the course of four days, and I haven't done that with a computer game for over a decade, including the first iteration of the revamped X Com series which I also really enjoyed.  Some plot spoiers below-
Pros:  Tactical combat (obsessively interesting and never boring)
Good gameplay balance - despite being afraid to lose the game to the computer due to not enough resources, not enough time, not enough good armor or weapons at several points in the early game, able to pull out a hairs-breadth escape by games end.  Mid to late game became complacent that my outstanding squad could handle anything, but had to replay the last two scenarios a couple of times because they were tough!  Felt a sense of satisfaction at winning them at long last

Great graphics, great game art!  Squad member customization options are endlessly interesting and the best of a tactical game of this kind.
Great squad battles!  That's the core of the game, and this does not disappoint.  Just when you think you've figured out each type of map and each type of enemy combination, the game throws you a surprise every few missions.
Cons:  Slow framerate and glitchiness to be expected with new games of this magnitude before their first patch these days.  However, letting my nVidia game configure routine work fixed the game with one click of the "optimize" button with no apparent loss in graphical quality (on my system at least)
Surprisinglingly small number of technical advances and goodies to research.  Didn't really bother gameplay until at the end you get a tricked out "avatar" with weapons you never really had to work for.
Irrelevance of Psionics and the Psi Lab.-  I won the game on normal without ever having to put a recruit through psionics training, and thus missed a lot of game play options.  Never needed any psionic abilities to win, with mindshield and will conditioning bonuses, psionic use on the part of the computer opponent was never an issue until the last mission.  You get your powered armor suits, you get your "gremlin" upgrades, but you don't get to play with your own battlefield robotics.  In the first game, you had that, but since it took a squad slot it was only useful if you couldn't field a complete squad.

Conclusion - Minor flaws do not detract from the enjoyment of an outstanding and immersive tactical game, as long as you get around your particular system set up to smooth out the framerates.  Sure this will be fixed soon.  Really enjoyed this game and didn't mind paying the big bucks for what I got, warts and all.

Right from the start i'll tell you this : i love this game.
XCOM 2 took everything from the previous game and improved on it in every way, and as of now, i haven't found anything they did worse then the last game, but my opinion asside, here's the review!
REVIEW :
XCOM 2 is the successor to the tactical, squad-based, turn-based, strategy game XCOM : Enemy Unknown and the expansion Enemy Within.
I have put hundreds of hours into the previous games on console and i loved it to death.
The combat was exciting, the strategy layer lets you make difficult choices and the feeling you get when you lose that high-ranked soldier you named after a friend due to a random crit is horrible, which makes the game even more interesting!
XCOM 2 is all of the above, but improved in every way.
The combat is, in my oppinion, more challenging then the previous game, the addition of more alien species and buffs to the classic ones really make them more of a challenge to take down.
In the previous game, seeing sectoids or thin men on a map wasnt really a big deal, their abilities weren't all too dangerous and in the late game they just become cannon fodder for your troops.
In XCOM 2 the sectoids have way more health and can mind controll your men right from the second mission and the poison spitting thin men?
Well, they're snakeladies now with the ability to drag troops towards them with their tongues and binding them, rendering them unable to move or act.
They can also spit acid and dodge bullets, so they're anything but cannon fodder.
The "replacement" for the cannon fodder would be the regular ADVENT troops, human-alien hybrid soldiers acting as a police force, yet if these fellows flank your low-ranked troops you can be sure a crit will kill your men right away.
With all these aditions, the enemies are waaaay more powerfull then their predecessors with more abilities and variation in strength.
But don't you worry, your own troops got some neat upgrades as well!
Your classic 5 classes are still in the game under another name, Heavies being the Grenadiers, Supports being Specialists etc...
All of them have a new set of skill, divided into two subclasses, for example : you can spec out your Sharpshooter to be your good ol' sniper, taking down aliens from far far away with squadsight, or turn them into gunslingers, granting them skills with their sidearm like free shots or shooting at all enemies in sight with your pistol.
Customisation!
Yes, customisation is even more fleshed out then the previous game with tons and tons of gear to kit your troops out with.
Going from bandanas, aviators, helmets, cigars and even hockeymasks if you'd like to add in Jason Voorhees with a machete, go right ahead!
Mods mods mods.
Firaxis did a great job of supporting the mod community with the addition of the Steam Workshop and giving the modders access to ALL assets they used in creating XCOM 2.
Yep, all of them, the full 50GB of sounds, buildings, textures, models... all of it!
They even partnered with Long War Studios, a modding studio that made the famous mod for XCOM Enemy Within : Long War, which added a more lengthy game, items, classes and abilities.
I was also surprised to see a few abilities from the Long war mod incorporated into the game itself like the Aim ability for the sharpshooter, which was in Long War under the name of Steady Aim as well as several other mechanics.
the mods will only lengthen the lifespan of XCOM 2 just like mods did to Skyrim and i forsee tons of interesting additions to the games mechanics.
In short :
XCOM 2 is a fantastic game, i have already finished the story in my first playthrough which took around 26 hours, the final mission being really challenging and feeling more like an end game unlike the headshot-the-uber-ethereal-and-win ending of the last game. The story itself is way more engaging and interesting, explaining why the aliens came here in the first place and why they are abducting people.
If you liked the last game, buy it, just buy it, you'll love it just as much as the previous game.
But if you didnt like it, i wouldnt recommend buying it since its very similar (in a good way) to XCOM : EU.
As for a score, i'd give it a 9.8/10

Hi! Before I leave my review I want to say I'm a "casual" gamer. I don't really play games on the hardest difficulty unless it's a series I really, really love. I don't find joy or amusement in dying repeatedly - I know winning after lots of deaths is rewarding for some but I like a challenge that doesn't feel impossible. With that said, I recommend this game to for both casual and hardcore gamers.
I haven't yet beaten the game but I'm really close(according to viewers in stream) and I have beaten some bosses on the first try. To give you an understanding of how the fights go think of The Witcher 3 bosses or any of your fave RPG boss battles - challenging but fun and they felt like worthy opponents. That's how EVERY mob in Dark Souls is to me. The mobs aren't just weak shambling skeletons that crumble after one hit to give you a sense of dominance or empowerment, but every mob is fighting to win, and kill, just like yourself.
There isn't any music until boss fights so when you're exploring and wondering, there's this feeling of hopelessness that follows you. It doesn't bother me much and I think it helps set the tone of the game.
As a gamer, when things get tense, I'm someone who button mashes out of panic. The game punishes this like crazy - this game is all about patience really. It'll beat the lesson into you. To give you an example... One boss took me a total of 1:12:51 , while another took a mere 7minutes on my first try.
I keep all my boss fights recorded on twitch in order of completetion so check it out if you wish!
Now onto my issues with the game...
1. This game doesn't teach you anything at the start except how to swing your sword and move out of the way of incoming attacks. No info on secondary characters, items, quests, lore ect. This is a problem to me because as I said I'm almost done with the game and didn't even know about quests in this game at all. I've just been hunting bosses. If you recruit companions and don't fufill their objectives, which they never freaking tell you, they die or leave or become hostile. Also no way to keep track of said quests.
2. I'm not sure of the lore of this game, viewers help me out there and explain the significance of characters that otherwise seem boring or unimportant to me.
3. Online is horrible. I didn't know using a helpful item in game allows other players to invade. Maybe this is fun for veterans of the series but as a newb trying to make my way through? Being hunted by people who have done NG+++ isn't fun at all....
4. DiSGUSTING CREATURES! What depraved soul designed the monsters for these games? Got a playa wanting to go back to church. LAWD
5. Optional/hidden bosses and/or companions that lock if you don't complete the hidden prerequisite before advancing. This goes back to the game not explaining crap. I got to really difficult bosses that people said are done with companions but turns out I couldn't ask for help because I didn't do something way back when at the start of the game where I was just terrified of everything coming at me. Before anyone poops on me for complaining about this, admit it, when you first played you probably didn't know either(unless you cheated and used a guide) and missed out of quests/characters/story. I'll likely play again to discover everything but it's slightly annoying learning I skipped a lot of the game because I didn't complete obscure actions.
Verdict?
It's a thumbs up for me. If you're considering buying but hesitant because of how hard it appears - wait for a sale. The game can be brutal and is frustrating at times as it doesn't hold your hand at all. No tips or anything. But it's not impossible. If you get angry fast and are prone to throwing controllers, stay away. If not and you are up to the challenge and willing to learn from trial & error tactics, definitely get it! It's a fun adventure :D with replayability. Just stay away from Online play until you at least get the basics down.

Really enjoyed this game despite minor flaws.  Played it to its end over the course of four days, and I haven't done that with a computer game for over a decade, including the first iteration of the revamped X Com series which I also really enjoyed.  Some plot spoiers below-
Pros:  Tactical combat (obsessively interesting and never boring)
Good gameplay balance - despite being afraid to lose the game to the computer due to not enough resources, not enough time, not enough good armor or weapons at several points in the early game, able to pull out a hairs-breadth escape by games end.  Mid to late game became complacent that my outstanding squad could handle anything, but had to replay the last two scenarios a couple of times because they were tough!  Felt a sense of satisfaction at winning them at long last

Great graphics, great game art!  Squad member customization options are endlessly interesting and the best of a tactical game of this kind.
Great squad battles!  That's the core of the game, and this does not disappoint.  Just when you think you've figured out each type of map and each type of enemy combination, the game throws you a surprise every few missions.
Cons:  Slow framerate and glitchiness to be expected with new games of this magnitude before their first patch these days.  However, letting my nVidia game configure routine work fixed the game with one click of the "optimize" button with no apparent loss in graphical quality (on my system at least)
Surprisinglingly small number of technical advances and goodies to research.  Didn't really bother gameplay until at the end you get a tricked out "avatar" with weapons you never really had to work for.
Irrelevance of Psionics and the Psi Lab.-  I won the game on normal without ever having to put a recruit through psionics training, and thus missed a lot of game play options.  Never needed any psionic abilities to win, with mindshield and will conditioning bonuses, psionic use on the part of the computer opponent was never an issue until the last mission.  You get your powered armor suits, you get your "gremlin" upgrades, but you don't get to play with your own battlefield robotics.  In the first game, you had that, but since it took a squad slot it was only useful if you couldn't field a complete squad.

Conclusion - Minor flaws do not detract from the enjoyment of an outstanding and immersive tactical game, as long as you get around your particular system set up to smooth out the framerates.  Sure this will be fixed soon.  Really enjoyed this game and didn't mind paying the big bucks for what I got, warts and all.

Right from the start i'll tell you this : i love this game.
XCOM 2 took everything from the previous game and improved on it in every way, and as of now, i haven't found anything they did worse then the last game, but my opinion asside, here's the review!
REVIEW :
XCOM 2 is the successor to the tactical, squad-based, turn-based, strategy game XCOM : Enemy Unknown and the expansion Enemy Within.
I have put hundreds of hours into the previous games on console and i loved it to death.
The combat was exciting, the strategy layer lets you make difficult choices and the feeling you get when you lose that high-ranked soldier you named after a friend due to a random crit is horrible, which makes the game even more interesting!
XCOM 2 is all of the above, but improved in every way.
The combat is, in my oppinion, more challenging then the previous game, the addition of more alien species and buffs to the classic ones really make them more of a challenge to take down.
In the previous game, seeing sectoids or thin men on a map wasnt really a big deal, their abilities weren't all too dangerous and in the late game they just become cannon fodder for your troops.
In XCOM 2 the sectoids have way more health and can mind controll your men right from the second mission and the poison spitting thin men?
Well, they're snakeladies now with the ability to drag troops towards them with their tongues and binding them, rendering them unable to move or act.
They can also spit acid and dodge bullets, so they're anything but cannon fodder.
The "replacement" for the cannon fodder would be the regular ADVENT troops, human-alien hybrid soldiers acting as a police force, yet if these fellows flank your low-ranked troops you can be sure a crit will kill your men right away.
With all these aditions, the enemies are waaaay more powerfull then their predecessors with more abilities and variation in strength.
But don't you worry, your own troops got some neat upgrades as well!
Your classic 5 classes are still in the game under another name, Heavies being the Grenadiers, Supports being Specialists etc...
All of them have a new set of skill, divided into two subclasses, for example : you can spec out your Sharpshooter to be your good ol' sniper, taking down aliens from far far away with squadsight, or turn them into gunslingers, granting them skills with their sidearm like free shots or shooting at all enemies in sight with your pistol.
Customisation!
Yes, customisation is even more fleshed out then the previous game with tons and tons of gear to kit your troops out with.
Going from bandanas, aviators, helmets, cigars and even hockeymasks if you'd like to add in Jason Voorhees with a machete, go right ahead!
Mods mods mods.
Firaxis did a great job of supporting the mod community with the addition of the Steam Workshop and giving the modders access to ALL assets they used in creating XCOM 2.
Yep, all of them, the full 50GB of sounds, buildings, textures, models... all of it!
They even partnered with Long War Studios, a modding studio that made the famous mod for XCOM Enemy Within : Long War, which added a more lengthy game, items, classes and abilities.
I was also surprised to see a few abilities from the Long war mod incorporated into the game itself like the Aim ability for the sharpshooter, which was in Long War under the name of Steady Aim as well as several other mechanics.
the mods will only lengthen the lifespan of XCOM 2 just like mods did to Skyrim and i forsee tons of interesting additions to the games mechanics.
In short :
XCOM 2 is a fantastic game, i have already finished the story in my first playthrough which took around 26 hours, the final mission being really challenging and feeling more like an end game unlike the headshot-the-uber-ethereal-and-win ending of the last game. The story itself is way more engaging and interesting, explaining why the aliens came here in the first place and why they are abducting people.
If you liked the last game, buy it, just buy it, you'll love it just as much as the previous game.
But if you didnt like it, i wouldnt recommend buying it since its very similar (in a good way) to XCOM : EU.
As for a score, i'd give it a 9.8/10

XCOM is known to be a punishing game. Unfortunately, XCOM 2 is punishing in the wrong way, and in such ways that it begins to feel cheap instead of a fair challenge.
Take your time and play a mission carefully so your soldier will recover from being Shaken? Oh, that's too bad, you missed the exit area by one turn. Take a risk and hack a beacon to possibly get an advantage? ♥♥♥♥ you, enjoy your mission-ending reinforcements or enemy buffs. In the meantime even not including possible reinforcements, you're regularly facing several enemies per mission that can (permanently, in case of Stun Lancers) incapacitate your soldiers regardless of cover (Sectoids, Stun Lancers). Save-scumming is essentially the only way to make progress with the odds being so stacked against the player. This is coming from a player who found the difficulty of XCOM:EW on Ironman Classic to be about just right, though perhaps too easy towards the end.
The music is uninspired and the UI has a few annoyances. I won't go in to the technical issues and bugs, though at the moment there are many, one of which can be game-ending: a savegame with an active burrowed Chryssalid on the map is automatically corrupt.
Positive new features include the improved destructible cover and added customabilizity for your soldiers.
Waiting for a major revamp patch (official or unofficial, due to active modding base one should be coming out sooner rather than later) is highly recommended before playing the game. As such, I can't recommend it in its current state.

I was never good at this game. I got it because I loved watching livestreams of it, and on my first day, neither of my starting characters made it to town, and my new party wiped on their third mission. After that, I didn't really play anymore, but I still paid attention to its development and still loved to watch the streams. But over time, I noticed that the game was getting worse and worse as it got longer. In the state where I first took interest, with just the Ruins, Warrens, and Weald, the amount of content and difficulty scale overall seemed ideal. The introduction of the Cove seemed to stretch things a little thin, but I was still willing to overlook that because as a work of art, this game is beyond outstanding. The art, the atmosphere, the voice work, the character and enemy design, it's all pretty close to perfect.
And then... the Darkest Dungeon came out, with that more than
the amount of grind present in the game - starting with quadruple because of the dungeon's unique mechanic:
, and actually being much worse because RNG at Darkest difficulty level is *horribly* stacked, virtually guaranteeing a huge number of failed runs and deaths for each actual success. And at that point, this game went from cruelly hard to virtually unplayable.
Oh, it wasn't
the Darkest Dungeon's fault. To some extent, it just seems that every new feature added to this game only serves to make it more punishing, the most notable example being the horrible disease system that
the number of debilitating penalties a hero can suffer from, but that was the final nail in the coffin. This used to be one of the games I was most proud to have in my library, even if I was too much of a chicken to play it much myself. But these days... you need to ask yourself, is it worth trying to play a game that requires dozens of hours playing through the same content over and over, getting continually screwed by the RNG in the process? This game isn't 'random' in the usual sense of the word - you don't get a streak of good rolls and win, because luck only carries so far before its benefits are removed or canceled out. We're not talking about beating a hard mission once, we're talking about
them to truly gain ground. The only randomness here? Whether or not you'll make it through each grinding session without having your progress completely set back again.
As a work of art, this game deserves a spot in a museum, and to have classes of college students studying it and writing papers on it. As a game... it's not a game, it's just grim, soul-crushing, uphill toil. I suppose, considering its subject matter and intended effect on the player, that this is only fitting.
Edit: Changes made by Red Hook over time have done quite a bit to alleviate the problems mentioned in this review, and I'm now in the process of playing through it fully; currently I'm too strong for Apprentice missions but not
upgraded enough for Veteran yet. If I find that the changes don't go far enough, my recommendation will remain unchanged, but if they prove to have adequately resolved the worst issues, I will write a new review recommending the game.

Just finished XCOM 2, took about 50 hours to complete on Commander difficulty (the one below the most difficult setting) and I have to say I was not disappointed.
I only experienced two major glitches during the time I was playing, other than that just having a choppy framerate through almost all the missions was pretty common but not irritating.  The first glitch was on a map where aliens endlessly assault your ship while you try to destroy a beacon and then escape, what happened was the game continually slowed down with each wave of aliens until the alien wave would not end.  Restarted the game and everything worked again.  The second glitch worked in my favor, it basically caused all of my units to be in permanent concealment, allowing me to literally walk right up next to an alien and attack it without any retalition, not to mention almost every shot was a critical shot.
The game is good, real good, real fun too.  The story is kind of cheesy at times with the dialogue but its not all bad.  The base management is pretty similar to Enemy Unknown although you won't need to worry about adjacency bonuses or having more than one lab/workshop, I actually made it through my whole playthrough without even needing a workshop.  The biggest difference is that you have to manage your engineers, you can't get anything done without them and they enable you to "power up" your current facilities so they can provide more resources.
Combat is pretty good, people complain about the random number system but it's not fixed like some people say.  It does seem like if you load your game and try the same action, you get the same result but little changes such as moving to a different location or having another soldier take their turn first can change your result.  Aside from the random number generator, combat is also different now with the addition of concealment and patrolling aliens.  Before, you would have enemies placed at different locations on the map just waiting to be discovered, now they wander around providing a field of vision which will detect any soldiers who pass through it.  However, once spotted by the aliens, then they get their free action like in the previous game, so just make sure you have plenty of people on overwatch before breaking concealment.
The game's plot is alright, not the greatest but still good and they did a good job making you feel like you're leading some kind of resistence.  Like before, you advance the plot by completing combinations of research and the plot based missions that follow this reserach.  Pretty similar to Enemy Unknown.  There are only about 3-4 of these plot missions and they are mildly interesting, one of the final ones you can actually get through without even fighting anything.  The games final level is pretty good but has just a meager ending, with an ending much like you would expect.
The biggest change is the Avatar Project, which is a game ending project compelted by the aliens, shown to you as a series of squares which light up as the aliens get closer to completing it.  It seems overwhelming, watching each one of those litte squares light up while your only squad is barely able to handle its own with unupgraded weapons and armor, however...it's all just to scare you.  Once you start winning the Black Site missions, those little squares are erased and by the end of the game the aliens will most likely be back at absolutely no progress toward their goal of completing the project.  So don't worry about it.
Hacking is a great tool, once you get the ability to increase your ability at it you become able to take control of almost every mechanized unit.  Not to mention hacking things like a lamp post looking Advent beacon give you some pretty awesome bonuses like extra resources or reducing your resource gathering rates by 50% for several weeks.  There are drawbacks if you fail, such as alerting soldiers to your presence, giving the mech unit extra defense and aim or sometimes added defense for all active soldiers for a couple turns.  But considering you can take control of enemy units, even advent soldiers, for a few turns as well as gain global bonuses outside of missions, it's safe to say hacking is a very useful ability.  Oh almost forgot, if you have a soldier who is a specialist you can have them hack locks and mission objectives from far away too.
Overall, XCOM 2 is a great game.  The customization for the soldiers is a lot of fun and you're no longer stuck with having a really good, but horrible sounding/looking soldier anymore.  I think the system is great, the new units are a lot of fun and if anything, I'd really like to see a Long War version for this game come out.

Okay so first things first:
Yes the performance issues suck.  I really don't like having to have action cam turned off and the ugly textures here and there.  I don't like the occasional lock ups and the rare (but not VERY rare) crashes.  There are some odd difficulty spikes here and there.
But this is a great game.  Many of the things that made XCOM:EU and XCOM:EW so good are present and improved on.  Here's my summary:
+ Great tactical combat with more emphasis on superior height
+ Excellent depth for modifying and thereby empathizing with your team
+ Nice range of new baddies to kill
+ Really satisfying sound design.  The sound effect of the Magnetic Rifle is gorgeous
+ The new campaign structure is less grindy, always being short of resources is a cool challenge
+ The theme is great, really nicely thought out
+ It's an XCOM game and I love those
- Glitchy performance
- Occasional issues with multiple heights
- Occasional issues with the AOE effects (fire, poisen) affecting people when they shouldn't
- I don't really understand all of the campaign map stuff at the moment so my first play through was stunted by this a bit
All in all I really enjoyed this and will gladly slice up Sectoids and bloody Vipers some more, especially now I have a Fusion Sword!

I was never good at this game. I got it because I loved watching livestreams of it, and on my first day, neither of my starting characters made it to town, and my new party wiped on their third mission. After that, I didn't really play anymore, but I still paid attention to its development and still loved to watch the streams. But over time, I noticed that the game was getting worse and worse as it got longer. In the state where I first took interest, with just the Ruins, Warrens, and Weald, the amount of content and difficulty scale overall seemed ideal. The introduction of the Cove seemed to stretch things a little thin, but I was still willing to overlook that because as a work of art, this game is beyond outstanding. The art, the atmosphere, the voice work, the character and enemy design, it's all pretty close to perfect.
And then... the Darkest Dungeon came out, with that more than
the amount of grind present in the game - starting with quadruple because of the dungeon's unique mechanic:
, and actually being much worse because RNG at Darkest difficulty level is *horribly* stacked, virtually guaranteeing a huge number of failed runs and deaths for each actual success. And at that point, this game went from cruelly hard to virtually unplayable.
Oh, it wasn't
the Darkest Dungeon's fault. To some extent, it just seems that every new feature added to this game only serves to make it more punishing, the most notable example being the horrible disease system that
the number of debilitating penalties a hero can suffer from, but that was the final nail in the coffin. This used to be one of the games I was most proud to have in my library, even if I was too much of a chicken to play it much myself. But these days... you need to ask yourself, is it worth trying to play a game that requires dozens of hours playing through the same content over and over, getting continually screwed by the RNG in the process? This game isn't 'random' in the usual sense of the word - you don't get a streak of good rolls and win, because luck only carries so far before its benefits are removed or canceled out. We're not talking about beating a hard mission once, we're talking about
them to truly gain ground. The only randomness here? Whether or not you'll make it through each grinding session without having your progress completely set back again.
As a work of art, this game deserves a spot in a museum, and to have classes of college students studying it and writing papers on it. As a game... it's not a game, it's just grim, soul-crushing, uphill toil. I suppose, considering its subject matter and intended effect on the player, that this is only fitting.
Edit: Changes made by Red Hook over time have done quite a bit to alleviate the problems mentioned in this review, and I'm now in the process of playing through it fully; currently I'm too strong for Apprentice missions but not
upgraded enough for Veteran yet. If I find that the changes don't go far enough, my recommendation will remain unchanged, but if they prove to have adequately resolved the worst issues, I will write a new review recommending the game.

Having played for a loooong while, I believe I'm nearly at the end of my first playthrough (though I could be wrong). I've never finished a game of Xcom before, I was introduced through Enemy Unknown on my PS3, though I never finished my first playthrough and I was probably 13 so had no idea how to play properly.
With XCOM 2, I have been absolutely sucked in, and I've enjoyed a lot. But, do not think the game is handed to you. At the beginning, I had happy faces all around as my team finished a couple of missions that were rated "Excellent". This is all on normal difficulty (called Veteran in the game, I believe). Not long after, I'm struggling to even finish missions at all, reloading autosaves to stop my whole team being destroyed. There would be panicking soldiers, soldiers that end up being mindcontrolled, soldiers that end up being grabbed from a long distance by a Viper and screwing up my strategy. My happy team suddenly became not so happy, as my ratings went to "Good" and even "Poor", most of the time with 1 or 2 of my team being KIA. And this was while I was loading old saves, chances are my team would have all been KIA if I hadn't.
The easy thing is to blame the game for failing against what seem impossible odds. You go on the Steam forums, you see people ranting about broken mechanics. But what you have to remember is: the actions you take off the battlefield are just as important as the ones you take on it. If you haven't been sensible, then you will end up going up against impossible odds, and you WILL lose.
All this became apparent once I managed to buy the Guerilla Tactics School. I thought having more soldiers on my team was what I was missing. And I was bang on right. From then on, my time against the aliens was a lot easier. Especially once I had upgraded my weaponry and armour. You don't buy armour and weapons 1 at a time for each soldier, once you buy, for example, Magnetic Rifles, every person on your team that uses rifles can then equip them. Having two extra soldiers to take advantage of these investments changed the game for me, and I realised I shouldn't have left building the GTS so late. Everything became so much easier.
But even then? I have been reloading old saves when things didn't go my way. More recently, I had to deal with a Retaliation attack. Most of my badass team made up of Colonels and Liuetenants had been injured. I didn't think it would be so bad, I had some decent people in there. But I was wrong on that one. I lost a Captain Sharpshooter, I didn't want to reload because I had a second injured Captain Sharpshooter who I could use, and I wanted to keep to the spirit of the game. Then I mindcontrolled a Codex. Then I destroyed a Sectopod. But all the misses added up, someone panics and I'm quite sure I lost another soldier. And I had already lost the mission because too many civilians were dead. At that point I gave up, and reloaded my old save which put me back at base before the mission began.
And I wonder, if I had focused on healing my 1st team by staying at my base and doubling my healing rate rather than jetting around the world and picking up supplies and intel, before the Retaliation attack happened,  would I have won? I'm pretty sure I would have. My 1st team had easily dealt with similar threats before, without loading up old autosaves. Once I managed to skulljack a Codex and destroy what came after, as well as a couple of mutons, a Sectopod, heavily armoured MEC, and another few small  guys, AND extract my whole team including the VIP in less than 12 turns. And that was incredibly satisfying.
The reason why this game is so fun is because it makes you work for your victories. If you start taking winning for granted, it will come back to bite you. And while people certainly won't always be happy for it, a lot of other people would respond: That's XCOM.

Edit: With the addition of paid mods being introduced I can no longer recommend this game. I was willing to tolerate some of the changes they had made in the Fallout formula but this overpriced micro transaction BS is unacceptable.
