Reduced RPG mechanics
Over reliance on settlement mode
I have to admit that despite its faults, I have sunk a lot of hours into this title. This is not because the main story is good, because it's not, it's terrible. It's because the world keeps drawing me back, because FO4 scratches that post-apocalyptic itch really well depending on how you choose to play.
Yes, the RPG mechanics are reduced, but it doesn't mean you can't have a build focused to one specific play style. Technically after enough time you can max out everything and have every skill, but by that point I highly doubt you'll have anything left to do.
The gun play is a vast improvement over the previous titles, and makes for a much better experience.
Where I feel the game really fails is with the voiced protagonist. It was an interesting concept but ultimately felt painfully restrictive, especially in the dialogue department which had been the butt of many memes. The options are Yes,Yes,Yes and more information which will count as a yes. The past titles gave me a sense of connection to my character but this time, less so, much less so.
The main character back story is also fixed, like FO3. No matter what you do, you will always start at the same place with the same prior experience (soldier or lawyer). My courier in NV was a patriotic NCR citizen, dedicated to the the imperialistic spread of the NCR in one playthrough; and the next play through he was a capitalistic, egotist with a god complex working with Mr House. FO4 I am war veteran, that's it. Every time.
The main quest. Well, it's rubbish, but that's par for Beth, you don't buy a Beth game for the main plot.
The other issue is the heavy approach to the settlement system, with three whole DLC's focused on it. I will say that I have sunk far too many hours into it, because I actually like the system, but as a fun little side activity I do when I want to build a two story gold♥♥♥♥♥♥ However, the settlements don't do anything. They're a model train set that you set up and then look at. There's no real reason to build them and there in lies the biggest problem, you never feel like it's actually contributing to the world. Your settlements aren't spoken of or acknowledged. The world doesn't expand because of them, thankfully there are mods that improve this and add more purpose but it seems like a wasted opportunity that  was given too much attention.
Which brings me to mods, like any good Beth game there are fantastic mods, along with the standard, cringe mods for pubescent 15 year olds that gives every women massive t.its and armour that covers nothing but the nipples.
I actually bought this game again for the PC mods, which breathed a lot of life into this game.
Buy this game on sale, don't pay full price. I have enjoyed this game and will continue to do so as the modding community continues to produce new quests and the like.
Since Beth expects the fans to complete this game, then the fans should be expected to pay half the price, which again, is my recommendation.
Finally don't buy the season pass unless it's on sale as well, probably a given, after the paragraph above.
Verdict.
6/10 (Standard edition)
6.5/10 (with DLC, namely Far Harbour)
7/10 (DLC & Mods)
4/10 (With the introduction of paid mods)

Update 5/15/16: I'm updating this but keeping the original review up.
Do I like this game? Big time.
Do I like everything about it? No.
There are pros and cons and some stuff I wish was in it but it seems the devs decided not to do. I will now list them with a "+" for a pro, a "-" for a con and a "=" for something that is neither a pro nor a con.
Pros:
+The vast amount of aliens themselves
+The difficulty of the game is nice even when on a the "Rookie" difficulty (I start at the lowest possible level when I play)
+A stealth mechanic that XCOM Enemy Unknown/Enemy Within lacked
+Recovering Loot on the battlefield
+Can capture enemy VIPs
+Can carry wounded/dead soldiers off the battlefield
+Can train a soldier into the class you want (requires a certain Avenger Facility)
+The mods available to this game
Cons:
-The Avatar Project itself
-How quickly the Avatar project fills up
- - (Double Negative) YOU CANNOT CHOSE WHEN TO DO SUPPLY RAIDS!!
- You cannot chose when to do missions in general
- Not doing a mission has too extreme of punishment (I lost a region [not permanently] for skipping a VIP Extraction because I wanted all my troops available)
- Aliens and ADVENT get a Free Move even during an Ambush. Why would they get a free move during an ambush?
- - - - - - (MEGA NEGATIVE) Despite HATING Sectopods and Chryssalids in XCOM Enemy Unknown/Enemy Within, I find them to NOT BE SCARY IN XCOM 2! Seriously! In Enemy Within, I'm always afraid of encountering Sectopods but in XCOM 2, they're cannon fodder, LITERALLY! Chryssalids? A LOT SCARIER with their zombification of civies during Terror Missions, now they just turn their victims into cocoons that spawn THREE more! Think that's scary? Not when you just cut them down in seconds! Also, LIDS DON'T TARGET CIVIES IN XCOM 2!
- You have to do EVERY mission given to you (story missions not included) or else you get punished so badly it kills the game (mods help with some but not all). You CANNOT go into hiding to try to get ADVENT to cool down and "forget" about your little resistance thus letting their guard down.
Neutrals:
= The vast assortment of equipment you can make
= The weapon tier auto upgrade on troops
= The armor tier auto upgrade on troops
Basically, this game improves upon XCOM Enemy Unknown and Enemy Within but it also lacks some stuff.
I would like to see the devs actually add the ability for the player to turn the Avatar Project on or off because of how short it is in general and it KILLS the game because you HAVE TO RUSH YOUR DECISIONS! That kills the game!
Then there's the lack of being able to "go into hiding" like an actual resistance would. I'm now fighting Sectopods, Gatekeepers, Andromedons, etc. and I'm growing tired of all of them! I want to be able to let ADVENT cooldown and make them "lower their guard" thus making them go down to using Tier 1 Troopers, Officers, Stun Lancers, Shield Bearers and MECs. I can understand their facilities staying super heavy on the troops but other missions......I want to be able to let ADVENT cooldown because of all the crap they're throwing at me. Is it too much to ask for a system that depending on how many missions you pull off against ADVENT, the more they throw at you and the less you do, the less they throw at you? And by "going into hiding" you don't HAVE TO DO EVERY FREAKING MISSION!
Also, I hate not being able to chose my own missions WHEN I WANT TO AND WHERE I WANT TO! SERIOUSLY! YOU'RE A FREAKING UNDERGROUND RESISTANCE! YOU SHOULD BE ABLE TO CHOSE WHEN TO DO MISSIONS NOT WAIT TO BE GIVEN THEM! The only missions I can understand are XCOM 2's version of Terror Missions but they have no impact on the notoriety concept I laid down; meaning they neither raise nor lower it because you're defending your stuff. This area is especially bothersome because you can't chose when do to a supply raid! Certain missions though, aka Avenger Defense, I can understand those as being event required. But every other mission; VIP Extraction (both from city and vehicle/structure), VIP Capture, and Supply Raid, need to be able to be CHOSEN WHEN AND WHERE YOU WANT TO.
Also, the punishments for NOT doing a mission are too high! Losing a region for not doing a VIP Extraction?! That's a bunch of bull! I could understand it for a XCOM 2 version of a Terror mission but NOT a VIP Extraction mission! What I could see as more viable and more fun, would be a temporary lose of income from that region and/or an increase in recruitment costs even IF you have a certain continent bonus. IF you FAIL a mission, I could picture a mix of those two. Failing a Terror mission could be all three.
All in all, despite lacking some of the features I thought there'd be for this game, I really like this game.
8/10

+Game plays despite Fallout 4 being just as new but am unable to play Fallout 4.
+For me (do NOT assume this will happen for you as well) the higher the graphics, the better the game plays for me.
Original review: Despite not playing for very long, this game is extremely fun but a LOT harder than XCOM: Enemy Unknown and its expansion Enemy Within combined.
I will cover a few pros and cons from my experience:
Pros:
+Despite lacking some of the graphical requirements and using a Windows 8 laptop, the game runs fairly well and barely lags.
+New stealth system which XCOM Enemy Unknown and Within needed
+Looting system from killing enemies
+Recover unconscious/dead troops to save them or recover their equipment, respectively, if retreat is needed (haven't retreated)
Cons:
-No random seed generation upon reload (every action has the same consequence and yes, I'm that type of player)
-Advent quickly overpowers you outside of Training Mode
-Advent MECs will spam their AoE (Area of Effect) attacks given the chance thus resulting in cheap Advent tatics
-Advent Project Avatar
-Advent Project Avatar timer (negated by mods somewhat)
-Advent Project Avatar timer fill-up speed
Questionable:
-Promotional footage showed ability to train any class of your choosing, in-game does not have that feature (unsure if it was cut or if a base facility is required)
I realize that the Advent's Project Avatar timer might be more for a "game over" condition but to me, it just takes away from the feel of the game and ruins the whole resistance movement idea by pretty much rushing you to deal with everything that's going on.
Timer is also too short and fills up too fast (length is negated by mod, speed isn't).
All in all, feels like a good successor to XCOM Enemy Unknown but is much crueler, especially when it comes to new mechanics.

Review was written by a Closed Beta Partner.
Where as many free-to-play games focus too much on monetization and trying to win customers over with cosmetics, black squad simply allows players to focus on playing a good game. Skill, not wallet size, is the key to victory. The game features a handful of maps for each mode, as well as clans and squads. The game has various firearms and loadout slots, allowing players to hot-swap between playstyles. The weapons have a easy curve, and are just varied enough to have their own twist. Weapons are a simple decision between high-damage, high-recoil or low-damage, low-recoil.
The game also allows you to open two DLC packages that give you about half of the game's current guns for 15 days, so there's that. Being a beta partner, I watched Neowiz and their wonderful staff listen to feedback post after feedback post. It is obvious that they are passionate about fixing things, and are constantly doing maintenance/patches to the game, and are always active in their platforms (Discord, twitter, etc.).
Cosmetics are present, but only make the weapon look better. Skinned items have identical stats to the base items. The only microtransactions present are "Bullets", which are used to open crates for random items. However, you can also get the chance to earn "BS Coins", so that you can open crates with coins as opposed to bullets and still save money on cosmetics. You also earn medals from ranking up and completing tasks in the game, which you can use to purchase items.
Unlike other F2P shooters, Black Squad's items are ALL permanent, except for grenades. This allows you to ensure that when you want an item, you keep it. No "3 day rental" crap, no "permanent only through microtransactions", just items to be earned by playing.
All in all, Black Squad is a fun, bare-bones but addictive free to play shooter that constantly changes based on community feedback and offers a entertaining experience for any and all players, allowing people's skills to shine over their wallet size.

What used to be a flourishing indie game inspired from some of gaming's best retro is now a shell of it's former self. Spiral Knights was fun when it was under indie ownership and it was still great when Nick was leading the development team. He left with a somber note and now I see why; the developer is clearly more interested in adding grind walls to get money out of it's players than it is providing a fun and balanced gameplay. RIP Spiral Knights, SEGA ruins yet another good thing.
Good night sweet prince.
EDIT: READ ON FOR AN ACTUAL REVIEW, STILL DON'T PLAY THIS GAME.
Spiral Knights started out as an indie game developed and funded by Three Rings (simply called OOO from here on). It got many rewards and was lauded by critics cause of it's fun and unique playstyle for an MMO and easy to learn, hard to master approach. Like many games it has dual economy; in game money being >crowns< and the real world alternative >crystal energy<.
For a short while, one could easy get energy crystals from simply playing the game to earn crowns which they could then trade for EC. This worked for a while and it was very fair way for players to get the premium gear and goodies the game had to offer without ever needing to spending actual cash. The game did, however, limit how much you could play in a single day with MIST ENERGY, which you used to progress down floors into game's dungeons. You could get about an hour or so of play time of your 100 daily mist energy, so it was good incentive to buy an elevator pass so you could play the game as much as you wanted. For small price of $5.95, you could play the game for as much as you wanted for as long as you wanted (see how I racked up 2000+ hours?).
The game always had balance issues but with enough practice, you could overcome them. Swordsmen had the best selection of armor and weapons, dished out the most damage and had the most of the game's content dedicated to it. Gunners were gimped by poor damage output, a 3 bullet clip, and reduced movement speed when firing. Bomber probably had the worst of it all. Bombs take what feels like an eternity to charge, and you can only place down one bomb at a time. The blast radius was embracing unless you had a 4* or 5* weapon and even then, you were at large risk of dying because of how bombs functioned.
Did I mention they teased opening the Core for years?
Things started to turn sour, though, once SEGA purchased the developer. Content started to slow to a halt, and a steady increase in cosmetic promotions were now the common flavor of the month. SEGA, of course was more interested in milking the game's acclaim for cash rather than developing upon it's success as a wonderful, retro gaming-inspired masterpiece. It took almost a year for the guild hall update to finally release and it took even longer for Gunner Update to hit the players. In between that, there was dozens of promotional boxes featuring nothing but armor and weapon recolors and underwhelming chances of getting said items. It was a skinner box idea to start with that only got worse, as at this point in the game, the promo boxes didn't even provide the player with EC.
There were two nails in the coffin for this game: the first being the addition of the Furnace and the departure of head developer/game creative director Nick Popovich. This game was a love letter of gaming for Nick and it really showed. Sadly, he left on a subtly sad note and moved on with his life.
It was clear at that point that SEGA was simply using the game was means of collecting easy cash off of young people with no knowledge of how their gambling--erm--lockboxes work. rather than make an evolving game. OOO is now a money machine for SEGA and nothing else. The Furnace turned the game into an nigh painful grindfest and it's god awful at it too. "Heat" up your gear now and spend rare fire crystals at a chance at leveling up your gear.
Do yourself a favor, if you see this game in your recommended feed by Steam, click "Not Interested" and said yourself the wasted harddrive space.

Definitely one of the best competitive FPS games on the market right now. It's actually kind of sad that an F2P game beats most of AAA titles. I only play 5v5 demolition (a mode simillar to CS/CoD4 Promod), so that's what my review will be based on.
I play the game on the lowest settings (something I do in every competitive FPS) and the game works like a charm. I get almost constantly 200 FPS, which is understandable considering it's UE3. There is a FOV slider which goes up to 80, though unfortunately viewmodel FOV remains unaffected by it. The mouse feels amazing in the game. It's smooth as hell, very responsive with no acceleration whatsoever. It's such an improvement over today's AAA games that the moment I first launched the game I thought I was in heaven.
Movement is okay. A mix between CS and CoD. The animations could be a little less clunky, but it's nowhere near game breaking problem.
Weapons are pretty one dimensional. They either have low damage and low recoil or high damage and high recoil. In my opinion, that's perfectly fine. No need to make things overly complicated. Arguably the strongest weapon in the game is SR-47 which has a serious kick, but once you learn how to manage it, it's really great. There is also easier to manage G36 and MDR. If you're bad at controlling recoil and are looking for a good gun to start with, R5 is probably your best bet.
The pricing on items is amazing for an F2P game. You rack gold like mad for daily/weekly events. You also get gold for logging in daily. This will buy you most of the weapons in the game (including G36 and R5 mentoined earlier). Some guns can only be bought by medals which you also get for daily/weekly events as well as for leveling up and logging in every day for 7 days straight. The only thing you can buy with real money currency are skin variations of the guns buyable with gold/medals, so no P2W at all in this game so far. If someone is willing to invest some time into the game (which should be expected seeing as it's a competitive shooter) then he won't have any problems buying things. The only annyoing thing is that you have to buy grenades every day once your free 7-day trial runs out, however, the daily log in bonus covers the grenade prince and leaves you with a lot of gold left, so it's not that bad.
As for balance, shotguns definitely need some work (especially KSG) and moveshot accuracy of sniper rifles should be nerfed as well (maybe in favor of faster scoping in?). When it comes to map balance, Castle and Carrier are way too much in favor of attacker side - rotating from one site to another takes way too long and there's no way to do it in time unless you sprint the whole time. The overall round timer is way too long as well in my opinion. Something like 2:00 or even 1:45 should be enough, especially considering how short the bomb timer is.
There's also a matter of server stability, but the game's still in early access and I believe that the server problems will be sorted out eventually.

I want to write this review not only to give potential players some insight to how awesome this game is, but to also debunk the negative comments of any naysayers out there writing negative reviews.
First of all I am a pretty casual gamer and find it hard to completely delve into a game obssesively. Darkest Dungeon has commanded my full attention. I have recently stopped playing Dark Souls 3 (another awesome game) to dive into Darkest Dungeon whole heartedly. All of the elements of the game come together to form a glorious experience.
Story:
While Darkest Dungeon doesn't really possess a changing storyline based on your choices throughout the game like most of todays RPGs. What it does provide is a rich atmosphere for you to play in. The Narrators desperate call to the unknowing heroes and tragic end (don't worry I'm not spoiling anything it's in the opening cinematic) sets the mood for this horrific Lovecraftian fantasy/horror story. His narration continues throughought the game. While in town and deep in the dungeons his cautionary tales and reactions to your continuous battles are so descriptive and dark I exclaimed to several friends "We have to track this guy down to be our next DM!" As your journey progresses you uncover lost journal entries that further detail the follies of those who came before you to conquer the depths and makes you ever fearful of the horrors you will inevitably encounter. Some negative reviewers have a problem with the lack of an everchanging and expanding story but you have to accept a game for what it is. It's definintly the atmosphere of the game that keeps you interested and the setup alone carries me through it's twisted corridors. I've read other reviews complaining about the narrator's use of "10 dollar words" but seriously it's fantastic! I forgot such words existed and just like the antiquities you find down in the dark he unearths them to give his descriptions of your actions a rich and darkened tone.
Graphics and Sound:
The graphics in Darkest Dungeon are not the supremely detailed worlds of the Elder Scrolls series or Call of Duty but the flash style animations are superb and every obstacle that stands in your way and even the backgrounds are very well crafted and detailed. In combat every attack you launch has it's own unique animation. When characters are whacked with a grotesque tentacle or attacked by some arcane assault they reel in horror as blood sprays out of them in a satisfying way. The game zooms in slightly on the characters and monsters as they give and receive assaults to really emphasize the action of combat. Paired up with the game's grisly sound effects it makes combat an awesome visceral feel. Every hit is emphasized by heavy thunks or sickening slices and the death cries of your enemies are very rewarding as they fall to your blades. Deep in the corridors of the dungeons you hear every step your party takes adding to the suspense of the crawl. As your torches dim the squeels of rabid swine or moans of undead flesh eaters can be heard echoing through the halls reminding you of the evils that lurk in the darkest corners of these catacombs. When your torches completely burn out they grow even louder making it truly unnerving to be wandering around down in the dark.
Gameplay:
As good as the other elements of the game are the gameplay is what i find the most satisfying. An awesome party and character roster management system makes even your downtime fun and rewarding. In town there are trinkets to equip, buildings that enhance your abilities and gear and even places like the tavern, abbey, and sanitarium which are used to treat stress and different stress related ailments. Ah yes, stress. During your battles characters take stress damage and will eventually go insane or die of heart attacks if not managed properly, adding a whole new element to the game. Acquiring strange personality quirks (both positive and negatively affecting your stats) gives each character on your roster an added depth. My Crusader class character; Reynauld, is a very strong melee fighter yet is crazy as a loon, prone to fits of egomania and cleptomania. This means he occasionally will take actions on his own without my prompts, insult his fellow party members (causing them stress), or will just straight up steal items when I discover them. It really makes you question who you bring down into the dungeon with you. Good thing a steady flow of hapless souls arrives on the stagecoach after every quest ready to sacrifice their lives or sanity to the expedition of the dungeons. The battle system is solid too. A turn based combat system where you use cool abilities that cause your enemies to bleed, become poisoned, become stunned, or take so many other debuffs I can't name them all here is emphasized by a "marching order" mechanic which makes you think tactically about where you position your party. There are even attacks launched by both you and your enemies that can shuffle this order to their advantage, bringing back row fighters to the front so they can be destroyed by strong front row fighters or driving those same front row characters to the back where they become almost useless until they can climb their way to the front again. It's an awesome system and has me crying out in triumph every time I land a powerful strike or perfectly synchronize my attacks to decimate the enemy party.
Playability:
First of all, the game is unforgiving, and some new players might be discouraged as their characters die or give in to madness, but there IS hope! As you learn the combat system and the inner workings of the dungeons you eventually find a rhythm and start to mount victories, one grueling step at a time. With proper management and smart decisions you can overcome the game's difficulties without to much heartache. There are no do-overs and the game does warn you that characters will die and you must learn to let them go without becoming too frustrated. There will be more. Just surviving is a happy experience and really advancing is a truly rewarding endeavor. Hitting a groove is awesome but just know that it can be shattered by a bad foray in the dungeons at any time if you have a stroke of bad luck or were unprepared for the journey. There are settings in the menu that can make the game a little easier if you are having a hard time but it can definitely be conquered without these handicaps with determination and smart choices. The game is a solo experience and not something you need to be totally dedicated to the whole time you play. If it aggravates you too much you can always walk away in the middle of combat and vent for a while. The challenge really drew me in though because every victory is a victory well earned.
I'm telling you guys, this game is great. When I bought Darkest Dungeon it was on sale for about 17 bucks but I would have gladly payed more. It has been one of my favorite games in a long time and the only one I felt necessary to write such a lengthy review for. If you're into a challenging, butt-kicking experience set in dark, horrific catacombs wrought with dangers and terrible antidiluvian evils pick it up! Soon, like me, you'll find yourself totally immerrsed in the twisting tunnels and blood soaked corridors of... THE DARKEST DUNGEON!

This is the best game since the XCOM: Enemy Within.
And for the most part, it's very similar to the last XCOM; veterans of the previous war will find themselves sliding in without too much trouble. The only real differences in the 'base building' side of the game are some tweaks in how scientists and engineers work (for the better, in my opinion). Now, instead of having a small, faceless army of both, you get a handful of individuals who can be assigned to projects to speed them up.
The mission selection aspects have also been massively expanded - you'll always have a multitude of missions to choose from spread across the globe, as well as the usual random VIP, Council and Terror missions as before. Essentially, you don't spend nearly as much time just waiting around as you did in the previous game. The game comes at you quickly and doesn't pull it's punches, even from the start (all you tough guys who kept making out the last XCOM was too easy are finally going to get that challenge you've secretly been dreading!), with each enemy unit having a clear tactical purpose and not just varying degrees of 'better at shooting'.
2K worked with the Long War guys on some parts of this new XCOM game, which was a fantastic idea given the popularity of the Long War mod, and it shows. You will find yourself fighting rearguard actions and retreating or regrouping and you will have disproportionately hard missions thrown at you occasionally. Not to the same extent as Long War, where you had no chance of winning some missions and the only option was to run, but enough that you really get the feeling that the aliens have every advantage and you're fighting as part of an under resourced resistance movement. There seem to be problems flying at you from every angle, as you work against 'The Avatar Project' (the new Doom Meter), try to thwart alien 'Dark Events' (alien operations which give them advantages over you), make contact with new resistance cells (which provide greater coverage and resources, like launching a satellite in the previous game) all while prioritising which of the areas to investigate and missions to undergo.
Fans who liked the previous XCOM for it's story, drama and suspense will also find these portions of the game to be well stocked - there are plenty of high action cut scenes and desperation missions, invigorated by old and new characters. The new 'Concealment' mechanic adds to the suspense of sneaking up on an enemy patrol and helps you set up ambushes.
The only real disappointment so far is that air combat seems to have been removed, but it was such a marginal part of the last game that I can understand why they'd leave it out.
A lot of people have complained about lag and long load times, citing their computers load times for games like Witcher 3 or CoD 10,000: Advanced Zombie Black Ops (or whatever) as evidence of poor optimisation by XCOM developers and therefore proving nothing except that they know less about these things than they think. I'm running the exact rig I had for the last XCOM game, which would quickly and happily run with ultra settings all round. XCOM 2, I play with medium settings but it looks great and runs fine - no lag, occasionally a mission will take a while to load.
What people fail to realise is that First Person Shooters and games like Witcher are mostly a big 2D background with a few static props and landscapes designed to disguise short draw distances. Add to this that their AI is relatively uncomplicated and you should understand that they are not nearly as challenging to run as XCOM, which 3D renders every part of an almost totally intractable/destructible map that combines a variable cover system with 15+ moving units and a decent AI.
TL;DR: The 'super kewl' PC your Dad brought you 5 years ago can't run everything on Ultra anymore. If you want improved performance, get over it and turn your graphics settings down.
All in all, the complaints about XCOM 2 are mostly unwarranted. What we have here is the perfect sequel - a game that is mostly similar to the one we love, but improved and reinvigorated in almost every way.

Dark Souls 3 is one of the best RPG'S ever made. If you want the short answer, than yes Dark Souls 3 is worth every dime. While the story is nothing extravagant, hell there really isn't a story at all (there is lots of lore, but that requires you talking to NPC's and reading lots of background info on weapons), it is still a great and unforgettable journey, with great combat and decision making. If you're looking for an RPG you can dump tons of hours into (I'm nearly 50 hours in and I'm only halfway in at BEST) then Dark Souls 3 is the game for you. Now if you want the long answer as to whether or not you should buy this game, then keep on reading.
The story is nothing extravagant, and nothing is shoved in your face. It's really up to you on whether or not you want to know the lore behind the game as you progress. Lore is not exactly story though, lore is more of a background and gives you more clarity on what's going on.
Dark Souls 3 is nothing but gameplay. You aren't bombarded with menus and tutorials, the game doesn't tell you what you need or can't do. You can kill anyone you want (while you can kill whoever you want, there will sometimes be concequences). As for the combat, it is very fluid and is amazing on PC. There are loads of different weapons to choose from, with most having a unique "weapon art". Weapon arts are basically special skills linked to a certain weapon. While these weapon arts cannot be changed, it can be something that really makes a difference when choosing between two weapons of the same group/class. Dodging by rolling is very vital and key to success in Dark Souls, and is something every Dark Souls player should master. While you can hide behind your sheild, dodging by rolling can be more effective, and feels much more rewarding. You are bound to find a weapon that you like throughout your Dark Souls experience, whether your using a weapon for fun or to make certain areas of the game easier. While you can use swords to slash your foes you can also use magic and pyromancy (fire magic). While magic and pyromancy might not always be effective, it is an alternative to using swords and bows. You can make magic/pyromancy your main source of damage, there are weapons and items exclusively benefical to people that use magic/pyromancy.
The Soulsborne games have been known for being difficult, but how difficult is Dark Souls really? I am someone who played and completed Bloodborne before truly hopping into Dark Souls 3, so I had a good understanding and pretty good mechanics while playing. I didn't have much issue and rarely died up until fighting the
, after that the game became much more difficult. The truth is though, this game is difficult because it is one of the few games that treat you like every other enemy in the game. Once your HP drops down to zero
. There are no "revives" or "second chances". Once you die, you die. Bosses can be difficult without a doubt, as well as basic enemies. It's up to you how to decide to face each enemy. Once you get down the mechanics, Dark Souls won't be easy, but it won't be near impossible to play either.
The online aspect of Dark Souls 3 is pretty good for the most part. You can invade other players, join covenants, and help other players as well, but you can also be invaded and summon other players. This is an aspect I feel everyone should use, and I feel no one should go offline. Invading other players works like this, you invade someone else's world as a phantom, and your goal is to basically kill them. You get rewarded based on your covenant, but you will always gain souls. You cannot interact with their world, open doors, reveal illusion walls, attack enemies, etc, but enemies will not be aggresive towards you. Summoning works like this, you either put down a White Sign Soapstone in a certain area, and anyone that has their ember restored will be able to summon you into their world. You can either leave by using a Black Seperation Crystal or if you die. You do not lose the souls you gain from their world if you die. You can interact with the enemies in their world. Alternatively, if you're the one that needs help simply use an ember and go to a white summon sign mark (if it's there) and the person will come into your world. You can also summon NPC's, depending on the choices you've made throughout the game. Covenants are basically clans you join. You will find more throughout your journey, and each covenant has a different effect. For example, Way of the Blue makes it so that anyone in the Blue Sentinels covenant will be able to help you if you end up getting invaded.
The atmosphere is great in Dark Souls, and it really makes you feel like as if you're part of the world. The atmosphere could be very spooky and dark if you're in the
but can be very lighthearted and welcoming if you meet some NPCs in the

In one environment you will be surronded by lava and fire while in the next you're in the catacombs. At one point you walk out of a boss room, only to be treated by a beautiful view of

Not much to say here, other than the fact that the music is amazing. Even the main menu has a great song that plays. The music can seriously set the mood and tone of a boss fight.
Boss fights are phenominal in Dark Souls. While the earlier bosses can be very easy (definitely not for new players to the franchise, but it very easily can be for anyone with a good understanding and execution of the mechanics), once you reach the
bosses can start to become more difficult. Boss fights are very creative though, and you will be bound to enjoy a few of them, regardless of difficulty. Boss fights are very unique and while some can be lackluster and dissapointing, they are still very creative. The boss fights are definitely one of the best aspects of this game, and I encourage everyone to beat every bosses, optional and non optional.

There aren't many games that can make me feel the range of emotions that Firaxis' XCOM remakes can. The Microprose original will forever be the king when it comes to atmosphere, but XCOM2 manages to be just unfair enough to be a challenge, without being actually unfun.
XCOM 2 surpasses Firaxis' first outing in just about every way. The player is under much more pressure throughout the game and failure is always a spectre on the horizon if you spend too long messing around. Soldier customization has also been improved, allowing you to develop even deeper attachments to your hapless soldiers before they inevitably bite the dust. Particularly nice is the character pool, which allows you to create soldiers and VIPs that can appear naturally in the game without you customizing them on the fly. The multiplayer experience has also been improved, with ranked play now available and the ability to make squads comprising of both alien and human forces.
If any criticism can really be levied at this game, it's that the injury system could do with some tweaking. Grievously wounded soldiers can suffer temporary penalties to their will stat, but in the early game even taking one point of damage can result in a grievous injury being rolled, which doesn't seem right. TLDR; It's XCOM 2, just buy it :D It takes everything great in XCOM EU and EW and improves on them. It was awesome for me.
Review bassed on my experience in finishing a campaign on Veteran, taking my sweet time to get everything researched and built.
Pros:
* Liked the story. It's in the same style as the prequel, with new and returning characters. The dialogue blurbs nicely add character and flavour, as well as prequel references.
* Trade-offs amped up in the early- and mid-game. That feeling of being pressured to make trade-offs on a strategic level is greater than EU/EW, such as which facility to build first, where to stick the engineers, whether to get more supplies or grab a new engineer, or which Dark Event is the lesser evil at this point in time. It peters out in the late-game, as everything settles down into a routine. EDIT: Some people don't actually like this, so YMMV.
* The same pressure is applied on tactical maps, with turn timers that force you to cover ground faster, as well as constant reinforcements on certain types of missions. EDIT: Again, it seems a lot of people dislike this to the point of hating it. But there are mods to turn it off, so the point is moot.
* Even on "Veteran" difficulty, the aliens have health levels that feel like "Classic" on EU/EW. Even with end-game weapons, it's uncommon to be able to one-shot aliens (varies by skill set). Exactly like what the difficulty description says - a good challenge.
* New aliens, and new alien abilities. They are great additions, as they each need different strategies to counter. Armour on aliens just adds to the tactical variables that you need to take into account.
* New concealment mechanic allows for overwatch ambushes to soften the first pop. Get the right skills and mobility PCS, and you can have a concealed scout skirting the edges to scan the map.
* New soldier enhancement options - weapon mods and PCS that are attachable to weapons and soldiers.
* Lots of soldier visual customisations. I initialy didn't care much for this, but once I started tinkering with it...
Meh:
* The line-of-sight thing still bothers me. Some stretches of cover just seems to block line-of-sight unintuitively.
* There are new missions types not found in EU/EW, but a lot of them involve the timer (either a timer to reach a point, or a timer to get out). It would 've been nice to see more non-timed mission types. You also lose out on UFO interceptions (but the UFO chase is still there, but with a nice twist).
* The skill trees are not well-balanced. I tried out both trees, and I tried mixing them - some skills are just way more useful than their alternative. Oh, and a well-trained Psi Operative is really fun to play.
* Ambivalent about the change to scientists. I liked the change to engineers, but scientists? The diminishing returns sort of makes sense, but the Laboratory felt like a waste - most of the time, I don't have enough supplies to build stuff, so speeding up research is not so crucial. Plus, I can spend Intel to speed it up if I really need to.
Cons:
* The loading time to transition from the strategic screen to and from the tactical map feels really slow. EDIT: Apparently, someone found out that hitting Caps Lock on the misson-completed loading screen helps.
* Stutters and lags galore on the higher graphics settings. It's just annoying to lag as if I running minimum specs. It occurs less frequently when you tone the graphics, but it still happens.
* Didn't like that building a standard weapon/armour makes it available to every single solider. Prefer to EU/EW approach of needing to build one weapon for each soldier (cheaper).
* While the Proving Grounds projects does build exactly one item, it's also very odd that it's actually random:
Commander: "Hey Shen, build me a new type of ammo/grenade/armor/heavy weapon/powered weapon."
Shen: "What kind, sir?"
Commander: "Surprise me."
* Tactical map clipping issues, animation errors, and other graphical bugs. Nothing breaking (except maybe having my hacking options obscured by a truck my soldier was standing next to), but they're numerous enough for me to want to list it down.

Darkest Dungeon is very well made, spectacularly designed, and should be a glowing recommendation... but I can't bring myself to recommend a game that flawlessly executes being utterly unenjoyable.

Firaxis has successfully pulled off a sequel better than the original XCOM Enemy Within.  Listening to the community and studying what good things the "Long War" modders did for the first XCOM, they incorporated those changes into this game and fixed some annoyances.  Not only this but they also added many other useful tools such as hacking and gun modifications.
Here are some positives:
XCOM 2 is more easily moddable by the community.   Now we will see some very interesting ideas that the developers either didn't think about or didn't have time to incorporate into their game.
Some actions (like reloading) does not take up your full action as it did in the first XCOM.  This enables more interesting scenarios (like more AI baddies dropping into your zone)
Hacking adds another layer of fun and excitement.  If you succeed you usually can choose a temporary augmentation that will either help the hacker or the whole squad!
Beginning some levels concealed.  This is an awesome addition that enables you to have the surprise on the first group of aliens.  You can also get the Ranger class to remain concealed and scout around the map without "popping" groups.
Timed Limit on missions.  Missions being timed is that you can no longer crawl your way overwatching as you go to complete a difficult mission.  This adds another layer of difficulty to the game that was somewhat neccessary. I will say that the bad thing is that it does force the player to become agressive and take chances they aren't normally accustomed to taking.  Thankfully not every single mission has a time limit.
Modular level creation.  Now the maps can be completely different from each other and you won't be easily bored.
Here are some Negatives:
The game does framerate dip a lot.  The game doesn't run as smooth (and I have a Nvidia GTX 970 graphics card)
Timed Limit on missions.  I will mention this again because this game was already fairly difficult even on the lower difficulty levels and now this game can become a bit stressful during these missions.
Not enough classes.  The "long war" mod introduced many different and interesting classes to have and yet in XCOM 2 you still are only presented with 4 classes in the beginning.
Buggy.  This game is still buggy and is at best a late beta release.   Although I have not encountered anything game breaking, it is worthy to note this since it is a full priced triple A release.

I've played Darkest Dungeon quite a bit, as evident from the playtime I've logged. I enjoyed the game a lot, at first. As the game went on longer, I saw my motivation fading, due to a real lack of reason for success. This may sound vague so far, and many reviews cover the points completely and eloquently. I will therefor use an analogy.
Darkest Dungeon: Live Action Role Play Version
Step 01: Find a six-sided die (dice)
Step 02: Find a friend
Step 03: Find a playing surface, such as a table
Step 04: Roll the die on the playing surface
Step 05: Since you are a "beginner" at this point in the game, rolling an even number is safe and you "progress." If the number is odd, however, your "friend" kicks you in the groin as hard as he or she can.
Step 06: If you happened to roll an even number, you get a second roll. If you roll a two, you get a magical "cup." This "cup" can be worn for groin protection. The "cup" is also ringed with spikes on the exterior. These spikes are aimed at the inside of your legs. Now you can protect the groin, but the area around it will be painfully shredded in the process.
Step 07: Regardless of which number is rolled, if at any time you vomit, you lose. If you lose, you have one day to recover and must return to Step 01 the next day.
Step 08: If you rolled an even number, and disregarding the outcome of Step 06, you now move onto the "Intermediate" or "Veteran" difficulty. On this difficulty level, roll the die again. If you roll a 1 or 2, you are safe and can move onto the next difficulty level. If you roll a 3, 4, 5, or 6, your friend kicks you in the groin as hard as he or she can. Same rules apply to recovery.
Step 09: If you rolled a 1 or 2, you are now on the highest difficulty level. This being said, you get to roll the die once more. If you roll anything other than a 6, your friend kicks you as hard as he or she can in your groin.
Step 10: If you managed to roll a 6, congratulations. Your reward? You don't get kicked in the groin. If your roll resulted in groin kicking, go back to step 01 after one day of rest.
Step 11: If at any time you don't enjoy this game, and decide to quit, do not purchase Darkest Dungeon.

Pretty good! Worthwhile sequel. Addresses virtually every criticism of the last one. Handful of issues though:
- Performance is all over the place! Seems like lots of developers have added so many postprocessing effects to UE3 over the years that it's getting difficult to optimize well... and using a wrapper rather than doing OpenGL builds for OSX and Linux doesn't help. There's also hilarious bugs like the game thinking 12 PM is midnight and 12 AM is noon as far as your savefiles are concerned -- of course, _only_ C++ doesn't have a standard library to handle this for you, but that does suggest a minor lack of polish.
- The base-building optimization puzzle is a little too solvable, but it's the sort of thing you'll inevitably get wrong the first time through. This carries through to a lot of the game's design, where you seem to be encouraged to savescum or fail on your first time through, with neither option being particularly satisfying. There's no reason this game couldn't have borrowed Invisible Inc's autosaving-with-a-fixed-number-of-rewinds mechanic as an alternative to Ironman mode, and it'd have been better for it.
- Late game has a bit of Civ syndrome where once you've seen all of the tech it's a bit of a slog to push through to the very end.
- Narrative comes on too strong at the start with all of the military stuff and the power fantasy of repeatedly addressing the player as "commander," though the mid-game scripted events are well-handled.
- The starting swords are ridiculously anachronistic.
This is already a good game, but I expect it will be much, much better in a year. It's probably fair to be frustrated by that in the meantime.

I am very sad about this game. I had such high hopes for it. It is a great concept, it has great art, it has a great vibe, the voice acting is terrific so what could have gone so wrong?
The gameplay.
It all boils down to one problem. If you want to have a game about psychological damage the most important thing is that the player should care about the characters, a lot. You have to set it up to say "you are stuck with this guy however insane it gets". You have to feel like you are on a minecart ride to hell where then only way out is to go all the way down.
Instead what this game does is throw hundreds of characters at you. You need 4 per week to make an adventuring squad but you can get up to 8 replacements! So yeah you end up with a massive squad of 16 adventurers whose names you don't even know. Has one of them gone insane? Chuck them out and get another to fill their place. Everyone is disposable.
Drowning in characters means it's impossible to care about any of them. It's such a shame because this game could have been a true great, instead it's a complete fail.
If they just made it so that you had a small squad which you needed to cherish, with maybe a replacement every once in a while. If only you had to sit in the town thinking "I really want to stay here for another week to rest but I need to keep pressing on deeper into the dungeon because I have to beat the timer" this really could have been a huge win.
Instead they bungled it.

Did you like XCOM: Enemy Unknown? Then you'll like this.
If XCOM: Enemy Unknown simply isn't/wasn't for you, this won't be either.
If XCOM: Enemey Unknown had some nitpicks that made it undesirable to you, this game MIGHT be to your interest.
It's pretty common knowledge now that XCOM 2 follows the 'canon' that XCOM lost in the first game. Does that mean your XCOM game was essentially 'wasted' storywise? Not really. You find out in the tutorial that the Commander (ie the player) was captured and was forced to play 'war games' so the aliens could learn about human tactics. So your playthroughs of XCOM were essentially those simulations, so your game still 'counts'.
Combat is mostly the same. The new 'classes' aren't really new, they match the archetypes from XCOM. Sharpshooter = Sniper, Grenadier = Heavy, Ranger = Assault, Specialist = Support. They're basically 'the same but better'. PSI is also still a thing, though rather than being a trainable sub-class for a small number of soldiers late game, here it is it's own fully unique class avaiable VERY early (within the first few missions) should you choose to pursue it. You need a Sectoid autopsy, followed by a PSI lab. From there, any Rookie can be trained into a PSI class in 10 days in the PSI Lab (5 days if the Lab is staffed by an Engineer).
This game also has a lot more meaningful choices. Unlike the abduction sites in XCOM, where the game basically said 'yeah you can only do one because reasons', here you may be presented with more objectives than you have the time to deal with, so it's up to you to decide which is best based on your circumstances. There are still 'pick between one of these' missions every month, called 'Dark Events'. There are 2-3 each month and you can only deal with one. However, unlike abductions which could lead to a state leaving the Council, the Dark Events you choose not to attend will grant a buff to the enemy for 1 in game month, such as increased health, armour (every point of armour reduces damage taken by 1 until it's removed by grenades or special class abilities), special ammo types etc. So it's almost a case of 'do the mission to remove the most worst debuff and take the less worse one'.
The game does have some stutter issues, but being turn based this has zero effect on gameplay. There are also still some 'how can you shoot through a wall' situations, but not as bad as before either.
This game also seems to be much harder than the first, to me at least (coming from someone who has completed Enemy Unknown on Normal). Sectoids are now much more dangerous, with double health, Mind Control, and the ability to create a PSI Zombie from any humanoid corpse (ADVENT soldier,civillain or XCOM) and you still encounter them from the word GO. ADVENT soldiers also seem to be much better shots than the early game aliens of before.
Basically, if you played and liked XCOM, this is more of the same but slightly better. If you didn't like it, this probably isn't the game for you.

Darkest Dungeon oozes with style. The dungeons are dangerous, even your strongest character is at risk.  One dungeon takes usually 15-30 minutes, and so you can attempt a dungeon even if you don't have much time to play in the day.
You cannot save scum, so you won't get stuck in saving and reloading when you encounter unfavorable events (which you will). You have to live with your choices. Unless special circumstances take place, high level characters will refuse to enter lower level dungeons with low level characters, and so even lower level dungeons will continue to be threats.
There is a good variety of team compositions with the 15 different character types. Characters have different styles depending on where they stand in the 4-person formation. Forced movement abilities from your own characters and the enemies keep combat encounters varied. Bosses are unique from one another and cannot be beaten by the same strategy. Some team compositions will simply never work versus a particular boss.
Things can go badly instantly or can slowly creep up on you. Throughout the dungeon you can manage your risk by torchlight, brighter light, less risk, but also less reward. Mismanaging Stress can bring a halt to your dungeon attempt.
Critical hits not only sinks into your characters' health pools, but they also demoralize (increases stress) the team. The reverse is true too -- if your character hits a critical, they reduce stress for themselves and perhaps some of the team. You may have a healthy team, but if one teammember snaps, they can bring down the entire dungeon run (quest). Having to manage Health and Stress makes dungeoning unique to this game. Thankfully you keep what you've found, trinkets, heirlooms, and gold, from unsuccessful dungeon runs. However, your characters will not earn experience from failed dungeon runs and they still bring back their Stress, quirks, and diseases.
Out of dungeons you manage your small town, which serve as upgrade shops, recruiting station, and stress, quirk, and disease management. Your characters will develop both negative and positive quirks throughout the dungeoning as well as diseases. Characters with high stress are liabilities and will need to be managed in one of the stress-reducing buildings, Abbey or Tavern.
---
I'd recommend this to anyone who likes dunegon-looting games or team-based strategy games and is looking for a new experience.  It's important to know that you will lose characters permanently and will fail quests. If being denied success at times is not something you like in a game, then you probably won't like the flow of Darkest Dungeon. You'll be placing your established characters in harm's way.

Before I begin, do NOT bring my play time into account of this review. I played back when the game had a much more appealing idea behind it and wasn't 100% reliant on Promos to keep it alive.
Now honestly what can be said about this game that hasn't already. From its core it was a very promising game. Frequent updates, fun gameplay, and interesting lore are what made this game so great from the very start. The majority of that changed for the worse when accessories were implemented as it gave the developers a false ideal that accessories are what should keep the game a float instead of pure content that most other games thrive off of to survive. For the most part the game in itself was a great one from the start, but with every level, every floor, every depth you went down further it started to lose the magic that it once had. It became less of a challenge for the player and just ended up turning into a limitless grind to see who could have the best looking set overall. Cosmetics can be nice and mix things up in games, but when that game survives off of that simple factor alone then it is truly not going to last forever. This game could have been something special if it truly didn't rely on cosmetics and reskins to keep it going.
I may have a great deal of a time in this game, but it took me much longer than it should have to truly realize how the devs were handling it after countless promo that managed to root itself in with every event. On its own the gameplay stands out, it's fun whether you enjoy solo play (only for so long), and can be even better when you have a party of friends to play with, but you will quickly lose all enjoyment that you originally had once you reach the end-game content as it doesn't have much to offer other than reskinned bosses with extra challenge added to them. Other than the never-ending grind that presents itself for end-game there truly is no goal afterwards as it gives you nothing to strive for.
For what it is the soundtrack is great, and can easily be memorable if you happen to enjoy calm tunes when relaxing in Haven or enjoy dramatic music when engaging in battle. The graphics are also quite nice with how everything seems to be made to appear cute, but at the same time present some sort of danger. The community (although much smaller now) also happens to be a pretty good part of what makes the game what it is (except the PvP part of it. You know who you are). Other than that the only true flaw that makes me not want to recommend this game is that the devs have basically given up on putting out any true content updates, and mostly focus on reskins and cosmetics like most F2P models fall victim too.
I can’t say I’d ever go back to this game either since it lost all of its charm as soon as I started playing other games and noticed the only real reason I originally played it was due to a nostalgic feeling that it gave. For the most part it reminded me of Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past, and when I had first started this seemed like a wonderful experience since this was what I thought I was missing out on especially since it had co-op functionality.
All - in - All great idea, and interesting mechanics, but the devs have basically become greedy, and have chosen to take the lazy route only to release cosmetics that add no value to the game other than making it another bland dress-up game to see who has the most valuable and shiniest sets.
TL:DR This game is decent, but like most F2P games it has its flaws, and won’t last you too long nowadays like it used to for enjoyment if you want a truly memorable experience.

Dark Souls 3 is one of the best RPG'S ever made. If you want the short answer, than yes Dark Souls 3 is worth every dime. While the story is nothing extravagant, hell there really isn't a story at all (there is lots of lore, but that requires you talking to NPC's and reading lots of background info on weapons), it is still a great and unforgettable journey, with great combat and decision making. If you're looking for an RPG you can dump tons of hours into (I'm nearly 50 hours in and I'm only halfway in at BEST) then Dark Souls 3 is the game for you. Now if you want the long answer as to whether or not you should buy this game, then keep on reading.
The story is nothing extravagant, and nothing is shoved in your face. It's really up to you on whether or not you want to know the lore behind the game as you progress. Lore is not exactly story though, lore is more of a background and gives you more clarity on what's going on.
Dark Souls 3 is nothing but gameplay. You aren't bombarded with menus and tutorials, the game doesn't tell you what you need or can't do. You can kill anyone you want (while you can kill whoever you want, there will sometimes be concequences). As for the combat, it is very fluid and is amazing on PC. There are loads of different weapons to choose from, with most having a unique "weapon art". Weapon arts are basically special skills linked to a certain weapon. While these weapon arts cannot be changed, it can be something that really makes a difference when choosing between two weapons of the same group/class. Dodging by rolling is very vital and key to success in Dark Souls, and is something every Dark Souls player should master. While you can hide behind your sheild, dodging by rolling can be more effective, and feels much more rewarding. You are bound to find a weapon that you like throughout your Dark Souls experience, whether your using a weapon for fun or to make certain areas of the game easier. While you can use swords to slash your foes you can also use magic and pyromancy (fire magic). While magic and pyromancy might not always be effective, it is an alternative to using swords and bows. You can make magic/pyromancy your main source of damage, there are weapons and items exclusively benefical to people that use magic/pyromancy.
The Soulsborne games have been known for being difficult, but how difficult is Dark Souls really? I am someone who played and completed Bloodborne before truly hopping into Dark Souls 3, so I had a good understanding and pretty good mechanics while playing. I didn't have much issue and rarely died up until fighting the
, after that the game became much more difficult. The truth is though, this game is difficult because it is one of the few games that treat you like every other enemy in the game. Once your HP drops down to zero
. There are no "revives" or "second chances". Once you die, you die. Bosses can be difficult without a doubt, as well as basic enemies. It's up to you how to decide to face each enemy. Once you get down the mechanics, Dark Souls won't be easy, but it won't be near impossible to play either.
The online aspect of Dark Souls 3 is pretty good for the most part. You can invade other players, join covenants, and help other players as well, but you can also be invaded and summon other players. This is an aspect I feel everyone should use, and I feel no one should go offline. Invading other players works like this, you invade someone else's world as a phantom, and your goal is to basically kill them. You get rewarded based on your covenant, but you will always gain souls. You cannot interact with their world, open doors, reveal illusion walls, attack enemies, etc, but enemies will not be aggresive towards you. Summoning works like this, you either put down a White Sign Soapstone in a certain area, and anyone that has their ember restored will be able to summon you into their world. You can either leave by using a Black Seperation Crystal or if you die. You do not lose the souls you gain from their world if you die. You can interact with the enemies in their world. Alternatively, if you're the one that needs help simply use an ember and go to a white summon sign mark (if it's there) and the person will come into your world. You can also summon NPC's, depending on the choices you've made throughout the game. Covenants are basically clans you join. You will find more throughout your journey, and each covenant has a different effect. For example, Way of the Blue makes it so that anyone in the Blue Sentinels covenant will be able to help you if you end up getting invaded.
The atmosphere is great in Dark Souls, and it really makes you feel like as if you're part of the world. The atmosphere could be very spooky and dark if you're in the
but can be very lighthearted and welcoming if you meet some NPCs in the
. The environments are great. Unlike Bloodborne where while they were great environments everything felt the same. Dark Souls is not the case at all. In one environment you will be surronded by lava and fire while in the next you're in the catacombs. At one point you walk out of a boss room, only to be treated by a beautiful view of
.
Not much to say here, other than the fact that the music is amazing. Even the main menu has a great song that plays. The music can seriously set the mood and tone of a boss fight.
Boss fights are phenominal in Dark Souls. While the earlier bosses can be very easy (definitely not for new players to the franchise, but it very easily can be for anyone with a good understanding and execution of the mechanics), once you reach the
bosses can start to become more difficult. Boss fights are very creative though, and you will be bound to enjoy a few of them, regardless of difficulty. Boss fights are very unique and while some can be lackluster and dissapointing, they are still very creative. The boss fights are definitely one of the best aspects of this game, and I encourage everyone to beat every bosses, optional and non optional.

Despite the fact that it doesn't show any PC prompts in menus or anywhere at all it'll take about 5 minutes to know and memorize which buttons mean what on the keyboard. It runs well on both NVidia and AMD cards (from past experience). The PC version is truly the best way to experience Dark Souls 3. But is important to note that

Dark Souls 3 is a masterpiece and is an example of a near perfect RPG. If you're looking for a challenge, a game you can put tons of hours into, an RPG game, and/or one that is well crafted and put together, than Dark Souls 3 is the perfect game for you.

Xcom 2...is just too hard.
Xcom 2  is a very well-made game. The atmosphere is grisly and creepy, and perfectly sets up a strong Lovecraft theme -- and I mean that in every sense of the term, Along with the aesthetics, From's mastery of level design is on full display here, with clever pathing and shortcut placement. In this sense, Xcom 2 feels very much like a superb 3D Castlevania.
However, Xcom 2's combat asks much more of the player than previous Firaxis games. This shift was clearly a calculated design choice, but it was tough for me to appreciate the differences after becoming so aggravated from dying to the same cheap shots over and over.
Xcom 2 is a game brimming with secrets: daunting and multilayered mysteries that sunk into my subconscious, tracing snaking paths across my brain until I was literally seeing mazes every time I closed my eyes. It hooked me in with its masterful puzzle design and gorgeous visuals, then compelled me forward as I began to carve out my own purpose.      It’s a freedom granted by a world as welcomingly open to exploration as it is enjoyably challenging to solve.
With its recycled map and wildly overpowered abilities, playing Xcom 2 feels like a lot like enabling god-like cheat codes in Xcom 2 and going nuts. Its ridiculous story, goofy characters, self-aware humor, and amazing character editor make it all work, especially for those of us who’ve played the previous games and can appreciate its in-jokes. But its appeal is shortened by the ludicrous speed at which we can zip across it and grow tired of its lack of challenge.

Darkest Dungeon is a new take on classic turn-based games.  The art direction is superb and really sets the overall mood of the game, which is matched by quality voice overs and sound design.  Unlike most traditional RPG's, DD adds a stress system to the game which is quite unnerving at times.  Characters' stress levels increase when taking damage, walking around in the dark, or various other things.  Stress can be lowered by achieving critical hits, party companions performing helpful deeds, or by more traditional manners while in town by using the ♥♥♥♥♥house, sanctuary, bar, etc.  If a character gets too stressed they can become even more crazy and paranoid or they could go the other route and become even more brave and let their true inner hero shine while under pressure.
Combat mechanics are interesting and there's a lot to love there.  I've spent countless hours getting my butt handed to me, and even though the RNG can feel unfair at times, overall I love the combat.  Exploration is also really interesting in this game as you never know from one room to the next if you're going to encounter a mini-boss or find hidden treasure.  Maybe you'll find both but your stress level dings and one of your party members goes all psycho on you and drives the rest of the party into madness.
Perma death makes things even more rewarding but challenging, very similar to the way XCOM: EU made me feel.
Anyway, at this price point, DD is a game everyone should own.  I play it on my desktop gaming PC when I'm home but also on my Macbook when I'm traveling.  Runs great on both and it's hard to find games at this price point that can offer hundreds of hours of enjoyment.  DD nailed it and the devs continue to release new content on a regular basis (so far for free!).
Buy this, everyone should own at least a copy of DD - buy two and gift one to a friend.

Dark Souls 3 is one of the best RPG'S ever made. If you want the short answer, than yes Dark Souls 3 is worth every dime. While the story is nothing extravagant, hell there really isn't a story at all (there is lots of lore, but that requires you talking to NPC's and reading lots of background info on weapons), it is still a great and unforgettable journey, with great combat and decision making. If you're looking for an RPG you can dump tons of hours into (I'm nearly 50 hours in and I'm only halfway in at BEST) then Dark Souls 3 is the game for you. Now if you want the long answer as to whether or not you should buy this game, then keep on reading.
The story is nothing extravagant, and nothing is shoved in your face. It's really up to you on whether or not you want to know the lore behind the game as you progress. Lore is not exactly story though, lore is more of a background and gives you more clarity on what's going on.
Dark Souls 3 is nothing but gameplay. You aren't bombarded with menus and tutorials, the game doesn't tell you what you need or can't do. You can kill anyone you want (while you can kill whoever you want, there will sometimes be concequences). As for the combat, it is very fluid and is amazing on PC. There are loads of different weapons to choose from, with most having a unique "weapon art". Weapon arts are basically special skills linked to a certain weapon. While these weapon arts cannot be changed, it can be something that really makes a difference when choosing between two weapons of the same group/class. Dodging by rolling is very vital and key to success in Dark Souls, and is something every Dark Souls player should master. While you can hide behind your sheild, dodging by rolling can be more effective, and feels much more rewarding. You are bound to find a weapon that you like throughout your Dark Souls experience, whether your using a weapon for fun or to make certain areas of the game easier. While you can use swords to slash your foes you can also use magic and pyromancy (fire magic). While magic and pyromancy might not always be effective, it is an alternative to using swords and bows. You can make magic/pyromancy your main source of damage, there are weapons and items exclusively benefical to people that use magic/pyromancy.
The Soulsborne games have been known for being difficult, but how difficult is Dark Souls really? I am someone who played and completed Bloodborne before truly hopping into Dark Souls 3, so I had a good understanding and pretty good mechanics while playing. I didn't have much issue and rarely died up until fighting the
, after that the game became much more difficult. The truth is though, this game is difficult because it is one of the few games that treat you like every other enemy in the game. Once your HP drops down to zero
. There are no "revives" or "second chances". Once you die, you die. Bosses can be difficult without a doubt, as well as basic enemies. It's up to you how to decide to face each enemy. Once you get down the mechanics, Dark Souls won't be easy, but it won't be near impossible to play either.
The online aspect of Dark Souls 3 is pretty good for the most part. You can invade other players, join covenants, and help other players as well, but you can also be invaded and summon other players. This is an aspect I feel everyone should use, and I feel no one should go offline. Invading other players works like this, you invade someone else's world as a phantom, and your goal is to basically kill them. You get rewarded based on your covenant, but you will always gain souls. You cannot interact with their world, open doors, reveal illusion walls, attack enemies, etc, but enemies will not be aggresive towards you. Summoning works like this, you either put down a White Sign Soapstone in a certain area, and anyone that has their ember restored will be able to summon you into their world. You can either leave by using a Black Seperation Crystal or if you die. You do not lose the souls you gain from their world if you die. You can interact with the enemies in their world. Alternatively, if you're the one that needs help simply use an ember and go to a white summon sign mark (if it's there) and the person will come into your world. You can also summon NPC's, depending on the choices you've made throughout the game. Covenants are basically clans you join. You will find more throughout your journey, and each covenant has a different effect. For example, Way of the Blue makes it so that anyone in the Blue Sentinels covenant will be able to help you if you end up getting invaded.
The atmosphere is great in Dark Souls, and it really makes you feel like as if you're part of the world. The atmosphere could be very spooky and dark if you're in the
but can be very lighthearted and welcoming if you meet some NPCs in the
. The environments are great. Unlike Bloodborne where while they were great environments everything felt the same. Dark Souls is not the case at all. In one environment you will be surronded by lava and fire while in the next you're in the catacombs. At one point you walk out of a boss room, only to be treated by a beautiful view of
.
Not much to say here, other than the fact that the music is amazing. Even the main menu has a great song that plays. The music can seriously set the mood and tone of a boss fight.
Boss fights are phenominal in Dark Souls. While the earlier bosses can be very easy (definitely not for new players to the franchise, but it very easily can be for anyone with a good understanding and execution of the mechanics), once you reach the
bosses can start to become more difficult. Boss fights are very creative though, and you will be bound to enjoy a few of them, regardless of difficulty. Boss fights are very unique and while some can be lackluster and dissapointing, they are still very creative. The boss fights are definitely one of the best aspects of this game, and I encourage everyone to beat every bosses, optional and non optional.

It runs well on both NVidia and AMD cards (from past experience). The PC version is truly the best way to experience Dark Souls 3. But is important to note that

Dark Souls 3 is a masterpiece and is an example of a near perfect RPG. If you're looking for a challenge, a game you can put tons of hours into, an RPG game, and/or one that is well crafted and put together, than Dark Souls 3 is the perfect game for you.

So this game is a masterpiece, but it's not for everyone, including many of the gamers you might think would enjoy it.
Darkest Dungeon is a difficult game, but its difficulty is in contrast to other challenging games. Take Dark Souls for example. That's a tough game which can require hours of attempts to beat a single boss. So you might think, "Well Dark Souls players will like Darkest Dungeon."
Not really. Dark Souls is challenging but it gives the player a huge amount of control to overcome that challenge. When you die in Dark Souls, it's pretty much your fault. You know what you did wrong. Usually at a mechanical rather than mental level.
Darkest Dungeon's difficulty is, however, on a mental level. Yes you need to master your mechanics, but it is entirely possible that you can prepare and play perfectly and STILL lose heroes.
Some players can't handle that. They're not wrong to get upset. It's basic game design that you should never force the player to fail even if they've done everything right. Such design would be madness.
Which is the very reason I call this a masterpiece. The game requires of the player the same thing the player require of his heroes: Mental fortitude even in the face of madness. If players do manage to persevere to the end (as I did), they'll find that - thematically speaking - this punishing game design is essential.
So it's a great game. Beautiful. Strategic. Addictive. Immense gothic / cosmic horror flavor, and a voice over up there with the likes of Bastion. But know what you're getting into. This game will test your resolve.
Bland, unoriginal and ultimately boring.

Darkest Dungeon oozes with style. The dungeons are dangerous, even your strongest character is at risk.  One dungeon takes usually 15-30 minutes, and so you can attempt a dungeon even if you don't have much time to play in the day.
You cannot save scum, so you won't get stuck in saving and reloading when you encounter unfavorable events (which you will). You have to live with your choices. Unless special circumstances take place, high level characters will refuse to enter lower level dungeons with low level characters, and so even lower level dungeons will continue to be threats.
There is a good variety of team compositions with the 15 different character types. Characters have different styles depending on where they stand in the 4-person formation. Forced movement abilities from your own characters and the enemies keep combat encounters varied. Bosses are unique from one another and cannot be beaten by the same strategy. Some team compositions will simply never work versus a particular boss.
Things can go badly instantly or can slowly creep up on you. Throughout the dungeon you can manage your risk by torchlight, brighter light, less risk, but also less reward. Mismanaging Stress can bring a halt to your dungeon attempt.
Critical hits not only sinks into your characters' health pools, but they also demoralize (increases stress) the team. The reverse is true too -- if your character hits a critical, they reduce stress for themselves and perhaps some of the team. You may have a healthy team, but if one teammember snaps, they can bring down the entire dungeon run (quest). Having to manage Health and Stress makes dungeoning unique to this game. Thankfully you keep what you've found, trinkets, heirlooms, and gold, from unsuccessful dungeon runs. However, your characters will not earn experience from failed dungeon runs and they still bring back their Stress, quirks, and diseases.
Out of dungeons you manage your small town, which serve as upgrade shops, recruiting station, and stress, quirk, and disease management. Your characters will develop both negative and positive quirks throughout the dungeoning as well as diseases. Characters with high stress are liabilities and will need to be managed in one of the stress-reducing buildings, Abbey or Tavern.
---
