I haven't put that many hours on the game yet, but I figure I can write a review about what I've seen so far.
Pros:
1) Excellent art style. Everything is interesting to look at.
2) Solid music. Not anything super special, but it's moody enough.
3) Satisfying sound effects. A little silly, maybe, but for me - sound goes a long way.
4) Playing with friends is different than playing solo -- as in levels adjust their difficulty slightly if you're playing by yourself. That doesn't mean you can breeze through everything if you just go solo all the time, but expect some levels to be more difficult when you have a team together.
5) The levels are slightly randomized, so when you have to play one level multiple times, it's not so tedious.
6) Though the game as the pay-to-win features, there are still ways to get around that - as the game allows you to use in game currency to purchase the real-money currency. While it still takes a long time, I appreciate not feeling so pressured to spend real money on a free-to-play game...though the rates of purchase can be a little extreme.
Cons:
1) This is a grind heavy game. And I mean grind HEAVY. You'll be playing levels over and over to get money, items, crystals, minerals, and whatever you need to upgrade your gear and your battle sprite (if you use one). While the game is enjoyable enough to take the sting off of it, I can acknowledge that this isn't something everyone will enjoy.
2) Also listed above -- the pay-to-win features. Some real cash and you can access the best of everything at earlier points in the game, leaving those of us who don't have money to spend left with hours of grinding. Not to mention that the game expects up to 40USD for things like armor and costumes, which is hefty for virtual items. Being able to circumnavigate this is good, but the rates can be painful. For example, I've spent something like six hours trying to get enough energy to purchase a key so that I can open a lockbox I got on a prizewheel. 100 Energy costs ~7500 crowns, and I'm getting about ~500 crowns per level run. It's time consuming and kind of annoying.
3) The game always seems to put you in the most crowded instance of Haven, which can lag out many computers with lower performances.
That's all I can think about for right now. It's an enjoyable game, I really like it, and I intend to keep playing it. I'd recommend it to anyone who enjoys this particular brand of game.

Overall, a great game that doesn't change that much from Enemy Unknown but really doesn't need to.
Tactically, the game is similar to its predecessor but introduces the nice Concealment mechanic that allows your squad to get the drop on the enemy in most missions, vastly improving the flow of the missions. You also have a lot of utility items to use, far more than in EU/EW, which greatly improves variety in combat. The difficulty (on Commander) is quite well balanced if you plan and execute carefully, and mostly stays consistent through the entire game while EU was hell at the start but became faceroll from the mid-game onwards.
Strategically, satellite spam is gone, and good riddance. Instead you choose which regions of the globe to expand to, albeit your progress is guided by the need to stop the alien's Avatar Project, which is their "win condition" so to speak; if you neglect it, you lose. This ends up working quite well as you allocate your limited time and ressources to best further your goals, especially early game where you have a lot of choice in which building to construct but not enough space for them all.
Complaints: Unfortunately, the game is prone to camera bugs, especially if you use the Action Camera. More frustratingly, it doesn't perform very well at all on my six core Phenom, R7 260x setup, having difficulty breaking above 30 FPS on medium settings with frequent dips below 20 and long-ish loading times. I expect better from a PC exclusive.
A lot of people have been complaining about timers, but I thought they were great, adding tension to every mission while still always giving you enough time. I literally never ran out of time even when my squad was getting battered. The only possible compromise I could see is stopping the timer until concealment is broken. Removing them outright whould change the game's design too much.
Hopefully Firaxis will patch those issues, because the core of the game is just amazingly fun, and the apparently extensive mod support will make it even better.
TLDR: buy it.

[EDIT: My computer crashes were proven to be unrelated, and the recent patch has fixed a TON of performance issues.  Disregard those issues in this review.]
An Andromedon punched my soldier so hard that my computer crashed.  10/10
[scroll down for pros/cons]
But seriously, this game does have quite a bit of poorly-optimized issues here and there, though there are guides on how to help mitigate that.  The most frequent are rather minor annoyances (camera freezing up during attacks, windows exploding before anything jumps through it/shoots it, bodies seeming to clip through floors) but I did have one bug that cost me a mission when an enemy was said to be in on space but nothing was there and AoE attacks did nothing.  I have had a couple of computer crashes while playing this (like the aformentioned one) but I can't confirm if it's XCOM 2's fault or simply having a sub-par processor/power supply.  Still, these kinds of bugs are not excusable on a major release with professional QA testers, and you should be cautious with your purchase until they are resolved.
Bugs aside, as those tend to be patched out later, the game is pretty solid.  If you'd played the original XCOM: Enemy Unknown and/or it's expansion you will find this game is basically just a hard mode for that, a really solid and really difficult hard mode but not TOO much different in terms of gameplay.  Stealth is a fun new addition to the game but I feel it is rather constrained by the missions themselves.  Since enemies are aware of all your troopers (save for rangers with a special ability) when you are spotted or event complete an objective on a mission it doesn't allow for a ton of all-stealth missions.  I can excuse that under the reason of it not earning you experience so but some more stealth options would have been delightful.
The game's main story is that you are trying to prevent the aliens from completing some project by sabotaging facilities and completing story missions, and to represent that is a story timer.  It can seem rather out-of-sight, out-of-mind in the early game as in order to sabotage any of those facilities you must perform a number of small tasks and gather a lot of resources in order to even GET to said facilities, but the sabotage missions themselves are laughably easy so it kinda evens out there I guess.  The timers that are more restrictive are the in-mission ones that seem ABUNDANTLY present; it heavily penalizes the old turtle strategy of crawling forward and using reaction shots on enemies, but also restricts their new stealth mechanic as it tends to rush you into ambushing just the first enemy group you see.  HOWEVER!!! If this feature bothers you, there are already mods up which lengthen the timers and some which remove them altogether, so I wouldn't let that be a purchase-making decision unless you are a puritan.
Pros (Cons)
+Increased difficulty through new enemy tactics / units rather than just increasing stats
++VERY weighty decision-making, even outside of combat (-can be kinda nullified by save-scumming [see below])
+++GREAT mod support on LAUNCH, to the point where it nullifies a lot of cons (-Not too many as of writing)
+Fantastic character customization, and in-game pregenerated units aren't too bad either (+/-?Can end up with multiple copies of the same trooper for some reason in-game)
+Intriguing story, gets rid of a lot of immersion-breaking faults of previous game's story (-Gets predictable at about the 60% mark but by then you're pretty into it)
+Improves the core gameplay of previous title a lot (-does not innovate too much aside from the stealth mechanic)
+Rich number of tactical options (--Hampered quite a bit by restrictive timers)
+/-Game autosaves VERY frequently, saving the last 3 turns in a mission and right before starting the mission (can encourage over-reliance on saves [can be turned off though])
+Great feel of running a resistance campaign against a superior foe
+Sequel does not require extensive knowledge of previous title but still is enjoyable for returning players
Verdict: Buy if you feel you're ready for a harsh challenge or love the theme/gameplay of it.  You can alter this game a LOT through the difficulty settings and mods alone so it'll have a good amount of replayability.  Look up a guide on how to mitigate current performance problems now if you do intend on buying it.

Overall, a great game that doesn't change that much from Enemy Unknown but really doesn't need to.
Tactically, the game is similar to its predecessor but introduces the nice Concealment mechanic that allows your squad to get the drop on the enemy in most missions, vastly improving the flow of the missions. You also have a lot of utility items to use, far more than in EU/EW, which greatly improves variety in combat. The difficulty (on Commander) is quite well balanced if you plan and execute carefully, and mostly stays consistent through the entire game while EU was hell at the start but became faceroll from the mid-game onwards.
Strategically, satellite spam is gone, and good riddance. Instead you choose which regions of the globe to expand to, albeit your progress is guided by the need to stop the alien's Avatar Project, which is their "win condition" so to speak; if you neglect it, you lose. This ends up working quite well as you allocate your limited time and ressources to best further your goals, especially early game where you have a lot of choice in which building to construct but not enough space for them all.
Complaints: Unfortunately, the game is prone to camera bugs, especially if you use the Action Camera. More frustratingly, it doesn't perform very well at all on my six core Phenom, R7 260x setup, having difficulty breaking above 30 FPS on medium settings with frequent dips below 20 and long-ish loading times. I expect better from a PC exclusive.
A lot of people have been complaining about timers, but I thought they were great, adding tension to every mission while still always giving you enough time. I literally never ran out of time even when my squad was getting battered. The only possible compromise I could see is stopping the timer until concealment is broken. Removing them outright whould change the game's design too much.
Hopefully Firaxis will patch those issues, because the core of the game is just amazingly fun, and the apparently extensive mod support will make it even better.
TLDR: buy it.

[EDIT: My computer crashes were proven to be unrelated, and the recent patch has fixed a TON of performance issues.  Disregard those issues in this review.]
An Andromedon punched my soldier so hard that my computer crashed.  10/10
[scroll down for pros/cons]
But seriously, this game does have quite a bit of poorly-optimized issues here and there, though there are guides on how to help mitigate that.  The most frequent are rather minor annoyances (camera freezing up during attacks, windows exploding before anything jumps through it/shoots it, bodies seeming to clip through floors) but I did have one bug that cost me a mission when an enemy was said to be in on space but nothing was there and AoE attacks did nothing.  I have had a couple of computer crashes while playing this (like the aformentioned one) but I can't confirm if it's XCOM 2's fault or simply having a sub-par processor/power supply.  Still, these kinds of bugs are not excusable on a major release with professional QA testers, and you should be cautious with your purchase until they are resolved.
Bugs aside, as those tend to be patched out later, the game is pretty solid.  If you'd played the original XCOM: Enemy Unknown and/or it's expansion you will find this game is basically just a hard mode for that, a really solid and really difficult hard mode but not TOO much different in terms of gameplay.  Stealth is a fun new addition to the game but I feel it is rather constrained by the missions themselves.  Since enemies are aware of all your troopers (save for rangers with a special ability) when you are spotted or event complete an objective on a mission it doesn't allow for a ton of all-stealth missions.  I can excuse that under the reason of it not earning you experience so but some more stealth options would have been delightful.
The game's main story is that you are trying to prevent the aliens from completing some project by sabotaging facilities and completing story missions, and to represent that is a story timer.  It can seem rather out-of-sight, out-of-mind in the early game as in order to sabotage any of those facilities you must perform a number of small tasks and gather a lot of resources in order to even GET to said facilities, but the sabotage missions themselves are laughably easy so it kinda evens out there I guess.  The timers that are more restrictive are the in-mission ones that seem ABUNDANTLY present; it heavily penalizes the old turtle strategy of crawling forward and using reaction shots on enemies, but also restricts their new stealth mechanic as it tends to rush you into ambushing just the first enemy group you see.  HOWEVER!!! If this feature bothers you, there are already mods up which lengthen the timers and some which remove them altogether, so I wouldn't let that be a purchase-making decision unless you are a puritan.
Pros (Cons)
+Increased difficulty through new enemy tactics / units rather than just increasing stats
++VERY weighty decision-making, even outside of combat (-can be kinda nullified by save-scumming [see below])
+++GREAT mod support on LAUNCH, to the point where it nullifies a lot of cons (-Not too many as of writing)
+Fantastic character customization, and in-game pregenerated units aren't too bad either (+/-?Can end up with multiple copies of the same trooper for some reason in-game)
+Intriguing story, gets rid of a lot of immersion-breaking faults of previous game's story (-Gets predictable at about the 60% mark but by then you're pretty into it)
+Improves the core gameplay of previous title a lot (-does not innovate too much aside from the stealth mechanic)
+Rich number of tactical options (--Hampered quite a bit by restrictive timers)
+/-Game autosaves VERY frequently, saving the last 3 turns in a mission and right before starting the mission (can encourage over-reliance on saves [can be turned off though])
+Great feel of running a resistance campaign against a superior foe
+Sequel does not require extensive knowledge of previous title but still is enjoyable for returning players
Verdict: Buy if you feel you're ready for a harsh challenge or love the theme/gameplay of it.  You can alter this game a LOT through the difficulty settings and mods alone so it'll have a good amount of replayability.  Look up a guide on how to mitigate current performance problems now if you do intend on buying it.

Perks and Skils are watered down and feel more like it's holding your hand than anything else. Item condition only applies to power armor. Overview
Xcom 2 Is a wonderful Turn Based Strategy game with elements of base building despite the few flaws it has. It is a lot more story driven and better written than the first xcom game. There are 5 different classes of soldiers and they are all fleshed out and none of them to me felt underpowered in any way. They have their uses and they come in handy.
,
but if you were to turn it down you should be fine (It still looks great at some of the lower graphics settings as I played through the game using those). There are time limits on SOME not all missions in order to discourage overwatch turtling. Playing aggressively is needed and In my opinion enhances the pacing of the game. Now your experience may vary with the difficulty because I played about 500 hours of the long war mod for Xcom Enemy within and had a good handle for the game and did not have a lot of trouble with it.
Note Just stating a fact: I used an integrated amd attached to the motherboard that put out about 768MB of video ram
Pros
+Effects and graphics are Amazing probably better if you can run it on max.
+Gameplay is facepaced and the strategy is deep
+More to base building than the last game
+A degree of precedural generation in map creation in order to keep things not dull.
+Wound timers seem to be more forgiving and missions are spaced out to keep the aliens from bulldozing you (atleast from my experience on veteran and I got 3 flawless missions out of the 37 that I did.
+ALL COVER IS DESTRUCTIBLE INCLUDING THE WALLS AND CEILING.
+A wider variety of missions available than the usual kill all the aliens and storm alien craft
+Tech Tree and costs are well balanced
+If you create something in the engineering department all of your soldiers get to use it. No more splashing ufos just to make one gun.
+Very well created atmosphere through great storytelling and gameplay
+The Classes all have their uses and specialities making them well fleshed out
Cons
-A few visual glitches when shooting at aliens
-Some hanging at the end of missions
-Hanging
-It won't work on low end computer but is to be expected out of a triple A title and might run slowly on some mid end rigs.
-Now I didn't like how you had to choose between 3 different guierlla missions to stop dark events (these buff the aliens if you don't stop them but they really aren't too deadly for you)
-I think the swords on rangers should have a bit more power to them in order to make them more appealing to use than just running up and blasting them with a shotgun. THEY STILL HAVE THEIR USES AND THEIR INCENTIVES TO USE THEM THOUGH
Final thoughts
If you like a challenging strategy game and liked xcom eu/ew and have a good setup then by all means BUY IT. WHY ARE YOU HESITATING? BUY IT!

A great entry, personally more enjoyable for me than II was, namely due to the enemy placement feeling a bit more fair.  Improvements include a return to some old form from the first Dark Souls.  Enemies won't just stop respawing because you want to grind an item drop or you just happen to suck like a certain writer called "me."  There aren't a limited number of the multiplayer items, the humanity or human effigy-equivalent, "embers."  Weapons don't degrade like they're made of paper mache.
Buuut, there might as well not be a weapon degredation system in the first place...I can count on one hand the number of times my claymore got below half durability in nearly 70 hours.  DS1's system was basically just busywork, but at least there were some chances to have weapons break.  DS2's was basically a big lazy glitch that the devs left.  And now they've basically rendered it a non-mechanic.
Does pyromancy suck or is it just me?  The requirements are so restrictive, removing a lot of the fun I had with it in DS1 since anyone could use it.
They have a serious infatuation with one-way doors, one-way doors
, making levels more linear than they should be because you can only open doors
and you will go through these levels the way they want you to and

Then there's the bonfire placement.  You can frequently find a bonfire literally within sight of another bonfire.  Often, they're a hallway away from each other with no enemies in between.  What were they thinking?  Were they thinking at all?
I may sound harsh, but overall I liked the level design.  Again, it feels more enjoyable to navigate this world than DS2 did, more of a return to form minus the occasionally janky levels from DS like Blighttown.  But this game feels like two steps forward, two steps back.  Dark Souls 1 had a genuinely organic-feeling, interconnected world, DS2 tried to do something similar, although it made considerably less geographic sense, and DS3 just didn't even try.  You're essentially jumping into worlds ala Mario 64, a far cry from the metroidvania-esque interconnecting level design the series had formerly aspired to.  Why make levels interconnect in sensible ways when we can just let them warp from firelink??  Rather, we don't want to invest the effort to design such a complex world, so let's just let them warp right away to save ourselves the effort.  So you can forget picking the master key as your starting item and exploring an area before you're "supposed to," since you get spoon-fed levels when when they darn well please.
I guess what I'm saying here is that the game itself?  Is fun.  The gameplay for me is a lot more fun and it feels better than DS2's did.  DS3 is a better (or at least more enjoyable) game from a very basic gameplay perspective.  The world is visually beautiful in a way that neither of the previous games can match.  But it is
derivative of DS1's story and lore, it doesn't even try to aspire to the level of world design previous games did, and it's still chock-full of design decisions (like the bonfires) that could only have been made while drunk.
A lot of these complaints you'd have no reason to care about if you've never played the previous games.  If you want to jump in, this is actually one of the best places to.  Multiplayer is still lively and this game has
co-op system in the series (as in, it's not completely broken without mods ala DS1).  But for fans of the series, you might get where I'm coming from--it reverses some design decisions that you may or may not have liked from 2, while adding new ones of its own, creating a competent game that fails to really bring anything new to the table for the series.

Ok let's get to the brass tacks: this game overall is better than 2012'a XCOM ever hoped to be. Non-linear game play, superb graphics, great soldier customization and the story/subplot is immersive and engaging. You'll be starting as a "guerilla" unit this time and so very often it feels and plays that way.
Now, the ONE hangup I have: the difficulty is brutal. No no, take what you THINK is hard, and multiply it by a factor of four. Remember starting or loading missions in XCOM because you lost one of your favorite soldiers? Forget it: you'll lose them and frequently, despite your best planning and efforts. That in and of itself isn't so bad, except that very often you'll be facing missions with massively under-experienced soldiers or find yourself on maps massively outnumbered. How massively? How's 16 enemies to four soldiers? And that's on NORMAL difficulty. I gave up on Veteran two hours and endless restarts into the game.
Should you buy it? Yes, it's as deep and good a turn-based strategy game as you'll ever play.
Should Firaxis have ever let it out of internal testing at this difficulty balance? No, never.

I have now pumped in several days of play before I wrote this review.
X Com 2 is a game that for me lived up to and exceeded expectations. Good story and the diffuclty is based on strategy rather then just gear now (yes I beat the game and didn't really start researching Mag Weapons and better armor until I was near the end. Had too many other important things to research), I beat the game with mostly Mag Weapons and heavy plasma in the end. Classes feel more useful now and better able to adapt to different play styles. Story was a shocker and has left me wondering just what I was doing in X Com 1.
I recommend the game for anyone who enjoyed X Com 1 and for those who enjoy the turn based strategy genre in general. I eagerly await the DLCs. *Thumbs up*
Pros:
* Expanded on a good framework for combat and fixed old problems with the turn based system.
* Good Unit Customization (Blows X Com 1's out of the water)
* Custom Units can be saved.
* Good balance between units and enemies, missions require a bit of care and strategy to win even on Easy.
* Psi Units are their own class and can become much more powerful compared to their X Com 1 counter parts.
Cons:
* Like all X Com Games: Difficulty ramps up fairly steadily and quickly.
* Some issues with lower end machines, my recommendation is take the recommended specs and add 2gb to the RAM.
* No 'Second Wave' options (Hopefully will be brought back soon)
* (Wasn't for me but I know some people didn't like this) Psi Units are their own class, you can't promote another class into Psi.

While there, there are objects you can inspect for loot, but it's ultimately pointless because 20% they're empty, 70% there's a trap, and 10% of the time there's actually some sort of mediocre reward waiting. You also fight groups of disgusting beasts or menacing undead/bandits in a turn-based setting.
One of the main mechanics of the game is stress. At 100 stress you gain afflictions that basically make your characters destroy themselves. Of course, this usually happens to all 4 of your pathetic underpowered characters at once, so you have to sit there and wait for them to take damage everytime they are about to take a turn. Pretty fun. Not. At 200 stress your character has a heart attack and dies. Stress is something that is ultimately dealt to you 10x more than it could ever be healed in battle. You gain about 20 stress per hit eventually, and the developers throw a big ♥♥♥♥ you in your face by giving you petty skills that heal 3-6 stress. Yes, let me spend 3 turns healing that 20 stress while I gain it 3x over. How about no, go ♥♥♥♥ yourself. Of course, you can heal your stress by basically incapacitating your characters until the next mission is over, and you must pay a lump sum of cash to do so. This is cash that you probably won't have because you need to grind for it. You'll find yourself investing gold in characters and then watching them die because of the unfair gameplay mechanics. Eventually you will be totally broke and unable to heal any stress or buy food, torches, etc (which are necessary). That's where this game really excels: stressing the player out.
The thing that really peeves me the most, is that even if you are smart about how you play, the enemy usually is 2x faster than you, and they hit the same, if not more damage than you do. All characters have about 8 skills in total and you must pick 4 to use in battle. Most of these are terrible. They have horrible damage modifiers, so you are mostly stuck using the same two skills. On top of that the RNG is almost never in your favor. You will find yourself hitting in the lower half of the damage range of your already-weak skills most of the time. Because of this, utility skills usually don't proc their debuff, so you just wasted a turn. Yet another ♥♥♥♥ you from the developers.The game gives you hardly any reward. It only punishes you.
I could go on and on about what's wrong with this game and the horrible design choices that were made, but now I'm going to discuss some good things about the game:
The narrator's voice. Yep. that's it.
Can I have my $20 back? Please? The amount of stress this game generates will probably give you a heart attack. Thankfully, I stopped playing the game at 100 stress, where I began to suffer from severe disappointment, intense regret, and a really sore ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ from getting ♥♥♥♥ed so hard. lol. Seriously though, don't buy this ♥♥♥♥ing game. I'd rather do jumping jacks in an iron maiden than play this.

Wow, just wow... I've been a Darkest Dungeon lurker since the kickstarter days. I didn't think they'd pull it off in such an appealing way. This game is the quintessential rpg dungeon crawler with a twist that puts you on the edge of your seat EVERY time you prep to dive into the dungeons. I don’t care how many times you think you’ve got it, your fate is an RNG away from total destruction, or total success, OR success by a slim margin, OR FAILURE by a slim margin. The game is so appealing in every way; it’s addicting, it makes you think before you move, it entertains you at EVERY turn, and no matter how mad you get, you keep coming back for more. The combat is somewhat repetitive at lower levels, but once you level your characters, more options become available to choose from. The dungeons are limiting as well, but you level them, and they progressively get harder. I’m hoping that DLC in the future will add more. Finally, the events that were added creates an additional layer of things that could go right AND things that could go wrong.
If you want a game to blaze through, and get to the end in hours, then this is not for you. If you want a challenging experience, full of depth, atmosphere, and a voice commentator that puts it through the roof (admittedly, if the voice over wasn’t there, I actually drop it to 9/10 stars… yeah, it’s THAT good), then Darkest Dungeon is what you’ve been waiting for.

Mechanics- RNG, RNG, a roll of the dice decides your fate (in a fantastic old school D&D kind of way)

VOICE OVER – not near perfect… PERFECT.

To be honest, when I was looking for a new game to play and saw this one, I wanted to buy it. At first, I was scared because of all the reviews and about how difficult the game is. Yet, I still bought it and I enjoy the game.
Now about the RNG everyone complains about. This game is not for people that can't stand facing bad "luck" or easily get upset losing a well trained party, character or items. It happens, and people blame it on RNG. You WILL face a monster that crits you multiple times in a row, you WILL face a monster that dodges 3 of your team's attacks, you WILL fail that escape and face a team wipe. But it could turn your way too, you could double crit monsters, evade all their attacks, open a chest that has a pretty good trinket and clear the dungeon. People don't realize that everything doesn't turn out their way, you can't expect the game to just give you that needed crit or dodge. Depending on RNG to win for you isn't a good feeling or even entertainment for most people. Pushing your luck is guaranteed to result in a bad ending.
On to the trinkets and rewards.
Yes, I do agree that some of the items you can get in the game are useless, but only some. Most every item has a good effect paired along with a bad effect, some way too negative, or even a trinket that has no negative effects. It sorta reminds of Team Fortress 2 items, And speaking of which, you need trinkets that fit your playstyle and character. Doing this will boost the positive side of the character and minimize the negative side. Equipping a random item you think is good, could do more harm to you than having no trinket. It's all about balance, and some trinkets can completely reduce the bad side effects of your other trinket.
As for the talk about stress damage, it is a bit harsh. It's harder to heal than physical damage and can be a pain if someone goes crazy because of it. (Or becomes a OP from that chance of virtue)
Pros:
+Unique (stress management)
+Customization, from characters, to skills, to items
+A bit suspenseful (interactive objects, unexplored places)
+Cool Mechanics (torch light, obstacles, character quirks)
+Voice acting, sets a very ominous tone
+Character development.
+Kinda addicting despite RNG
Cons:
-Need to learn how to overcome challenges quickly (gold, stress, upgrades, etc.)
-Has more RNG than most games
-Stress damage a little high or atleast the affliction cap
-Story is not too appealing, could use some work
-Not for players that get frustrated easily
-Somewhat Forced playstyle, some parties/character combinations would get utterly destroyed
All in all, its a good game, and if you're like me and don't care about money, you could buy this game if it interests you. Don't chicken out because of some RNG, unless you're one of those people

Dark Souls is what happens when a developer gets tired of making the game easy so that everyone can play it. Yes, Dark Souls is hard. It's also fair and when you get the hang of the combat system, it's incredibly rewarding. This is about when you get cocky and think you have this game figured out. It has no problem putting you in your place, reminding you that you need to stay on your toes.
The enemies at the beginning killed me so many times. The first boss was impossible for me until I watched someone else beat him. The boss at the beginning is the basics. Pay attention to the enemy and how they move. Do not be overly aggressive. DODGE. Learn how to position yourself in relation to your enemy, their weapon, and where they swing. The combat in this game is all about timing and paying attention. There are many different enemy types, and they're all pretty different. Learn their tells, preferably by playing it safe and paying attention versus dying a thousand times.
Anyway, that's my rant. Here's my breakdown:
Graphics: Stunning. This is a beautiful game with a lot of atmosphere. Excellent enemy designs, particle effects, lighting, textures, models... everything. It's beautiful.
Sound: There's some great music in Dark Souls. Sound effects are spot on.
Gameplay: Difficult. Everything in this game must be done with intention. I'm pretty sure this game can tell when you button mash, and it'll punish you with a quick death. That being said, learning the gameplay is incredibly rewarding. People don't love this game because it's hard, they love it because they get good at it and it feels good.
Story: Intentionally ambiguous, dark, and sad. If you're looking for something happy or uplifting, look elsewhere.
Overall: There is a lot to learn in this game. Weapon and attack types, spells, leveling up your character, techniques, enemies, level designs, hidden areas... there is a lot. Stick with it and you will be rewarded. Give up, and join the legions of gamers who couldn't do it.
Side note: Dark Souls 1 and 2 are definitely worth picking up, although it doesn't seem like you need to have played them before Dark Souls 3. I watched a "summary of Dark Souls 1 and 2" and that was probably good enough.

A Spoiler Free Review
I make reviews of games I purchase, especially the games that I spent in excess of 10 hours getting my fix of caffene and explosions. *grips his coffee mug like a crack addict*
I prefer to put my reviews in "Overview", "The Good" "The Bad" and "Conclusion" format.
Overview
The hype train was going full steam and the breaks were carefully removed and discarded with scorn. Leading up to this game, we had heard amazing things and this was the very first time I have ever heard of a community largely accepting a studio's decision to postpone launch by 3 months. Partially, I think, because they actually delivered on time. The first X Com made by this studio was generally accepted as a worthy remake of the original game (though some purists felt too much was lost and too little was gained), and this particular game stood up to the behemoth that was X-Com 2:Terror from the deep. It released on time with a bizzare release schedule that no one understood (and many people bypassed with scorn thanks to VPN clients)
and I, just starting my vacation between contracts, dedicated way too many waking hours to it and ruined my sleep schedule as a result.
Disclaimer: I pre-ordered this game. I don't know anyone who worked on it.
The Good: There is a LOT to list here. It's graphically beautiful and it's pretty clear the art team attacked the challenges of making this game like a rabid dog. I will have to separate this section out so it's not a wall of text.
Gameplay: The devs had a working mechanic and they stuck to it. Taking examples from the previous game and expanding on them in a huge way. There are many more powers that involve multi-round effects, many old powers have been toned down while new ones really make things interesting on a whole new level. The new classes are very diverse and work differently (mostly) from their old counterparts. The only one which feels and plays roughly the same is the Sharpshooter, though you won't have an "In the Zone" map cleaner like you did in the past... sorry folks. Needless to say, even on normal mode the game was a challenge, the enemy has WAY more toys at their disposal and it makes for a far more dynamic game. Psionics are handled amazingly and are a LOT of fun
The Story: We all know the basis of the game is "you lost the first game bad, this is the result". The story had me gripped and wondering, and considering the last several games I tried to play had utterly horrible plots, this was like cracking open a lovecraftian novel after reading childrens stories. The mystery kept on going right to the very end. The writers deserve a lot of credit.
The Enemies: Wow. Every time a new alien enemy appeared my response was a mix of "Holy ♥♥♥♥ that looks awesome" to "Oh god I am gonna die." While there are a few aspects that are repeated (andromedan walking animation is the same as the muton walking animation), they all are strikingly unique and all require different tactics to defeat. You will have moments of awe and horror right up to the very end (at least I did). The Elite Muton Day 1 mod was the least inspiring of the new enemies and still looked amazing, so that should tell you something about how impressive the foes are.
The Base/World map: The layout of the base and world map are very similar on the surface and familiar to anyone who played the previous game, but there are critical differences. Your 'base' is randomly placed at the start of the game and you spend very little time there. Your mothership flies around the world from location to location instead of launching from home base. You don't intercept UFO's, THEY INTERCEPT YOU (providing one of the most intense combat situations I ever experienced in the game). Managing the several layers of ticking time bombs, any of which could end your game if not handled right, is a big part of the game as well. You need to ration your time at the start of game and be careful how you use it.
Day 1 Mods: These were fun on the whole. You don't gain much from the Elite Muton aside from a more heavily armored Muton with a fancy helmet, but I don't see any reason to turn it off. The Leader mod I didn't get much of a chance to experience but I probably will in my second play through, but new abilities are always fun and they are all just as diverse and intuitive as the ones found normally in the game. The SMG pack is EASILY the best of the three though, providing a set of great looking items that work in a very unique way and are beautifully integrated into the game. I recommend all of them.
The Bad
Interface: Buttons are tiny, sometimes difficult to select, and if you get impatient you may end up activating the wrong power. When you have large numbers of abilities you run out of keybindings across the top of the keyboard and manual power selection can be tedious.
Slowdown: Yeah this happens a lot. I don't think it's my computer (it's a beast, even if it's 3 years old). I wonder if this is something related to the game as a bug. When slowdown happens, either in loading screens or between powers, it can annoy the hell out of you.
Camera and targetting:I think we all know this. The targetting is a little clunky for area effect weapons and the camera loves to screw with us. It may just be a fact of the engine at this point.
X-Ray vision: Some enemies and even your own troops sometimes can see foes that have complete cover (no LOS at all), and shoot through the wall (or even their own bodies) to get at you. Probably will be patched but it can be annoying as hell.
Bugs: Yeah it has a fair few, it makes you wonder what bugs existed before to require three months of fixes before release. The most annoying one by far is the corrupted save file bug, I had one happen to me on the last mission. Nerd rage.
Conclusion: This game is amazing, and was worth the pre order. If people will criticize it for basically being a remake of the first game, then holy hell they did a great job. The ending was great for setting up the next game/dlc, and we have two upcoming DLC packs to look foreward to.
Final Score: Happy to have bought it and sperglorded over/10.

This is also a game where you yourself determine how much your players can take. That means if you have the highest level soldier with all of the best upgrades and skills, he doesn't become invincible, regardless of his stats. Short View:
Some bugs, if you want 60 FPS everywhere, you might want to wait.
Details
-/+This game is hard; harder than EU/EW
-/+This game is faster in both areas
+The combat is more intense
+More customization
+Mods
--Bugs
XCOM 2 is a strategy game developed by Firaxis, the developers of Civilization. Most of the game is played in the turn based tactical combat portion with you commanding between 4 to 6 soldiers against numerically superior and technologically superior (at least in the beginning) aliens. However you must also develop a long term strategy and research new weapons and armor in the strategic portion. The strategy portion is “real-time” and careful management in both sections is required for success.
XCOM 2 is descended from Firaxis’ XCOM Enemy Unknown and Enemy Within remakes rather than the original XCOM. I have played XCOM EU/EW and I thoroughly enjoyed EU/EW. The games were hard but quite doable if you had patience to learn the mechanics. XCOM 2 is somewhat harder in the missions, the enemies, and especially the pacing.
The pacing in EU/EW was slow and methodical. The pacing felt right for those games and the optimal strategy was to carefully inch your way across the battlefield by overwatching every few steps. XCOM 2 is built to make you move quickly through a level. From the greatly despised mission timers to many enemy abilities, you are constantly forced out of the slow and methodical crawl and into a run. Enemies can easily disrupt your soldiers hiding behind cover and draw them out. This is exacerbated by the timers which ensure you must work at a brisk pace. Thematically this makes sense (you are a resistance movement that is on the run), and I believe that it can work, but increasing the amount of time on many missions would make the experience better. I often had to rush, which may be unthinkable to XOCM EU/EW veterans.
Frankly I used a mod to increase the timers; removing the timers is another mod, but I believe this removes a crucial piece of the game.
Combat is incredibly fun and intense. Each of the classes has been reworked and there are far more options available in combat. In this portion of the game, XCOM plays incredibly well. There are so many scenarios. Do I want to use up one of my grenades and shred this MEC’s armor? Should I try to break this wall and flank another enemy? When XCOM 2’s combat starts, you are drawn into XCOM’s seemingly hopeless struggle for survival.  You’ll cry in frustration as the RNG gods curse you and your soldier misses a target right in front of them with a 97% hit chance and you’ll gasp in surprise as your sniper manages to nail that enemy on overwatch from halfway across the map to save your bacon.
For XCOM EU/EW veterans, there are quite a few changes to the basic mechanics. One very noteworthy feature is the reworked overwatch system. Now your soldiers will fire sequentially and all your overwatches won’t be wasted on a single sectoid that charges you. This works very well and entire pods can be mopped up in a single turn. Another change is the initial concealment phase in many missions. In this phase, your soldiers are “hidden” and you can supposedly set up ambushes. However the rushed nature of many of these missions often caused me to rush into pods and ruin this advantage before I could set up a good ambush. When it works, it is a beautiful sight as your squad mows down 1-2 pods of enemies.
In terms of customization, this game is much better than EU/EW. You’ll spend a lot of time dressing up your soldiers and their weapons. There are also many more tactically benefiting items that can be applied and most importantly, there are no clear advantages between light/medium/heavy armor suits. You can change out armor without worrying about reducing your HP enormously.
One of the biggest gripes that many people have with this game other than the timers is the performance. This game looks fine graphically; it isn’t amazing, but it isn’t bad either. However it can run terribly as some graphical options are for the future and some are plainly badly optimized. The max graphics options includes 8X MSAA. This will reduce the FPS enormously regardless of the power of your rig. This option should have been added in a later patch or maxed out at 2-4X with an option to set 8X. Vsync, and Ambient Occlusion are actually badly optimized. The Vsync can cause many issues when the game drops below 45 FPS and simply locks the game at 30 FPS. Loading can be excessive if you do not have a SSD. In fact if you have a HDD, you are simply out of luck and will have to suffer through jarring stuttering and long (2-3 minute) load times. My final note regarding performance is the hanging and slow down for calculations form environmental destruction and alien turns. Many times the action will stop for 3-6 seconds as a single enemy decides what it is going to do. Whenever you blow up any walls, there will be extreme slow down and loss of FPS.
Overall, I do not regret buying this game and would recommend buying this title despite the bugs.  The gameplay is simply that good. If you definitely want 60 FPS at every location then you might want to wait for a patch. The timers are easily addressed by mods.

Everything that went wrong with EU was fixed and improved in XC2.
The good:
-The new story setting suits way better the gameplay, the hindrances and hardships of working as rebel force, .
-The modding should be the star of this game, it's open, free and encouraged (if you tried to mod EU you will remember what a pain it was); and some problems i found are already being "solved" by modders.
-The new classes are awesome and well balanced.
-Customization is pretty fun, including the ability of previously creating the pool of characters.
-The random maps are better and, well, random. While in EU the maps were all the same, they were also HUGE, meaning that sometimes you would waste a LOT of time LOOKING for that solo alien that was hidding, the maps now are smaller (but not too small) and the objectives are more clear.
-The new enemies look more "serious" and better designed.
-A nice set of missions variations.
-Weapon modding.
-Starting the game concealed is fun, but don't think this is Metal Gear, don't simply sneak throught aliens, or you WILL end up flanked.
-No more "satellite rush".
The Bad:
-Its VERY hard. When some reviews said that the game was too hard i thought it was an exageration, but after a few battles i saw that this game major problem is actually the balance, betwen easy and veteran (normal) there is a HUGE diference in dificult, while easy is a walk in the park, Normal is hell : full cover is useless for you, you will find 2 or 3 times more enemies in the field,encounter top tier enemies even before researching a better armor, all of this with a timer against you. While this would be a deal breaker for me, once again, the world was saved by modders, with mods like Better aim, More time and more units in the field, Normal dificult is actually pretty much playable.
-I'm missing the huge mecha units, but knowing how popular they were in the EU (EW) i assume Firaxis is going to launch them in a DLC, but while it's just a guess, i'll treat this as a mistake.
-The new management system get time to get used too, it's overwhelming for some time, and i don't really enjoyed it, too many things happening at once and it takes a lot of time to actually progress in items.
As you can see, there are way better things than bad in this game, while the bads are sure an hindrance, they are easily fixed by mods.
This is a game that i surely will be playing for some years.

Wow, just wow... I've been a Darkest Dungeon lurker since the kickstarter days. I didn't think they'd pull it off in such an appealing way. This game is the quintessential rpg dungeon crawler with a twist that puts you on the edge of your seat EVERY time you prep to dive into the dungeons. I don’t care how many times you think you’ve got it, your fate is an RNG away from total destruction, or total success, OR success by a slim margin, OR FAILURE by a slim margin. The game is so appealing in every way; it’s addicting, it makes you think before you move, it entertains you at EVERY turn, and no matter how mad you get, you keep coming back for more. The combat is somewhat repetitive at lower levels, but once you level your characters, more options become available to choose from. The dungeons are limiting as well, but you level them, and they progressively get harder. I’m hoping that DLC in the future will add more. Finally, the events that were added creates an additional layer of things that could go right AND things that could go wrong.
If you want a game to blaze through, and get to the end in hours, then this is not for you. If you want a challenging experience, full of depth, atmosphere, and a voice commentator that puts it through the roof (admittedly, if the voice over wasn’t there, I actually drop it to 9/10 stars… yeah, it’s THAT good), then Darkest Dungeon is what you’ve been waiting for.
PROS
Amazing atmosphere – they nailed the genre
Gameplay – amazingly complex yet easy to handle
Graphics – SPOT on, for what it is, it’s near perfect
Mechanics- RNG, RNG, a roll of the dice decides your fate (in a fantastic old school D&D kind of way)
Sound – see graphics
VOICE OVER – not near perfect… PERFECT.
CONS
Really looking forward to more dungeons and more variations of monsters and ghouls, if this initial release is evidence to the creativity of the developers, then we’re in for a treat.

This pool allows you to have characters you created already available to hire in the armory or even as a part of the starting squad. To be honest, when I was looking for a new game to play and saw this one, I wanted to buy it. At first, I was scared because of all the reviews and about how difficult the game is. Yet, I still bought it and I enjoy the game.
Now about the RNG everyone complains about. This game is not for people that can't stand facing bad "luck" or easily get upset losing a well trained party, character or items. It happens, and people blame it on RNG. You WILL face a monster that crits you multiple times in a row, you WILL face a monster that dodges 3 of your team's attacks, you WILL fail that escape and face a team wipe. But it could turn your way too, you could double crit monsters, evade all their attacks, open a chest that has a pretty good trinket and clear the dungeon. People don't realize that everything doesn't turn out their way, you can't expect the game to just give you that needed crit or dodge. Depending on RNG to win for you isn't a good feeling or even entertainment for most people. Pushing your luck is guaranteed to result in a bad ending.
On to the trinkets and rewards.
Yes, I do agree that some of the items you can get in the game are useless, but only some. Most every item has a good effect paired along with a bad effect, some way too negative, or even a trinket that has no negative effects. It sorta reminds of Team Fortress 2 items, And speaking of which, you need trinkets that fit your playstyle and character. Doing this will boost the positive side of the character and minimize the negative side. Equipping a random item you think is good, could do more harm to you than having no trinket. It's all about balance, and some trinkets can completely reduce the bad side effects of your other trinket.
As for the talk about stress damage, it is a bit harsh. It's harder to heal than physical damage and can be a pain if someone goes crazy because of it. (Or becomes a OP from that chance of virtue)
Pros:
+Unique (stress management)
+Customization, from characters, to skills, to items
+A bit suspenseful (interactive objects, unexplored places)
+Cool Mechanics (torch light, obstacles, character quirks)
+Voice acting, sets a very ominous tone
+Character development.
+Kinda addicting despite RNG
Cons:
-Need to learn how to overcome challenges quickly (gold, stress, upgrades, etc.)
-Has more RNG than most games
-Stress damage a little high or atleast the affliction cap
-Story is not too appealing, could use some work
-Not for players that get frustrated easily
-Somewhat Forced playstyle, some parties/character combinations would get utterly destroyed
All in all, its a good game, and if you're like me and don't care about money, you could buy this game if it interests you. Don't chicken out because of some RNG, unless you're one of those people

This review is based solely on Battleye.
.:TL;DR:.
If you have a history of not being able to access multiplayer or mandated internet singleplayer parts of games due to Battleye, this game will be no different.
If you've played Insurgency or CS:GO and faced the dreaded and non-fixable "VAT" issue, this game will be worse.
However, if you've never experienced the problem, then you might like the gameplay. It's a mix between Dirty Bomb and CS.
.:End TL;DR:.
Many FPS games love using Battleye as their anti-cheat client for some reason.
Maybe it's cheaper than other anti-cheat software on the market?
Maybe it's more flexible?
Maybe the offer handy's in exchange for the publicity?
We may never know.
What many of us DO know is how game breaking Battleye is.

Excellent game with fresh elements of roleplaying.
Guide your bunch of desperate adventures through horrific dungeons and darkest woods, fight, hack, stun and kill your enemies, watch them losing their minds over the abominations they will meet and the horrific scenes they will encounter.
Grab as much loot as you can but keep in mind that your inventory has to hold also rations, keys and ingredients of various sorts, because you will need them to help your group through hell and back. After each mission you will face the results of sever traumas that your group has to deal with. Level up and increase your chances by buying improvements for the coach that brings new characters, the gipsy trinket dealer, the guilde, the ranger, the sanitarium, the smith and so on....
The gameplay might be looking repetitive, and to some degree it is. But it will open you hundreds of different ways how to get to the end, allow you to create differently composed adventurer groups again and again and find out step by step, who your true heroes are.
I am playing RPGs since my childhood but this one is so different in a very good way, so much fun and so nicely set with respect to sound and scenery (Edgar Allen Poe would have loved it), that you will be positively surprised.

Combat in XCOM 2 is nothing like XCOM: Enemy Unknown. The problem is when you buy the game assuming that it is.
The first game was relatively simple by comparison, concentrating on a sturdy two-action tactical system with a manageable number of special abilities on both sides; this ensured that for the normal player, the game was always about movement and positioning. You were always playing for those flanking shots or using a highly limited means of getting through cover.
XCOM 2 is overwrought and utterly overbearing. Although the general thrust of the tactical game is visually recogniseable, the manner in which it now plays is not. Emphasis now falls on overpowered special abilities, with the positional gameplay of XCOM: EU consigned to the bin by endless timers that force you into ugly engagements with enemies that are themselves increasingly overpowered, thus also forcing you into honing down your strategy into the most brutal spam of special abilities possible in a single turn, because you will be effortlessly one or two-shotted in many cases by aliens if you leave any of them able to retaliate.
To finally hammer this tactless, ability spamming manner of gameplay directly into your face, mid to late game enemies become heavily armoured enough to take little damage to their fat health sack without said armour being 'shredded' by explosives (or a single gun ability available on the class that deals with all the explosives). You don't outmaneuver aliens in XCOM 2 in order to get that golden flanking shot, you simply destroy the entire area with a squad consisting 50% of grenadiers. Every single time. Anything left alive is now 'flanked' due to cover having all been destroyed, which usually doesn't matter because you'll be throwing out other cover-ignoring abilities to kill, shut down, or infallibly misdirect aliens (mimic grenades, notably) to ensure that their own spam of devastating special abilities doesn't slaughter your team like yours did to them.
And to punch that ability spamming nail into your face for insult, lots of later enemies don't even use cover and have built-in defence bonuses that replicate it anyway, then the game sprinkles on the new passive ability of dodging for some enemies, so regular shots that manage to hit can STILL end up being ablated into uselessness. That'll teach you for trying to do something normal, like just fire a gun, like an XCOM: EU scrub. Use psionic death rifts or grenades with no accuracy needed next time, loser, now get out while I sell the rights to Michael Bay.
The strategic layer of the game is immaculate, being a well balanced challenge of resources in its own right, unlike the simply inevitable grind of the original game. Added to this is a more extensive and genuinely engaging plot which is, quite frankly, the only reason I'm going to finish this game. Unfortunately, the extremely short amount of time I'm spending talking about the strategic layer is indicative of how much it saves the game next to the profoundly unpleasant combat.
In the end, this game was made for the vocal fanbase that played the Long War mod. It's made for people who write off poorly conceived, arbitrarily punishing, and frustrating gameplay with 'lolXCOM' meme garbage. It's made for people like BeagleRush who spend their time powergaming a system in order to crush it. It is electronic sadism for gameplay masochists, with really nothing else to offer anyone who never wanted to play that game.
XCOM 2 cannot be recommended in the slightest as being an intrinsically enjoyable process. it's not fun to simply *play the game*. It's not like picking up Dragon's Dogma and having a blast running around and climbing on every giant monster you can see because it's just plain fun. XCOM 2 is about winning. That is the enjoyment. The actual gameplay is a relentless barrage of overbearing horses**t and the only 'fun' to be had is climbing atop that pile of s**t in order to feel victorious.
Do you want to play that game? Maybe. Plenty do, it seems.
I sure as hell don't.

You're required to choose a group, and slaughter the rest - including the friends you made in the other groups.  There's no option to say "Hey, I'm leaving your group. I'm honestly not sure whether I should reccomend this or not.
It is extremely well made - the music is exciting, the sound, dialogue, and voice acting is great, and it has an amazing visual style.
It is challenging but actually fairly balanced IMO - once you know a general good structure for a team and the the bad luck that usually crops up in different places then things will become a lot less random. The first few runs will be a gong show while you are figuring things out though. As will the first time in a new area, or with a new team, or after leveling up, or against a boss . . .
This is kind of why I am not sure about reccomending it - the struggle is real and constant.  Usually you get 'better' as you play a game - you have new skill, or the game gives you better weapons etc. In DD your team gradually levels up and at a certain point are too 'skilled' to run easier dungeons. Suddenly your 'A Team' absolutely sucks and you are getting out by just the skin of your teeth.
On the one hand, this keeps the challenge up - you need to find new stategies and group configurations and there is always that anxiety about entering a dungeon.  Characters have a set suite of skills and can only be leveled up so much and even high level items seem to have some crippling negitive aspects along with the good.
On the other hand, while you continue to achieve more difficult and amazing tasks, it is not actually satisfying. I would come to dread my characters leveling up. Most of the time I felt like a stressed out HR manager trying to fill vacancies.
This was probably intentional though - the whole game is a bit of a commentary on what 'adventuring' would be like in the real world. Having to go out in the dark  and murder a bunch of horrible monsters would actually suck quite a bit wouldn't it?
You know what - I'm going to reccomend this. It is something different and even if I didn't actually 'enjoy' it , it definitely had me thinking about it long after I was done a session.

Dark Souls 3. The very first Dark Souls I've ever played. Combat is fast and fluid. There is a variety of classes to choose from. I started with a Mercenary with the dual twinblades. The soundtrack is memorable. Regular enemies hit like a truck. Mini-boss like mobs hit like a bullet train and sometimes hits harder than the actual bosses. The bosses are difficult as well. They are aggressive and they can melt your face. You will die a lot, I mean A LOT! You may lose your souls and you will rage like never before. Git gud and you'll eventually beat all the bosses, even the optional ones.
Single-player is an overall fun experience. I plan to reach NG+7 with my DEX + Faith build twinblades character.
Multiplayer on the other hand is a mixed experience. Things can go both ways. You're the Embered Host, you can get invaded by players who hide behind a mob of enemies. You die, lose your ember, and you have to pick up your souls before dying again. There are some invaders who will fight you 1v1 but you won't see that often. When I'm the invader, I want to fight 1v1 (note: an honorable invader will win less than half of the time). I see a Host with 2 phantoms and a blue guy and I would get smeared across the floor and all of them would point down on me. My worst invasion experience is when I enter the world of hackers who would do crazy things to me like picking me up and throwing me like a rock, the hacker that brings a message "Humanity is Stolen" and I have to look it up because I didn't know what it means and I haven't played any other souls games.
If you have the DLCs, you can have a pvp arena where you can fight fair with other dualist.
I also like to help out other players beat bosses. I like to camp and wait for people to summon me to fight the really hard bosses. I also co-op with my brother and I can say co-op is pretty fun.
Overall, I like this game.

Dark Souls is what happens when a developer gets tired of making the game easy so that everyone can play it. Yes, Dark Souls is hard. It's also fair and when you get the hang of the combat system, it's incredibly rewarding. This is about when you get cocky and think you have this game figured out. It has no problem putting you in your place, reminding you that you need to stay on your toes.
The enemies at the beginning killed me so many times. The first boss was impossible for me until I watched someone else beat him. The boss at the beginning is the basics. Pay attention to the enemy and how they move. Do not be overly aggressive. DODGE. Learn how to position yourself in relation to your enemy, their weapon, and where they swing. The combat in this game is all about timing and paying attention. There are many different enemy types, and they're all pretty different. Learn their tells, preferably by playing it safe and paying attention versus dying a thousand times.
Anyway, that's my rant. Here's my breakdown:
Graphics: Stunning. This is a beautiful game with a lot of atmosphere. Excellent enemy designs, particle effects, lighting, textures, models... everything. It's beautiful.
Sound: There's some great music in Dark Souls. Sound effects are spot on.
Gameplay: Difficult. Everything in this game must be done with intention. I'm pretty sure this game can tell when you button mash, and it'll punish you with a quick death. That being said, learning the gameplay is incredibly rewarding. People don't love this game because it's hard, they love it because they get good at it and it feels good.
Story: Intentionally ambiguous, dark, and sad. If you're looking for something happy or uplifting, look elsewhere.
Overall: There is a lot to learn in this game. Weapon and attack types, spells, leveling up your character, techniques, enemies, level designs, hidden areas... there is a lot. Stick with it and you will be rewarded. Give up, and join the legions of gamers who couldn't do it.
Side note: Dark Souls 1 and 2 are definitely worth picking up, although it doesn't seem like you need to have played them before Dark Souls 3. I watched a "summary of Dark Souls 1 and 2" and that was probably good enough.

I like the most the fact that we have a voice acted protagonist, for which I were more than fine with sacrificing dialogue options for. I do feel the dialogue options in fallout 3 were a tad overwhelming and didnt always impact your gameplay as much, really didnt go well with the silent treatmet.
They improved the gun mechanics soooo much, almost a FPS quality level, very nice with the gun modifications, i appreciate that they removed weapon degredation.

The graphics are alright, its not as 'wow' as what fallout 3 was when it came out, but cmon people, us who played  previous fallout games obviously dont mind it, since yes, it was a bit dissapointing, but its not supposed to be the main concentration of the game, go play a single pathed AAA Title like metro last light if you care so much about the looks (dont compare fallout 4 to witcher 3 because then you'll be even more dissapointed)

My problem with this early-access game in particular is the customer experience. There has been mutliple occasions where the Chucklefish developpers, out of frustration, have censored criticism, banned people for no reason, and all around been insulting to everyone.
First of all, the developpers never interact with the Steam boards. The only time they did since December release actually, was when one of their coders had a meltdown and decided to ban dozens of people for no reason at all other than what was fair and unloaded criticism about the game.That was before the same coder insulted another user, calling her mentally ill before editing his post and eventually apologizing if people had their jimmies rustled.
Second, the game was sold as a beta. It's not. 6 months later the game still feel like an Early Alpha. In fact, if we are to believe the lead dev's own words on Reddit, it feels more like a tech demo than anything else, and it is true. The problem is that the Store page said otherwise. It also promised 'thick and fast updates' but in the 7 months of developement following release on EA, we had mods incorporated into the game and a few cosmetic changes here and there.
What is odd, hoever, is that the devellopers have been using the money they made from pre-orders/kickstarter and early-access to invest in their game publishing empire. Yet, they still pretend to be an indie game company. They have also started developmment of another game, hired devs for it, while Starbound is dying not being updated, falling from an average of 60K+ players to about 2500 in a few months. Now Chucklefish defenders will say that we have the Nighlies now, and that it is proof that the devs are delivering on their promises. I can't recommend it. All the right ingredients are there, and it should be the best XCOM game ever made according to the sum of its features.
Yet the restrictive turn counters that appear in most missions utterly ruin the game, and indeed go against what has always been XCOMs central concept. No longer do you carefully plan your way to victory, but instead find yourself scrambling to rush to an objective completely arbitrarily. Apart from anything else, it simply restricts the way you can play a mission. In the past, if people wanted to rush an objective, that was one of many possible strategies. Now, in most missions, it is the only possible strategy.
The problem is only exarcebated because most of the maps are randomised, meaning there is no guarantee an objective is even completeable in the time allowed. When your entire squad can be wiped out on failure of certain mission types, this becomes a simply inexcusable and frankly game ruining design feature.
In all other aspects this is a truly fantastic game, and those 1 out of 10 missions where there are no timers can be incredibly gripping. But knowing that a potentially game ending mission (through no fault of my own) could be just around the corner makes it increasingly difficult for me to play this.

I'm honestly not sure whether I should reccomend this or not.
It is extremely well made - the music is exciting, the sound, dialogue, and voice acting is great, and it has an amazing visual style.
It is challenging but actually fairly balanced IMO - once you know a general good structure for a team and the the bad luck that usually crops up in different places then things will become a lot less random. The first few runs will be a gong show while you are figuring things out though. As will the first time in a new area, or with a new team, or after leveling up, or against a boss . . .
This is kind of why I am not sure about reccomending it - the struggle is real and constant.  Usually you get 'better' as you play a game - you have new skill, or the game gives you better weapons etc. In DD your team gradually levels up and at a certain point are too 'skilled' to run easier dungeons. Suddenly your 'A Team' absolutely sucks and you are getting out by just the skin of your teeth.
On the one hand, this keeps the challenge up - you need to find new stategies and group configurations and there is always that anxiety about entering a dungeon.  Characters have a set suite of skills and can only be leveled up so much and even high level items seem to have some crippling negitive aspects along with the good.
On the other hand, while you continue to achieve more difficult and amazing tasks, it is not actually satisfying. I would come to dread my characters leveling up. Most of the time I felt like a stressed out HR manager trying to fill vacancies.
This was probably intentional though - the whole game is a bit of a commentary on what 'adventuring' would be like in the real world. Having to go out in the dark  and murder a bunch of horrible monsters would actually suck quite a bit wouldn't it?
You know what - I'm going to reccomend this. It is something different and even if I didn't actually 'enjoy' it , it definitely had me thinking about it long after I was done a session.

I enjoyed XCOM 2 quite alot, mostly because I played quite alot of XCOM: EU, EW and the Long War mod. The game makes some pretty good improvements over the original while, managing to stumble on few of the new things.
Now I am simply gonna state some things about the game.
- Perfomance & optimization is bad. I run GTX 560 Ti.  Max & High were unplayable. Medium & Low took heavy hits every know and then. Even after turning off most of the luxury graphics, the game had extreme issues. Even few additional particles in a map would start causing performance drops. The overhub was no better, the mere action of going to the geoscape causes a performance hit. This kind of stuff needs to be fixed, there are no excuses.
- Enemy desing had both good and bad. Enemies with always always ready teleport abilities that they can use to auto-flank you are not creative or strategic, they are pure ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. First time meeting a new enemy needs to be a surprise, but after that, not so much, this game is about strategy. Hidden enemies were a nice addition, there could have been more tools to dealing with the though. Too many enemies seemed to have incredible movement ranges, to top it off, most of them even had quite large HP pools, armor & defensive stats. This made damage dealing methods that did not rely on chance (Explosive, Psi & some others) something the player needs to hoard, otherwise they would not be able to deal with most enemies in the game.
- The gameplay outside of mission was quite pleasing, the change was nice from XCOM. It made you work quite hard, so you don't fall behind the aliens in power & progress. The resources you had worked quite fine, though some of them at times seemed quite redundant as you had nowhere to spend them and by the time you need them, you have too much. The black market could have been a lot better. You should have been able to make request for a small-medium payment in order to have something to look forward to when visiting there.
- The proving grounds annoyed me a little. Having to rely on RNG to make the best items & tools in the game was a little bit akward. Weapon modding is one of the games highlights, so why the hell am I not able to gain access to the, mods trough anything but drops & shop, which BOTH rely on RNG. Even worse, some of the mods are completely stupid. Instant kill mod? Additional move mod? Misses deal dmg mod? What? Those are completely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ concepts in a game of strategy & chance. I don't want mods that introduce more RNG, I want mods that are able to tip the scales in my favour trough the choices I make. Bipod? Grenade tube? Bayonet? Why is holo targetting still a skill no one will ever pick, not a mod?
- Mission were extremely nice. Timed missions at first hard, but after you got the hang of traversing the terrain, scouting the areas and knowing which pods were worth it to break concealment for, the missions became very very interesting. (Thank the heavens for specialist scanning & battlescanners) VIP & Dark VIP rescues were a bit annoying, the player should have been allowed to choose the spot for EVAC atleast in the mission where the VIP had to be rescued from a room/cell/van. Could have balanced it out by making the evac square require a bit more free space.
- Character customization is good, I expect to see more stuff added by both Firaxis & modders.
That is all I can think of now.

The reason I didn't write a review for this game a while ago was, I didn't know what to write. I love this game, but it's hard to put how interesting it is into words.
Starbound is NOT a ripoff of Terraria, though often that is one of the first impressions people get. Like Terraria, it is an Indie Sandbox game with crafting, bosses, etc. However, there are some major differences. Starbound has a huge array of different enemies, put together from a few sprites to make random and sometimes funny-looking enemies. In Starbound, it is a little bit more on the surviving and exploration side, with LOADS of structures and strange blocks to fin, and strong enemies. Ores are more scarce. Starbound has many races to play as, each with their own pros and cons. There's too much more to talk about...
For an early access game, Starbound is amazing. AMAZING. I agree with the devs: "Starbound is already extremely playable and contains a vast amount of content". For an example, take the sheer amount of different planets. Here's the rundown:
5 sectors (galaxies)
A LOT of star systems
Each star system has 1 - 8(?) planet clusters
Each planet cluster has 1 - 4 different planets/asteroids to land on
There's so much content. I would highly reccomend this game to people who enjoy games with the option, but are not totally created around the ability, to build cool stuff. People who enjoy games that have the RPG feel of "I need to get better! I need the best stuff! To defeat all the bosses!" will enjoy this game.

A great entry, personally more enjoyable for me than II was, namely due to the enemy placement feeling a bit more fair.  Improvements include a return to some old form from the first Dark Souls.  Enemies won't just stop respawing because you want to grind an item drop or you just happen to suck like a certain writer called "me."  There aren't a limited number of the multiplayer items, the humanity or human effigy-equivalent, "embers."  Weapons don't degrade like they're made of paper mache.
Buuut, there might as well not be a weapon degredation system in the first place...I can count on one hand the number of times my claymore got below half durability in nearly 70 hours.  DS1's system was basically just busywork, but at least there were some chances to have weapons break.  DS2's was basically a big lazy glitch that the devs left.  And now they've basically rendered it a non-mechanic.
Does pyromancy suck or is it just me?  The requirements are so restrictive, removing a lot of the fun I had with it in DS1 since anyone could use it.
They have a serious infatuation with one-way doors, one-way doors
, making levels more linear than they should be because you can only open doors
and you will go through these levels the way they want you to and

Then there's the bonfire placement.  You can frequently find a bonfire literally within sight of another bonfire.  Often, they're a hallway away from each other with no enemies in between.  What were they thinking?  Were they thinking at all?
I may sound harsh, but overall I liked the level design.  Again, it feels more enjoyable to navigate this world than DS2 did, more of a return to form minus the occasionally janky levels from DS like Blighttown.  But this game feels like two steps forward, two steps back.  Dark Souls 1 had a genuinely organic-feeling, interconnected world, DS2 tried to do something similar, although it made considerably less geographic sense, and DS3 just didn't even try.  You're essentially jumping into worlds ala Mario 64, a far cry from the metroidvania-esque interconnecting level design the series had formerly aspired to.  Why make levels interconnect in sensible ways when we can just let them warp from firelink??  Rather, we don't want to invest the effort to design such a complex world, so let's just let them warp right away to save ourselves the effort.  So you can forget picking the master key as your starting item and exploring an area before you're "supposed to," since you get spoon-fed levels when when they darn well please.
I guess what I'm saying here is that the game itself?  Is fun.  The gameplay for me is a lot more fun and it feels better than DS2's did.  DS3 is a better (or at least more enjoyable) game from a very basic gameplay perspective.  The world is visually beautiful in a way that neither of the previous games can match.  But it is
derivative of DS1's story and lore, it doesn't even try to aspire to the level of world design previous games did, and it's still chock-full of design decisions (like the bonfires) that could only have been made while drunk.
A lot of these complaints you'd have no reason to care about if you've never played the previous games.  If you want to jump in, this is actually one of the best places to.  Multiplayer is still lively and this game has
co-op system in the series (as in, it's not completely broken without mods ala DS1).  But for fans of the series, you might get where I'm coming from--it reverses some design decisions that you may or may not have liked from 2, while adding new ones of its own, creating a competent game that fails to really bring anything new to the table for the series.
