I've run into a wall with PC gaming. Mostly due to finances and the inability to upgrade my PC because of it. So being stuck with a x32 Motherboard, I find sadness every time I see a game I really want to play (Why hasn't steam come in with software that scans your system for compatibility yet?). So my search always ends with me (most times) saying "maybe in the near future" or on the rare occasion "it WILL work" only to have said game freeze while playing the tutorial.
In comes Darkest Dungeon.
I had just about given up torturing myself with my Steam account when I read a faint whisper of this gems release. Lovecraft you say!? Dungeon crawler? But... what of the dreaded 4GB minimum RAM that EVERYTHING is released with (why 99 Levels to Hell? you're not 4GB worthy!). So I kept my eye out. Then the whispers became chattering, they also mentioned a potential PS4 release! "I'll wait for that!". Then the day came... 2GB RAM! My heart nearly leapt from my tired and abused gamer chest! Instantly decided that I was buying it for both PC and PS4. I couldn't wait the extra year or 2 for the console version.
I was not disappointed.
Being that I have loved Lovecraft since my youth and played a SMIDGEN of Call of Cthulhu Tabletop RPG; Darkest Dungeon brought to the table where other lovecraftian games failed in my opinion (besides Amnesia)... the dreaded sanity loss. I no longer felt fear of dying by the hand of some horror of the deep. But found myself dreading my party breaking one by one till their OWN fear or other mental abnormality felled my entire party.
I was crushed... But not dis-hearted what so ever.
I began my long path to The Darkest Dungeon. Even now with so few party members above level 3 I find myself dreading the sacrifice the ruins of the mansion almost seem to require. Upon embarking I always wonder if it's worth sacrificing my level 4 vestal and man-at-arms for more money and heirlooms to upgrade the Hamlet. Sometimes I push forward and watch in horror as the party rips itself apart with selfishness, fear, masochism or abusiveness in the vague hope that just 1 will overcome the brutal mental lashing from witnessing the horrors and carry the party to the end. But to no avail.
But it never seems unfair.
I am generally a purist with gaming and often avoid guides. I feel guides have ruined gaming in my opinion. Yet I feel that even with a guide, the ruins will take whomever they see fit to fill my Hamlet's graveyard as a sort of foundation to up hold the horrors that lay in wait. Learning which skills work with certain characters/party combination is half the fun!

The concept seems interesting and thoughtful, but it's not. The Cthulhu-based story drew me in. The terrible design drove me away. Challenge comes only through non-sensical design choices and the intense over-use of RNG.
Want to do something? RNG will stop you. Want to heal out of combat? You can't, even though you are a healer. Want to kill monsters? Well, you may get an occasional kill, but bodies just pile up, even though you are killing less than 3 at a time. Said bodies will block you from attacking. Everything is range based, and the game keeps finding ways to randomly change your positioning. The monsters can get though the piled up bodies just fine though, for some reason. If this were an action game, zombies and skeletons would be more nimble than humans. All of this doesn't entirely matter though, because your party usually dies from massive amounts of stress damage, which can't be mitigated much, in a handful of fights. It can be mitigated, sure, but you take about 500 damage in a dungeon, and you can mitigate about 20.
Party members are essentially canon fodder, and your goal is to build up your estate as they all die from horrible deaths. Yet, you will not be interested in doing so, because it's an excessive RNG-based grind fest where you see the same tiles and the same monsters over and over and over again....
I tried to return the game, but they won't let me. Maybe there's $2 worth of original ideas in this game, not $10 or $20+, not nearly so.

I cant recommend this game enough for fans of the series or tactical turn based games in general. Alot of hate is directed at the game currently because it has "some" timer based missions. I am currently playing on the legend difficulty and get around 40%-45% of my missions as timer based ones. And there are always more than enough turns to complete all objectives at a nice easy pace. So, after putting a lot of hours into all of the Dark Souls games ( mostly Dark Souls 1 and 3 ) i decided to write a review about this awesome game! Dark Souls 3 is the third and possibly the last Dark Souls game in the franchise, and frankly, it is a worth end to the series. Now let's talk about some aspects of the game.
The Story
Ever Since Gwyn has linked the first flame, there were countless other heroes that relinked the first flame so that the age of fire can continue. The three main Lord of Cinders ( SPOILERS : or rather i should say four, if you count Lothric as a Lord of Cinder. I personally don't, because he never actually lit the first flame ) rise from their grave because the fire is threatened. These lads are supposed to re-link the flame so the age can continue, but instead of doing that, they would rather watch the flame die out. So the flame ( or..rather the Bell of Awakening? i don't know ) wakes up the Unkindled. You are one of these unkindled ash. Your job is to bring the Lords of Cinders back to their thrones. Either Alive or as Ashes. My overall opinion of the story is that its pretty awesome, but can be really confusing sometimes..and it needs a lot of reading. Some portion of the story isn't actually there, you have to theorise.
The Gameplay
Dark Souls 3's gameplay is basically Dark Souls 1's gameplay, but with a lot of fixes and balances ( and some ♥♥♥♥ups xD )
You still have the same main stats, but some of them either got removed, or they were made into one stat ( Endurance no longer gives you more equip load. Instead, equip load can be raised by spending points in Vitality.  And also, the Resistance stat from Dark Souls 1 is completely gone, you can't invest points directly into resistance ) Also, because of a lore aspect, you no longer have the option to stack up Humanity. Actually, Humanity is quite gone from this game, instead you use Embers to restore your link to the other worlds and also give you an HP boost which lasts as long as you're alive. ( To Simplify it , once you use an ember you can be invaded, but you can also summon other people to help you at certain areas ) Summons ( also Invaders ) also have the option to use Estus ( although the overall Estus you can use while being summoned is reduced ) Now you can also equip up to four Rings! Quite better than just two rings. Oh and one other thing, Poise is completely broken. Covenants also return, and quite frankly some of them are really fun and they give you good rewards, and some of them are totally dead. For example, The Blade of the Darkmoon ( my favourite covenant from DS1 ) is utter♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in this game, since you can't level up, because the covenant itself relies on another covenant ( Way of Blue ) which is a completely dead covenant on levels above 25 SL. Also in this game, as my good friend Jack would say " Medium Roll actually works ". In DS3 medium roll still has the same Iframes, but now your character recovers much faster at the end of the roll. Overall , the gameplay is pretty cool, you have a lot of variety in Magic Stuff ( Pryomancy, Offensive or Healing Miracles, Sorceries , Dark Sorceries/Miracles/Pryomancies ) and you also have a ton of Melee weapons to use. This makes DS3's replayability INSANE, because you can literally make *ALMOST ANY KIND OF BUILD* you want.
Controlls
I highly recommend using a controller. 'Nuff Said. I think the controlls are good, but if this is your first Souls experience, you gotta get used to it first.
The Graphics, Areas and Armour
This game is super gorgerous! It looks amazing in almost every area! I especially love how Irithyl looks like, with all that snow and stuff. Superb! I really like how some weapons got some extra details ( Boss Weapons look amazing! ) The enemies are also very nicely detailed. Almost all of the areas look very cool, but honestly there were some areas that could've been bigger and better detailed. For example, the Profaned Capital is a joke. It's basically a 5 minute run to the boss and that's it. The Armour in Dark Souls 3 is really good! There are a lot of armour from DS1, for example you can get Lautrec's armour..or Artorias's armour ( Sadly Lord Blade Ciaran armour didn't make it into the game ) You can do a lot of cosplay by combining other armour pieces together. Overall they have a lot of variety.
Some things i wanted to mention as either cons or pros
*SPOILERS*Dark Souls 3 continues DS1's and DS2's trend with having some ridicolously easy bosses. Wolnir, Deacons of the Deep, Crystal Sage and the Anchient Wyern are basically a joke. Dark Souls 3 also continues the other trend from the other games, which is that the main guys you are supposed to defeat are probably one of the easiest bosses. The Abyss Watchers themselves aren't so hard, Yhrom the Giant is a complete joke. Aldrich isn't so particularly hard either. Although thank god the Twin Princes actually manage to put up some kind of challange. I would've enjoyed if most of these bosses put up some kind of challange *SPOILERS ARE OVER*
Also, there are the Invaders. I myself don't have a really big problem with invading, but some people really don't like how some of the community handles invading. Some invaders tend to come to you, use gestures and get you to do an Honor Duel, which is cool. Some invaders particularly like hiding behind enemies and gank you while you're trying to defeat the enemies so you can kill the invader. Overall, yeah, the community isn't perfect, but hey, that's not the game's problem. You can easily punish these invaders by using a Seed of a Giant Tree, or you can ♥♥♥♥ with them some other way too.
Alright, I think that covers most of what I wanted to say. Let's gather the cons and pros
Pros :
-Fitting end to the Series
-Lore is quite interesting
-Awesome gameplay mechanics
-Good variety of magic or pure melee weapons
-INSANE ammount of builds. You can almost make any kind of build you want.
-Graphics are awesome

For my final verdict, skip straight to the end. If you want some explanation about the systems and what I think of them, read on!
About 1.5 years ago, I would have recommended this game to all of my friends. While a lot complained about the mist system, it actually wasn't a bad thing. It helped limit people from becoming too addicted to the game unless they wanted to completely sink their time and not make very many crowns/energy in the process.
1 year ago they removed the cost to go down the elevators, completely freeing people from that "detrimental" mist system, but in its place came a much worse one: the forge. While the forge could have been good and not a huge detriment, the developers eventually started reducing the drop rate of fire crystals, especially Radiant Fire Crystals, which are needed to heat your end game gear. It now takes forever to get enough crystals to fully level a piece of gear up to 5*.
As for the spark of life system, I'm neutral on it. The drop rate of sparks is actually quite tolerable if you aren't dying twice every floor. They even gave players a free revive (up to 30 health) per floor. That's quite the generous system, in my opinion.
The orbs of alchemy crafting system is a double edge sword. While the removal of mist means buying orbs costs an extra 100 energy for 3*, 4*, and 5* (effectively) over the old system, those who are patient enough can earn their way to craft items 100% free. I was able to do this for a few 5* items on my alternate account, which I played from the ground up after the new systems were in place until mid 2014.
The game is nice to play IF you have a guild of helpful people and friends that are willing to run with you day in and day out. Also do not grind in the same places all of the time. It will destroy your interest in the game. Do danger missions, explore the arcade, make challenges for yourself, etc. Try to craft weapons you wouldn't think of normally using, just for fun!
While the systems in place might hinder fun slightly, it has always been ultimately up to the player to find how they can make the given game fun. Find what you like and do it enough so that it always stays enjoyable, but doesn't become a grind.
I give this game a thumbs up, barely. Try this game long enough to get through to the 3* areas before you decide if you love or hate it. Don't expect this game to wow you in the first hour. That won't happen. It's a community driven game now, mostly.

First impressions after just a couple of hours of play:  very similar to the previous offering in mechanics and play, though the story line seems more interesting.  Weapons upgrades are a new, and kind of cool, feature (you can add laser sights, high capacity mags, autoloaders, etc., to individual weapons).   There seems to be a similar upgrade option for individual soldiers ("PCS" attachments), but I haven't figured out how to use them yet.   If you're into dressing up your squad, there are more uniforms, face paint options and color options than before.  There's a split economic system--intel and supplies--not yet sure of the implications.
Most missions are on a pretty tight timer, that requires you to move quite quickly.  This is mitigated somewhat by the interesting "concealed" mechanism (and by one character class, the Ranger, that can remain concealed after the enemy alerts to your presence).  The upshot is that you'll leave a lot more enemies alive and just run past them to complete your mission.  This makes for a somewhat different flavor than the "search and destroy" missions from Enemy Unknown, but I don't find it disturbing as do some other reviewers.  It just requires a different tactical approach.
Now, the bad:  the cut scenes are fun once, but you can't skip past them, so if you end up going back to an old save or playing a second time through, they're just obnoxiously repetitive.  Likewise, if you need to go back and check out your current objectives, you've got to watch them scroll excruciatingly slowly down a screen that you don't have a scroll bar for.  That's just annoying.  The load screens that come up as you're going to and from missions are interminable--do they really have to be so long?
This could have been a much better game if the designers hadn't decided to make you watch their cool cut scenes whether you wanted to or not.  Instead, it rapidly becomes annoying as you wait for your helpers to ramble through speeches you've already heard.  This limits the replay value tremendously.
4 out of 10.  Should be a 7.  Could be a 9.  But the designers like wasting your time, so 4.
UPDATE:  Having played through the game, I'm even more disappointed with the time-wasting nonsense I discuss above.  The cut-scenes last waaaaay too long (like up to 2 minutes before and after every mission--I've got time to get up, get a beer and come back, only to find my troopers still flying around in the cut-scene.  This isn't loading time; when I load a saved game it finishes in about 10 seconds.  It's just bloody-minded time wasting.)  Also, the dramatic cut scenes for various mission points can't be skipped.  Some of them go on and on.  This really limits replay value.
Lots of people have complained that the game is too tough.  I don't agree.  The tactics are a bit different from the prior game--using concealment (and rangers who stay concealed after the fighting starts) is a bit tricky, but once you figure it out the aliens are still pretty easy to drop.  The mission clocks are rarely too tight, and the Avatar Project progress is easy to stall.  Overall, the game would be a worthy successor to and improvement on its predecessor, but the annoying, unescapable, time-wasting cut-scenes just kill it.

Darkest Dungeon is a very atmospheric and tactical game. From a roster of over a dozen ragtag heroes chosen from those constantly arriving into your forsaken village of Hamlet, you will select 4 to go into the dungeons, and hopefully come out alive, as well.
Each hero has some individuality - apart from the distinct and memorable classes (which there are 14 of currently), each hero will, over the course of his or her adventures, pick up up to 5 positive and 5 negative quirks, which are permanent unless replaced by another quirk or removed for money in the Sanatorium. These quirks may affect anything from how the hero may relieve stress in the Hamlet (they may find a love interest in the Brothel and refuse to spend time elsewhere, or overhear a disturbing conversation over prayer and refuse to pray in the future), how they behave during the dungeon crawling (They may develop an unhealthy fascination with death and go rummaging around every cart of bodies, for better or worse, or they may become cleptomaniac and steal some of the loot for themselves), or how they act in battle (they may become familiar with one of the 5 dungeons and get a fighting bonus in that dungeon, or they may get a phobia of the walking dead and get more stressed when fighting skeletons and the undead). And these are just a few from what seems like dozens of possible quirks.
Each hero can have 4 active skills (out of 8 available) and 4 camping (out of 8 available). Each recruit starts with 4 random skills in each category unlocked, but if you want to develop particular synergies, you will need to unlock other skills and mix and match them, picking whichever are relevant to what team the hero is going with, where in the formation they will stand, and which enemies you're likely to meet in the dungeon you're headed for. Each skill can get upgraded, each hero's active skills and half of the camping skills are unique to that profession. Many heroes will be able to work together, since some have skills that expose the enemy to effects another hero can inflict, etc.
The battles themselves are turn-based - you will come across up to 4 enemies in the dungeon, each relevant to the dungeon where you meet them, each also with unique skills and synergies. After the stat-based turn order is automatically determined, each enemy and hero gets 1 (with exception of some bosses) turn, one at a time, to use one of their skills. Each skill is sensitive to which position in the formation the hero or the enemy is in, and which enemy they mean to target. For instance, Vestal's healing skills may only be used when she's in the two rear positions, while most of the Crusader's skills can only target the front two opponents, and won't reach in the rear rows. Some enemies and heroes have skills that may change their or the enemies' positions thereby changing which skills may be used in the next round. Some skills can affect more than one enemy or hero. Each skill's success or failure depends in large part on your hero's and the enemy's skill level, stats, equipped trinkets, and equipment, and in large part on the RNG.
There's much more to the game than the battles - there's the metagame in your village of Hamlet, where you will upgrade, train, and equip your heroes, and there's the wandering around the dungeons between battles, where your choices of which supplies to buy and which objects in your way to disturb will affect your heroes with various buffs, debuffs, damage, healing, or even permanent effects that stick to the hero unless you remove them at a cost when (and if) you return.
Each hero is potentially disposable - unlike most other games, the one resource you have in abundance is new recruits arriving on the cart, and recruiting them is always free. Death is permanent, so if you get wiped in the dungeon, you will always be able to recruit more heroes when you return to Hamlet. This takes hero management to the next level - you're no longer eager to spend money to heal their negative quirks or upgrade their skills and equipment - they may die in the very next run, wasting all your money. You have to decide which of your heroes are worthwhile, and treat their quirks quickly, since if they are not treated within a few days, the quirks lock in and become even more expensive to get rid of.
The Stress mechanic is novel and interesting. In addition to health, your heroes may receive stress for various actions - from wandering in the dark or choosing to read scribbles on human skin parchment, to a stress-inducing spell of an enemy mage or a critical hit suffered from a skeleton. Stress must be managed during battles via tactics and knowing which enemies have abilities that cause stress, or certain heroes' stress-affecting skills; between battles when choosing how to spend your time camping, or which curios to disturb; between dugeons when assigning your weary heroes to one of 6 stress relief activities in the town, which all cost money. High stress may make your heroes become masochistic and looking for trouble in battle, or abusive and cause stress to their fellow adventurers, or paranoid and refuse heals or skip turns, and more. Stress climbing too high will cause a heart attack which will bring you to Death's Door, leaving you with very little time to save your hero by healing, lest they be finished off.
The Narrator's voice is creepy, frequent, and absolutely awesome. Your dead Ancestor will narrate your mistakes and successes, giving you advice and commenting on the events.This is one of those games you will always wish he had even more lines.
I consider all of the above good things about the game. Now, the ones you may find annoying:
Yes, the RNG is unforgiving. But unlike some other games with this problem, you do get a feeling your tactics are helping. Pick the right team, good trinkets, well-synergized skills, and the RNG God is no longer deciding if you live or die, but if you will get damaged or badly damaged - and that's a big difference. But you WILL get frustrated, mad, ragequit, and yell at the RNG God for your favorite hero you just spent so much money on dying to a jellyfish sting. You WILL miss hits you thought were sure thing in the worst possible time, so plan ahead. This is balanced by what I think most people complaining about it don't understand - Darkest Dungeon is a game of knowing when to pull out. It is too tempting to continue fighting when your heroes are on the verge of death, just so you don't leave empty-handed, but, as your Ancestor (the narrator) warns you, "Remind yourself that overconfidence is a slow and insidious killer". You WILL get to keep the loot you've gathered so far if you try to escape battle and return to Hamlet before you complete your main objective. And the heroes ARE disposable, and there's always more fresh meat coming in. If your heroes keep dying, don't blame bad luck. Blame your miscalculation of their survival chances when you decided to press on.
Another fair objection is to this game's lack of reward. You DO get more money, and you do get to upgrade the Hamlet, but the only reward for leveling your heroes is more difficult enemies. Lower level heroes are useless in high level dungeons, and high level heroes refuse to go to the lower level dungeons. Trinkets you equip your heroes with almost always have harsh trade-offs, which is a good mechanic, but, once again, makes you question why you just defeated the Spawn of the Devil for a trinket you will never wear because it adds so much stress.
Also, the quirks, despite being very important to the gameplay, are hard to manage and keep track of.
Overall, I would certainly recommend this game. Its novelty and complicated, but rewarding mechanics, as well as excellent art direction and voice acting will immerse you in the Darkest Dungeon world and you will spend many hours customizing and improving your heroes one quirk and skill at a time.

This game rewards the chicken-hearted. Stubbornly trying to finish a dungeon that's gone badly from the start leads to a deathmarch.
This game rewards the detail-minded. Did you remember to unequip your trinkets? Did you re-equip them? Did you check to see if that monster is going to easily resist that attack? Dude, did you even make a provisions checklist?
This game rewards the heartless. Sometimes the best thing to do with a syphilic, boozed-up "hero" with a bad case of nerves is to fire her. Sometimes deciding to let her die of a heart attack gets you a shiny.
This game rewards the persistent. Not giving up after a humiliating party wipe is more of a key to success than flashes of tactical brilliance. Completing the game in less than 99 weeks (each week is a dungeon run that takes up to half an hour) is considered fast and gets you an achievement.
This game rewards the flexible. Sometimes you don't have a lot of choices. Your healers are all too diseased and crazy this week. Your tank went AWOL, and your barbarian needs to have a pesky trait removed. Can you scrape together a viable party? Or maybe your tactics went well only up to a point. Will you come up with new ones or will you pack it in, mumbling bitterly about the unfairness of it all?
It's not for everybody.

Ignore the negative reviews. The trolls are out in force deliberately downvoting  all the possitive reviews reguardless of their content.
That out of the way, you should definitely buy this game. Yes, it does have some performance issues, but then so did Enemy unknown when it was first launched, and these were quickly patched. The perfomance issue the game does have have been greatly over exagerated by many people. I'm running an i3 processor and 6gb of ram with an Gforce GT 610 graphics card, which is low end for a gaming rig, and I can run the game with all textures etc on high with no lag. The only performance issue I've suffered is that the loading time between missions can be a minute or two while your stuck on the skyranger screen.
As for gameplay... yes there are more timer missions, but your certainly not forced to suffer them every mission. I've run infiltration missions, sabotage missions, base defence etc and there are no forces turn timers upon them. Again, another massively over-exagerated feature claim.
That said, this game does not play like XC1. Its a totally different play style where you are a guerilla opperative fighting with limited resources rather then an elite organisation with worlwide funding. If you try to play it like the first game, you are going to loose and get frustrated.
All that out of the way, XC2 is a massive improvement over the first. Better customisation, gameplay, level design, AI and a better variety of mission types. Overall its a game that feels to have much more replayability value to it too as there are now so many more different choices that affect the overall gameplay beyond simple starting location and what you chose to research first. In XC2, every decision matters. Hell, even selling stuff at the market could screw you over if you find yourself suddenly short on intel or an item you traded for supplies.
As it stands, X-com 2 is a solid 8 of 10. Once they fix the load lag, its a good 9. It'll never be able to please everyone,  but any true fan of the genre or the x-com franchise won't regret buying this game. As said, the trolls and 'fair weather gamers' are out in force.

While I'm still playing through the campaign, I can say that XCOM 2 is overall a well-made game, but there are some downsides with it. For me, mainly two: the game isn't as optimised as it should be, I'm running a 650 Ti 2GB currently but I feel like it should be able to run the game at higher frames (although the game has never outright crashed). I also feel like the difficulty of the game needs some tweaking - I've been playing on the second difficulty and it feels too punishing in certain areas.
If you make one mistake in your research, mission choices or facility choices, you can find yourself in completely frustrating situations, like not having enough squad member slots, or wasting all your money on new soldiers because you didn't buy the facility needed to use the speed boost that heals your current soldiers faster and in time for the next mission. Once you realise your weaknesses and start trying to correct them down the road, the Avatar counter will keep ticking up as expected, not giving you enough time unless you want the red bar almost completely filled by the time you're prepared for the mission.
Making these types of oversights can make the game extremely tedious unless you constantly revert saves, which isn't how you want to play it. You can find yourself saving after every mission so you can revert to any point of the game and change your choices so that you can avoid the problem that made you revert in the first place.
Overall, good game for strategy players and one that improves on Enemy Unknown. Don't buy if your graphics card is old or if you don't want to constantly revert saves or constantly lose all time and effort you invested into your playthrough.
(Yes, I understand XCOM is meant to punish bad decisions, but personally I feel it went too far in that direction and could have been more forgiving at least a few times, especially on the first two difficulties).
P.S. I wrote this review for the Pillar of Community badge.

Overall I enjoyed and recommend this game.  In my opinion its later levels are too dominated by randomness and grinding, and with the stakes as high as they are (permanent loss of characters and items that took immense time investment to get that far), that randomness starts to feel very cheap and oppressive.  That turns into tedious play, and the game stops being as fun in the end.
There are ways to play that help to mitigate the RNG threat, but you'll never be free from bad rolls of the dice totally hosing your progress.  This is the disadvantage of a game like this -- the main (and most tempting) tool for upping the difficulty is easily overused.  I suspect this is a game I will never finish, simply because I cannot dedicate the time to it, and because tedium isn't fun.  I've been playing champion dungeons for about 10+ hours now, and I'm kinda tired of it.  Further, I'm told the final dungeon has even more tricks to artificially lengthen the game and force you to grind even more.  I'm just not up for that.  :(
Don't get me wrong... The game can be grindy or infuriating at times, but overall it's been a fantastic experience.  That's why it gets a thumbs-up from me.  The experience falls apart in later levels and I'm disappointed by that, but I've had enough fun with the game that I cannot justify down-voting it just because of a poor end game.  The theme and mechanics treated me *very* well through most of the game, and it delivers fantastically before the RNG and grindy issues start to really hurt.
Unless you're a completionist who would feel very uncomfortable walking away from the game before the end, then I greatly recommend this game.  Up until the end stages, it's hard in a fair and reasonable way, and you feel very smart when you figure out ways to mitigate the threats and have mostly successful runs.  The severe penalty of failure only sweetens success.  There are ways to make forward progress in the late game, but they're too slow for me and I've moved on to other games; please see other reviews' coverage of that content.
Pros:
-Fantastic Theme and Presentation.  This kept me coming back even when I was frustrated.
-Very Interesting and Fun Mechanics.  Again, I kept coming back because the design is compelling, and I wanted to try out new ideas and strategies (which you can do easily in early levels).
-I sank lots of hours into this game and don't regret them
Cons:
-Steep Learning Curve.  Game does very little to teach you, and expects you to learn by doing.  This is pretty harsh given the sharp penalties of failure, though you can always recover (early game is pretty easy to bounce back).  But it can be difficult to learn the system without getting your rear handed to you an awful lot until it's discouraging.  I recommend checking the guides & wiki from time to time, if not often.  (and some guides are very out of date, so be careful)
-Late game is dominated by grinding and randomness, and it's difficult & tedious to minimize those issues.  You're stuck playing a certain "correct" way, and it quickly becomes tiresome and unrewarding.
-I'll probably never finish this game, and at this point I'm okay with that.  With my time so limited, I have to know when to call it quits.
Overall: Good.  I recommend you pick it up.

The best way to describe Starbound is Terraria in space.  What was done in Terraria is expanded at least ten fold in Starbound.
Players choose a race, choose from a starting set of clothes, progress through tech tiers, and fight bosses.  As of 2014-02-22, the first four tech tiers a locked until you kill a boss.  There are rumors of a fifth boss, but it has not been implemented as of this review.  It is my hope that every tech tier will eventually have a boss to defeat.
Just like Terraria, players can get items and equipment from friends.  There are no equipment requirements, so this can significantly boost your power level without passing the boss gate.  This is both good and bad, since progression is a huge incentive.  Being given tier ten (aka max tier) gear removes that sense of accomplishment.
Unlike Terraria, players are free to travel between 12.667 quadrillion planets.
reports this number is expected to reach 422.22 quadrillion upon full release.  Planets are currently divided between five sectors (alpha, beta, gamma, delta, and X).  Each sector is designed for a certain tech tier:  A is 1, B is 2, G is 3, D is 4, X is 5-10.  Players will notice the mineral content and enemy strengths change according to these tiers.
One criticism of Starbound vs. Terraria.  In Terraria, you had the one world to explore.  You could build a great fortress or palace as your home base.  In Starbound, you may set a home planet to do this, warping directly to the home planet from your ship, no matter what planet the ship is currently orbiting.  In my opinion, the best replacement to Terraria’s home base is a mod like
Want Star Trek’s Enterprise?  Star War’s Death Star?  Firefly’s Serenity?  Build and design to your heart’s content!
If you’re not sure about Starbound, I encourage you to pick up Terraria.  You should be to pick it up for $10 (or less during sales).  If you enjoy it, Starbound is definitely worthy in its current state and will only get better as more features are added.  Starbound is still subject to character wipes, but 12 quadrillion planets provide plenty of variability in gameplay for each mandatory restart.

*I HAVE NOT FINISHED THE GAME SO THIS REVIEW IS SUBJECT TO CHANGE CURRENTLY*
Im conflicted on whether to say this is worth picking up at the moment. Several patches can easily fix issues that are gameplay related. Optimisation wise, there is somethings to be decided. So lets jump into the good, the bad and the ugly.
The game picks up in a future where xcom lost in EW (roughly around the 3 month mark from memory). The story is intriguing and the lore is interesting. Some nice throw backs to EW, but nothing super necessary.
Graphics -
The game looks nice, has a nice 'feel' to it. Things look on point. Enemy pod reveals are cool, the camera can be a little clunky but does give a satisfying feeling most of the time.  Textures are appealing and soliders look cool. Alien designs vary but Xcom 2 does a great job of the models imo.
Sound -
The soundtrack on this game is stellar. The music gets you right into the spirit of whats going on, the tension exists. Sounds are all nice, game does a great job using audio to its advantage.
Gameplay -
This is where things get shaky. Starting with difficulty. The game itself is not 'Impossible' and this is very apparent on veteran and lower difficulty. I found commander was a fair challenge. Legend has me ripping my hair out, but thats what you sign up for. The issue is apparent in veteran and lower where the game is disgustingly easy until it spikes.
Xcom 2 introduces constant mission timers. I found several issues with this. It seems very divided by players if its good or bad, it creates tension but I found timers were sometimes stupidly short and were too unforgiving. This is reinforced by procuderal generated maps. I have had missions come up where it is not viable for me to reach the objective or vip and get out in time due to the map generation. This is when I have a issue. There is nothing worse than coming into a mission and straight up accepting its a failure because you cannot reach a point in time. MODS CAN ADDRESS THIS ISSUE AND EXTEND TIMERS/TRUE CONCEALMENT.
Most of the aliens seem to be implemented well, with the exception of the faceless who punishes the player for doing what the game forces you to rush. Not a great system, but with time you can get strategy to get around these issues.
Geoscape wise. Building is more streamlined, unfortunatley the early game is very forceful and you have to take a pretty forced build order. You have to manage time more effectively. Issues arise again from the avatar project and how quickly it can accelerate in comparison to how long it takes you to do things.
Optimization -
Yeah no. Its not optimized well and that impacts the game significantly. High performance rigs can struggle to pull decent frames when it is not something that appears to be all that demanding. Hopefully the game can be optimized and this fixed.
Should you buy it?
If you have played EU/EW you have a semi idea of whats going on. The game is a fun TBS with a cool premise and interesting elements.
However, do not buy this game if you do not enjoy getting punished constantly. You can extend timers through mods or remove them entirely so dont fear them.
I am enjoying the game a lot and am having a lot of fun. The game is in a state where its playable, but some fine tuning could really polish this to be easily game of the year.

**DISCLAIMER**SLIGHT SPOILERS AHEAD**
Fallout 4 is a good game, but it's not a Fallout game. So before I get discredited as another Fallout 4 hater, hear me out bruv. I'm going to address it's good parts first, before addressing it's flaws.
Fallout 4 has good graphics for Bethesda standards and the ranged combat feel has improved drastically since F03 and F:NV. The crafting system to modify weapons and armour, mix your own meds and chems are also stellar improvements. The effects of broken limbs, especially your head are a nice detail when playing in first person.
And here's where the good parts find an end.
The biggest flaws of this Fallout installment have to be the story and dialogue.
Story:
Bethesda somehow manages to destroy the whole premise of the story from the get go, by forcing you to establish a connection to a predifined character that has a family. You'd think Bethesda would know how to create a nobody for you to start off your adventure choosing who you want to be, since you barely have any backstory other than being a criminal in their TES games. Like with F03 you're forced into a specific role off the get go. At least in F03 they kept it malliable enough by having you be a young adult whose moral and ethical values aren't set in stone. You can decide who you want to be after you leave the vault in search of your father, so the player can still RP to a certain extend. F04 throws that right out the window. You're married with a child, the war starts, you get to a cryogenic vault where you freeze for 200 years, witness your spouse get killed and your son kidnapped, then get frozen at least another 60 years, before you get released into the game. Your main mission is to retrieve your son and avenge your spouse to whom the player has no connection whatsoever other than making her/him look pretty in front of the mirror, prior to them getting blasted in the head with a revolver.
The liberty of exploring the wasteland as whoever you want to be is out the window, the backstory has been written for you.
Now as you progress through the Wasteland, you keep getting interrupted from your main quest all the time. Sometimes it's unavoidable even. While this game weighs the main mission so heavily, it floods you with often times completely unrelated side quests. Better get to Nick Valentine's office so he can help me find my son, "Hey Mister, wanna buy a swatter? Oh btw, I know you lookin for your little one, but could ya put that on hold and fetch me some f***ing pre-war Baseball junkifacts for me? I'll pay ya some nice caps!". My first instinct was to gun him down, best quicksave of my life. Not to spoil it completely, the story continues with too many plot holes and inconsistencies, next to all the nagging of side characters wanting you to do♥♥♥♥♥♥for them. Why should you waste time, looking for your 1-year old, right? Might aswell be polygamous and have three women dating you at the same time, "Nora who? Who is that? My wife? Shot by some brand of corn flakes? Doesn't ring a bell".
Dialogue: You get four options to pick from, which are mostly: Yes, not right now, sassy clever joke, I need to know more on this. Or in some cases you even get three different ways of saying "yes". Speech checks are based on your Charisma, since there are no skills anymore, plus they don't show you the percentages to flip the coin or if you need a specific requirement in a skill to win the speech check. For all we know: Yellow is easy, Orange is medium and Red is spamming F9 for five minutes until RNG is in your favour (curse you if you do that). Remember witty answers that would pop up if one of your skills were high enough, adding more depth into problem solving via dialogue? Kiss that out the window. Also the fact that your character speaks for you and more often than not, doesn't add the right emotion into what you say at that particular moment is revolting, wishing they'd never introduced voice to begin with.
Further things that are bad which I'll spare you a wall of text:
- Companion depth: They try to add instances of dialogue based on your affinity threshhold and even give you the option of being more than just companions, but honestly they're the same pack mules that Lydia was.
- Town location and presentation: Bigger towns or settlements are straight in the hotbed of gang warfare between Raiders, Gunners, Super Mutants and the likes. In a post-apocalyptic world every movie or series, every book every other media simulating any of this recommends you don't settle in towns. They're the hot zones for the infected or deformed and the lawless. You reinforce an area away from town and go on supply runs or make your own crops to survive. Furthermore, every town you visit is a trash bag. You'd think 200 years after the bombs fell, people would get their asses up, fixed their ragged clothing, got the trash lying around out on the wrecked ruins and would try to live as pre-war as possible. They don't. 200 years have passed and they all live in dirt, trash, tattered rags living off a non-existant economy, since you're almost always the only visitor in that town and most unnamed Settlers just wander about and do nothing resembling any work for which they should earn their keep. It makes little to no sense who even buys anything at the markets. If there were at least more simulated unnamed drifters having a stay in town for some food and rest, get some equipment then leave, you'd at least give those towns some life.
- Open camera: The open camera during dialogue scenes does not recognize when a companion or any other npc stands next to you, blocking the field of view, same goes for walls. Essentially the whole dialogue rips you out of this immersive interactive movie that you're playing, with small annyoing details like these.
- Enemy variety and tactics: Humans and Humanoids shoot from a far or get close in a straight line to jump on you or even kamikaze you. The formula never changes. Most creatures use some dodge or burrow mechanic to close the gap to you. It gets rapidely repetitive, you'll know what to expect and often enough you can predict their movement ahead of time to mitigate damage and minimize ammo consumption.
- Realism: Even if you put on hardcore mode or whatever it's called in this one, there's no feeling of realism whatsoever. You'd expect a headshot to be a one-hit kill, it isn't. You have to unload a whole clip of any gun to the head of a foe to get them killed, or even just low on health, it's absurd. Radiation doesn't leave you with ill effects anymore or somehow influences your vision, no it just reduces your maximum health cap until you rinse it off with some old-fashioned Rad-Away.
There's more that comes to mind, but this is long enough for a basic steam game review. Fallout 4 is a good game on it's own, but it's the worst within the whole franchise. If you can look past the success and beauty of the non-Bethesda developped Fallouts (F01, F02, F:NV), then this game might satisfy you for one run, two at max and then you'd wish you were given all of those wasted hours back.
I'll leave you with a quote of Ghandi about this game:
"Todd Howard took the RP from my G!" Ghandi, 2015, PAX East

Ah yes, yet another Free-To-Play online FPS game... I'll be honest, I wasn't really expecting a lot from this game, that being said, I was pleasantly surprised.
Let's address the elephant in the room, that being the cash shop and premium items. Yes, there is premium stuff, no, there is nothing you can buy to give you a stat advantage. The only thing money will buy is a currency called Bullets, which are just skin crates. that's it, so far. It's wayy too early to tell if this will evolve into something more sinister, time will tell on that front.
Since that is out of the way, on to the rest of my unduely long review!
this game looks pretty nice, animations are good, the maps follow their own colour palettes, some are brown and grey, some more colourful. Overall map design is all very simple and easy to get a hold of, the maps are easy to learn and navigate.
Textures look good, haven't seen anything blurry or that stands out as weird, the graphical design is all very coherent if not a bit dull. The guns look very nice and tacticool.
are good, there are a couple music tracks and they're decent enough, mostly rock\metal style music, some songs sound a little bit quiter than others but it's nothing major. Gun sounds are everywhere from unique and good sounding to mediocre and bland. The starter pistol sounds like an airsoft gun. However you can generally tell the weapon type being fired pretty easily. Footsteps are loud as hell, making walking a very important tactic to employ since it'll make you completely silent.
is very reminiscent of Call of Duty meets Counter-Strike: Global Offensive. If you played any of these titles, you'll feel very comfortable in this game. The guns have almost no recoil making assault rifles feel very samey, they mostly are the same aside from varying stats, such as one rifle might do more damage with a slower rate of fire and smaller magazine size, while the other has a much large mag size, and fires faster but has lower damage.
The available primary weapons are Assault Rifles, SMGs, Shotguns, Sniper Rifles, LMGs and Designated Marksman Rifles (DMRs). They're all very straight forward, however shotguns in this game are brutal, they can take someone out with a single shot from quite far away, they have barely noticable recoil, and they fire quickly. Basically, matches, especially in Demolitions, will come down to who has the most KSG shotguns on their team, and who sees who first.
Game modes are fairly straight forward.
You have good ol' Team Deathmatch which is addictive.
Demolition 8v8 & 5v5 which is identical to DE defuse game modes in CS:GO, minus the buying.
Assassination, where one team defends a VIP (controlled by a brain dead AI, mind you.) that can die in like 4 shots, as he waddles to a helicopter. The other team has to kill the enemy team and the VIP, or kill the VIP and extract from their own helicopter. This mode is very... meh. It's out of place and not fun.
And last, but not least, Battle Match, where you have to work with your team to destroy the enemy base, which are giant supply crates or something. This mode is where classes come into play, and it's pretty hectic and clearly the main gamemode. It's okay, it's certainly one of the better modes. The maps for it are quite large as well, which is nice.
The combat is very, very fast. The time-to-kill in this game is intensely low, and fire-fights rarely last more than a couple seconds. Pretty much every weapon kills in 2 - 1 headshot, in some cases like the shotguns and close range, headshots aren't even needed to take someone out in a split second.
Grenades in this game, unlike CS:GO, are lethal. While easy to avoid, catching one will seriously injure or just outright kill you from full health.
There is "sprinting" in this game, but it's just pulling your knife out ala CS. However the interesting thing here is you have the option to hold a button to take your knife out, and then swap back to the last weapon you had upon button release. It acts like a sort of sprint button, very different feature I've never seen before. Knives themselves are just 1-hit kills if you manage to land a stab, 2 - 3 hits if you just swing it.
is where you purchase weapons and stuff like that, and I was pleasantly surprised with it. There is really nothing to buy with actual money, and they give you a LOT of cash to start with. You get 215k just for starting and doing the tutorial, guns range from 96k - 192k, and they are permenant, no repairs or anything like that, once you own a gun, you keep it forever and can use it forever. Cash is very easy to earn, you get 15K just for logging in each day, 20K or so for dailies, and around 800 for each match completed.
You also have weeklies. They award Medals which let you purchase more novelty items, like player cards, side-arms, skins and stuff like that. A Desert Eagle costs 1,500 medals, after only about 15 matches I had a little over 1,000, so it's not hard to obtain.
Overall, the store is quite nice, the menus are a bit hard to navigate, though. It remains to be seen if this game will turn P2W, only time will tell.

*I HAVE NOT FINISHED THE GAME SO THIS REVIEW IS SUBJECT TO CHANGE CURRENTLY*
Im conflicted on whether to say this is worth picking up at the moment. Several patches can easily fix issues that are gameplay related. Optimisation wise, there is somethings to be decided. So lets jump into the good, the bad and the ugly.
The game picks up in a future where xcom lost in EW (roughly around the 3 month mark from memory). The story is intriguing and the lore is interesting. Some nice throw backs to EW, but nothing super necessary.
Graphics -
The game looks nice, has a nice 'feel' to it. Things look on point. Enemy pod reveals are cool, the camera can be a little clunky but does give a satisfying feeling most of the time.  Textures are appealing and soliders look cool. Alien designs vary but Xcom 2 does a great job of the models imo.
Sound -
The soundtrack on this game is stellar. The music gets you right into the spirit of whats going on, the tension exists. Sounds are all nice, game does a great job using audio to its advantage.
Gameplay -
This is where things get shaky. Starting with difficulty. The game itself is not 'Impossible' and this is very apparent on veteran and lower difficulty. I found commander was a fair challenge. Legend has me ripping my hair out, but thats what you sign up for. The issue is apparent in veteran and lower where the game is disgustingly easy until it spikes.
Xcom 2 introduces constant mission timers. I found several issues with this. It seems very divided by players if its good or bad, it creates tension but I found timers were sometimes stupidly short and were too unforgiving. This is reinforced by procuderal generated maps. I have had missions come up where it is not viable for me to reach the objective or vip and get out in time due to the map generation. This is when I have a issue. There is nothing worse than coming into a mission and straight up accepting its a failure because you cannot reach a point in time. MODS CAN ADDRESS THIS ISSUE AND EXTEND TIMERS/TRUE CONCEALMENT.
Most of the aliens seem to be implemented well, with the exception of the faceless who punishes the player for doing what the game forces you to rush. Not a great system, but with time you can get strategy to get around these issues.
Geoscape wise. Building is more streamlined, unfortunatley the early game is very forceful and you have to take a pretty forced build order. You have to manage time more effectively. Issues arise again from the avatar project and how quickly it can accelerate in comparison to how long it takes you to do things.
Optimization -
Yeah no. Its not optimized well and that impacts the game significantly. High performance rigs can struggle to pull decent frames when it is not something that appears to be all that demanding. Hopefully the game can be optimized and this fixed.
Should you buy it?
If you have played EU/EW you have a semi idea of whats going on. The game is a fun TBS with a cool premise and interesting elements.
However, do not buy this game if you do not enjoy getting punished constantly. You can extend timers through mods or remove them entirely so dont fear them.
I am enjoying the game a lot and am having a lot of fun. The game is in a state where its playable, but some fine tuning could really polish this to be easily game of the year.

At the time of this writing I’ve devoted only a few hours to the single player game and I can see many more hours being devoted.
It has already been said but I’ll mention it again…this is a game for fans of Terraria and Minecraft. If you come into it with knowledge how the gameplay mechanics of those games work, you’ll be that much more ahead.
The learning curve is not long, but you will die often at first. When you die, you loose pixels the currency that is used for crafting and buying items in the game.
The graphics are not amazing. But that’s what makes it great. Each new species that I discover is unique and it takes some knowledge to figure out which ones will attack or not.
Honestly, I’ve only scratched the surface of the game…literally. I have not dug down into the depths to discover what’s below the planet that I’m on but I cannot wait.
There is no pausing in the game as of yet. Which is frustrating for the folks that play for a few and then get up. But, you could just craft a safe bed near some heat and sleep while you do what you do in the real world.
I would highly recommend this game to the folks who enjoy the exploration games and I cannot wait to see what the game eventually develops into.

This game is astounding. Currently it is in the beta but despite that fact it is getting wonderful support from their dev team and updates come fairly often and are certainly welcome. As everyone else has said before, this game is like Minecraft and more so like Terraria (although I must regrettably admit I have not played that game so I can't compair much there). I believe the best statment that ca be made about this game is that it is a 2D RPG based game with sandbox elements. There are delvable dungeons, boss fights brought on by a series of mini-quests/ achievements, and there are interactions between NPCs that lead to quests (the chat context is in the game although actual quests aren't available from NPCs yet). One of the qualities that makes this game almost endlessly replayable is the exploration factor. If the thought of piloting a spacecraft to an almost endless number of randomly generated planets ( in my opinion every planet seems to actually be generated from a seed in the form of x,y coordinates) then this game will be a blast.
As for the regrettable cons that every game must have, this games fall under the relm of simply being an unfinished game. There are only about 4 or 5 main boss fights as of now and with those acting as the main quests besides adventuring into the currently repetative dungeons can be a bit of a drag but again this is early game access and these things will be updated and changed. Also after you craft the final tier (as of now) weapons and armor, there is less modivation to explore and mine new materials, it also leads to less exploration in general because the craftable sets of armor and weapons are better than anything you can find while adventuring.
Again I just want to point out that the game is in beta and with one of there more recent updates adding different difficulties including permadeath I can easily see 100 hours happening from this game. And what more can you ask for from a beta?

I don't want to write a giant wall of text, so i will keep it short (or atleast try to) and summarize the pros and cons of this game. Please keep in mind that these are based on my own experience with this game. Some people have little to no issues with this game. That is why the reviews are not all negative nor are they all positive. Anyhow, back to the pros and cons:
Pros:
- it has the potential to be a great game, if playable (some recurring new mechanics that i did enjoy: timed missions,
blacksites and class mechanics (all classes are good and none of the builds are inherently weaker than the other builds.
It really depends on the mission, to determine which build is more efficient. Also, don't be afraid to experiment with
your builds. You have the option to retrain your soldiers at some point in the game.)
- most issues people have with this game are fixable
- a great and friendly community (a lot of people, who have small performance issues, can find help in the steamforums
of XCom 2)
Cons:
- crashes and freezes that leads to crashes (black, grey, red, blue screens, i have experienced them all atleast once in the
last 4 days)
- poor optimization (low to mediocre fps even on high end rigs)
- a lot of bugs and/or glitches ranging from aliens detecting/shooting you through walls to allies sinking in the floor
- poor technical support on the side of the developers (a friend of mine was advised to use the same strategy as with
XCom EU/EW. That is to play untill you crash/freeze with XCom EU/EW, then start up XCom 2 and play untill you reset
your pc. Repeat this process, if you want to play XCom 2 without black screen (or whatever colour you're
experiencing))
- no patch announcements, so you can forget about short term improvements and/or resolutions.
Conclusion (Well, i did promise to keep it short, so here are my final thoughts regarding XCom 2):
I loved XCom EU/EW and XCom LW, but sadly i am unable to enjoy and play XCom 2 due to technical difficulties. So even if i wanted to, i just can't recommend this game to anyone, untill the game is properly patched. Which is a shame, because the game has a lot of potential. I just have to wait a few weeks (or more likely months) for the game to be patched, so i can enjoy the game thoroughly and on my own terms, instead of making compromises due to poor optimization and or technical issues.
I sincerely hope, that i have dissuaded atleast some of you from buying this game in its current state, because i really want you gents and/or ladies out there, to have a great and memorable (first) experience with this fantastic franchise.
Cheers!

Fallout 4 is a game of great scale and impressive worldbuilding. It has an exceptional amount of content, and the early sense of exploring the wasteland is thrilling . Unfortunately, it turns out to be a massive letdown. Here are five reasons why.
 
1) The engine is not up to the task. Its handling of shadows is infamous. On a GTX1080 it suffers significant framerate drops, even with settings turned down. It is also plagued with glitches, such as characters sinking into the floor or the player getting stuck.
 
2) The UI is poor. Endlessly scrolling through the Misc section of your inventory to find the latest note or disc which you picked up is infuriating. The lack of any sort of indication of the locations of your companions is a glaring omission, especially given how prone they are to lag behind or disappear altogether (I had to use console commands to retrieve Dogmeat at one point).
 
3) It’s not a good RPG. You are rarely given compelling choices, and most of those are crude binary options. Skillchecks are limited to dialogue, based on RNG and are easily maxed out regardless of your character build due to the levelling system. I never felt like I was playing *my* character. I completed Fallout 2 six times just to try different character builds and choices. Once is enough for this game.
 
4) The writing is bland and forgettable for the most part. It doesn’t help that I came to this after Shadowrun: Hong Kong – a game with a compelling storyline and deep characters. Nothing about this game made me care about the people, factions or places it depicts. It was hard to choose between factions not because each had strong merits, but because I disliked them all. As the story funnelled me into wiping out person after person, I realised that I didn't care about the named characters any more than the countless faceless enemies who I'd wiped out in the wasteland. It all felt so meaningless.
 
5) It’s packed full of busywork. Settlement building is utterly pointless and inconsequential; it doesn’t matter if my settlers have no food or beds. Radiant and miscellaneous quests just act as tedious busywork to fill out the playing time. If a fraction of the time spent on this was spent on the UI, the game would be a better experience.
And a bonus negative for Australians - as usual, Bethesda have imposed a big price gouge. Make sure to buy it somewhere other than Steam.

I'm loving it, it improves nicely on the first XCOM (not the original one, haven't played it).
The fact that many missions have some sort of time pressure will irritate some (c.f. some reviews. CLARIFICATION: you can take as long as you want to make your moves, the only limit is the number of turns you get.). Be aware that there's already mods that increase the turn limit or get rid of it completely, so if it's really not your thing, you can easily play the game differently. But I think the frequent time pressure is great and it improves the game. Here's why:
-having to manage time as a resource IS strategic, contrary to some opinions. While it does remove the option to take it absolutely slow and cautious, so far, I've found there's plenty of wiggle room and making a mad dash for the objective is NOT your only option.
-time pressure is thematically very coherent with the game's premise of being resistance fighters. Not having it would create ludo-narrative dissonance.
-what the turn limit basically does is force you to give up the most effective XCOM: EU play-style, which is take it super slow, only activate one bunch of enemies at a time, spam overwatch and reload after each encounter. Unless you didn't care about winning, XCOM forced you to play like that. There were no rewards for finishing early, afaik (there were some rewards for taking risks in the expansion, though). Favouring such a slow playstyle is a bit like wasting the player's time.
-time pressure lets you experience a different, thrilling playstyle the same way playing without saves (ironman mode, iirc) helps you enjoy the game in a different way that you probably wouldn't, with saves enabled. Unless you're super disciplined, you know you end up reloading when your favorite soldier dies. Same goes for taking yet another turn, reload- and overwatch-spamming.
MISC COOL STUFF:
-A memorial for your soldiers with the option to write them an epitaph. So far, my only casualty's reads: "Whatshername will not be forgotten."
-Enemy Reinforcements: (not sure, if these also happened in XCOM: EU). It totally fits the scenario and it's very exciting to see a dropship come in and worry about what it might bring, as well as very satisfying to set up an ambush for them and wipe them when their feet touch the ground.
FINAL THOUGHTS:
If you liked XCOM:EU, you'll love this one. Give it a try as it is, and if you absolutely must play ultra-slow, simply use a mod.

I don't want to write a giant wall of text, so i will keep it short (or atleast try to) and summarize the pros and cons of this game. Please keep in mind that these are based on my own experience with this game. Some people have little to no issues with this game. That is why the reviews are not all negative nor are they all positive. Anyhow, back to the pros and cons:
Pros:
- it has the potential to be a great game, if playable (some recurring new mechanics that i did enjoy: timed missions,
blacksites and class mechanics (all classes are good and none of the builds are inherently weaker than the other builds.
It really depends on the mission, to determine which build is more efficient. Also, don't be afraid to experiment with
your builds. You have the option to retrain your soldiers at some point in the game.)
- most issues people have with this game are fixable
- a great and friendly community (a lot of people, who have small performance issues, can find help in the steamforums
of XCom 2)
Cons:
- crashes and freezes that leads to crashes (black, grey, red, blue screens, i have experienced them all atleast once in the
last 4 days)
- poor optimization (low to mediocre fps even on high end rigs)
- a lot of bugs and/or glitches ranging from aliens detecting/shooting you through walls to allies sinking in the floor
- poor technical support on the side of the developers (a friend of mine was advised to use the same strategy as with
XCom EU/EW. That is to play untill you crash/freeze with XCom EU/EW, then start up XCom 2 and play untill you reset
your pc. Repeat this process, if you want to play XCom 2 without black screen (or whatever colour you're
experiencing))
- no patch announcements, so you can forget about short term improvements and/or resolutions.
Conclusion (Well, i did promise to keep it short, so here are my final thoughts regarding XCom 2):
I loved XCom EU/EW and XCom LW, but sadly i am unable to enjoy and play XCom 2 due to technical difficulties. So even if i wanted to, i just can't recommend this game to anyone, untill the game is properly patched. Which is a shame, because the game has a lot of potential. I just have to wait a few weeks (or more likely months) for the game to be patched, so i can enjoy the game thoroughly and on my own terms, instead of making compromises due to poor optimization and or technical issues.
I sincerely hope, that i have dissuaded atleast some of you from buying this game in its current state, because i really want you gents and/or ladies out there, to have a great and memorable (first) experience with this fantastic franchise.

This game was fun, at the start. It has a nice Zelda style gameplay, good design and art, plus a good crafting system and auction house and all that kind of stuff. The problem is the game just gets outright redundant before too long. The variety of the missions and the maps in the depths leaves a ton to be desired. After awhile it also becomes clear that there isn't as much weapon variety as you may have thought, and there are some weapon and armor combos that simply overpower others making many of them pointless.
The biggest problem is that while many MMO's deal with content issues early, they continue to develop and expand the game as time goes on. The issue here is that Three Rings has hardly developed a thing in the many years since the game came out. A few maps and missions have come in, but overall the story and main questing route all stalls exactly where it has since the very beginning. They're really good at developing new prize boxes to get people to pay real money for the chance of getting some rare cosmetic item, but development of the actual game has seemingly outright stalled. This last big update they hyped for quite awhile took over a year to come out and really just consisted of a few new guns and a couple new pieces of armor.
Spiral Knights is just a great example of a good game and a good concept losing its steam due to mismanagement and greed. If they cared as much about making progress on their game as they did about finding new ways to get people to spend cash on prize boxes then their game might have a larger playerbase and they wouldn't need to stoop so low to milk the cash cow. I'd love to see this game get back on its feet as I enjoyed the content it did have, but I just don't see that happening until the developer starts to care again. When all is said and done the game is dead now.

It's fallout 3 but with slightly better graphics and a TON more content. If you haven't played 3 or New Vegas, you might as well start here, no reason to go backwards. It's a pretty typical post-apocalyptic story, it has some details but if you're not interested you don't need to worry about it. It's got that solid retro vibe to it, though it is in the future, people never left the 50's Americana behind. If you havent' played any of the recent Fallout games (shelter not included) this is a FPS/RPG hybrid, a better hybrid than Fallout 3. Obviously Bethesda acquiring iD rubbed off and helped them design a better shooter. However their VATS system is still a major focus of the game, VATS basically lets you pause the combat and select a enemy and a specific area of their body and do a 'dice roll' to see if you hit them. These attacks are more accurate and often do far more damage than you just pointing and clicking. The graphics are... ok... Fallout 4 is actually just built on the Fallout 3 engine, but modified, so for an engine that old they couldn't do much. It shows too. While animations are smoothing out more and more in games, they're still real clunky in Fallout 4. Overall, Fallout 4 does everything it can to distract you from the desperately aged engine supporting it all. They do a decent job too. Great characters, good voice acting/dialogue, a broad interesting open world, curious story, fun building mechanics, weapon building and lots of story driven side question really keep you going. Now whatever my play hours on here are, add 140 to that, because that's what I put into this on the Ps4. I ended up buying Fallout 4 on Steam because I had the original Vanilla on the console and got Fallout 4 with all its DLC on a Steam sale a year later. The DLC is pretty good, though I never ended up playing most of it. Knowing what I could do in fallout, I got rather overwhelmed at the idea of doing it all over again + lots more with the DLC after the console edition. I did the Harbor DLC which was quite good and puttered out myself. Still, if you haven't tried it, for $30 or less this is a seriously good game to get. You can easily burn 60 hours on this and not feel like you're forcing yourself. The ending is a bit bland, but Fallouts always struggle with endings much like Elder Scrolls games. Bethesda is more about telling the story and less about concluding it, their endings are typically a bit drab and blatant, or otherwise completely screwball and almost meaningless. But everything up to that is always a solid ride.

Where as Minecraft is about exploration, survival, crafting, decorating and creating your own bulidings or art projects (and for some people programming and music projects), Trove is more about fighting, mini-dungeon crawling, player progression through weapons, clothing items, RPG leveling and LOOT. Crafting as more of an after thought. You do need to find materials to make items in the world as in Minecraft but it isn't really the feature that sticks out in my mind when you play this. Crafting is more or less the thing you do so you can get even more loot to upgrade your character instead of for survival and to make your time trying to exist in the game easier. In that way Trove is essentially Destiny with a Minecraft skin on top. You'll repeatedly do the same tasks and dive into the same but only slightly different dungeons over and over again so you can get your loot and upgrade your character. The loot you get is in itself random so every time you get an item or defeat a dungeon boss it's like gambling. I somehow struck 777 on the "slots" during my time playing and got a super rare and expensive Tron Bike. Another way to put it is that this is a game that relies on Skinner Box to keep players hooked, where it apparently succeeds based on the number of people I've seen playing.
It's a nice game to waste a little time with, but for me it holds no redeeming value beyond that. I never got the feeling like I was being challenged or that I was progressing in anything beyond character progression with no story or really a point to what I was doing being made clear. That sounds like the same kind of criticism you could put for Minecraft but playing Minecraft has always been more like a "Zen Garden" thing I like to do when I feel like it. It's something I do to keep me calm with moments of excitement thrown in. Trove throws all that Zen stuff out the window to focus only on pretty mediocre action mechanics and in doing that it loses all appeal to me.
If this game is going to be more action and loot oriented it could at LEAST have a story to it to keep me interested so I know what I'm fighting for like in every other dime a dozen online massively multiplayer online game they throw at you for free on the internet. It feels like I was just being set loose in a randomly generated block world simply to beat up monsters to get loot and do other things just to get more loot to upgrade my character. The game doesn't bother to tell you everything you need to know about your character's fighting abilites (it does most, but not all) or how to find the items you need around you and just EXPECTS the player to go to a Wiki. Minecraft pretty much expected players to go to a wiki, but Minecraft started from a single group of people's website as an in beta indie project that didn't reach a major release till much later. It was already widely known from many sources that you needed to use a Wiki for information. Trove was released as a full game on Steam with dedicated servers and as a complete project, not as a work in progress like Minecraft. It just pretentiously expects you to go to the Wiki right off the bat with no hint that you should even look at one.
If you're the kind of person who likes "stuff" and getting "stuff" is the main thing that keeps you interested in video games, then you'll like this game because "stuff" and being important because you have more and better "stuff" than the other person is the main point of this game. Otherwise, if you're looking for something really exciting with some amount of depth, with a small story or something calm to do, you may be better off looking elsewhere. Also, good luck if your friends are a higher level than you and more interested in this game than you because due to monster difficulty levels you can't join them without getting slaughtered. Joining you would probably be boring unless they make a new character that is around your level. Pretty much once they've sunk more time into this game than you, you'll probably never see them very often even though you're both playing at the same time.
Trove feels like a very very striped down flashier version of Minecraft to me that takes out all the things I enjoy to focus on the things I'm kind of ok with but don't really enjoy that much.
There's a reason this game is called Trove. As in Treasure Trove. It's all about the Loot which ironically will all be gone when they eventually stop supporting this game.
On the plus side when you get loot in the environment it can't be taken by the other people in your party. Every person gets their own loot.

Fallout 4 is a game of great scale and impressive worldbuilding. It has an exceptional amount of content, and the early sense of exploring the wasteland is thrilling . Unfortunately, it turns out to be a massive letdown. Here are five reasons why.
 
1) The engine is not up to the task. Its handling of shadows is infamous. On a GTX1080 it suffers significant framerate drops, even with settings turned down. It is also plagued with glitches, such as characters sinking into the floor or the player getting stuck.
 
2) The UI is poor. Endlessly scrolling through the Misc section of your inventory to find the latest note or disc which you picked up is infuriating. The lack of any sort of indication of the locations of your companions is a glaring omission, especially given how prone they are to lag behind or disappear altogether (I had to use console commands to retrieve Dogmeat at one point).
 
3) It’s not a good RPG. You are rarely given compelling choices, and most of those are crude binary options. Skillchecks are limited to dialogue, based on RNG and are easily maxed out regardless of your character build due to the levelling system. I never felt like I was playing *my* character. I completed Fallout 2 six times just to try different character builds and choices. Once is enough for this game.
 
4) The writing is bland and forgettable for the most part. It doesn’t help that I came to this after Shadowrun: Hong Kong – a game with a compelling storyline and deep characters. Nothing about this game made me care about the people, factions or places it depicts. It was hard to choose between factions not because each had strong merits, but because I disliked them all. As the story funnelled me into wiping out person after person, I realised that I didn't care about the named characters any more than the countless faceless enemies who I'd wiped out in the wasteland. It all felt so meaningless.
 
5) It’s packed full of busywork. Settlement building is utterly pointless and inconsequential; it doesn’t matter if my settlers have no food or beds. Radiant and miscellaneous quests just act as tedious busywork to fill out the playing time. If a fraction of the time spent on this was spent on the UI, the game would be a better experience.
And a bonus negative for Australians - as usual, Bethesda have imposed a big price gouge. Make sure to buy it somewhere other than Steam.
