I'm loving it, it improves nicely on the first XCOM (not the original one, haven't played it).
The fact that many missions have some sort of time pressure will irritate some (c.f. some reviews. CLARIFICATION: you can take as long as you want to make your moves, the only limit is the number of turns you get.). Be aware that there's already mods that increase the turn limit or get rid of it completely, so if it's really not your thing, you can easily play the game differently. But I think the frequent time pressure is great and it improves the game. Here's why:
-having to manage time as a resource IS strategic, contrary to some opinions. While it does remove the option to take it absolutely slow and cautious, so far, I've found there's plenty of wiggle room and making a mad dash for the objective is NOT your only option.
-time pressure is thematically very coherent with the game's premise of being resistance fighters. Not having it would create ludo-narrative dissonance.
-what the turn limit basically does is force you to give up the most effective XCOM: EU play-style, which is take it super slow, only activate one bunch of enemies at a time, spam overwatch and reload after each encounter. Unless you didn't care about winning, XCOM forced you to play like that. There were no rewards for finishing early, afaik (there were some rewards for taking risks in the expansion, though). Favouring such a slow playstyle is a bit like wasting the player's time.
-time pressure lets you experience a different, thrilling playstyle the same way playing without saves (ironman mode, iirc) helps you enjoy the game in a different way that you probably wouldn't, with saves enabled. Unless you're super disciplined, you know you end up reloading when your favorite soldier dies. Same goes for taking yet another turn, reload- and overwatch-spamming.
MISC COOL STUFF:
-A memorial for your soldiers with the option to write them an epitaph. So far, my only casualty's reads: "Whatshername will not be forgotten."
-Enemy Reinforcements: (not sure, if these also happened in XCOM: EU). It totally fits the scenario and it's very exciting to see a dropship come in and worry about what it might bring, as well as very satisfying to set up an ambush for them and wipe them when their feet touch the ground.
FINAL THOUGHTS:
If you liked XCOM:EU, you'll love this one. Give it a try as it is, and if you absolutely must play ultra-slow, simply use a mod.

While the game is fun to play with the similarities to Terraria and having supposedly endless worlds... AND IN SPACE, there is something that I simply cannot forgive nor accept: character and world wiping.
I played the game for aprox 35 hours and had an error with my computer(not the games fault) and it restarted, and when I got back into the game, all my progress had been wiped.
So I basicly wasted 35 hours and have to do everything all over again.
Not ok.
I have no intentions to go back into the game even when it reaches full release.
To me the game wasn't fun enough to go through all that again.
It will just be a bore.
Another thing I don't like is the combat.
The melee weapons aren't very good for combat at all.
You can't swing up or down with any of the melee weapons.
And I never came across any ranged weapons that was better than the steel bow that is very weak and limited to use.
And while the enemies become harder and harder to kill, it's almost required to have a friend or get a good gun(which I never found any of).
A shield did improove a little against normal enemies solo, but when more joins the battle and the big guys come, then the shield wont help you at all.
Then you might think, "well get better armor" well sure, I just need to kill a guy that almost instakills me first before I get access to better materials.
The difficulty curve is way too steep, and does not follow the progression of the game.
And then comes the fact that there are so many worlds and most of the time, the planet you go to does not have anything usefull to you.
There is a reason people share coordinates so people don't have to search blindly in so many masive planets.
But even that has problems.
When ever the game has an update, the coordinates regenerate and the entire cosmos is renewed, making every coordinates explored before non-usable.
All of this stuff are something that can be fixed and probably is when the game is fully released, but untill then, the game isn't worth it.
I won't be playing this again since I already got through the first part of the game and won't go through it again when the game finally have been fixed.
But please bare this in mind, that all this is only while the game is in early access.
When the game is fully released, then I recomend buying the game.

Trove is a decent game that seems to base itself around its many different customization options and seemingly endless amounts of dungeons to explore that may or may not be randomly generated. However if what you are looking for is a challenging MMORPG game with an in-depth leveling system such as skill trees that highly affect how well your avatar does in combat; this is not the game you are looking for. For the 6 hours of Trove I played I find this to be a game about the adventure's and loot collecting with friends more than anything else which can greatly appeal to certain audiences. Yet the combat system is very basic and not challenging at all, I only needed one other person to travel the Trove world with in order to completely dominate this game. I never had to focus on the crafting system or anything that might improve my character because raiding dungeons will give the player all they need to become over powered.
Nonetheless this game is completely free and will be fun to even the hardcore RPG gamers for at least 3 hours minimal. Thus why I recommend you give this game a download if you have spare time.

This game is astounding. Currently it is in the beta but despite that fact it is getting wonderful support from their dev team and updates come fairly often and are certainly welcome. I believe the best statment that ca be made about this game is that it is a 2D RPG based game with sandbox elements. As for the regrettable cons that every game must have, this games fall under the relm of simply being an unfinished game. There are only about 4 or 5 main boss fights as of now and with those acting as the main quests besides adventuring into the currently repetative dungeons can be a bit of a drag but again this is early game access and these things will be updated and changed. Also after you craft the final tier (as of now) weapons and armor, there is less modivation to explore and mine new materials, it also leads to less exploration in general because the craftable sets of armor and weapons are better than anything you can find while adventuring.
Again I just want to point out that the game is in beta and with one of there more recent updates adding different difficulties including permadeath I can easily see 100 hours happening from this game. And what more can you ask for from a beta?

TLDR, Fallout 4 just doesn't meet the standards of most AAA games, and is boring ride filled with bugs and a forgetable story.
It's just an average day. You say good morning to your wife and baby, and sit down for your cup of coffee. Across from you, the news is playing on TV. Everything's calm and peaceful... Until the newscaster on TV starts to act up. "We do have... Yes, we do have coming in, confirmed reports. I repeat, confirmed reports, of nuclear detonation in New York and Pennsylvania. My God." You rush to the vault, the underground bunker the government set up in case this happened. All of a sudden, a peculiar whizzing sound. The screen flashes and a giant cloud of smoke and fire erupts in the distance. A wave of hurricane-strength winds filled with smoke and ash shoots towards you with incredible speed, just as you lower youself into the vault.
A great start to a game, but, unfortunately, the excitement ends there. I bought this game originally for the ps4, beat it, and was not impressed. It was disappointing, because I was pretty excited for it. A while later, when my pc was finally repaired, I bought the game here on steam with the mindset that the ability to add mods and play with better graphics might make the game more enjoyable. Even though I had some fun installing mods and such, the game still felt like it was missing something.
Now I love the Fallout series. Ever since the first installment I've loved Fallout. The world is so interesting, both before and after the nukes that destroyed it. So when you make a Fallout game, you have every advantage, and so much to work with. But did Bethesda use any of these advantages? No. Besides improved graphics, they have not innovated at all. It's the same mediocre story we saw in Fallout 3, just instead of a missing father, there's a missing son.
The dialogue choices are boring and hardly impact what happens, except for making your followers increase or decrease their fondness for you with the poorly implemented relationship system. Most of the time doing what's fun will make your followers hate you, so if you want to have a good relationship, expect to have to be nice all the time. Maxing out your relationship with a follower is a grind, and you are hardly rewarded for doing it anyway. You get the option to have a romantic relationship when you have a maxed out relationship, but all that really does is make them call you "Honey" or "Sweetie" and things along those lines.
Most of the followers are boring and aren't unique. The only follower I enjoyed having was the dog, because he didn't constantly badger me with the same voice lines that the other followers will constantly repeat. It's ironic that the most enjoyable follower is the dog that doesn't talk or do anything interesting.
Side quests are abysmal. After I beat the story, I went around and completed some of them. They're forgetable, and extremely repetitive. By now I'm sure you've heard the meme, "Another settlement needs your help! I'll mark it on your map!" Well, that's a line from Preston Garvey, the leader of the faction "The Minute Men", who's goal is to improve the lives of the people in The Commonwealth. (The game's setting) Now, this goal's pretty good, right? Well, it is, but not when those 11 words are repeated every time you go back to him.
This leads me to the next topic, the factions. Now, most of the factions are underwhelming, but there is one that stands out, and is by far my favorite part of the game. I'm talking about The Brotherhood. The Brotherhood faction is this giant military force where everyone has Power Suits and rocket launchers. Also, their base is a blimp. And let's not forget about Liberty Prime, the humongous robot that shouts hilarious Conservative propoganda as he obliterates the enemy. I thoroughly enjoyed that questline, and I will give credit where credit is due, it's pretty damn awesome. Unfortunately, that's really the only interesting faction.
I guess this is the part where I talk about the pros, now that I've gone on and on about the game's cons.  There are definitely some good parts to this game. The soundtrack, for one, is fantastic. Bethesda again has shown their talent when it comes to making a great sounding game. With songs like, 'It's all over, but the the crying", "Atom Bomb Baby", and "The Wanderer", you are guaranteed to tap your foot or sing along.
There are a lot of interesting creatures, as well. There's an alien, the zombie guys, and, of course, the Deathclaws, just to name a few.
Besides those things plus the Brotherhood, a lot of this game is just very forgetable and not worth $60.
If this game was $30, I would probably recommend it. But for a AAA, $60 game, this is at best a mediocre experience. With a world and backstory as interesting as Fallout, they have so many things to work with. But they didn't do anything different. And that's the main problem here. It's unexciting, and basically the same as Fallout 3. With uninspired dialogues, quests, and followers, I just can't recommend this game.
So, if you're on the fence still, here's my suggestion. Play Fallout 3, it's cheaper and basically the same thing. Mod the game with some ENB's and other graphics mods and BOOM (Nuke pun intended). Fallout 4 for $20.
That, or wait till this goes on sale.

Xcom is NOT a game for everyone. Xcom is designed in such a way as to test your ability to stay calm and collected in the face of adversity, and sometimes, extreme loses. Unless playing on "easy" or "normal", losing squad members and even missions IS THE WAY XCOM PLAYS.

I've played Xcom Enemy Unknown (and LongWar) for over 280hrs. What draws me to this turned based tactical shooter is the challenge, the frustration, followed by the (eventual) exhilaration of succeeding. Personally, I'm not impressed by games that are 95% eye candy with only 5% challenge... Games that the path to victory is all but guaranteed. I want a game that pushes me to my limits and, right when I think I cannot take it anymore, draws me back in due to interesting and dynamic game mechanics that makes me think "just one more mission" or, after failing the campaign and restarting for the 4th time, "just one more try, let me try some other tactics".
Xcom 2 is in my mind the ultimate turned based strategy with NO equal, either in the past or contemporary. You have procedurally generated maps, randomized missions, a refreshing variety of mission types, greatly improved AI, significantly improved story, large tech tree to explore, more balanced classes with interesting skills to choose from, and lots of tactical possibilities to name but a few. The cherry on top of the cake: The game itself (unlike Xcom EW/EU) is very mod friendly = unlimited future possibilities, playability, and customization.
To be fair, there are some cons. First, performance in Xcom 2 is not super responsive. There seems to be input delays, pauses and freezes when blowing things up as well as when the enemy AI is plotting their move. Nothing that is game breaking, but it does need to be addressed and fixed. Second, the timers on both certain missions as well as the Avatar Project should be tweaked. While I like the sense of urgency, at times I also feel too rushed… Some missions are even timed so short that the only path to success is to rush it in concealment and hope you don’t run into the enemy and get surrounded and swarmed by every bad guy on the entire map! And when that happens the mission is a 99% failure with moderate to heavy casualties guaranteed. In fact, the timer mechanic has been, overall, responsible for every one of my campaign fails.
In a nutshell, Xcom 2 is not for everyone… It’s certainly not for anyone who expect glass-like FPS performance with straight forward tactics and paths to victory. Xcom 2 is ultimately an extreme thinking game that FORCES you accept and manage failure and crises, while keeping the big picture in mind. While there are some issues that need to be addressed and balanced, Xcom 2 is a master piece and I suspect will go down as the ultimate turned-based cult classic.

Playing for free in Spiral Knights can be summed up thusly, Grindan: The Grindaning. To even upgrade your equipment, you have to go through the same level repeatedly for a slim chance that a rare upgrading ingredient might drop, or you can grind for money and buy another type of premium currency to buy the ingredient. Pets are useless, especially in the first 30 levels where they have a lack of skill points. The storyline is just an excuse for your characters to go grind some more in the dungeons. You can also spend real money to skip all that grinding and get to the good stuff, like weapons, boss fights, and accessories.
Otherwise, it is a nice little rpg with weapon trees, good controls, cute pets, costumes, accessories, trading ingame premium money, and all that classic junk you would expect from a mmorpg these days. Even if grinding is a large part of the game, 7/10 would reccomend again.

I'll begin by stating that Starbound is an amazing game even at an early stage. Countless worlds lie at your fingertips, waiting to be discovered and plundered of their treasures. An assortment of player and npc races add tremendous depth and flavor to Starbound, giving one the impression of the vastness of space. For those of you that think Starbound is essentially "Terraria in Space", you're only slightly correct. The gameplay is quite the same, with a few changes in mechanics that seem to have streamlined and polished the original concepts (like being able to place and remove multiple blocks at once). The graphics are very much improved and there are many different biomes already, offering a wide range of colors and textures to enjoy. Starbound's soundtrack is excellent and provides the right atmosphere and mood for the game. A sense of discovery and adventure or exploration takes you over as the tracks subtly blend into one another.
Finally, the core aspect of Starbound's gameplay progression is simple and effective: collect the necessary materials to build a device and subsequently create or obtain a "key" item, that unlocks the next tier in progression or the ability to travel to more challenging areas. Although it sounds mundane, what you actually experience along the way is what Starbound is about. Finding cool new planets and lifeforms and treasure!
For an Early Access release, this is an exceptionally polished version of what Starbound will ultimately become. Buy it now and don't think twice.

First of all, if you love XCOM:EU, get XCOM 2. There is no question. Get it and enjoy.
Let me share with why my experience with this game has been so completely amazing.
1) Ironman!
- I never got into Ironman in EU/EW, and as I read up on XCOM2 subreddit, I convinced myself that this was going to be how I would play it. On commander. First mission: I miss two flanking shots and lose a rookie as a result. That became the story that I tell that convinces others to play the game. Ironman forces you to make the most of bad situations. Ironman forces you to embrace the death of that mind-controlled top level Grenediar who was executed on an overwatch shot by her brother. It truly is the best way to play the game. I've lost missions and I've lost some of my best and brightest, but that's the game.
2) Defeat is possible.
- Again, I never retreat in games. Never throw up my hands in surrender. One gurrella op I was tasked with picking up some data. I got hung up with my high level squad fighting some ADVENT. Running out of time: I dashed up with my ranger, which activates a sectopod. And I am still fighting parts of two other groups. The mission was out of control and I knew it. I had a choice: either attempt to dash in and save the data, which would likely lead to the death of my ranger, or call for evac. I drop the evac point in the center of the battle, and get out of dodge. Game calls it a defeat. I call it a win since I'm coming home with six well-trained troops.
3) More forgiving.
- This may seem odd due to the first two points, but its very true. You have some amazing tools in your inventory this time around that really save the day. Because of that, I have botched ambushes or activated pods at all the wrong times, and yet was able to pull the victory out without losing a soldier. In one example, I was about to ambush two groups, because I didn't see another choice and I thought I could handle them all in the ambush. A third group patrols in, and I want to wait until it passes. Instead of going around the building on the path, they come into the woods, revealing my soldiers and dropping one to two hp. Overwatches pop, and I'm in a bad way. Drop a mimic beacon (life-saving) and use all the tools at my desposal and use all the crazy tools at my disposal, and I'm ready for that sectopod that comes in two turns later.
4) Smaller maps/faster fights.
- All the maps seem much smaller pieces than many of the EU/EW ones. Three buildings seem to be the norm. The most I've seen on a mission is in the neighborhood of 4 groups of enemies. This fact, timed missions, and concealment truly makes each battle go that much faster than I ever felt in EU/EW.
5) Strategic map improvements.
- At this point in the game, my tactical map game is going well. I can still lose a soldier if things go wrong, but I am past the nail-biting-waiting-for-that-one-roll portion of that game. My tech and skills give me everything I need to do the job. However, the strategic map is a whole different story. Twice the AVATAR project countdown has hit max only to be brought down in the 12 day counter and be set back. I never have enough resources to do what I want to do. The next blacksite is still two territories away. The strategic layer this time away demands as much engagement and planning as the tactical side. Choices have to be made, some things prioritized over others. It truly makes that mission your guys go on that much more important when the resource you are getting is what you need to save the Earth.
Those are my reasons why this game is so great, besides the basics that you see on most any review. Yes there are graphical bugs, and yes there are times when the turn switches and I can feel my computer chugging to process all the enviromental effects going on. But here's the reason that people who love this game give those a pass: not one of these bugs have diminished gameplay in the slightest. The one time when I attempted a hack and I couldn't see the choice, I hit Esc, and tried again and it worked.

After playing this game for 40 hours I figured i'd share my thoughts on it with you.
Seing as it's been out a few days now, i figure most of you know the general story of this game, but just in case here is a short synopsis: It's 20 years after the events of XCOM. during that time, the aliens overthrew the human governments and founded their own. They are currently in control of everything. XCOM is njow little more than a  small group of freedomfighters, with very little to their name. The goal is to stop abductions, overthrow the aliens, and get the cake. Although not a very innovative story, it is certainly interesting enough to keep you hooked.
Firaxis have let the story show through in some of its game mechanics-in both good and bad ways.  You are constantly on a timer, meaning you have to prioritize production of gear, research and facilities well. You may alos find yourself abandoning areas of the world to help out another. Every choice feels important, and this really helps carry the story forward.
On the flipside of the coin however we have the idea of timed missions. In XCOM I enjoyed them as a nice little break from the normally slow phasing, But in this game they have taken it to the extreme. Practically every mission have some sort of mission timer, usually 8 or 12 rounds, but sometimes also 6, or via the use of a "dont let the aliens blow up the computer" mechanic.
These timers are extremelly short for what you need to do, and you often find yourself forced to double move into unknown territories, just to keep up with the timer. This means you cant really react to what you find, and there's a big chance you put yourself in a flank. This mechanic would've been fine if Firaxis added a few turns  on each mission, but as it stand it is just infuriating.
The game is also extremelly buggy. there are countless amounts of visual glitches, such as bladestorming a Viper as he is entangling you causing you to be stuck in the entangled animation for the rest of the mission, or falling through a recently blown up floor causing you to lose all your animations every once in a while. The list of minor bugs can go on practically forever. This however was probably anticipated as we saw similar issues with the release of XCOM.  There are however several game breaking bugs, such as falling through roofs and getting stuck in an enviromental piece, doors on the final mission not opening, or certain enemies on the final mission warping off the map.
Enemy design is overall great. All enemies have a counterplay (although cryssalids are extremelly infuriating and not enjoyable in any way), and they all look great. They have all evolved in some way since XCOM, and it's always enjoyable to see Firaxis keeping their story at heart.
The gameplay itself is just what you'd expect from XCOM, and with the exception of the timer, and classes being reworked it is near identical. The missions have different goals, and the game focuses more on destruction of cover.
In short: The game is enjoyable, it plays mostly like XCOM EU/EW. It does have a glaring issue in the form of the mission timer, and it is absolutelly littered with bugs.  If you can overlook these two issues you will have a blast.

Only after many crippling losses, frustrating encounters, unfortunate outcomes, and landing myself in a situation where even the most mundane quests seemed impossible to complete did I truly fall in love with this game. To say that Darkest Dungeon is a hard game would be an understatement, as disaster is always a possibility and dare I say inevitable. What makes this game different from other RPGs is that luck is more involved than any objective mechanic, as anyone who has played more than ten minutes would be able to tell. With this in mind, anything is possible at any point, whether it be searching through an inconspicuous bookshelf or in a chance-encounter with a boss. In a way, you the player are in the same position as your heroes fighting for your estate, but whether you prevail against adversity or crack under pressure and end up leaving a bad review is not up to RNG. Ultimately, Darkest Dungeon is a game that demands a lot from the player mentally, and it is understandable to feel hopeless, fearful, or abusive as that is all a part of the game, but unfortunately this frustration can lead people to hate the game for being what it is; an unforgiving and unrelenting RPG that will refuse to allow everything to go in the player's favor but instead require the player to react to a poor situation.
Before buying, it is vitally important to understand what it is you're getting, and that is true with anything and is no different with this particular game. Aside from outlining the gameplay, the artstyle is incredible and I would be remiss to not mention it. The art alone was enough to entice me into buying, and I was not disappointed by that aspect of the game. All in all, everything is subject to opinion so I can only hope more people get to enjoy this game where others would not.

Great game marred by questionable design decisions. Claims that the game is completely unbalanced are overstated, as once you get a hang of the mechancis, you'll be able to overcome about seventy-five to ninty percent of the game's challenges whether you happen to be particularly good at the game or not.
And then, you'll spawn a dimensional shambler, randomly, not by interacting with the curio,walking down the hall in a short level one dungeon with a party that couldn't hope to deal with such a creature at full health, not to mention while exploring the very last hallway on low health after 'completing'  the dungeon. You won't be allowed to run away or withdraw and your stressed out heroes will do stupid things that will get the whole party killed. You'll watch helplessly as your party dies. It will have nothing to do with your knowledge of the game or your personal ability, it'll just be random bad luck and either you'll suck it up 'git gud' by senselessly griding out another party of adventurers or you'll go play games that are actually challenging because of the decisions you make rather than completely random rolls on the encounter table. Beating this game isn't so much a question of skill as it is persistence.
It is a testament to how otherwise fun this game is that I'll probably come back in a week or two and pointlessly bang my head against the pseudorandom challenge that is Darkest Dungeon again.

After playing this game for 40 hours I figured i'd share my thoughts on it with you.
Seing as it's been out a few days now, i figure most of you know the general story of this game, but just in case here is a short synopsis: It's 20 years after the events of XCOM. during that time, the aliens overthrew the human governments and founded their own. They are currently in control of everything. XCOM is njow little more than a  small group of freedomfighters, with very little to their name. The goal is to stop abductions, overthrow the aliens, and get the cake. Although not a very innovative story, it is certainly interesting enough to keep you hooked.
Firaxis have let the story show through in some of its game mechanics-in both good and bad ways.  You are constantly on a timer, meaning you have to prioritize production of gear, research and facilities well. You may alos find yourself abandoning areas of the world to help out another. Every choice feels important, and this really helps carry the story forward.
On the flipside of the coin however we have the idea of timed missions. In XCOM I enjoyed them as a nice little break from the normally slow phasing, But in this game they have taken it to the extreme. Practically every mission have some sort of mission timer, usually 8 or 12 rounds, but sometimes also 6, or via the use of a "dont let the aliens blow up the computer" mechanic.
These timers are extremelly short for what you need to do, and you often find yourself forced to double move into unknown territories, just to keep up with the timer. This means you cant really react to what you find, and there's a big chance you put yourself in a flank. This mechanic would've been fine if Firaxis added a few turns  on each mission, but as it stand it is just infuriating.
The game is also extremelly buggy. there are countless amounts of visual glitches, such as bladestorming a Viper as he is entangling you causing you to be stuck in the entangled animation for the rest of the mission, or falling through a recently blown up floor causing you to lose all your animations every once in a while. The list of minor bugs can go on practically forever. This however was probably anticipated as we saw similar issues with the release of XCOM.  There are however several game breaking bugs, such as falling through roofs and getting stuck in an enviromental piece, doors on the final mission not opening, or certain enemies on the final mission warping off the map.
Enemy design is overall great. All enemies have a counterplay (although cryssalids are extremelly infuriating and not enjoyable in any way), and they all look great. They have all evolved in some way since XCOM, and it's always enjoyable to see Firaxis keeping their story at heart.
The gameplay itself is just what you'd expect from XCOM, and with the exception of the timer, and classes being reworked it is near identical. The missions have different goals, and the game focuses more on destruction of cover.
In short: The game is enjoyable, it plays mostly like XCOM EU/EW. It does have a glaring issue in the form of the mission timer, and it is absolutelly littered with bugs.  If you can overlook these two issues you will have a blast.

This game starts off as being a cute mindless distraction, but quickly slammed me into a paywall.
The game is divided into missions that transport you to the same few stages over and over again.  The only difference is the enemy layout, and the placement of the beginning and goal of the course.  In some respects, it's similar to Monster Hunter in that way.  Gameplay is arcade-style brawler/SHMUP, with lots of avatar customizability.
The wall comes in the form of equipment prerequisites before being able to move onto the final missions in certain chapters.  Basically "you must have a full set of X-star gear before moving onto the next mission".  This wouldn't normally be a problem, except that you have to first grind the level of the equipment to a certain threshold by using it in battle, and then use materials and money gathered to forge the item into a higher level, and then, once a level threshold is reached, use more mats and monies to forge it into the next tier item of your choice.
Stuck behind the mission leading to the final chapter because I didn't have 5 star gear. and determined to figure out if playing the game legitimately was possible, I started grinding the levels en masse, and investing it into the auction house, playing the dual-currency economy to quickly (read: slowly) amass the materials and money required to level all six or seven items that I needed.  It took two weeks of dropping everything I was doing every two hours, logging on to manage the auction house to gather resources, and then an hour or so a day just grinding to get the equipment I needed to gain entrance to the mission and move on with the game.
Did it feel like an accomplishment when I completed the task?  Yes.  That is, it did until I realized that I could have just paid OOO like, 5 or 10 bucks and have bought the materials needed with real cash and moved on earlier.
It wouldn't have stung as much if the game had more content past that last equipment threshold, but there were only a few missions after that, which equated to maybe 45 minutes of game time.  Should I have paid $10 to basicaly access the end of the game sooner?  I don't think so.
I have played this game off and on for a few years, and it's gone through a few iterations, but I can say for certain that the implementation of the crystals as materials was not a good idea.  I would have liked much more endgame, elite-tier content than I received.  Even when considering the optional sidequests and the DLC, they just amount to different equipment, and don't add anything to the story.
I think OOO should consider a recalibrating the way the crystals work, and creating a meatier, story-driven DLC/add-on, instead of just making the game a skinner box.  Heck, I would even tolerate ads in the loading screens if that's what it took to make it lucrative enough for the team to make more content.
It's time to open the Core, guys.

SNAPSHOT
A Lovecraftian game built to mirror the stress and sanity loss between the player and the characters in the game.
OVERALL - 6 / 10
PROS
+ great atmosphere / aesthetics
+ satisfying meta progression
CONS
- huge emphasis on very poor RNG
- game is balanced heavily against the player early on
- gameplay gets repetitive quickly
DETAILS
I'm going to say this up front: I save scummed the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of this game, and I don't feel one iota of remorse. Overall, the game has a lot of fun elements to it, but the fun parts are dwarfed by the stress and frustration that it creates due to poor design choices, mostly those that were added post-alpha. Pre-alpha the game was a lot of fun, often pitting the player into darkness but giving them eventual hope and opportunities to climb out of it. Post-alpha the player is pushed into a well with no rope to climb back up. The game is built to be challenging, but what Darkest Dungeon delivers is an iron maiden of epic proportions: the more you play, the more you bleed out what little energy you have left to come back and get slapped in the face by the massive amounts of RNG you have to rely on.
Darkest Dungeon pits players against a perpetually stacked deck, which only gets worse the longer you play. The game is built to put the PCs into a dying state quickly and often, which is compounded upon by the heart attack mechanic. Introduced sometime after alpha, and a longstanding point of contention, heart attacks cause a PC to instantly enter a dying state, regardless of health, or die permanently if they are already dying. Because of this, often times the game ends up chaining multiple events together that can easily wipe a party, regardless of how well you are doing.
Sanity loss for PCs leads to afflictions, which basically makes the given PC suicidal for the rest of the dungeon. More often than not an afflicted PC will skip their turn, refuse healing, shift the party order around, or somehow injure or debuff themselves. It would be one thing if an affliction only caused one of these things, or even if there was a limit as to how often they could happen, but instead they often happen in succession, which causes other party members to lose sanity and gain an affliction, and the cycle repeats. This quickly leads to an entire party wiped because 75% of your turns are either skipped or used to re-arrange heroes because they can't do anything else (not even defend). This is, in short, not fun whatsoever.
Aside from the in-dungeon frustrations, the game also has a level restriction on those that can enter the dungeon, with PCs claiming that they "wouldn't learn anything from the experience", or some other ridiculous reasoning. This is actually probably my biggest gripe, even moreso than heart attacks. This level restriction makes it extremely frustrating to try and level up other heroes to replace the ones that die or are otherwise unable to function for the dungeon. Unfortunately, it appears that the lowest level dungeons are also the least well balanced, so the player is forced to trudge through them again and again, re-living the nightmares they thought they had previously overcome.
Overall, I do like Darkest Dungeon, when the dice are in my favor. When they aren't (which is ~75% of the time, it seems), the game is just an unending stream of frustration. The thrill, charm, and balance this game had with heroes constantly teetering on the brink of death in pre-alpha has given way to the hopelessness and malaise introduced with the post-launch changes, and given that I play games to relieve stress and have fun, this is the opposite of the desired result. As such I cannot recommend that others willingly subject themselves to it, however if you do make sure you keep the lights on and bring a lot of torches.

So, I'm not insanely far into the game, so this will be kind of just a, first few hours of gameplay impression kind of review.
Now, from what the images and videos of this game suggested, this game is supposed to be super hard, anxiety inducing, just all kinds of stressful. Me being the individual I am, Dark Souls is my kind of game to simply relax to and most every game I play, I play on the hardest difficulty. It's just what I do. So when I saw this game advertising itself as some super difficult, stressful experience, I was immediatley intrigued on how large of a challenge it would actually present itself as. First thing I notice when I started was that there was not a difficulty setting which made me a little skeptical that the game would be too easy. However, once I really got into the game itself and started experiencing what the dungeons and fights were like... Oh my goodness. I am happy to say this is one of the best, difficult games I've played that actually IS difficult and quite a stressful, challenging experience with every dungeon that you set out to explore.
What I really love about the game and its dungeons is that it makes you think really hard on what items you'll need to bring, what characters you'll want to take, and how you want to them ot operate in their formation. Let me elaborate on the characters here.
You have several differnt classes that you can hire in the game and you can only take four of them into a dungeon at a time. Each of these characters has their own skillsets that match them to what role theyr're supposed to fulfill and with that role also comes with where you want to put them in formation. Your formation determines what skills they are allowed to use and what enemies those skills will hit. it's a pretty awesome way to tackle a single player party system in my opinion.
All of your items begin to feel sacred as you learn to treasure them more and more because of how important it is to have food or shovels or torches at a specific time. You also can't just waste a bunch of money on items thinking you'll be cool, because then by the time your done with that dungeon, you will need to have made a good enough haul to be able to by more items for the next trip, help relieve the stress of your characters by spendning thousands on them, improving gear so that fights become easier, all while also trying to keep some of that gold on the side in order to make a steady profit and not just breaking even.
At a certain point you can start to relax a little though once you're able to recruit four new people at once, which as grim as it is, makes people more disposable because you will always have a full party. However this does, by no means, mean that the game gets less stressful when actual fighting through the dungeons.
This is basically the extent of my experience in the game thus far and I look forward to delving deeper into the madness of Darkest Dungeon. I hope this review helped.

Bad:

TL;DR: Try this game out, it's rather enjoyable.
Okay, so. I have obviously delved a bit of time into this game recently. Here's why.
- The game is easy enough that you don't just want to quit from the grind, as the grind is actually quite fast and enjoyable. You won't be spending long times at each dungeon, in fact I can usually clear dungeons in about 1 minute. And because of how close dungeons are, you will be clearing out biomes in about 10-15 minutes.
- Getting resources is relatively easy aswell, which makes it less troublesome to farm that stupid amount of resources it takes for some things.
-Making a guild is free. Yeah, which in a game like this is typical, however what is not typical is the fact you end up getting to make a guild world without a fee. Which is pretty darn fine.
- Each class is a seperate character, much like a co op game such as Team Fortress 2. You can freely swap into any class you have already unlocked, and their gear, and stats are retained from last you played them. This adds game time as you are constantly working on getting a class to max level, and unlocking classes takes very little time. Once you've done the tutorial and gotten to Mastery 30, you will probably have unlocked at least 4 classes.
Bad stuff:
All games have something bad, and here's what I think is BAD about Trove.
-Classes are far too linear, there is absolutely no skill structure to anyone. An ARPG like this should have ability trees.
LITERALLY, each class has: A passive, and 3 active abilities. It's sad, I really wish there was something more to the leveling up aspect of this game, which brings us to part 2.
-You are entirely dependant on gear, rather than your skill. Yes, like most MMOs you aren't exactly relying on skill to get you through a tough spot. And while yes, this game DOES require you to bob and weave in and out of combat to keep yourself alive, once you've gotten max level gear on a max level character... you are unkillable. And you can easily just swap this gear onto another similar class of a lower level and get THAT character to max level in no time.
Where this game could use a revision is the aforementioned ability tree. Give players a bit more customization to their characters than just aesthetic.

Only after many crippling losses, frustrating encounters, unfortunate outcomes, and landing myself in a situation where even the most mundane quests seemed impossible to complete did I truly fall in love with this game. To say that Darkest Dungeon is a hard game would be an understatement, as disaster is always a possibility and dare I say inevitable. What makes this game different from other RPGs is that luck is more involved than any objective mechanic, as anyone who has played more than ten minutes would be able to tell. With this in mind, anything is possible at any point, whether it be searching through an inconspicuous bookshelf or in a chance-encounter with a boss. In a way, you the player are in the same position as your heroes fighting for your estate, but whether you prevail against adversity or crack under pressure and end up leaving a bad review is not up to RNG. Ultimately, Darkest Dungeon is a game that demands a lot from the player mentally, and it is understandable to feel hopeless, fearful, or abusive as that is all a part of the game, but unfortunately this frustration can lead people to hate the game for being what it is; an unforgiving and unrelenting RPG that will refuse to allow everything to go in the player's favor but instead require the player to react to a poor situation.
Before buying, it is vitally important to understand what it is you're getting, and that is true with anything and is no different with this particular game. Aside from outlining the gameplay, the artstyle is incredible and I would be remiss to not mention it. The art alone was enough to entice me into buying, and I was not disappointed by that aspect of the game. All in all, everything is subject to opinion so I can only hope more people get to enjoy this game where others would not.

After completing the game, I can say without a doubt that Xcom 2 is one of the most well crafted games I've ever had the pleasure of experiencing. It takes everything the reboot did well and refines it. Upon writing this I spent 35 hours on my first playthrough, over the course of four days, and I could not stop playing this game. It's just so damn good.
I suppose you could say Enemy Unknown/Within's Story was pretty good. A lot of people were upset that in this game the "orginal" Xcom lost the war. Personally, I think it makes the game far more personal. It allows the story to have far more depth, especially with characters who lived or have been affected by the loss of the war. The new scientist Dr. Tygan and enginerr Lily Shen are both interesting characters. Some of my favorite moments were when they would drop a comment in the Avenger, the game's base. The return of Bradford adds a warm familiarity to all the new, but gives you a look into how much the world has changed. These three characters "make" the story, adding to a already great plot. The alien's involvement is well written, and fits in well with EU/EW. You feel compelled to discover their plans and stop them.
Overall I think it's a fantastic story from a genre that doesn't require one. It just makes the game that much better.

I'll split this into two parts, your time spent on the Avenger, the game's base, and the actual missions.
When I first heard about the Avenger and the new "hologlobe" I was worried it become overcomplicated, and drag away from the game. I'm so pleased I was wrong. The amount of choices you can make are incredible, but not overbearing. So much so that each playthrough differs, giving the game more replay value. Moving away from the "satillite meta" of EU/EW, the game offers you random events, some of which are missions and others are resources, which you can respond to. During which your Scientists research, and your engineers construct, create, or maintain the different facilities of the Avenger. This leads to the similar micromanagement of the first game that makes you almost hate when a mission pops up. There are many small changes that make the formual feel fresh and fun.
The missions take the Xcom turn based combat and crank it up a notch. They fixed a lot of the issues with the first game, like overwatched soldiers all firing at the same enemy. This makes the game feel more fair, but still challenging. With the new concealment mechanic you can set up ambushes and quickly take out your foes, which looks great with the action camera. Occassionally the game gives you a mission timer, pushing you towards your objective. This breaks the "Move and Overwatch" strategies from the first game, forcing you to think and react to your surroundings. For some, this can be a little challenging, but Xcom has never been a easy game. I find they really add to the game, in the same way Meld from the Enemy Within DLC changed the way you play. When there is a objective, it is clearly defined on the playfield so you don't have to go searching for it. The mission variety itself feels quite diverse, really immersing you into the world of a Guerrilla Xcom.
The new skill trees are more distinct than the orginals. Each side promotes a specific style of play, but you can easily cross between them to fit your tactics. Do you want a Specialist who provides Healing for the team, or a offensive hacker abusing the alien's reliance on machines? It's all down to how you want to play, and having multiple of the same class really helps. The reworked five classes work really well in the game, and the cooldowns on abilities allow your soldiers to make critical plays, without making them overpowered. I have a fondness for each class, it would have been far more difficult to complete the game without any of them.
As for the customization, Firaxis has outdone themselves. It isn't on the level of a RPG, but they have enough choices to make your characters far more unique than they were in EU/EW, and of course more heart breaking when you lose them. I loved spending time writing stories for each of my soldiers, creating my own little substories while the campaign goes on.

Xcom 2 is awsome but i like Xcom more.
This is pretty much how I felt the last time I started playing XCOM, way back in 2012, but I’d liken the game more to XCOM’s “Enemy Within” expansion in 2013. A comprehensive update to the gameplay, customization, and flow of the original, “Enemy Within” made XCOM the game it should have been at launch.
XCOM 2 is better. Not only are customization options far more varied even than the expanded XCOM, the game is simply deeper, more challenging, and more fun in almost every way. Still, it’s not without its problems.
Lets take a look at the Good, The Bad, and The Insulting of Firaxis’ ambitious sequel.
Customization- I have way too much fun customizing my soldiers. This was severely lacking in XCOM, massively expanded in “Enemy Within” and has reached critical mass in XCOM 2. If you like customization options, they are here in abundance, from language and voice options, to props like sunglasses and baseball caps, to facial hair and scars. When a soldier reaches a certain rank, even more options are opened up
Enemy Variety- Enemy variety is almost overwhelming at times. You learn to tread carefully and start making a kill-priority list very early on
More Tactical- Alongside the increased enemy variety is an increased sense of panic at the rest of the challenges. Whether that’s rescuing civilians, blowing up an enemy base, or getting to an enemy data bank before it self-destructs, there’s often some sort of primary or secondary objective that makes your life even harder
Features- Adding to the tactical flavor are some new game features. Often you start the map out in Concealment mode, and can move through the map unseen by the aliens. This allows you to set up masterful ambushes and take out multiple bogies in one fell swoop.
Swords - Using swords is awesome. Every game should have swords.
The Scenario Makes Way More Sense- Here we had a global effort to fight back against an alien horde, and we were barely able to fund it. And why were so few soldiers taking on these missions? This time around you lead an underground resistance to the aliens and their global domination organization ADVENT. Having limited resources and a small, elite squad makes way more sense.
More Strategic Depth- Alongside more tactical missions, your base of operations and world-map are now way more complex. There’s a consequence for every action, too, which means you’ll probably screw up a lot. Or at least, I screw up a lot, or I think I do.
It’s All A Bit Too Much - You can barely get one thing done without being interrupted a bazillion times by all the various projects you have going, by new missions popping up, or new resource collecting timers going off. Even when you get through a month and the powers-that-be send you your supplies, you have to go spend a few days picking them up. During that time any number of horrible things can happen, and all the while the ADVENT clock is ticking, leading toward some new calamity.
Frankly, it’s just too much going on at once to be enjoyable at times. There’s almost no breathing room, even in the very beginning, and it’s very easy to slid into chaos.
Mental Distress- Let me give example for you: I’ve got my four squad mates lined up just right to take out some bad guys. A dudes is in Overwatch, and the girl I have shooting has an 87% chance of success. Then she misses. My Overwatch dudes miss. Everyone misses and the enemies flank me. One of my squad mates gets hit by an alien with a sword, knocks them unconscious, so they’re out of the game. Then two of my squaddies panic and shoot wildly at nothing. Then a Sectoid takes over the mind of my fourth soldier and I’m out. I can’t do anything. There was nothing I could have done any better, either. I set it all up perfectly. I had a good chance of landing a shot and then taking out at least a couple of the aliens with Overwatch. But because half my squad panicked, one was knocked out, and the other got mind-controlled, I had no options left.
(After this incidence i took a 3 hours nap)
Repetition- In missions where you have to save civilians, you’re going to lose a bunch of them no matter how good you are. Aliens start picking them off instantly, and it’s a race just to grab the bare minimum. But each time the aliens kill someone, your right-hand man “Central” pops up on the screen to chastise you. “We cant afford to loose too many civilians, Commander!” he intones, or something like that. Many times over. The game pauses while he says his bit, which is really irritating. Stuff like this happens throughout the game. It’s repetitive, slow, and annoying. You should at least be able to play while the NPC’s are dressing you down for being a pathetic loser.
My character fall of a building and KIA. One time the game just went black. Sometimes animation freezes for an agonizingly long time when Overwatch is triggered, ETCs.
It’s top of the class when it comes to turn-based tactical gameplay, and I honestly can’t get enough.

Even though this game was (and after 125 hours still is) the most engaging and satisfying experience of 2016 for me, it is rather hard to analyze why exactly that is.
I guess at its core the game found a combination of buttons to push to make me love it to bits. While the dungeons never quite become a walk in the park, you realize after a while, that you're not supposed to turn into an unstoppable killing machine, steamrolling towards the end credits powered only by your growing boredom. Instead, you are repeatedly told and shown that the horrors your little henchmen face are way more similar to the stress you feel yourself when trying to guide them through.
Yet the stress you face in the dungeons and, above all, the anticipation of horrors that await you next, is what makes the whole experience surprisingly Zen. Yes, you will find yourself nerd-raging and screaming obscenities at the screen quite a lot, however, even if you faced the worst outcome, you come to realization that it won't ruin your life, and in the grand scheme of things it's nothing you can't overcome. I guess there is a valuable life lesson in that.

The graphics are beautiful, and the map variety is a huge step up from the X-Com EU and EW.
The customizations and individualization of the soldiers is top-notch. Options include weapon and armor patterns, tattoos, eye color, glasses, and bandannas. Attitudes determine how they behave in the Skyranger during loading screens, and what they say on the battlefield. Soldiers who are gravely wounded will even get scars. You can design your own soldiers and put them in a pool that will used in the game.
Weapons can be upgraded with parts found in missions or purchased from the Black Market. Is your sniper constantly reloading? Give them a larger clip or a free reload each mission. Instead of having to share weapons, once a weapon is researched and built, it becomes equipment that any soldiers of the correct class can use. This means that you spend less time mining for elerium and alloys. Armor gives you a general upgrade that everyone can use, but you do still have to build each special armor individually.
The aliens have a wide variety of troops to field, including hidden troops that can ambush your soldiers. Old favorites are back, and a whole slew of new ones. Advent troopers are near human, sectoids have gotten an upgrade, and the rest are more advanced than the first game.
Everything about the game is top notch.
The learning curve on Veteran mode is extreme. During my first play-through, I was suffering 50% or higher casualties per mission and had to save scum constantly just to survive. Many aliens could one-shot kill my soldiers and took two hits each to take down. They traveled in groups of three and moved fast enough that one of them was always able to flank for their shot. Many of the missions had timed objectives, meaning that we had to charge headlong towards the extraction point instead of moving cautiosly. Getting bogged down in a firefight for a couple of rounds meant we weren't going to make it and the squad would be captured.
I restarted the game in Rookie mode. Fewer and weaker enemies meant that I could I get a better idea of how to fight them and a feel for the game's rhythm. I was able to progress through the story line and get a better feel for what my squad was capable of. When I went back to Veteran mode, it felt more even, although I still have a lot of save scum moments.
Concealment doesn't feel like it adds much to me. Most maps have an objective that is heavily guarded. Being concealed to that point means that aliens will converge from all corners of the map once you are spotted. This results in your squad being surrounded and having to take on 12 or more aliens from all sides. For me, it was better to blow concealment early and face them in waves.
Overall, the game looks and plays well. I've seen a few glithces here and there, but nothing game stopping. The real challenge is the difficulty. Too often, missions hinge on luck of the RNG rather than strategy.

After completing the game, I can say without a doubt that Xcom 2 is one of the most well crafted games I've ever had the pleasure of experiencing. It takes everything the reboot did well and refines it. Upon writing this I spent 35 hours on my first playthrough, over the course of four days, and I could not stop playing this game. It's just so damn good.
I suppose you could say Enemy Unknown/Within's Story was pretty good. A lot of people were upset that in this game the "orginal" Xcom lost the war. Personally, I think it makes the game far more personal. It allows the story to have far more depth, especially with characters who lived or have been affected by the loss of the war. The new scientist Dr. Tygan and enginerr Lily Shen are both interesting characters. Some of my favorite moments were when they would drop a comment in the Avenger, the game's base. The return of Bradford adds a warm familiarity to all the new, but gives you a look into how much the world has changed. These three characters "make" the story, adding to a already great plot. The alien's involvement is well written, and fits in well with EU/EW. You feel compelled to discover their plans and stop them.
Overall I think it's a fantastic story from a genre that doesn't require one. It just makes the game that much better.

I'll split this into two parts, your time spent on the Avenger, the game's base, and the actual missions.
When I first heard about the Avenger and the new "hologlobe" I was worried it become overcomplicated, and drag away from the game. I'm so pleased I was wrong. The amount of choices you can make are incredible, but not overbearing. So much so that each playthrough differs, giving the game more replay value. Moving away from the "satillite meta" of EU/EW, the game offers you random events, some of which are missions and others are resources, which you can respond to. During which your Scientists research, and your engineers construct, create, or maintain the different facilities of the Avenger. This leads to the similar micromanagement of the first game that makes you almost hate when a mission pops up. There are many small changes that make the formual feel fresh and fun.
The missions take the Xcom turn based combat and crank it up a notch. They fixed a lot of the issues with the first game, like overwatched soldiers all firing at the same enemy. This makes the game feel more fair, but still challenging. With the new concealment mechanic you can set up ambushes and quickly take out your foes, which looks great with the action camera. Occassionally the game gives you a mission timer, pushing you towards your objective. This breaks the "Move and Overwatch" strategies from the first game, forcing you to think and react to your surroundings. For some, this can be a little challenging, but Xcom has never been a easy game. I find they really add to the game, in the same way Meld from the Enemy Within DLC changed the way you play. When there is a objective, it is clearly defined on the playfield so you don't have to go searching for it. The mission variety itself feels quite diverse, really immersing you into the world of a Guerrilla Xcom.
The new skill trees are more distinct than the orginals. Each side promotes a specific style of play, but you can easily cross between them to fit your tactics. Do you want a Specialist who provides Healing for the team, or a offensive hacker abusing the alien's reliance on machines? It's all down to how you want to play, and having multiple of the same class really helps. The reworked five classes work really well in the game, and the cooldowns on abilities allow your soldiers to make critical plays, without making them overpowered. I have a fondness for each class, it would have been far more difficult to complete the game without any of them.
As for the customization, Firaxis has outdone themselves. It isn't on the level of a RPG, but they have enough choices to make your characters far more unique than they were in EU/EW, and of course more heart breaking when you lose them. I loved spending time writing stories for each of my soldiers, creating my own little substories while the campaign goes on.
No game is perfect, but Xcom 2 nearly reaches it. Here are some of the issues I found with the game.
If you have any questions for further information, feel free to ask.

SNAPSHOT
A Lovecraftian game built to mirror the stress and sanity loss between the player and the characters in the game.
OVERALL - 6 / 10

CONS

DETAILS
I'm going to say this up front: I save scummed the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of this game, and I don't feel one iota of remorse. Overall, the game has a lot of fun elements to it, but the fun parts are dwarfed by the stress and frustration that it creates due to poor design choices, mostly those that were added post-alpha. Pre-alpha the game was a lot of fun, often pitting the player into darkness but giving them eventual hope and opportunities to climb out of it. Post-alpha the player is pushed into a well with no rope to climb back up. The game is built to be challenging, but what Darkest Dungeon delivers is an iron maiden of epic proportions: the more you play, the more you bleed out what little energy you have left to come back and get slapped in the face by the massive amounts of RNG you have to rely on.
Darkest Dungeon pits players against a perpetually stacked deck, which only gets worse the longer you play. The game is built to put the PCs into a dying state quickly and often, which is compounded upon by the heart attack mechanic. Introduced sometime after alpha, and a longstanding point of contention, heart attacks cause a PC to instantly enter a dying state, regardless of health, or die permanently if they are already dying. Because of this, often times the game ends up chaining multiple events together that can easily wipe a party, regardless of how well you are doing.
Sanity loss for PCs leads to afflictions, which basically makes the given PC suicidal for the rest of the dungeon. More often than not an afflicted PC will skip their turn, refuse healing, shift the party order around, or somehow injure or debuff themselves. It would be one thing if an affliction only caused one of these things, or even if there was a limit as to how often they could happen, but instead they often happen in succession, which causes other party members to lose sanity and gain an affliction, and the cycle repeats. This quickly leads to an entire party wiped because 75% of your turns are either skipped or used to re-arrange heroes because they can't do anything else (not even defend). This is, in short, not fun whatsoever.
Aside from the in-dungeon frustrations, the game also has a level restriction on those that can enter the dungeon, with PCs claiming that they "wouldn't learn anything from the experience", or some other ridiculous reasoning. This is actually probably my biggest gripe, even moreso than heart attacks. This level restriction makes it extremely frustrating to try and level up other heroes to replace the ones that die or are otherwise unable to function for the dungeon. Unfortunately, it appears that the lowest level dungeons are also the least well balanced, so the player is forced to trudge through them again and again, re-living the nightmares they thought they had previously overcome.
Overall, I do like Darkest Dungeon, when the dice are in my favor. When they aren't (which is ~75% of the time, it seems), the game is just an unending stream of frustration. The thrill, charm, and balance this game had with heroes constantly teetering on the brink of death in pre-alpha has given way to the hopelessness and malaise introduced with the post-launch changes, and given that I play games to relieve stress and have fun, this is the opposite of the desired result. As such I cannot recommend that others willingly subject themselves to it, however if you do make sure you keep the lights on and bring a lot of torches.

This game has been getting some bad rap from some people. Said people walked into the game expecting something that the game isn't. So here's a fair review of Darkest Dungeon:
1. Yes; the game is a rougelike. It is tough, dark, challenging, and will be punishing at times. Is it an impossibly difficult game? No. But it is difficult. At times it will have you frustrated, but that's the point. The game sets out to make sure you DON'T get too attached to your heroes. They will, in all liklihood, die. And that's what people hate. They hate that they can't just waltz through a game, get a few boo-boos, and then truck through the rest of the fight with no danger. The fights don't work that way. Hero death happens, and it's critical that you avoid it if at all possible obviously. But there are times when you weigh your options and you make the wrong choice. This game won't hold your hand for you. You are the master of your actions: you deal with your consquences.
People often complain that their tactics in one dungeon didn't work in another dungeon. That's because each dungeon offers a range of new challanges that must be faced with new tactics. Why would your blight heavy party, who was able to destroy the blight-prone skeletons of the ruins meet the same monotonous victory in the warrens, where the pig men are used to disease and blight? Pick new heroes ffs. Get some curse and bleed up in there. (Pro tip, a party with no tank goes really badly. A party with no capability of healing also goes really badly).
This game does what it's supposed to, and it does it rather well. It shows the player that your actions have consequences, and you need to put a decent amount of forethought into your strategies. Don't get too bummed out when a hero dies. It happens. Total party wipes happen. You can avoid those if you know when to retreat. But if it does happen, just move on and assemble a new team and learn from your mistakes, as you do with any other game (dare I say, and life in general).

A pretty great game with an awful story. Gunplay and systems in a bethesda game are the best they've ever been, some of the smoothest gameplay in their titles, and most of the weird quirks that were present in skyrim haven been adjusted. Asides from that, the quest system and story are worse by almost tenfold. The radiant quest system that was awful in Skyrim(go to x dungeon, kill y draugr) has become the settlements system and feels like even more busy work, most of the quests and characters outside of the main questline don't have strange quirks or memorable storylines. The additions to gameplay and the crafting system have helped make a satisfying town management metagame, but doesn't fix the weak story and forgettable characters. I am not even sure how they managed in a quirky off-future radioactive wasteland, but Bethesda have made one of the most playable games with absolutely no charm whatsoever. This is easily their worst vanilla experience, and it shows across the board, it's still a perfectly servicable game, but there's nothing sci-fi, hard fantasy, about it. The graphics look hit or miss, but usually miss, the texture work is pretty bad, and the engine powering it is ancient at this point. Performance is some kind of enigma, all over the place at times, but typically pretty smooth, the loading times without an SSD are obnoxiously long. Gunplay is pretty tight and smooth, no COD or BF by any means, but definitely the best they've been. Dialogue is the worst it's been, choosing a VA for the main character really was the worst selection in bethesda's case. When choosing a VA you should always consider how much you are gonna pay them based on the dialogue, which in bethesda's case, it's an RPG, there's gonna be a bunch, except instead of writing intricate dialogue or multiple options for scenarios across the game, they chose the simplest option: Every option equals yes unless it begins a quest. They wrote three factions to choose from which are all comically unlikeable, no intracacies across any of them, no grey zone strange compromises at all, You're either a hippie trying to liberate sears electronics, some kind of weird patriot that fixes every leaky sink in town, or a hardcore soldier who don't like no technology and nothing different, It's comical how awful the factions are written, since Fallout NV, which was written by Obsidian, but a nearly 7 year old game, which exists in your same universe has you outclassed. I can easily recommend this game based on the fun of playing it for about 50 hours, but the wear at the edge of this grilled cheese becomes soggy at about 20 hours in, and you start to notice they've placed no emphasis on anything about the RPG aspects since Skyrim almost immediately.

After a long wait, XCOM 2 is out, to grab us by the balls once again, whip our backs, and command us to call it Mama Susie. This is not an easy game. This is not a fun game. You will feel hype, enthusiasm as you hit your first shot, you will curse at your buddy Billy that you named your best soldier after, because he missed a 95% shot. GET YOUR♥♥♥♥♥♥TOGETHER BILLY.
You will feel the excitement when you finally get that ♥♥♥♥♥ mission that you were stuck on for hours, immense satisfaction when you finally kill that mo$^£$%"£ piece of $"$%"%&^ c*cksucking codex that keeps teleporting around the map and clones itself, and it just WON'T ♥♥♥♥ING DIE.
You will feel your balls shrinking up as the aliens almost complete the avatar project, and you only have 20 days to stop them, and the eventual relief when you barely manage to achieve that 4 days before you lose, OR the pity for yourself when you do lose and you have to start all over again.
If i could describe this game in 3 words i would say :Uphill battle simulator.
Improvements from xcom 2 and general pros:
-Much wider mission variety.
-Many more and deeper customization options. You can even give them cigars now.
-Late game is harder now. In fact, i lost one of my campaigns, even though it had reached late game.
-Classes are much more diverse than before, and every class is useful, with it's own merits. You will see what i mean, when you enter a hard mission and you don't have a specific class with you, and how you will feel it's skills missing from your arsenal deeply affects you.
-A new loot system is in the game, that lets you individually upgrade your weapons, which you LOSE if the soldier carrying them dies on the field and you don't extract his dead corpse.
-Also, the effect of "billy panics, and shoots his friends dead" is much less prevelant than before, althought this might just be on the default difficulty. I imagine things get much tougher later on.
Pros or cons: (depending on your point of view)
-The game has the whole mentality of "Even if you do everything perfectly, you can still lose", and it's obvious in this game. You WILL get shot from half way across the map, you WILL lose your best sniper from a random crit that came out of nowhere, and  you WILL get shased down by ufos when you least expect it. This aspect, everyone can take it on a different light, but you have been warned.
Cons:
-New players to xcom will feel lost. If you don't know what xcom is, i recommend to get xcom enemy unknown first, as it is a smoother transition and will explain much of the mechanics of this game. I guess firaxis thought that the only people that will buy this game are players who already know about xcom, but still, i feel it's a misfire on their part
-Hacking is in the game now, but i feel like more could be done with it. You can hack robots, towers, and some objectives, and that's pretty much it. It also follows the same mechanic, so be prepared for your friend Tommy to ♥♥♥♥ up his hacking with 90% chance of success, and suddenly you have a super mech chasing after you.
-Several performance issues, either minor either major. For me personally, the game suffered from some framedrops after a lot of hours of playing, and it can't really handle alt tabbing that well. Some visual bugs, and also only 1 heavy crash (again due to alt tabbing), but thankfully, there is a new autosave function now, so use that.
In conclusion:
If you are familiar to xcom and you love a good challenge (and you are also a masochist) you will love this game. Be prepared to lose friends, family, your dog, your 3rd cousin from your mothers side. This is a tough game, and even harder in higher difficulty levels. Recommended ONLY for those that know what's coming to them.
Right now, with the minor performance issues, it's an 9/10 for me. Once patches are introduced and further customization is implemented, it's a clean 10/10.

Having now surpassed over 150 hours on Darkest Dungeon (~40 in EA, ~110 since full release), it's long overdue for me to give this game the praise it deserves.  Simply stated, I would rank this in my top 10 games of all time - it's truly a phenomenal piece of work, and for anyone who's a fan of tough, turn-based RPG combat, you really need to buy this game.
The good stuff:
- The game's aesthetic; fantastic art, in a very gritty, dark style that sets the tone perfectly
- Really cool music that uses some unusual sounding instruments; yes, I bought the OST DLC for this one
- A turn-based combat, roster management style game that never lets you coast.  In fact, the difficulty ramps up pretty steadily, and on the top level missions one slight error in judgment could easily get that high-end hero you sank tons of gold into permanently killed
- Nice variety of mission length, perfect if you sometimes only have a short while to play, but with longer missions that can last up to a couple hours
- Cool variety of characters, all with unique skills, and all of whom can be used in many different ways depending on how you develop them
- Some of the coolest bosses in any game, ever (Formless Flesh is truly the stuff of nightmares!)
Guess I have to find something bad to say about it, too...?
- Could definitely seem like a grind to some....and in a lot of ways it can be, but if you're (red) hooked on this game you won't care
- The lack of anything to do with the currency you use to improve your town after you've puchased all the upgrades; maybe let us trade it for gold, or find something new to use it for once the town is maxed?
Fans of dark, Lovecraftian fantasy or anyone who enjoys a challenging, turn-based RPG dungeon crawler, do yourself a favor and get this game.

I like Fallout 4.
Let me start out by saying that I'm not very emotionally attached to the Fallout games as a series. I consider the original Fallout a masterpiece in both gameplay and presentation, but don't much care for Fallout 2; it just feels tedious, slow, and too big for its own good without enough compelling content. I played and enjoyed 3 and New Vegas on console, but didn't pour tons of time into either one. To make the inevitable comparison to The Elder Scrolls series, I find that Fallout's more-or-less real-world setting and somewhat derivative elements make it feel like a less special series to me. I can understand, sort of, that many old fans are upset with how Fallout 4 handles the lore, because I felt that way about Skyrim, but I never found the Fallout lore particularly compelling. For me, many factions, individuals, icons, etc, of the Fallout series could be different and the game would, I think, feel pretty much the same. That's why what Bethesda did with Fallout 4 bothers me less than Skyrim did in that regard.
It's true that it's not as much of an RPG as earlier games, but the perk system isn't at all bad, and the combat mechanics and AI are leaps and bounds ahead of anything Bethesda's done in the past. And the "dumbed-down" progression has the convenient side effect of allowing the game to avoid the dire level-scaling that made Skyrim a pain to play after a while. I'd also say the crafting system is much improved, relying more on generic components than Skyrim's very specific recipes and skill/perk requirements. The armor system's fantastic and the individual slots for arms, legs and chest armor, as well as split damage types, is a welcome change to me.
The story, while unfortunately forced, isn't presented badly and can be surprisingly fun to follow, especially compared to Skyrim's. My biggest problem with the game is probably that the game world itself is larger and emptier than it needs to be, but there are thankfully some very memorable locations and impressive vistas.
It's just a fun game, and I'm by and large done with being cynical about games just to be cynical. If you want an old-school Fallout experience, play the old games. They hold up well. Fallout 4 is a marked departure, but it's quite good if you can detach yourself from the series' roots and enjoy it for what it is. I'm not a casual gamer, and I enjoy plenty of deep, engrossing, classic RPGs, but I'm also not ashamed to admit I get a real kick out of Fallout 4. It still offers an incredible amount of depth, choice, and breadth as far as gameplay goes when compared to the myriad other modern titles which blur the line between action-adventure, shooting, and RPG.
