This is a clear case where the sequel could never live up to the original.  For better or worse, Xcom : Enemy Unknown, and Enemy Within were as close to perfect as it was possible to get.  With flawless strategy, and perfectly paced combat, the game trancends what you might call entertainment and becomes an experience.
That is the problem with being too good, the first time around...  you have to follow it up with another act.
XCOM 2 hits most of the notes -- it's character creation has a lot of welcome options, and it's nice to see so many cool details, such as squad member's faces being tossed up on wanted poster holograms.  It feels life the first game, but the focus is a little fuzzy.
I understand there's a time limit now.  I already disabled it.  I haven't played the game with any timer enabled, nor will I.
Other than that, there's not so many overt problems... just a whole bunch of little ones that drag down the whole experience.  Things like touchy controls, unresponsive bindings, random bugs, and ugly animations.
Essentially, Xcom 2 feels half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥  It's poorly optomized, load time is atrocious, and it dosn't even have controller support.  It has steam controller support, but not standard controller support -- a ploy to get you to drop 100 dollars on yet ANOTHER controller.
In short, XCOM 2 to me, is an unworthy sequel -- half finished, half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.. pushed out the door for full price, just assuming the community will fix it.

A pretty great game with an awful story. Gunplay and systems in a bethesda game are the best they've ever been, some of the smoothest gameplay in their titles, and most of the weird quirks that were present in skyrim haven been adjusted. Asides from that, the quest system and story are worse by almost tenfold. The radiant quest system that was awful in Skyrim(go to x dungeon, kill y draugr) has become the settlements system and feels like even more busy work, most of the quests and characters outside of the main questline don't have strange quirks or memorable storylines. The additions to gameplay and the crafting system have helped make a satisfying town management metagame, but doesn't fix the weak story and forgettable characters. I am not even sure how they managed in a quirky off-future radioactive wasteland, but Bethesda have made one of the most playable games with absolutely no charm whatsoever. This is easily their worst vanilla experience, and it shows across the board, it's still a perfectly servicable game, but there's nothing sci-fi, hard fantasy, about it. The graphics look hit or miss, but usually miss, the texture work is pretty bad, and the engine powering it is ancient at this point. Performance is some kind of enigma, all over the place at times, but typically pretty smooth, the loading times without an SSD are obnoxiously long. Gunplay is pretty tight and smooth, no COD or BF by any means, but definitely the best they've been. Dialogue is the worst it's been, choosing a VA for the main character really was the worst selection in bethesda's case. When choosing a VA you should always consider how much you are gonna pay them based on the dialogue, which in bethesda's case, it's an RPG, there's gonna be a bunch, except instead of writing intricate dialogue or multiple options for scenarios across the game, they chose the simplest option: Every option equals yes unless it begins a quest. After 800+ hours of playtime, i think now is the right time to review the game. i recently completed the game again (which is my 3rd playthrough) and i used 100+ mods and also tried the survival difficulty which in my opinion is the best way to experience the game. Firstly, this game isn't great, it has a lot of issues and problems and other things that i will discuss later in the review.
Let's discuss the "pros" first:
1. It has FAR BETTER shooting mechanics than Fo3 and New Vegas.
2. The settlement system (it's not perfect but its a good addition to the fallout franchise).
3. Improved graphics and animations from Fo3 and NV (Obviously).
4. The use of color, unlike fallout 3 where the world is really "bland" looking.
5. The "Survival Difficulty".
6. Interesting companions.
7. The Far Harbor dlc, which improved the roleplaying mechanics.
8. The Vertibird, a really awesome way to traverse the wasteland.
9. The Commonwealth, it has a lot of interesting places to go
10. The Overhauled Power Armor, which also introduced the addition of a FU$%#NG JETPACK
11. The Brotherhood Of Steel. Bethesda made a great job implementing the BOS, They're More Awesome and Badass in here.
12. Good mod support. While its still not as good as modding in skyrim, i'm pretty sure it'll grow over time.
13. The Character Creation. This is by far THE BEST character creation in a bethesda game and its probably one of the best Character Creation in games in general.
it probably has a few more but those are the "Pros" IMO.
Now to the "Cons":
1. Lack of Role-Playing in a Role-Playing Game!
2. Limited choices in quests, unlike New Vegas.
3. Textures and Player Models can look like S%#T for a modern pc game on ultra settings.
4. Dissapointing side quests.
5. The new factions are not that interesting, especially the Minutemen.
6. BORING fetch quests. (F%#K YOU PRESTON)
7. Dissapointing Endings.
8. The dlc's are not that good, except for Far Harbor which i mentioned earlier in the "pros".
9. The Voiced Protagonist. While the actor and the actress certainly did a great job, it just doesn't fit in fallout because it limits the role-playing options.

Wow, what an adventure. While nothing in my humble opinion compares to that original experience of your first Dark Souls 1 playthrough, this hits all the right notes exactly where they're needed. It got to that same point, where I was right at the end, and decided to get as much stuff, looting, treasure hunting and farming purely so I could keep the game going - much like in the first one, I didn't want the experience to end. Though unlike DS1 I will defiintely crusade onto New Game +, I want twin demon fists!
The mystery and crypticism synonamous with Dark Souls is here, the answers are out there if you're brave enough to find them. The weapon arts add an entirely new dimension to gameplay, perhaps perfecting the mould of the franchise. Do you pick a spear with a dash rushing forward, lighting spewing from the tip but leaving your sides exposed, or do you pick a sword with a sweeping fire attack that does less damage but plays safer? Do you want to keep your enemy at a distance with a crossbow, but catch them offf guard with a shoulder tackle when they close the distance, or do you want to blacken the sky with a hail of pointed crystal?
Amongst the hordes of AAA big budget games that promote hand-holding cinematic CGI ♥♥♥♥fests and useless DLC♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ this franchise is oldschool as it gets in 2017 - brutal, unrelenting but rewarding, with a pure gameplay aesthetic. Gameplay is the word here. No quicktime events or anything like that, just you, your wits, your reflexes, and most importantly, your resolve.
I don't feel like I have the linguistics to do it justice, but I will simply say, that the Dark Souls franchise (particularly 1 and 3) - are modern game classics that deserve to be held in the pantheons of the greatest games of all time, to be remembered much in the same way Mario, Zelda, Metal Gear Solid are = as the games that defined the industry.
It is sad that the series has now come to an end, but perhaps it is tasteful again to bow out gracefully at the top of your powers, amidst a rising genre of games that this series has single-handedly produced (yet it will always remain the king of the mountain!) - as opposed to living long enough to see yourself become the villian, ala Assassin's Creed and COD etc.
Thank you for some of the best moments of my adult gaming life, From Software.

First off, XCOM 2 WILL. KICK. YOUR.♥♥♥♥♥
Yes, you are now officially a terrorist organization from the ADVENT government (alien/human coalition) perspective. You fight with bare minimum resources, manpower and logistics support. Your monthly credit/supplies are going to be pathetic, bordering on it being a sick joke at a run-down strippers club staffed by fat hippos.
You are going to fight EVERY BATTLE outnumbered, outgunned, and ill-equipped. You will be firing good óld 5.56mm rounds and popping 40mm grenades while the opposition fires plasma based weapons at your team.

This is a clear case where the sequel could never live up to the original.  For better or worse, Xcom : Enemy Unknown, and Enemy Within were as close to perfect as it was possible to get.  With flawless strategy, and perfectly paced combat, the game trancends what you might call entertainment and becomes an experience.
That is the problem with being too good, the first time around...  you have to follow it up with another act.
XCOM 2 hits most of the notes -- it's character creation has a lot of welcome options, and it's nice to see so many cool details, such as squad member's faces being tossed up on wanted poster holograms.  It feels life the first game, but the focus is a little fuzzy.
I understand there's a time limit now.  I already disabled it.  I haven't played the game with any timer enabled, nor will I.
Other than that, there's not so many overt problems... just a whole bunch of little ones that drag down the whole experience.  Things like touchy controls, unresponsive bindings, random bugs, and ugly animations.
Essentially, Xcom 2 feels half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥  It's poorly optomized, load time is atrocious, and it dosn't even have controller support.  It has steam controller support, but not standard controller support -- a ploy to get you to drop 100 dollars on yet ANOTHER controller.
In short, XCOM 2 to me, is an unworthy sequel -- half finished, half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.. pushed out the door for full price, just assuming the community will fix it.

I don't usually write reviews for games I don't care about, but Xcom 2 has certainly caught my attention.
Whether you are a long-time xcom fan or just have a fetish for mass murder and genocide of the extraterrestrial species - you definitely need to pick up Xcom 2.
It is a turn-based, 3rd person, shooter strategy game. The commander "you" gets to control an elite unit of macho men and sexy women that are humanity's last hope to reclaim Earth. Xcom: Enemy Unknown/Within never happened. You did not save Earth from the aliens! You failed dammit! You know what they told you in school? If you screw up, go and fix it. So, buy Xcom 2 and stop being the loser you were for losing the war from Xcom: Enemy Unknown/Within.
Anyways, on a serious note. This game is phenomenal. The scenery is nicely done and the gameplay seems very flushed out, for the exception of a few glitches that usually involve the katana-wielding, but-kicking, swag-like, Ranger class. Oh well, you will see them when it happes\ns but it's nothing game breaking.
The game features destructable environments and procedurally generated maps. That means that the chances of you playing on identical maps are very slim, considering the game auto-generates them each time. There are plenty of environments involving various climates and divided into jungle/forested regions and cities/towns.
Base-building is still a thing, although this time it can fly. The map was completely redesigned and you have to fly around gathering supplies (currency) and intelligency to keep your operations rolling and aliens in check. There are no Xcom Funding Nations to appease, but there is still a "Doom Tracker" in the form of the Avatar Project. However, if you are a casual gamer and you don't like to rush games, there are easily accessible mods in the workshop to disable the timers.
As far as soldiers go. Soldier classes got flipped around, but for the most part it all feels improved. Psionics are can acquired very early into the game, if you are into Harry Potter type magics, but there are no MECs from the previous game. So far, that has to be the only thing I don't like. No MECS! However, there is special armor that acts like a mec suit by giving soldiers additional slot for heavy weaponry like Boba Fett wrist rockets or flame throwers.
Speaking of Boba Fett, this game has very well-done customizations. You want a ninja? Sure! How about Freddy Kruger with a katana and his blood soaked ski mask? Done! Justin Beiber with a goatee and a minigun? Eh, why not. Although if it were up to me I would have 6 Megan Foxes running around in no time.
Back to topic at hand. Research and development is similar to the previous games. Base building is unchanged. However, scientists and engineers work a little differently now. Engineers are used to clear out rooms instead of excavating them and then used to power different facilities for bonus effects.
As far as bonus stuff goes. Were you ever a fan of the Long War Mod? Well, a lot of the newer stuff will be familiar then. Experimental weapons have been added, researching which gives random grenades, ammunition, armor, etc. It was never more fun to drown enemies with fire, gas, and acid. Hey, they deserve it!

Seriously, a nightmaresterpiece has officially been unleashed upon traditional RPG fans craving a four-party system alongside more robust and psychologically driven character and development.  If Ironman runs are your preferred form of self flagellation, steel yourself for the Darkest Dungeon.
GAMEPLAY
In Darkest Dungeon, you start out on the receiving end of a grim letter from a relative begging for your return home after he unwittingly opens a "festering abomination" below the family estate. The player is quickly introduced to the oppressive evil permeating Darkest Dungeon via the forlorn narration of your estranged relative alongside macabre imagery and equally sinister vocabulary.
From there, any seasoned RPG player will recognize the old standby’s: an HP bar, status effects, weapon efficacy based on the style and opponent, and opposing forces of magic. Where Darkest Dungeon breaks away from its counterparts is in the addition of a stress level represented in similar fashion to the character's HP. Quickly, you’ll find that your characters stress level is just as important to your success as keeping your party’s health in the green. Many of the foes you encounter will target your stress instead of health leading to severe penalties if a character is allowed to reach their breaking point.
There is the possibility of virtuous results from these tests of will, resulting in truly great gaming moments, but masochistic and abusive character flaws are par for the course and often lead to skipped attacks, shuffled party order, or attacks you have no hand in choosing. It’s unfortunate that the enemy doesn’t have a similar mechanic you can manipulate but, thematically, I can see why the choice was made not to.
The mechanics (and your inevitable failure the first time around) will quickly force you to decide what a successful party looks like, thus, physical & emotional healers take on equal importance and provide a refreshing approach to party construction. Characters capable of shuffling the enemy's own party order find themselves in high demand as well. and become crucial in tackling more nuanced bosses later on in the game.
While outside of combat during an expedition, you are often given the choice to interact with various objects with equal amounts risk and reward (though a well placed supply item can eliminate many negative effects). This constant choice of digging deeper both mentally and physically is just another way DD keeps you from turning on the autopilot while grinding away at enemies.
In relation to grinding, the level a character is at will also determine if they will participate in lower level missions (they won’t); so management of the flow of adventurers in your employ via the stagecoach is an imperative and a science I'm still working out the kinks to.
The tension and emotional weight each character begins to take on in your own mind is genuine and refreshing when compared to the conventional brooding emo archetypes so prevalent in RPG’s as of late. DD, using only a fraction of a typical RPG character's dialogue, does what many larger budget titles fail to do:
It makes you care.
Partially this is due to permadeath (without exception) but also because DD weaves such a rich tapestry of mysterious yet interesting affectations into each character. More thematically driven gamers might find themselves creating backstories as well as how they think a character might sound  for the sheer enjoyment of it all.
Effective use of party organization (finally!) and positioning will leave you cringing as your rearguard healer is yanked to the front line for a macabre♥♥♥♥♥pounding by enemies specialized in bleeding you out. Effective use of characters such as the Occultist, is crucial to your own success in battle by pulling enemies with an abysmal tentacle, for example, into front line positions. And don't judge yourself too harshly when a sadistic grin of pleasure crosses your face as you unleash your heavy physical hitters such as the Leaper to annihilate ill-positioned enemies in a single devastating swipe of your executioner's blade. Seriously, the satisfaction derived from successful party organization and execution in DD is simply something you have to experience for yourself alongside the carpal tunnel you’re likely to get from fist-­pumping in success.

Having now surpassed over 150 hours on Darkest Dungeon (~40 in EA, ~110 since full release), it's long overdue for me to give this game the praise it deserves.  Simply stated, I would rank this in my top 10 games of all time - it's truly a phenomenal piece of work, and for anyone who's a fan of tough, turn-based RPG combat, you really need to buy this game.
The good stuff:
- The game's aesthetic; fantastic art, in a very gritty, dark style that sets the tone perfectly
- Really cool music that uses some unusual sounding instruments; yes, I bought the OST DLC for this one
- A turn-based combat, roster management style game that never lets you coast.  In fact, the difficulty ramps up pretty steadily, and on the top level missions one slight error in judgment could easily get that high-end hero you sank tons of gold into permanently killed
- Nice variety of mission length, perfect if you sometimes only have a short while to play, but with longer missions that can last up to a couple hours
- Cool variety of characters, all with unique skills, and all of whom can be used in many different ways depending on how you develop them
- Some of the coolest bosses in any game, ever (Formless Flesh is truly the stuff of nightmares!)
Guess I have to find something bad to say about it, too...?
- Could definitely seem like a grind to some....and in a lot of ways it can be, but if you're (red) hooked on this game you won't care
- The lack of anything to do with the currency you use to improve your town after you've puchased all the upgrades; maybe let us trade it for gold, or find something new to use it for once the town is maxed?
Fans of dark, Lovecraftian fantasy or anyone who enjoys a challenging, turn-based RPG dungeon crawler, do yourself a favor and get this game.

I don't usually write reviews for games I don't care about, but Xcom 2 has certainly caught my attention.
Whether you are a long-time xcom fan or just have a fetish for mass murder and genocide of the extraterrestrial species - you definitely need to pick up Xcom 2.
It is a turn-based, 3rd person, shooter strategy game. The commander "you" gets to control an elite unit of macho men and sexy women that are humanity's last hope to reclaim Earth. Xcom: Enemy Unknown/Within never happened. You did not save Earth from the aliens! You failed dammit! You know what they told you in school? If you screw up, go and fix it. So, buy Xcom 2 and stop being the loser you were for losing the war from Xcom: Enemy Unknown/Within.
Anyways, on a serious note. This game is phenomenal. The scenery is nicely done and the gameplay seems very flushed out, for the exception of a few glitches that usually involve the katana-wielding, but-kicking, swag-like, Ranger class. Oh well, you will see them when it happes\ns but it's nothing game breaking.
The game features destructable environments and procedurally generated maps. That means that the chances of you playing on identical maps are very slim, considering the game auto-generates them each time. There are plenty of environments involving various climates and divided into jungle/forested regions and cities/towns.
Base-building is still a thing, although this time it can fly. The map was completely redesigned and you have to fly around gathering supplies (currency) and intelligency to keep your operations rolling and aliens in check. There are no Xcom Funding Nations to appease, but there is still a "Doom Tracker" in the form of the Avatar Project. However, if you are a casual gamer and you don't like to rush games, there are easily accessible mods in the workshop to disable the timers.
As far as soldiers go. Soldier classes got flipped around, but for the most part it all feels improved. Psionics are can acquired very early into the game, if you are into Harry Potter type magics, but there are no MECs from the previous game. So far, that has to be the only thing I don't like. No MECS! However, there is special armor that acts like a mec suit by giving soldiers additional slot for heavy weaponry like Boba Fett wrist rockets or flame throwers.
Speaking of Boba Fett, this game has very well-done customizations. You want a ninja? Sure! How about Freddy Kruger with a katana and his blood soaked ski mask? Done! Justin Beiber with a goatee and a minigun? Eh, why not. Although if it were up to me I would have 6 Megan Foxes running around in no time.
Back to topic at hand. Research and development is similar to the previous games. Base building is unchanged. However, scientists and engineers work a little differently now. Engineers are used to clear out rooms instead of excavating them and then used to power different facilities for bonus effects.
As far as bonus stuff goes. Were you ever a fan of the Long War Mod? Well, a lot of the newer stuff will be familiar then. Experimental weapons have been added, researching which gives random grenades, ammunition, armor, etc. It was never more fun to drown enemies with fire, gas, and acid. Hey, they deserve it!
I would really hate to spoil the game, but do give it a try! The UI and controls are smooth, graphics are good, gameplay is not stale. The cutscenes are well-made and the storyline is actually entertaining. You may feel overwhlemed and that's fine. This game was not designed to be easy. Set the difficulty to low and play around with it. It took me the first 10 hours just to get into the thick of things. I came from beating xcom on impossible ironman and lost on normal in 8 hours. Mistakes were made. You will make them too. Just don't let it get to you. It's fun to struggle and that is what the game is about. You control a guerilla force that is trying to take back a whole planet. It was never meant to be easy.
Good luck and I really hope you enjoy this product as I have done and will continue for the many hours ahead.
Cheers!

I can't recommend this game highly enough. It's genuinely, in my opinion, one of the best games of the past decade.
It is punishing but fair. It makes every little accomplishment feel amazing. The challenge of this game is part of what makes it so fun. You gradually learn how to fight, and progress from struggling to fight little dogs to killing literal gods.
The atmosphere is so dense and rich. The game itself looks amazing (look up screenshots of Irithyll of the Boreal Valley for some stunning examples). Each region has its own distinct enemies and style, most of which are engaging and enjoyable. (Except the Irithyll Dungeon with those stupid jailers -_- )
The story and plot is very bleak and dark, but in a refreshing and captivating way. It isn't thrust in your face like many modern titles do. It's dripped to you in subtle little hints in such a way that you gradually piece together what is happening in this miserable world you find yourself in. Being able to pick up on little hints rather than having a massive sign with neon lights pointing at every plot point is a smart way to reward exploration, and really helped me to immerse myself in the world.
Compared to DS1, it feels more responsive, less buggy, more pretty and more well designed overall. One gripe is it is definitely slightly more linear than previous titles in the series, but that is in a way a trade off, as this game is able to balance itself far better than DS1 was (particularly in the end game) and doesn't have a massive drop off in quality at any points.
It's freaking great, not a tonne more I can really say at this stage.

After finishing my first game, I figured I'd write a little review for XCOM 2.
So, to begin, the TL;DR of XCOM 2 is that it is an excellent example of what a sequel should be:  Bigger and better, as well as doing a few things different from it's predecessor.
First impressions were good, the game looks impressive and exciting.
The plot follows 20 years after the fall of XCOM from XCOM: Enemy Unknown, we lost the war and the aliens have occupied Earth.  XCOM is now an underground guerilla op, fighting back against the alien overlords.  But this is long odds, the world is happy under the aliens.  So, thematically, it really feels as though you're in a tough spot from the beginning.
From here, it only gets better.  Plot points are sprinkled throughout missions and research, giving you more of a reason to investigate them.  It has a little more of a narrative than XCOM: EU/EW, but if there was one complaint I had it was making the Commander character more of main character.  I realized that the player is supposed to be the 'Commander', but it felt a little forced to be inserted so much into the story.  That's as far as I'll go without going into spoilers.
First off, I've had some performance issues with this game (I'm running Mid-High Specs).  Stuttering and long load times are somewhat common, but it doesn't really detract from the gameplay.  I would hope that they will have an optimization patch soon (review written just after release: 2/8/2016).
Otherwise, the graphics look great.  The beginning armors look rather patchwork and cobbled together, while higher end armors have a nice sleek, Iron man like sheen to them.  Weapons and effects on the battlefield are impressive.  The aliens have also gotten an upgrade as well, looking meaner and more menacing than ever.
Soldiers look more emotive than their XCOM: EU/EW counterparts, as well as being a whole lot more customizable.  Being someone who likes to customize my troops, this is a welcome benefit.  Also included is the language packs from other nations, so a number of your troops can speak their native tongue (there are even options for Australian English and UK English options for Irish and Scottish accents).  Oddly, Russian is not present as it was in XCOM: EW.
Sound design is great, with the weapons having a good "omphf" to them, as well as the chit chat from your soldiers in battle.  The VO is good, couldn't really see too many complaints with it.
And now the big one.  This is the crux on whether XCOM 2 is good or not, I suppose.  Well, XCOM 2 surpasses it's previous entry in a lot of ways.  First, let's talk about the Tactical layer.
Tactical Layer:
All four of the XCOM: EU classes have been revamped for the sequel.  Each class gaining a few new tricks as well as losing some.  For instance, the Assault has become the Ranger, wielding a sword now.  Support got it's upgrade in the Specialist, with a Gremlin like drone that can heal from afar or hack mechanical enemies.  There is nothing like the feeling of terror at seeing a Sectopod, then hacking it and gleefully laughing as you rip your enemies to shreds with it's devastating power.  The Psi class of EU is now it's own separate class known as the Psi Operative.  And it is basically a wizard, flinging psi abilities left and right.
The new classes feel more powerful from the originals, but to offset this, the aliens have gotten a huge upgrade now as well.  Not only do the aliens all look quite a big more menacing, they have been given some new abilities of their own.  Sectoids can bring dead units back from the dead, Mutons counterattack melee attacks.  If a Chryssalid kills a unit in melee, or with poison, that unit becomes a cocoon and after a turn *THREE* Chryssalids burst forth.  With the newer aliens, you'll frequently think to yourself "Oh, that looks really cool" before realizing the terror in seeing them.
However, it was a little sad to be missing a few of the original aliens (Cyberdisc you will be missed!  As well as,
).
Strategic Layer:
There have been numerous improvements in the strategic layer.  For those that didn't like the Interception mechanic from EU/EW, it it no longer in the game.  Now you move the Avenger, a repurposed alien supply ship, around the world hitting alien targets.  XCOM 2 has replaced the throwing satellites up from EU/EW with making contact with new regions and setting up radio towers.  This also allows you to complete guerilla ops (basically your missions) in that region.
You will need to make contact with regions quickly as the aliens win condition, the Avatar Project, ticks away and they build more facilities.  As stated before, you can't launch a strike on a facility without having contacted the region, so quite a few times I found that the aliens would throw up a facility in some other corner of the world that I had no contact with.
Research and engineering are for the most part remain unchanged, with the exception of new weapons and armor.  You only have to build them once, then everyone in your roster can have it.
Soldier mechanics have changed, so now that anytime a troop is damaged in anyway they will be wounded now and have to sit out for some time.  I found this to be rather welcome, making it feel more 'realistic' and really making the player have to not just use one 'A-team' to take care of everything.
XCOM 2 is excellent and I would say a must buy for anyone who loves XCOM/X-com and/or turn based games.

A few things you need to understand before you pick this up, or even start to play it for that matter. This game is not a series known for holding your hand, and more importantly the developers decided the last reboot was too simplistic and easy for their tastes. They have made the enemy AI slightly better, buffed the opponents, and modified the overview/direction of development/ and tactical behavior. You are simply on the run and on the clock constantly at full tilt. This game does not accept blunders without incredible repcussions, and even with the supporting infrastucture it becomes manageable. The AI is designed to be completely unfair, you are the underdog. Higher levels of play completely encourage you to fight dirty and quickly, limiting engagements to preferable 1 turn to kill the entire opposing party, about 3 to 4 times any given mission. That being said, its a series for masochists, and some of us prefer that. I recommend it, within a few months it will have the modding community release a full conversion im sure.
Pros:
Mods are easy to use and fully adjustable without impacts on achivements
The is enough time to complete every mission even timed
It has improved on the framework by adding in an entirely new level of customization which is completely moddable without penalty
Campaigns are notably shorter yet more open in terms of time
Interceptor games are removed
You now have complete control over missions besides dark events
Classes are now far more balanced
Endgame still keeps you on your toes
While the game is designed to move quickly, you have the full freedom to prolong the game for as long as needed within reason
Full stealth is now an acceptable option
Maps are non static
Legend difficulty redefines the pace of the game completely
Cons:
Protection missions late game are the worst besides the final mission. Considering I've beaten the game I'm not joking.
Minor glitches and occassional game breaking bugs need working out.
AI has some rediculously unfair abilities such as literally dragging you through cover.
Hacking system needs some work in terms of rewards.
Some class builds are intunitive
Avatar Program has some minor flaws with implimentation
Without adjustment the rate of loot is too damn low
Retaliation missions have several annoyances such as audio and faceless design.
There should be another way to reduce progress on the avatar project than story progression and base destruction

A pretty great game with an awful story. Gunplay and systems in a bethesda game are the best they've ever been, some of the smoothest gameplay in their titles, and most of the weird quirks that were present in skyrim haven been adjusted. Asides from that, the quest system and story are worse by almost tenfold. The radiant quest system that was awful in Skyrim(go to x dungeon, kill y draugr) has become the settlements system and feels like even more busy work, most of the quests and characters outside of the main questline don't have strange quirks or memorable storylines. The additions to gameplay and the crafting system have helped make a satisfying town management metagame, but doesn't fix the weak story and forgettable characters. I am not even sure how they managed in a quirky off-future radioactive wasteland, but Bethesda have made one of the most playable games with absolutely no charm whatsoever. This is easily their worst vanilla experience, and it shows across the board, it's still a perfectly servicable game, but there's nothing sci-fi, hard fantasy, about it. The graphics look hit or miss, but usually miss, the texture work is pretty bad, and the engine powering it is ancient at this point. Performance is some kind of enigma, all over the place at times, but typically pretty smooth, the loading times without an SSD are obnoxiously long. Gunplay is pretty tight and smooth, no COD or BF by any means, but definitely the best they've been. Dialogue is the worst it's been, choosing a VA for the main character really was the worst selection in bethesda's case. When choosing a VA you should always consider how much you are gonna pay them based on the dialogue, which in bethesda's case, it's an RPG, there's gonna be a bunch, except instead of writing intricate dialogue or multiple options for scenarios across the game, they chose the simplest option: Every option equals yes unless it begins a quest. They wrote three factions to choose from which are all comically unlikeable, no intracacies across any of them, no grey zone strange compromises at all, You're either a hippie trying to liberate sears electronics, some kind of weird patriot that fixes every leaky sink in town, or a hardcore soldier who don't like no technology and nothing different, It's comical how awful the factions are written, since Fallout NV, which was written by Obsidian, but a nearly 7 year old game, which exists in your same universe has you outclassed. I can easily recommend this game based on the fun of playing it for about 50 hours, but the wear at the edge of this grilled cheese becomes soggy at about 20 hours in, and you start to notice they've placed no emphasis on anything about the RPG aspects since Skyrim almost immediately.

Great game as usual.  Enter the space time continuum and realize hours have passed from getting so sucked into the game.  You will also be yelling at your team for missing a 94% point blank shot or attack with a blade.
XCOM 2 has some great upgrades from Enemy Within.  I love the different types of rounds and grenades you can research.  The environment is now interactive for example, destroying the roof makes the enemies fall and get damaged.  I like that you don't have to build similar facilities next to each other.  I found that I quickly ran out of things to research and ended up needing more engineers than scientists.  You will learn to love the grenade launcher and that the snipers always have squadsite.  My favorite class, as in Enemy Within as well, is the sniper who can almost take out an entire screen full of enemies with the right skills.  I find that the ranger is the most useless class.  I can see it trying to mimic the assault class, but I think the assault skill tree was much better.  The specialist is a nice added class to the game allowing for remote healing and controlling of enemies.  I find it best to have two on your team, one with each skill tree.  The grenadier is awesome for destroying enemy armor.  I find that side of the skill tree to be more effective than the other.  The ability to destroy armor with grenades and their weapons is most definitely useful.  There are also a lot of cosmetic changes in case that is of interest.  Your team shows battle scars as they get damaged too.
There are a few bugs I have noticed so far.  Sometimes it will show enemy movement is happening but not zoom in on it like it should when they are clearly in your view.  Enemies will sometimes fall through the floor when they are on the bottom level.  You will sometimes shoot through trees and the ground.  It is also a pain waiting a minute plus to finish the mission and return back to the map.
Overall though, awesome and addicting game.  If you liked the Enemy Unknown/Within, you will for sure like this game.  If you are new to XCOM, it is a great strategy game to play and easy to learn.

My main issue is with the story and Roleplaying elements. Because the single player narrative is so forced, it's hard to get into the character. The limited dialogue also doesn't help.
The factions in the game you are sort of rail-roaded into, making sure you are forced to see them all, instead of happening upon them naturally. It feels like too much development time went into the crafting/building system than the story or game design.
Exploring feels unrewarding, the map is more cramped than before, hardly any of the characters are memorable outside of the Vault Tech salesman, and once you get to a certain point in the main storyline, I just felt like stopping or puttering around doing anything to avoid finishing the story.
As for the gameplay, once again there's no in-depth Melee system. It's an odd complaint, but I still want to be able to Fist of the North Star my way through the Apocolypse, and the current melee system doesn't help foster a good feel for that. Tying the grenade to the melee button and not being able to change it in the menu is annoying.  It was also hard to care about any of the characters.
Overall, FO3 was better for exploration, and FO:NV was a better overall story and gameplay. I haven't played the DLC for FO4 yet, so no comment there.
I hope whatever the next fallout game is, it takes a bit more imaginative a turn for it's location, like Florida or the great lakes area.
Overall, I'm really not enjoying my time in this game as much as I did the previous 2 fallout titles.

A solid sequel with numerous welcome additions and changes, particularly mod support. XCOM 2 is superior and an overall upgrade to the first of the rebooted XCOM series and should serve to be highly enjoyable for those who were a big fan of vanilla XCOM 1, though poor performance is a concern.
Despite the advancements, vanilla XCOM 2 shadows in comparison to XCOM 1 Long War mod. Gameplay balance and rules have ultimately gone in the wrong direction when Long War went the opposite way. Super powerful abilities and equipment use, both alien and player have removed a lot of tactical mechanics and good positioning. I feel XCOM 2 is played by exploding, decoying and bluescreening your way to victory in a sorched earth, 'cheese everything before you get cheesed' way. Class trees lack balance and while they are more indepth than XCOM 1 Vanilla, are still inferior to the multiclass, large group system from Long War. While random maps was one of the most needed additions to XCOM, for some reason, XCOM 2s maps feel crowded and small in comparison to XCOM 1. As someone who played so much Long War, XCOM 2 had to stand up to that mod instead of the vanilla game for me and sadly it missed the mark. They have all the means in the vanilla game to artifically prolong the length of the campaign, like what Long War did, but once you play, you realise even 40 hours is nowhere near long enough. You're rushed through the story and tech upgrades that the game is over before you get to have a feel of all the features available.
At the end of the day it's a good start but the game *desperately* needs its own 'Long War' style partial conversion single mod, the tools and means are there to create something that shadows Long War, so I'm hoping someone will take up the challenge. There's quite a large list of individual mods that are pretty mandatory in improving the game, but they hardly work, even the Firaxis supported SMG pack from the Long War team doesn't work right now, you can't upgrade the SMGs in game. Such an addition to the game is pointless in such a short lived game.

I like Fallout 4.
Let me start out by saying that I'm not very emotionally attached to the Fallout games as a series. I consider the original Fallout a masterpiece in both gameplay and presentation, but don't much care for Fallout 2; it just feels tedious, slow, and too big for its own good without enough compelling content. I played and enjoyed 3 and New Vegas on console, but didn't pour tons of time into either one. To make the inevitable comparison to The Elder Scrolls series, I find that Fallout's more-or-less real-world setting and somewhat derivative elements make it feel like a less special series to me. I can understand, sort of, that many old fans are upset with how Fallout 4 handles the lore, because I felt that way about Skyrim, but I never found the Fallout lore particularly compelling. For me, many factions, individuals, icons, etc, of the Fallout series could be different and the game would, I think, feel pretty much the same. That's why what Bethesda did with Fallout 4 bothers me less than Skyrim did in that regard.
It's true that it's not as much of an RPG as earlier games, but the perk system isn't at all bad, and the combat mechanics and AI are leaps and bounds ahead of anything Bethesda's done in the past. And the "dumbed-down" progression has the convenient side effect of allowing the game to avoid the dire level-scaling that made Skyrim a pain to play after a while. I'd also say the crafting system is much improved, relying more on generic components than Skyrim's very specific recipes and skill/perk requirements. The armor system's fantastic and the individual slots for arms, legs and chest armor, as well as split damage types, is a welcome change to me.
The story, while unfortunately forced, isn't presented badly and can be surprisingly fun to follow, especially compared to Skyrim's. My biggest problem with the game is probably that the game world itself is larger and emptier than it needs to be, but there are thankfully some very memorable locations and impressive vistas.
It's just a fun game, and I'm by and large done with being cynical about games just to be cynical. If you want an old-school Fallout experience, play the old games. They hold up well. Fallout 4 is a marked departure, but it's quite good if you can detach yourself from the series' roots and enjoy it for what it is. I'm not a casual gamer, and I enjoy plenty of deep, engrossing, classic RPGs, but I'm also not ashamed to admit I get a real kick out of Fallout 4. It still offers an incredible amount of depth, choice, and breadth as far as gameplay goes when compared to the myriad other modern titles which blur the line between action-adventure, shooting, and RPG.

I have 38 Hours at the time of writing - I've beat the SP and played some MP (No spoilers below - Summary at the bottom).
Neutral Points
--Gameplay wise this is VERY akin to Enemy Unknown. This is not a negative or a positive. I enjoyed the repeated forumla, butI did feel there wasnt a lot of innovation.
--The new enemis are an additional challenge are very well designed (looking) but very quickly end up being simple bullet sponges of differing degrees of sponge-ness.
Positives
--The story is quite good and the character interration with the science, and tech leaders, as well as Central (your second in command) is very good for an XCOM game. I was motivated and really wanted to win FOR EARTH!
--Character customization is FANTASTIC. Weapon patterns, armor patters, face, helmet, legs, chest, arms, color, race, nationality, etc. ALL and MORE are under you control. You can literally make an entire rookie team of Stormtroopers (Prove you can hit something and I give you back a name).
Negatives
--This was a big problem for me, but might not be for others: Difficulty. I started playing on the third level (veteran I think, but that might be the second level) and was brutalized for a few missions, but through superior tactics and very careful play was making it work. As I advanced further, however, problems started to present themselves. Simply put, I think this game ♥♥♥♥ing cheats! As I started to get Maj. and Col. level characters, they'd be missing 80-90% shots CONSTANTLY, and the enemy would crit them from across the map on a steady basis. In response, I lowered it down to the second level. Then it started spawning in 9 enemies at a time, where they would link pull and swam my troops within the first move of deployment. Then I lowered it down to rookie, and the enemy spread their legs and asked me to shoot them. There isnt a very good balance of super easy, and unfair hardness. This is my subjective opinion so take that as you will.
--Another problem, for me, is preformance. The game chugs when the battles get busy, and on city map with a lot of destruction there is FPS dips every deployment. I'm running a GTX 980ti for reference, so yeah, its pretty bad.
--The online servers are WRECKED at the time of writing this. Matchmaking doesnt work for unranked, and the matches lag on ranked (I'm talking 40 second gaps of lag, not a little stuttering). THIS WILL CHANGE WITH TIME.
Summary
Overall I had a blast with this game, and though I'm not really interested in replaying it at the moment, mainly because its stressfull as hell, I know in a week I'll be back trying to play on the hardest difficulty just to see my troopers get killed. I really enjoyed the gameplay, the characters, and the story, and in general, have pretty positive views about the game. The preformance was pretty bad, but it wasnt bad enough that I wanted to stop playing, and there werent any crashes (though I did have to restart the game twice due to bugs).

Awesome! It looks like Terraria but all action is in space and different planets. You can explore them, you can build your own spaceship, you can hunt different animals and aliens, you can craft all you want.

Performance issues aside, which CAN be patched, this game is head-and-shoulders above its predecessor(s). The strategic layer of gameplay isn't just "Press A to pass time, wait for something to happen, and maybe build buildings" anymore; now it's "Move from country to country, press A to pass time, wait for something to happen, maybe build buildings, and manage scientists and engineers," which makes more of an impact than you might think. It also makes the game harder, since there's no real train track to follow anymore in the story. I'd recommend it to anyone that can stomach the performance issues and enjoys turn-based games. Wow, what an adventure. While nothing in my humble opinion compares to that original experience of your first Dark Souls 1 playthrough, this hits all the right notes exactly where they're needed. It got to that same point, where I was right at the end, and decided to get as much stuff, looting, treasure hunting and farming purely so I could keep the game going - much like in the first one, I didn't want the experience to end. Though unlike DS1 I will defiintely crusade onto New Game +, I want twin demon fists!
The mystery and crypticism synonamous with Dark Souls is here, the answers are out there if you're brave enough to find them. The weapon arts add an entirely new dimension to gameplay, perhaps perfecting the mould of the franchise. Do you pick a spear with a dash rushing forward, lighting spewing from the tip but leaving your sides exposed, or do you pick a sword with a sweeping fire attack that does less damage but plays safer? Do you want to keep your enemy at a distance with a crossbow, but catch them offf guard with a shoulder tackle when they close the distance, or do you want to blacken the sky with a hail of pointed crystal?
Amongst the hordes of AAA big budget games that promote hand-holding cinematic CGI ♥♥♥♥fests and useless DLC♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ this franchise is oldschool as it gets in 2017 - brutal, unrelenting but rewarding, with a pure gameplay aesthetic. Gameplay is the word here. No quicktime events or anything like that, just you, your wits, your reflexes, and most importantly, your resolve.
I don't feel like I have the linguistics to do it justice, but I will simply say, that the Dark Souls franchise (particularly 1 and 3) - are modern game classics that deserve to be held in the pantheons of the greatest games of all time, to be remembered much in the same way Mario, Zelda, Metal Gear Solid are = as the games that defined the industry.
It is sad that the series has now come to an end, but perhaps it is tasteful again to bow out gracefully at the top of your powers, amidst a rising genre of games that this series has single-handedly produced (yet it will always remain the king of the mountain!) - as opposed to living long enough to see yourself become the villian, ala Assassin's Creed and COD etc.
Thank you for some of the best moments of my adult gaming life, From Software.

Pros and cons below, but summary first:
As a turn-based rpg - it's clever. Not awesome or revolutionary, but certainly clever and can hold a person for a while; and it's a good game for fifteen minute sessions or for sessions of an hour or two, because it's broken up into dungeon crawls of bite-sized lengths. What it does awesomely is that it is wrapped in pitch-perfect flavor, art, and sound. It's a 'buy' - particularly if Hallowe'en is a holiday you enjoy!
Pros:
- For any fan of Lovecraft, there's just tons of clever homage.
- Fantastic art style and atmosphere
- Great voice-over
- A good variety of skills for each class leads to an impressive amount of different viable tactics - building synnergies between heroes is important. Quirks layer onto this effectively.
- The battle system manages to make even turn-based combat be stressful.

This is a great game for anyone who's never played it before. It's casual so everyone can enjoy it, but offers a sense of progression. It's an absolute blast if you have friends to play with. If you like the idea of a 4-player Legend of Zelda, give this game a shot. It's truly free-to-play now, and you don't need to spend money to progress. PvP can be insanely fun but does require a big time investment. The game mechanics are very simple but offer a lot of room for skill growth (reactions, etc.)
That said, I've played this game since it came out on beta in early 2010 and there have been zero progression updates to the game ever since SEGA acquired them in late 2011. The same final boss that appeared in 2010 is still the same final boss in 2014. The "final gate" that was locked to players in 2010 is still locked. The "hardcore" content is simply recycled dungeons and locked behind a bad paywall, but luckily you never have to touch it. The game has basically devolved into a cycle of minor updates with no progression content, and a bunch of cosmetic items. Hats. And more hats.
The fact that it's coded in Java is also a huge problem, as there are some fundamental issues with the code that make the game poorly optimized. The biggest problem is Java having to dump its memory every time it reaches the memory cap, causing the game to occasionally stutter as Java does this, even on beast computers. See these threads:
1.
2.
I recommend this game especially if you have friends to play with. It'll offer a solid hundred hours of enjoyable, challenging fun. But if/when you get to the end, don't expect them to add any more progression content... because they won't, and haven't since 2010.

If you played the first XCOM and found alot of the little things like when as soon as you'd encounter the aliens on the map they'd get to make their move, or how when you'd want to move to flank or take a shot at an enemy you'd find yourself unable to when it looked like you could, those kinds of things, you'll find that most of those annoyances have been dealt with. While nothing enormous has really changed within the mechanics themselves, aside from the new concealment system which lets you set up an ambush for your first attack, much remains the same. However, I feel Total Biscuit was right in saying that this is XCOM x12, they really amped up the enemies and I loved it.
While the vast array of new enemies is a complete headache to deal with at first when you don't know what they're capable of, and they're capable of ALOT, when you work your way through the campaign and become aware of the multiple ways an enemy can ♥♥♥♥ you over, you'll adapt to it and find yourself taking full advantage of ways to exploit the enemies position at that given moment, it's almost like a game of chest...CEPT WITH ALIENS AND LASERS AND♥♥♥♥♥♥
Aside from the enemies recieving new and seemingly overpowered abilities, I have to commend Firaxis for making every single skill tree for your troops viable this time. I did not find one skill trees that was useless in the slightest, each class adds ways to counter specific problems you'll run into on the field and some of the ways you can combine those abilities with other abilities makes for a whole new level of play this time around. Squads with variety are highly recommended so that you can make full use of the versatility every class provides!
Mechanics aside, the global map itself is alot more interesting this time leaving you with multiple opportunities for resource scavenging and extending your influence, but you'll need to make smarter decisions as to what you want to respond to seeing as you'll constantly be working against the clock. Thankfully you'll also have opportunities to set back this clock and even delay it. While at first you may feel irritated by countdowns on both the global and mission maps, it gives you a sense of urgency which without it would slow down the game dramatically, although I do feel that there could have been a tad fewer countdowns in the mission variety themselves. Even though you'll be working against the clock alot of the time, once you complete the objective that is leading that countdown, you'll have all the time in the world to finish off the remaining forces so the stress mainly originates from having to secure that objective each time.
Finally I'd love to commend Firaxis on their collaboration with the Long War team to ensure an open sourced means for modders to work their magic on the game, seriously impressed. They're honestly one of my favorite developers now for a move like that. The fact that they'll admit that someone can purchase a game and do with it what they wish because it's their damn product is a amazing mentality and has earned my respect, love ya Firaxis.
TL;DR: If you liked XCOM EU/EW then you'll love this one. RNG is still and thing and always will be, deal with it or become a save scummer like me and everyone else or go hard and legendary+ironman the hell out of it. Looking forward to the bright future of XCOM!

Mechanically speaking, it feels like some weird middle ground between the combat of Bloodborne and Dark Souls, and not always in a good way. The backstory is likewise a jumbled mess with inconsistencies and hanging threads everywhere, despite the actual plot you follow being basically a retread of the first game. That isn't a bad thing in itself, but it compounds the other story issues when the first kept things so much more coherent even in ambiguity. There's still some brilliant level design to be found, although it's balanced out by some equally stupid design choices. As well, the setpiece fights are as gorgeous as ever, but some enemies are so big and visually busy as to obscure their own tells (a problem leftover from Bloodborne), making fighting them that much worse. Netcode seems noticeably sloppier too, given how often phantoms get bugged out of joining boss fights- I've been on both ends of that problem myself.
If you're a big fan of the series and dead set on playing this final entry, I guess I can't blame you. Just know that this swan song stumbles as much as it succeeds, and if you came for closure, you're going to be disappointed.

To preface my review (one of the few I've ever left) let me say I've never been one of those gamers that says "git gud". I'm not "hardcore" and whilst I certainly don't think I'm a "casual" I'm sure many would say I am.
I dislike hard games overall. Games that are difficult just for the sake of it. I like games that punish me for my mistakes, where there is a constant back and forth. Games shouldn't essentially complete themselves and nor should they make completing them a chore. Darkest Dungeon manages this perfectly. There are punishing mechanics that will constantly knock you down if you make a mistake. I see reviews from people who have encountered this not recommending this game and it physically angers me. Put in some time to learn the game, to learn how it works and you can deal with those mechanics. Nothing is unfair in Darkest Dungeon. Everything is in your control.
People who turn others away from this game because of the difficulty I say this to you: Not everyone is you. Most people will put in the effort to actually play a game and figure out an actual solution to the problem they're faced with. If you want a turn based combat game then yes, this will let you down purely because it is so much more, and it is wrong to refuse to accept what you are offered.
Darkest Dungeon would be an awful game if it was less than it is but all the parts come together to make one well oiled machine that will make a worthy player come back for more time and time again.

So after several hours of gameplay, I can honestly say I recommend this game and love the new changes.  I played XCOM: Enemy Unknown and Enemy Within as well so I will give an honest review of the game.
Quick Overview of Pros and Cons:
Pros:
* Really really fun - Matters because reason we buy and play
* Good solid graphics
* Great strategic play - Well thought out - Better than XCOM: EU/EW
* Lots of options makes for very diverse play
* Lots of maps - Really good maps/variety
* Extremely immersive gameplay - You feel like you are trying to save the human race/world
* Surprises, twists, and mystery - Great story telling so far
* A large range of different enemies to fight
* Mobile base and travel is well done and you have to make hard decisions
Cons:
* Could take some learning for new players - you might die :)
* I did find one bug in the game during play so far - It was while in base, under the armory tab, and happened during customizing my units.  When I clicked on the "menu back" button it would not back out of the menu.  I did eventually get back out by switching to customizing another player and was then able to use the menu back.  Have not been able to duplicate this bug, only happened once.
I know some do not like the "time limit" or number of turns you have, but I really thought it added to the game and made it a lot of fun so far.  It is an immersive element, you need to accomplish some parts of some missions fast and I liked it.  It gives some depth and weight to your choices on the battlefield and it makes sense from a story telling perspective as well.  It is well done, should try it before you mod it out imo.
I know some have experienced some performance issues, I have not.  My system is good, but not top of the line.  If you have a below average system you will need to upgrade to play this game.
My system:
* i7 4790k
* 8GB Ram
* 120 SSD (game not on SSD)
* 1TB HD
* AMD 280 with 3GB video mem
Perhaps the current AMD video card drivers are better for this game than the current Nvidia drivers - I don't know that, but perhaps that is why some are experiencing some lag/stutter issues.
*I have not had a single crash or freeze with this game.
Overall this is a great game and extremely fun to play!  Lots of ways to customize and it's just a blast to play.  I think it is well done.  There are some out there that say it is poorly optimized, however most are probably not programers or developers.  I have electrical engineering and computer science experience and it seems fine to me.

Well I fell in love with this game about 3-4 years ago when I saw it in an advertisement and loved the graphics. I've spent 38 days in game (I only recently linked it to Steam so it probably says something different) so I think I can give a decent review on the game.
Graphics: Awesome graphics 10/10
Soundtrack: Awesome music 10/10
PVE: Fun until you hit very late game and are sort of forced into grinding Firestorm Citadel (the final 'main' boss) because it gives the most loot. Although if you're actually interested in having fun and don't care too much about loot you can just delve into the Clockworks which have random levels or do Danger Missions which is probably the hardest content in the game (other than Shadow Lairs). 6/10
PVP: There's two PVP gamemodes; Lockdown and Blast Network. I've only played a couple games of Blast Network and it is somewhat similar to Bomberman with a bird's eye view of your player. Then there's lockdown, which is much, much more popular and basically a capture-the-flag type game where you fight each other to capture the points. Tier 3 Lockdown is really fun but somewhat unbalanced if you don't have the best armor/helmet/weapons and people with UV'd gear have an unfair advantage over those without them (UVs or Unique Variants are bonuses on your gear such as  Attack Speed Increase and Charge time Reduction). 7/10
Gear: There's lots of weapons and armory to choose from and they all have interesting and unique basic attacks and charge attacks. However, the gear is really unbalanced. For example, bombs (which only have charge attacks and no basic attacks unlike handguns and swords) are pretty much inferior to swords and even guns. The Mad Bomber Set is literally a completely inferior armor set to the Chaos set (They both have the exact same stats except one gives bomb dmg increase: medium and bomb charge time reduction: medium while the chaos set gives the exact same bonuses to the bomb, handgun AND sword). 4/10
Payment Mode: The game is completely free-to-play and everything can be accessed without paying money, but obviously paying money lets you advance faster and gain extra gear. I personally don't regret the money I've put into the game.
Updates: The game has had only one actual content update in 2015 although the game is somewhat polished so it doesn't really need updates but they wouldn't hurt. 2/10
I don't play it too much right now (although I checked it out for the Gunner Update) but if you're looking for a fun, casual MMO then this is for you.

Despite inevitable comparisons to Terreria and Minecraft, Starbound stands out in its character design and world feel. You choose a race and are tasked with escaping a planet near which you've run out of spaceship fuel. The game shines in multiplayer and there are already several online guides for setting up a mini-server from your own copy of the game. I think it would be easy to not "get the point" of this game. To those people, I ask what the point of any game is? Typically it's a way to relax, and that works for me.
It's hard to know when to comment on software in development. Gmail was in beta for several years, but it was still a good product right?  I see room for improvement in the procedural generation of sound design. In particular, the loop on overworld music is too quick and it can become a bit annoying. More annoying is the sensitivity to begin battle music for every aggro thing on screen. This includes monsters which fall in poisonous water or lava in dark caves (a common event), so fight music will start too often for seemingly no or little reason. Starbound may be in development for a fairly long time, but I still recommend it quite highly.

So now that I've seen some improved performance through the most recent mods such as "Stop Wasting my Time" the game has vastly improved to where I now can recommend it. The reason it was a not recommended wasn't because of the gameplay reasons such as timers but due to all the buggy issues with the game.
XCOM 2 is the next step in the Firaxis XCOM franchise. The game does a neat job of switching the roles where we are the invaders and some of these features really felt missing in the first XCOM. Concealmeant is without a doubt my favorite system in the game but I also love fighting against the high tier enemies.
The thing about fighting a sectopod or a gatekeeper is that when you defeat one of those enemies, it feels great. There are some enemies that are very annoying that I think should've been scrapped and reworked (Stun Lancer for example) because they aren't fun to fight against early on.
The story is a strategy game story, it's not supposed to have a Bioshock Infinite level of plot twists. There are a couple of references to the X-COM franchise (Terror From the Deep) but whether or not Firaxis will actually make a TFD I don't know.
At $60 the game is currently enjoyable for XCOM fans but not so much for anyone else. The new player experience is pretty bad because they do not give you enough of an introduction to show you all the neat little things about the game. This will make it very hard for newcomers to actually play the game. Of course they can watch a tutorial which is what I would do but the game doesn't teach you how to play that much.
Mods will also keep this game alive for a long time. I bet in about a year or so, we will see a Total Conversion Mod where the Rebels fight the Empire in XCOM Empire at War.

great game with amazing modding ability. my thoughts after beating Veteran difficulty with the stock rules and a lot of save-scumming.:
the timers are by and large way too short for most of the guerilla ops missions, like most people are saying. particularly in the lategame, bounding forwards to make up time is incredibly risky more often than not and it feels like I'm being forced to make awful moves in order to actually get something done. also had a couple of sharpshooters get captured because they couldn't make it to the evac point in the final turn after providing fire support to clear said evac point - probably the only soldier losses that I felt were complete BS. most of my save-scumming was to find a way to possibly get people close enough to the evac zone before the timer ran out. the best way to fix this seems to be to have the timers start upon breaking squad concealment instead of on mission start.
however, the combat layer is improved in pretty much every other aspect over EU. sequential reaction fire is a godsend, and it's always fun to watch a tank get chewed up by bullets after stumbling into a killbox. the class system is much more interesting, especially when the Advanced Warfare Center is up and running you're rolling abilities for soldiers that wouldn't normally get them. (Kill Zone for life!) procedural maps are amazing to have, though sometimes I did feel starved for cover when I really needed it.
the strategy layer is... eh. not much to talk about, since it's very much slimmed down, even from EU. having some degree of staff management is nice, but i do wish that engineers and especially scientists had more of an use than they normally do. seems strange to only be having about 5 of each one by the end.
the character customization is very extensive, and it's fun to mess with. the option to add biographies was a great touch, since your soldiers eventually become their own little writing prompts as you take them on missions. nice music all-around, too.

Pros and cons below, but summary first:
As a turn-based rpg - it's clever. Not awesome or revolutionary, but certainly clever and can hold a person for a while; and it's a good game for fifteen minute sessions or for sessions of an hour or two, because it's broken up into dungeon crawls of bite-sized lengths. What it does awesomely is that it is wrapped in pitch-perfect flavor, art, and sound. It's a 'buy' - particularly if Hallowe'en is a holiday you enjoy!
Pros:
- For any fan of Lovecraft, there's just tons of clever homage.
- Fantastic art style and atmosphere
- Great voice-over
- A good variety of skills for each class leads to an impressive amount of different viable tactics - building synnergies between heroes is important. Quirks layer onto this effectively.
- The battle system manages to make even turn-based combat be stressful.
Cons:
- The gameplay doesn't really change a huge amount once you figure out the tactics.
- There is a moderate amount of grind, particularly in replacing lost heroes and in affording the higher-tier upgrades to your hamlet
Mixed:
- The randomness factor. It's not a con, per se, but it does require a different mindset to deal with effectively - the more you can deal with loss, and hedge against it with your tactics, the better you can put yourself into the 'manager of a team of heroes' role you need to be in rather than playing as a hero yourself. I have a feeling that most of the complaint comes from people who don't realize that .. yes, sometimes it's better to cut losses and retreat from a quest than try to shove through. That instinct to try to win is hard to resist, and it leads to frustrating party kills.

To preface my review (one of the few I've ever left) let me say I've never been one of those gamers that says "git gud". I'm not "hardcore" and whilst I certainly don't think I'm a "casual" I'm sure many would say I am.
I dislike hard games overall. Games that are difficult just for the sake of it. I like games that punish me for my mistakes, where there is a constant back and forth. Games shouldn't essentially complete themselves and nor should they make completing them a chore. Darkest Dungeon manages this perfectly. There are punishing mechanics that will constantly knock you down if you make a mistake. I see reviews from people who have encountered this not recommending this game and it physically angers me. Put in some time to learn the game, to learn how it works and you can deal with those mechanics. Nothing is unfair in Darkest Dungeon. Everything is in your control.
People who turn others away from this game because of the difficulty I say this to you: Not everyone is you. Most people will put in the effort to actually play a game and figure out an actual solution to the problem they're faced with. If you want a turn based combat game then yes, this will let you down purely because it is so much more, and it is wrong to refuse to accept what you are offered.
Darkest Dungeon would be an awful game if it was less than it is but all the parts come together to make one well oiled machine that will make a worthy player come back for more time and time again.

The closest Dark Souls III comes to this is you can fight the Dancer early, before Vordt even, but there's no reason to as you still can't get to the fourth lord and get his cinders until you kill the other 3 lords. In one you could go snag Nito's lord soul as soon as you reached firelink, in two the Rotten's soul was up for grabs as soon as you got to majula pretty much. In three you can fight the dancer as soon as you get to the high wall but you can't get the cinder of the lords there until the game wants you to so there's little reason to. In two even though it was less seamless there would be times I didn't know where to go and times when it felt there was too many places I could go, in one it was so seamless and free flowing and yet still structured that it was a master piece in that regard. In three there's never much question as to where to go next and there's never too many new places to go to at a given time, you go to the next area it's pretty much that simple. So yeah three has some wiggle room but ultimately you do have to fight almost every boss and the events and map are both far more linear then previous installments. That aside it's still a great game. I think the boss fights in this game are some of the best in all of Dark Souls, like the lothric princes and the nameless king. However, it also has some of the crappiest like the decons of the deep and wolnir. But most of the bosses have tons of diversity and differ greatly and will require different tatics to fight. You can't just melee tank and out poise literally every boss and estus spam in front of them wearing full havel like in one, and you can't get hit by every other attack without any real consequence since you have a million lifegems on your belt. That said if you can consistently i-frame your rolls most everything will be easy since rolls are OP this time around. More over, the PvP in Dark Souls III has the most active players of any the games and is, in my opinion, the most balanced and overall best in the seiries. Invasions feel exetremely unfair but a good amount of those invaders end up killing me anyways so I guess they find ways to make the best of it. All around it's still a great game because being non-linear isn't by any means the most important feature of a game and though Dark Souls III lacks the seamless and open world of OG Dark Souls and feels much more spoon fed in terms of progression it's still a great game that I highly reccomend to all who are interested.

I'm not sure whether to reccomend this game or not.
On the one hand...
-It's absolutely beautiful. The handdrawn style really does deserve a HUGE amount of credit. It's evident from that alone that a lot of time and effort has been put into this game.
-It's a refreshing change of pace for RPGs. If you're a RPG fan, you will love this game. Character management and stats alone are enough to give any lover of the genre shivers of delight. Stats are clear with noticable effects, each character plays vastly differently, and the equippable trinkets allow so many different builds for one character. The amount of skills learnable by each character are expansive but not overwhelming.
-Darkest dungeon offers a well-thought out return of turn-based combat, while retaining none of it's tedium. It's wonderfully oppressive and build tension like nothing else.
HOWEVER. Despite having these things going for it (And trust me they carry it a LONG way), it has some real stinkers in it's design. If you're someone who plays games just to have a stab at them and leave it unfinished, these previous points will probably carry the game for you. if you want to be playing this long-term and have the satisfaction of beating it... WEEEEELLLLL...
-It seems almost incomplete from both a story perspective. Granted, the setting is delightfully atmospheric, but it's no replacent for a real juicy TALE. What fragments exist of a narrative seem to revolve around discovering the sins of your anscestor and cleansing them, but we're given no real motivation to do it. Sure, there might be a possessed-demon pig in the basement, but... He's not threatening me, and seems rather content to sit there while I kill all his grunts. Why do I need to bother clearing out bosses at all when the story's given me no real reason to care? Any real story seems to be self generated, but in the words of Zero Punctuation: "I don't find myself very engaging, I'm QUITE the bellend".
-It gets tediously repetitive after a while. Clearing out dungeon after dungeon with no pause, uninterspersed with cutscenes or any real exposition gets boring eventually (Although to the game's credit, I was hooked HOURS longer every play session than expected, so the randomly-generated dungeons ARE very immersive).
-Lastly, the RANDOM NUMBER GENERATOR IS ♥♥♥♥ED. This one comes at the end, in all caps, just so that you will ALL notice it. To the game's credit, it requires a large amount of skill. Most of that skill is in regards to weighing up risk and reward, something that plays a large part in managing your inventory to balance treasures and supplies, and trying to guague whether a 50% chance at stunning an enemy is REALLY worth it. HOWEVER. When a character (Especially the weaker classes) Can fall to two critical hits and a side of bleed damage, the player is only being punished for something that isn't their fault. This does NOT reflect good game design.
In conclusion, Darkest Dungeon is described best when it's said to be rougelike, but it would be best if it would decide what sort of rouge it wants to be. Does it want to be the Han-Solo sort of rouge that'll kiss me and charm me despite it's frustrations and quirks, or is it going to be the kind of rouge who'll kick me in the nutsack and steal my money? Because I know I want it to be the first, but the more I grind through this tedium (And ESPECIALLY the third Darkest Dungeon expidition, what the hell is that all about?!) I notice Red Hooks' hand creeping towards my wallet and their knee towards my testicles.

So now that I've seen some improved performance through the most recent mods such as "Stop Wasting my Time" the game has vastly improved to where I now can recommend it. The reason it was a not recommended wasn't because of the gameplay reasons such as timers but due to all the buggy issues with the game.
XCOM 2 is the next step in the Firaxis XCOM franchise. The game does a neat job of switching the roles where we are the invaders and some of these features really felt missing in the first XCOM. Concealmeant is without a doubt my favorite system in the game but I also love fighting against the high tier enemies.
The thing about fighting a sectopod or a gatekeeper is that when you defeat one of those enemies, it feels great. There are some enemies that are very annoying that I think should've been scrapped and reworked (Stun Lancer for example) because they aren't fun to fight against early on.
The story is a strategy game story, it's not supposed to have a Bioshock Infinite level of plot twists. There are a couple of references to the X-COM franchise (Terror From the Deep) but whether or not Firaxis will actually make a TFD I don't know.
At $60 the game is currently enjoyable for XCOM fans but not so much for anyone else. The new player experience is pretty bad because they do not give you enough of an introduction to show you all the neat little things about the game. This will make it very hard for newcomers to actually play the game. Of course they can watch a tutorial which is what I would do but the game doesn't teach you how to play that much.
Mods will also keep this game alive for a long time. I bet in about a year or so, we will see a Total Conversion Mod where the Rebels fight the Empire in XCOM Empire at War.
