great game with amazing modding ability. my thoughts after beating Veteran difficulty with the stock rules and a lot of save-scumming.:
the timers are by and large way too short for most of the guerilla ops missions, like most people are saying. particularly in the lategame, bounding forwards to make up time is incredibly risky more often than not and it feels like I'm being forced to make awful moves in order to actually get something done. also had a couple of sharpshooters get captured because they couldn't make it to the evac point in the final turn after providing fire support to clear said evac point - probably the only soldier losses that I felt were complete BS. most of my save-scumming was to find a way to possibly get people close enough to the evac zone before the timer ran out. the best way to fix this seems to be to have the timers start upon breaking squad concealment instead of on mission start.
however, the combat layer is improved in pretty much every other aspect over EU. sequential reaction fire is a godsend, and it's always fun to watch a tank get chewed up by bullets after stumbling into a killbox. the class system is much more interesting, especially when the Advanced Warfare Center is up and running you're rolling abilities for soldiers that wouldn't normally get them. (Kill Zone for life!) procedural maps are amazing to have, though sometimes I did feel starved for cover when I really needed it.
the strategy layer is... eh. not much to talk about, since it's very much slimmed down, even from EU. having some degree of staff management is nice, but i do wish that engineers and especially scientists had more of an use than they normally do. seems strange to only be having about 5 of each one by the end.
the character customization is very extensive, and it's fun to mess with. the option to add biographies was a great touch, since your soldiers eventually become their own little writing prompts as you take them on missions. nice music all-around, too.

TL;DR: Spiral Knights provides a dynamic, action-based experience with engaging combat and a fun, free spirited world - but the lack of content updates and throttled crafting system can leave many players quickly feeling burned out.
The pros:
-Engaging, action oriented combat. No ability rotations or hotbar jungles here - Spiral Knights relies on a more Diablo/Torchlight-esq system, with a few unique quirks of its own. Gameplay focuses heavily on movement and weapon mechanics - on avoiding or blocking enemy attacks and striking back with a vast array of wildly different tools.
The game has a huge variety of gear and weapons which all noticably change your gameplay, and most weapons have unique "charge attacks" which can unleash huge damage or powerful effects.
From heavy cleaving swords, to fast nimble rapiers, to precise peacemaking revolvers, to crowd-busting magnus cannons, to debilitating haze fields - heck, there are even literal black hole bombs. The list goes on - there's a lot of ways to customize your gameplay.
And although this game doesn't offer abilities in the traditional fashion, you can still earn a trio of special, slighly customizable abilities by leveling up your personal pet. From the Drakon's enraging firestorm, to the Maskerwraith's devious stealth, to the Seraphynx's dauntless overshield - there's something for every playstyle.
The cons:
-Severe lack of content updates. This is the biggie. Aside from the endless stream of promotions, this game has gone mostly unchanged for several years. Once you complete the game's mission system, there isn't much to do beyond spam the single endgame dungeon or try your hand at the single popular PvP minigame.
Sure, you can do special challenge missions once a day for pixel prestige points, and you can pay a hefty fee to try amped up variants of the boss levels, but those don't provide a sustainable experience for most people.
-Throttled crafting system. Leveling up and crafting new gear requires special "forge crystals" which can take many hours to find in adequate quantities. Although the mission system gives you roughly enough resources to make your first endgame set, after that you're on your own - and the time and resources required to progress any further can be a bit daunting for anyone who isn't already an established veteran.
Granted, grinding is to be expected in a F2P MMO, but Spiral Knight's crafting can often leave one feeling like they're dragging their feet through the mud. Given the game's huge emphasis on equipment, this is a pretty notable issue.
There's a lot more I could say about this game but those are the big points for me. I've been playing this game on-and-off since the official pre-Steam release over three years ago, and recently ported to Steam so I could use the in-game voice chat with my younger siblings. Ultimately, I've enjoyed my time with Spiral Knights, and while the game has its faults I would still absolutely recommend giving it a try. It's a fun experience.

If you're looking for a completely new game, which is exactly like the old one - please enjoy playing the old one. Fallout 1, 2, 3, NV, Tactics. They are affordable and run on a anything. But to give this game a thumb down based on your expectations is simply not fair. Many people sound like Bethesda "butchered a franchise". Maybe choosing a faction was a more important part of Fallout 1 and 2, or maybe the game has been a bit streamlined as a shooter with an RPG system, rather than the other way around. I prefer the changes.
The diamond shaped dialogue opton is an improvement to the pile of text of the previous titles. A is a confirmation, B is a rejection, X is a provocative or sarcastic remark, Y is always a question. So, if somebody asks you: Dude, want some chems? You can reply without reading! This is far more immersive than the dialogue in previous games.
Also the shooting, assuming you unlocked the framerate and disabled the mouse acceleration, the shooting feels good. Responsive.
Ah, the building, This feature alone justifies the purchase. You'are able to build. ANYTHING. Yes, you're limited to the in-game assets, but there are plenty. Electric wiring alone will keep you entertained for hours. Some of the already present objects don't always attach to the new ones and sometimes the allignment is off, but still it's a great feature to have.
Survival-mode. It changes the game...Completely. Now you cannot save, only autosave at sleeping locations(sleeping bags, beds) Those become your checkpoints. You cannot fast travel. Every object has weight, except for quest-items and misc-objects. This means you have to decide: Will i take the stimpack, water and fruit or the weapon. How much ammo? These important decisions you will have to make in order to survive. Wow, really feels like survival...And...you can play the survival mode right from the start, unlike in NV,
So, basically Fallout 4 is full to the brim with several well-made mechanics and a huge wasteland full of secrets. I assume the bad reviews refer to the way the publisher decided to handle mods, or whatever. I don't care. Fallout 4 is worth your time.

So whats to say about XCOM 2...
Starting with the negatives: Performance issues, especially with physics, destroying a section of a building with explosives can and most likely will tank your framerate, general stuttering (wich i was able to somewhat fix by tinkering with config files) and moderately long load times if you are not on a SSD.
Difficulty curve is not very smooth, the beginning is fairly punishing but the midgame until the very last mission is generally smooth sailing.
Class balance is not perfect, explosives are a bit too strong making my squad comp always lean towards multiple grenadiers, they were super effective. (heh.)
At times the game can feel "sluggish", both allies and enemies might just decide to stare into the sunset for a few seconds before remembering they actually have to act their turn.
With that out of the way... XCOM 2 is still a really damn solid tactical game, the story picks up right from where it ended in XCOM and does not disappoint. Voice acting is good, the aliens look great and varied.
Its what you expect from this game and then some more.
Mod support is icing on the cake and if Firaxis smooths out the rough edges it will be remembered as a classic just like the XCOM of yore.
If you are on the fence... might aswell jump in.

This game is ugly.  If Roblox and Chex Quest had a kid, and that kid was fed into a wood chipper, one could glue the remains together into a semblance of Unturned.  If you're looking for a game that makes you want to hit that screenshot button and make wallpapers for your PC, slowly step away from the install button.
If you are the kind of person who took their best friend's ugly sister to the prom because you're just a good guy at heart, stick around.  Unturned is ugly on par with Gilbert Gottfried's voice through a loudspeaker.  But it has it where it counts - gameplay.
Let's see.  Survival, Sandbox, Stealth, Multiplayer, Character Customization, Character Advancement, Weapon Customization, Horror (admittedly cute), PUBG-style Battle Royale.  And it does most of these very well.  I mean, one can only be so terrified by a lego character scooting across the ground with red pixels painted on its face.  But the Arena mode in Multiplayer was the icing on a very solid survival game for me.
This game does a lot of little things very well.  Directional VOIP chat in multiplayer.  Free items with a frequency akin to TF2, including those oh-so-wacky hats.  Sneaking on your belly behind a Zombie to grab that crossbow, only to have it suddenly whip around and jump on your square tush.  Base Building.  This game grows on you like an urban zombie plague.  Seriously, at the time of writing I've put in 33 hours.  That's 33 hours on a free to play Quasimodo when I could be back in Skyrim, Dishonored, TF2, Elite Dangerous, or any of my other more beautiful games.  Give it a chance!
TL;DR It's an ugly game that is completely worth the download!

The revived XCOM series is a testiment to the original turn-based tactical combat game created years ago.  And while XCOM2 retains all of what makes XCOM and its predecesors great, I found the depth ultimately disappointing.  XCOM2 is for all intents and purposes a reskined XCOM game with a minor storyline.  The game still consists of four classes with four weapon concepts, three tiers of weapons (firearm, mag, plasma) and a small selection of other secondaries.  The armor is almost identical as is much of the psionics, and it doesnt even delve into the true mech and gene therapy options found in XCOM: Enemy Within.  While additional customization options for your soldiers allows for better immersion, this much work could easily have been incorporated into another expansion to the original XCOM.  Firaxis should have put much more effort into a longer storyline with multiple outcomes or ethical choices, more technology choices or even differing/counter tech trees for replayability, additional ranks and class abilities/choices, and additional ship based content or global resource management.  The story could have allowed for any number of plot twists which were not followed, leading to a predictable, lackluster ending.
The hacking concept was a fantastic addition, most noteably the skulljack :)  This was probably the best new feature of the series.  Starting in stealth is also a nice new feature but is ultimately inconsequential as you can effectively ambush a single group and then its back to normal combat, in which newly discovered enemies are diving into cover or going into immediate overwatch.  Some of the tactical skills were designed to overlap effectively to great effect, creating unique options for combat superiority, but due to the frequency of injured soldiers it is hard to keep a cohesive unit to take advantage of those options.  The concept of creating a random item (e.g. under-armor and heavy weapons) is just silly - if I am building something it doesnt just come out with a random result.  If I want to build hellfire under-armor then the game should let me, not force me to make various other under-armors until I get what I want.
Performance was less than spectacular also (worse than the original XCOM game).  With an NVIDIA GTX970 I was getting framejumps galore and even lost video completely during one mission load.  Also suffered long load times for missions (I run 8-core i7 3.5GHz proc, 32GB and Samsung EVO SSD).
Overall XCOM2 is still a great game and terrific fun.  If you havent played the XCOM series before its totally worth the purchase.  But as an experienced XCOM fan-atic, I pretty much consider it to be XCOM: the XCOM2 Expansion.

Rather than making a review. I want to adress two of the main complaints people seem to have with this game :
- Poor optimisation : Yes. It is poorly optimized. I have a high-end PC and I do have bugs, loss of frame rates at times. To me it's not so bad that the game isn't enjoyable. But If my PC has this issues, I can only imagine how poorly the game runs on other PCs. SO it is a valid concern and FIRAXIs need to fix and polish the game ASAP! I can still play it and I love the game, but clearly the game is not polished... Not acceptable. If you have a high end PC, buy the game... You will have some issues there and there but overall it's ok. If you do not have a high end PC. DOn't buy it just yet, wait for FIRAXIS to fix the bugs and polish the game with patches.
- The new timer on mission : Honestly, people giving the game a negatice review exagerate on this issue. Yes... Most missions have a timer now. Yes you can't simply place your operators, set them on overwatch and wait for the alien to come to you. However, those who say that the game has no tactical or strategy to it because of the timer or absolutly full of♥♥♥♥♥♥ For one, the timer isn't so bad that you need to dash all the time to the objective. It's a bit hard the first missions but once you get the detection grenade, you can use it and work on the best course of action from there. The timer does force you to move forward, but never to the point that you have to expose yourself to the enemy without a solid strategy. Yes people, the timer makes the game more challengy... YOu can't just sit around and wait for the aliens to come to you. You have to move, and make the best of the situation. With enough skill, and i dare say "TATICS" you can clear a mission and get your entire team out alive. Yes, sometimes the random nature of the maps will put you in a situation where you will be forced to lose some of your soldiers in the battlefield. But that's part of the game! You have to deal with loosing operators. And it's not nearly has bad as all of the cry babies pretend it is. SImply send rookies on easier missions from time to time to train them enough so that they can replace your Elite ones should they fall. Loosing operators is part of the game. If you can't deal with that, then sorry sweety, XCOM (this one or the the previous version), is NOT a game for you. The timer doesn't remove any tactical element in this game. If you do not optimise every unit your have to their full potential in the field, you will pay dearly. So no... Don't listen to these morrons who overdramatise a feature they don't like by saying ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t like that.

So whats to say about XCOM 2...
Starting with the negatives: Performance issues, especially with physics, destroying a section of a building with explosives can and most likely will tank your framerate, general stuttering (wich i was able to somewhat fix by tinkering with config files) and moderately long load times if you are not on a SSD.
Difficulty curve is not very smooth, the beginning is fairly punishing but the midgame until the very last mission is generally smooth sailing.
Class balance is not perfect, explosives are a bit too strong making my squad comp always lean towards multiple grenadiers, they were super effective. (heh.)
At times the game can feel "sluggish", both allies and enemies might just decide to stare into the sunset for a few seconds before remembering they actually have to act their turn.
With that out of the way... XCOM 2 is still a really damn solid tactical game, the story picks up right from where it ended in XCOM and does not disappoint. Voice acting is good, the aliens look great and varied.
Its what you expect from this game and then some more.
Mod support is icing on the cake and if Firaxis smooths out the rough edges it will be remembered as a classic just like the XCOM of yore.
If you are on the fence... might aswell jump in.

The revived XCOM series is a testiment to the original turn-based tactical combat game created years ago.  And while XCOM2 retains all of what makes XCOM and its predecesors great, I found the depth ultimately disappointing.  XCOM2 is for all intents and purposes a reskined XCOM game with a minor storyline.  The game still consists of four classes with four weapon concepts, three tiers of weapons (firearm, mag, plasma) and a small selection of other secondaries.  The armor is almost identical as is much of the psionics, and it doesnt even delve into the true mech and gene therapy options found in XCOM: Enemy Within.  While additional customization options for your soldiers allows for better immersion, this much work could easily have been incorporated into another expansion to the original XCOM.  Firaxis should have put much more effort into a longer storyline with multiple outcomes or ethical choices, more technology choices or even differing/counter tech trees for replayability, additional ranks and class abilities/choices, and additional ship based content or global resource management.  The story could have allowed for any number of plot twists which were not followed, leading to a predictable, lackluster ending.
The hacking concept was a fantastic addition, most noteably the skulljack :)  This was probably the best new feature of the series.  Starting in stealth is also a nice new feature but is ultimately inconsequential as you can effectively ambush a single group and then its back to normal combat, in which newly discovered enemies are diving into cover or going into immediate overwatch.  Some of the tactical skills were designed to overlap effectively to great effect, creating unique options for combat superiority, but due to the frequency of injured soldiers it is hard to keep a cohesive unit to take advantage of those options.  The concept of creating a random item (e.g. under-armor and heavy weapons) is just silly - if I am building something it doesnt just come out with a random result.  If I want to build hellfire under-armor then the game should let me, not force me to make various other under-armors until I get what I want.
Performance was less than spectacular also (worse than the original XCOM game).  With an NVIDIA GTX970 I was getting framejumps galore and even lost video completely during one mission load.  Also suffered long load times for missions (I run 8-core i7 3.5GHz proc, 32GB and Samsung EVO SSD).
Overall XCOM2 is still a great game and terrific fun.  If you havent played the XCOM series before its totally worth the purchase.  But as an experienced XCOM fan-atic, I pretty much consider it to be XCOM: the XCOM2 Expansion.

This game is ugly.  If Roblox and Chex Quest had a kid, and that kid was fed into a wood chipper, one could glue the remains together into a semblance of Unturned.  If you're looking for a game that makes you want to hit that screenshot button and make wallpapers for your PC, slowly step away from the install button.
If you are the kind of person who took their best friend's ugly sister to the prom because you're just a good guy at heart, stick around.  Unturned is ugly on par with Gilbert Gottfried's voice through a loudspeaker.  But it has it where it counts - gameplay.
Let's see.  Survival, Sandbox, Stealth, Multiplayer, Character Customization, Character Advancement, Weapon Customization, Horror (admittedly cute), PUBG-style Battle Royale.  And it does most of these very well.  I mean, one can only be so terrified by a lego character scooting across the ground with red pixels painted on its face.  But the Arena mode in Multiplayer was the icing on a very solid survival game for me.
This game does a lot of little things very well.  Directional VOIP chat in multiplayer.  Free items with a frequency akin to TF2, including those oh-so-wacky hats.  Sneaking on your belly behind a Zombie to grab that crossbow, only to have it suddenly whip around and jump on your square tush.  Base Building.  This game grows on you like an urban zombie plague.  Seriously, at the time of writing I've put in 33 hours.  That's 33 hours on a free to play Quasimodo when I could be back in Skyrim, Dishonored, TF2, Elite Dangerous, or any of my other more beautiful games.  Give it a chance!
TL;DR It's an ugly game that is completely worth the download!

Welcome to the Darkest Dungeon, young blood. Be warned: many adventurers have ended in the cramped cemetery - covered in the poisoned earth and awaiting merciful oblivion. Vicious foes and traps lie in the dark, preying on such fools.
If however you intend to survive and overcome what may be the darkest trial of your short life, then by all means watch your step. Never let your guard down, never take a fight for granted, never allow yourself a moment of easy respite or vain triumph. In the end it will all be worth it: there is gold, glory and knowledge to be secured here... at a dire cost.

Success requires a forceful strength. The lifeblood of your efforts will come from a crowd of adventurers of various trades and backgrounds, men and women molded by a life in crime, war or arcane. Do not delude yourself with bonds of affection or pity: they will serve as cannon fodder for your ambitions. You’ll need to keep these tools sharp: trained, equipped, and mentally sound - if by sound we mean blind enough to venture through the gates of hell.
So ransack everything you can from the dungeons and put your loot to good use. Gold and relics will help you to rebuild the Hamlet and bolster your troops. A visit at the flagellation room or the brothel will raise the mood of your broken men. The sanitarium will purge diseases and negative quirks. The guild house and the blacksmith’s workshop will improve their combat skills and gear of the high level fighters. Preparation is half the battle – the easy half.

You may have heard the squeals (or read the reviews) of the weak and the soft-headed calling this adventure overly difficult. Is it so? It has been beaten by myself and many others. Yes, I left my sanity back there and many of my henchmen have lost worse... but the Dungeon of my ancestors has been purged, and those monsters who pretended to bar the way are now laying in pools of their own coagulated blood!
Now there is some truth in all this nonsense: survival is a tenuous proposition in this sprawling tomb. The game can harshly punish mistakes, as you will probably learn the hard way. Do not be cheap when packing torches, food or bandages (much needed in the Cove). Never let the light die, unless you really know what you’re doing. Always replace a warrior pushed out of position to make the best of his/her tactical skills. Don't hesitate to abandon a quest and go home if most of your team hit max stress or Death’s Door. There is a solution to every problem you can face.

Deep in the maze shines a glint of mad hope: victory. The road is as long as it is treacherous, but if you keep your eyes peeled at all time you will see the end of it. The Darkest Dungeon is doable and extremely rewarding. Now go forth, madman, and hold your torch high and bright!

I've played a lot of this game, way more than I would have liked to in retrospect.
And I sit here wonder only what could have been.
My initial attraction to the game was through its gameplay reminicent of top-down zelda games and its art style because, I admit, im a sucker for cute♥♥♥♥♥♥ And while I frequently reminice of my days of old when the game was still fresh and new to me, I today am only disilusioned and disenfranchized to it all. I'll start by getting the good out of the way.
As I said the gameplay is reminicent of earlier zeldas. There are a variety of damage and armor types as well as different enemy factions with strengths and weaknesses in acordance to these types. The enemy types are nicely varied and require different tactics to them. There are swords, guns, and bombs to use and equip. The arcade is essentially a sandbox element where you trek through different randomized levels. And there is good fun to be had when you take your first steps into Cradle.
Then you hit it, the massive brick wall called "end game". A herculian task of overcoming frustrating RNG and tedium to get the 2nd highest level armor, then tripled that for the highest quality. Now that might not sound so bad, I mean reallly good gear should be worked for right? Well the thing is that its required to progress through the game. It's not fancy gear you can choose to get, you must get a full set of certian quality gear in order to progress through the story as there are missions that quite literally only serve as a gear check. And then you see the energy bar in the bottom corner taunting you to spend some cash to make the pain stop.
After smashing your head against said brick wall for hours on end, or simply paying to make the pain stop, you are introduced into an end game world of freakishly overpriced fashion items and RNG prize boxes. This is a game where the endgame is cosmetic items, but due to the abhorent RNG and rarity of these items, they cost upwards of 20$-100$+ of real money. You can spend in game currency to buy premium currency (energy) which is whats often used for trading of these accessories, good luck getting anywhere if you dont plan to grind one single level and one single boss for all eternity. So unless you have enough money to smash your way into this impenetrable market, the accessory trade is strictly for veterans and no one else.
By the time you have the end game gear, you have already done most of everything this game has to offer. That deceptive climb to the top was just padding. All but the shadow lairs which are the games only end game content that a regular player would probably enjoy. But those have an up front cost of 1800 (~20$) energy just to get a key to play one. And these lairs are just altered versions of already existing boss levels.

Review Done on Veteran Difficulty (Normal) - savescumming only used to check mechanics (eg can I hack this remotely? Lets test)
The Good
- Turn timer removes the extremely dull, slow overwatch to win method that is a test of your patience rather than skill. Expect nail biter endings. There are some missions that still permit this, which allow a more cautious approach now and then.
- Missions less of a win / fail binary. Easier to extract or half complete missions.
- Tweaks to classes introduce new choices and mechanics - pistol snipers are now a serious class, the specialist can basically heal from anywhere on the map, whilst still staying in combat, reducing medikit micro
- Enemies harsher, but more predictable - they signal who they are going to attack, their attacks are nastier but tend to give you a turn to deal with them (eg snake binds you, sectoid mind controls a dude or revives a zombie). Deaths feel more fair than thin man plasma rifle crit across map
- Actual variety in geoscape strategy - spam satellites is no longer the path to victory - game encourages carefully balancing a variety of resources (engineer, scientist, alloy, elerium, cash, intel)
- Soldier customisation rises to new levels
- New setting is a little derpy, but mostly brilliant. Allows new worldbuilding and character exploration that builds on XCOM 1, while presenting a different and interesting premise.
- Abductions are gone
- Game now indicates when enemies can shoot you and where they can't, and what moves will trigger enemy overwatch.
The Bad
- Optimisation (protip, turn down AA and turn off DoF to fix 80% of problems) - this will challenge your computer
- Not knowing some mechanics will get your men killed a few times in a first playthrough (same as original XCOM)
- Missions start to feel pretty abstract - hack mcguffin X, shoot VIP Y, Feels transparently like a gameplay mechanic rather than strong link to story
- Enemies can be a little binary. They use their super move, it either a) Ruins you, and sets you on course for a wipe or b) You kill them in the next turn.
- Animations can be a bit slow - long term players will likely get irritated with the wait
The Misc
- Storyline kind of just pops you in 20 years after the occupation. Oh no, the aliens are about to do something super bad? Kind of feels a little odd. What has the resistance been doing the last 20 years?
- Still derpy XCOM animations. Stepping off buildings to take a shot. Attempting to smash already broken windows. Firing through the tinest crack. At this point I basically consider it part of the charm.
The Things People are Complaining About that Are Rubbish
- Reducing number of classes. Yes they got rid of the SHIVs. Deal with it.
- Turn timers allowing only a mad dash to the end. Nope. Amount of enemy groups you have to deal with are quite small. Moderately aggressive playstyle has not caused me to miss a deadline yet.
- "The RNG is lying" - Hahahahahahah
- "The RNG is predetermined" - HAHAHHAHAHAHA, (no seriously, go read about save seeds on original XCOM. Stop whining that your savscumming is not supported  by default)
Things I'm Not Sure of Yet
- Commander difficulty (yet to play)
- The full plotline

Awesome game. An improvement I didn't think was possible from Enemy Unknown.
The story is deep and the missions are ruthless.
There clearly are some people whom are having trouble adjusting their play to the new timed scenarios but I'd say that they are without a doubt the best thing to happen to UFO/XCOM in a long time, especially so if you like playing on Iron Man. The reason is that they force your hand to action. You are no longer able to play ridiculously defensively going inch by inch through the level with all your guys always on overwatch but are going to have to make some really tough calls.
Sometimes you'll make the wrong call, people will die, sometimes you'll make the right call and people will die anyway. Sometime leaving your guys to die is  the right call in the longer campaign. Previously Iron Man was simply an excercise in patience, since there were heavy consequences to having your guys shot at, the valid strategy was the one spent hammering overwatch and end turn never putting any of your guys at risk. If you never put anybody at risk, you don't need to load save games.
In XCOM2, this is a luxury you seldom have. Usually there is something pressing you on, be it a beacon calling in enemy reinforcement, civilians getting eaten by aliens, a bomb timer ticking or just hordes and hordes of enemy reinforcements whittling you down. This calls for action and decisiveness, but if you over-extend and act too hastily, the game will still be there to punish your overconfidence.
There are some missions where there is no timer or the timer will start very late in the mission or the timer might not start until you leave concealment (more about this later). These are usually the missions with the stiffest resistance as well. It allows you to revel in these occasions to really cheese the aliens as much as you can, pay them back for past transgressions, savor the ambush. (Un)fortunately these are also the missions where the aliens are the most well equipped to raise you on your cheese and give you a run for your money. The first such mission I ran into the only survivor was a sole rookie, objective in hand, runnning for her life from hordes of alien reinforcements. The mission was a success albeit a pyrrhic one as my best sniper, my best ranger and my last grenadier were left dead on the battlefield.
Other pros:
- The whole setting being insurgents against a state of dystopian alien opressors is awesome and surprisingly(!) fits the gameplay much better than the original secret government agency schtick that most other x-com games have had.
- The new concealment system allows for some glorious ambushes though it doesn't hand it to you on a silver platter, you really have to be clever about it utilise it to it's full.
- The game seems a lot longer and more content rich than previous Firaxis x-com games, that being said there is some heavy borrowing here and there especially on the gear side, but all in all more is more and there are few things without some new refinement.
- The base building and management of the avenger (flying around doing missions on the map) feels a lot more refined and is more fun than in previous games. Also, it's no longer just about MOAR LABS, MOAR SCIENTISTS! Engineers are really nice and have a lot of versatility and tasks to balance.
- There is a lot more verticality in the missions, allowing better and more varied level design.
- Voice acting is good and the characters in your base have a lot of non-critical monologue/reflectections that are fun to listen to but easy to skip.
- All aliens are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s
Cons:
- All aliens are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s
- The user interface feels very laggy at times, especially during combat.
- The framerate will suffer at times, more so than you'd expect from a turn based game. With that being said though, since it's a turn based game it's not a game breaker, but somewhat of an annoyance.
- The game has a significant amount of minor bugs, nothing game breaking or super annoying though
- The line of sight system is supposed to be super simple, but it turns out instead to be very unpredictable at times as it sometimes allows enemies and players to shoot through walls (it at least makes holes in the wall when they do). Also, what counts as cover from what angles is kinda gamey and you can have situations where it looks like you can clearly see an enemy but it turns out he's in heavy cover. The rules for when they are or are not are rather simple, so you can learn them but it does take you out of the moment sometimes.
- You can only rotate the camera in 90 degree increments and have very low zoom in/out capabilities. I suspect this is due to the line of sight thing, since trying to look down from where your character is looking won't actually help you tell if there'll be line of sight or not.
- Sometimes, especially when fighting in enclosed spaces, the wall transparence effect that's supposed to allow you to see what you're doing even if there's a wall between you and your character will also make the wall behind your character transparent making it very hard to see what's where and where there are walls and where there aren't.
Overall, great game. I was pleasantly surprised despite high expectations.

The most annoying, aggravating, and anxiety-inducing game you'll love to play.
The greatest thing about Darkest Dungeon - and the thing that many players hate and fear - is that it is a FAIR GAME. As in, actually fair. Balanced. It is NOT "fair" in the sense that one measly hero can develop god-like power and squash everything in his/her way. Darkest Dungeon is fair in the sense that your heroes and the enemy are almost a 1:1 ratio in power. Every blow you land on the enemy is dished out right back at you. Bosses fights are actually tough, and unique, not just a formality. Instead of winning 99% of the time and b*tching about the ONE TIME YOU FAIL, like in most RPGs, you will have to make a decision whether or not to cut your losses and "fail" more than you will feel comfortable with. The game rewards wise choices and stacking the odds in your favor as much as you can - most of the time. Sometimes it just doesn't matter, because the % chance just didn't go your way.
And considering that's how things have gone for the MILLIONS AND BILLIONS of monsters who have died to feed our egos over the years, that's more than fair.

The game hosts a great number of unresolved bugs and glitches regardless of whether a player decides to use mods or not.
Just to mention some of the most glaring ones...
There are instances in which the game freezes simply because the player enters VATS,
There are instances in which the game closes randomly without so much as an error window.
There are instances in which a player may experience infinite loading screens.
Companions will often be incapable of carrying or equipping anything despite having an entirely empty inventory.
Dialogue options for completing quests will sometimes be absent and a quest NPC will sometimes not even enter dialogue at all with the player despite the  player having completed the related quest objective.
The  game itself is playable and can be enjoyed, but I've reached a point where the question, "will it work or will it crash or freeze again?" just puts too much worry and stress on my mental state for me to even bother trying anymore. And the Survival mode fails to enhance the game; instead, it enables all the notorious problems in the game, forcing players to use mods to bypass all of Survival's rules just so they don't end up having their time wasted by bugs well outside their control.
This game is presented as a finished product, but it should have stayed in development for a little while longer for quality assurance purposes. And because it wasn't, I cannot recommend this game at any monetary value.

If you cannot get past the idea that you may do everything right and correct and still lose an entire party then this isn't for you, the RNG is strong with this game and you can either deal or not. This is not a case of people 'playing it wrong' its simply a case of people not liking what is a core part of the game. Another thing I would caution people with is getting too attached to your party members, in the early parts of the game the optimal strategy is to use them till they drop and simply replace them - as little sanity management as possible and just leave the quirks. All in all I like this game but I can understand why people dont like it, it can be very frustrating at times! My best recomendation if you are still unsure is to read more reviews and watch playthroughs.

A. As a super rare drop in rare versions of loot boxes throughout stages
B. Accumulate tons of 'crowns' to purchase them (the community accepted value always rising, too)
C. Pay with real money

While I respect that people have to earn a living, I was baited in by getting used to an otherwise good game then surprised by the grind paywall. When the game was first released, it instead limited the number of levels a person could play, which restored over 24 hours and of course, could be improved with payment. This I didn't mind as much in hindsight because it's a totally transparent mechanic: from the first level I was made aware of it, it encouraged me to get the most of my play time and ensured I didn't spend too much time.
Also, most of the stages are shared between 'rank' and 'arcade', making repetition set in real fast: this would have been acceptable if the grinding wasn't insane when it sets in. Starbound is a sandbox 2-D platformer that lets you travel between planets, meeting tribes of people and fighting strange alien creatures.
The game plays similarly to Terraria or 2-D Minecraft, as you start with a basic tool from which you can harvest the resources you need to craft better equipment. As you upgrade your equipment you will be able to craft the items needed to summon bosses, who hold the technology required to advance to the next zone of space and the next tier of equipment.
There are quadrillions of planets to explore, and you an designate a home planet which you can teleport to at any time. this gives you a base of operations and a place to build your ideal fortress/city/monument with the blocks you discover while travelling the universe. The tier-like progression also rewards you for fighting enemies and the game plays similarly to an RPG in that respect.
The game is still in beta at the time of writing, and this means that some crash bugs are yet to be resolved and there are still several pieces of content missing (e.g Quests).
Nonetheless, the game is excellent, a pleasure to look at (although no super-realistic graphics) and fun to play alone or with friends in a shared universe.

After a successful battle the haunting voice of the narrator of Darkest Dungeon speaks to me, stating that “overconfidence is a slow and insidious killer”. Before I might have shrugged this off, assuming it was simply clever writing done to help set an ominous tone. But I’ve played enough of this game to know that this is more than just a line, it’s a warning.
Darkest Dungeon is a fantastically illustrated roguelike dungeon crawler with a sense of style unlike any game I’ve ever seen before. The gothic-inspired visuals are extremely appealing and are paired perfectly with a haunting soundtrack as well as one of the best narrating voices I’ve ever heard in a game. Beyond this impeccable atmosphere and great writing there lies a game that is incredibly fun and addicting.
The premise of the game is simple; you have inherited the estate of a deceased relative and now must enlist the aid of various adventurers to help you explore the dungeons that lie below your land. In order to do so you must build up a network of these heroes and send them into the dungeons, four at a time, to complete various tasks. Achieving the quest at hand requires a bit of thought as you must take into account various aspects which your success hinges on. This includes your heroes, their mental and physical well-being, their equipment, and the supplies they are carrying to help aid them and keep them alive.
There are a variety of classes of heroes to choose from, each with their own unique abilities that bring a different advantage to your group. Your heroes travel through the dungeon in a line, and their placement in that line dictates what abilities they can use and what positions they can attack in the enemy’s line. You must ensure that you are using heroes that are best suited for the dungeon and/or boss you are about to face and have them arranged in a way where their abilities will not be hindered.
Perhaps the most important aspect of Darkest Dungeon is the affliction system, which dictates the psychological state of your heroes. Every hero has a stress bar which displays their current stress level. If their stress level gets too high, they will respond physically to their emotional state. In rare cases this might actually give them a bonus, but in most cases it will cause a penalty which will negatively affect your chances of making it out of the dungeon alive. The stress system is not something to be ignored, and doing so will cause you to witness your otherwise healthy heroes to suffer heart attacks and die before your eyes.
Before even setting foot in a dungeon you must go through the provisions screen, where you will have the option to buy items to aid your heroes in that dungeon. It is important to pay attention to what dungeon you are going into; as certain dungeons will contain enemies that focus on a particular type of damage. By paying attention to these things you can better equip your heroes with supplies that will prove useful while saving your hard earned gold. It is worth noting that the items bought here do not carry over if you are left with a surplus at the end of the dungeon. This might be an annoyance to some, but I think it adds a bit more strategy to the game as it forces you to find a balance in how you handle your money.
With the game saving automatically as you go along, there’s no ability to fall back on save-scumming to avoid disastrous situations. A mistake in planning can prove to be fatal, causing you to lose not only your heroes that you spent precious time leveling, but also the rare trinkets you had them equipped with. In order to avoid this heartache you will likely find yourself consulting outside sources for information about the boss you are about to face. Making an effort to think ahead and plan can help get you through some of the most difficult encounters. Progressing past the more difficult fights gives an immense feeling of success that I believe only comes with games that actually challenge you.
I truly love this game and can’t recommend it enough to those who will not let death deter them but will instead soldier on to the next darkest dungeon.

This game is so freaking awesome! Although it is in early access, just in case you didn't find that out already, Starbound is a  2D adventure survival sandbox game and seems to fill some nostalgia for those who played Terraria though Starbound is much different than Terraria. You explore countless worlds around the infinite universe in Starbound which adds to the replay value of the game. In addition, the mobs in each world seem to be different with unique powers (more to come) such as shooting flames from their mouths, rocks, and heck even using telekinesis and there are various world biomes such as forest biomes, desert biomes, snow biomes, and volcanic or magma biomes only to name a few. I recommend Starbound to any gamer that has played Terraria or anybody that likes survival sandbox games, but remember this is an EARLY ACCESS game so there will be problems or bugs and waiting for updates but if you have no problem with that go right ahead. Wonderful game. I adore it. Played since beta. Some changes have been real improvements, some less so, but overall it's a good balance.
You can do almost all the content for free, or all of it if you're willing to save up the in-game currency (crowns) to exchange for the real-money currency. The only downside is paying monthly for weapon expansions. But again, you can earn crowns and buy them that way. Just takes more time.

You'll almost certainly want to buy this if you enjoyed XCOM: Enemy Unknown.
There are some glitches (e.g. dodgy LOS that activates VIPs when the squad is three full moves away) that mean the game isn't ready for ironman playthroughs yet, and loading times are oddly long (even returning from missions when there really isn't anything the game could be loading)
For the record, yes, combat is indeed chance-based - the outcome of an (most) attacks is based on the roll of a die, and not the player's ability to aim with the mouse. If you don't like that idea, then XCOM is not the game for you. XCOM simply isn't "Rainbow Six with aliens"

I own this game since early access, and I have seen it progress through several stages of EA-development, all of which I am rather fond of. I figured I might as well write a review, because why not..?
Your task is to take control of a group of 4 heroes, which you assemble on your own, and lead them through different, randomly generated dungeons, with different inhabitants, and objects to interact with. A lot of loot awaits, both powerful and valuable. While doing your dungeon-crawling, you will not only have to defeat enemies in turn-based-combat to keep your merrymen alive, you will also need to keep them from getting stressed out. Health and sanity are both valuable resources, which you will need to handle with care.
Before moving out you can buy provisions, food, medical herbs, holy water, shovels, you name it. Said provisions allow you to use certain interactive objects more safely and/or effectively.
Upon completing a dungeon, your heroes will be given XP, which leads to level-ups sooner or later. Higher level heroes can use higher tier armour and weaponry, as well as improve their skills.
To provide the best possible care for your crews, you will need to upgrade your very own, small village, to unlock more efficient methods of curing mental deseases, quirks, or sicknesses, like the black plague, for example. Training and gearing up also takes place in town, in corresponding buildings.
Well, this has been discussed a lot, and everybody has a different point of view on that subject. My point of view is, that this game is neither too difficult at all, nor does it contain "false difficulty" (I always have to laugh when someone uses that term. A game is either difficult or it is not, and how difficulty is "created" is purely a choice of design).
What makes this game challenging is that, no matter what you do, everything is based on odds, or RNG as some might say.
One does not simply hit/stun/crit all the time.
Your job as a player is to identify threats, and prioritize targets according to the current state of your party at any given point in time, as well as playing the odds in your favour as much as you possibly can. That being said, even if you are doing everything "right", your mileage may vary, such is the way of things. If the thought of that happening throws you off, this is the wrong game for you. Should you enjoy having success, eventhough your heroes lives are constantly at risk, stop reading my wall of text, pick up the game, and dive right in.
You have an abundance of hero classes to choose from when you want to assemble a party. Tanks, healers, dmg-dealers, debuffers, stunners, etc allow you to be creative with your lineups.
All your heroes start out with at least 4 combat skills, and some camping skills for longer endeavours, but they can learn, and master seven different skills during their careers. You will, however, always have to choose 4 skills for combat, all of which define the role your hero plays in conjunction with other party members. Furthermore certain skills are only useable from a certain position.
There is a lot of creative leeway here, and experimenting with different lineups is highly recommended and encouraged by the diversity of encounters in the different dungeons.
The actual combat plays the most significant role as far as gameplay goes. Each area has a different roster of enemies which you may or may not encounter. Some enemy lineups are rather straightforward: A couple melee brawlers with ranged support, for example. Other lineups, on first glance, are a bit more subtle as to what what manner of threat they pose, but be warned: Some enemies are pretty much designed to "attack" your heroes mental stability, trying to drive them insane. Furthermore there are lineups which are based on certain combinations of the monsters' individual abilities. Your job is to dismantle them all. Did I mention bosses already? No? Well, this game has bosses too, so be sure to think fast on your feet, when you encounter them for the first time.
Not only is the composition of your party a relevant factor, also the order in which you assemble them plays a huge role. The same logic is applied to your enemies as well. If you manage to shuffle enemy groups, you can capitalize on that by taking out high-dmg monsters with lower health quickly, for example, your enemies might attempt the same however.
Art-style sure is a matter of personal preference, be it visual, or audio. I believe it is safe to say that the overall style of this game is very appealing, because visuals and audio go hand in hand, add a really good narrator to the mix, and you're in for quite an immersive experience.

Hello Commander!
Shooting aliens has never been so much fun, while at the same time being so deliciously difficult.
XCOM 2 manages to completely capture the XCOM spirit, while improving upon the shortcomings of the predecessor.
The basic premise of XCOM 2, taking Earth back from the aliens, elegantly solves a conceptual weakness of past XCOM games: If the whole world is at stake, why have resources always been so limited? Why doesn't the Commander have all of Earth's resources at his command? Why does he have to please individual countries lest they not drop out of the XCOM project?
The guerilla approach serves XCOM2 very well, it serves as a natural and logical explanation for the limited resources the player has to operate with.
A great change in XCOM 2 is that most missions now have a turn timer. It makes missions a lot more intense, you now have to constantly move forward and take risks if you do not want to loose the mission.
The new and changed alien units seems to have been specifically designed to be as annoying as possible. They can all easily wipe your squad if not dealt with appropriately. The AI makes good use of the abilities of the various unit types.
These changes make the game a lot more challenging, but also far more rewarding. I highly recommend this game, it's a lot of fun.
Good luck, Commander!

First thing: My playtime is at about 145 hours. Got SPiral Knights first, and then I got Steam
So, lets start:
In Spiral Knights you play your Knight, run through the ever harder layers of the clockwork, defeating monsters and boss monsters to get materials and money to build better armor and weaponry.
Story:
The story has an interesting base. The story that is told before you start playing and during the tutorial is very exciting I think. But later you are just sent on many missions to get materials for the Spiral scientists, foil the plans of the Gremlins who claim the clockwork for themselves and want to kill all Spiral Knights, kill some boss monsters and eventually get to the planets core. By these missions, which you complete to progress in story and equipment you´re allowed to wear, the story gets unimportant. Just do the next missions to progress in the story, finally slay a boss and get the permission to explore the next layer of the clockwork.
Music:
The music is overall relly good I think, but it just becomes repetitive and most of the compositions are a bit slow.
Graphic:
Nothing special, but not bad. Just look at the pictures above and you´ll see.
Community and Development:
The community is nice as far as I know (never really read forum). There is a huge place in the middle of the basevillage, where you always see some people just hanging out, chatting and trading. It can be a nice place just to have some nice talks and relax.
The development is very slow. There is a patch maybe every one or two months. But those are just yearly events like christmas or so, new price boxes for real money or very much ingame money which contain mostly cosmetics, texture changes and one or two bug fixes. The last REAL content was released one year and four months ago.
Antoher thing is that it´s programmed in Java. The programmers seam do not have programmed the game very good, because everytime get hit by an enemy, everytime you activate a pressure plate which spawns enemys, the game stands still for the fraction of a second. You´ll also have to wait ten or 20 seconds on every loading screen between the levels or the parts of the village and the patches always take ten to 20 minutes even if only a single texture was changed.
Gameplay:
The combat system is realtime, it´s much about timing. When to use your melee weapon, when to better use ranged attacks. When to keep the distance and when to use your ability or your block. When an enemy wants to attack with a melee attack, they try to get near to you, then stand still and get a coloured indicator in the direction they are attacking. You have a short time until they launch their attack.
That the clockwork is ever changing is not completely right. If you do the same missions, every layer is the same.
You will only see changes if you are doing regular levels which reach from newbie level to the highest level. You just take a start point (those available depend on your mission progress) equal to your equipment level and run through the layers. Every layer the same enemies deal more damage and can take more hits. You have a map on which you can see, which levels are in the next depth and wait at the elevator until the level you want comes in. In every layer there are one to five different possible levels and those are the same everytime you enter the same gate. There are four gates at any time, every week the oldest gate disappears and is replaced by a new one. The levels which may come into the layers of the new gate are chosen from a level pool which are always the same. This means that, after hours of playing, you´ll  see
only levels you already know. The fights are diversified enough to not become boring, but the levels are not going to be something new.
The armor is sub-divided into head armor and body armour which vary in defense strength and defensetypes (there are multiple damagetypes) and small things like giving extra health bars or so.
Then there is the shield which has the same stats like armor, but also a health bar which goes done by using it to block attacks. The defensestats of the shield determine how much damage it will tank until it has to reload.
Then there are two slots for offensive equipment. There are melee weapons, guns for ranged  attacks and bombs which you can charge and then lay onto the ground to damage everything destructable and hostile nearby a few seconds later.
Melee is stronger than guns are, but also more dangerous because enemies can easily hit you at those distances.
Guns are always safe to use, if you only use guns you will barely be ever killed.
I cant tell about bombs because I dont use them.
The realmoney-currency can also be sold on the market for the ingame curency, so you can get it. If you couldn´t you´d barely be able to craft equipment, because grinding alchemy orbs can take countless hours.
But in the end it is much about farming. You´ll need to farm much for alchemy orbs or get the money to buy premium currency and then buy alchemy orbs. But the farming is not that boring. The combat is diversified enough to not get boring unless you play many hours consecutive.
Conclusion:
The game can be really fun, it is realtime combat which is good because you will have to farm for many hours if you want to get good equipment without paying real money. It can be a bit laggy and slow sometimes, probably because it´s in Java and not programmed very well. The developers are very slow, so do not expect new content being released when you play the game. The communtiy is nice and good for little talks, the graphics and music are okay, but not special.
I would recommend to give it a try. It has its little faults but it can be a really exciting game for many hours.

If you're looking for a completely new game, which is exactly like the old one - please enjoy playing the old one. Fallout 1, 2, 3, NV, Tactics. They are affordable and run on a anything. But to give this game a thumb down based on your expectations is simply not fair. Many people sound like Bethesda "butchered a franchise". Maybe choosing a faction was a more important part of Fallout 1 and 2, or maybe the game has been a bit streamlined as a shooter with an RPG system, rather than the other way around. I prefer the changes.
The diamond shaped dialogue opton is an improvement to the pile of text of the previous titles. A is a confirmation, B is a rejection, X is a provocative or sarcastic remark, Y is always a question. So, if somebody asks you: Dude, want some chems? You can reply without reading! This is far more immersive than the dialogue in previous games.
Also the shooting, assuming you unlocked the framerate and disabled the mouse acceleration, the shooting feels good. Responsive.
Ah, the building, This feature alone justifies the purchase. You'are able to build. ANYTHING. Yes, you're limited to the in-game assets, but there are plenty. Electric wiring alone will keep you entertained for hours. Some of the already present objects don't always attach to the new ones and sometimes the allignment is off, but still it's a great feature to have.
Survival-mode. It changes the game...Completely. Now you cannot save, only autosave at sleeping locations(sleeping bags, beds) Those become your checkpoints. You cannot fast travel. Every object has weight, except for quest-items and misc-objects. This means you have to decide: Will i take the stimpack, water and fruit or the weapon. How much ammo? These important decisions you will have to make in order to survive. Wow, really feels like survival...And...you can play the survival mode right from the start, unlike in NV,
So, basically Fallout 4 is full to the brim with several well-made mechanics and a huge wasteland full of secrets. I assume the bad reviews refer to the way the publisher decided to handle mods, or whatever. I don't care. Fallout 4 is worth your time.

I recommend Starbound to any gamer that has played Terraria or anybody that likes survival sandbox games, but remember this is an EARLY ACCESS game so there will be problems or bugs and waiting for updates but if you have no problem with that go right ahead. In my honest opinion the game so far is looking pretty good with a bunch of potential to become successful since this has been in development for about two years and a steady community from my experience. This game is suffering major launch pains. At least for me and my system (Windows 10 Pro). I'm running a 3.4 ghz 64 bit multi-core i7-3440 CPU with 16GB of RAM and an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 660 Ti with updated drivers. The game crashes regularly if you do anything "special". By special, I mean doing anything other than playing "straight-through". It crashes when I customize characters, reload a save mid-mission, and sometimes when training characters I select "Continue training."
The game is much less stable than its predecessor at launch. I had none of these issues with XCOM: EW, although granted it'd been out a while before I purchased it. I've worked in Product Development in the past, so I understand the balance of getting a product to market "complete" and getting one out to off-set capital costs, but this feels rushed. Games certainly be tested to the point of avoiding complete system freezes. But it is tough to test "every system", "every OS", and "every piece of hardware".
I'm the first to be sympathetic to the developer, I understand the struggles. This really feels like a product that was given a possibly arbitrary or finanicial launch date. I've experienced this where the business dictates a date and works backwards, rather than providing requirements and working forward to a reasonable lauch date. I would recommend anyone looking to purchase wait until these MAJOR crash issues are resolved. I love the game and the franchise, but having to force quit and relaunch because I would prefer my specialists hair be blonde instead of brown is unacceptable. Having to reboot because I wanted my PSI-OP to continue training is equally frustrating.
I recommend the game, but wait until the first major patch / fix.

This isn't Fallout, this is a kid's game.
I feel like I spent almost 70 hours of my life playing a game that "cool kids" play, and then run to their friends to say how much violent and hard their new game is.

-RPG elements are non-existent, basically. I felt like I had no choice other than the one the game imposed me to take.
-Didn't like much companions, especially because the Lone Wanderer perk basically killed my interest in them (this is my fault tho, not the game).
-The DLC's are maybe the worst thing that could happen to this game, except for Far Harbor. Automatron and Vault-Tec Workshop are just useless DLC's that let you make cool things, but they are just wasting your time. Nuka World is maybe THE worst DLC in the entire franchise. No storyline, bad map, bad characters, and god awful ending to an awful DLC. Far Harbor was good, it didn't bore me and even tho it hadn't any cool exclusive equipment or such, the story was good and you could link it to the main questline (synths and♥♥♥♥♥♥ ya feel me). Oh, and the Old Longfellow might be my favorite companion in the game, even tho I never used it.
Overall the game just feels like a kid's game. The story is bad, the choices you can make are so little and bad, the factions are bad, the DLC's are cancer, companions are killed by Lone Wanderer perk, no RPG elements, repetitive dungeon and quest system like in Skyrim, and a settlement system that made my stomach suicide by how tideous, annoying and cringy those things are.
I really had hopes, I really liked it in the beginning. Then it got worse the more I went on.
My advice is, if you like Skyrim and you didn't play any of the previous Fallout games, give it a try. You will like for sure, because it's a really accessible game with his easy FPS style and shooting systems, which btw it's the best thing this game has. If you only played Fallout 3, still give it a try. If you played either Fallout 1, 2 or NV, just don't buy it. I was lucky enough to try and finish the game for free, with the DLC's included.
Final Verdict: 4/10. Disappointing.

Great game sofar.  Being in beta still, this game is alot of fun, and shows great promise.  In short, the game is Minecraft meets Megaman.  Fun gameplay, easily played with a controller even, although thru habit, I have reverted back to using the keyboard+mouse.  Old habits die hard I suppose.  I eagerly await what comes next.  Each player (or you if playing single player) gets dumped off in orbit of a random planet with simple quests at first to teach you how to play.  There are ways to goto other systems, including friends that are on the server.  As in Minecraft, there are some buildings you run across that can be makeshift shelters or flat out bases.  The way the starting area is setup, since the game is 2d, you will be limited to how far to each side you can go with each technology level you achieve, needing the next step to progress.  Fans of Minecraft Survival mode will definitely enjoy this one.
Several deficiencies due to its beta status are apparent sofar, most notably bad adminning tools for those that run their own server.  This is promised to be fixed, but is currently not something that will arrive soon from what I have been able to gather.
The other one, that I have not yet researched is the rather weak toon customization options.  I would love to run around as a cousin of Thor or as a pirate, but the current state of affairs doesn't currently allow for that.  Hopefully thats a "yet".
That said, I would say a solid 8/10 sofar, with more refinements and a cleanup of gameplay.

In all honesty, I could recommend this to you but I'm not sure if I should since if you are looking for some singleplayer shooting action with some RPG elements in the mix, you might have a great time with it but Fallout 4 is overall a bad RPG and even worse of a Fallout game as it lacks most of the things the fans love about Fallout franchise (like the karma system, unique and memorable RPG quests that are more than just the "run, fetch and kill"-type and the very atmosphere of a nuclear wasteland).
Don't get me wrong, it's not all bad... But it's clear that Bethesda wasn't paying attention to the right things as they did do some things well. The guns are so well done (they could've added more of them though), the power armor feels amazing, it's got great songs in there when ever you get to hear them, few interesting companions that you can travel with (Nick Valentine, John Hancock, Deacon and maybe even Strong) and the overall combat is just fun.
But the game can get boring very quickly as well, since it's all very repetitive and the quests are for the most part just way too similar, though there are few good ones as well (Diamond City Blues, for example).
If you're looking for a solid RPG-experience, just turn your head towards either Fallout 3 or New Vegas (I'd recommend New Vegas a bit more, though).

About 7 hours in and I am enjoying the game so far. Trove has some interesting classes and what appears to be some alright synergy between some of them. Enemy variety is there although a lot of the creatures do the same thing. There are a lot of dungeons but they aren't all that different from eachother. It also seems like the game is really easy, even with my 7 hours of gameplay, but maybe it's because of the craziness of some of the spells from some classes combined. Difficulty might change later on but I doubt the gameplay will be too different since you don't have too many abilities to choose between. I thought there would be a skill tree with unlockable abilities but there seems to be no such thing. It might come later in some way though.
The game sure has a lot of silly stuff in it and plenty of items (and there are a lot of items...a whole lot. Your inventory is filled up all the time) which are references to other games or movies which is alright but it can be a little too much at times. The game is also really damn random... a bit too much for my taste. It seems like the world has been built by a really poor generator and all the biomes and dungeons are connected in very weird ways. The game also lacks atmosphere and it's hard to get immersed in the world. There's a lot of comparison between Trove and Cube World and with good reason, but Cube World did a better job with the world generation and atmosphere (too bad that game was abandoned). I also feel like Troves graphics style is a little dull but that's just a personal opinion.
Trove still has a lot to offer though so I will continue playing and I feel I will be surprised later on so I might have to edit this review at some point.
Oh and btw, the game is free but you won't feel it at all when you play the game. The only times you will notice is in the hub area where you get a pop-up window with stuff you can buy. It's no big deal and you really don't have to buy anything which is great. THERE IS ONE IMPORTANT THING TO NOTICE THOUGH: My friend bought a backpack expansion and it seems to not be what he expected at all! Read up on things first before you buy 'em!
EDIT: After about 100 more hours of gameplay all the things I've written before still apply. I have been grinding a whole lot more and have been doing a lot of shadow arenas. They don't do much though. I haven't tried the new Shadow Tower but from what I've heard it's just a bigger, more grindy version of a Shadow Arena. I am done with this game and that won't get me back into it. It's way too grindy (gettin the gear (which all have the same stats in the end by the way), the challenges, getting mounts and everything else) in a way that get's pretty boring later on and the lack of immersion just made me lose interest completely. Was fun for a while but they need to add a whole lot more (even something simple as an auction house would make the game 10 times better because of all the grinding) to get me back into the game.
Still, give it a try - you've got nothing to lose! Would be cool to see what they'll add if enough people play the game and give feedback.
PS: I've been playing with a friend and that seems to make the game a lot more fun so find a buddy to slay with!

XCOM 2 is everything that you loved about XCOM: Enemy Unknown and XCOM: Enemy Within… but better. You will again find yourself in the position of the “Commander,” managing both strategic assets on your mobile base, and your soldiers in tactical actions on missions in the fight against aliens who have taken over Earth.
The game largely takes place within these two spheres – strategic, and tactical.
In the strategic side of things, players will have to make choices on the Geoscape and within the Avenger.
The Geoscape allows you expand your ‘resistance’ contacts, unlocking missions in new areas, chase rumors of supplies and intelligence, and view the progress of the “Game Over” counter that is constantly ticking upwards, against you. The choices on what to pursue are meaningful, as you generally can’t do it all; missions will expire after a set time. Investing time into improving the areas you’ve contacted provides a significant amount of long-term benefit in terms of resource income in the form of ‘supplies’ (your money), at the expense of other missions which might provide more short-term gains.
The Avenger gameplay will consist largely of managing your base; much like XCOM: Enemy Unknown, you have a fixed area in which to build, and you must clear out alien debris and plan your structures out within that space. There are more optimal placements if you want to conserve the power necessary to operate your facilities, or to boost your existing power generation structures. There is enough space to construct everything; it’s more a matter of prioritizing which research structures you want over others. While constructing and managing your facilities, you will have the option of re-assigning engineers that you’ve  picked up on missions to increase facility construction speed, upgrade facility roles (generating more power, healing soldiers faster), or make item construction faster. This represents an interesting worker-placement challenge, as you will not have enough engineers to have everything fully upgraded and working at full speed. It is necessary to move engineers from one task to another task as needs change/arise. You will also spend time prioritizing which research you want to pursue, and which experimental weapons/armors/items you would like to make (they’re not all insta-build.)
The tactical gameplay utilizes a squad of 4-6 highly customizable soldiers (XCOM operatives) to complete various missions. This will be very familiar to XCOM: Enemy Unknown players; combat takes place on a grid, with various structures and obstacles to use in the fight against the alien menace. Unlike previous games, there is a significantly greater amount of urban combat, and far fewer “fighting in the woods” type missions. The action is well-paced, and well-calculated choices will make the difference in ensuring you leave missions without too many casualties. Many missions have timers associated with them to force you to take an aggressive stance on the tactical map; this is overall an improvement, in my opinion, as previous games allowed a much slower pace (to the detriment of the action of combat.) During missions you will also have the opportunity to pick up gear that your enemies drop; this too is on a timer, incentivizing aggressive action to pick up powerful upgrades. Enemy A.I. is much improved over previous versions, and enemies will tactically retreat to their comrades if they’re overwhelmed. The enemy variety is also very interesting – you will have to adjust tactics, frequently, based on the variety of alien soldiers that you will face.
Overall, the game is very difficult, especially in the early months where you are constantly out-gunned and pressured into tough missions to make ends meet. There is a constant tension on missions where you are working against a timer, and there is a near constant tension on the geo-scape as you are forced to choose between equally compelling missions. If you expect to walk into a game and dominate it on the first try, you really won't be able to in XCOM 2.  Learning the nuances of the mechanics of the strategic gameplay and the enemies your facing (along with the squad that you carefully build up) will allow you to remove a lot of the randomness that you'll face, but you will lose soldiers, or have to retreat from certain missions; soldiers, at the end of the day, are a strategic asset that you will sometimes need to sacrifice in order to complete an important strategic goal on your missions. The challenge can be daunting, but eventually you'll get the hang of it and be able to run very smooth  missions that allow you to take on very difficult setups.
Plot-wise, the game is well-written and compelling as you try to lead Earth in a rebellion against your alien overlords. Overall, I don’t think that the supporting cast was as well-developed as in previous games; Lily and Tygan are interesting enough, but don’t seem to have the same flair that Shen and Vahlen had in the original. Bradford returns, a bit gruffer, a bit grumpier, but perhaps not as funny as in XCOM: Enemy Unknown. The role and personality of the Commander play a greater part of this game, interestingly enough. The trajectory that humanity is on, and the fate of the Earth are interesting enough in this post-alien dystopia; exploring and seeing details of what that future entails are one of the joys of the game.
Graphics-wise, this game is more intense than its predecessors; even with a good medium-end rig, you can expect some slowdowns/framerate drops if maps get too hectic. The environments, textures, and characters are all wonderfully detailed in this future sci-fi dystopia. The world itself has a lot of personality as you conduct missions within it, whether you’re aiding an isolated rural Resistance base, or running a high-powered mission into the heart of A.D.V.E.N.T.-controlled territory.
Overall, the game is a worthy successor to XCOM: Enemy Unknown. I look forward to the DLC installments for this game, and I feel there is a great deal of replayability in this particular game. I highly recommend this game to anyone with a PC!

Beyond the artistic merits, I was largely unimpressed.
The game is inexplicably punishing to the point of frustration. Hear me out. I am no meek gamer in the strategy world. I have completed Shogun 2 on Legendary, Xcom on Impossible Iron-man, and Xcom 2 on Legendary Ironman. I can take the beatings if the game world and mechanics make sense, and I get a feeling that I am contributing to my goal.
In Darkest Dungeon there is one difficulty. I suppose the designers have tried to incorporate what is known as cognitive flow in game theory [1], by allowing your to choose the level of dungeon you enter with your party. You can roughly match your party to a suitable dungeon in level-wise as well as tactics wise (if you go ruins, don’t take bleed damage, for one example).
Then it becomes apparent that the designers have know idea what they are doing and then BREAK the cognitive flow by not allowing you to 'game the game'. You can't take a level 3 character into a level 1 dungeon. You can't use your 'battle' skills outside of battle, but then you can't take an extra 2-3 rounds in battle to heal wounds and stress... because the game will punish you with more stress for bothering to try. Entering a level 5 dungeon is less like a move from 3 to 5, and more like a move from 3 to 10 if you know what I mean.
Beyond the obvious imbalance in the game, the game will then double and triple punish you with the inane random dice that I wonder why even try in the first place? It feels like my skill and knowledge of the game becomes more irreverent the higher the dungeon level. Ironically the stress attacks in the game cause real stress to the player -- that is they are so frequent and critically boosted that it causes no-end to frustrations. Where is the fun lads?
Minor gripes include the carry space is far too small for the amount of item types in the game, forcing more contrived choices with the only goal of annoying me further. There is not enough gold earned in the game, used for nearly everything useful. There are too many heirloom item drops in the game (used to unlock and build up your town).
I am left to assume that the refusal to balance the game properly and provide either adequate difficulty modes or a proper working cognitive game flow, is a sign of artificially inflating the playtime of the title. Taken into account the annoying slow pop-ups that lock the control on the party, the tedious animation loops, and the drawn out combat; all of which compound to my suspicions.
I hope with their financial success, they make another game and address these issues forthwith, but for me I didn't like this game despite really trying and pouring 50 hours into it. This is the counter point to looking for 'long games' to use as an example of 'good games'.
