Some Good, Some Bad
The general gameplay is pretty decent, a turn-based dungeon explorer. That said, there's a lot of elements that are really just frustrating to deal with. The stress system, while sometimes fun (It feels pretty awesome when you hit 100 stress and your character gets a heroic bonus instead of crumbling under the stress like the majority of characters do) is more annoying than anything. When maximum stress hits the character has a heart attack, dropping their health to zero and debuffing them for the remainder of the dungeon, which can be a group killing experience. To avoid this you're expected to "treat" the character's stress by leaving them in the local bar or church while you go on your next adventure. This leads to a lot of characters leveling up at different rates. This wouldn't be too bad, but there's invisible barriers between characters of certain levels. For instance, level 3 characters can't embark with level 2 characters. This causes problems where the only characters available on your roster are two level 3s, and two level 2s, because everyone else is healing from stress or illness. Except you can't embark with that group, because theyre separate level groups. So what do you do? Well, you can either take a highly stressed character out of the bar or church because you need some lower leveled guys to adventure with to get some people up to level 3. I realize its supposed to be a matter of how to manage the team, but it's more frustrating than anything. A high stressed character IS going to have a heart attack during the dungeon and ruin the run, and dismissing them to hire a new recruit is just really annoying.
Then there's the spontaneous difficulty spikes. For instance one dungeon, suggested for level 1 characters, asks you to kill a specific character, a "boss". The "boss" character all of a sudden is able to knock two characters down to 1 health in one attack, and gets multiple attack turns in one round. Meanwhile all before this I had been playing level 1 dungeons, others with boss characters that were nowhere near this difficulty. It's just ridiculous, because there's no reason or expectation of such power in a level 1 dungeon.
There's also the low drop rates of gold, which you need to spend more and more of on supplies just to survive the dungeon, but then also need to use to upgrade characters and heal their stress and ailments. There's barely enough money to go around, which makes advancing characters a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ especially when they'll just die to an encounter with an enemy like I mentioned in the last paragraph.
Overall, I find the game frustrating, but there are redeeming aspects, like having a solid team making dungeons a challenging, but rewarding experience (but like I mentioned with the level-tier separations that can get messed up really quickly) I'd recommend it to people that like repeating tedious elements, because you will be losing characters, and re-running the same dungeons to level up new characters again. I've read that the game is more of a team-management game than a dungeon crawler, which kind of rings true. The important part of the game seems to be more in how you handle healing characters and the meager funds you get. If you're into that aspect, and dont care that much about whether your characters survive in the long run then you might like the game. I feel the game is misrepresented as a dungeon crawler RPG, and thats only a part of the game, which is more often frustrating than enjoyable. If all you want is to dungeon crawl, a different game might be more up your ally. If you want to manage your team of weaklings, and can accept that most of them are going to die then you might like the game.
Generally, I don't recommend the game, because I don't think it appeals to a wide audience and most people are going to go into it expecting an experience much different than what it actually is, but if you fall within a specific niche of gamers that prefer team-management games and grim-dark fantasy you might be one of the people that really like Darkest dungeon.

I love this game. I don't play early access games, since I'm more interested in the finished product; I made an exception for Darkest Dungeon prior to its release.

If you enjoy, say, Nuzlocke runs of Pokemon, I feel like the two are similar when it comes to developing strategies. Darkest Dungeon is really one of my favorites. You will have runs that go down the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, but that's the exception, not the rule. tl;dr:
I've had no problem in beating the timer in EVERY SINGLE MISSION I've played so far. In fact, only once came as close as T-2. Mobile combat tactics, covering retreats etc. play very differently than overwatch spam of xcom 1. I very much enjoy the game the way it is, on normal difficulty. My only grief is that I played through xcom 1 doing trench warfare, which is considerably less fun.
The rest:
What people seem to whine about the most is that Firaxis presses them into running and gunning... and in that all strategy (which TBS games are all about) goes out the window. That's only partially true. Yes, you are forced into a more dynamic and less comfortable model of gameplay. Yes, your old strategies will be no good here. Most modern gamers, the auto-heal generation (as opposed to the medkit generation), may not be used to playing genuinely difficult games, where the odds are stacked against you and the game is challenging in every single way it could be. Here, you need to adapt and develop new tactics. There's plenty of time to complete every mission, if you think about what you're doing. It's still a turn based strategy, take your time to consider the next move!
What the game excells at is constantly throwing new challenges at you. The aliens are always one step ahead, no matter what. Even if you push them back a bit, they always come back and the gameover clock is inevitable. You're always losing.
One more major complaint about the game that I see come up so often is that the aliens don't play smart, they just play unfair. I must disagree with the first part - personally I find the AI slightly more challenging and unpredictable than in xcom 1. As for the latter part, I do agree and enjoy this fact very much. The game isn't arbitrarily challenging - the unfairnes is based on how well you're doing, as it was in previous XCOM games. Now it's just more nasty :D

TL;DR
Great game early to mid-game, but gets too grindy endgame. Still an 8/10
Full Review
I think I just want to address this first: If you really think that this game is 100% RNG based that can instantly wipe out your entire party in a single dungeon run, I can assure you that is not the case. A lot of the game is based on RNG, but unless you're being really stubborn, a crit hit on you or a few misses in a row won't be the end of you. You're given plenty of options in hero choices, trinkets, and skills to rig the odds best in your favor for a particular mission. But once a mission starts heading south, REMEMBER THAT YOU CAN QUIT THE MISSION AT ANY TIME. I hear a lot of complaints about how BS stress can be, but you always have the option to abandon the mission if too many party members are afflicted, diseased, ect. Pick your battles wisely, and you'll never have a party wipe. I beat the game without one, just check my achievments. The only place where RNG really plays a huge role is with Deaths Door, when a character reaches 0 hp. And thankfully because of that mechanic, it prevents instant one-hit party wipes. Though they are debuffed for the rest of the quest
Now, onto the main bulk of review.
The story: An ancestor of yours accidentally unleashed an eldritch abombination into the world, so it's up to you to fix it.
The main bulk of the gameplay revolves around sending heroes out to do various quests to collect gear, gold, and heirlooms, mainly to prepare for the assaults on the Darkest Dungeon. Doing missions levels up their resolve, which allows them to get better gear, better skill upgrades, and do harder missions. If you wanna purchase the better gear/skill upgrades, you need heirlooms from your various missions in order to unlock these. Later on, with a high enough Blacksmith and Guild(Used for skill updgrades), you can even upgrade your stagecoach to bring in heroes with pre-upgraded armors in skills, all the way up to level 4, which helps with the grind a bit. For stress and afflictions,  as your heroes explore, they'll accumulate stress and may develop ununfavorable traits. If stress gets to 100 in a dungeon, they'll either become afflicted negatively which will cause them to act irrationally depending on the affliction, or they have a slight chance of gaining a great buff, which can seriously help out your party. If stress reaches 200, they'll suffer a heart attack, which will either reduce their health to 0, or if they're already at Death's Door, instantly kill them. You can reduce stress in the dungeon by using certain skills, from camping. Out of the dungeon, you can use the Tavern or Chapel. Sometimes the traits can be really bad (E.G, -10 accuracy against a certain enemy type), but for the majority of the time, you don't have to worry way too much about these traits.
When it comes to the main dungeon crawling, you take 4 heroes through a variety of missions, from simply explore the area to collect 3 amount of artifacts, to work your way up to the boss. As you start off, your worst opponent will be inexperience. As you continue to play, you eventually learn which team combos work best where, along with the fact that your heroes should have beter gear as you go on. It's a difficult yet fun curve, which takes a while to get over. Once you get over the curve though, that's when you start to notice the repetitiveness of the dungeons. Stronger enemy varients for just about every enemy is just a different name and higher stats, so you don't really see too much variation between enemys in later areas. It's the exact same for the bosses. You have to re-fight each boss 3 times, each one stronger than the last. This really contributes to the feeling late-game that you are pretty much only just grinding since you're seeing the same place and enemies over and over again because you need to level up heroes or need more gold/heirlooms. And trust me, the darkest dungeon is insanely hard, and you need to grind A LOT in order to prepare for it to prime your lv 6 heroes to perfection. Not to mention the "Never Again" penalty that your heroes get when they finish a Darkes Dungeon quest. Any heroes that successfuly assauled the Darkest Dungeon will never return there again, which means you need 16 lv 6 heroes ready to go. Because of this, I seriously don't recommend creating throwaway parties for suicidal gold runs.
The Darkest Dungeon, the final area in the game, is true hell. All the enemies deal insane bleed, blight, and stress damage. Not only that, abandoning the mission will take the life of a random hero. On the plus side, there's no obstacles, no traps, and no chance of ambush, and the dungeon isn't randomly generated. The "abandoning takes a random hero" is really the only major flaw of the dungeon. Darkest Dungeon is a game where you NEED to learn from your mistakes, the Darkest Dungeon especially. For learning from your mistakes there, you're guaranteed to grind up at least one new hero. But the satisfaction from beating each darkest dungeon assault is imeasurably satisfying. All the odds were against you, and you still won.
SPEAKING OF SATISFACTORY (SPOILER TERRITORY AHEAD)
The second greatest flaw of the game has to be the ending. It's a forced bittersweet ending, and I mean FORCED. It's "Well you may have literally killed this god, but you merely delayed the inveitable", coming full circle and ending on "Ruin has come to my family." TL;DR, some dimwad decided to re-awake the monstrosity that lived down there AGAIN despite the (likely) 14 heroes you had who already knew about the terrors of the dungeon. The eldritch abomination was awoken because the Anscestor didn't know what he was getting into at first. WHAT REASON WOULD ANYBODY HAVE TO AWAKEN THE THING AGAIN? Hell, if they wanted to end it on a lovecraftian note, why not end it like how the Rats in the Walls ended, by just flat out destroying the entire estate that sat upon the dungeon? This ending is a forced punch to the gut saying, "Lol I know you suffered a lot but that was pointless". There are a million different ways this could have ended, and Red Hook took the "Blatantly forced edgy" ending.
Despite it's shortcomings, the game is still great. The art and sound design is amazing, the dungeon crawling (for a majority of the game) will always keep you on your toes, and the stress mechanic is something pretty original that adds a new layer to the game's dungeon crawling. It's a good 8/10 game if you can tolerate the pain early-game brings

Alright, I normally don't write a lot of reviews but I really like this game so I suppose I will.
The good.
There are a lot of good parts about this game. Mostly in that it combines the creative "sandbox" aspect of games like minecraft with a classic adventure style MMO where you have to go into dungeons, team up, and fight bosses. The loot system in this game is very cool because rather than having to constantly find new loot as you play, if you like the stat variety in a certain piece of equipment you can just upgrade it until it is the highest level. I also found it very cool that your characters level is not just dependent on the number of experience points you have, but also based on your items.
Another thing I really like is that all of the classes can be played (once you earn the cubits for them) and so you can switch between different classes to your liking. Also, like WoW and other games, the maximum level is very easy to attain, in Trove it is actually very very easy to get to the highest level, which is 20, and start focusing on raising your level by getting better items. Overall I really enjoy this game
Also, most free games feature content that makes the game basically unplayable if you don't buy a bunch of stuff with cash. This game is definitely not like that. Most of the things available for purchase are cosmetic, or are obtainable in the game through some other currency (in game currency), and the things that are not, just give players an xp boost or jump boost, but seeing as it is not a competative game in any way, that is not really an issue
The Bad
The unfortunate thing about this game is the servers are quite frequently down, choppy, or having large queue times. This is understandable as it is a fairly new game with large volumes of people already playing it, so I would hope/expect to see this problem resolved in short time. The other bad thing is that while it combines the "minecraft" type game with the MMO type game, the aspects of each of these are very limited. You only have 3 abilities, which makes the combat extremely simple. This could be a good thing if you enjoy that sort of game and don't like to deal with complicated battle rotations because I assure you this game has none. Additionally, the dungeon and shadow arena team combat is limited compared to other MMOs which typically have a designated tank, healer, and combat characters. It seems in most cases that everyone just haphazardly runs into an Arena and then a giant killfest ensues. Again, this is not necessarily a bad thing if you don't mind highly simplified combat.
In general this game is very fun, and I will continue to play it, mostly because for all the server issues there may be, it is free so I cannot complain much.

Beyond the artistic merits, I was largely unimpressed.
The game is inexplicably punishing to the point of frustration. Hear me out. I am no meek gamer in the strategy world. I have completed Shogun 2 on Legendary, Xcom on Impossible Iron-man, and Xcom 2 on Legendary Ironman. I can take the beatings if the game world and mechanics make sense, and I get a feeling that I am contributing to my goal.
In Darkest Dungeon there is one difficulty. I suppose the designers have tried to incorporate what is known as cognitive flow in game theory [1], by allowing your to choose the level of dungeon you enter with your party. You can roughly match your party to a suitable dungeon in level-wise as well as tactics wise (if you go ruins, don’t take bleed damage, for one example).
Then it becomes apparent that the designers have know idea what they are doing and then BREAK the cognitive flow by not allowing you to 'game the game'. You can't take a level 3 character into a level 1 dungeon. You can't use your 'battle' skills outside of battle, but then you can't take an extra 2-3 rounds in battle to heal wounds and stress... because the game will punish you with more stress for bothering to try. Entering a level 5 dungeon is less like a move from 3 to 5, and more like a move from 3 to 10 if you know what I mean.
Beyond the obvious imbalance in the game, the game will then double and triple punish you with the inane random dice that I wonder why even try in the first place? It feels like my skill and knowledge of the game becomes more irreverent the higher the dungeon level. Ironically the stress attacks in the game cause real stress to the player -- that is they are so frequent and critically boosted that it causes no-end to frustrations. Where is the fun lads?
Minor gripes include the carry space is far too small for the amount of item types in the game, forcing more contrived choices with the only goal of annoying me further. There is not enough gold earned in the game, used for nearly everything useful. There are too many heirloom item drops in the game (used to unlock and build up your town).
I am left to assume that the refusal to balance the game properly and provide either adequate difficulty modes or a proper working cognitive game flow, is a sign of artificially inflating the playtime of the title. Taken into account the annoying slow pop-ups that lock the control on the party, the tedious animation loops, and the drawn out combat; all of which compound to my suspicions.
I hope with their financial success, they make another game and address these issues forthwith, but for me I didn't like this game despite really trying and pouring 50 hours into it. This is the counter point to looking for 'long games' to use as an example of 'good games'. tl;dr:
I've had no problem in beating the timer in EVERY SINGLE MISSION I've played so far. In fact, only once came as close as T-2. Mobile combat tactics, covering retreats etc. play very differently than overwatch spam of xcom 1. I very much enjoy the game the way it is, on normal difficulty. My only grief is that I played through xcom 1 doing trench warfare, which is considerably less fun.
The rest:
What people seem to whine about the most is that Firaxis presses them into running and gunning... and in that all strategy (which TBS games are all about) goes out the window. That's only partially true. Yes, you are forced into a more dynamic and less comfortable model of gameplay. Yes, your old strategies will be no good here. Most modern gamers, the auto-heal generation (as opposed to the medkit generation), may not be used to playing genuinely difficult games, where the odds are stacked against you and the game is challenging in every single way it could be. Here, you need to adapt and develop new tactics. There's plenty of time to complete every mission, if you think about what you're doing. It's still a turn based strategy, take your time to consider the next move!
What the game excells at is constantly throwing new challenges at you. The aliens are always one step ahead, no matter what. Even if you push them back a bit, they always come back and the gameover clock is inevitable. You're always losing.
One more major complaint about the game that I see come up so often is that the aliens don't play smart, they just play unfair. I must disagree with the first part - personally I find the AI slightly more challenging and unpredictable than in xcom 1. As for the latter part, I do agree and enjoy this fact very much. The game isn't arbitrarily challenging - the unfairnes is based on how well you're doing, as it was in previous XCOM games. Now it's just more nasty :D

Some Good, Some Bad
The general gameplay is pretty decent, a turn-based dungeon explorer. That said, there's a lot of elements that are really just frustrating to deal with. The stress system, while sometimes fun (It feels pretty awesome when you hit 100 stress and your character gets a heroic bonus instead of crumbling under the stress like the majority of characters do) is more annoying than anything. When maximum stress hits the character has a heart attack, dropping their health to zero and debuffing them for the remainder of the dungeon, which can be a group killing experience. To avoid this you're expected to "treat" the character's stress by leaving them in the local bar or church while you go on your next adventure. This leads to a lot of characters leveling up at different rates. This wouldn't be too bad, but there's invisible barriers between characters of certain levels. For instance, level 3 characters can't embark with level 2 characters. This causes problems where the only characters available on your roster are two level 3s, and two level 2s, because everyone else is healing from stress or illness. Except you can't embark with that group, because theyre separate level groups. So what do you do? Well, you can either take a highly stressed character out of the bar or church because you need some lower leveled guys to adventure with to get some people up to level 3. I realize its supposed to be a matter of how to manage the team, but it's more frustrating than anything. A high stressed character IS going to have a heart attack during the dungeon and ruin the run, and dismissing them to hire a new recruit is just really annoying.
Then there's the spontaneous difficulty spikes. For instance one dungeon, suggested for level 1 characters, asks you to kill a specific character, a "boss". The "boss" character all of a sudden is able to knock two characters down to 1 health in one attack, and gets multiple attack turns in one round. Meanwhile all before this I had been playing level 1 dungeons, others with boss characters that were nowhere near this difficulty. It's just ridiculous, because there's no reason or expectation of such power in a level 1 dungeon.
There's also the low drop rates of gold, which you need to spend more and more of on supplies just to survive the dungeon, but then also need to use to upgrade characters and heal their stress and ailments. There's barely enough money to go around, which makes advancing characters a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ especially when they'll just die to an encounter with an enemy like I mentioned in the last paragraph.
Overall, I find the game frustrating, but there are redeeming aspects, like having a solid team making dungeons a challenging, but rewarding experience (but like I mentioned with the level-tier separations that can get messed up really quickly) I'd recommend it to people that like repeating tedious elements, because you will be losing characters, and re-running the same dungeons to level up new characters again. I've read that the game is more of a team-management game than a dungeon crawler, which kind of rings true. The important part of the game seems to be more in how you handle healing characters and the meager funds you get. If you're into that aspect, and dont care that much about whether your characters survive in the long run then you might like the game. I feel the game is misrepresented as a dungeon crawler RPG, and thats only a part of the game, which is more often frustrating than enjoyable. If all you want is to dungeon crawl, a different game might be more up your ally. If you want to manage your team of weaklings, and can accept that most of them are going to die then you might like the game.
Generally, I don't recommend the game, because I don't think it appeals to a wide audience and most people are going to go into it expecting an experience much different than what it actually is, but if you fall within a specific niche of gamers that prefer team-management games and grim-dark fantasy you might be one of the people that really like Darkest dungeon.

TL;DR
Great game early to mid-game, but gets too grindy endgame. Still an 8/10
Full Review
I think I just want to address this first: If you really think that this game is 100% RNG based that can instantly wipe out your entire party in a single dungeon run, I can assure you that is not the case. A lot of the game is based on RNG, but unless you're being really stubborn, a crit hit on you or a few misses in a row won't be the end of you. You're given plenty of options in hero choices, trinkets, and skills to rig the odds best in your favor for a particular mission. But once a mission starts heading south, REMEMBER THAT YOU CAN QUIT THE MISSION AT ANY TIME. I hear a lot of complaints about how BS stress can be, but you always have the option to abandon the mission if too many party members are afflicted, diseased, ect. Pick your battles wisely, and you'll never have a party wipe. I beat the game without one, just check my achievments. The only place where RNG really plays a huge role is with Deaths Door, when a character reaches 0 hp. And thankfully because of that mechanic, it prevents instant one-hit party wipes. Though they are debuffed for the rest of the quest
Now, onto the main bulk of review.
The story: An ancestor of yours accidentally unleashed an eldritch abombination into the world, so it's up to you to fix it.
The main bulk of the gameplay revolves around sending heroes out to do various quests to collect gear, gold, and heirlooms, mainly to prepare for the assaults on the Darkest Dungeon. Doing missions levels up their resolve, which allows them to get better gear, better skill upgrades, and do harder missions. If you wanna purchase the better gear/skill upgrades, you need heirlooms from your various missions in order to unlock these. Later on, with a high enough Blacksmith and Guild(Used for skill updgrades), you can even upgrade your stagecoach to bring in heroes with pre-upgraded armors in skills, all the way up to level 4, which helps with the grind a bit. For stress and afflictions,  as your heroes explore, they'll accumulate stress and may develop ununfavorable traits. If stress gets to 100 in a dungeon, they'll either become afflicted negatively which will cause them to act irrationally depending on the affliction, or they have a slight chance of gaining a great buff, which can seriously help out your party. If stress reaches 200, they'll suffer a heart attack, which will either reduce their health to 0, or if they're already at Death's Door, instantly kill them. You can reduce stress in the dungeon by using certain skills, from camping. Out of the dungeon, you can use the Tavern or Chapel. Sometimes the traits can be really bad (E.G, -10 accuracy against a certain enemy type), but for the majority of the time, you don't have to worry way too much about these traits.
When it comes to the main dungeon crawling, you take 4 heroes through a variety of missions, from simply explore the area to collect 3 amount of artifacts, to work your way up to the boss. As you start off, your worst opponent will be inexperience. As you continue to play, you eventually learn which team combos work best where, along with the fact that your heroes should have beter gear as you go on. It's a difficult yet fun curve, which takes a while to get over. Once you get over the curve though, that's when you start to notice the repetitiveness of the dungeons. Stronger enemy varients for just about every enemy is just a different name and higher stats, so you don't really see too much variation between enemys in later areas. It's the exact same for the bosses. You have to re-fight each boss 3 times, each one stronger than the last. This really contributes to the feeling late-game that you are pretty much only just grinding since you're seeing the same place and enemies over and over again because you need to level up heroes or need more gold/heirlooms. And trust me, the darkest dungeon is insanely hard, and you need to grind A LOT in order to prepare for it to prime your lv 6 heroes to perfection. Not to mention the "Never Again" penalty that your heroes get when they finish a Darkes Dungeon quest. Any heroes that successfuly assauled the Darkest Dungeon will never return there again, which means you need 16 lv 6 heroes ready to go. Because of this, I seriously don't recommend creating throwaway parties for suicidal gold runs.
The Darkest Dungeon, the final area in the game, is true hell. All the enemies deal insane bleed, blight, and stress damage. Not only that, abandoning the mission will take the life of a random hero. On the plus side, there's no obstacles, no traps, and no chance of ambush, and the dungeon isn't randomly generated. The "abandoning takes a random hero" is really the only major flaw of the dungeon. Darkest Dungeon is a game where you NEED to learn from your mistakes, the Darkest Dungeon especially. For learning from your mistakes there, you're guaranteed to grind up at least one new hero. But the satisfaction from beating each darkest dungeon assault is imeasurably satisfying. All the odds were against you, and you still won.
SPEAKING OF SATISFACTORY (SPOILER TERRITORY AHEAD)
The second greatest flaw of the game has to be the ending. It's a forced bittersweet ending, and I mean FORCED. It's "Well you may have literally killed this god, but you merely delayed the inveitable", coming full circle and ending on "Ruin has come to my family." TL;DR, some dimwad decided to re-awake the monstrosity that lived down there AGAIN despite the (likely) 14 heroes you had who already knew about the terrors of the dungeon. The eldritch abomination was awoken because the Anscestor didn't know what he was getting into at first. WHAT REASON WOULD ANYBODY HAVE TO AWAKEN THE THING AGAIN? Hell, if they wanted to end it on a lovecraftian note, why not end it like how the Rats in the Walls ended, by just flat out destroying the entire estate that sat upon the dungeon? This ending is a forced punch to the gut saying, "Lol I know you suffered a lot but that was pointless". When I first picked up Trove, I began expecting some sort of Minecraft ripoff with MMORPG elements here and there. Trove is so much more than that.
There is nothing particularly new or innovative or even that good design wise in Trove. It's common MMORPG style with combat, with left click as your basic attack and the number keys for your abilities. Exploration and movements nothing special either, with just WASD to move around and mouse to control the camera. Seems just your common MMORPG so far.
But then you get into the game. It throws your right in as soon as you sadly have to install Glyph for a launcher. This is common, but I personally find having to install a launcher annoying for games ported to steam. But I digress. As soon as you install the game through Glyph, you are thrown right in. You pick your characters name and class and you're free to have your world. You get a small minute long tutorial of "move and shoot this enemy". The game gives you missions to introduce you to a lot of the concepts better, which is useful, but I found it fun to explore the game's mechanics on your own. I still recommend doing the missions because it gives you money for the shop, but still it's fun to figure out all the different types of crafting tables and forges and such.  So if you chose to ignore the tutorial missions for a bit like myself,  you just kind of started walking in one direction to find something interesting. You find your first dungeon. Probably a small castle or tree house with a few enemies in it. For the first time you really felt like an explorer. I didn't particularly know what the castle marks on the map meant, I assumed it meant where people's houses were. But finding a dungeon and going in and looting it is so weirdly immersive and incredibly fun. So you continue to loot and plunder. Level up, find better equipment, upgrade your house. It seems sort of repetetive and routine but if you go to say the Subreddit and see a picture of someone's giant house or cool loot it immeadiately sparks your sense of "I wanna get that" and reignites your interest. It's weirdly addictive in a way.
There are only a few cons I have to list: Having to install another launcher is sort of annoying, but that's a bit more on the personal prefrence side. You can't collect a lot of the blocks and decorations you see in dungeons, so you still have to stick to "a bunch of different colored blocks and all the crafting tables" for your houses decor. Theres a lot of pay to win parts in the shop. Luckly they're not shoved in your face, but it sort of bugs me. Lastly, the servers are all global opposed to regional, so having to find someone of your same language to say help you in a dungeon or join your group of adventurers.
Lastly, I want to bring up the community. The community is... not amazing. A lot of spam bots constantly promoing there credit card stealing websites. A great part is how the developers keep in touch with the community at least! You're allowed to submit designs for weapons and other gear to the developers for a chance to them to actually be added to the game! That's really really cool! I'd actually consider it a big selling point to the game.
To sum up everything, a simple pros and cons list for TL;DR purposes:
Pros:
-Lots of fun!
-Free to play with not a lot of pay to win stuff!
-A lot of exploration with a lot of loot and treasure to find!
-Appealing graphics!
-Good developer community connection!
Cons:
-Have to install a launcher
-Limited building materials and decorations
-Spambot filled community
-Sound is repetetive and music cuts out randomly
But in short, I'd recommend Trove. It's free, so you don't need to purchase anything. It's a lot of addicting fun and building so if you're a fan or Minecraft or WoW you'll enjoy it.

I played the original XCOMs to completion along with the EU reboot.  I enjoyed these games.
I am a tough critic.  I expect a game to be fun and enjoyable from my first hour to my last hour.

(+)Great atmosphere
(+)Competent tactical combat
(+)Large variety of aliens, items, structures, and skills
(+)Customization of troopers

(-)Bugs.  One such bug is the game allowing troops to shoot through one or more solid walls/ceilings/floors.  If the cover system doesn't work in a cover based shooter, then the core functionality of the game is broken.  I don't understand the problem here because these mechanics worked fine in EU.
(-) Poor optimization.
(-)The first mission is a 100% on the rails "tutorial" followed by a far(far) more challenging real mission that is very unforgiving -- this is an "interesting" design decision.
(-)Time limits along with procedurally generated maps & random spawns = lol, you were punked situations on occassion.
(-)Development traps, RNGesus, unforgiving gameplay, and uneven difficulty limit the way you can play the game.  Over reliance on grenades is almost a requirement in many places.
(-)Save scumming is how many (if not most) people will deal with the above "challenges".  Designing a game to require save scumming from many players is a questionable decision (imo).

When I first picked up Trove, I began expecting some sort of Minecraft ripoff with MMORPG elements here and there. Trove is so much more than that.
There is nothing particularly new or innovative or even that good design wise in Trove. It's common MMORPG style with combat, with left click as your basic attack and the number keys for your abilities. Exploration and movements nothing special either, with just WASD to move around and mouse to control the camera. Seems just your common MMORPG so far.
But then you get into the game. It throws your right in as soon as you sadly have to install Glyph for a launcher. This is common, but I personally find having to install a launcher annoying for games ported to steam. But I digress. As soon as you install the game through Glyph, you are thrown right in. You pick your characters name and class and you're free to have your world. You get a small minute long tutorial of "move and shoot this enemy". The game gives you missions to introduce you to a lot of the concepts better, which is useful, but I found it fun to explore the game's mechanics on your own. I still recommend doing the missions because it gives you money for the shop, but still it's fun to figure out all the different types of crafting tables and forges and such.  So if you chose to ignore the tutorial missions for a bit like myself,  you just kind of started walking in one direction to find something interesting. You find your first dungeon. Probably a small castle or tree house with a few enemies in it. For the first time you really felt like an explorer. I didn't particularly know what the castle marks on the map meant, I assumed it meant where people's houses were. But finding a dungeon and going in and looting it is so weirdly immersive and incredibly fun. So you continue to loot and plunder. Level up, find better equipment, upgrade your house. It seems sort of repetetive and routine but if you go to say the Subreddit and see a picture of someone's giant house or cool loot it immeadiately sparks your sense of "I wanna get that" and reignites your interest. It's weirdly addictive in a way.
There are only a few cons I have to list: Having to install another launcher is sort of annoying, but that's a bit more on the personal prefrence side. You can't collect a lot of the blocks and decorations you see in dungeons, so you still have to stick to "a bunch of different colored blocks and all the crafting tables" for your houses decor. Theres a lot of pay to win parts in the shop. Luckly they're not shoved in your face, but it sort of bugs me. Lastly, the servers are all global opposed to regional, so having to find someone of your same language to say help you in a dungeon or join your group of adventurers.
Lastly, I want to bring up the community. The community is... not amazing. A lot of spam bots constantly promoing there credit card stealing websites. A great part is how the developers keep in touch with the community at least! You're allowed to submit designs for weapons and other gear to the developers for a chance to them to actually be added to the game! That's really really cool! I'd actually consider it a big selling point to the game.
To sum up everything, a simple pros and cons list for TL;DR purposes:
Pros:
-Lots of fun!
-Free to play with not a lot of pay to win stuff!
-A lot of exploration with a lot of loot and treasure to find!
-Appealing graphics!
-Good developer community connection!
Cons:
-Have to install a launcher
-Limited building materials and decorations
-Spambot filled community
-Sound is repetetive and music cuts out randomly
But in short, I'd recommend Trove. It's free, so you don't need to purchase anything. It's a lot of addicting fun and building so if you're a fan or Minecraft or WoW you'll enjoy it.

The Darkest Dungeon was suprisingly enjoyable on many levels, the player sends adventurers into areas where they must overcome the challenges within while making sure you keep their induvidual stress in check. What sets Darkest Dungeon apart from other RPGs in my opinion is the stress system.
From certian damaging attacks to simply dwelling in the dungon for a duration can stress a minion out. When your stress reaches the threshhold of 100 their mind is tested and you have a chance of them breaking down mentally or overcoming their stress with their own types of perspective buffs or de-buffs. Should you near 200 you minion has a chance to suffer a heart attack and instantly die.
With that mentioned a large number of things aside from RNG goes into the Darkest Dungeon. If you pick up on what events and certian mobs do you have a better chance of surviving runs and encounters. The game can be difficult but is still fair. Often times you must think carefully about your party comp and if they synergise well together.
Should you play the Darkest Dungeon?
If you enjoy a RPG with a spot of challenge, and dont mind some RNG aspects. This one will melt some faces.

Darkest is a gothic, lovecraftian dungeon crawler that is as punishing as it is rewarding. Hope is a dangerous thing in darkest, as the RNG can wipe your party with ease if you dont keep your wits about you and the majority of your hard won loot is spent fixing up your heroes and provisioning for the next dungeon. A string of bad luck can leave your heroes broke and broken and leave you praying that your next foray wont end with four new graves. Its harsh procedural play ensures that your heroes will sometimes be left out of comission, and with limited funds and an unreliable source of fresh meat for the grinder, a well built and maintained party is a serious investment and some serious luck. Often times you will find yourself dungeoning under provsioned, under prepared or with a poorly built party because one (or more) of your heores got really unlucky and needed treatment or a casket. However all this makes being able to blast through a dungeon and have your party come out sane and safe incredibly satisfying, especially when its won through preparation rather than the roll of the dice. Overall, with its somber and eldritch tone darkest somehow manages to give you hope, however fleeting it is, that you can prevail despite the odds and that you can win, no matter how bitter the victory is.

XCOM 2 is a wonderful game. This game, I would reccomend more than anything. There are a few bugs, which hopefuly will be wrinkled out in time, but the rest of the game is absolutely perfect. Why is the game perfect? Because the game as a very fun, strong gameplay rotation, and complete mod support from the developers. This means that you can customize the game to fit your needs. Three examples of mods will show just how fundamental mods are to the experience of XCOM 2.
Firstly, you have the three commisssioned mods created by Long War Studios. These mods include a more specialized skill tree, a brutal enemy, and a new weapon type which is weaker but faster. Mods like these add layers to the game, providing even higher replayability and longevity to a sequel rebuilt on the pillar of replayability.
Secondly, you have mods like Free Camera Rotation by wasteland_ghost. This kind of mod shows how free the reigns are for the modding community. And, its a great mod.
Lastly, you have mods like TimerTweaks by Sashka, Disable Timers also by Sashka, and True Concealment by Takeru Shirogane (which is the one in this list I use), These mods each address a problem some players have with a part of the game. The ingame timers on most missions. TimerTweaks adds 4 turns to timed missions besides one type, Disable Timers disables them, and True Concealment causes concealed turns to not count against you in the timed missions. These three mods show how quickly the community rallied through mods against a system that was not well recieved by some players.
Because of the sheer support Firaxis and 2K are giving to the modding scene, and the sheer power of the modding scene already, just at launch, I cannot recommend any game more highly than XCOM 2.

It is a very classified project which you get some info about when you attack one of the facilities reducing the Xcom 2 equivilent of the Doom tracker. This equivilent is known as Avatar Progress, it increases over time and you can reduce it by attacking facilities or continuin with the story.
Dark events are also an aspect of the game where unless you take on a mission to counter them, an event that will make things more difficult for you will occur such as getting hunted down by a UFO.

+: Combines aspects from other games in a way that makes the game truly unique in its own way.
+: One of the only if any MMO's that allows you to dig on the terrarian itself (although you can't build on the terrain unless it's in your own 'cornerstone' which is basically your own portable headquarters that you craft things at).
+: For an MMO this game took an interesting style of graphics that I haven't seen done before (in an MMO).
+: A bunch of classes to chose from, all seeming quite different from one another.
+: The game is free.
+: Can be a good MMO for someone who's never played one.
+: You can 'deassemble' a weapon or accessory you don't want to turn it into crafting materials that you may find more useful.
(Stating this) Many reviews on here say that the problem with the game is that it takes so long to connect to servers but this has been fixed (to my understanding).
-: Although there is a huge arsenal of weapons (that you are pre-assigned based on your class e.g. Shadow Archers will ONLY receive bows) none of them actually change the way you fight or for that matter give you any feeling of variety.
-: You progress so quickly that an item you picked up that you may have considered to be really good at the time can quickly become outdated in terms of stats. The game tries to make you feel good with this system of constant rewards and progression although it fails because you don't actually feel accomplished.
-: No storyline, NONE.
-: This game is repetitive, most of your objectives in this game are basically 'kill this and receive this' or... 'mine this and receive this'. Due to there being no storyline you find yourself asking 'why am I even doing this?!'.
-: No actual quests, you have a pre-determined set of quests that every player in the entire game is also doing. You have no freedom to do what you want (that is if you want to actually make progress within the game), you MUST complete the assigned quest to move onto the next one.
-: The entire game is randomly generated making there feel like there's nothing to actually explore, it's just randomly generated terrain and dungeons (that also seem to be very repetitive).
-: You must make an account for the game itself, this isn't so bad on its own however it can be very frustrating trying to get your verification code from your email to work (both me and my friend had the problem).
-: Character customization itself is bad, (not the hats, there's plenty of those). there aren't many color options, as far as physical traits just about all you can do is change your skin color (e.g. you cannot change your height, width, etc.).
-: Things in the tutorial seem to be out of order, for example around my first hour of gameplay I was being being told the buttons used to attack even though I had already killed loads of enemies.
-: Does not have very much music.
-: All drops are marked as uncommon/rare+ when it comes to the rarity tag of an item, I've never seen a single item marked as 'common'. I feel the game does this to make you feel more accomplished.
This game has/had a lot of potential, it really did. Sadly I have to say that I must give this game a 3/10 for the reasons listed above.

I've enjoyed the past XCOM games so much that I have over 3000 hours in the last game. The past 2 games have had their share of flaws and annoyances but they were easily overlooked because the game was fun. This I can also say about multiplayer, my favorite part of xcom, however this new game is a big disappointment to me and I feel robbed of my money. It is chock full of bugs, performance issues, and aside from the occasional cinematics, it gets quite boring. Even in the beginning I've done over 12 "missions" which LITERALLY was just moving your soldiers to the "intel" that you "hack" and then the mission is "flawless." Where the hell are the aliens? Eventually some aliens started showing up but by then they were already upgraded in armor and weapons since the "dark events" had progressed but with no damn aliens to kill for so many missions I didn't get all my parts I needed to research.
The multiplayer also is terribly designed. Not only did they remove the fine customization options you had in the past but it is full of bugs also. I literally had 4 matches where people would join my game and it would kick them or we just sat there both of us with the "ready" status and nothing happening. To add annoyance, the clock would go from 69 seconds to 4 seconds randomly, then zero and just hang there. With nothing happening. Then all of a sudden the opponent's acctions would start coming through. It was unplayable period. For as many "bugs" as the old XCOM had, at least those bugs allowed the game to be playable and added meta gaming to the tactics. This just adds frustration.
The only thing I found even remotely good was the soldier appearance customization (even that needs work), being able to save their appearance was good too, and the ability to do small "upgrades" to weapons was neat. The level of textures and graphic options are pretty nice too. The story seems intriguing enough for any xcom player, however it really isnt anything much. I am hoping a future mod will make this game worth it. As it stands now I can't recommend it, especially the MP side of the game.

I've never left a review on Steam before, but I'll make an exception for XCOM2. In the short of it, this is an absolute must-buy for any fan of the prior game, or indeed anyone with a love of turn based strategic combat games.
I'll presume you're familiar with the broad concept of XCOM and this game, so I'll cover some of the notable new features:
- The strategic layer is far more interesting than XCOM:EU. Gone are the random, uninteractive UFO hunts and spending 2 weeks hitting 'scan' while waiting at the base. You'll be given more random map events than you can realistically handle, so you'll have to make choices about which sites to hit. It's a constant trade-off between grabbing the event rewards and expanding your territory to prevent the Avatar project getting out of control.
- Mission variety is vastly improved. EU had effectively a single mission type of 'kill aliens', along with terror/council missions (outside of DLC). Now there's a lot more variety and objectives, as well as interesting features such as hacking Advent tech for loot. Some will be races against time, others are the old style of slowly creeping infiltration, or even base defence.
- The timers are an excellent addition with a lot of undeserved criticism. The old XCOM style made 'move one tile, overwatch, repeat' the best strategy with no downside apart from Meld. This led to tedious gameplay. The timers force you to make hard choices about how far to advance, weighing up the cost of carefully engaging enemy spawns against the risk you might get bogged down and get left behind.
(a tip if you're really struggling - use a Phantom Ranger w/ Conceal. They can just scout the entire map ahead of your squad, letting you sprint to the end while avoiding pods or at least engaging them favourably)
- As to be expected, there's a lot more content. More interesting aliens, more interesting abilities, some great new bits of gear such as heavy-weapon wielding EXO suits and unique ammunition types.
There are a few cons though.
- Performance is terrible. While it's not unplayable, load times are long and fps drops are common. I can run far more visually impressive games than this at far better fps, so this level of optimization is inexcusably bad.
- As expected, there's bugs. Teleporting pods, untargetable enemies, a squad member setting themselves on fire when they shoot... I wouldn't recommend Ironman for a while. Nothing that's totally gamebreaking if you can reload, but if you have an Ironman save this will likely frustrate.
- There are some odd balancing issues. By 6 months in I've researched every tech available, as it seems that after the Interceptor/Interrogation side of tech was removed they just didn't replace it with anything, so you can beeline the best weapons/armor. Certain mob types such as the new invisible, burrowing chrysalids that can activate and attack on your turn are a bit ill-conceived, even if they are beatable.
Despite the above, I'd still completely recommend it. It's refreshing to see a game come out that isn't afraid to challenge the player and take risks - they could have quite easily released XCOM:EU/EW but with a new coat of paint, but instead they've taken bold strides.

You get two choices in a review: yes or no. In its present state, this game is a "No". It is a crying shame really, it has a lot going for it: great graphics, compelling story, a complete release (unlike EU) and often great gameplay. But it has a flaw that makes enjoying the game without modding it (and in fact cheating) very unenjoyable and ultimately not fun to play: timers.
There are timers on everything, if you do not feel rushed you're not paying attention. Most missions have a timer restricting the number of turns you get. Then there's the avatar timer, forcing you to derail whatever you are currently doing to sometimes send troops out to quash the aliens, then there are the constant events (which are familiar to the franchise since the 90s) which distract you from whatever you are trying to accomplish. The entire game is doing its best to push the player into action that would not logically make sense, and is deliberately unclear can be ignored. In fact some things can be ignored: the avatar timer can be delayed until the last second, some missions do not have to be taken immediately, etc. But there are plenty of things that can't be ignored: mission timers are for real, the avatar project will kill you if you do not progress the core research & acquisition projects at least far enough, etc. Generally I understand "why" they want you to feel this way, but it ruins the fun of the game.
However, they did make one brilliant concession: they released the mod tools to players alongside the game. With the "Disable Timers" mod, my biggest complaint is thrown out the window. It is a cheat, to be fair: some missions were clearly balanced around limited moves, and the AI is definitely not smart enough to anticipate you coming from anything other than the most direct route. It's almost like using flanking strategies is OP, and slamming the hammer against the anvil is cheating.
If you like your strategy/tactics games without any strategy/tactics, then this game may be for you. If you prefer a slower paced, more cerebral game, then at the very least get the "Disable Timers" mod and up the game difficulty level. The game is enjoyable once you undermine some of its design decisions,  but it could have, and should have, been much better.

This game is pretty good. Its game engine by From Software is fairly response and there are some peculiarities to the way From handles certain events. There is not a lot of visual que outside of the enemy moving, casting their spell, etc, so there are sufficient cue's for you (the player) to respond to the enemy but there are not buzzers and lights whcih pop up on the screen to help you react to danger. Enemies of course have wind-ups before attacking and sound effects which hint at the way they are about to kill you. The way From has put the game together does the same thing with its "understatement" of everything that's going on in the story. The understatement generates enough mystery for most players like me to completely feel story-agnostic, and there are enough mythological lore tidbits and mentions in the item descriptions and revealing NPC dialogue you will have the opportunity to indulge the occassional inkling for some lore-y-ness during your gaming session.
A mention on PVP. I love PVP and my background is mostly games sharply tuned for competition, so I have to trash DS3 PVP because while there is tons of variety in weapons, character builds, and such, the net code is awful and results in wonky invisible swings from enemies taking place, and you will often believe you have just taken advantage of an enemy's mistake when the game suddenly reveals your enemy player was in i-frames on a dodge roll while on your screen they appeared to still be on their feet eating your axe's blow. Also, great axes are really pitifully bad although they are really appealingly cool and the moves have style, they are all bark and no bite, players interested in having a good time PVP'ing need to select from the top-tier weapons.
So what of the PVP? Point is there is plenty of fun in the pvp and there are some spots where the net code feels really sloppy (this is largely a infrastructure problem imo, not so much From's fault), my main message here is to play DS3 and enjoy the PVP AND CHOOSE TOP-TIER WEAPONS don't get stuck wishing you had a non-meta style because the meta is baked in pretty well by this time in the game's life.
The single player experience is great for the adventure through the gameworld. The game's combat and overall handling are response although a few non-essential functions are difficult to reliably trigger for some players (e.g. kicking requires a combination of move forward & attack, but even a veteran fighting game player will randomly fail to trigger the kick as they wished, or trigger a kick accidentally.). The point is you can go through the whole game without kicking or using the jump attack (which also posses problems for a lot of people), so this weakness in the game's handling isn't going to impinge on your enjoyment to too great a degree.
Anyway, buy it for the single player action-adventure-RPG and excellent take on third person combat. Hop into PVP just don't get your hopes up about being a cool guy who outplays with bottom-tier weapons.

TL,DR: Significant upgrade over its predecessor.
The previous game, XCOM: Enemy Unknown was riddled with plot holes and the gameplay never really flowed well with the story, but luckily for it the gameplay was so good that nobody cared that the story was weak or otherwise terrible.
Now in the new game, they've done a lot to fix that and in the process, they've coincidentally made the game a lot harder.
Now I've seen a lot of people complaining that a lot of missions in the game have turn limits before you're forced to withdraw, but in reality that's just them meshing story elements with the gameplay as Earth is occupied territory and you're running an under-manned and under-supplied resistance force; you can't go into a major city center and expect that the aliens/collaborators wouldn't be able to bring down a massive force on your little team if you stay in the area too long, so you have a set number of turns before your team is hit with enemy reinforcements and you have to achieve the mission and get out while you can.
The turn limits also eliminate the go-to strategy in XCOM: Enemy Unknown where if you got two snipers to max rank, and used a slow approach overwatch-based advance on missions, then from that point on you had won the game at any difficulty level and any team configuration.  In XCOM 2 you can no longer take a slow advancing approach in most missions (there are some missions without time limits) as you'll run out of time before you complete the objective and have run from enemy reinforcements, which means you have to employ different strategies and take risks.
With these new strategies, the new special abilities of each class becomes incredibly important; you specialists can remotely shield or heal your teammates, or disrupt the enemy; you rangers can haul *** around the map and cause major damage with a shotgun or their new sword; your grenadiers provide much needed fire support with their cannons and grenade launchers; and your snipers are able to contribute as their pistol sidearms are actually useful in this game.
All in all, there is a lot more depth to XCOM 2 than there was in XCOM: Enemy Unknown, sure you have to take more risks, but with those risks comes a much better sense of reward for getting a Flawless score on a mission than you ever got with Enemy Unknown.  That's also to say nothing about the atmosphere and the music in the game, which are both excellent and improved over the first game.
It's a harder game, and you're constantly bombarded with calls for help against the alien overlords, or opportunities that you need to find a way to take advantage of, but it's a worthwhile challenge; the only thing I can say against it is that it could be optimized better but I'll give that a pass since it's a brand new game.
Overall rank: 9.5/10

Trove has a lot of potencial, I think, but I just didn't fall in love with it. For a start, because of its free to play nature, you are kind of expected to be willing to buy the in game currecy, or suck it up. At the start, you are asked to pick your class, and the little flavour texts are not nearly enough to help you make a choice that will define your first 10 hours of play. I picked knight, and was less than blown away by it. Fortunetly, I got a sample a second class when Trion gave everyone a free class token for our patience during the cueing nightmare that followed release. So I tried Ice Mage, which was pretty fun. There isn't enough challenge, here, I think. The dungeons are really easy, the loot flows far too freely, and the fact that you can just pop your personal base down almost anywhere means that a resupply is never far away. Even the advanced worlds are not as challengeing as I would like. The combat is fun, but, as with so many MMOs, it feels like a race to the highest DPS.
Multiplayer worked great, very easy to set up, once you bypass the cues. True, this makes an easy game a little easier, but I think it's made up for. However, I think my biggest problem with the game was the scale of the world. This is a game with randomly generated worlds, and so I feel like we should see the scale that Minecraft offers. Dungeons should occure maybe only once in each biome, or the biomes should be huge! I think the biomes should be huge, anyway. Never once was I anywhere that I couldn't see another area from where I was. And I think that that is taking some of the real joy out of a fantasy world: the endless treking through vast landscapes. Some of the biomes look FANTASTIC, like the Neon City, or the Volcano, and so it's really sad that we can't spend an hour in them, and never find our way out. Even on Slow Sebastion, who's really not that slow. I realise that having to trek so far could get boring. And, in a forest biome, it would. Especially if you treked for ten minutes, only to find that some other random player had beaten you to the dungeon. But I think this can be solved, maybe with dungeons that reset after a few minutes?
The another big problem with this game is the building, which feels like an unqualified disaster, added over the weekend. You can hit TAB to change into building mode, at which point, your character disappears, and you can break blocks with a laser, often destroying more than you meant to. You can collect different coloured blocked, which are named things like Red Block, Green Block, etc, which is a nice touch. There are always plenty of Green Blocks, the easy forest areas being made out of them, but blocks like White Block are really hard to find. I was an Ice Mage, so I wanted to build a cool little white castle for myself as my personal base (called a corner stone; can be placed down at any vacent cornerstone plot). I looked for white blocks for a while,  but all I could find was a big white temple, which was actually a dungeon, and so unbreakable. In the end, I ended up just sticking with the regular cornerstone house, which, again, is silly, because not only will you only be there to stock up, but you don't need a house, just a line of the various machines on your empty plot. It's not like anything that might wander in would be more than a minor inconvinance.
I feel like Trove would be a great game if everything was BIGGER. Bigger biomes, bigger dungeons, bigger monsters. But, for now, it's a game where you can jump in, slay some guys, and jump around. And that could be just what you want from a casual MMO. I approched this as a serious RPG, but it doesn't have to be. I just sometimes feel that they took the concept of OORT Online, and dumbed it down.

I've enjoyed the past XCOM games so much that I have over 3000 hours in the last game. The past 2 games have had their share of flaws and annoyances but they were easily overlooked because the game was fun. This I can also say about multiplayer, my favorite part of xcom, however this new game is a big disappointment to me and I feel robbed of my money. It is chock full of bugs, performance issues, and aside from the occasional cinematics, it gets quite boring. Even in the beginning I've done over 12 "missions" which LITERALLY was just moving your soldiers to the "intel" that you "hack" and then the mission is "flawless." Where the hell are the aliens? Eventually some aliens started showing up but by then they were already upgraded in armor and weapons since the "dark events" had progressed but with no damn aliens to kill for so many missions I didn't get all my parts I needed to research.
The multiplayer also is terribly designed. Not only did they remove the fine customization options you had in the past but it is full of bugs also. I literally had 4 matches where people would join my game and it would kick them or we just sat there both of us with the "ready" status and nothing happening. To add annoyance, the clock would go from 69 seconds to 4 seconds randomly, then zero and just hang there. With nothing happening. Then all of a sudden the opponent's acctions would start coming through. It was unplayable period. I've never left a review on Steam before, but I'll make an exception for XCOM2. In the short of it, this is an absolute must-buy for any fan of the prior game, or indeed anyone with a love of turn based strategic combat games.
I'll presume you're familiar with the broad concept of XCOM and this game, so I'll cover some of the notable new features:
- The strategic layer is far more interesting than XCOM:EU. Gone are the random, uninteractive UFO hunts and spending 2 weeks hitting 'scan' while waiting at the base. You'll be given more random map events than you can realistically handle, so you'll have to make choices about which sites to hit. It's a constant trade-off between grabbing the event rewards and expanding your territory to prevent the Avatar project getting out of control.
- Mission variety is vastly improved. EU had effectively a single mission type of 'kill aliens', along with terror/council missions (outside of DLC). Now there's a lot more variety and objectives, as well as interesting features such as hacking Advent tech for loot. Some will be races against time, others are the old style of slowly creeping infiltration, or even base defence.
- The timers are an excellent addition with a lot of undeserved criticism. The old XCOM style made 'move one tile, overwatch, repeat' the best strategy with no downside apart from Meld. This led to tedious gameplay. The timers force you to make hard choices about how far to advance, weighing up the cost of carefully engaging enemy spawns against the risk you might get bogged down and get left behind.
(a tip if you're really struggling - use a Phantom Ranger w/ Conceal. They can just scout the entire map ahead of your squad, letting you sprint to the end while avoiding pods or at least engaging them favourably)
- As to be expected, there's a lot more content. More interesting aliens, more interesting abilities, some great new bits of gear such as heavy-weapon wielding EXO suits and unique ammunition types.
There are a few cons though.
- Performance is terrible. While it's not unplayable, load times are long and fps drops are common. I can run far more visually impressive games than this at far better fps, so this level of optimization is inexcusably bad.
- As expected, there's bugs. Teleporting pods, untargetable enemies, a squad member setting themselves on fire when they shoot... I wouldn't recommend Ironman for a while. Nothing that's totally gamebreaking if you can reload, but if you have an Ironman save this will likely frustrate.
- There are some odd balancing issues. By 6 months in I've researched every tech available, as it seems that after the Interceptor/Interrogation side of tech was removed they just didn't replace it with anything, so you can beeline the best weapons/armor. Certain mob types such as the new invisible, burrowing chrysalids that can activate and attack on your turn are a bit ill-conceived, even if they are beatable.
Despite the above, I'd still completely recommend it. It's refreshing to see a game come out that isn't afraid to challenge the player and take risks - they could have quite easily released XCOM:EU/EW but with a new coat of paint, but instead they've taken bold strides.

You get two choices in a review: yes or no. In its present state, this game is a "No". It is a crying shame really, it has a lot going for it: great graphics, compelling story, a complete release (unlike EU) and often great gameplay. But it has a flaw that makes enjoying the game without modding it (and in fact cheating) very unenjoyable and ultimately not fun to play: timers.
There are timers on everything, if you do not feel rushed you're not paying attention. Most missions have a timer restricting the number of turns you get. Then there's the avatar timer, forcing you to derail whatever you are currently doing to sometimes send troops out to quash the aliens, then there are the constant events (which are familiar to the franchise since the 90s) which distract you from whatever you are trying to accomplish. The entire game is doing its best to push the player into action that would not logically make sense, and is deliberately unclear can be ignored. In fact some things can be ignored: the avatar timer can be delayed until the last second, some missions do not have to be taken immediately, etc. But there are plenty of things that can't be ignored: mission timers are for real, the avatar project will kill you if you do not progress the core research & acquisition projects at least far enough, etc. Generally I understand "why" they want you to feel this way, but it ruins the fun of the game.
However, they did make one brilliant concession: they released the mod tools to players alongside the game. With the "Disable Timers" mod, my biggest complaint is thrown out the window. It is a cheat, to be fair: some missions were clearly balanced around limited moves, and the AI is definitely not smart enough to anticipate you coming from anything other than the most direct route. It's almost like using flanking strategies is OP, and slamming the hammer against the anvil is cheating.
If you like your strategy/tactics games without any strategy/tactics, then this game may be for you. If you prefer a slower paced, more cerebral game, then at the very least get the "Disable Timers" mod and up the game difficulty level. The game is enjoyable once you undermine some of its design decisions,  but it could have, and should have, been much better.

So, here I sit, in the hamlet outside my former home, gnawing on a leg-bone of a fallen party member, writing of my experiences in the Darkest Dungeon…
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
What can I say about Darkest Dungeon that hasn’t already been said? The game is awesome, it’s received high ratings by players and critics alike and it’s been nominated and received numerous awards. I’ve enjoyed it so much that I had to write a review, my first ever for those who care.
At its heart, Darkest Dungeon is a side-scrolling dungeon crawler. The graphics, sound and gameplay are works of art and it has the high polish and feel of a commercial game from a much larger production house. The UI (User Interface) is intuitive and the story narrative is immersive. The gameplay is at once challenging, unforgiving, deceptively deep, and highly rewarding. It’s not what I would consider a game for the typical, casual player or someone that’s going to freak out if a player dies, let alone losing an entire party. Trust me, it will happen.
In Darkest Dungeon, you begin the game with the Highwayman (an AOE [Area-of-Effect] and DPS class) and Crusader (a Paladin-like tank) taking you to the hamlet. On the way you learn the basic game mechanics and pick up a few rewards. And maybe they both survive the journey. Once you arrive in the hamlet, you pick up the Vestal (i.e. Healer) and Plague Doctor (a utility/support class with buffs/AOE/DPS capabilities).
At this point, the game begins and from here on you control a party of four adventurers. You recruit from a randomly generated selection of the 15 different character types/classes. Every decision you make will have tactical and strategic implications; from the position of each member, their skills and party load out to the hamlet building upgrades where you train, treat and improve the skills of your roster of adventurers.
As I said, gameplay is challenging and unforgiving, yet simple and deceptively deep. Each character has a set of unique skills whose availability depends on their position within the party. Each building allows you to either treat and reduce a character’s stress or diseases, improve their skills, upgrade their gear, increase the number of available random characters to place on your roster or increase the size of your active roster to have a larger selection of characters to choose from.
Your party ventures into the dungeon with limited supplies that you purchase in the hamlet, torches, food, bandages and other supplies. Bring plenty of torches, each torch produces a certain degree of light which fades over time. The darker it gets the more stressful it is for your characters. Bring plenty of food or your characters will starve. Food is also the only way to heal outside of combat.
Each character has a health bar and stress bar. When a character’s health bar reaches zero they don’t immediately die but instead are considered at death’s door. Each time a character is at death’s door the stress bar for all party members will increase. Given enough stress a character’s resolve will break, resulting in a myriad of psychological conditions and afflictions. Afflicted party members will act out in a number of interesting and frustrating ways from refusing to fight, stealing treasure for themselves, doing their own thing or berating other party members.
So, if you're up for the challenge and want to support Indie Game development at its finest, I'd strongly recommend purchasing this game.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Look upon our once proud house … Perched upon high, peering down upon the Moure … Can you cleanse it of its foulness, brave the peril and stem the tide of its horrors? Or will you too fall victim, your once hopeful flame extinguished, as you perish, screaming, in the clutches of the nightmarish horrors … of the Darkest Dungeon?

This game, well. Unfortunately I've been unable to play for a while because of work and other commitments. But I felt that this game deserves a review.
The game at a first look seems like it is designed for little kids to run around and whilst that is very true it also makes plenty of room for the more hardcore gamers.
You start the game with a class that you choose which is randomly generated. You can then choose your look at your pre built safe house which you can openly customise whenever the hell you want! By that I mean no one players house looks at all the same! (unless you've got two players that have just started) Like, you can edit and change every individual block and there's no limits either, resources are super easy to obtain and special blocks are a little harder but to build your basic safehouse you have a whole world of mineable blocks around you! and it doesn't end there. You can build where ever you are. It doesn't have to be in your designated safe house area. (of course it won't stay there, but you can build outside of the home area if you want. this is just another example of the kind of freedom you get in the game)
The combat is indeed repetative, but strangely satisfying! Like, you just don't get tired of it. Choose your class wisely as this is going to be your class for a while but shortly after playing into the game a bit you will be able to unlock anothe class until you eventually unlock all the classes. (don't get me wrong, at the start you can choose any class to start with) when you unlock all the classes you can seemlessly switch between any of the classes on a single account. I'm talking, you can be halfway through a dungeon and be like "I'm bored of this class now" press the shortcut key and switch to another unlocked class on the fly!
The crafting on the game seems bottomless with tonnes of new amazing things you want to craft in the game giving you tonnes of new things to do, dungeons are easy to find and range from easy to difficult to clear and then you have shadow arena's which are even harder and require a team. Each have better or worse drops depending on difficulty, magic find and how lucky you are and everything contributes in one way or another to crafting.
and then there's the customisation! just to start, this game is very moddable. You can find all sorts of visual mods on the web, from HUD mods and armor mods and even the colour and effects of the visuals. But if you don't fancy messing around with the modding side of things you have unlimited options inside the game. You find some really amazing weapon with the best stats ever after completing a really hard shadow dungeon with your Neon Ninja. The only problem is that this badass weapon is a giant lollipop... Whilst some might like that idea, some might want a badass ninja with a flaming radient sword! By simply pressing C you can literally change the skin of your sword to any of the other weapons you've broken down previously in the game. I'm talking every sword you ever picked up from anywhere. If it has rubbish stats you still want to pick it up if it looks good. Chances are, you might not have the skin for it yet. So you can break it down to get the skin and of course some valuable flux (which helps you craft and serves as currency in the game)
Of course, it's not all rainbows and butterflies. On some days you can get unbareable lag (which gets better and better every day with constant communication from the devs I might add)
The trade system is something you will get into eventually in the game. This game is still in early days yet. But trade is literally tapping into trade chat and selling things the old mmorpg way (WTB 2 pentaforge) bla bla. And then to trade you have to teleport to the player you want to trade with (it's easy to do when you get the hang of it) and use a nearby trading post which is a tad buggy at times. I get the feeling and kind of hope that this is just a quickfix solution for trading until they decide to implement something more concrete into the game.
I can't really think of too many negative things about the game but what I can say is that the Positives most definitely outweigh the negatives!
Definitely worth a try, it's free so what you got to lose?
