I've never left a review on Steam before, but I'll make an exception for XCOM2. In the short of it, this is an absolute must-buy for any fan of the prior game, or indeed anyone with a love of turn based strategic combat games.
I'll presume you're familiar with the broad concept of XCOM and this game, so I'll cover some of the notable new features:
- The strategic layer is far more interesting than XCOM:EU. Gone are the random, uninteractive UFO hunts and spending 2 weeks hitting 'scan' while waiting at the base. You'll be given more random map events than you can realistically handle, so you'll have to make choices about which sites to hit. It's a constant trade-off between grabbing the event rewards and expanding your territory to prevent the Avatar project getting out of control.
- Mission variety is vastly improved. EU had effectively a single mission type of 'kill aliens', along with terror/council missions (outside of DLC). Now there's a lot more variety and objectives, as well as interesting features such as hacking Advent tech for loot. Some will be races against time, others are the old style of slowly creeping infiltration, or even base defence.
- The timers are an excellent addition with a lot of undeserved criticism. The old XCOM style made 'move one tile, overwatch, repeat' the best strategy with no downside apart from Meld. This led to tedious gameplay. The timers force you to make hard choices about how far to advance, weighing up the cost of carefully engaging enemy spawns against the risk you might get bogged down and get left behind.
(a tip if you're really struggling - use a Phantom Ranger w/ Conceal. They can just scout the entire map ahead of your squad, letting you sprint to the end while avoiding pods or at least engaging them favourably)
- As to be expected, there's a lot more content. More interesting aliens, more interesting abilities, some great new bits of gear such as heavy-weapon wielding EXO suits and unique ammunition types.
There are a few cons though.
- Performance is terrible. While it's not unplayable, load times are long and fps drops are common. I can run far more visually impressive games than this at far better fps, so this level of optimization is inexcusably bad.
- As expected, there's bugs. Teleporting pods, untargetable enemies, a squad member setting themselves on fire when they shoot... I wouldn't recommend Ironman for a while. Nothing that's totally gamebreaking if you can reload, but if you have an Ironman save this will likely frustrate.
- There are some odd balancing issues. By 6 months in I've researched every tech available, as it seems that after the Interceptor/Interrogation side of tech was removed they just didn't replace it with anything, so you can beeline the best weapons/armor. Certain mob types such as the new invisible, burrowing chrysalids that can activate and attack on your turn are a bit ill-conceived, even if they are beatable.
Despite the above, I'd still completely recommend it. It's refreshing to see a game come out that isn't afraid to challenge the player and take risks - they could have quite easily released XCOM:EU/EW but with a new coat of paint, but instead they've taken bold strides.

You get two choices in a review: yes or no. In its present state, this game is a "No". It is a crying shame really, it has a lot going for it: great graphics, compelling story, a complete release (unlike EU) and often great gameplay. But it has a flaw that makes enjoying the game without modding it (and in fact cheating) very unenjoyable and ultimately not fun to play: timers.
There are timers on everything, if you do not feel rushed you're not paying attention. Most missions have a timer restricting the number of turns you get. Then there's the avatar timer, forcing you to derail whatever you are currently doing to sometimes send troops out to quash the aliens, then there are the constant events (which are familiar to the franchise since the 90s) which distract you from whatever you are trying to accomplish. The entire game is doing its best to push the player into action that would not logically make sense, and is deliberately unclear can be ignored. In fact some things can be ignored: the avatar timer can be delayed until the last second, some missions do not have to be taken immediately, etc. But there are plenty of things that can't be ignored: mission timers are for real, the avatar project will kill you if you do not progress the core research & acquisition projects at least far enough, etc. Generally I understand "why" they want you to feel this way, but it ruins the fun of the game.
However, they did make one brilliant concession: they released the mod tools to players alongside the game. With the "Disable Timers" mod, my biggest complaint is thrown out the window. It is a cheat, to be fair: some missions were clearly balanced around limited moves, and the AI is definitely not smart enough to anticipate you coming from anything other than the most direct route. It's almost like using flanking strategies is OP, and slamming the hammer against the anvil is cheating.
If you like your strategy/tactics games without any strategy/tactics, then this game may be for you. If you prefer a slower paced, more cerebral game, then at the very least get the "Disable Timers" mod and up the game difficulty level. The game is enjoyable once you undermine some of its design decisions,  but it could have, and should have, been much better.

TL,DR: Significant upgrade over its predecessor.
The previous game, XCOM: Enemy Unknown was riddled with plot holes and the gameplay never really flowed well with the story, but luckily for it the gameplay was so good that nobody cared that the story was weak or otherwise terrible.
Now in the new game, they've done a lot to fix that and in the process, they've coincidentally made the game a lot harder.
Now I've seen a lot of people complaining that a lot of missions in the game have turn limits before you're forced to withdraw, but in reality that's just them meshing story elements with the gameplay as Earth is occupied territory and you're running an under-manned and under-supplied resistance force; you can't go into a major city center and expect that the aliens/collaborators wouldn't be able to bring down a massive force on your little team if you stay in the area too long, so you have a set number of turns before your team is hit with enemy reinforcements and you have to achieve the mission and get out while you can.
The turn limits also eliminate the go-to strategy in XCOM: Enemy Unknown where if you got two snipers to max rank, and used a slow approach overwatch-based advance on missions, then from that point on you had won the game at any difficulty level and any team configuration.  In XCOM 2 you can no longer take a slow advancing approach in most missions (there are some missions without time limits) as you'll run out of time before you complete the objective and have run from enemy reinforcements, which means you have to employ different strategies and take risks.
With these new strategies, the new special abilities of each class becomes incredibly important; you specialists can remotely shield or heal your teammates, or disrupt the enemy; you rangers can haul *** around the map and cause major damage with a shotgun or their new sword; your grenadiers provide much needed fire support with their cannons and grenade launchers; and your snipers are able to contribute as their pistol sidearms are actually useful in this game.
All in all, there is a lot more depth to XCOM 2 than there was in XCOM: Enemy Unknown, sure you have to take more risks, but with those risks comes a much better sense of reward for getting a Flawless score on a mission than you ever got with Enemy Unknown.  That's also to say nothing about the atmosphere and the music in the game, which are both excellent and improved over the first game.
It's a harder game, and you're constantly bombarded with calls for help against the alien overlords, or opportunities that you need to find a way to take advantage of, but it's a worthwhile challenge; the only thing I can say against it is that it could be optimized better but I'll give that a pass since it's a brand new game.

Others may think that starting from the beginning is best, but I believe that if you want a good introduction to these types of games (Genre: Souls-like/Action RPG) then this is the best game for that. Though an issue is that, although the game has a considerable amount of bosses, the singleplayer is short in vanilla game. My first play-through took a short 50 hours and the rest were finished repeatedly in 10-20 hours. Another issue is the replayability, after 3 or 4 runs of the vanilla game the rest of the game gets boring because there isn't any variety or change. New Game Plus (or Plus Plus (etc.)) doesn't have any change, except for harder enemies, more souls/money, and maybe a few rings...
But that's just me, that was my opinion on this game. It's up to you to decide.
P.S. The game may have its fair share of issues, but even with them this game certainly dominates my favorite games list.

Disclaimer :
- I play disconnected
- I finished  the game in 230 weeks, in "strict mode", at my first campaign
------------------------------------------------------------
This is not a review in itself (by now, you should know what the game consists in), but my perception on how the game evolved since early access.
I bought the game in early 2015, when the game had a 95%+ satisfaction rate. I played it for a bit and, on reaching the 5-6 tier missions, decided to wait for the final release. It was before the Arbalest and Abomination classes, and "The Cove" were added, and before the "corpses patch".
Then I saw the approval for the game sink, I saw the negative reviews multiply with each and every new patch. I was nearly convinced Red Hook had lost control of their game.
Fast-forward one year, and I'm back on
: I realized all this collective hysteria was pure crap. The game is
.
- I find the corpses, which I feared would disrupt the "unravelling of enemy groups" (the substance of the fights),  work both ways and are a great tactical addition. They make the fights more subtle, less lazy. How they could loose the game 10% approval is insane...
- I find the game is not unfair : I finished the game with only one wipe, during my only "dark run". I can complain
. Truth is that when you die, in
, it's because of your greed. Of your gluttony. You die because you took risks you knew you should not have taken.
- I find the game is not brutal : I found it
. At each new tier, there's a fair rise in difficulty, but it's dosed with care. It helps you rethink the way you played (and sliced through) the lower tier. It requires you to refine your tactics, to look for new combinations, to consider resources you neglected. It's brilliant. Understanding how to beat the 16 Pounder after retreating 3 times (best fight of the game) was extremely rewarding. Even on week 200, I kept learning and discovering stuff. And probably will continue to discover more in the NG+ mode or if I want to win under 99 weeks.
- The game is not "impossible" : actually, it's not even difficult (in a
way), once you have understood the way it works, and what it expects from the player. It's challenging, and remains challenging, which is a good thing in the long run. From time to time, you loose a hero, sure. I lost 40 of them in 220 weeks (most of them at lvl 6 rank, 2 from heart attack, 2 from hunger, 6 or 7 in the Darkest Dungeon, 2 of which against the final boss). But it's the way the game works. You have to manage your roster to provide a constant flow of efficient heroes.
This is the main obstacle, I think :
is a game of GRINDING. You have to farm to restore your hamlet, to level your heroes, to pay for their spells, to pay for their weapons and armours, to cure them... Then, when your hamlet is restored, when your roster is full of upgraded lvl 6 characters, you may want to grind missions to get some special relics. And then you grind more, and more and even more to cycle and lock the quirks you want to worm your way into the Darkest Dungeon. The "definitive" aspect of the Darkest Dungeon final missions (you can't retreat for free) adds to the tension in a great way, but makes you think a lot before adventuring there. Many times, I chose to procrastinate and grind more instead, to get "that special quirk".
While it's repetitive, I never found that to be tedious, because the level 6 missions do not allow auto-cruise, and I always grinded in a strategical perspective, with objectives. But I understand it may not be to everyone's taste.
The nice thing about it is that you can leave the game for a while, and come back at it very easily.
My only real complaint about the game is about the stress mechanic. While I like it during the missions and the fights, I think it could have been implemented in a less gimmicky way outside the missions :  Why would a hero become "ruins phobe", "bulimic", or catch syphilis after a run in the cove is not clear. I wish the mechanic was more rational and clear : I would find enjoyment in trying to outplay/defeat/manage it. As it is right now, I fail to see any clear link between the stress endured/its source/ the actions performed by the heroes and the positive/negative quirks (or even diseases). It smells of randomness and money-sink, and it's not on par with the rest of the game's mechanics.
Final word : if you're on the fence about buying
, but still hesitating because of the negative reviews that whine about difficulty, know that it's all ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t from useless crybabies that play only Ubisoft games.

Aside from some performance issues, this game is absolutely fantastic! The issues are not game breaking, and can be addressed for now by turning down some settings.
Now the big issue people have a problem with: Most missions have turn limits. This is guerrilla warfare. You do not have all the time in the world to finish your missions. People are just LOVING to complain about this, but not only does it make sense, it prevents the old Overwatch-until-win boringness of Xcom 1. The people complaining are simply realizing that they aren't the Xcom masters they thought they were. This DOES NOT limit strategy AT ALL. In fact, not being able to win simply by overwatching over and over, means you have to actually USE strategy, and it punishes you without mercy for screwing up. You are hit and run guerrilla fighters. Act like it. Or you could install the mod that removes the turn limits if you need a "very easy" mode.
That said, there are still missions that only call for eliminating all enemies and have no timer, and many of the ones that do only require that you take care of an impending task, such as hacking a device before it self destructs, then allows you to clean up the area at your leisure.
I've not lost a single soldier in 24 hours of play so far. It took almost completely restarting a few missions, but I know sooner or later it just may not be possible to keep everyone alive, and that's just part of the game. If you play this like Xcom 1, you will lose. If, however, you're up for a rewarding and immensely satisfying strategic challenge, look no further.

Minecraft meets MMO, except the MMO elements are very poorly executed.  The game becomes a woeful gear grind after about 6 hours of play.  You're essentially stuck doing lower levels of content until you can upgrade your items, which increases your effective level.  It's similar to the WoW item level system, but poorly implemented as the grind gets exponentially longer, but the material gathering does not follow suit in the slightest.
Moreover, for an MMO to be playable, you need stable servers.  It has been years since I've had such terrible rubber-banding and random "teleporting" because of the server's inadequacy.  I've died many times to easy content because hitting the potion key didn't result in driking a potion for >6 seconds, or because the server believed I was standing in fire.  If the server-side is the source or truth for player positionig, you'd better have much more stability than the Trove servers are capable of.
I'm also quite disappointed in the difficulty scaling.  Moving from Uber 3 to Uber 4 (essentially tiers 8 and 9 in the difficulty) causes every boss fight to be a minion fest.  The bosses start spawning minions at an alarming rate, which makes the fights require AE abilities to deal with the rapid spawn quickly enough to not be simply overwhelmed.
The game, while entertaining for a while, has lost all of the MMO appeal, and now it's just another Minecraft clone in my book.

THE BEST: The Concealment mechanic is absolutely the best change from the 2012 title. Until your squad attacks or enters enemy sight lines, enemy pods (groups of units) will not trigger, unlike the last game. This allows you to set up ambushes or try to reach an objective unseen. Even after the initial concealment phase ends, Rangers (with the right skills) can continue to act as scouts and spotters for Snipers and Grenadiers. It's just way too fun.
THE WORST: At the time of writing, there are some performance and UI issues. The game especially seems to have trouble with figuring out multi-unit damage with certain kinds of explosives, and Overwatch reactions. The game seems to pause or slow down for a while while it's figuring everything out. You may have experiences similar issues in XCOM 2012, however this time they're even more pronounced.
VERDICT: Buy this game! It's extremely good as-is, and the level of mod support and community involvement only means it will get better.

Here we are again. Aliens invaded the Earth and noone is here to stop them... except you. 20 years after aliens conquered the Earth, you take control of Xcom project with only one goal - Wipe out invaders out of this planet.
EDIT 1: I updated the review 21.4.2016 to let you know, what changed since the game was released. These "EDIT" texts were written after my second playthrough after some patches.
---Game wont go easy on you---
What looks like an impossible missions is truly close to it. Although the game offers 4 difficulty levels, even the easiest one represents QUITE a challenge. Most players start the games on normal difficulties, expecting fine challenge. Your expectations will be very likely blown up as the game throws at you mind control aliens and heavy forces right from the first mission. Tutorial teaches you the control of soldiers but wont teach you the strategizing, which is key element of xcom 2. The only way to survive in this world is to careful plan every move. Every small mistake may result in great injuries, big mistakes may cost you the whole mission. If you feel like you are REALLY good in tactical games like this, go for veteran difficulty, otherwise i highly recommend starting on lowest "rookie" difficulty.
---No more camping---
As you progress through the game, you will notice that majority of missions are timed - there is enough time in the early missions, but as you progress through campaign, you may have to restart a mission few times just to be able to complete mission just one turn before it fails. Timed missions offers so short time, that it may look like the only way is to rush through all aliens - which will most likely result in getting your whole squad wiped out. Be prepared to save and reload often to go for different strategies, which may show better results than... death...
EDIT 1: My second playthrough was on ironman veteran difficulty, which i had to restart 4x to be able to win. I learned that the hardest part of the game is the beginnings - once you research the important technologies, you will be able to survive with all your soldiers with minimal or no injuries at all. I think im prepared for commander difficulty in next playthrough.
---Control Everything---
You will control not only soldiers in the field, but also your xcom base - from prioritizing various research to building facilities. Soldier customization is very enjoyable part of the game. You will control what you want to do - your goal will be to get support of countries all around the world and you decide if you want to fight, look for supplies or just chill until ufo lands somewhere. Often you will get random missions that you will have to complete immediately... well you dont have to, but in that case be prepared for some kind of serious disadvantage. Time goes fast and aliens will not wait until you get your soldiers healed. Every injury may mean that your soldiers will not be able to participate in any mission for next few weeks.
---They shoot through walls---
Game offers 30-hour long campaign and very addictive gameplay. Game in current state is playable, but its filled with quite big collection of bugs and problems - The first one you may notice is FPS drop - its not about the computer hardware, its about bad optimization. If you would buy the game now, you may have to spend some valuable minutes in graphic settings to get FPS on playable level. FPS is not the only problems - aliens can sometimes hit your soldiers through walls, sometimes camera moves to aliens for 15 seconds without anything happening and sometimes the animation of grenade wont show up and you can just see building falling apart for no reason. Most bugs are just visual and in most cases wont affect gameplay too much. However these bugs are common thing in current state of game.
EDIT 1: Patches with fixes already hit the game and second playthrough was smoother. FPS doesnt seem to be that much of a problem now, bugs are less frequent. Now is good time to buy this. :)
---Conclusion---
Thats about it. Id recommend checking out my xcom: Enemy unknown review, where i wrore more about gameplay, which is very similar to xcom 2. The expansions are a must buy for me !

- I play disconnected

------------------------------------------------------------
This is not a review in itself (by now, you should know what the game consists in), but my perception on how the game evolved since early access.
I bought the game in early 2015, when the game had a 95%+ satisfaction rate. I played it for a bit and, on reaching the 5-6 tier missions, decided to wait for the final release. It was before the Arbalest and Abomination classes, and "The Cove" were added, and before the "corpses patch".
Then I saw the approval for the game sink, I saw the negative reviews multiply with each and every new patch. I was nearly convinced Red Hook had lost control of their game.
Fast-forward one year, and I'm back on
: I realized all this collective hysteria was pure crap. The game is
.
- I find the corpses, which I feared would disrupt the "unravelling of enemy groups" (the substance of the fights),  work both ways and are a great tactical addition. They make the fights more subtle, less lazy. How they could loose the game 10% approval is insane...
- I find the game is not unfair : I finished the game with only one wipe, during my only "dark run". I can complain
. Truth is that when you die, in
, it's because of your greed. Of your gluttony. You die because you took risks you knew you should not have taken.
- I find the game is not brutal : I found it
. At each new tier, there's a fair rise in difficulty, but it's dosed with care. It helps you rethink the way you played (and sliced through) the lower tier. It requires you to refine your tactics, to look for new combinations, to consider resources you neglected. It's brilliant. Understanding how to beat the 16 Pounder after retreating 3 times (best fight of the game) was extremely rewarding. Even on week 200, I kept learning and discovering stuff. And probably will continue to discover more in the NG+ mode or if I want to win under 99 weeks.
- The game is not "impossible" : actually, it's not even difficult (in a
way), once you have understood the way it works, and what it expects from the player. It's challenging, and remains challenging, which is a good thing in the long run. From time to time, you loose a hero, sure. I lost 40 of them in 220 weeks (most of them at lvl 6 rank, 2 from heart attack, 2 from hunger, 6 or 7 in the Darkest Dungeon, 2 of which against the final boss). But it's the way the game works. You have to manage your roster to provide a constant flow of efficient heroes.
This is the main obstacle, I think :
is a game of GRINDING. You have to farm to restore your hamlet, to level your heroes, to pay for their spells, to pay for their weapons and armours, to cure them... Then, when your hamlet is restored, when your roster is full of upgraded lvl 6 characters, you may want to grind missions to get some special relics. And then you grind more, and more and even more to cycle and lock the quirks you want to worm your way into the Darkest Dungeon. The "definitive" aspect of the Darkest Dungeon final missions (you can't retreat for free) adds to the tension in a great way, but makes you think a lot before adventuring there. Many times, I chose to procrastinate and grind more instead, to get "that special quirk".
While it's repetitive, I never found that to be tedious, because the level 6 missions do not allow auto-cruise, and I always grinded in a strategical perspective, with objectives. But I understand it may not be to everyone's taste.
The nice thing about it is that you can leave the game for a while, and come back at it very easily.
My only real complaint about the game is about the stress mechanic. While I like it during the missions and the fights, I think it could have been implemented in a less gimmicky way outside the missions :  Why would a hero become "ruins phobe", "bulimic", or catch syphilis after a run in the cove is not clear. I wish the mechanic was more rational and clear : I would find enjoyment in trying to outplay/defeat/manage it. As it is right now, I fail to see any clear link between the stress endured/its source/ the actions performed by the heroes and the positive/negative quirks (or even diseases). It smells of randomness and money-sink, and it's not on par with the rest of the game's mechanics.
Final word : if you're on the fence about buying
, but still hesitating because of the negative reviews that whine about difficulty, know that it's all ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t from useless crybabies that play only Ubisoft games.

Okay, to put it plain and simply, Dark Souls III most definitely lives up to the lofty reputation created by its predecessors. It is, overall, a fantastic game for anyone who has that Souls itch in need of scratching. It takes several steps forward from the strengths and weaknesses that made up Souls I, II, and Bloodborne. However, I also feel that it takes a step or two back in the way that these new features are implemented.
So, The Good:
-GORGEOUS. Like, holy hell. DaSI was passable, II was okay, but III blows them out of the water. The enviroments will make your eyes melt, the bosses look fantastic, and it runs very smoothly on PC. The best-looking of all the Souls.
-Combat. It encourages the fast and agressive playstyle of Bloodborne, which took me a while to realize. To put it in perspective, on your first run in DaSI your shield and one-hander were your best friends. You prayed to them every night before you went to sleep. Now, the creatures and bosses are more agressive and attack faster, so hiding behind your shield all the time will get you pummeled. It's much more effective to roll out of attacks and use big ol' two-handed weapons. However, not all enemies are like this. Some of them can be solved with a high-speed high-damage approach, and some of them can be solved by digging in with a high-stability shield and cosplaying as an M-1 Abrahams, so you have to be flexible.
-Merchants and Upgrades. When you're looking to spend souls on upgrades, spells, and consumables, it's much easier as all the services have been consilidated into several NPCs in the hub area. All of the higher-level stuff is contained with in scrolls, tomes, and umbral ash found in the world that can be gifted to NPCs to unlock better spells, upgrades, and items. The weapon-upgrading system built off of DaSII's approach and made it much easier. You no longer have to hunt for colored titianite and make long treks to far-off merchants to get that dank +10 weapon, it's all done through Andre in Firelink Shrine. In addition, the "infusions" that can be done support all character builds. High Faith/Intellegence builds can get weapons that have fantastic scaling with their caster skills, and pure quality characters can get weapons that scale better with only Strength, only Dexterity, or both at once.
-Variety. Swords, and spears, and polearms, and rapiers, and bows, and claws, and scythes, and HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥ There are a multitude of new and old weapons, spells, and armor available and the sheer number of things to try out will make you salivate.  Armor sets look cool as hell. Some of them have flowing capes, some are grungy and dark, some are shiny and noble, and you dont have to grind titianite to make them useful anymore so you can just slap on anything you like and head out without having to worry about your gear being underpowered.
-Length. As of writing this with almost 40 hours under my belt, I'm only just now reaching the end of my first NG, and you can bet your♥♥♥♥♥I'm going to NG+7.
The Meh:
-Magic. This is my main criticism. Yes, magic has variety, yes it can be powerful in PVP if you focus on it, HOWEVER, it is very underpowered early game. Each type seems to have been gimped in its own way. For Sorcery, a LOT of bosses resist magic, and even at low STR/DEX levels your weapons will outdamage your spells. For Pyromancy, you have to invest twice the levels, as scaling is done off of FTH and INT, plus you can't get any optimal weapon infusions until late-game. Faith got the shaft the worst IMO, as it not only has the same problems as Sorcery, but it only has three tiers of Lightning Bolt like DaSI and II had. That would be fine if not for the fact that the second tier can only be found in the SECOND TO LAST area and only after grinding THIRTY sunlight medals, which is a VERY time-consuming task, and the third can't even be aquired until NG+. On top of all of that, you still won't hit as hard or as fast with any magic build as if you were using a pure melee build. But there is a light at the end of the tunnel, magic is far more viable once you have plenty of levels under your belt, so once you hit NG+ it will FINALLY be good. (by that time you'll be drowning in souls and buying up all the spells from merchants is a breeze) There is also a covenant ingame that lets you esentially respec your levels, so you can go for a melee build in the beginning of the game then reallocate your levels to use magic once you're set up with all the requisite rings and spells.
-Linearity. While this isn't a huge problem, I always loved the twisted and conected paths of DaSI, but III is very linear. It makes up for this, however, by having complex individual areas.
-Online Features. Somehow not as good as it was in II. There are only a few covenants and most of them are meh. Only useful for the rewards, but grinding enemies for covenent items is far more difficult if you don't have internet connection. Way of the Blue/Blue Sentinels are back, and you'll still never be summoned for them. Darkmoon Blades are back, but it's just reskinned Blue Sentinels. Rosaria's Fingers are the new Darkwraiths and they're not bad. Warriors of Sunlight are still alive and kicking and that dumb FTH requirement is gone. Oddly enough, you can earn Sunlight Medals from them through PVP. Wierd, right? But, aside from that, online is almost exactly the same as it was in DaSI. Not bad, but not as good as it could be. The DLC offers an arena that you can use to challenge your friends through a password system, but that should have been something offered in the base game.
Overall, there are some gripes that I have, but those should not put you off from a great finalie to the Dark Souls series. I reccomed it wholly.

EDIT / ACTUAL REVIEW:
I have spent some time reading other reviews of Darkest Dungeon and here's some real talk addressing the most common complaints:
1) "RNG PLEASE!!!"
- Yes this game contains RNG, why not learn to play around that?
Sometimes your Leper will be crit from 100-0 by a fat man in chainmail. Your move Crusader. Man, if only King Arthur, 1st of His Name, Biggest of Jockstraps, Defender of the Realm and Slayer of Harems had thought to bring a band-aid to get Ol' Compost the Leper off of death's door then he might have lived. Oh wait he totally has that skill. You just didn't equip it because biggest sword is best sword. Big RNG crits sink happy little adventurer's ships, so run a very low level heal skill on 3/4 characters and a stun on 1 to keep people alive when terrible things happen. The Leper lives, and you don't have to go home and tell his, ah, remaining foot that the rest won't be coming home. You do get better at the game, you are rewarded by learning from your mistakes. I've run 20-30 level 5 long dungeons in a row without losing a character. To those who say "TOO MUCH RNG, NOT EVEN A GAME": proper prior planning prevents♥♥♥♥♥♥(urine) poor performance.
2) "TRINKETS ARE TRASH, NO REWARD!!!"
- Trinkets have upsides and downsides, why not combine two trinkets? *brainexplosion*
e.g. +30% heals, +20% stress. "THIS IS TERRIBLE I'LL DIE OF STRESS" says big bubba. Oh wait what's this? A trinket that says -20% stress? What if we added those two together and now suddenly we have a dirty dirty healer at the back of the team that'll poke your organs back in to roughly where they should be. Legendary trinkets are legendary, proper use of them and being able to manage the drawbacks make them very powerful. There's no free hand outs, use strategy and planning to win dungeons.
3) "THE GAME IS TOO MUCH OF A GRIND!!!"
- If you're taking forever to finish the game, then you're losing too many people. The game is easily finishable within 60 hours. True end game dungeoning can take a long time, because of certain factors which come into effect. However at the end game there are catch-up mechanics to speed up levelling and get you where you need to be fast. Procedurally generated rogue-like games such as this, you are essentially doing one dungeon after another. The only time it becomes monotonous is when you can play the game safely every time, and by then you should be finishing the end game bosses, which have their own surprises.
I wholly recommend this game to people who are fine with:
1) Difficult gameplay, where consequences are real.
2) Brothels
3) Tentacles

Darkest Dungeon is definitely a good game, but it is also a very demanding game and has some problems, if I had to rate it I would give it a 3.5/5.
+ Challenging game
+ Nice artstyle and atmosphere
+ Long game
+ Fair price
- Questionable difficulty design choices
- Hard grinding required
It's a pretty unique title with an awesome artstyle inspired by Lovecraft and a nice concept. The battle system is classic, but fun, and provides lots of interesting classes and combinations to try out. It's nice to see the city being gradually rebuilt as you purchase upgrades and the narrator commenting on every action you take.
You will explore lots of randomly generated dungeons in search of loot, heirlooms or trinkets but every step you take could be your last. The exploration part of the game is very basic: you just need to select the room you want to go to and then fight your way through.
The game is hard and forces you to choose wisely every action you take, every piece of loot you discard to make room and every item you interact with.
What sets this game combat apart from the classic titles is the stress mechanic: while hp will determine the life or death of a character, the stress meter will determine his sanity and when it reaches 100 the hero will have his resolve tested with a small chance of passing it and become stronger or a very high chance of failure resulting in pretty much a constant rng debuff giving stress to all the party or passing turn, and this creates fear in the player because there are few ways to mitigate stress and it tends to hit a critical level when you're on your way to complete a mission, potentially screwing it.
At the end of each dungeon you stress meter will remain filled and you'll need to address it sending your soldiers into the tavern or the abbey, heroes will also gain quirks (good and bad) or diseases that will require your attention.
You will get emotionally invested in you heroes and you will need to face their death, and that's a very interesting part of this game atmosphere.
The game progression is very slow (even if it's a bit faster compared to the pre-antiquarian build), you'll need to collect lots of heirlooms to upgrade the town buildings to a reasonable level and a lot of gold (and I mean A LOT) to upgrade the equipment for your heroes, but you'll need only a few amounts of exp to level up your party. A high-level dungeon will provide a lot of loot compared to an apprentice-level one, but to have a fair chance in there you'll still need to spend a lot of resources in upgrading skills and equipment.
High level heroes will refuse to visit lower level dungeons and that at first acts like a barrier against grinding, but since you need so many resources you will be forced to hire a lot of low level heroes and throw them in dungeons just to take as much as you can get and then dispose of them, especially at the beginning of the game where you won't have resources to upgrade your high level heroes' equipment, making them almost useless. This is an even worse form of grinding than the traditional one and results in an incredible slow and boring progression that affects game immersion.
Once you reach the point where you have a reliable high level party or two you can start to farm resources a bit faster, but you'll probably have already completed all the necessary structures (armory+guild).
To me the biggest disappointment is that the game feels always the same, some heroes will perform better at high level but essentially you'll always see the same enemies (except for 1 or 2 extra enemy type at veteran and champion) and bosses, just buffed enough to provide the same or just a bit more challenge. Your strongest heroes don't feel powerful because they always face enemies balanced for them and that is a let down for the time you require investing.
The difficulty is brutal and that's fine or... that would be fine if you could really use your ability at the game to mitigate every bad situation, but sometimes the rng is gonna screw you no matter what, and that would still be acceptable if the game didn't have permadeath for your heroes. That said it's also pretty clear that an experienced player can reduce the amount of devastating rng by quite a lot, even Ng+ is beatable with enough experience, and some of the most hated mechanics like corpses and hearth attacks can be easily kept in check by an experienced player. The game has however the option to disable most of the hardest combat mechanics, but frankly those are what makes this game unique and I think there are better ways of making the game more accessible to the casual gamer.
The last problem I found is that there are some useless abilities, particularly the self-buffs and that makes some potentially versatile characters bound to a certain skillset .
Darkest Dungeon Achievements are fun and some of them require lots of thinking and effort to unlock (like "Dysfunction" if you're not lucky), and that's always a plus.
The main reason this game isn't a "great game" but is only a good game is the rng+permadeath+ huge timeloss combo that lies in its very core design. There is no ultimate fail state (except on NG+), that means that losing your whole party isn't a problem, but the time you require investing in maxing gear and abilities of that party is a lot, too much in my opinion, especially because losing a single party member will make the other 3 guys useless (due to a fixed party size of 4) until you can level up another 4-people party.
A hard and punishing game is fine but you should be able to use your in-game experience to cut progression time is a smart way like in other "hardcore games" (like Dark Souls) or to have a manual save (like in XCOM), so far you only have the antiquarian class as a choice to get some extra cash.
This is a good game that sometimes feels hard just for the sake of it and not for a unique design and requires a huge time investment that not many people can provide: if you can commit to it buy it, otherwise there are way better games for you. It's still one of the best games coming out of kickstarter and I enjoyed it.
I would suggest the devs to consider making an option for a mode where you can save in the hamlet or for a "fast mode" with upgrade prices (especially for abilities and weapons) cut by 40-50%  while maintaining classic strict mode and ng+ always available for diehard harcore players (with those 2 achievements as rewards): that, in my opinion, would make the game more accessible and enjoyable for many people.

People say the game gets repetitive - which I don't know how it is possible, because this game has a story which people with 200+ Hrs havn't even completed yet, aswell as UNIQUE cinematics for each boss/lvl and sercret rooms. The game is meant to be this hard and unforgiving - you require skill and patience when fighting, you can't just select a skill and click on the enemy and expect it to die! Characters traverse the dungeons in single file, their position in the line dictating which abilities are able to be used and the enemies on which they are able to use them on.
To have fun and not die you'll need to gather your 4 leaf clovers for some luck, because the game... sadly (for some) is RNG based ( Mostly Loot wise ), you'll also need to know your basic and some complex abbreviations for RPG's, that's why the game has a glossary book when your at your Estate menu on the bottom right of the screen.

The crusader has this one skill where he gives everybody stress relief with a speech he gives and where others can take watch while the rest of the party sleeps... all those skills take "Time Points" ( The hovering number above your camp menu ) and eventually when you decided you've used enough of those points the rest of the time is how long the party sleeps - the longer the more they heal and stuff.

I want to get this out of the way right now. If you dislike RNG heavy games then this might not be for you as pretty much everything is RNG. You can tip the scales in your favor but everything is all about the roll of the dice.
With that out of the way, Darkest Dungeon is one of my favorite games.
The presentation as a whole is so wonderful. The gloomy atmosphere, the dark artstyle, and the music all come together to bring a masterfully made world.
The gameplay is hard to compare to anything else. The closest I can think is like, (classic) Final Fantasty mixed with X-Com. Turned based battles where the position of your characters matter greatly. This game makes you think about every move you make before you make it. Even healing because you have to think. "Is it worth healing my characters over killing this monster that could make my heroes stressed?" Speaking of that, the stress system is what drew me into this game in the first place. An RPG where it explores the themes of the stress a "Hero" would go through when exploring these dungeons filled with horrors and fiends. It had me hooked as soon as I first heard about it.

Unturned is a great game and I would recommend it to anyone who wants to play something new with some friends on a server. I've been playing the game since the very first edition on steam and it's evolved in so many different ways mostly for the better. The singleplayer on its own is great to play for the first time, I remember going into unturned 1.0 on PEI and I spawned at the light house and got completely destroyed by zombies but soon I figured out how to survive the hard way. After a while the main map got boring (this is after all its changes to PEI till 3.0) and by that time there were new maps with lots of different enviroments and stratergies to survive at least in singleplayer and it entertained me for a while. I'll be honest I never play singleplayer anymore cause I've just overplayed what I enjoyed about the single player.
The multiplayer I started off playing was a server with a few of my friends one of which recommended me the game and we built a base on the big mountain near the farms. The PvP aspect of the game was amazing even in 1.0 where weight was pretty annoying, I had managed to trick my friend into telling where his location was through questions but he still killed me due to timberwolf. Anyways, the multiplayer now personally is a lot less unenjoyable on public servers due to all the servers with kits and tpa and home making the vanilla aspects of grinding your way to good loot completely useless. Which is why I recommend playing with a group of friends on a private server if you want a more vanilla experience. Multiplayer unturned gave me a feeling of constant fear at all times especially on PEI, since the map is pretty small compared to newer ones there was always someone in every town and you weren't sure if you could kill them or not (at least in the old 2.0-3.0 vanilla servers). Although the multiplayer definetely gave me a great time, it was so unlike any other game I had played and still is unlike any, you could get some people who just were big fresh spawn killers or you could get dudes who would help you out (it was hard to distinguish between them since a big portion were people who would kill you in an instant). It was just so diverse I think is the right word. Once I was again playing with my friend who recommended me the game and we got assaulted by a man in a sky blue plane trying to 'aluakba' us while his friends surrounded us in military gear. I had to say I didn't believe him about the plane till it was too late.
Honestly I really do not like the current multiplayer. All it is, is a PvP fest and it's just so bleh. I miss the servers where you needed to know what to craft to make a makeshift rifle instead of typing in a kit for full military gear. I miss when you had to pack food for the trip to a location and get back as well as making sure no one follows you to your base. It was better for online servers a while ago, hopefully some more gems shine through the cancer of PvP servers.
Anyway as you can tell I haven't told you much about actual gameplay cause if you think it looks cool you should experience it yourself not told it from me. In the end my opinion on gameplay mechanics won't matter if you hate the game.
Unturned 9.5/10

Okay, to put it plain and simply, Dark Souls III most definitely lives up to the lofty reputation created by its predecessors. It is, overall, a fantastic game for anyone who has that Souls itch in need of scratching. It takes several steps forward from the strengths and weaknesses that made up Souls I, II, and Bloodborne. However, I also feel that it takes a step or two back in the way that these new features are implemented.
So, The Good:
-GORGEOUS. Like, holy hell. DaSI was passable, II was okay, but III blows them out of the water. The enviroments will make your eyes melt, the bosses look fantastic, and it runs very smoothly on PC. The best-looking of all the Souls.
-Combat. It encourages the fast and agressive playstyle of Bloodborne, which took me a while to realize. To put it in perspective, on your first run in DaSI your shield and one-hander were your best friends. You prayed to them every night before you went to sleep. Now, the creatures and bosses are more agressive and attack faster, so hiding behind your shield all the time will get you pummeled. It's much more effective to roll out of attacks and use big ol' two-handed weapons. However, not all enemies are like this. Some of them can be solved with a high-speed high-damage approach, and some of them can be solved by digging in with a high-stability shield and cosplaying as an M-1 Abrahams, so you have to be flexible.
-Merchants and Upgrades. When you're looking to spend souls on upgrades, spells, and consumables, it's much easier as all the services have been consilidated into several NPCs in the hub area. All of the higher-level stuff is contained with in scrolls, tomes, and umbral ash found in the world that can be gifted to NPCs to unlock better spells, upgrades, and items. The weapon-upgrading system built off of DaSII's approach and made it much easier. You no longer have to hunt for colored titianite and make long treks to far-off merchants to get that dank +10 weapon, it's all done through Andre in Firelink Shrine. In addition, the "infusions" that can be done support all character builds. High Faith/Intellegence builds can get weapons that have fantastic scaling with their caster skills, and pure quality characters can get weapons that scale better with only Strength, only Dexterity, or both at once.
-Variety. Swords, and spears, and polearms, and rapiers, and bows, and claws, and scythes, and HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥ There are a multitude of new and old weapons, spells, and armor available and the sheer number of things to try out will make you salivate.  Armor sets look cool as hell. Some of them have flowing capes, some are grungy and dark, some are shiny and noble, and you dont have to grind titianite to make them useful anymore so you can just slap on anything you like and head out without having to worry about your gear being underpowered.
-Length. As of writing this with almost 40 hours under my belt, I'm only just now reaching the end of my first NG, and you can bet your♥♥♥♥♥I'm going to NG+7.
The Meh:
-Magic. This is my main criticism. Yes, magic has variety, yes it can be powerful in PVP if you focus on it, HOWEVER, it is very underpowered early game. Each type seems to have been gimped in its own way. For Sorcery, a LOT of bosses resist magic, and even at low STR/DEX levels your weapons will outdamage your spells. For Pyromancy, you have to invest twice the levels, as scaling is done off of FTH and INT, plus you can't get any optimal weapon infusions until late-game. Faith got the shaft the worst IMO, as it not only has the same problems as Sorcery, but it only has three tiers of Lightning Bolt like DaSI and II had. That would be fine if not for the fact that the second tier can only be found in the SECOND TO LAST area and only after grinding THIRTY sunlight medals, which is a VERY time-consuming task, and the third can't even be aquired until NG+. On top of all of that, you still won't hit as hard or as fast with any magic build as if you were using a pure melee build. But there is a light at the end of the tunnel, magic is far more viable once you have plenty of levels under your belt, so once you hit NG+ it will FINALLY be good. (by that time you'll be drowning in souls and buying up all the spells from merchants is a breeze) There is also a covenant ingame that lets you esentially respec your levels, so you can go for a melee build in the beginning of the game then reallocate your levels to use magic once you're set up with all the requisite rings and spells.
-Linearity. While this isn't a huge problem, I always loved the twisted and conected paths of DaSI, but III is very linear. It makes up for this, however, by having complex individual areas.
-Online Features. Somehow not as good as it was in II. There are only a few covenants and most of them are meh. Only useful for the rewards, but grinding enemies for covenent items is far more difficult if you don't have internet connection. Way of the Blue/Blue Sentinels are back, and you'll still never be summoned for them. Darkmoon Blades are back, but it's just reskinned Blue Sentinels. Rosaria's Fingers are the new Darkwraiths and they're not bad. Warriors of Sunlight are still alive and kicking and that dumb FTH requirement is gone. Oddly enough, you can earn Sunlight Medals from them through PVP. Wierd, right? But, aside from that, online is almost exactly the same as it was in DaSI. Not bad, but not as good as it could be. The DLC offers an arena that you can use to challenge your friends through a password system, but that should have been something offered in the base game.
Overall, there are some gripes that I have, but those should not put you off from a great finalie to the Dark Souls series. I reccomed it wholly.

The crux of this game does definitly not lie in it's basic gameplay. The basics are very, very simple... and that's excactly what's so great about it! Whilest other mmo's extend there basics to a complex, hard to learn game system that forces the player down a certain road of character development, skill specialisation, etc... this game remains beautifully 'sandboxed', but with easy, well defined goals. But the beauty of it lies in the vast amount of options and content presented: hopefully they add (even) more activities and add more game mechanics (just add, don't change/complicate the basics!) in the future, because that's what this game needs: lots and lots of content, whilest keeping the basic game functionality simple. for example: don't add a skill tree, but at a furnace to apply elemental effects to your weapon/change your ult or make it  weapon dependent. A very fun game alltogether, compared to other mmo's: not grindy at all. maybe the characters need more different skills, or at least a wider choice, but definitly nothing to complicated: it's the simplicity of things that make this game so awesome, together with the variety of constructions (lots of player created content, a variety of dungeons that are as well procedural as high in variety, do to the mix in design and content generation). not pay2win at all, you can easily collect in game cash and buy stuff.

Let me just start by saying that, in my honest opinion, this game is great.  I have been on the fence about making this purchase for a while now and I'm so glad I finally did!
I'm not going to go into the whole story and what you're trying to do but I will touch on some of the great points and my one and only criticism of the game.  First off, I love the dark sense of the game.  The setting, the illustration, and especially the narrator all catch the theme very very well.  Second, the upgrade system and differences between the classes are a must for a rogue-like dungeon crawler and Darkest Dungeon nails it!  Not only are there 10+ classes but they all have 8 abilities each.  Each of which can be upgraded up to 4 levels I believe, however you can only utililze 4 at any one given time, which makes the exploring team more precise in regards to the way and style you want to play.  Now, you not only have to worry about your characters and their life bar; you also have to worry about any negative ailments they may receive as well as diseases they may contract.  On top of that, you have to keep a watchful eye on their stress level because if it gets too high they may suffer a heart attack.  Yup, lost my first two warriors to that one lol.  With all of these important factors to keep on top of you'd think there would be a system to deal with that.  And there is, and it's done brilliantly!  You can place your stressed out characters in the Abbey (church) or let them have at it in the Tavern to gamble or even visit the brothel.  I'll touch on that one in a few....  Smh.  And to deal with additional ailments and diseases you can send them to medical wards etc. to get treated.
There are also upgradable places in your town where you can upgrade the characters weapons, armor, skills, all adding to the depth of this game.
Now, to touch on the battle system.  I think this is another strong point for this game.  I've read a few reviews saying that it gets very boring and repetitive.  I can say that, after 16 hours I still don't feel that way.  With the variety of character classes and the amount of abilities they have, the game is still fresh to me.  I should also mention that the character's placement is vital as they can only perform certain skills while in a certain position within the group, all adding to the depth of combat too.  There are a decent number of different enemies though I would like to see more but their abilities and types vary quite a bit, which definitely helps in that regard.  Now, when you meet a big enemy, they are fantastic!  I've faced 3 total so far and each one is so different and challenging that I look forward to the rest of them.  Overall, there are 24 listed enemies of this sort, and let me tell you, the first 3 have been very tough and are hulking beasts!!
So, to give you a little taste of what to expect, this game is not for the faint hearted.  It is very difficult at times and can certainly be unforgiving.  If you take your time and build a good party, you will always stand a chance though.  The computer has had as many bad breaks as I have and I have never felt cheated from the result of my decisions.
One experience I had that I feel compelled to share is when my wife died....  Oh yeah, I forgot to mention that you can change the character names and color or outfit/armor.   Speaking of my wife's death sounds grim, I know but its only a game right???  Anyway, on her second to last run out in the dungeons, I was very close to defeating the bossman known as the Prophet when the tides turned very quickly.  Her stress level skyrocketed but we were able to defeat him and head back to town.  While in town I realized that she contracted some sort of fear from her last battle and the only way I could relieve her stress was to send her to the Brothel..  Yes, my wife in a brothel.  Wasn't crazy about the idea but what was I going to do?   When the time came for her to return  I was notified that, "Andrea's debauchery has reached new heights-whereabouts unknown".  She was missing for an additional week...  The following week I was notified that she had done unspeakable things and that she was no longer allowed in the brothel!  It followed up by saying that she had the time of her life and engaged in pleasures of the flesh and recovered 81 stress but acquired Disease:  Syphilis....  Syphilis!!!  Wtf Andrea!!!  Lol.  Well, I opted not to treat the disease or the fears and onward she went to the next dungeon.  A rough run in with a few vagrants, eldriches, and a bout of poison and the next thing I knew, her untreated stress level got out of control and she suffered a heart attack mid battle.  Now she lies in the cemetary of fallen warriors...  Syphilis and all....
Now for the one criticism I have.  The one and only thing is that I wish certain things were clearer regarding some character stat abbreviations.  I'm still uncertain as to what each and every stat means when choosing the skills I want to equip and which ones to upgrade.  One good thing is in battle, once an enemy target is highlighted, clearer stats are displayed regarding the percentage of a hit or miss and the range of damage a successful hit will cause.
All in all this game is masterfully done.  Difficult but balanced very well and the developers nailed the characters, the upgrade system, overall gameplay and certainly the dark humour.  9.5/10.

I've been waiting for this damn game ever since they announced it back in mid-2015 or somewhere around that time. The evidence that this franchise is a great franchise mostly derives from the fact that when they did announce X-COM 2 my lazy♥♥♥♥♥was STILL playing Enemy Within from 2013. My expectations were set pretty low because of story said from the trailers of X-COM 2 seemed pretty corny, and the gameplay just looked like the same damn thing. Even if I loved Enemy Within/Unknown I knew game studios can't constantly put out masterpieces so I just expected X-COM 2 to be 'another one'.
Looking at and having played 20 hours and a lot more to come just in 4 god damn days you bet this is a good♥♥♥♥♥game. Due to my low expectations the game immediately blew me out of the water with visuals, customization, and the overall experience. The story to avoid spoilers I'm just gonna say is pretty corny at times but overall isn't nearly as bad as I thought. Once you get on the ship the game gives you a false sense of security by giving you baby steps through the new mechanics. My initial reaction was "Oh well these first missions are just gonna be tutorial cakewalks." As soon as the first mission showed up I went in expecting a boring tutorial mission on how the new concealment mechanic works but instead..It was actually pretty easy, but it wasn't a drag to complete.
Then from that point on the game throws you a curve ball by having every mission passed that point be overwhelming in terms of enemies forcing the player to think strategically, having them use the concealment mechanic for the advantage as opposed to other games that would probably force you to use it. On the battlefield you have so much choice and it's your job to decide which is the best one and nobody in the game is gonna decide that for you. You are more the 'Commander' than ever. It holds the classic X-COM feeling of rolling the dice where you have those miracle and disaster moments this franchise has always been famous for while at the same time bringing more to the table.
And for those who say this game is 'unforgiving' and 'too hard', you missed the point more than my rookie did that 99% shot.  The game is designed to be difficult and unforgiving, it's not gonna hold your hand. Even with that in mind I feel as if the normal 'Veteren' and below difficulties are way too easy. X-COM has always had that feeling of dread when it comes to facing your enemy and this game embraces that more than ever. Hell half the time I need to think for like two minutes about what to target in a battle due to the fact that every enemy presents a problem in their own way. The sectoid's psi stuff, the officer's mark you, the mutons have this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t melee attack that deals way too much damage, etc.
X-COM 2 is an emotional rollercoaster, and not in the sense that other games are where the emotions come from the conflict in the story. This emotion comes from the bonds the player themselves make with their soldiers having made them and that disappointment and frustration you feel when you lose one of your best guys is all part of the ride. This game doesn't have an identity crisis other games seem to when it decides what it's wants to be, either, it embraces the hard♥♥♥♥♥number game it is. It will grab you by the♥♥♥♥♥♥ have you by the edge of your seat, and it will throw you to the god damn moon. If you're a fan of TRPGs, turn-based strategies, or even any sort of tactical game I recommend you this masterpiece whole-heartedly. I hope everybody enjoyed it as much as I have been.

Not having played the first game still doesnt sap the game from its total splendor and absolute perfection. I haven't played a single game like Dark Souls 3 before and this was a stellar introduction. Others may think that starting from the beginning is best, but I believe that if you want a good introduction to these types of games (Genre: Souls-like/Action RPG) then this is the best game for that. Bloodborne is too hardcore, Dark Souls has the annoying element of realistic walking, and Dark Souls 2 is too focused on making the player feel comfortable. That doesn't mean that the others are bad, just that this game is a great game for introductions.
Though an issue is that, although the game has a considerable amount of bosses, the singleplayer is short in vanilla game. My first play-through took a short 50 hours and the rest were finished repeatedly in 10-20 hours. Another issue is the replayability, after 3 or 4 runs of the vanilla game the rest of the game gets boring because there isn't any variety or change. New Game Plus (or Plus Plus (etc.)) doesn't have any change, except for harder enemies, more souls/money, and maybe a few rings...
But that's just me, that was my opinion on this game. It's up to you to decide.
P.S. The game may have its fair share of issues, but even with them this game certainly dominates my favorite games list.

Doesn't matter how good your party is.
Doesn't matter what abilities they have or what level they are.
Doesn't matter how many resources you brought.
Doesn't matter how much time and gold you've invested.
Doesn't matter who you have in your party.
They will all die. Painfully.
You'll lose everything… and yet you can't help but love it.
Welcome to
, a brutal and unforgiving turn-based Lovecraftian dungeon-crawler from the team at Red Hook. The rogue-like design makes for near infinite replay value. But your biggest enemy here, however, is RNG and, similar to the
franchise, you'll watch your favourite heroes fall and suffer party wipes again and
Having picked this up a few days after the launch of Early Access last year and knowing very little of it, the level of detail, depth and polish that the small developer team has put into this was instantly engrossing. It wouldn't be that much of a stretch to say that this is one of the most unique games to emerge in recent years, especially from Kickstarter, and
has earned a passionate cult following to show for it, even with a modding community to boot. As one who has never really enjoyed turn-based or strategy games in general, (with exception to
and some cRPGs), I was pleasantly surprised at how much I enjoyed this, and still do, in fact. Must have sunk hours and hours into it within the first week; it's addictive and can't help but pull you back in for another shot at taking down that seemingly invincible boss.
is, undoubtedly, a great game, with an excellent gothic atmosphere that adds to the bleakness of your heroes' plight. The narration, especially in combat, can be repetitive at times, yet immensely satisfying when you land a game-changing critical hit as your party desperately clings to life. Classes are great and each come with unique and interesting abilities and styles, complementing the gritty and dark design nicely. The micro-management and balancing of resources also adds further to the almost survival-like aspects of general gameplay, so success depends on watching your gold deposits closely and the strength of the torch as you delve deeper still into the heart of darkness..
The most fascinating addition, however, is the stress mechanic which implements psychological, (as well as physical), diseases and maladies to reflect the extremely punishing nature of the game world. These can be alleviated and cured through lore-friendly outlets in your Hamlet, (which acts as the main player hub), such as the Tavern, Abbey and Sanatorium. All these buildings and more can be upgraded, as well as your party's armour and gear in a typical RPG fashion, once again complementing the depth and just how time-consuming this can be.
As you can no doubt imagine, the emphasis on such risk/reward stats in nearly all aspects of gameplay leaves you to the mercy of the random number generation (RNG) and it is this dependency on pure luck rather than skill or tactics that is the game's biggest fault.
While it certainly isn't punishing to the point of being broken or unfair, how much you're willing to endure at the whim of chance is ultimately whether or not I can recommend this game to you personally.
is certainly worth a purchase at full price but is equally crippled for some by the punishing nature of the RNG mechanics.
I am thus torn between both an up and down vote for a recommendation.
If you've played a (traditional) cRPG before or the likes of XCOM, then you should be right at home for an immensely satisfying, albeit hard-core, experience. But for the average, "new age" gamer then it once again comes down to how much you're willing to risk in
to enjoy the gameplay reward. Is it worth it? You must find out for yourself.
Proceed with caution; both treasure and death, friend and foe, await at every turn.

I've been waiting for this damn game ever since they announced it back in mid-2015 or somewhere around that time. The evidence that this franchise is a great franchise mostly derives from the fact that when they did announce X-COM 2 my lazy♥♥♥♥♥was STILL playing Enemy Within from 2013. My expectations were set pretty low because of story said from the trailers of X-COM 2 seemed pretty corny, and the gameplay just looked like the same damn thing. Even if I loved Enemy Within/Unknown I knew game studios can't constantly put out masterpieces so I just expected X-COM 2 to be 'another one'.
Looking at and having played 20 hours and a lot more to come just in 4 god damn days you bet this is a good♥♥♥♥♥game. Due to my low expectations the game immediately blew me out of the water with visuals, customization, and the overall experience. The story to avoid spoilers I'm just gonna say is pretty corny at times but overall isn't nearly as bad as I thought. Once you get on the ship the game gives you a false sense of security by giving you baby steps through the new mechanics. My initial reaction was "Oh well these first missions are just gonna be tutorial cakewalks." As soon as the first mission showed up I went in expecting a boring tutorial mission on how the new concealment mechanic works but instead..It was actually pretty easy, but it wasn't a drag to complete.
Then from that point on the game throws you a curve ball by having every mission passed that point be overwhelming in terms of enemies forcing the player to think strategically, having them use the concealment mechanic for the advantage as opposed to other games that would probably force you to use it. On the battlefield you have so much choice and it's your job to decide which is the best one and nobody in the game is gonna decide that for you. You are more the 'Commander' than ever. It holds the classic X-COM feeling of rolling the dice where you have those miracle and disaster moments this franchise has always been famous for while at the same time bringing more to the table.
And for those who say this game is 'unforgiving' and 'too hard', you missed the point more than my rookie did that 99% shot.  The game is designed to be difficult and unforgiving, it's not gonna hold your hand. Even with that in mind I feel as if the normal 'Veteren' and below difficulties are way too easy. X-COM has always had that feeling of dread when it comes to facing your enemy and this game embraces that more than ever. Hell half the time I need to think for like two minutes about what to target in a battle due to the fact that every enemy presents a problem in their own way. The sectoid's psi stuff, the officer's mark you, the mutons have this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t melee attack that deals way too much damage, etc.
X-COM 2 is an emotional rollercoaster, and not in the sense that other games are where the emotions come from the conflict in the story. This emotion comes from the bonds the player themselves make with their soldiers having made them and that disappointment and frustration you feel when you lose one of your best guys is all part of the ride. This game doesn't have an identity crisis other games seem to when it decides what it's wants to be, either, it embraces the hard♥♥♥♥♥number game it is. It will grab you by the♥♥♥♥♥♥ have you by the edge of your seat, and it will throw you to the god damn moon. If you're a fan of TRPGs, turn-based strategies, or even any sort of tactical game I recommend you this masterpiece whole-heartedly. I hope everybody enjoyed it as much as I have been.

Starbound as you should all know is basically Terraria in space. You start off as one of 6 different races, each of which have their own unique looking spaceship. You try to gather materials in order to advance onto more advanced areas of the universe. As you travel from planet to planet you will find them inhabited by different races-sometimes your own races. Some civilizations are hostile, while others are friendly towards you... Until of course you decide genocide is the best option. Of course, like Terraria, your entire existence in this world is to build structures and craft items. You advance your "level" per se by crafting and upgrading your armors and weapons. Your survival in the tougher sectors of the world relies on better items.
The game is currently in BETA and I think that is very important to remember both when the good and bad things happen. Even if they came out today and said we aren't doing anything more to the game, I'd recommend it to anyone with only one warning: Beware, this game can be highly addictive. The bad in this game all revolves around basic glitches that are sure to be fixed. For example; I need to go up but there isn't a way, so of course you start jumping and putting blocks underneath you, and then you get stuck in the block itself. I'm sure thats one of the many reasons it is still in BETA. But then all of these good things happen and you see all of the great potential. These developers are known for their want to improve on their own games and have the utmost confidence in saying that they will continue to do so. You might think to yourself; "Oh I wish this were in the game!" Well, it might not be now, and it might not even be planned. But with enough fans begging for it, they might just do it.

I've never been a huge fan of MMOs, but when Trove came along I was drawn to the art style and the fact that is looked as if it didn't take itself too seriously and it looked like a non-traditional MMO that I'm used to seeing.

Trove is what I would call a casual MMO. It has MMO elements but they are not forced. And you can just build and adventure as you'd like at your own pace. Its REALLY a great game to play with friends as you adventure or build together.
It's also part dungeon crawler. There are TONS of user created dungeons to explore. I find myself constantly finding new ones and laughing as I play through them, "I can't believe someone made an NES console dungeon!"- you can adventure your way through through tons of things that make you laugh. The candy biome is by far the best example of where this game can be taken in terms of absurdity.. there are lolipop men and cupcake people that yell "Eat me!" as they attack you.
I love that the community is passionate about the game and rightfully so-- they have a huge hand in creating it. Not just dungeons but what items look like too. And their names are crediting on the items they created.
As a result of the community created items, there are TONS of customization options for your character.. from hats, facemasks, helmets, mounts, costumes, weapon styles.. I can customize myself to be some sort of Psycho-Dentist wearing a Jason mask and wielding a Toothbrush sword.. or a Poultry-powered gunslinger with chickens that fire lazers.
I only have 6 hrs played on the steam version.. but I have played plenty in Beta. I keep coming back to see what's new and exciting because they are always updating the game.. adding new classes (that truely play differently and give a lot of replay value), dungeons, worlds, mounts, etc. It's a great game for collecting stuff, adventuring, and being creative in building your home base or home world. Some of the stuff people have created are absolutely mind-blowing.
For a free game that is always being developed and progressed forward.. this is a pretty awesome experience and has HUGE potential to become truely fantastic. It can be a casual experience or hardcore if you want it to be. No doubt I keep coming back for more!

I had been looking for some good fun online FPS game like GRP, so far Planetside 2 is doing good job satisfying that need.

I think it has four type of match modes, except for team deathmatch, rest are ok and with time people with enjoy it more I guess. But currently i'm enjoying its Team Deathmatch more due to its fast paced action.
So far only problem I have faced during gameplay is swirling left or right quickly during firefights is laggy and bit delayed. I have adjusted my mouse sensitivity many times too but it still persists. I really hope they fix it.
Other than that so far not faced any other issues, will update if find something else. It doesn't look like Pay to Win till now, good job there devs, now please find some strong way to keep hackers away in near future.
